APT

TUESDAY, MARCH 9, 1965 UNITED STATES SENATE, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN RELATIONS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, pursuant to notice, at 10:05 a.m., in room 4221, New Senate Office Building, Senator J. W. Fulbright (chairman) 

presiding. 

Present: Senators Fulbright, Sparkman, Morse, Long, Lausche, Symington, Clark, Pell, Hickenlooper, Aiken, and Williams.

For the 18th time since the Marshall plan was first authorized, the Committee on Foreign Relations is beginning hearings on an annual foreign aid authorization. It has been only a little more than 5 months since the Senate completed its consideration of last year's foreign aid bill. To open the presentation of the administration case, we have with us this morning the Secretary of State, the Honorable Dean Rusk. 

We are also pleased to have with him Assistant Secretary MacArthur, who, I believe, is making his first appearance at a hearing of this committee, and Mr. David Bell, who is Administrator of the AID program.

Mr. Secretary, it is always very nice to welcome you regardless of the circumstances. Will you please proceed in your own way. (S. 1367 is as follows:) [S. 1367, 89th Cong., 1st sess.]

A BILL To amend further the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, and for other purposes

Be it enacted by the Senate and House of Representatives of the United States of America in Congress assembled, That this Act may be cited as the "Foreign 

Assistance Act of 1965". 

CHAPTER 1-POLICY SEC. 101. Section 102 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, which relates to the statement of policy, is amended by inserting after the second full sentence in the thirteenth paragraph thereof the following: "Congress further urges that the United States and other free world nations place an increasing portion of their assistance programs on a multilateral basis and that the United States continue its efforts to improve coordination among programs of assistance carried out on a bilateral basis by free-world nations". 

CHAPTER 2-DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE TITLE II-TECHNICAL COOPERATION AND DEVELOPMENT GRANTS SEC. 102. Title II of chapter 2 of part I of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, which relates to technical cooperation and development grants, is amended as follows: 

(a) Amend section 212, which relates to authorization, by striking out "1965” and “$215,000,000” and substituting “1966” and “$210,000,000”, respectively. 1

TITLE III-INVESTMENT GUARANTIES SEC. 103. Title III of chapter 2 of part 1 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, which relates to investment guaranties, is amended as follows: (a) Amend section 221 (b), which relates to general authority, as follows: 

(1) Amend the introductory clause to read as follows: 

99 "The President may issue guaranties to eligible United States investors—' (2) In paragraph (1), strike out "$2,500,000,000" and substitute "$5,- 000,000,000". 

(3) Amend paragraph (2) as follows: 

(A) In the first proviso, strike out ", and no such guaranty in the case of a loan shall exceed $25,000,000 and no other such guaranty shall exceed $10,000,000". (B) In the fourth proviso, strike out "1966" and substitute "1967”. (b) Amend section 221(c), which relates to general authority, by inserting after the word "guaranty", the third time it appears, the words "of an equity investment". (c) Amend section 222(b), which relates to general provisions, by inserting after "(exclusive of informational media guaranties)," the words "and to pay the costs of investigating and adjusting (including costs of arbitration) claims under such guaranties,”. (d) Amend section 223, which relates to definitions, as follows: (1) In subsection (a), strike out "and" at the end thereof and in subsection (b) strike out the period and substitute "; and". 

(2) Add the following new subsection (c): 

"(c) the term ‘eligible United States investors' means United States citizens, or corporations, partnerships, or other associations created under the laws of the United States or any State or territory and substantially beneficially owned by United States citizens, as well as foreign corporations, partnerships, or other associations wholly owned by one or more such United States citizens, corporations, partnerships, or other associations: Provided, That the eligibility of a foreign corporation shall be determined without regard to any shares, in aggregate less than 5 per centum of the total of issued and subscribed share capital, required by law to be held by persons other than the United States owners. 

(e) Amend section 224, which relates to housing projects in Latin American countries, to read as follows: 

"SEC. 224. HOUSING PROJECTS IN LATIN AMERICAN COUNTRIES.-(a) It is the sense of Congress that in order to stimulate private home ownership and assist in the development of stable economies in Latin America, the authority conferred by this section should be utilized for the purpose of assisting in the development in the American Republics of self-liquidating pilot housing projects, the development of institutions engaged in Alliance for Progress programs, with particular emphasis on cooperatives, free labor unions, savings and loan and other institutions in Latin America engaged directly or indirectly in the financing of home mortgages, the construction of homes for lower income persons and families, the increased mobilization of savings and the improvement of housing conditions in 

Latin America. 

"(b) To carry out the purposes of subsection (a), the President is authorized to issue guaranties, on such terms and conditions as he shall determine, to eligible United States investors as defined in section 223 assuring against loss of loan investments made by such investors in- "(1) pilot or demonstration private housing projects in Latin America of types similar to those insured by the Federal Housing Administration and suitable for conditions in Latin America; "(2) credit institutions in Latin America engaged directly or indirectly in the financing of home mortgages, such as savings and loan institutions; "(3) housing projects in Latin America for lower income families and persons, which projects shall be constructed in accordance with maximum

unit costs established by the President for families and persons whose incomes meet the limitations prescribed by the President; "(4) housing projects in Latin America which will promote the development of institutions important to the success of the Alliance for Progress, such as free labor unions and cooperatives; or "(5) housing projects in Latin America 25 per centum or more of the aggregate of the mortgage financing for which is made available from sources within Latin America and has not derived from sources outside Latin America, which projects shall, to the maximum extent practicable, have a unit cost of not more than $6,500. "(c) The total face amount of guaranties issued under this section outstanding at any one time shall not exceed $350,000,000: Provided, That the total face amount of guaranties issued under subsection (b) (1) outstanding at any one time shall not exceed $250,000,000: Provided further, That no payment may be made under this section for any loss arising out of fraud or misconduct for which the investor is responsible: Provided further, That this authority shall continue until June 30, 1967.”

LO 

STATEMENT OF HON. DEAN RUSK, SECRETARY OF STATE; ACCOM- PANIED BY DAVID E. BELL, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT; AND DOUGLAS MacARTHUR, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE, CONGRESSIONAL RELATIONS 

Secretary RUSK. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

I do appreciate the privilege of appearing before you in support of the President's foreign assistance program for fiscal year 1966. 

This request will enable the United States to carry forward a program which, as President Johnson said in his message to the Congress in January, offers "strength to those who would be free; hope for those who would otherwise despair; progress. for those who would help themselves."

FOREIGN AID AND NATIONAL SELF-INTEREST 

Foreign aid continues to be an indispensable arm of our foreign policy in building a society of free nations in a stable world. The fundamental reason why we conduct programs of economic and military assistance is to support our interests, in the broadest sense, around the world. Our security is inextricably bound up with the evolution of a world of independent, peace-seeking nations. It is in our most elementary national self-interest to do what we can to help in strengthening the prospects for peaceful progress in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Economic and military assistance can make a crucial contribution to such progress, at very reasonable cost relative to our great economic strength and our vital interest in a decent world order. 

We should not let today's crisis or tomorrow's headline obscure the very real advances we have made in the years since World War II. 

While progress in some countries has been slow and frustrating, in many it has been steady and in some truly outstanding. 

This great endeavor will not be completed quickly. It will take patience, foresight, and courage. It will continue to require the understanding and calm judgment of the American people, if this progress is to continue. To have a foreign policy that has continuity, relevance, and direction is a constant test of a free people's ability to govern themselves in the modern world. It would be dangerous for our security and tragic for the future of the world if, out of frustration or fatigue, the United States were to turn back when we have come so far down the road. Winston Churchill said, in his prophetic speech in Fulton, Mo., 19 years ago this month: 

Our difficulties and dangers will not be removed by closing our eyes to them. 

They will not be removed by mere waiting to see what happens ***.

The United States has determined that it would not just wait "to see what happens."

U.S. INTERESTS AND OBJECTIVES IN COUNTRY PROGRAMS 

It is, of course, true that the interests of the United States are not always and everywhere the same, in each part of the world, in every country. The first question always faced in considering whether the 

United States should provide assistance to any country is: What interest do we have in this situation; what are our objectives here?

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, It is also quite true that the provision of aid is not everywhere or always a necessary or useful expression of U.S. interests. The second question that is always asked in considering whether assistance should be provided to a country: Can our aid be useful; what is the country prepared to do for itself; is the country prepared to make sacrifices, exercise self-discipline, and commit its own resources in a framework within which American assistance can be effective? 

Finally, there are, of course, other advanced countries and a variety of international organizations that can assist the developing countries. 

And consequently, in each case we ask: What resources are available to this particular country from sources other than the United States; is it necessary for us ourselves to be directly involved? 

Recognizing these qualifications, it is unmistakably plain that in a substantial number of circumstances, assistance from the United States has proved its great worth in the past, and is proving it at present. 

The program the President has recommended is tailored to the vary- ing situations in which we ought to help. It is highly concentrated in those cases where our assistance is most needed and will accomplish the largest results: 

1. Seventy-six percent of the funds requested for development loans are scheduled to go to seven countries: India, Pakistan, Turkey, Nigeria, Tunisia, Brazil, and Chile. 

2. Eighty-eight percent of the funds requested for supporting assistance are expected to go to four countries: Korea, Vietnam, Laos, and Jordan.

The total appropriation request for economic assistance in fiscal year 1966 is $2.21 billion. The military assistance program is $1.17 billion, for a total request for new appropriations of $3.38 billion. 

The new authorization for the economic portion of the foreign assistance program totals $848 million. As you know, Development Loan and the Alliance for Progress programs are operating under a continuing authorization.

I urge the Congress to give its prompt approval of the full amount requested.

LATIN AMERICA 

For Latin America, we are requesting an appropriation of $580 million for the coming fiscal year for the Alliance for Progress. The physical accomplishments already registered under the Alliance are encouraging. But perhaps more important is that the people of Latin 

America are beginning to know that the Alliance can succeed. Many of the Latin American nations have now turned to the hard tasks of reform and growth. The Castro experiment in Cuba has shown itself to be a failure. The Cuban dictator is becoming more and more isolated.

Brazil provides a striking example of what has happened. Prior to the advent of the new Government in April 1964 Brazil was seriously threatened by a steady economic and political deterioration which brought recurrent crises and growing popular unrest. Since then, the situation has changed dramatically for the better. Political stability has been restored. The environment which helped Communists and other extremists to infiltrate and exert a disproportionate influence has given way to an environment which discourages violent or extreme action.

year

The Brazilian Government has vigorously declared its common purpose with other democratic nations; its foreign policy is typified by the important role that Brazil played in the OAS adoption last of additional measures against Cuban subversion. It has launched a program for economic stability and growth; initiated major reforms; and at the same time maintained democratic institutions and a free press. Much remains to be done, but the first, difficult steps have been taken.

Recent developments in Chile have been similarly encouraging. The victory of the Christian Democrats in last September's presidential election, and in last Sunday's congressional elections, has expressed Chile's preference for peaceful reform. While the road ahead will be difficult, President Frei has, since his inauguration in November, set the stage for an ambitious economic stabilization and development program, including measures to reduce price inflation, substantially increase internal financing of the development program, and stimulate the agriculture and export industries. 

AFRICA 

Turning to Africa, the picture is highly diverse. Real progress is being made in some countries such as Tunisia and Nigeria; slower improvement in others. Our assistance programs are directed, as they should be, chiefly to training and to the building of institutions needed for planning and executing development activities. These programs are designed to develop human and social resources and to supply the ingredients of economic and social progress-education, technical skills, public administration, and managerial talents. Thus, the proposed program for Africa in fiscal year 1966 is $218 million, 42 percent of which is for technical assistance. 

Social and economic improvement is slow, and there are troublesome difficulties. East and central Africa are subject to active Communist machinations and blandishments. The competition in Africa between the Soviets and Chinese Communists has intensified, which adds to internal instability. 

The Congo, of course, presents a prime and immediate problem in Africa. We continue to support the legally constituted Central Government in response to its request for assistance and in conformity with U.N. resolutions. The Congo is primarily an African problem, and we seek an African solution; we look to other Africans, especially through the Organization for African Unity, to work together with the Congolese to this end. These African states have been addressing themselves seriously to this problem during the present meeting of the OAU in Nairobi. We expect that, once a measure of internal stability is established, progress can be made toward a broadly based National Government. This has not yet happened, and some fighting continues despite vigorous efforts of the Central Government to bring the rebellion under control. Increased aid to the rebels from external sources has threatened to prolong the struggle and create new difficulty for the Congo, for other African states, and for the United States. 

The Government of the Congo is faced with grave responsibilities in this trying period. It must better mobilize its own efforts and gain more support from its neighbors. We must continue to help. Without a peaceful Congo, there can be no stability in Africa.

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA 

In the Near East and south Asia, India, Pakistan, and Turkey are making substantial progress in their efforts to create modern economies. These three countries account for over $685 million--more than 

40 percent of the total development assistance proposed for fiscal year 1966. Iran, too, has been making encouraging headway and is moving ahead with programs of economic and social progress. 

We have extended aid to most Arab nations in the past, and currently we have programs in several, including the United Arab Republic. Compared with the size of our assistance to the major recipfent countries in this critical area of the world—India, Pakistan, and Turkey-our economic assistance program in the United Arab Republic has been quite small. But the troubled state of our relations with the United Arab Republic makes even that small program loom large.

Recent events in the United Arab Republic are naturally a matter of great concern to us. The United Arab Republic's public support of the 

Congolese rebels and the continued presence of substantial Egyptian forces in Yemen have led to some deterioration in our relations with Egypt. This strain was heightened by the destruction of the USIS library in Cairo.

We have sought, and we continue to seek, a basis for continuing a cooperative relationship with the United Arab Republic. External aid is vital to the United Arab Republic's development, and we believe that the economic progress of the United Arab Republic is a necessary element in a growing environment for peace and stability in the Middle East. However, while we desire to assist Egypt in its enormous task of social and economic advancement, there is plainly an inadequate basis of understanding at the present moment. We are, therefore, encouraging the United Arab Republic to examine with us the possibilities of reducing areas of difference. 

WESTERN PACIFIC 

In the western Pacific, two countries necessarily have recently occupied the center of our attention: South Vietnam where foreign assistance plays a major role, and Indonesia where our assistance has been steadily reduced over the last 2 years. 

South Vietnam has a right, as do all the nations of southeast Asia and, indeed, in the rest of the world, to live in peace, free from aggression from neighboring countries. Moreover, it has an understandable desire to be left in peace in order to use its resources on the economic and social development of its people, rather than for the harsh necessities of resisting aggression. 

Under the President's proposals for fiscal year 1966, we shall continue to provide sizable economic and military assistance. Indeed, the foreign assistance program is the principal vehicle for this support, not only of South Vietnam, but for the protection and safety of the nations in southeast Asia threatened by Chinese Communist. aggression.

As you can see in the presentation book before you, the technical assistance program in Indonesia is currently under review. The 

United States and Indonesian Governments have been at odds on

certain policies and courses of action pursued by the Indonesians. 

Over the past 2 years, there has been a significant change in our assistance program in Indonesia. No loans have been made during this period. No shipment under the Public Law 480 sales agreements for surplus food have been made to Indonesia for nearly a year and the agreement itself has now expired. In the same period, the technical assistance program, largely for universities, training, and malaria eradication, had dwindled. Under present circumstances, it is questionable that a basis will exist for further technical assistance in fiscal year 1966.

Elsewhere in the western Pacific, Taiwan has made such marked gains in growth, that it now stands on its own, and no longer requires AID assistance, even though programs under Public Law 480 and military assistance are continuing. The accomplishments of Taiwan, as a result of U.S. assistance, and their own ability and persistence, are an excellent example of success. South Korea is making considerable progress despite the necessity to maintain large military forces. 

Her expanding export earnings and economic growth are enabling us to shift increasingly from supporting to developmental aid within the overall program of assistance to Korea. In Thailand, our assistance takes fully into account the threat of Communist subversion and infiltration in the northeast. Despite these threats, Thailand has maintained a growing and stable economy over the last decade. 

I should like to turn now to two matters of concern. 

INCREASING LEVEL OF EXTERNAL PUBLIC DEBT OF DEVELOPING COUNTRIES 

First, the level of external public debt of the developing nations has been steadily increasing and, in some cases, alarmingly so. The accumulated burden is now about $30 billion. Even more significantly, the repayment volume on the debt is nearly $5 billion per year and is increasing 15 percent annually.

This is a heavy load for countries with limited resources, inconvertible currencies, and low foreign exchange earnings. The United 

States and other free world nations must continue their joint efforts to ease this burden, particularly during the early years-the crucial first decade of major development efforts. That is why it is imperative for the United States to maintain the current low interest rates and grace periods for development loans. That is why we are continuing to urge other donor nations to soften further the terms on which their aid is given. 

If we raise rates on long-term development assistance, the ultimate loser will be not only the recipient country, but the American taxpayer as well. For the higher the repayment burden, the longer development will take; and the day when nations will no longer need our aid will be further postponed. 

U.S. BALANCE-OF-PAYMENTS SITUATION 

Second, for several years we have given close attention to the relation of foreign aid to our balance-of-payments position. 

Since 1961, foreign aid has had a steadily decreasing impact on our balance of payments. 44-834-65- 2

The adverse impact is at the lowest level yet achieved. More than 

85 percent of the funds requested for the economic assistance program in fiscal year 1966 will be spent directly in the United States, for U.S. goods and services. 

The drain of dollars that still occurs through the aid program is due primarily to three factors-our contributions to international organizations, dollar expenses of employees overseas, and a small amount of commodity procurement in the less developed countries themselves.

It should be added that some of these dollars do return to the United States through such channels as procurement under United Nations projects. 

The net drain of funds from the economic aid program, taking into account repayments from prior aid loans, was about $300 million in fiscal year 1964. In 1961, the comparable drain was almost $1 billion. 

The committee should also bear in mind that foreign aid often opens the way for U.S. trade. Obviously, that is not the reason we extend foreign assistance, but it is one of the most helpful byproducts. Our aim is more trade, less aid. This is what has happened in Western 

Europe and Japan, and is happening in Taiwan, Greece, Israel, and other countries.

U.S. exports to Western Europe have doubled since 1950; exports to Japan have tripled in that time.

There are substantial future markets in the developing nations. As development picks up momentum, the peoples of these nations will be able to buy more from us and from other countries. The less developed countries are determined to grow-to buy more and to sell more. 

The United States can reasonably expect to get its fair share of these expanding markets. In addition, as these economies grow, there will be an increase in returns on growing American private investment in the less developed areas. Thus, foreign aid is a minor adverse factor in the current balance-of-payments problems; it is a strong positive factor over the long run.

CHANNELING AID THROUGH INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS 

The question has been raised whether a larger proportion of our economic aid for development purposes should be channeled through international organizations. It is a proper question and an important one, and we welcome full discussion.

The United States has strongly supported the establishment of international organizations providing assistance to development. We have been a major supporter of the World Bank, and we strongly backed Mr. Black when in 1959 he proposed the establishment of the Inter national Development Association. The United States energetically supported the establishment of the Inter-American Development Bank. We have been strong supporters of the United Nations Special 

Fund and the Expanded Program for Technical Assistance, now in process of merger into a single framework. 

In all these cases and others, we have been working for the expansion of aid given on an international basis as rapidly as other advanced countries have been willing to contribute a fair share to the common budget of these organizations. This remains our basic position. The

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 11 1965 Congress only last week accepted the President's recommendation and authorized an expansion in funds for the soft-loan window of the Inter-American Development Bank. We look forward to negotiations later this year under the leadership of the World Bank which we trust will result in enlargement of the funds available to the Inter national Development Association. 

I believe, therefore, that the executive branch and the Congress are in agreement on the desirability of enlarging the resources available to international aid-giving agencies on the basis of cost-sharing among the advanced countries.

Furthermore, I believe we are in agreement on the importance of steadily improving the arrangements for multilateral coordination of bilateral aid programs. The United States has taken a leading role in setting up international consortiums such as those for India, Pakistan, and Turkey, and international consultative groups such as those for Nigeria, Thailand, and Colombia. The World Bank is at present considering the possibility of establishing several more consultative groups over the next year or two, and the United States has supported this proposal.

In addition, the United States encouraged the creation of the Inter- American Committee for the Alliance for Progress (ordinarily referred to as CIAP) as a multilateral coordinating arrangement tailored to the special circumstances of Latin America. The CIAP has made a promising beginning, under strong leadership, and has our full support.

The United States has supported the establishment and the opera tion of the Development Assistance Committee of the OECD in Paris. 

The DAC has made some headway toward developing a common understanding and common policy positions among the major aidgiving countries.

Thus, both through our support for international development agencies, and through our support of multilateral coordination, we have made substantial progress toward achieving greater effectiveness with the aid made available to developing countries, and toward a more equitable sharing of the costs of aid among the advanced countries.

It is an impressive fact, as noted in the President's aid message, that- in fiscal year 1966, 85 percent of our development loans in Asia and Africa will be committed under international arrangements. All U.S. aid to Latin America is made available within the international framework of the Alliance for Progress. 

In Africa and in Asia, forces are now moving to strengthen multilateral arrangements on a regional basis. Properly organized, such arrangements could lead to more concerted measures of self-help within regions; to the emergence of more and better projects and plans for external financing; and to the mobilization from Europe, Japan, and elsewhere of additional development funds. Although the kind of arrangements created in Latin America, through the machinery of the Organization of American States, would not, of course, be exactly duplicated in other regions, we are prepared to play our part in encouraging further development of multilateral regional arrangements which have the effects described above.

BILATERAL AND MULTILATERAL AID 

To support international aid agencies and multilateral coordination, it is not necessary to derogate or eliminate our bilateral aid programs; quite the contrary. In our judgment, the United States clearly requires strong bilateral aid programs in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. The international aid agencies, while growing steadily, cannot hope to replace more than a fraction of the bilateral aid of the United States and other advanced countries in the immediate future. It would be a serious mistake, in our judgment, to abandon the principle of shared funding for the international aid agencies, and this necessarily will limit the rate at which those agencies can be expanded. 

SELF-HELP STANDARDS 

Moreover, I believe the executive branch and the Congress are in agreement on the very great importance of establishing proper standards for self-help performance on the part of countries which desire to receive assistance. Some-but not all of the international aid agencies have done well in this respect. But it is no exaggeration to state that for the last several years, the United States has taken the lead, both through its bilateral programs and through its participation in multilateral arrangements, in strengthening the insistence on sound self-help performance by aid-receiving countries. 

Nor has this insistence, if executed with full respect for the independence and sovereignty of the countries receiving aid, created unusual difficulties for our international relations. The relationship between donor and recipient is necessarily a delicate one, but it can be constructive and friendly if based on a shared commitment to the mutual objective of economic and social progress in the country in question. Our bilateral relationships are excellent in nearly all the cases where major assistance is involved. The cases in the world where our bilateral relationships are in difficulties do not revolve around aid, but around far broader and deeper political issues. 

The United States intends to rely to the maximum extent possible on international agencies and multilateral coordinating organizations to establish the self-help standards necessary to make development aid effective. But for the present, certainly it is necessary for us to continue to work bilaterally as well as multilaterally toward this objective.

NEED FOR A BILATERAL AID PROGRAM 

In summary, it is our conviction that U.S. interests require us to proceed with a strong bilateral aid program, as well as to contribute to the steady increase of aid funds available to international agencies and to use multilateral institutions or groups where it is appropriate. 

We believe our present proposals for bilateral aid authorizations are a prudent and sensible commitment of our resources, allowing concentration on those countries and those programs where they will do the most good. The task of assisting peaceful development_in 

Asia, Africa, and Latin America is a lengthy, difficult, and complex matter which in our judgment requires the best talent we can seek and mobilize on a bilateral as well as a multilateral basis. Relying

solely on either form of aid to the exclusion of the other simply does not meet the conditions as they now exist. 

CONCLUSION 

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I would recall that Winston Churchill, again in his Fulton address, spoke of "the power to save the future." 

Neither Mr. Churchill, nor any leader of the free world since World 

War II, has ever maintained that the United States or any nation has the power or the responsibility to control every event in every part of the world.

But our experience requires us to reject the idea that we must just wait to see what happens. Inaction in the face of challenge is the sure path to disaster.

Since 1945, the United States has been concerned with the peace of the entire world. Today, we can be secure only to the extent that the community of nations is secure on land, at sea, in the air, and the adjoining areas of space. 

Our policy has been, and will continue to be, to work patiently but purposefully toward a world of stability in which all nations are able to grow and prosper without fear of interference from outside. 

In pursuit of this goal, we are pledged to meet challenges, whether direct attack or subversion, which threaten our own security or the security of those who want to be free. 

We employ a variety of tools in this effort. Foreign aid is one of the most important.

Without it, we would be at the mercy of events. And the field would be left to our adversaries. We must not lose the future by default. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman and gentlemen.

European countries.

That figure has been constantly rising, has it not, over the years? 

Secretary RUSK. That is correct, sir.

SEPARATION OF MILITARY AND ECONOMIC AID 

Senator SPARKMAN. Do you have any feeling or do you care to express yourself on the proposal that has been made by the chairman. of this committee and has been recommended, I would say, at different times in the past by the majority of the committee, to the effect that the bill be divided and that we deal only with the economic aid part of it?

Secretary RUSK. Senator, my principal central concern is the program of aid recommended by the President. Over the years there has been considerable discussion in the Congress about whether that ought to be handled in a single bill, a single package, so that the Congress and the public will see it all together at the same time, or whether it ought to be broken up into two or more pieces in order to treat different parts of the aid program differently with respect to length of authorization, with respect to an examination of its component parts in detail. 

Quite frankly, I think this is at the moment not a primary issue between the executive and the legislative. The technique by which the Congress chooses to legislate the program requested by the President is basically for the Congress and its leaders to determine. I would prefer to allow a little discussion, between the two Houses and with the executive, to take place before I am called upon to give any view as Secretary of State or any personal view on that matter. 

Senator SPARKMAN. Yes. I thought that might be the case, and that is the reason I did not press you for an answer, but wanted to get the question on the record.

PROGRESS IN LATIN AMERICA Senator HICKENLOOPER. You mentioned Latin America, and you refer-if I can find it here-to Brazil and to Chile in some encouraging terms. And for the first time in postwar history there was a net reduction last year in Argentina's external indebtedness.

POSITION OF CASTRO IN CUBA 

I notice one interesting statement on page 5 of your statement here.

He still seems to be getting along all right. He seems to be having goods and commodities that he can ship to the militant Communist groups. 

Secretary RUSK. I think those are two very important things. 

Senator HICKENLOOPER. I presume the same thing could be said about the Red Chinese regime, but anyway there is no use arguing about it here, I guess.

ANTAGONISM TOWARD THE UNITED STATES 

I think a lot of us have been greatly bothered in trying to find a reason for the violent, and it has begun to seem almost universal, antagonism toward the United States. I have a list that has been compiled of some 85 or 90 rather recent incidents where citizens of other nations have attacked American Embassies, attacked American installations, burned the American Information Service, called us names, and accused us of everything imaginable. I think it has created the idea in a great many places that all you have to do to get money out of the United States is to insult us and kick us around. 

And it seems to be fairly successful. 

The point is that they do seem to be getting away with it. They do not seem to be drawing any closer to the Western idea of independent self-determination. I do not anticipate and I do not think it would be good if these countries followed the United States blindly in all political and economic activities. But I think our object is to have them try to assume responsibility for independence and genuine self-determination in a world of freedom, and I do not see much evidence that they are moving much toward that except in maybe one or two countries, perhaps three. 

Some of the countries in Africa that 3 or 4 years ago I had the greatest hope for seem to be going in reverse. I am not encouraged about Tanganyika. I had some hopes for that country under the present leadership 3 or 4 years ago. The same general leadership seems to be in power but they are drifting the other way. 

India now joins and says we are aggressors in southeast Asia. 

Pakistan is making goo-goo eyes at China, and they are wining and dining each other in great style; and criticism of the United States by our ally Pakistan--which we once thought was one of the strong arms of our mutual defense program down there is increasing. 

Pakistan seems to be for some reason or other veering the other way constantly. I do not know whether it is a fear of India or whether they think they will get more money out of the United States the more names they call us or the further they appear to be drawing away from us and toward Red China.

I did get some encouragement out of what looked like a cooperative action on the part of 12 or 13 small African nations in connection with the Congo situation which seemed to be in some support of our efforts there, but basically the whole picture does not look very good.

Of course, I think the most shocking situation to a great many of us is the Egyptian situation under Mr. Nasser. There is a nation that has been consistently receiving for some time now 25 percent at least or more of its wheat supplies from the United States. If you take other foodstuffs that we have furnished them under one program or another, it runs up to almost 40 percent, by certain calculations anyway, of the whole food volume that they have that we are giving it to them. So they insult us. They have wholly failed to keep their agreements on Yemen. It makes it rather difficult to keep getting kicked around by these countries to whom we keep putting out our largess in one way or another. 

I have here an interesting and quite a caustic column written by Jenkin Lloyd Jones in the Evening Star of January 23, which is a

little old now as things in the world currently move. I will not take the time now to read it into the record, but, Mr. Chairman, I would like to insert it in the record at this point. 

The CHAIRMAN. Without objection. 

(The article referred to follows:) [From the Evening Star, Washington, D.C., Jan. 23, 1965] JENKIN LLOYD JONES-TIME NOW TO RESTUDY FOREIGN AID 

A few months ago units of the Atlantic fleet arrived at Rio de Janiero. 

Some genius in our Embassy dreamed up a great public relations gimmick. A volunteer crew of American sailors would go up into one of the "favelas," or slum communities that cling to the beautiful Rio mountains. The sailors would paint a few shacks. And a Navy boilermaker would be sent to repair the boiler leak in a Rio hospital. 

No charge, of course. Just good will. Neighborliness. 

Well, what the Communists did to this Boy Scout performance was pathetic. "What," they asked the citizens of Rio, "can the Americans be up to? And how stupid do they think we are if they believe that we cannot see that there is a trick in this somewhere?"

And, sure enough, in a short time not only most of Rio, but most of Brazil was asking, "What is the American trick?"

Now, where the Embassy went wrong was in its failure to realize that nowhere does such altruism as painting a building or fixing a boiler for free exist in the philosophy of the average Brazilian. To do these things a man must be either crazy or devious. And since the American sailors didn't look crazy their deviousness was easy to believe. 

There are plenty of examples of idiotic foreign aid. Like the $23 million plastics plant we gave Yugoslavia, at the dedication of which both Marshal Tito and Nikita Khrushchev made glowing speeches about this example of the triumph of socialism. 

Or the $3 million air-conditioned yacht for Emperor Haile Selassie.

Or the TV sets for jungle villages with no electric power. 

Or the shipment of "royal bee” sex rejuvenator for Nationalist China.

But it is a mistake to pick over bits of lint. Even if foreign aid were the greatest discovery since the tinder box, the passing out of about $100 billion naturally would include boo-boos. It is the philosophy, itself, we should reexamine.

Our aid program got started reasonably and wisely under the Marshall plan. 

It was designed to rebuild the war-wrecked industrial economies of Europe and Japan, without which there would have been chaos, starvation and a probable Communist takeover. 

But then the whole world, including nations that had not only sacrificed nothing in the war but which had profited handsomely from it began rattling the cup and our global charity got underway. 

Mark Twain once made the cynical remark, "If you take in a homeless dog, feed him and make him prosperous, he will not bite you. This is the principal difference between a dog and a man.' 

There is some truth in this, as we have discovered. Nations hate to look upon themselves as mendicants. They like to imagine that they are giving something in return for what they are getting. And, in the case of U.S. aid, rationalizations were not slow in coming, particularly since Communist propaganda helped all it could. Samples include: 

Americans are embarrassed by their food surplus. It costs them nothing to give it away.

Americans are contemptuous of other nations, and think they can buy their friendship.

Americans are trying to control other governments for their own selfish purposes, and aid is the "Trojan horse."

So phase II followed. Foreign politicians, in an effort to prove to their people that they were not subservient to the Americans began to make it a point to be critical of U.S. policies. 

This brought on phase III. The louder foreign statesmen yelled about the 

United States, the more foreign aid we rushed to them. You could get more 

U.S. dollars by insulting Uncle Sam than by pumping his hand in gratitude. 44-834-65— -3

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, And so we have come to phase IV—blackmail. A recent issue of U.S. News & 

World Report asserts that the chief reason why U.S. aid continues to Egypt after Gamal Abdel Nasser made no move to stop the burning of our libraries, refused to apologize for shooting down an American plane and told our ambassador to jump in the Nile, is because we fear, if aid is cut off, Nasser will attack Israel.

Somebody ought to send the State Department a history of ancient Rome. 

When the Romans began paying peace tributes the end of the empire was near. 

The savage chieftains milked the Roman treasury for all they could get and then invaded anyway. 

Foreign aid has some uses. 

Our wheat can stave off starvation in India for a limited time. Technical assistance can help some backward countries increase their gross national products. But the lavish outshoveling of American wealth to friends and enemies alike in the face of continued U.S. balance-of-payments deficits, will not only not strengthen us in foreign affairs, but it will wreck the dollar.

It's that simple and it's time for another look. 

Senator HICKENLOOPER. I can only say, as I say, it is quite a caustic article. There is one interesting paragraph. He recites quite a number of illustrations, but there is one interesting paragraph in this article, about the middle of it. He says: "Mark Twain once made the cynical remark, 'If you take in a homeless dog, feed him and make him prosperous, he will not bite you. This is the principal difference between a dog and a man.'" It seems that we have taken in a lot of homeless and distressed people over the world and saved them from political suicide. We have saved them literally from starvation in many places, and now that they have got their strength, their teeth are strong again, and they are biting. I am not sure what the answer is, but I do think we ought to try to find the answer here in this committee as quickly as we can.

GIVING IN TO THREATS- -MALAYSIA 

There is one other thing that has concerned me, and I think it goes to the point of our willingness to surrender under threat. We negotiated a loan for military hardware and equipment with Malaysia. 

Those negotiations went on here and in Kuala Lumpur; agreements were all apparently reached, and it went finally to the Cabinet in Malaysia, as I understand it, for final action. All through these negotiations over a considerable period of time, the Malaysians did not raise any real question about the interest rate. The interest rate was established at 5 percent. It was an ordinary loan in which we charge other countries in most instances where they have an ability to pay, and certainly Malaysia has a surplus of convertible currency. The loan gets over to the Malaysian Cabinet, and in quite a dramatic statement, the head of the Government got up and condemned the United States as a "Shylock" and a profiteering country for asking 5 percent on this loan. They indicated they probably wanted it for nothing. 

This question was not seriously an issue until the final presentation over there.

I notice in the papers now in the last few days we have backed up and said, "Well, OK. If it is offensive to you, we will now drop it down to 3 percent. We back up on the originally agreed 5 percent. and we will let you have it for 3 percent." 

I am not so sure but what that probably contributes to the idea. among a lot of nations that if you yell loud enough, the United States: will give it to you for nothing or almost nothing or they will cut the interest way down.

Secretary RUSK. Senator, on that particular point, we and Malaysia are not in that type of "arms-length dukes-up" relationship. It is quite true that during all of the negotiations that preceded the public statements in Malaysia a few weeks ago that there had been no secret as among the negotiators or between the governments about the normal, expected conditions of loan for credit sales of military equipment. 

Our offer of November 1964 involved the use of MAP funds to guarantee a loan of $15.2 million from commercial sources. When the 

Cabinet learned of the terms, it rejected the offer because the terms were considered too onerous. Nevertheless, we wished to carry out

the offer made to the Malaysian Government last year and to demonstrate our support of Malaysia. So, in February 1965 we made a new military credit sales offer to Malaysia involving a loan of $4 million from MAP funds, repayable in 10 years at 3-percent interest. This offer involved a much smaller amount than did the November offer and could be made without bank credits. The terms, therefore, could be more favorable.

My own impression is that that particular episode is behind us and that this represents what would have been a normal kind of agreement between the two Governments had it been handled through diplomatic channels throughout.

Senator HICKENLOOPER. One of the points which I probably did not emphasize sufficiently, is that Malaysia is financially able to pay this. 

Malaysia is basically from a financial standpoint not a supplicant country. I can draw a difference. A country that is totally unable to keep current loans on, let us say, a bankable basis can justify a request for a soft loan on easy terms over long periods. However, I do not think that is the case with Malaysia in this particular loan. I think they are perfectly able to pay it. I think they have a surplus. Of course, everybody wants to keep their surplus, I guess, if they can and get things as cheaply as possible. But this is an illustration where we may have set a precedent for reducing all kinds of loans to all kinds of nations who are able to pay.

Secretary RUSK. Well, because of the considerations that you mentioned, Senator, we do not ourselves suggest at our own initiative that there be special concessionary rates applied to Malaysia as applied to other countries. It is true, however, that they have had to increase their military purchases, their defense expenditures in connection with the confrontation policy. They themselves have not set forth their own plans in this regard and the requirements that they were facing, so that despite the fact that they have been in good economic position, they face some very heavy and extraordinary expenditures. 

Senator HICKENLOOPER. Yes. 

Secretary RUSK. So we felt that this solution that was reached is a fair solution under all the circumstances. 

Senator HICKENLOOPER. For several years we have had to borrow money to pay our own bills. There is either a failure of understanding on the part of a lot of these countries or, I often think, a feeling that the United States is just an easy touch. 

I think that is all.

BREAKDOWN OF FOREIGN ASSISTANCE OF OTHER COUNTRIES 

The next memorandum that I would like to ask for, Mr. Secretary, is that you and Mr. Bell supply this committee with a detailed breakdown of the foreign assistance programs of other countries, not just what they call AID, but a detailed presentation as to what terms and conditions they enshroud their programs with in comparison with our very, in my judgment, lax ones the length of their grants or loans, the interest rates of their loans, and the grace periods that they allow. The information constantly is handed out by the administration that countries X, Y, and Z are providing such and such percentage of foreign aid in terms of their national product or in terms of some other statistical base that they want to use. Then when you dig into it, you discover it is like judging a mule and a horse in a show ring. They are different critters, and you don't have the same criteria of judgment.

I think we ought to go into that this year, in a cooperative spirit, rather than to have counsel for the opposition have to dig it out and thereby get themselves in somewhat of a litigous position. 

In fact, we occupy a very strange position in this debate. We have several hats that we have to wear, and the one hat I want to have at my right hand all the time is the hat whereby I work with you rather than against you. I have always said that I thought a lot of these problems could be resolved if there were more of the exchange of views that I am asking for in these memorandums that I am calling for. Now I will proceed to ask a few questions. 

Secretary RUSK. Let me just say, Senator, that we will be glad to furnish that information. There is some in the presentation book, but we will make that more detailed. 

We have been working very hard in the Development Assistance Committee to get more coordination with respect to criteria, terms, and grace periods and things of that sort. We will report on that in the memorandum. (The unclassified parts of the information referred to follow :)

VIII. CONTRIBUTIONS FROM OTHER INDUSTRIAL COUNTRIES 

Apart from the industrial OECD countries, Australia, Finland, New Zealand, and the Union of South Africa regularly extend assistance to less developed countries. While Finland and South Africa contribute exclusively to multilateral organizations, Australia and New Zealand have bilateral, as well as multilateral, assistance programs. In 1963, these four countries together contributed about $85 million. Of this amount, $20 million was in multilateral contributions.

The bilateral aid programs of Australia and New Zealand consist mainly of financial subsidies for the local budgets of dependent territories (Papua and 

Australian Trust Territory of New Guinea, Norfolk and Cocos Islands, Niue and 

Cook Islands). During the last few years, bilateral contributions have shown a continuous upward trend, mainly on account of rising disbursements by Australia to Papua and the Trust Territory of New Guinea. These amounted to about $45 million in the year to June 1963 or over three-quarters of total Australian bilateral assistance. 

Contributions by Australia and New Zealand to the Colombo plan and the Indus Basin Development Fund make up the remainder of the bilateral assistance by these countries. From the beginning of the Colombo plan in 1961 until June 

1963, Australia's contribution to the plan totaled about $110 million in grants, three-quarters of which were for development programs and projects and the remainder for technical cooperation. During the same period, New Zealand's contributions were $27 million, all in grants. In the year to June 1963, Australia provided $10.8 million and New Zealand $2.2 million. Contributions to the Indus 

Basin Development Fund, which are calculated in accordance with the original agreement on the establishment of the Fund, were $2.2 million by Australia and $0.3 million by New Zealand in the year to June 1963. These countries also contribute to other Commonwealth schemes, such as the Special Commonwealth 

Aid to Africa Plan (SCAAP). 

Senator MORSE. Of course, as you know, I haven't had the opportunity to study the presentation book this year, but I have every past year, and unless it is an entirely different presentation than it was in the past year, it will be completely unsatisfactory. The presentation last year did not give the breakdown that I am calling for in my memorandum.

Secretary RUSK. Right. 

Senator MORSE. And if it is in this year's presentation book, fine.

GREATER USE OF MULTILATERAL AGENCIES 

There has been some discussion here this morning, Mr. Secretary, about the greater use of so-called multilateral agencies. Of course, you know that I don't propose to not cooperate with the multilateral agencies. I do propose, however, to insist upon basic congressional checks in respect of the funds that we put in those agencies. If they don't want to accept our fund on the basis of our checks, they don't have to. It is up to them. 

But I think you ought to know that one of the great issues in this debate and one about which there is going to be very strong differences I think within this committee, is that some of us, at least, do not think we ought to turn foreign aid over to a multilateral agency. We think that we ought to cooperate in providing American contributions to those agencies, but not to do with as those agencies may decide to do, without what we consider to be basic checks. 

That is why some of us have strongly disagreed with the Department and the administration last week on the Inter-American Bank. 

I am a strong advocate of the Inter-American Bank, which has some-

thing to do in helping those who get it through the Congress. I am for it.

But I think you should understand in this debate that many of us feel that you are developing a foreign aid program in which the legislative representatives, in fact and in effect, have less and less control of American taxpayers' money that is being spent in the foreign assistance program. That is what I think the public is eventually going to resent. When we are fighting to preserve these checks, we are really on the side of foreign aid, although we are labeled as a "neoisolationist" and "anti-foreign-aiders," and so on, by writers who devote most of their time to reading their own writings. 

But I want you to know that I am concerned about the comments in your statement this morning which seem to indicate that it is the plan of the Department to make greater and greater use of these multilateral agencies. There is not a whisper from you in your statement as to the imposition of any American checks in respect to the use to which a foreign body or organization can put American taxpayers' money. 

I think we have to be reasonable about it, but I certainly think that it is reasonable to say that American money that goes into the International Monetary Fund or the World Bank, or any one of these so-called international multilateral organizations, should be subject to certain limitations imposed by the Congress. If they don't want to accept those limitations, just don't give them the money. 

There is a great void of difference, I think, that exists between some on this committee and the Department, if I read your testimony this morning right. Those of us who are concerned about a tendency in this country for the executive branch of Government to take over more and more basic legislative functions. 

I am, as you know, greatly disturbed about it, and I think we have an example in these multilateral international agencies. We have an example of what I consider to be a most dangerous trend in this Republic: of the Congress delegating more and more authority and power and decision to you gentlemen, estimable as you are, in the executive branch of the Government. I think that breaks down our system of checks and balances.

I don't propose to give you a lecture here this morning, but, as counsel for the opposition, to tell you at least what some of our fears are, and why we are opposed to your program as you have presented it this morning. 

Secretary RUSK. Senator, may I comment very briefly? 

Senator MORSE. Oh, I would be delighted.

Secretary RUSK. I talked this morning about a balanced program: strong support for those international agencies that appear to be able to do an effective job, plus a strong and vigorous bilateral aid program. 

In referring to the taxpayers, there is the possibility in many of these international agencies to multiply the dollars one and a half times straightaway through the matching, or more than matching from others, 40 percent as against 60 percent in the U.N. Special Fund, and 42 percent against 58 percent in IDA.

We participate in the management of those operations, and I think that we have felt that under men like Mr. Eugene Black, Mr. George 

Woods, and others, that they have achieved a very high standard of

managerial skill. It is a balanced program that we are talking about, where it can be effective through international bodies where we can mobilize additional funds, fine; where we need to do it on a bilateral basis, yes.

But I think I would have to say that when we elect to use an international body, there are some things which are not appropriate to the international rule. For example, we can't turn to an international body and tailor it exactly as the Congress might wish to tailor our own bilateral programs with respect to particular and special countries or highly sensitive situations. 

That is one of the reasons for having a bilateral program as well as an international program. Congress would have to make its own judgment as to how best and in what combination to support both the multilateral as well as the bilateral program. 

RETAINING A SYSTEM OF CHECKS AND BALANCES 

Senator MORSE. It is going to make its own judgments and lay down its own criteria as to the terms and conditions on which we will participate in such a body. If they don't want us to participate with those congressional checks retained, why then we just can't participate. 

Let me very quickly say that is what bothers me so much about the soft currency funds. Those are American dollars that go into them. 

My feeling is that you will get much more careful administration given to your hard loan funds than to your soft loan funds, that you have to always be on guard about that. 

You made an observation about the people that are involved representing our country on these international bodies. You see, I will never talk in terms of individuals. Let me be completely impersonal about it. I am going to talk about the fact that whoever the individual is, he is a human being. We have learned under our system of government, that you have to write in the procedures that protect the people from the administration by human beings to retain a government by law.

We talk about a government by law, but it is administered by human beings. You protect that government by law by getting the kind of restrictions and checks imposed upon your national policy that isn't going to permit any person, I care not how noted his name, from substituting himself and his judgment for what might be a better national policy. 

And so we are in a field, as you can see, of abstract principles of representative government. I happen to feel that our foreign aid program more and more is breaking down those principles. That is why you are going to find me urging to tighten the congressional checks. 

I think it is fair to say that the indication of your testimonyboth in what is written in your statement and in the remarks that you made in addition-cause me, at least, to conclude that you favor an expansion of the use of these international multilateral bodies. expansion of the If we do, how long do you think this 85-percent figure that seems to impress some of my colleagues so much-it never has me—will remain 85 percent?

Do you think if you are going to have the administration and the youating decisionmaking turned over to multilateral international bodies, that 44-834-65- -4

they are very long going to say 85 percent of these goods and services can be bought in the United States? 

They are going to have some goods and services that they are going to insist, knowing as I think you know that in international negotiations there is give and take and there is compromise and there is a tendency to prorate. Do you think this 85-percent figure will last very long?

Secretary RUSK. Senator, I think it might be well for me to submit a memorandum on the balance-of-payments effect of our contributions to international bodies. 

Senator MORSE. Delighted. 

Secretary RUSK. For example, in the case of the World Bank, our experience has been that World Bank financed the projects on the basis of international bids makes it possible for us to get in ordinary competition at least 25 percent of those funds. In the case of the recent request for an expansion of the Fund for Special Opera. tions of the Inter-American Bank, the Secretary of the Treasury testified that that increase would be used for procurement of goods and services very much like our own bilateral programs. 

But I think this is a relevant point and we will be glad to submit a detailed memorandum of the effect of balance of payments in international institutions. (The information requested appears on p. 692.) 

NATURE OF ASSISTANCE FROM OTHER COUNTRIES 

Senator MORSE. I don't know whether I had made clear or not, but I will make clear now for the record that when you supply this memorandum to us in regard to the foreign-aid programs of other countries, I would like to have it also include data showing their contributions to these international multilateral bodies. This you did have in the workbook last year, and I assume that it is in there again, but I want to mention it; would you also make perfectly clear what percentage of their aid goes to their present or former colonies in which they have great vested economic interests at the present time? 

When France, for example, gives aid to some of her former or present colonies or Portugal or Spain either, they are sort of aiding themselves to a degree-not entirely, but to a degree. 

Yet there is a tendency for the State Department and the AID people to call attention to the aid of these great colonial powers. 

We have to get the people to understand where that aid goes to and to what extent that aid is sort of taking money out of their right pocket and putting it in their left pocket.

Secretary RUSK. That is highly relevant, Senator, and we will be glad to do that. I think it is also fair to say that our own AID programs are, to a degree, in aid of ourselves in the same sense. 

Senator MORSE. Yes.

Secretary RUSK. Both from a training point of view and from the point of view of long historical relationships. 

Senator MORSE. That is why, Mr. Secretary, you could get more money out of me for aid than you are recommending if we had more of it really aiding us than it presently does. But that is going to be part of the case.

Secretary RUSK. Senator, may I interrupt for just a moment, because on the point you were discussing earlier, I think it ought to be pointed out that over the past 3 years we have had authorization in the AID program to commit 10 percent of the economic aid through international bodies, but in the appropriation process, that has been suspended. In other words, the Congress has expressed both views on this subject in effect as far as the present authorization and appropriation is concerned.

Senator MORSE. This is so typical of you. That is a very fair statement for you to make. You could also get more money out of me for the multilateral bodies if we could get a little more cooperation for the administration to write in some congressional checks. You wouldn't have had any trouble with me last week at all. 

Senator LAUSCHE. You are beginning to soften. 

Senator MORSE. Don't worry about my softening. 

Secretary RUSK. That is a tempting prospect.

Senator MORSE. I am simply asking for the checks. We could have gone on and on right down the road last week. Instead a continuing widening difference of opinion in the country I think is the result of the debate today.

This chart that is made a part of the record shows that 89 countries and territories in fiscal 1964 received more than $1 million of U.S. assistance of some kind or another. 

If I understood you correctly this morning, your figures this year will show 74 nations instead of 89. Those of us of the opposition are going to offer our own foreign aid bill this year, and one part of it, of course, will be to bring all foreign aid to an end at the end of fiscal 1967, stop the whole program and start all over again, limiting it to not more than 50 nations, and setting forth the terms and conditions that an applicant must meet. You note I use the word "applicant." They have to come and apply for it. It will be a novelty to some of them to apply for it, rather than to have it urged upon them. 

INFORMATION ON SELECTIVITY REQUESTED 

But I would like to have a memorandum on the selectivity question based upon this chart of fiscal 1964, and based upon what will probably be a corresponding chart for fiscal 1966. My question is why so many.

Isn't it possible to even eliminate a few countries? Do we have to continue to provide aid for 74? And I know you can say well, in some instances it is not too much, but if they don't need it every dollar is too much. If they can assume the burden themselves, then we can't justify giving them any. I would like to have a memorandum on that, and any comment you want to make now. 

Secretary RUSK. Thank you, Senator. We will be very glad to furnish a memorandum on that. I think it is important for the committee and the country to know that 95 percent of the 1966 country program funds will go to 31 countries where we have substantial AID programs. 

About 4 percent will go to 33 countries. 

Now the list of the number of countries is heavily explained by the fact that we do believe that we should help keep our doors open in the field of technical assistance so that our land-grant colleges and our

medical schools and our other institutions of training can help to prepare the manpower that is important for economic and social development in so many of these countries. So I think that the memorandum would show that there is a much higher degree of concentration that the mere listing of the countries on a single sheet would indicate. We will be glad to send that to you, sir. (The unclassified part of information referred to follows:) 

PLANNING AND CONCENTRATION OF AID COUNTRY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS Total country assistance programs: 

Fiscal year 1964. 

Fiscal year 1965-. 

Fiscal year 1966-. 

1 Includes 3 programs for Northern and Southern Rhodesia and Zanzibar. 1 82 76 228 72 AID assistance programs are developed on a country-by-country basis. Three basic principles determine the nature and amount of U.S. assistance allocations to individual countries. They are- 

The importance to the United States of strengthening the country's economy and development effort, its political and social structure and institutions its security situations; 

The needs of the country for assistance, and the availability to the country of assistance from other sources; 

The effectiveness with which the country is using its own resources. 

These principles are applied to the formulation of a U.S. assistance program carefully tailored to achieve U.S. objectives in, and the needs of each country situation.

Each proposed AID country program is developed over several months of review and analysis in the field and in Washington. Proposed country programs are reviewed in the field by the U.S. Ambassador and the AID Mission Director, and in Washington by the regional Assistant Administrators of AID and the Regional Assistant Secretaries of State, and by the AID Administrator. A continuing review process is maintained as programs are carried out, to make sure that adjustments are made to take advantage of new opportunities and to overcome obstacles.

This program review process and application of basic aid principles results in a highly selective and concentrated AID program. The program proposed for fiscal year 1966 will intensify the concentration of U.S. assistance in countries of priority need and best performance. 

Less than 1 percent of proposed fiscal year 1966 AID country programs is planned for countries in transition toward self-support. These countries should complete the transition of self-support over the next several years. 

Ninety-five percent of proposed fiscal year 1966 country programs is planned for limited programs of assistance in 31 countries. 

Two-thirds of development assistance funds is presently planned for seven countries which are engaged in strong, self-help development programs; Brazil, Chile, Nigeria, Tunisia, India, Pakistan, and Turkey. 

Seventy-four percent of development loan funds will go to these same seven countries.

Ninety percent of supporting assistance funds is planned for four countries whose security or stability depends on continued U.S. support: Vietnam, Laos, Korea and Jordan. 

In recognition of the priority the United States places on the progress of our Latin American neighbors and in response to the momentum achieved under the Alliance for Progress, Latin America will again be the scene of our most intensive assistance effort. The $596 million planned for Alliance countries during fiscal year 1966 represents nearly a third of total AID country assistance and a per capita aid level of $2.73, by far the highest for any region. 

MAJOR COUNTRY PROGRAMS 

AID conducts major programs of assistance in 31 countries which are of major importance to U.S. foreign policy, and which must deal with differing economic and political problems and opportunities.

Among the 31 major AID country programs proposed for fiscal year 1966, 24 are focused directly toward building development. Seven programs provide assistance to promote security and stability in critical country situations. 

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE PROGRAM 

In 24 major development assistance programs, the United States is attempting to induce and assist sound efforts toward lasting economic and social development. The goal is to help these countries reach the point where foreign assistance on concessional terms is no longer necessary. 

AID development assistance strategies and criteria are applied in all major development assistance programs. However, two main subtypes of development assistance programs may be identified. 

General support.-Each of these countries has relatively large needs for external assistance and each is expected to be able to use such assistance effectively in building development. Each is important to U.S. foreign policy. These countries are taking steps to improve self-help performance and to allocate investment funds and other resources effectively. Virtually all of AID's program loans for development are made to countries in this group. 

Qualified support.-Development in these countries is of major importance to 

U.S. policy interests and they have relatively good prospects for development. 

These countries have not, however, yet demonstrated an adequate and sustained commitment to sound development policies and effective resource use. 

In some cases, political and economic institutions in these countries have not been strong enough to undertake or effectively carry out needed self-improvements. 

Much of AID assistance to countries in this group is conditional on specific self-help performance. Assistance is carefully focused to develop bases of strength within their economies and to provide incentives for specific reforms and improvements. As countries in this group demonstrate willingness and capability to carry out major self-help efforts, the United States stands ready to support them further. 

SECURITY-STABILITY PROGRAMS 

This group consists of seven countries of critical importance in which basic conditions of internal and external security must be established and the government strengthened before serious development may be undertaken. Many of these countries face severe political and economic instability caused by internal tensions or Communist subversion and aggression. Security-stability programs are funded primarily from supporting assistance. Programs proposed in these countries for fiscal year 1966 will absorb 94 percent of the fiscal year 1966 supporting assistance program. 

The U.S. goal in these countries is to reach the point where improved security conditions permit elimination of supporting assistance and a shift to a development effort. In such countries as Pakistan, Turkey, and Iran this goal has already been reached. In Korea, United States policy in the past few years has been gradually to decrease that portion of its assistance which is directed to security-stability and to increase the development portion.
