RELATIONSHIP OF MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO FOREIGN POLICY 

Senator MORSE. If I may I will limit myself to this question. Mr. 

Secretary, will you give us your views as to the relationship of military aid in any country to American foreign policy in that country? To what extent do you have a voice in determining what that military aid will be, and to what extent do you have authority to veto a decision made by anyone under the President of the United States in respect to foreign military aid. 

Secretary RUSK. Yes. First, 72 percent of military assistance funds are planned for 11 countries around the periphery of the Communist bloc. This has been largely true since the beginning of military

assistance, although we pulled back substantially from Western Europe, of course.

I think we have to anticipate that the decade or so ahead of us is going to be very much affected by what happens on what the Communists call wars of liberation. There was a big argument in 1961 between Moscow and Peiping about the techniques by which one supports a world revolution.

Moscow at that time said that the sending of men and arms across national frontiers would very well stimulate what they call military reaction from the imperialists. Peiping made the point, tried to make the point that that technique was safe, and that they could do that without much "reactions from the imperialists." 

I think both of them have, in effect, accepted the fact that nuclear war is prohibitively expensive and destructive as an instrument of policy, that organized invasions by armies of a conventional sort is not the way to get on best with a revolution, but this war of liberation is a very important thing.

That means that we need to give attention to the capacity of friends and particularly our allies to organize their internal security and to protect themselves against that particular kind of penetration. 

We have thrown most of our weight in that direction. It means training. It means specialized training and equipment. It means civic action programs whereby the armed forces themselves knit themselves into the life of the people of the countryside by working on projects that contribute to economic and social development. It means in some cases shore patrols, patrols at sea to cover coastlines and things of that sort.

But I would think that this relatively modest military assistance program of $1,170 million is very much a part of our total security interests and total security burden around the world. 

Now as far as specific programs are concerned, the law itself gives the Secretary of State a policy responsibility for policy guidance. 

The President, the Secretary of State, and the Secretary of Defense keep in very close touch with each other on these matters. I have no doubt at all that we work as an effective team in making these decisions. 

I have not felt that I have been overrun by others in connection with these judgments.

I think the administration of that part of the law has proceeded very well. I must say that this has been facilitated by the team spirit and the readiness to cooperate of my colleague, the Secretary of Defense, but it also applies to our colleagues down the line who are in daily contact with each other on these military assistance problems. 

Senator MORSE. Mr. Secretary, in deference to my chairman, I want to say that your answer to my question raises many questions that I want to go into with you in depth at our next public hearing. I want this discussed in public, and I also will ask no more questions now other than to have you know that I shall press on the point that in my judgment military aid in the country is more controlling of foreign policy than any other one factor, if it is substantial aid. We have to face up to the fact that when you are dealing with military aid, you are dealing with foreign policy. 

Secretary RUSK. I have no question about it.

Senator MORSE. I want to be absolutely certain that you OK every dollar of military aid anywhere in the world and that there is no question about your power to say to the Pentagon Building, "You shan't grant that aid." I think that is so important under what my chairman calls the discussion of the theory of representative government, I don't intend to support any program that in effect turns foreign policy over to the Pentagon Building. 

The CHAIRMAN. The Senator from Delaware. 

Senator WILLIAMS. Mr. Chairman, I will pass. 

The CHAIRMAN. The Senator from Louisiana. 

Senator LONG. No thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

The CHAIRMAN. The Senator from Ohio. 

TOTAL FOREIGN INDEBTEDNESS TO THE UNITED STATES 

Senator LAUSCHE. I would like to ask a few questions. Mr. Rusk, some mention has been made of the debts owing to us by different nations, as a consequence, one, of World War I, and then, of World War II. Do you have available in round numbers the aggregate indebtedness that exists now, including the interest accumulation on the still existent debts of World War I? 

Secretary RUSK. I don't have that with me this morning, Senator.

I did mention the figure of just over $6 billion as it relates to France, but I don't have the others. I will be very glad to furnish those for the record.

Senator LAUSCHE. Do I understand you to say that the debt of 

France alone is $6 billion, or is that the aggregate of all the nations? 

Secretary RUSK. No, that is the World War I debt, accumulated principal and interest over time, in the absence of a final settlement or elimination of the problem. 

Senator LAUSCHE. Relating to France alone? 

Secretary RUSK. Yes, sir, according to the information—

The CHAIRMAN. If the Senator will yield, I put that in the record last year in a speech. I got the figure from the Treasury, and it is over $6 billion. Part of that is not yet due under the arrangements made after the war. The due date hasn't arrived, but that is the total up to now including what- Secretary RUSK. As far as the debts that arose out of World War 

II are concerned, France is current in its payments of those debts.

DISCUSSIONS ON AMERICAN TOURISM 

Senator LAUSCHE. Is the Department at all discussing with foreign nations their concern about our Government advocating a policy of inducing American tourists to visit the United States, and thus help our balance-of-payments problem? 

Secretary RUSK. We have had some exchanges on that, but our principal effort thus far has been to indicate to our Americans that if they are making on-balance judgments about what their own tourist plans are, that they might want to consider visiting parts of this country that they have not seen.

The net deficit in our tourist account is about $1.7 billion as I understand it. There has been an increase of about $400 million in the past 

4 years. We don't want to discourage tourism as such. 

We would like, however, during this period when we are working on the gold balance, to encourage Americans to have a good look at their own country, and if they are making on-balance judgments, to perhaps do some traveling here first. You see, the number of passports, for example Senator LAUSCHE. The amount has increased in the last 4 years. It is now up to $1.7 billion, did you say?

Secretary RUSK. I believe the net has gone up about $400 million a year compared to say 4 or 5 years ago, and similarly with passports. 

We are issuing now about 75 percent more passports than we did in 1961. 

In other words, there has been a very substantial increase. Now fortunately there has also been a very substantial increase in tourism coming the other way, but not quite enough to take up the energetic desire of the American people to travel abroad.

Senator LAUSCHE. If the imbalance resulting solely from tourism is growing worse, why are you hesitant about exercising greater efforts to discourage tourism abroad?

Secretary RUSK. Well, we hope that we can use it just as in the case of capital investment, we can try the process of persuasion, rather than going to compulsory measures that interfere very greatly with private decisions and judgments on the matter. 

Tourism itself is a very important element of our relations with other countries in both directions. We would not wish to move drastically on it if it were possible to have it make some contribution. 

Senator WILLIAMS. Would the Senator yield right at that point? 

Senator LAUSCHE. Yes.

Secretary RUSK. Yes; I will be glad to. I think you will find that this is not very much, but you might also be interested to know that we saved a half million dollars-2 years ago by moving our traditional, our regular class of air passengers across the Atlantic from first class to economy class for the State Department itself. 

We saved a half million dollars in 1 year on that. But I will be glad to furnish the information. 

Senator LAUSCHE. FOREIGN BORROWING IN THE UNITED STATES 

Senator LAUSCHE. Mr. Rusk, have you discussed, especially with the Western European countries, the good that would be served our Nation if they quit selling here or borrowing money from our American banks and getting dollars to go into their countries, thus aggravating our balance-of-payments problem?

Secretary RUSK. Well, at the present time there is a coincidence of concern on this matter from both directions, for different reasons. As you know, certain countries have been asking themselves whether the rate of American investment in their particular countries is not higher than it is, from their point of view, sound over a long period. 

We, on the other hand, because of our balance-of-payments situation, would like to see that rate of private investment reduced somewhat. 

We have asked our business people to undertake to see what can be done about this on a voluntary basis without getting into compulsory controls on the matter.

I think there is a chance that we can narrow this gap. I believe the imbalance on private investment is running just under $3 billion, for

example, as compared with $1.7 billion on tourism, and anything that can be done on those two points would be helpful. 

Senator LAUSCHE. My question is: Has that subject been under discussion, especially in view of the adoption of the interest equalization bill which was intended to provide relief against this outflow of dollars?

Secretary RUSK. Yes; this is a matter on which the Secretary of the 

Treasury has frequent discussions with his colleagues in other governments, and this is a matter which is being discussed in the Committee of Ten; it is still being discussed there, and when he goes to the NATO meetings, these come up with his other finance ministers. This is a matter of continual consultation. 

Senator LAUSCHE. I listened to a snatch of your presentation to a meeting in New York the other night. I was proud of you, not only in the method in which you said it, but the sincerity which dominated your expression to that gathering. 

Secretary RUSK. Thank you, sir.

Senator LAUSCHE. In my judgment you never were better, Mr. Rusk. 

Secretary RUSK. Thank you, sir.

Secretary RUSK. Thank you, sir.

PROBLEM OF POPULATION CONTROL 

Senator CLARK. Recently I was quite heartened by receiving a document which I believe is public. It is entitled "AID Policies on Population." It is dated March 2, and I am delighted to see that the AID administration is taking a more favorable position with respect to the problem of population control. This to my way of thinking is essential to bringing a just and lasting peace to the world through disarmament, which is the most important single thing that we can do to assure long life and some prosperity for our descendants. There are, however, one or two things in this memorandum I would like to you about. ask 

Secretary RUSK. Yes, sir. Excuse me, Senator, may I just ask is that the March 2 bulletin?

Senator CLARK. It is March 2. 

Secretary Rusk. Right.

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, Senator CLARK. But it is not the confidential one. 

It is the one that is marked as a public document. I note on page 3 that- 

The AID administration has set up a population reference research branch organized in the Health Service of AID's Office of Technical Cooperation and 

Research to serve as a focal point for information and coordination in the population field. The Latin-American Bureau has created a population unit and has requested each Latin-American aid mission to appoint an officer to be responsible for population matters. Further that every aid mission is being instructed to assign one of its officers as Latin-American missions have done to become familiar with the problems of population dynamics, program developments, and to keep the mission director country team personnel in Washington headquarters appropriately advised.

INSTRUCTIONS TO AMBASSADORS ON POPULATION CONTROL 

My first question is whether you have implemented this AID directive with instructions to our Ambassadors abroad to give strong cooperation to the heads of the AID missions. 

I ask the question because, in the course of a recent trip down the west coast of Latin America, I found that most of the AID people were seriously concerned with the population problem, and anxious to do very much about it, as much as they possibly could. But the Ambassadors whom I saw, fine gentlemen they were, seemed to think that this was something which was a little bit too far out front for their cooperation and support. 

Secretary RUSK. I think, since your visit here, I signed and sent a telegram on this subject, Senator. Let me say very briefly that we do believe this is a major problem. 

When you talk about economic and social development, you are talking about what happens to people. That is what it is all about. 

How many people and what kind, and what their talents are, and what their education facilities are going to be, all those things are part of any attempt to look ahead 5 or 10 years to see what can be done about a country.

We do not believe that the policy decisions on these matters should be made by the countries themselves, but that we ought to be as helpful as we can within the limits of their policy. We don't believe that we should go to them and say "There are too many of you." We have a pretty vigorous birth rate ourselves, and for all sorts of other reasons. This goes deeply into psychological and political problems that are extremely important. But nevertheless we know that while all the governments are working on the problem of increasing their resources, that many governments are concerned on the other side of the ledger because they do not see any answer in the longer run to their demographic problems as they look ahead.

And so when they bring themselves to a point where they want to get into that, they find us fully cooperative. This is the principal point I wanted to make. 

Senator CLARK. And this applies to the Ambassadors as well as to the heads of the agencies. 

Secretary RUSK. That is correct, sir. 

Senator CLARK. Thank you, sir. Now on this little memorandum

I note the first question has to do with the U.S. policy on population,

and President Johnson's most courageous statement in his state of the Union message which I will quote: 

I will seek new ways to use our knowledge to help deal with the explosion of world population and the growing scarcity of world resources. 

NATURE OF AID ACTIVITIES IN POPULATION CONTROL 

This I think is an excellent general and overall policy. But the next question gives me some concern. The question is: "Does AID advocate family planning policies for developing nations?"

The answer is "No. The United States opposes any effort to dictate population policies to another country." 

Of course, we oppose efforts to dictate population policies to another country, but why does it follow that we should not, if not advocate, at least advise and promote family planning policies for those developing nations where it is entirely clear that the increase in the gross national product is being absorbed and more than absorbed by an increase in population?

Secretary RUSK. Senator, I do believe that the basic policy responsibility on this, as between governments, is for the government of the countries concerned to decide what its involvement with this problem is going to be, and how it sees it from its own point of view. 

Beyond that our general view is that we ourselves would not want to be associated with an action in this field that is compulsory in character, that as far as the individual is concerned, it would be a voluntary matter.

Senator CLARK. We are in accord on that, no compulsion. 

Secretary RUSK. Yes. 

Senator CLARK. Why can't you advise and consent? Might it not be worthwhile to give a little thought in your own quiet way to whether that answer to question two is quite the way it ought to be. 

Secretary RUSK. I would say, Senator, that when you look at particular situations, the population question is far more complicated than it looks when you just look at it as a total worldwide scene. 

People are producers as well as consumers, and there has been a considerable connection between the development of the resources of the United States and a fairly rapidly expanding population here. 

In terms of what might be called the population problem, I suppose we had our greatest one in this continent before the white man arrived. 

Now this needs a very careful and deliberate and exhaustive examination in the country itself to see what the character of this problem is and what solution would lead to its 

POPULATION CONTROL AS A FORM OF SELF-HELP 

Senator CLARK. I just leave you with the suggestion that in my judgment you are a little more timid than you need to be, and ask this other question. No. 4 on that memorandum says:

Does AID regard the adoption of official family planning policy as a self-help condition for receiving U.S. aid?

If we were to strike out those words "for receiving U.S. aid," would not the answer be "Yes" instead of "No"? Isn't this probably the most effective method of self-help they can enter into? 

Secretary RUSK. Again, sir, I think that unless this requirement arises out of their own careful examination of their own demographic situation and leads them to the conclusion that further action by them in that field is necessary, I think it is not easy for the United States to say to them "You must as a condition for anything take these and those and other measures." 

Senator CLARK. Mr. Secretary, don't fence with me. You know I agree with you on that. There is no "you must" about it. 

The question is whether the head of the AID mission and the ambassador are going to say "Why don't you fellows do something in this regard? It will be very useful to you. Here are the reasons why. 

We will give you a jeep. We will send our people to give you technical assistance. You can make a lot of money out of manufacturing your own devices. This is a great idea. It is just as great an idea as it is in connection with improving your agricultural system." 

Nobody is talking about compulsion. You are not making them build any schools. I am going to leave the subject with that little, if 

I may say, "Morse lecture." 

Secretary RUSK. I would have to say, Senator, that within the framework of our present policy, what you describe I am sure frequently happens.

Senator CLARK. I am sure it will, but I will just encourage you to be a little bit braver. Mr. Chairman, I pass.

The CHAIRMAN. The Senator from Rhode Island. 

PURPOSE OF FOREIGN PROGRAM 

Senator PELL. Two questions, Mr. Secretary, one a rather general one. I was interested in your definition. We often get asked whether foreign aid is more a question of trying to create in foreign countries a climate in an area that will prove barren from the viewpoint of the development of a Communist society, or whether it is more directly related to the development of self-interest and national interest in our part and directly related to how they fit into our pattern of how we think nations should behave. 

I realize there are problems that you and Mr. Bell face in deciding who gets what and how much and how the pot should be divided. 

I will be interested if you could digest in a paragraph or two which of those factors plays the larger role. 

Secretary RUSK. Senator, in my opening statement I referred to economic and military assistance in support of our interest in the broadest sense around the world, and that phrase "in the broadest sense" I think is quite important.

I think the point to make is, that there now is in the present international scene a sharp conflict between two concepts of a world order. One of them is that sketched out in the United Nations Charter, a world society of independent states cooperating across international frontiers, and so forth. The other is the idea of a world revolution,

which in recent years has been put forward by Peiping with a militancy that has caused great problems even within the Communist world.

Now everywhere that there is an independent state secure and viable and able to live in peace with its neighbors, there is a situation which is of the deepest interest of the United States in terms of our concept of the world situation as a whole. 

We have 42 allies, but that is not really the important thing. What is important is that we have committed ourselves and so have most of the rest of the world, to an international world order sketched out in the United Nations Charter. Now, basically, that is what we are working toward. The principal threat to that does come from the militancy of a world revolution. But the main purpose is that peace and world order.

Senator PELL. The emphasis would be more in the development of areas that are barren to the fruition to the seeds of communism than it would be identity with American self-interest per se. 

Secretary RUSK. If we look at self-interest broadly enough, then 

I think we are saying the same thing. I have no doubt, for example, that if there were no Communists, we still would need a vigorous aid program to help build that kind of world order we are talking about. 

Senator PELL. My next question is perhaps going back to the old adage that the way that you secure a person's sympathy and affection is you let him do you a favor rather than vice versa. 

EMPHASIZING THE MULTILATERAL APPROACH 

Why don't we emphasize more the multilateral approach? I have always been struck in going around to different countries by this: 

I always ask the standard question, "Who is the head of the U.N. technical assistance program mission here and what are your relations with him?" You would be amazed at the number of posts where our man doesn't even know the name and I can cite them to you-of the technical assistance program director. There is no collaboration whatsoever. 

He is treated like a dog, as it were. 

I was wondering why we don't push more into that? I find myself in agreement with Mr. Fulbright on this point. 

Secretary RUSK. That is obviously wrong to the extent that it exists. 

We try to work with the host government, to work with them in the coordination machinery by which they coordinate international as well as bilateral aid and other things. 

Let me say again that we have had in our legislation for the past 3 years the privilege of moving up to 10 percent of the appropriated funds through international bodies beyond those specifically appropriated for international bodies, but at the appropriation stage that particular authority has been eliminated. 

We do think that the international machinery can play a strong and, from a political point of view, a very wholesome role in terms of the largest American interests. I think we feel, however, that it is important to have a balanced program which would include both international and bilateral.

Senator PELL. As you know, the whole United Nations technical assistance program is, I think, in the neighborhood of a quarter of a billion dollars, and ours is considerably more than that. 

Secretary RUSK. Not strictly in technical assistance terms. Our technical assistance is about $300 million. 

Senator PELL. Of the United Nations? 

Secretary RUSK. No; our own technical assistance is about $300 million.

Senator PELL. So we are more or less matching. 

Secretary RUSK. That is correct. 

Senator PELL. I see. 

Secretary RUSK. One of the problems I might say, Senator Pell, as you know from your own personal experience, is that the ability to give effective technical assistance is frequently limited by the availability of people, and the international agencies can draw upon a wider range of talented personnel from many countries than can a straight bilateral program. 

Senator PELL. You will forgive me for mentioning here, too, I think, that very often the caliber of man that can be secured for a 2or 4-year term of assignment abroad is higher, man for man, from European nations or other nations, where people are trained around the world, than it is from our Nation where most people really dislike going abroad.

Again I don't mean to sound un-American, but I have noticed our lower fellows in these programs don't have the caliber. I am sure 

Mr. Bell faces the problem as best he can, because there is no permanence to the whole program. If they go abroad, the European is the finest and highest type. A doctor or engineer or government official would give his eye teeth to go abroad for a 2or 4-year term. With us we really sometimes have to drag the bottom of the barrel to go and get somebody to do the same thing. I have one other question. 

Secretary RUSK. Sir, I think that perhaps at the present time there is not as sharp a contrast on that as there might have been earlier. 

In the first place, Europeans have their manpower shortage and recruiting highly trained people in Europe is not quite as easy. Under 

Assistant Secretary Harlan Cleveland, we have organized ourselves a very specific recruitment program to get talented Americans involved more in these international bodies, and we hope that is going to show some result.

Senator PELL. I share your hope. Another thought in this regard and I will wind up. Earlier I believe in the testimony-I read your statement and then got a rundown-you said that a good many of the chiefs of AID missions were also the heads of the Embassy's economic section. What would be the number of these?

Secretary RUSK. No, in many cases the Ambassador is also the principal AID administrator in his country. 

Senator PELL. Right.

Secretary RUSK. That is correct, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. Approximately $13 billion, and we were told it might cost $16 or $17 billion. 

Secretary RUSK. That is correct.

THE OEEC AND ADMINISTRATION OF MARSHALL PLAN The CHAIRMAN. How was the Marshall plan administered? What was the role of the OEEC? 

Secretary RUSK. The key role was played by the cooperative administration of the receiving countries; that is, they developed, devised their plan. They made recommendations with respect to where the key bottlenecks were, and what the major emphasis ought to be. 

We in turn were working with them advising with them as to what we might be able to do and how we felt they might best move forward. 

I think that was a rather remarkable combination of American and European cooperation in the administration of a very large program. 

The CHAIRMAN. In effect, the OEEC was set up, wasn't it, composed of Europeans with whom we worked. They determined to a great extent, they suggested and recommended the program, did they not? 

Secretary RUSK. Yes. 

The CHAIRMAN. Weren't you in the State Department in that period? 

Secretary RUSK. Yes, I was.

The CHAIRMAN. Didn't you play a part in that? 

Secretary RUSK. I was not directly and deeply in the Marshall plan program itself. I was then in the United Nations and Far Eastern affairs. But in effect Secretary Marshall's Harvard speech said "You

people get together and advise us as to what is required to put you back on your feet," and Mr. Bevan and others immediately picked that up, and they got themselves together, they got their organization; and the combination of Mr. Hoffman's organization, that is the part of it in Europe, and the Europeans themselves worked out the details of the plans. 

The CHAIRMAN. And it worked very well. 

Secretary RUSK. Yes. 

The CHAIRMAN. And it achieved its purpose. I have heard very little criticism of it-only one criticism, that it all should have been loans rather than part grants, which I think everybody agrees with hindsight. We thought they were more desperate and more likely to collapse than they actually were. 

ROLE AND FUNCTION OF CIAP 

Now isn't the role of the CIAP very similar to OEEC? 

Secretary RUSK. The basic concept is very close to it. 

The CHAIRMAN. The function you expect is the same. 

Secretary RUSK. The Latin American leaders-we have a representative on CIAP-will themselves review Latin American programs. 

They will themselves make suggestions to Latin American countries about how they ought to get on with their development plans. 

They also are extremely effective in reminding Latin American countries sometimes when the news is disagreeable, that there are self-help and discipline measures that have to be taken, if economic and social progress is to be achieved. 

The CHAIRMAN. They can do that with less resentment than when you do it directly, can they not?

Secretary RUSK. I think so, sir. I think it has worked out that way on the whole.

The CHAIRMAN. This is semimultilateral. It is multilateral because they are really making recommendations for the Inter-American Bank and the Alliance for Progress, aren't they? 

Secretary RUSK. That is correct, sir. They make recommendations.

The final decisions are made by those who have the ultimate responsibility, but nevertheless- The CHAIRMAN. It seems to me the OEEC experience alone, which was the most successful part of our AID program, is very persuasive argument for a greater degree of multilateralization. 

Secretary RUSK. But there is a combination again of a multilateral technique and a bilateral program in terms of financing. 

Now we hope also, Mr. Chairman, that this will multiply shall I say, multilaterally by providing a means by which other countries, for example, in Europe, can find a role to play in the Alliance for Progress with the greatest convenience to themselves. 

REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT BANK 

The CHAIRMAN. You mentioned very briefly I think at one point in your statement-I won't take the trouble to look it up-that you are giving thought, at least, to a regional development bank in other areas, such as Africa and possibly Asia, for that matter. Is that correct?

Secretary RUSK. That is correct, sir. The African Bank is in being. 

The African countries themselves have subscribed to it. I think it is a little more likely in terms of time than perhaps the Asian Bank, which is a little more remote in time. 

The CHAIRMAN. Not many years ago, I know, Mr. Eugene Black, as head of the International Bank, talked to me at considerable length about the development of a Middle East development bank. There were efforts made to get contributions from some of the big oil companies together with the governments for such a program. They did draft such a charter. I think it was drawn up by the technicians in the Bank. But there was resistance on the part of many people to contribute. I think that, in view of the success of these programs, it is perfect justification for our at least advocating, examining, and proceeding in this direction, ATTEMPTS OF CONGRESS TO ADMINISTER PROGRAM 

This other question perhaps you shouldn't commit yourself on, but I want to raise it. The Congress attempting to move into the area of precise terms of administration causes great difficulty for the administration. It is perfectly obvious, of course, and natural, that the 

Congress has the complete power to have a program at all. 

It can stop the power this year if it wants to, but as long as it agrees to have an AID program, then it moves into the administration of it, by setting down precise requirements for loans and even going to the extent of forbidding you to negotiate or to have relations with specific countries. It seems to me you create an intolerable administrative problem for any program of this kind. Do you wish to comment? 

Secretary RUSK. Yes, Senator, I would like to comment on that, because, we have had a number of occasions to get into this issue in the course of the consideration of aid by the Congress. We do believe that the law can properly establish policy and criteria. 

The CHAIRMAN. Broad guidelines. 

Secretary RUSK. Broad guidance, but we do feel that it puts manacles on us if administrative details are spelled out in the law, or if specific policy with respect to specific countries is made a matter of law.

The world situation moves far faster than the annual legislative cycle of the Congress, and we feel that there ought to be flexibility to deal with these matters as the interest of the United States require, on a week-by-week or month-to-month basis. 

I know there are certain cases, and we have gone into this in executive session, where the general feeling of the Congress with respect to a particular country turns out to be the view of the administration, and is the way in which relationships are developed. But even there we would not want to see that in legislation because these matters can change. We would like to have the freedom of movement. 

The CHAIRMAN. The object of your program is to change them in many cases, isn't it? 

Secretary RUSK. That is correct, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. And you can't change them if this is put into the law. 

Secretary RUSK. That is correct, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. The Senator from Oregon has gone, but anyway this is no secret-one of the main differences between us and one of the principal reasons why I feel the movement toward multilateralization of the program is so important, is the very fact that he and certain others, who share his view, are attempting more and more to restrict the administration. 

To be perfectly frank, one of the main reasons why I think it is good and proper to move in this direction is to avoid further and further restriction upon your administration. We have had several examples. 

One was the interest rate controversy. 

There were certain people who wished to make very high interest rates on a program that the main excuse for it is its soft loans. When you approximate it, if you ran the AID program on the same basis as the International Bank, there would be no need to have the AID program, would there? sir. 

Secretary RUSK. Basically that is right as regards interest rates,

The CHAIRMAN. The same way with this Inter-American Bank. 

If you put requirements that it all must be paid back in dollars under certain conditions, then there is no need in having it. So if the Congress makes the decision to have a program-and with very broad guidelines—it seems to me it is an impossible situation to expect you to achieve anything. 

Last year we had a controversy about whether or not you would be allowed to upgrade the quality of your personnel. This committee and the Senate agreed to allow Mr. Bell certain limited selections, but in the process of the congressional control it was denied. Now this seems to me absolutely intolerable, if we are going to have a good administration.

Secretary RUSK. Well, we wanted the same privilege we had for the foreign service.

The CHAIRMAN. I thought it was very reasonable. We had over 

80 amendments to this bill offered last year. They were not all, fortunately, voted on, but a great many were. A few of them were relevant to the foreign aid program. Most of them were not. 

But in any case, if we are going to have a program, it seems to me, and if it is going to make any sense in the future, it has to move more in the fashion of the OEEC, the Marshall plan, the CIAP, and in other cases where appropriate you follow the same pattern. 

It is in a sense distasteful to Members of Congress since we all have applicants in our own districts for a similar kind of aid. You understand that, I am sure. 

Secretary RUSK. Yes, I do, Senator.

The CHAIRMAN. If you are going to have a program, it seems to me it should be disassociated insofar as it can be from specific restrictions in the administration. 

Secretary RUSK. We fully agree, sir.

COUNTRIES IN WHICH AMBASSADOR HEADS AID MISSION The CHAIRMAN. One last question. You mentioned the 12 coun tries in which the Ambassador is the head of the mission.

Mr. BELL. We have moved in this direction, Mr. Chairman, as rapidly as we felt the load could be properly imposed on the Ambassador. To take responsibility for the day-to-day management of the AID program in a country where the AID effort is sizable would not be desired by most ambassadors, and I would agree with that. But in the cases of the small AID programs which you are referring to, we do think this is a system that has worked well, and we expect to extend it.

Mr. BELL. Yes.

Mr. BELL. Mr. Chairman, the issue arises really in the case of countries like Ecuador and Central American countries, and Panama. In total dollars these programs are relatively small, but they have a number of projects connected with them. They have quite a complicated administrative burden.

In those cases we have thus far felt that it was preferable administration, and the State Department has fully agreed with us, to have a chief of AID mission, so to speak, who is under the Ambassador's general supervision, there is no question about that, but he is not technically a part of the Embassy staff, and we have not technically asked the Ambassador to take on the supervisory responsibilities for each of the projects which exists in that country. 

This is where the decision, the judgment factor comes in, and I quite agree that we can and should do this in the larger number of cases. But my guess would be that it would be a matter of 30 to 40 countries in which it makes sense to maintain an AID mission chief, so to speak, rather than 15.

The CHAIRMAN. That might be very beneficial to your overhead, too, wouldn't it?

Secretary RUSK. We are also experimenting with administration of the smaller AID programs from outside the country by a regional office in Washington or by some arrangement in the field, so that one should not suppose that in whatever country there might be AID activity it has to be administered within that country.

WEDNESDAY, MARCH 10, 1965 UNITED STATES SENATE, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN RELATIONS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, pursuant to recess, at 10:10 a.m. in room 4221, New Senate Office Building, Senator J. W. Fulbright (chairman) 

presiding. 

Present: Senators Fulbright, Sparkman, Clark, Aiken, and Carlson.

The Committee on Foreign Relations this morning continues its hearings on the foreign aid program for fiscal 1966. 

We are glad to have this morning Mr. David Bell, Administrator of the International Development Administration. 

Mr. Bell, I believe you have a prepared statement. 

Mr. BELL. I do, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. CHAIRMAN. Will you proceed, sir. 

STATEMENT OF DAVID E. BELL, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. BELL. Thank you very much.

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I welcome the opportunity to appear before this committee in support of the President's recommendations for the foreign assistance program for fiscal year 1966. 

AID AS A FUNDAMENTAL INSTRUMENT OF U.S. POLICY 

The President's request will carry forward our programs of assistance to the countries of Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Foreign assistance, as this committee well knows, is a primary instrument of U.S. foreign policy. It is carefully tailored to advance U.S. interests in each unique country situation. 

The world with which the United States must deal is restless, turbulent, and uncertain. The likelihood of a direct military confrontation of the two big powers may recede somewhat; but there is an increasing and equally dangerous threat to the security, progress, and freedom of the less developed countries from the Communist world. 73 44-834-65--6

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, This threat to the less developed countries is also a challenge to the United States-to our nerve and to our steadiness of purpose. The 

United States could not live safely in a world where totalitarianism and hunger grew and freedom and progress were confined to those nations who now have the wealth to afford them. 

The fundamental interests of the United States are involved in what happens in Asia, Africa, and Latin America. Our own national security requires us to contribute to the strength and independence of the peoples of the less developed areas. It is important to our own economic progress to help expand the economies of the developing countries, thus opening opportunities for larger trade and productive investment. Our own self-respect requires us, as the richest nation on earth, to devote some portion of our wealth to the less fortunate elsewhere in the world. 

SUCCESS TO DATE OF AID PROGRAM 

We have achieved some success. The results of the Marshall plan in Europe and of our foreign aid programs in Japan, Greece, Taiwan, and elsewhere are well known. The strong forward strides now being made with the help of American assistance in such countries as Korea, India, Pakistan, Brazil, and Chile are solid evidence of the benefits our aid can bring benefits not only to the countries we are helping, but benefits to our own vital interests. We can expect further progress if we, and the nations we are assisting, persevere. 

AMOUNTS AND CATEGORIES OF AID REQUESTED 

New appropriations requested by the President for economic aid military assistance total $3,380 million. This is, in the President's judgment, the minimum amount needed to carry on these programs. 

If it proves inadequate, additional funds will be requested. 

We are requesting $2,210 million in new appropriations for economic assistance. Of this amount, $846 million require new authorizations. 

The authorizations previously enacted for development loans and the Alliance for Progress are sufficient to cover the appropriations requested for those two programs. 

The request for economic assistance breaks roughly into three categories. The chart that follows shows that more than 70 percent is proposed for aid for development; 18 percent is proposed for supporting assistance and the contingency fund. The remainder is for contributions to international organizations and for administrative and other expenses.

The first major element of economic aid consists of development assistance in the form of development loans and of technical cooperation grants, for which total appropriations of $1.67 billion are being requested for fiscal year 1966.

I am pleased to be able to report continuing progress toward putting aided countries on a self-sustaining basis and terminating AID assistance.

There are now 26 countries where our economic assistance has been brought to an end. The list will grow further. It now includes not only the countries of Western Europe, but less-developed countries as well.

CESSATION OF AID TO TAIWAN 

The latest, and one of the most notable, example of success is Taiwan. Economic assistance from the United States is ending in the present fiscal year. No funds are being requested for fiscal year 1966.

In our natural preoccupation with the immediate crises that confront us, we should not overlook the remarkable achievement of Taiwan and other countries like it, where the combination of strong self-help measures and major external assistance has brought about rapid and lasting economic progress. Ten years ago, the prospects for stability and growth in Taiwan looked dim. Since then, a strong commitment by the Taiwanese and a crucial margin of U.S. help have brought success. Per capita gross national product in Taiwan has risen 45 percent; industrial output and exports have tripled; and 

Taiwan has joined other former aid recipients as a sizable cash customer for U.S. goods and services.

PROGRESS OF AID RECIPIENT COUNTRIES 

There is substantial evidence of progress also in countries that have not yet progressed far enough for aid to be ended. In the last 7 years, less-developed nations have increased their investment in education by an average of 15 percent per year. They increased the value of their exports from $19 to $29 billion between 1950 and 1962, despite falling world prices for many of their exports. 

Since 1950, they have increased industrial output at an average of nearly 8 percent per year. By 1963, roughly half of all the people living in malarious regions in the underdeveloped countries were being reached by malaria eradication programs. 

Perhaps most important of all is the growing evidence in many less-developed nations of a sustained and substantial commitment to the steady social and economic betterment of their peoples. For every dollar of our bilateral assistance to 20 major recipients of U.S. aid in fiscal year 1965, these nations are committing for development an average of $6 from their own meager resources. 

EMPHASIS ON SELF-HELP PROGRAMS 

U.S. assistance can be effective only to the extent that recipients are determined to help themselves. AID development assistance is increasingly designed to insist on and to induce needed improvements and self-help measures. 

Emphasis on self-help leads directly to the concentration of assistance. About two-thirds of the development assistance request is expected to go to seven countries-India, Pakistan, Turkey, Nigeria, Tunisia, Brazil, and Chile. These nations all have underway major development programs based on strong self-help efforts. If they continue their efforts and we continue to provide assistance, their prospects for further progress are good. 

IMPORTANCE OF DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 

The sum of $580 million of the development assistance request will go to continue the work of the Alliance for Progress. This great effort on the part of the peoples of the hemisphere is now taking hold and is demonstrating the opportunities for progress in freedom. 

The request for development assistance has been carefully calculated as the minimum necessary for the coming fiscal year. It is based on a realistic estimate of the self-help measures likely to be undertaken by the developing countries. 

I urge the committee, in considering this aspect of our program, to bear in mind that development assistance leads to lasting progress. It is plainly in our own interest to make development funds available when we can be sure they will be well applied. To do so will lead to the most rapid progress and the earliest possible termination of economic assistance.

SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE REQUEST 

A second major element of the proposed fiscal year 1966 request includes $369 million for "Supporting assistance" and $50 million for

the "Contingency fund." These funds are used primarily in countries where security considerations predominate. 

Supporting assistance is provided to countries threatened by or fighting Communist aggression and to promote stability in other politically sensitive areas. Supporting assistance funds are highly concentrated, with 88 percent planned for four countries-Vietnam, Laos, Korea, and Jordan.

Over the past several years, we have reduced sharply the amount of funds needed for supporting assistance. In fiscal year 1960 more than a billion dollars was used for this purpose. The fiscal year 1966 request is close to one-third of that amount. 

In countries such as Greece, Taiwan, the Philippines, and Turkey successful progress toward greater stability has enabled us to end supporting assistance grants and shift to development loans. Since 1960 supporting assistance has been ended in 14 countries. Korea is a current example of how careful programing of different assistance tools can help build stability and lay the basis for development. In 1960 almost $200 million in supporting assistance grants were required for Korea. By fiscal year 1964 progress toward stability and growth had enabled this figure to be reduced to about $75 million. Over the same period, development loans increased from $1 million to almost $30 million.

The decline in total appropriations for supporting assistance has been halted over the last year or two as a result of the heavy requirements in southeast Asia. These requirements are still rising, and additional military and supporting assistance funds may be needed in that part of the world. The President has accordingly requested a special standby authorization for Vietnam. If additional funds do prove necessary, the case for them will be presented to this committee at the same time the appropriation request is made. 

INTERNATIONAL CONTRIBUTIONS AND ADMINISTRATIVE EXPENSE 

A third element of our economic assistance request is $155 million for contributions to international organizations such as the United 

Nations Special Fund, UNICEF, and the Indus Basin Development Fund. 

Finally, we are asking for some $65 million for administrative and other miscellaneous expenses.

AID EFFORTS TO IMPROVE EFFECTIVENESS OF PROGRAM 

I have summarized the elements of our recommendations for fiscal year 1966. I should like now to call to the committee's attention some of the efforts we are making to improve the effectiveness of our aid programs.

First, we have steadily improved the ways in which we plan each country assistance program. 

The AID programing process is rigorous and comprehensive. It involves- 1. Planning and review on the ground by the AID mission and the country team under the direction of the ambassador. 

2. Further review in Washington by the regional assistant administrators and myself.

3. Continuous interchange of questions, ideas, and information between the field and Washington. 

The process involves evaluation of self-help efforts and shortcomings, discussions with host governments, coordination with other donors, and longer range analyses of opportunities, needs, and problems. 

The results are programs carefully worked out to further U.S. objectives in each specific country. Where stability and self-help efforts warrant, our program may provide major development assistanceprimarily in the form of loans. Where security considerations require, our program may focus on major support of defense and counterinsurgency efforts, or maintaining stability-usually through supporting assistance. In many situations, AID assistance is limitedoften to small programs of technical cooperation. This is true, for example, when another advanced country is providing the bulk of the assistance needed by a recipient country. 

In summary: 

1. Ninety-five percent of AID funds proposed for fiscal year 1966 country programs will go to 31 countries. 

2. Five percent will go to 41 countries.

Mr. BELL. May I, before passing that chart, Mr. Chairman, interrupt my prepared statement to call your attention to one set of figures on this chart. In the left-hand column you will note the indication of the volume of American bilateral aid per capita. It shows that in 

Latin America we are providing under the Alliance for Progress $2.73 per Latin American.

This shows that the aid the United States is providing per person in the recipient areas is substantially higher in Latin America than we are providing elsewhere in the world, but it is also notable that the figures on per capita aid during the Marshall plan were upward of $20 per capita per year, that is $20 per European per year. This indicates very graphically the difference between the kind of aid program we are operating today and the kind we operated in the Marshall plan. 

In Europe, where the basic technical and managerial skills existed, we were able to put in very large amounts of capital in a very brief period of time and accomplish what we were after. 

In the less-developed countries, we are necessarily working at a slower pace with a much, much smaller volume of assistance, and the progress-while it is there shows more slowly and over a longer period of time.

HOUSING LOAN PROCEDURES IN LATIN AMERICA

Mr. BELL. No; AID has made a number of direct loans to savings and loan financial institutions in those countries. 

Senator AIKEN. Financial institutions. 

Senator AIKEN. Who in turn lend to the organization at a considerably higher rate of interest, do they not? Including service charges and so on?

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; that is right. They are, of course, on a selffinancing basis. They cover their costs, build up reserves, and the earnings that they may obtain from the differential interest rate is of course plowed back into further loans to the savings and loan associations.

Senator AIKEN. But they do not lend directly to building and loan associations.

Mr. BELL. No. I think we have done it in one or two very special cases, but ordinarily- Senator AIKEN. I have heard complaints that that slows work considerably by forcing them to go to a bank which in turn increases the interest rate. Are you looking into that? 

Mr. BELL. We have.

Senator AIKEN. I am asking if you are looking into it to see if the situation can be improved. 

Mr. BELL. We have looked into it. We are continuing to do so. 

The basic objective we need to serve is to establish a system of housing finance in these countries. It is necessary for them to have centralized institutions to which these individual savings and loan institutions can turn just as we have them in the United States. 

So it is very much in our interest to help establish both a central financial institution of some kind and individual savings and loan associations. We are trying to work to accomplish both objectives. 

If we simply bypassed the central institutions and worked directly with the savings and loan associations in these countries, we would be in a position where we would in effect be saying, "Well, we will operate the central bank for these savings and loans." 

Senator AIKEN. But even if the central bank approved the loan directly to the building and loan association, you still would not make it, would you?

DEALING WITH COMMUNIST INSURGENCY 

Returning to the statement, Mr. Chairman, a second problem we have been concerned with, and increasingly concerned with, is the problem of Communist inspired internal insurgency. The insurgency problem arises in many forms-from rural guerrilla warfare in Vietnam to urban terrorism in Venezuela. It is made all the more serious by the rivalry between the Russians and the Chinese. Most recently there has been an obvious effort by the Communists to organize and promote insurgency movements in Africa. 

A major effort has been made by our Government in the last several years to discover the best ways and means of dealing with insurgent movements. We have made considerable progress. For example, the improvement of police activities in a number of countries has been of great value. In Venezuela, to cite an illustration, American advisers helped the Venezuelan police improve their effectiveness in dealing with terrorists in Caracas.

Moreover, in Vietnam and other countries where insurgency is a threat, the relationship between military and civilian activities is now better understood. In addition to providing military aid, we are now placing emphasis on the kinds of economic assistance necessary to bring hope and progress to the peoples of such countries. 

The discipline and tactics of well-trained insurgent groups are extremely difficult to deal with. But if free institutions and societies are to grow and expand, we must continue to improve the techniques, methods, training facilities, and leadership that will enable us to overcome this problem. 

ASSISTING PROBLEMS OF POPULATION GROWTH AND FOOD PRODUCTION 

Third, we have been increasingly concerned with the problems of food and population growth. 

Following the leadership of this committee and its members, AID has been assisting in studies of population problems and the statistics of population growth. We do not advocate any specific policy for any given country. But we do recognize the seriousness of the problem. And when a country wishes to carry out a family planning program of its own, we are ready, upon request, to provide information and some assistance-if the program is based upon freedom of choice for the families and individuals concerned. It is our objective to move ahead in this area constructively, with careful and deliberate consideration of all the economic and social factors involved. 

Food demands are increasing rapidly as a result of both growing populations and rising incomes. This is already a serious problem, and is likely to become even more serious. 

We are, accordingly, considering how to expand our already sizable effort to help increase agricultural production in developing countries. 

This will require greater use of the extensive technical skills of the Department of Agriculture, the land-grant colleges and universities, and private organizations of many kinds. It will require the rapid expansion of production of fertilizer and other items needed for raising agricultural output. Finally, we must continue to make our own agricultural surpluses available through Public Law 480-being sure we do this in a way which encourages the expansion of food production in the developing countries themselves and their ability to purchase food internationally when it is uneconomic for them to produce it. 

ENCOURAGEMENT OF U.S. PRIVATE INVESTMENT 

Fourth, as this committee is well aware, we have been steadily seeking to expand the role played by private American resources in helping to achieve progress in developing countries. The Advisory Committee on Private Enterprise in Foreign Aid, chaired by Mr. Arthur K. Watson of IBM, has been engaged in studying ways of enlarging this process and will make its report later this year. We are also urging prompt enactment of the 30-percent tax credit for new U.S. investment in less developed countries proposed by the President in his foreign aid message.

During the past year, some significant advances were made: 

1. A special task force chaired by Mr. John Gardner, president of the 

Carnegie Corp., made several important recommendations to improve

the relationship between AID and the 129 colleges and universities now involved with us in more than 300 technical assistance contracts. We are now putting these recommendations into effect. 

2. The specific risk investment guarantee program expanded dramatically, from 186 contracts for $426 million in 1963 to 486 contracts for $708 million in 1964. The chart "Investment Guaranties Written" illustrates the growth of the investment guarantee program.

USES FOR PROGRAM LOANS 

Fifth, we have been seeking to improve the effectiveness of U.S. development assistance in our use of loans to finance equipment, supplies, and raw materials. These loans are called program loans, to distinguish them from loans for specific projects. 

Program loans are of particular advantage in maintaining and expanding the role of private enterprise and in inducing and supporting needed self-help measures. 

As the less developed countries expand, the private sector in both industry and agriculture requires steadily larger amounts of raw materials, equipment, and spare parts, both for enlarging output from existing plant and for new investment. The traditional loan to finance major projects-in particular the loan to finance major projects in the public sector-does not meet these private sector needs. 

Accordingly, in selected cases we make program loans to finance the importation of U.S.-produced equipment, spare parts, supplies, and raw materials. We have found these loans very helpful in supporting and stimulating private investment and expansion. We estimate that almost 80 percent of U.S. goods provided through program loans in fiscal year 1964 went to private industry and agriculture. 

For program loans made thus far in fiscal year 1965, that figure is more than 90 percent. .

Furthermore, it has often been possible to couple these loans with an agreement on the part of the borrowing country to take needed self-help steps and improve its economic policies. To take one example, when Pakistan was assured last year of a major program loan from us, they felt able to eliminate licenses on raw materials imports into that country. This was a very important step toward reducing Government redtape and permitting a freer and more efficient reliance upon market forces to guide the volume and flow of materials and equipment in the Pakistan economy. 

We expect to continue and increase the use of such "incentive programing." At the same time, for obvious reasons, we can do so only in those few cases where we are sure the country is fully committed to a major development effort and is following sound economic policies which will insure that the commodities financed by our program loans will contribute to solid economic progress. Program loans

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, were made to only eight countries in fiscal year 1964. They will be made in only seven or eight in fiscal years 1965 and 1966. 

As in every other aspect of our development lending, we must assure ourselves that the financing provided by the United States is part of a program which will overcome the economic problems confronting the country in question. We are not interested in providing an economic crutch which would permit a less developed country to avoid coming to grips with the problems that face it. 

IMPROVING THE ADMINISTRATION OF AID 

The sixth area in which efforts toward increased effectiveness are continuing is the management of AID. We have made progress, although we still have much to do. From June 30, 1963, to June 30, 1964, we reduced our total direct-hire employment worldwide from 16,800 to 15,600. This trend will continue-although at a slower rate-unless the demands of the Vietnam program exceed the reductions we can achieve elsewhere. We have at the same time expanded use of contracts to tap directly the skills and talents of American private institutions and enterprise. 

We have sought to simplify our organizational structure and working procedures. But we are still not satisfied with our efforts to increase efficiency.

With respect to personnel, it is important to the effective operation of AID that we increase the interchange of persons between Washington assignments and oversea assignments. In order to achieve this result, we have steadily enlarged the number of persons rotating back into Washington for assignment here. In addition, however, we need general authority which we do not now have, to appoint officers in the Foreign Service Reserve for duty in Washington prior to oversea experience. We are requesting the legislative amendments which will permit us to do this. 

COORDINATION OF UNITED STATES AND OTHER FREE WORLD AID 

Before closing, I should like to discuss briefly an area which Secretary Rusk emphasized yesterday-the relationship of bilateral and multilateral assistance. 

Two weeks ago I had a series of discussions with officials responsible for the assistance programs of three major donor countries- France, Germany, and the United Kingdom. I found these discussions rather encouraging. There is no doubt of the commitment of these countries to continue a major and coordinated assistance effort. 

European donors also agree with us on the need to emphasize better self-help performance. 

In the months ahead, I expect improved coordination of our aid effort with those of other donors. I expect further progress in strengthening multilateral coordination through the Development 

Assistance Committee. 

Senator CLARK. What is the Development Assistance Committee? 

Mr. BELL. That is the subcommittee of the OECD in Paris which constitutes the liaison and policymaking committee of the donor nations. There are some 12 or 13 members on it besides ourselves. 

Senator CLARK. They are all European nations?

Mr. BELL. No, sir. They also include Japan and Canada. I believe those are the only non-European nations apart from ourselves. 

Senator CLARK. Thank you.

Mr. BELL. I am hopeful that there will be new consultative groups under the leadership of the IBRD. The groundwork of cooperation laid among the major donors over the past few years is now resulting in increased opportunities for closer, more effective partnership in the aid field.

INCREASED AID THROUGH INTERNATIONAL AGENCIES

VARYING ABILITIES OF COUNTRIES TO REPAY LOANS 

It is necessary to improve coordination among all donors. This is particularly so in view of the rising burden of foreign debt in lessdeveloped countries. Debt repayment obligations in these countries have been climbing sharply in recent years and will continue to rise. 

In Latin America as a whole, for example, the debt-service burden is already the equivalent of one-half of the gross capital inflow. 

It has been necessary in some cases, such as Brazil and Chile, for creditors to agree to reschedule the debt obligations of less-developed countries and stretch out the period of payment. 

It is because of this rising debt-service burden-which is out of proportion to the repayment capacity of many of the less-developed countries that the United States has adopted a policy of extending loans on terms related to the repayment capacity of the country concerned. 

For most of the countries to which we extend development loans, minimum AID terms are necessary- -a grace period of 10 years with the interest charge of 1 percent, and a subsequent maturity span of 30 years with interest at 21½ percent. 

As countries progress toward self-sustaining growth, AID raises its interest rates and shortens maturities. For example, the most recent loans made to Iran and Israel have interest rates of 312 percent, grace periods of 3 to 5 years, and maturities of 15 to 20 years. 

In conclusion, I should like to make one or two comments on the relations of our aid programs to the U.S. economy.

The job requires a steady and continuing effort by the United States and other advanced countries-and by the recipient nations themselves. 

Our own interests demand that we stay the course. 

It is in this spirit that we present our proposals for the committee's consideration. 

Thank you, sir.

MOTIVES OF COMMUNIST FOREIGN AID 

The CHAIRMAN. You mentioned the large step-up in the commitments of the Communists. How do you regard this? Is this in the interests of development which is our major emphasis? Do you welcome it?

Mr. BELL. We look at it about like this, Mr. Chairman. We think that the intent and effort of the Communist countries in extending economic or military assistance, as the case may be, is plainly to put themselves in the position to seek to achieve political domination. This is conspicuously evidenced, for example, in some of the African countries where during the past year the Chinese Communists have been making a strong effort. They have been virtually trying to buy the allegiance and buy their way into domination over the countries in question. 

Accordingly we would feel that the countries which are considering accepting Communist economic aid should be extraordinarily cautious is avoiding a situation in which it will result or can lead to the result of a political takeover or political control or domination.

UNOBLIGATED AND UNEXPENDED BALANCE FIGURES 

The CHAIRMAN. There is always one very troublesome problem that arises during the course of these hearings. It is the matter of the figures on unobligated and unexpended balances. Do you have these figures available so that we can raise the question and discuss it further later? 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. This is a particularly favored point of those who oppose the program. 

Mr. BELL. Our unexpended balances for the AID economic assistance programs as of June 30, 1964, were $3,826,991,000. 

During the present fiscal year, fiscal year 1965, we anticipate expenditures of $2,018,252,000. We had new funds and some transfers and reimbursements during the year, so that we estimate the unexpended balance as of next June 30 will be slightly larger, $3,957 million.

The reason this is rising is that our loan program in Latin America is still new enough so that we are committing loans, we are committing new loans faster than expenditures are flowing under the old loans. 

We have just about caught up, and I would not anticipate that our unexpended balance would rise significantly beyond fiscal 1966, perhaps 

1967 at the latest.

The experience with any lending program, as I am sure you know, Senator, from your other committees, is that in the early years of a lending program, if loans are made, their unexpended balances begin to accumulate, and then as the rate of expenditure catches up to the rate of new commitments, then your unexpended balance levels off, and it may well decline. This has been the experience of the World Bank and the Export-Import Bank, not just ourselves. I have doublechecked this to make sure that we are not letting something happen here which is unusual or unnatural. 

Furthermore, the development loan program is now old enough so that that is in fact the case, and we are in fact expecting the unexpended balances under our development loans outside of Latin America to be declining. Already we expect it to be declining in the present year, and it will decline further in the subsequent year. For each of the other appropriation accounts we expect the unexpended balance to be declining from year to year, not rising. Is this responsive to your question, Mr. Chairman?

CHANGE IN HOUSING GUARANTEE PROGRAM PROPOSED 

You said there was a change offered in the proposal this year on the housing guarantee program. What change is proposed there? 

Mr. BELL. Up to now, Senator Sparkman, that program has primarily operated to support individual projects-a group of houses built in Colombia or Lima, Peru, or wherever it might be with the effort organized primarily by an American builder and with the U.S. financial agency providing 100 percent of the funds under our complete guarantee.

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, This is a program which has been effective, and it could go on being effective as long as we, the taxpayers, are prepared to carry the complete risk, because there is no reason why American banks, insurance companies, and others wouldn't be willing to provide the funds under those circumstances.

The program has a number of benefits, among others some important demonstration benefits of modern, rapid construction of quite a significant number of houses. 

We felt, however, for some time that the program should be moved in the direction of getting a larger multiplier effect, a larger participation of Latin American funds, and the money we use, that we put into Latin America under this program, should help to establish institutions and to draw in Latin American funds as well as U.S. funds. 

With the advice of a special subcommittee of our Housing Advisory Committee, we have worked out the proposal which is now before the Congress, under which we would propose in the future to concentrate the use of the housing guarantee authority to guarantee American private funds going into housing institutions in Latin America, and into middle- and low-income housing as distinguished from middle and slightly higher, which is where most of it has been going up to this point, and into special cases such as housing projects organized by unions or by co-ops, where there is an institutional development aspect as well as a housing construction aspect. 

These are the principal elements in our plans. There is one other element also. We are also prepared to look at cases of the kind we have been financing up to now, where at least 25 percent of the fund is going to be put up from Latin American sources, and it will no longer be 100-percent American or U.S. money. These are the changes.

We think they will enable us to move forward with a good housing guarantee program, but one which will have much larger effects than the recent ones had in encouraging the establishment of Latin American institutions, which one of these days can stand on their own feet and will not require aid from outside. 

PROGRESS OF THE HOUSING PROGRAM 

Senator SPARKMAN. Has the housing program grown satisfactorily? 

Mr. BELL. It has been a very difficult program to administer. None of us are particularly proud of the delays which have occurred. 

We have now, however, quite a number of projects actually under construction, and several have been completed, and the complete authority which the Congress has given us, which is $250 million, will all be committed by the end of the present calendar year. 

We have subcontracted a large part of our review process to the FHA. They have assigned special people to work with us in going down and looking at these sites and reviewing the plans, and so on. 

They have provided a lot of technical expertise that we don't have, and have speeded up the process since we got them to do that a year or so ago.

Nevertheless, with all of its delays and complexities, there are some thousands of houses in Latin America which have been built or are being built under that program, and more coming along every day.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 105 1965 

SUCCESS OF THE SAVINGS AND LOAN ASSOCIATIONS 

Senator SPARKMAN. The savings and loan industry is still making headway?

 It varies by country, but we think that is one of the most successful things that the United States has contributed to establishing. I think there are savings and loan associations, now in some nine different countries. The gross deposits total more than $75 million.

There are some thousands of houses, the figure is not here, but as I remember it there are about 25,000 houses which have been started under the saving and loan associations. We are very pleased with the progress in that field. 

We quite agree with Senator Aiken. There will continue to be delays, especially in some countries. The central group in Chile, for example, that is helping to establish savings and loans is a very fast moving outfit, and has been doing a very good job. 

Senator SPARKMAN. The savings and loan institutions have given you considerable assistance, have they not?

Mr. BELL. Oh, yes. These savings and loan institutions in Latin 

America have been established by leaders of the American savings and loan industry working as consultants to us, putting in a great deal of time and energy, and at what for them is really on an unrecompensed basis.

We pay their expenses, but these are men who earn a great deal of money, and they are contributing a large share of their time, and we are extremely grateful. They have done a very fine job. Some of them have been down to Latin America now time after time to a given situation in a given country. They helped originally to set up a law that permitted savings and loan associations to be established, and they go back periodically to advise on the problems that have come up, and to stimulate the people that are working in the field and help to meet the issues that have arisen. It is a splendid relationship that we have had with the American savings and loan industry. We couldn't be more pleased. 

Senator SPARKMAN. Thank you very much, Mr. Bell. Senator Aiken? 

DIFFICULT ADMINISTRATION OF ECONOMIC AID PROGRAM IN VIETNAM 

Senator AIKEN. You still have a substantial program in South Vietnam, do you not? 

Mr. BELL. Very substantial, Senator.

Senator AIKEN. Do you find any particular interference in operating that program from the Vietcong? 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; a great deal. 

Senator AIKEN. In what way?

Mr. BELL. Well, a large part of our prorgam in South Vietnam consists of trying to help establish some degree of economic and social progress out in the countryside. We have AID advisers stationed out in all of the provinces of South Vietnam, and many of these men, while they are civilians, run very severe risks. 44-834-65--8

They are driving over these mined roads. Two of them have been. kidnaped. We believe they are all right in the sense that they are alive, but we don't know when they will be released. 

When you go and visit these men as I have done, and as others in Washington do every now and then, you feel very proud of them. 

They are working effectively under the most difficult circumstances. 

Some of them take risks that I think are perhaps excessive. 

They are accustomed to working directly with the villagers in areas where the Vietcong are very active. They are doing an admirable job, but necessarily, to answer your question precisely, the existence of the Vietcong and the restrictions that the Vietcong establish against the movement of our people and the Vietnamese Government people certainly does hamper our work in large parts of the rural areas of the country.

Senator AIKEN. But you are operating in areas that are virtually politically controlled, almost governmentally controlled, by the Vietcong. 

Mr. BELL. Let me answer your question this way, Senator. There are substantial areas in Vietnam which are in effect controlled by the Government in the daytime and by the Vietcong at night. 

Senator AIKEN. Moonlighting. 

Mr. BELL. We have got people operating in areas like that. Now if there is an area which in effect is controlled by the Vietcong all the time, day and night, where, for example, you can't go into the area unless you have a substantial body of troops escorting you, our people will not ordinarily be able to operate in a place like that. But in the areas where the control is shifting and uncertain, and where there may even be fighting going on, our people are in those areas. There 

Senator AIKEN. Are the French operating in the same area?

Mr. BELL. There is no French assistance group like ours. are French plantation owners and managers who are still operating in rural areas in many parts of Vietnam; yes, sir. 

Senator AIKEN. Do they meet with the same hazards?

Mr. BELL. Yes, they do. Some of them have been kidnaped also. 

Senator AIKEN. Why would they want Frenchmen? 

Mr. BELL. They probably want ransom.

Senator AIKEN. Perhaps they take them as advisers.
