(The following additional information was subsequently submitted:)

RESERVES OF THE UNITED NATIONS SPECIAL FUND 

The governments contributing to the Special Fund make annual pledges to this program but the work projects have an average duration of about 5 years. The Governing Council of the Special Fund has therefore adopted a policy of fully funding projects at their outset in order to insure that the projects started can be financed to their conclusion and to avoid incurring obligations in excess of the Special Fund's financial resources. Thus, when a project is actually started funds are allocated for the entire cost of the project to its completion. 

The cumulative total of pledges to the Special Fund from its inception in 1959 through 1964 totaled about $331 million. This sum was fully committed for projects which had already been approved, but expenditures from inception through December 31, 1964, had amounted to about $128 million. Thus, while the Special Fund's resources were fully earmarked, it had as of December 31 an unexpended balance on hand of about $203 million of which about $140 million is in liquid form (in convertible currencies, not restricted by deposit agreements with banks, etc.). It is estimated that expenditures in 

1965 by the Special Fund will run from $65 to $100 million. 

The recent U.S. pledge of $60 million represented our calendar year 1965 commitment to both the Special Fund and the expanded program of technical assistance. Of the $60 million, about $37 million will be contributed to the 

Special Fund and about $23 million to the technical assistance program. 

Actual payments to these program by the United States are made on the 40percent matching basis as receipts from other governments are reported by the U.N.

Senator AIKEN. Why, after telling the U.N. that we were not going to make a contribution to the Special Fund until certain countries pick up their back dues, did we suddenly change our minds and make à contribution of $60 million?

States was whether we should go ahead and put up our normal appropriate share of U.N. development activities, which are, as you know,

financed by voluntary contributions and not by assessments. That was the decision that was taken the other day.

FUNDING OF U.S. CONTRIBUTIONS TO UNITED NATIONS ACTIVITIES 

Budget estimates for U.S. voluntary contributions to special U.N. programs such as the expanded program of technical assistance, the Special Fund, and the Children's Fund, are submitted to the Congress in advance of the U.N. financial period to which they relate. 

On the other hand, budget estimates for U.S. assessed contributions to the 

U.N. relate to the U.N.'s financial year which is already underway when the estimates are submitted to Congress. Thus the U.S. contribution to the U.N. regular budget for the calendar year 1965 is included in the President's fiscal year 1966 budget presently under consideration by the Congress.

ADMINISTRATION BY AID VERSUS INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS 

Senator CLARK. Now it occurs to me as a new member of the committee that one of the problems over which seems to be some controversy is the relative effectiveness of the multilateral as opposed to bilateral aid. I would like to get your opinion on several of these questions. 

The first one would be: in your opinion are international agencies any more successful than the AID program in accomplishing results? If you don't want to answer it, just say so. 

Mr. BELL. No; I am perfectly prepared to answer that, Senator. I would say that the aid that is going to leave aside if we may the supporting assistance type of case in which the international agencies are not normally involved the aid that is going to development under our bilateral program is today being administered as effectively as the aid going for development being administered by the international agencies.

Now they will vary. Some of the international agencies are clearly stronger, more strongly administered, have longer traditions than some others. But in general I think the development aid that we are providing today is very effective, and as effective in general as the aid going under the international agencies. 

This is of course in part true because, as I pointed out in my statement and as the Secretary did yesterday, so much of our aid is going, even if it is bilateral aid, to the developing countries under a system of multilateral coordination, such as CIAP for Latin America, such as the consortiums organized by the World Bank. We are therefore in constant and continuous contact and collaboration particularly with the World Bank, the IMF, the Inter-American Development Bank, and we are all trying to use similar standards for decisions as to the kinds of projects we undertake and the ways by which we carry them out, and so on. 

SELF-HELP PROJECTS BY INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS 

Senator CLARK. Now in terms of enlisting self-help from the countries to which we give assistance, what is your opinion as to whether the international agencies such as the World Bank are generally more successful than you have been able to be in getting the maximum amount of self-help from these countries? 

Mr. BELL. Well, now here again, Senator, of course you are asking me questions on which I am sure different people would have different judgments. 

Senator CLARK. I understand. That is why I want to get your opinion.

Mr. BELL. My own feeling is that again the international agencies have varied. The best of them, the World Bank, has done an extremely good job of requiring careful standards to be met for the projects which they have been willing to finance. Indeed I would say that 

Eugene Black and the World Bank led the world some years ago in

establishing high standards. I think we have been catching up to those standards since.

U.S. POLICIES ON SELF-HELP PROJECTS 

There is another area of self-help standards, however, which goes beyond the individual project, and relates to the overall economic policies of a country. When, for example, we worked out with the 

Brazilians plans for bringing this very severe inflation to a halt, and overcoming the other very difficult economic circumstances that the new government had inherited from the Goulart administration, there was a long period of discussion as to what the proper and appropriate Brazilian program was. We were eventually quite well satisfied that the Brazilians understood their problem well and were tackling it well. 

We had made it quite plain that until we were satisfied along those lines, we were not prepared to provide major assistance to them. Now that is the kind of discussion leading to very strong self-help commitments on the part of the country receiving assistance, and very strong support from us, which we and the IMF have been doing very well, and in which the banks by and large have not usually participated on quite the same basis. 

In this sense I think it has been fair to say that the American bilateral program and the IMF have in some respects been developing stronger ideas about how to look at the overall economic position of a country and how to relate an aid program to the overall economic policies of the country than other international agencies have. 9 

INCREASING AMOUNT OF MULTILATERAL AID PROJECTS 

These are distinctions which I do not in any sense want to exaggerate. I repeat the main point, the main response to your comment is that the World Bank, the Inter-American Development Bank, the IMF, the United States, the other donor nations are increasingly working together and increasingly under multilateral arrangements, increasingly trying to apply the same kinds of standards. This is a direction in which we are making progress and we all expect to continue to make progress. 

I certainly would be wrong, however, to denigrate or not to recognize the important role that the United States has played, especially in the last several years, in trying to work toward-along with these international agencies to work toward a situation in which the efforts that a country makes for itself are examined and carefully analyzed, and the aid that other countries and international agencies are prepared to make available to them is related to the self-help effort which they are willing to undertake. There has been really a very significant gain over the last several years, and the United States has played a very important part in it. 

Senator CLARK. Now in terms of resentment incurred in the borrowing countries, do you notice any difference in your experience or in the experience of your agency between the resentment which is incurred toward the aid administrators as a result of these loans, and the international loans made by institutions whose governing board or executive officers are not sort of gringos?

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 119 1965 Mr. BELL. I think there is no doubt that an international agency operates from a position where it can ask for a meeting of technical standards without carrying any particular political overtones, whereas the United States has a somewhat more delicate job. 

We ask for the same technical standards to be met. It is possible for us to be accused of doing something for political reasons, or the political element may be brought in. In this sense I think Senator 

Fulbright's point, which he has made frequently, is a very sound point. 

The international agencies certainly can operate from a nonpolitical setting, so to speak, and certainly we, the American program, operate under the leadership of the international agencies wherever we can. 

We strongly encourage the Bank and the Fund and others to take the lead, because there is less direct political risk.

On the other hand, it is quite possible for us, for the United States, and has been possible for many years, and in country after country, to handle the delicate relationship between aid giver and aid receiver without rancor, without difficulty.

Looking back, for example, during the Marshall plan days, Bill Foster has told me how he had some very severe knockdown dragout fights in private, in which he said to one or another of the Euronan countries:

Look, you are a sovereign nation and you can adopt whatever economic policies you want, but we are also a sovereign nation. If we are going to make our aid available to you, we have to be satisfied that your economic policies make sense.

Now we are saying that today in private and quietly, and normally without any difficulty. You look around the world and the places where the large amounts of American aid are going, these are not the places where there is difficulty, where there is resentment, where there is argument. The places where there is a lot of controversy are cases where there is very little aid involved, where the real problem is not aid at all, but the political differences between ourselves and the country in question. I would be delighted to expand on this point in executive session. I think the point is perfectly obvious. 

Let me state it in a slightly different way. We have found that it is possible to insist on very strong self-help standards in many countries under our bilateral aid program. It is easier to do that, and it is preferable to do that within a multilateral framework, within a consortium or within CIAP or in any way that provides participation by the country in question and a joint agreement on the technical standards that ought to be applied.

But we don't take a back seat to anybody in asserting that we have been able to apply very strong self-help standards under our bilateral program.

My own view is that most of the problems confronting the world today are a result of the exaggeration of the nation state as the be-all and end-all of political organizations of society, far more so than

the alleged struggle between communism and capitalism. Therefore 

I would like to see personally, and I know many of my colleagues would strongly disagree, a gradual development of these multilateral and even worldwide institutions, and a gradual phasing out of our bilateral and national aid programs and a lot of other programs also. 

I take it from your close experience with this problem during the last 2 years that you would conclude that the time for that is not yet, although perhaps we can make some progress along that line. 

Mr. BELL. Oh, yes. I want to be perfectly clear. As the Secretary testified yesterday, we have strongly advocated and we strongly advocate today steady movement toward more funding through international agencies and more and better arrangements for multilateral coordination. We think those trends are in being and we agree with them and support them. 

We think that there will continue to be the need for a bilateral aid program and a strong one for at least several years to come.

MAXIMUM USE OF AGRICULTURAL SURPLUS AS AID 

In the first place, we fully agree with the policy suggestion that the gentleman makes in that letter. It is clearly in the interests of the 

United States to make our aid available in the form of agricultural commodities of which we have a surplus to the maximum possible extent. We believe we are doing that. The Public Law 480 program is now running in the order of magnitude of $1.5 to $2 billion per year of surplus agricultural commodities going almost entirely to the less developed countries. In every case where we can meet the needs for external resources of these countries with American agricultural commodities, our flat instructions to the embassies, to the AID mission directors, to the agricultural attachés who are the people on the spot figuring out what is going to be helpful in the particular country in question-our flat instruction is that they always use food and other American surplus commodities, such as cotton, to the maximum possible extent.

We have reviewed this matter repeatedly over the last 2 or 3 years during the period in which the balance-of-payments policy of the Government has been steadily tightened. 

We have not only focused on the question of making the maximum use of the American surplus commodities, but also of substituting the resulting local currency for dollar expenditures wherever that is conceivably possible. So that while we have no difference whatever with the policy, I can assure you that we are bearing down on this matter. We have continually done so, and I do not know of any significant opportunity for large-scale improvement. 

Now, this is not a matter that we can just let go. It is something we have to pursue, and we do daily, weekly, monthly, because there are always new questions coming up. Therefore, there is always a question facing us. Are we today in making the maximum use of American surplus agricultural commodities? 

AID PIPELINE ONLY FOR PROJECTS ALREADY BEGUN 

So far as the pipeline is concerned, I am sure that you know, Senator, having been an executive branch manager yourself at one stage, that the pipeline of obligational authority committed to contracts and to projects which are underway represents funds which can only be used to finish jobs which have already been started, and that it takes new obligational authority to undertake new activities of any kind. 

So that if there were no new obligational authority voted by the Congress, the projects which are underway would be completed. They are fully funded. It is our practice in the AID program to fund fully each capital project financed by loans, and they would be continued to completion, but we would be unable to undertake any new action of any kind, to commit any new funds to the purposes that the President and all the rest of us believe are so important. 

So that we do not have the option, it seems to me, of running on the pipeline. The only thing the pipeline would permit us to do would be

to complete the projects that are underway, and it would not permit us to meet the current-for example, it would not permit us to make any new commitments in Vietnam, and obviously that is a matter which would be of the utmost- 

Senator SYMINGTON. I do not think that is 

Mr. BELL. Right, I am sure that would not be the intent.

EFFICIENCY OF EMPLOYING U.S. CONTRACTORS FOR AID PROJECTS 

Has 

Senator SPARKMAN. Let me ask you just a few questions. the requirement to limit yourself to the use of U.S. firms in such fields as construction and engineering resulted in the lack of competition and higher costs? And answer this. How do the costs of the AID engineering and construction contracts compare with those of the World Bank for comparable work? 

Mr. BELL. This is a matter on which I would like to supplement for the record what I say now, Senator, because I do not have precise figures in my mind. It is not my impression, however, that we are

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 125 1965 encountering any difficulty because we are relying almost entirely on American engineering construction firms. 

So far as construction contracts are concerned, we of course make sure that our borrowers use competitive bid practices and the American firm which wins the contract is the low bidder. Therefore, we get the same kind of competition among American contractors that we do with any other Government program. 

So far as design contracts and engineering supervision are concerned, of course those are not let in our program or in any other on a competitive bid basis. We do review the abilities, the capabilities of the firms that are interested in a particular job, and we select the firm that we think will give us the best quality result, which is the same practice that is followed by the Corps of Engineers and other 

American Government agencies.

RELATIVE COSTS OF ENGINEERING PROJECTS 

It is not my impression that the costs that are involved in the engineering design and supervision contract, while they may be higher for American firms, they certainly are not enough higher to make it a significantly serious additional cost to the total value of a given project.

I would like, as I said, Mr. Chairman, to ask our engineering staffs and submit for the record, if I may- Senator SPARKMAN. We will be very glad to have that. 

Mr. BELL. I might be able to give you some sort of estimate of the differential cost of using American engineering firms. I would doubt very much that the American construction firms would have higher costs than those of other countries. They are accustomed to bidding internationally on international tenders and winning contracts for construction in cases that are financed by the World Bank and other international organizations, but I will doublecheck this. (The information referred to follows:)

COSTS OF USING AMERICAN CONSTRUCTION AND ENGINEERING FIRMS 

Direct comparisons of engineering and construction costs on different projects are extremely difficult. However, it appears from discussions with the Inter- 

American Development Bank and the World Bank that the costs of these services under the three programs are fairly comparable. 

As a general rule engineering fees are based on fee schedules established by the various U.S. engineering societies and accepted as common practice in the industry. The individual fees for initial investigations are very small. 

Costs for complete design, preparation of bidding documents, contract awards, and supervision of construction have run between 10 to 12 percent of estimated construction costs, depending on the magnitude and complexity of the project. 

If training in operations and maintenance of a facility is added, the cost might run as high as 18 to 20 percent.

In most cases involving capital construction, contractor selections are made by the borrowers with AID approval of the selection. While it is Agency policy to give preference to U.S. firms, it is also a fundamental goal of AID to improve the capability of host countries and local companies, and where the competence is available locally, these firms may be used. Construction contracts are let on a competitive bid basis. 

Of course the use of host country firms is less expensive for reasons of salary differentials, mobilization costs, and logistic support requirements. However, U.S. firms have developed a high level of know-how in foreign operations over the past years and frequently affiliate with local firms and employ local people, thus reducing costs to a comparable level.

Although borrowers now make most engineering contractor selections, 81 U.S. contractors were employed out of 91 contracts awarded in the fiscal year 1964 AID program. The experience in the Inter-American Development Bank over the past 3 years has been that U.S. firms were awarded 18 projects out of 28. 

We are advised by the World Bank that U.S. engineering and construction firms are competing favorably with foreign firms on an international basis. 

Discussions with officials of the Inter-American Development Bank and the World Bank do not indicate any significant disparity in costs between their work and ours although strict comparability in engineering work is almost impossible to attain. It

In comparing construction costs where AID allows equal competition between U.S. and local firms and the Inter-American Development Bank and the 

World Bank advertise on an international basis, we find that U.S. firms fare very well, except where large-scale procurement of equipment is involved. is AID policy to require such procurement from U.S. sources and costs may be higher for this reason. The Inter-American Development Bank¹ and the World 

Bank do not have such a policy and contractors are free to solicit competition for equipment purchases on the world market. U.S. construction firms are doing well also in private work overseas.

AMBASSADORIAL RESPONSIBILITY FOR INTEGRATED AID PROGRAM 

May I take this opportunity to say that the process by which these aid decisions are made is a far more sensible and unified process today than it was a few years ago. We now have a programing process for each country which starts in the country, and the ambassador is charged-working with his military advisers and his civilian advisers, his aid mission if he has one, his economic counselor and so on-to examine the situation in that country, the interests of the United States in that country, the opportunities for assistance if any and what the country is doing for itself, and the funds that will be available to that country from other sources than the United States, from other bilateral programs, and from multilateral agencies. 

It is the ambassador's responsibility to submit to us here in Washington an integrated program, so that, as I said to Senator Symington earlier this morning, if we can meet a need in a country under the Public Law 480 program, obviously we should not meet it by using dollars under the economic aid program.

The ambassador is responsible for being sure-and we review these decisions very carefully that the military assistance and the economic assistance make sense in relation to each other, and in relation to the situation in that country. 

So that each of these programs is intended to be, and the process is such, that we review this country by country, a very careful, uniquely tailored program for that country. Therefore, it is entirely appropriate to look at the Public Law 480, the military aid, the economic aid, in the context of any given country, and we should be able to justify to you gentlemen and to anybody else who is concerned why we think this particular combination of aid resources makes sense in the interests of the United States in that country. 

MOST ECONOMIC AID CONCENTRATED IN A FEW COUNTRIES 

May I add just one last point. It is very significant because looking at the countries in this way, we have increasingly concentrated the assistance in fewer countries. Of the 72 countries in which some economic assistance is scheduled for next year, is requested for next year, only 5 percent of it will go to 41 of those countries. Ninety-five percent of it will go to 31 of those countries. That is a very highly concentrated result, because we are trying to put the money where the opportunities are and where it will do the most good.

(The information referred to follows:) REGISTERED FOREIGN AGENTS DEALING WITH AID 

There are registered foreign agents who deal with AID. When the agent is representing an AID recipient government, he normally appears in an advisory capacity to that government. Applications for assistance come from the government directly. Sometimes these activities involve agents who are engineers by profession; e.g., in feasibility studies. At times registered agents appear seeking contracts with AID. Normally they do so on their own behalf and not in their capacity as agents. 

It should be pointed out that the foreign agents are selected for contracts on the basis of their professional standing and qualifications. 

In addition, officers and employees of corporations and partners of partnerships which are registered foreign agents must themselves register. In at least two cases, former employees of AID are officers of registered corporations. In another case a partner of a registered law firm was previously employed by the former development loan fund. 

Under an informal arrangement made with the Department of Justice in 1963, the latter sends copies of initial, supplemental and amendatory registration statements of foreign agents likely to have contracts with AID to the Office of the General Counsel of this Agency for review. That office distributes these copies to the appropriate functional offices for circulation to all officers who may have any contact with the agents concerned or their activities. These officers are required to submit comments regarding the registrant and the accuracy of his registration statement and also to report past contacts and future contacts, as they occur, with the registrant. Similar comments and reports are requested from the field missions concerned. 

The comments received are evaluated by the Office of the General Counsel. 

The described procedure is intended to apprise the interested AID officers of the identity of registered agents with whom they may have to deal. 

In the distribution of registration statements as described above the following form is used: "In accordance with established practice, the Department of Justice has sent to AID for review and comment a registration statement and attachments filed by the subject registrant, since the registrant is likely to have contacts with AID. Two copies of this document are attached. "Please circulate one copy of the statement to all AID/W officers in your region who may have had, or may be expected to have in the future, any official contacts with the registrant. The officers should be asked (a) to submit any comments they may have on the accuracy and completeness of the documents; (b) to report any contacts with the registrant that have occurred; and (c) to promptly report in the future any such contacts which may develop. Contacts previously reported need not be reported again. "The other copy of the statement should be sent to the U.S. AID with the request to comment and report in a similar manner. Please have this office included in the distribution of the message to the U.S. AID. "To prevent any misconception on the part of the AID/W and U.S. AID officers concerned. I should like to point out that registration under the Foreign 

Agents Registration Act in no way places any limitation on the activities which may be engaged in by an agent of a foreign principal. Hence, the fact that a person is a registered agent does not per se affect his eligibility for contracts with, or financed by, AID. However, in some instances the obligations of the agent to his foreign principal may be incompatible with the agent's obligations under a particular AID contract. 

"It is requested that comments and reports be forwarded through you to this office on a priority basis. The registration material need not be returned."

OBJECTIVES FOR GRANTING MILITARY ASSISTANCE

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 139 1965 Now, I phrase it that way because as you know, sir, in Latin America we have shifted sharply in the last 3 or 4 years away from a concept that the military forces of the Latin American countries should be primarily designed as part of a hemispheric defense and toward a policy that the military forces in the Latin American countries should primarily be thought of as contributing to internal security in these countries, and to some extent toward civic kinds of activities, using their engineer battalions to build roads and schools. and water facilities. 

DIFFERENT TYPES OF MILITARY AID TO MEET NEW MILITARY THREATS 

In consequence, the kinds of equipment that have been going to the Latin American countries under the military assistance programs have been decreasingly destroyers and tanks and things like that, and increasingly jeeps and communications gear and lighter armaments which are more appropriate for the current threat which is intended. to be met, and that threat is, of course, principally the threat of internal subversion stimulated and led by people trained and supported from Cuba and from the Communist bloc.

States.

REGULATIONS CONCERNING USE OF U.S.-OWNED LOCAL CURRENCIES BY U.S. 

OVERSEA PERSONNEL 

There are various requirements concerning the use of U.S.-owned local currencies by oversea personnel. 

In all countries where the United States hold local currencies in excess of foreseeable requirements and in certain other countries, the Department of State has required U.S. personnel to obtain their local currency requirements from the local funds held by the United States. For example, Circular No. 104 distributed by the American Embassy in Pakistan states: "The Department of State has instructed that all personnel in all agencies, without exception, be directed to purchase from U.S. Government disbursing officers their total rupee requirements for personal use except that all personnel in all agencies are permitted to import into Pakistan an amount not to exceed PRS 0.80 per person. All other rupees for personal or other rupee expenses will be purchased only from a U.S. Government disbursing officer."

This requirement, which applies not only to direct employees of the United States but also to employees of Government contractors, has been in force in Pakistan for over 14 years. Procedures for checking on compliance have been adopted, and anyone found violating the requirement is subject to discipline. 

The executive branch, after successful discussions with the governments of the excess currency countries and with the airlines, has promulgated policy statements designed to insure that excess currencies are used to the maximum extent in paying for air travel. AID Circular A-154, issued to implement this policy, states that it is mandatory that "All air travel to, from, and within [the excess currency] countries which is charged to U.S. funds will be paid in the appropriate excess foreign currency" and that this ruling applies to travel of not only all AID employees and their dependents but also to others; such as, experts and consultants, participating agency personnel, contractor employees, and participant trainees. Missions are required to submit monthly reports on air travel, and the circular makes clear that no deviation from the directive will be acceptable.

AID contracts attempt to insure that local currencies owned by the United States will be used. A normal provision states: "The contractor shall make all U.S. dollar payments under this contract in the 

United States of America and shall wherever possible obtain all local currency requirements for expenditures to be made in the cooperating country from the cognizant U.S. disbursing officer, American Embassy, of the U.S. AID controller, as appropriate, in exchange for U.S. dollars." 

This provision is designed to help implement AID Policy Determination No. 24, which states that local currencies shall be used to pay for logistic support of contractors and their employees, and that AID dollars may be used only when no reasonable alternative exists by which such support can be provided with local currencies or in kind.

U.S. DOLLARS TRANSFERS UNDER THE FOREIGN AID BILL

(The statement referred to follows:) STATEMENT OF HON. DAVID E. BELL, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT, BEFORE THE SENATE BANKING AND CURRENCY COMMITTEE, MARCH 9, 1965 

Mr. Chairman, thank you for the privilege of appearing before this committee.

As Administrator of the Agency for International Development, I am particularly pleased that these hearings are being held, for they present an excellent opportunity to give the facts to the Congress, and to attempt to clear up some of the misconceptions surrounding the relation of aid to our balance of payments.

Foreign aid is by its very nature closely involved with the flow of payments. 

Thus each action and step taken by AID is and must be evaluated from the point of view of our balance-of-payments situation. 

The foreign aid program provides goods and services to other countries which they cannot obtain through normal means-through their export earnings and through obtaining capital on commercial terms and by private investment. 

A successful aid program is one which enables the recipient country to strengthen its economy to the point where it can obtain goods and services it needs for steady expansion and growth by normal trade and normal capital movements--and without further need for aid grants and soft loans. This is what was achieved in Western Europe under the Marshall plan, and has since been achieved in Japan, Spain, Greece, Taiwan, and other countries. 

It is plainly important to seek to carry out this important national program, like any other, at minimum cost to the United States. 

In the first years of the U.S. foreign aid program after World War II, during the Marshall plan and most of the 1950's, our aid appropriations were, in general, spent wherever in the world prices were lowest. During the Marshall plan period, of course, the United States was the only major source in the world for most of the goods those countries needed. Therefore, most of the aid dollars, although not tied to U.S. procurement, were spent in this country. 

Later in the 1950's the revived European economies became increasingly effective competitors for U.S. aid purchases. 

Beginning in 1959, in response to the changed situation of the U.S. balance of payments, our policy respecting aid purchases was changed. Today, with small exceptions, aid appropriations can only be spent in the United States, for goods and services produced in this country. This has undoubtedly raised the cost to the Federal budget of providing a given amount of goods and services under the aid program, since some items are being purchased with aid appropriations in the United States which could be bought more cheaply in other countries. But our present policies are intended to minimize the adverse effect of the aid program on the balance of payments, even if that results in some increased cost to the budget. There are two approaches to measuring the impact of AID's expenditures on the balance of payments. The first, which might be called the accounting approach, measures the direct result of the AID spending: are the dollars appropriated by the Congress spent directly in this country or are they spent abroad or transferred to another country or to an international organization. 

Under this method of measurement, which is similar to the Department of Commerce figures on the balance of payments, during fiscal year 1964-the latest data available the gross adverse effect on the U.S. balance of payments of AID's economic assistance programs was about $513 million. 

We have now received preliminary estimates for the calendar year 1964 which show substantial further improvement. The payments abroad dropped to about $400 million. This is offset by repayments of past assistance extended by AID and predecessor agencies of over $150 million, making a net effect of about $250 million. 

The current expenditure rate under our economic assistance program is almost exactly $2 billion per year. 

Thus in 1964, for every dollar of economic aid extended, 20 cents showed as a current adverse impact in our balance of payments-not considering current or future receipts.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 145 1965 Put the other way around, 80 percent of AID's expenditures last year represented not dollars going abroad, but steel, machinery, fertilizer, and other goods and services purchased in the United States. 

Under these circumstances, of course, a cut in AID appropriations would primarily reduce U.S. exports, and would have only a very small effect on the balance of payments. 

Moreover, the proportion of appropriations spent in the United States is rising. Eighty-five percent of new obligations are being committed for direct expenditure in the United States. 

The $400 million of AID offshore payments in calendar 1964 is made up of the following major elements:

One hundred and twenty million dollars representing payments of U.S. voluntary contributions to international organizations, such as U.N. agencies, the 

Indus River project administered by the IBRD, and the Social Progress Trust 

Fund. 

Seventy-eight million dollars for commodity purchases in other less developed countries-cases where, for example, required goods are unavailable in the United States or shipping costs are too high. 

Nineteen million dollars for commodity purchases in other developed countries. These are either tag end expenditures of major projects approved before aid was tied in 1959 or items unavailable from any other source, approved on a case-by-case waiver basis. 

Sixty-six million dollars in cash transfers, transfers of funds made in a very few cases where normal procedures for providing assistance are not feasible or made in small amounts to cover local costs of technical assistance projects. The amount of such transfers has been reduced sharply in recent years and is expected to be only $40 million in calendar 1965. 

Thirty million dollars for local expenses of AID direct hire personnel stationed abroad. This represents the local expenses which could not be met by use of Treasury-owned local currencies.

Eigty-seven million dollars for other expenditures outside the United States. 

This includes payments by U.S. contractors for such necessary items as wages. 

It also includes payments to schools and hospitals abroad, disaster relief expenditures, offshore expenses of participants, and other project costs. 

As indicated above, this $400 million was offset by about $150 million in repayments of principal and interest on loans extended by AID and its predecessor agencies.

II 

This then is the "accounting" measure of the direct flow of dollars abroad resulting from our economic aid program. 

The true net economic effect of foreign assistance on our balance of payments cannot be measured so simply. This is because there are indirect effects not revealed by the direct accounts. A substantial portion of the dollars that go out under our aid program, to the United Nations, for example, comes back through regular commercial channels for purchases of U.S. goods. 

Dollars which go out and enter the economy of a less developed country may be used later by that country to buy needed goods in the U.S. market or may go through trade channels to a third country, which will use the dollars for purchase of goods in the U.S. market. 

These are examples of the so-called "feedback" effect, which means that the effect of aid outflows on the U.S. balance of payments is overstated, because dollar outflows to a considerable extent are immediately reflected in increased U.S. export sales for dollars. 

When an aid But there is another indirect effect in the opposite direction. recipient is able to buy U.S. imports under a tied loan-that is, has a letter of credit opened in a U.S. bank which can only be spent in the United States, then that country may use the tied dollars to buy goods that it would have otherwise bought with dollars it already owns. These other dollars-free exchangeare thus available for other purchases either in the United States or elsewhere. 

This is the so-called "substitution" effect, meaning that to some extent aidfinanced imports are "substituted" for imports that would have been bought with "free" dollars, and to this extent the effect of tied aid on the U.S. balance of payments is understated.

There are no good estimates of the size of the feedback and substitution effects. Only indirect evidence is available. With respect to the question of how much substitution occurs, for example, it is clear that most of the less developed countries have severe shortages of dollars, and need more goods from the United States than they can afford, even with the addition of aid. Furthermore, statistics do not indicate that a dropoff in commercial trade occurs when there is an increase in aid. Quite the opposite. The most frequently cited example is Latin America. While expenditures under the Alliance for Progress have been increasing over the past 3 years, so have Latin American purchases from the United States through regular commercial channels. In fact, according to preliminary estimates, commercial U.S. exports to Latin America increased by $500 million in 1964 alone. Thus it is the best guess of the economists who have studied these matters that the amount of substitution is relatively small.

Overall, it is our conclusion that the indirect economic effects of aid on our balance of payments roughly balance each other, and even allowing for some variation from time to time, the true effect of aid on our balance of payments would not differ very much in either direction from the figures shown by the accounting estimates referred to earlier. 

To sum up, our balance-of-payments figures show, by the "accounting" measure, the share of our expenditures made directly for U.S. goods and services is 80 percent and rising, and the share paid to foreigners and international organizations is 20 percent and falling. These figures do not take into account indirect effects, but it is our best guess that they would be little different if they did. AID dollars spent abroad which return quickly in payment for commercial exports roughly offset the amount of AID financing for goods that would have been exported anyway. As nearly as we can tell these two imperfections roughly cancel each other out and 15 to 20 percent is a valid indication of the real adverse impact of aid on the U.S. balance of payments. 

III 

I should like to say a word about the relationship of U.S. aid and holdings of U.S.gold.

Some aid recipients have bought gold from the United States in the past few years, mostly to finance their gold subscription to the International Monetary 

Fund. 

In the main, however, gold transactions between United States and aid recipients result in a net gain in U.S. holdings. During 1964, for example, lessdeveloped countries purchased $28 million worth of gold from the United States (of which all but $3 million was subscribed to the IMF), but they sold $89 million worth of gold to us for dollars in the same period. 

There is thus no direct relation between aid and an outflow of gold to aid recipients. In fact, the reverse is true. The U.S. gold problem lies with the industrial countries of Europe, not in our relations with the aid recipient nations.

IV 

I have been speaking thus far of AID expenditures. There are other U.S. programs which can properly be referred to as foreign aid in a broad sense. 

I should like to mention these briefly, with a word about their balance-of-payments impact.

Military assistance consists principally of the provision of U.S.-produced military equipment. Taking into account the costs of U.S. personnel overseas to administer the program, some oversea training costs, and other oversea expenditures, the estimates are that over 85 percent of military assistance expenditures are made directly in the United States, and the remainder are made offshore.

The Public Law 480 program provides U.S. surplus agricultural commodities by sale and donation to other countries. In view of the nature of the program, virtually all of the expenditures under it are made directly in the United States, with only minor and unavoidable offshore costs in foreign ports. The same is true of expenditures under the Export-Import Bank loans. 

The Peace Corps expenditures are almost entirely for the living expenses of the volunteers abroad, and for their training and supervision in the United States. It is estimated that about 75 percent of Peace Corps expenditures are made in the United States and about 25 percent offshore.

Finally, U.S. contributions to international agencies such as the International 

Development Association are paid in dollars and are shown in the Department of Commerce statistics as 100-percent outflows. In fact, however, a substantial share of the total expenditures of these international organizations is made in the United States. Consequently, the accounting estimate of balance-of-payments impact in this case overstates the true effect. 

I should also like to stress that we are seeking in every way we can devices to use local currencies, owned by the United States as a result of food-for-peace sales or other U.S. assistance, to meet the local costs of our aid missions. The net effect of this policy is to enable us in many countries to substitute U.S.produced commodities for what would otherwise be dollars used to purchase local currencies to cover the local costs of U.S. Government activities. V

President Johnson's message of February 10 said "Until we master our balances of-payments problem AID officials will send no aid dollars abroad that can be sent instead in the form of U.S. goods and services." We are doing just that. 

I have asked that every project and every commodity order be closely examined. 

Waiver of tied procurement regulations will be allowed only when it is clearly justified in the U.S. interest. Local costs will be paid for out of U.S. local currency holdings wherever possible.

We expect, as I have indicated, to see some further increase in tied purchases and expenditures in the United States, but we are close to the limit. Some minimum offshore expenditures will remain-principally the local expenditures of our employees and those of our contractors who are stationed overseas, the contributions of the United States to international organizations, and a few special cases where tying to U.S. procurement is unfeasible or unwise. 

The President, advised by his Cabinet Committee on the Balance of Payments, has concluded that this small remaining element of offshore expenditures under the aid program is a cost to our country which is far outweighed by the benefits to our own interests that will accrue from the achievement of economic and social progress in the less developed countries. 

A similar judgment underlay the distinction drawn by the President in his recent balance-of-payments message between U.S. private investment abroad in advanced countries-which for the time being is to be discouraged-and U.S. private investment abroad in less-developed countries, which the U.S. Government is continuing strongly to encourage. 

VI 

Looking beyond the immediate present, the foreign aid program has a number of effects which are positively beneficial to our balance of payments. 

Frst, our aid today is overwhelmingly in the form of dollar repayable loansunlike the situation under the Marshall plan, when 90 percent of our aid was in the form of grants. Future repayments of interest and principal on today's loans will be a positive factor in our balance of payments. 

Secondly, the evidence is plain that countries which with our aid achieve steady economic growth become increasingly better markets for U.S. exports and more attractive places for U.S. investment abroad. Over the last 15 years our exports to Europe have doubled and our exports to Japan have tripled. As other countries-Spain, Greece, Taiwan, and so on-gain economic momentum and our aid comes to an end the same kind of result is evident. 

Morover, the aid program in case after case has directly led to the introduction of American products and services in other countries, and to follow-on markets unrelated to the aid program. Aid has in fact been one of our best export promotion mechanisms.

VII 

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to report that since 1961 we have steadily reduced the effect of foreign aid on our balance of payments. We are continuing the efforts to minimize the effect as part of the action program announced by President Johnson last month.

We will do more. But the upper limit may soon be reached, as the adverse impact has already been reduced to $400 million, not including repayments. 

In addition, it is important to recognize that a continuation of the present program will have a long-range positive impact on our balance of payments as a result of a dollar repayment flow, expanding markets for our exports, and improving opportunities for our private investment abroad.

U.S. CONTROL OVER THE USE OF PUBLIC LAW 480 COMMODITIES 

Senator CASE. I take it for external funds. Do we have any control over what a country does with Public Law 480 commodities, for example? 

Mr. BELL. With the commodities?

Senator CASE. Yes. 

 We follow the commodities not only under the Public Law 480 program but under our economic aid program. 

We follow the commodities right to their end use, and indeed we have people on our staff who are called by a rather ugly bureaucratic gobbledygook term, end-use inspectors. Their job is to go all the way and follow the commodity and be sure it went where it is supposed to go. As I said to him, in addition to our own staff of inspectors and auditors, we have an external audit within the State Department from Ken Mansfield in the Inspector General's office. We also have the GAO continually checking on these matters. We also, of course, have the staffs of Senate committees. I have had the feeling that our inspections have been improving in competence steadily. Nevertheless, when you are talking as you are in the Egyptian case of thousands of tons of wheat, you have a very large volume of commodities to keep track of. 

Our main objective in the situations is to try to help the host government have inspection services that are better, and that steadily improve in quality, but we follow them, too, and try to bring about improvements wherever we find anything wrong. We are continually finding points of difficulty, and we are continually working to improve the control system, the inventory systems, the recordkeeping and all the rest of the machinery that can assure us that the goods go where they are supposed to go and accomplish what they are supposed to accomplish. 

Senator CASE. Perhaps you know whether one of the requirements for any kind of foreign aid or other assistance is to give a recipient country something so that it can use its own products of the same sort. 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; we have very careful policies on that matter and a review system. There are two issues involved really. One, we make our surplus commodities available only for what are additional needs, that is to say we are not trying to disrupt the normal marketing system around the world, the normal commercial exports from the United States or from any other countries, so that there has to be a demonstration that is satisfactory to the Agriculture Department that the commodities going into a given country are of the nature and in the amount which will not disrupt the normal marketing system.

Second, we want to be absolutely certain that we are not providing commodities to a country which they simply substitute for some of their own production of a similar commodity and which they then

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 149 1965 export, because that would obviously cut into our markets and other people's markets, and this is a complicated but very closely watched set of calculations. We have had some recent cases which are quite significant as to how we make this calculation. In the case of Korea recently, for example, we reached an agreement. The Koreans are natural rice producers and exporters, and obviously we do not want to prevent them from increasing their own economic strength as they can gradually produce and sell more, but also we do not want to substitute or allow them to export by making available an equal amount of our commodities. And so we have an understanding with them that insofar as they export rice, they will purchase from us an equivalent volume on a commercial basis of wheat or whatever it is, so that we are not in a position of supporting their exports with our Public Law 480 local currency sales.

MANSFIELD AMENDMENT TO CUT DOWN SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE 

Mr. BELL. Our record over the last several years with respect to suporting assistance I think is excellent. You will recall that 4 or 5 years ago the Senate under the leadership, I believe, of perhaps Senator Mansfield-I think there is something called the Mansfield amendment which was put in, saying in effect, "Let us reduce this supporting assistance business as much as we can." We have followed that instruction. Four or five years ago the corresponding figure to this $369 million was over $1 billion. During this period of time we have eliminated supporting assistance all together from some 14 countries, and we have transferred-we have either put the countries on their own feet wherever that was possible, or have shifted them from a basis of getting support from us to a basis in which we are helping them with their development leading to economic independence, so that in Turkey, in Pakistan, and in a number of other countries we are no longer providing any supporting assistance. 

Senator SPARKMAN. What about Greece? 

[Deleted.] 

Mr. BELL. But 5 years ago; I believe, there was some supporting assistance going into Greece. There was to Taiwan. So that not only has this figure been reduced, but the number of countries in which we are involved in any kind of supporting assistance is now way down, and we anticipate only nine countries for fiscal year 1966 will receive any supporting assistance.

Now, it is conceivable that some emergency would come along during the year which would add a country or two to that number, but as we see it today, in only nine countries de we expect to have to use supporting assistance. 

Senator SPARKMAN. If such an emergency came along, does it come out of this $369 million, or does it come out of the President's contingent fund?

Mr. BELL. It would come out of the $369 million if we could possibly reprogram within the available funds, or if necessary we would go to the contingency fund.

JUSTIFICATION OF AID TO CERTAIN AFRICAN COUNTRIES 

The CHAIRMAN. I wonder if you could give us your justification for such programs, and I will mention a few and there will be others, such as the Cameroons. I know these are small. 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. Central African Republic, Chad, Congo, Brazza ville, Gabon, Ghana, Malawi. In Ghana we are already involved in the dam; I guess it is too late to do anything about that. Mali, Niger, Senegal, Togo, Upper Volta. 

Mr. BELL. This is sort of a group of countries.

The CHAIRMAN. Right. 

They are very similar, and maybe we should discuss the specifics. 

I am interested in the justification for our having an AID program in all of these areas. The other day, as you will remember, there was a good deal in the press-I did not intend it that way-but it was in connection with the examination of the new Ambassador to Zambia. 

It turned out we were starting an aid program there even before we

appointed a new ambassador to this new country-which has a considerable potential but has just recently became independent from British rule. Generally speaking, why do we feel it necessary to establish an aid program in this type of country? 

Mr. BELL. You are quite right, Mr. Chairman. The question applies to a substantial number of countries in Africa. It really applies more in Africa than anywhere else in the world at the present time, although in a few cases it applies elsewhere as well. 

The CHAIRMAN. I could mention a few others. We had someone talking about Paraguay a while ago and Uruguay in Latin America and the other places, but take this as a group, what is your justification? 

Mr. BELL. We have given a great deal of thought to this, and I have talked personally and at length on numerous occasions with the Secretary, with many of the others in the Department, with Averell Harriman and with our own people. We have come to the following conclusions:

First, our interest in these countries, in their independence and their point of view is a real interest. They exist. They are independent countries. They are members of the United Nations. I will come to the question of colonies separately, but the ones that you indicated are all, I believe, independent countries. What should the U.S. attitude toward these countries be? It has been our conclusion that we should make it plain that we support their independence and their progress, and that we should do so at minimum cost to ourselves. 

Now, in certain cases, in all the cases that you have indicated, we have concluded that it would be appropriate and desirable from the standpoint of the United States to provide some assistance. Now, in many of these countries the assistance is limited to one or two technical assistance projects or perhaps one loan. We have limited the personnel that we have located in these countries to what we believe is the absolute minimum in some of them we have no AID personnel at all. We operate entirely by sending people in on trips when it is necessary to make some decision or take some action respecting an AID project. 

The bulk of the assistance in the ex-French colonies is coming from France. We believe that that should continue to be the case. The last thing that we intend to do-and fortunately the last thing the French want us to do is to displace their operations and their support. 

AID IN THE BASIC INTERESTS OF DEVELOPING COUNTRY AND THE UNITED STATES 

In the British case, the former British colonies, that is to say Malawi, Zambia [deleted], the crucial question is why do we have to do anything at all by way of aid.

The CHAIRMAN. That is right. 

Mr. BELL. The answer that we have consistently come to is that it is appropriate for the United States to be helpful where we can do so at reasonable cost to ourselves, because these countries exist and the United States has an interest in their independence and progress. 

Furthermore, there is a second argument which frequently applies, not in all of them but in many of them. It would be very awkward politically for the leaders of these countries to be dependent exclusively on a single foreign source, especially if that foreign source was

the former metropolitan area of which there were colonies. It is not hard for the leader [deleted] if he can say also, "Yes, and look, we have got assistance coming from the United States as well." It does not have to be big assistance, and it is not big assistance, but it is something, and it exists. The United States is providing it, and it is a demonstration to his own opponents in his own country that he is not dependent solely on the former metropole, and he has not led his country really into a new form of colonial relationship. 

So these are the two key elements which lead us and have led us to decide that it is appropriate to provide some assistance in the cases that you cite.

But coming back to your earlier point, while we propose to eliminate these programs as rapidly as the economic circumstances in these countries permit- The CHAIRMAN. Well, that is not likely to occur in many of these because you have just started them. 

Mr. BELL. That is right.

The CHAIRMAN. And many of them are very backward countries. 

Mr. BELL. Exactly. It would be my expectation that under present policy- The CHAIRMAN. COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATION: MULTILATERAL AID TO AFRICAN NATIONS

SPREADING OF AID BRINGS CONGRESSIONAL OPPOSITION 

It does not necessarily mean there is not another way to do it. I think this bilateral responsibility, which AID seems to assume-the local politicians know we have one no matter how small or how large- I think this is a relationship that has within it very serious problems in the future, and it has a way of sucking us into more and more responsibility of a political nature. I question in my own mind the wisdom of being there as a nation in this particular role. Of course, we could have, as I say, a consulate or whatever it is that is customary.

COMMITTEE RECOMMENDATIONS FOR SPECIFIC PILOT PROJECTS 

We have also made specific recommendations. Most of this happened before you came into this particular job. In Latin America, for example, we very specifically recommended in the beginning to concentrate on four specific countries in order to make a really successful pilot project. This, in itself, would prove to other countries that something can be done in these countries instead of spreading it so thin that we delay the accomplishment of a real success almost indefinitely. If we concentrate on, say, four countries with the best projects, within a much shorter time we could come up with a real success. This is far more persuasive to other countries than any kind of preachments or promises that we could make. And yet the Agency has not followed either of our suggestions in either Latin America or Africa. This is what I would call a basic difference of policy in the whole AID field.

STATEMENT OF DAVID E. BELL, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT; ACCOMPANIED BY JACK VAUGHN, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR INTER-AMERI- CAN AFFAIRS; WILLIAM D. RESEARCH CONDUCTED BY AID 

The CHAIRMAN. Does the AID have contracts of a research nature of this kind?

Mr. BELL. We do, sir; to some extent. 

The CHAIRMAN. Could you describe the nature of them? How much do you spend on such contracts?

Mr. BELL. The amount has been rising. The AID and its predecessors traditionally have done very little in the field of research, far too little in the opinion of those who have studied the progress of the developing countries most closely. In 1961 as part of the endeavor to improve the foreign aid program, a special study was made in this field by a group of scientists, primarily from American universities. The President's Science Adviser was also involved, and a provision in the act was proposed and adopted by the Congress which authorizes us to conduct a research program, and we have been doing so since that time. 175

In the 3-year period ending June 30, 1964, we obligated about $17 million. The current authorization is $12 million. During fiscal 

1964 we obligated $6 million, and we are this year operating, as I say, at a level approaching $12 million. 

We have a very distinguished Research Advisory Committee whose 

Chairman is Dr. Walsh McDermott of the Cornell University Medi cal School, and it includes not only university scientists but also a couple of high-level research administrators of private American corporations. We have tried to move with some caution in this field. 

I have personally tried to make sure that that is the case since I came into the Agency at the end of 1962. To any degree that the committee wishes we can provide full details on the research projects which we are funding at the present time, and those that we have funded in the past.

Do you wish me to stress any of the individual projects, Mr. Chairman, or otherwise go into this subject further? 

The CHAIRMAN. Yes; I think we are quite interested in that subject. I wonder if we could have a list of the projects with a short discussion of what they are about and the reasons why you think they are vital. Your research is now at the $12 million level. That is substantially more than that of the Disarmament Agency. Some of the studies that were submitted to us before seemed frankly rather farfetched or irrelevant to the major purposes of the Disarmament Agency. This was, I think, the purport of the criticism of the committee. I did not realize how extensive your contracts with these agencies are. These are contracts with such organizations as Brookings or National Planning. 

The information referred to appears on p. 694.) 

RESEARCH ON TSETSE FLY CONTROL 

Mr. BELL. That is right, also with some of the Federal agencies. 

I think perhaps the largest single contractor with us is the Agriculture Department's Research Service. We have some extremely interesting research projects underway with them. One of them which the committee might be interested in, as an illustration, is the contract under which they are seeking to apply to the tsetse fly in Africa the control methods which have proven so extremely successful with the screwworm in the United States.

In the southeastern part of the United States, as you perhaps know, a special control method has in recent years eliminated the screwworm entirely, which was a very damaging pest, and the scientists who worked on that and who are now working on the control of the tsetse fly in Africa believe that it may be possible to eliminate the tsetse fly in this way relatively cheaply from very large areas which are now rendered virtually unproductive because of the infestation of that particular pest. This work, as I say, is being done by the Department of Agriculture's Research Service, so that we have tried to draw upon research scientists in the Government, in the universities, and in nonprofit institutions. 

The CHAIRMAN. I notice a great many of these are good. fnise? 

Mr. BELL. Yes.

The CHAIRMAN. They are quite similar to the agricultural research in this country, are they not?

Mr. BELL. In general nature; yes, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. Of course; adapted to the problems of the particular country.

Mr. BELL. Exactly. 

RESEARCH ON IMPROVED METHODS OF PLANNING AND ALLOCATING U.S. ASSISTANCE 

The CHAIRMAN. One contract that was brought to my attention seemed rather interesting. It is research on improved methods of planning and allocating U.S. assistance. This seems to me, if it produces anything, very appropriate. 

The CHAIRMAN. Could you tell us what it did produce? What was the result of that? 

Mr. BELL. Which one?

The CHAIRMAN. This is by the Rand Corp. 

Mr. BELL. Oh, yes.

The CHAIRMAN. Through the Department of Defense. 

Mr. BELL. That is right.

The CHAIRMAN. The investigator is F. T. Moore, the action officer is Mr. D. Meyer, and it cost apparently $539,000. 

Mr. BELL. The project is still underway. 

The CHAIRMAN. Is it? 

Mr. BELL. It has produced initial results. Perhaps the most striking product under that research contract thus far was a team that visited Vietnam for us nearly a year ago now, I believe, and examined our economic assistance effort in relation to the precise difficulty, the precise kind of problem that exists in Vietnam. They made two major recommendations, both of which have been to a considerable extent adopted. One was that the program which had focused almost entirely on the rural areas up to that time needed to be augmented by efforts in the cities because there were very severe economic and social problems in the cities which were beginning to be the basis for Vietcong-type subversion in the cities themselves. 

Secondly, this research team from Rand-and of course they went on and discussed the precise nature of the problems and made a series of specific recommendations and so on-made the point that in our work in the rural areas which they believed was sound and sensible and should be continued as strongly as we could do it, we were not distinguishing sufficiently between the areas where the Vietcong did and did not control.

So that some of the things we were doing were inadvertently having some benefit for the Vietcong or at least for the farmers who were in Vietcong controlled areas and that we should try in everything we do to make plain that say the fertilizer that we are providing-should be available only to those farmers and those villagers who are endeavoring to stand up against the Vietcong control. 

This is obviously very difficult to do, and there are many parts of the countryside of Vietnam where the control shifts from day to day and where indeed sometimes the Government controls the area in the daytime and the Vietcong controls the same area at night. But this was an important and valuable suggestion which we accepted and

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, agreed with and which we are now trying to apply in the programs that are carried in the countryside in Vietnam. 

The CHAIRMAN. The research intended to point up the problem, not to give you the solution how to do it? 

Mr. BELL. They make recommendations, Mr. Chairman. We would not expect that they did their job if they stopped with just an analysis of the problem. We also want them to advise as to what they think we ought to do about it. We obviously will not necessarily accept their views 100 percent.
