Mr. BELL. I would be very glad to, sir. (The information referred to follows:)

PROJECT TITLE RESEARCH ON IMPROVED METHODS OF PLANNING AND ALLOCATING U.S. ASSISTANCE 

Contractor.-The Rand Corp. (through the U.S. Air Force). 

Project objectives The purpose of this project is to adapt for AID's use in planning, and in allocating resources among and within recipient countries, techniques now used by the Department of Defense to increase the effectiveness of their plans and programs. The research aims first to assess the effectiveness with which AID is handling selected problems and, second, to study in depth, by the use of advanced decision-making techniques, improvements in those AID policies and procedures identified in the first step. Justification Since its inception, the U.S. foreign aid program has developed its own methods for planning and allocating assistance in the face of uncertainties arising out of economic, social, and political changes. Recently, the Department of Defense has also developed techniques to assist its decision makers in the face of uncertainties. The resulting substantial gains in military program effectiveness warrant the effort to apply the techniques responsible for these gains to AID problems. Accomplishments

The problems selected for assessment of AID's effectiveness include: evaluation of country programs, programing of capital assistance, returns on investment in education, measurement of economic performance and self-help, assistance based on sectoral plans, and comparison of the effectiveness of different methods of economic aid. Studies in depth to improve AID's effectiveness have so far been undertaken on the first two problems listed. 

One country aid program-the one for Vietnam-has already been evaluated, with the results already mentioned in the testimony. The value of this pilot study was so great that two more such studies are now being carried out. Since this research contract is intended to cover only the costs of adapting the appropriate methods and techniques, and not the costs of applying them throughout

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 179 1965 AID, each of these additional evaluations is being financed by the regional bureau concerned. 

The study of capital assistance programing is developing: (a) guidelines on the use of loans to achieve broad U.S. objectives as well as to finance individual projects; (b) improved procedures for screening loans and insuring compliance with their terms; and (c) recommended adjustments of administrative practices to permit the improvements noted above to be carried out. 

PROJECT TITLE-RESEARCH IN FOAM PLASTICS FOR HOUSING Contractor.-University of Michigan. 

Project objective To determine the feasibility and to evaluate various ways of using different kinds of plastics in the development of low-cost housing for underdeveloped areas. Justification This Housing investment requirements in the less developed countries are extremely large. Consequently, the development of a satisfactory new technology making possible lower unit construction costs would be of major significance. project is an imaginative effort to design and test entirely new approaches to very low-cost housing construction which, if proved satisfactory, would be of major importance in less developed areas. Accomplishments

Five structural systems have been developed which look promising enough to justify additional study. Additional experiments are underway on the use of filament-winding techniques adapted from rocket engine technology for the production of housing shells.

The structural system based upon rigidizing of a reticulated foam is being studied for possible application by Rice University and the Ford Foundation in a community development project in Chile. An experimental building constructed by the Dow "spiral generation" process is in use in Ann Arbor and is being observed during its second winter of service. 

A useful method for the economic design of a sandwich panel is now available. 

Structural elements such as roofs, doors, curtain walls, etc., can now be designed from any of the systems. Considerable data have been accumulated on the status of cellular plastics materials in mature economies (for comparative purposes) on problems that might inhibit use of plastics applications and on process and production requirements from raw material to final product. 

The project has attracted considerable attention; more than 400 inquiries from 

Brazil, Colombia, Finland, Germany, Ghana, Israel, Italy, Samoa, and the United Kingdom have been received by the AID research staff. Articles referring to the project have appeared in numerous periodicals. 

Many companies in the plastics industry have contributed materials, facilities, and technical services to the project. Major contributions have been made by the Dow Chemical Co., Union Carbide Corp., Wyandotte Chemical Co., Binks 

Manufacturing Co., Pyles Indusries, Kimberly-Clark Co., Scott Papare Co., and 

Hercules Powder Co.

PROJECT TITLE THE INTERACTIONS OF SOCIAL VALUES AND POLITICAL RESPONSIBILITY Contractor.-University of Pennsylvania. 

Project objectives

This study is aimed at illuminating critical problems in the initiation of community activities at the grassroots or village level in India. It will first examine how traditional values held by local leaders affect the policy decisions they make on community development programs. It will then identify certain conditions (such as patterns of authority, communication channels, etc.) which can alter the impact of those values on the leaders' commitment to community development.

Justification The results of the study are expected- (1) To provide AID administrators with more effective methods of gaining the assistance of local leadership in implementing community development programs;

(2) To provide AID community planners with means of tailoring development alternatives to prevailing social structures. Accomplishments

Since the contract was signed in October 1964, the investigators have concluded arrangements to conduct the study with the cooperation of three local academic and research institutions and are currently developing their research instruments. The actual collection of data is scheduled to begin in June 1965; the initial results should be available in the spring of 1966. 

PROJECT TITLE-SYMPOSIUM ON RESEARCH ON THE DEVELOPMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE CAPACITY IN EMERGING COUNTRIES Contractor.-Brookings Institution. 

Project objectives 

By bringing together some 25 eminent social scientists and experts in public administration problems of the less developed countries, this symposium is intended: (1) To identify key research issues involved in the improvement of public administration in emerging countries, and thus to provide guidelines for an effective research program in that area; (2) To produce a volume integrating the prepared papers, the discussions, and the conclusions reached at the symposium, which will be widely distributed for use by AID and indigenous public administrators and researchers. Justification The shortage of adequately trained public administrators and, more generally, the limited administrative capacity of emerging countries are continuing to be major obstacles to development. The success of many AID programs depends on the extent to which these obstacles can be overcome. 

This symposium will help AID strengthen its research attack in this area and also help to enlist some of the best scientific talent for this purpose. Accomplishments

Since the contract was signed in November 1964, several planning conferences have been held at which the key issues have been sharpened and an agenda further developed. Advance research papers are being prepared, and a list of participants has been selected. The symposium is scheduled for the fall of 1965. 

PROJECT TITLE-VENEZUELAN DEVELOPMENT STUDY Contractor.-Simulmatics Corp. (through the Central University of Vene zuela).

Project objectives 

The purpose of this project is to test the usefulness in development planning of an advanced analytical technique-mathematical simulation—that has already proven useful in dealing with certain types of complex military problems. This technique involves developing a mathematical model which describes the effects of a change in one economic activity on all the others to which it is related. The model so developed permits more precise comparison of the potential effects of alternative policy decisions. 

The kinds of problems being addressed in the Venezuelan pilot study include the effects on rate of economic growth of changes in government policies regarding: public expenditures, balance of payments, investment patterns, and related matters. Justification

AID has recognized the need for improved planning by the less developed countries through its policy of providing planning assistance. Experience with this form of technical assistance has highlighted the need for new planning techniques. This project is testing one of the most promising techniques which, in identical or modified form, appears likely to be applicable to a number of countries. Accomplishments

Two simulation models have been developed. The more complex one is now being used to assist the Venezuelan Government planning organization (CORDI- PLAN) in developing certain elements of the 4-year plan for 1965-68. This has

demonstrated the utility of the simulation technique for this type of analysis. 

The simpler model is now being used by the university for training purposes. 

Thus the project's major objectives have been attained on a pilot basis, and the foundations are being laid for Venezuelan organizations (Central University, CORDIPLAN, and the central bank) to take over complete operation of the model, using people being trained in the ongoing study. 

An unanticipated benefit of this project was that it drew attention to significant improvements that can be made in the development, analysis, and use of information originating in the local economy. 

PROJECT TITLE-RESEARCH IN HEALTH MANPOWER PLANNING FOR SELECTED LESS DEVELOPED COUNTRIES Contractor.-Johns Hopkins University. 

Project objectives (1) To determine the health manpower needs of selected countries at different stages of development, and the current and projected availability of adequately trained manpower, with a view to identifying the nature and extent of shortages. (2) To compare alternative means of alleviating health manpower shortages and to determine the means most appropriate for selected nations and stages of development. (3) To devise appropriate methods of planning to meet national health needs. Justification

One of the most critical problems limiting the extension of health services in underdeveloped countries is the lack of qualified manpower. Methods currently employed are often not sufficiently responsive to local conditions and development trends and, therefore, are not fully effective. This study will attempt to devise means of alleviating the shortage rapidly and effectively. 

Accomplishments Field studies have been completed in Peru, Taiwan, and Turkey and are still underway in Nigeria.

Preliminary reports indicate that the findings should make possible more rational planning of health services and training of the requisite manpower by relating health planning to the needs and available resources at various stages of national development. The methodology will be applicable to the countries under study and, it is hoped, will be adaptable to other developing countries. 

PROJECT TITLE-MATHEMATICS CURRICULUM DEVELOPMENT IN AFRICA Contractor.-Educational Services, Inc. 

Project objective To develop and test new textbooks, work books, and teacher guides for improving instruction in elementary and secondary school mathematics in the Englishspeaking countries of Africa. Justification

A sound grasp of basic mathematics and science is essential for people in developing countries who wish to use technology for purposes of modernization. 

The present traditional mathematics curriculum, a holdover from colonial days, is deemed inadequate by all African countries. A new mathematics curriculum development program, involving Africans from the start, would not only produce superior instruction in this subject but would demonstrate to ministries of education an effective process whereby reforms in science teaching and other subjects could be effected. 

Accomplishments Three summer workshops have been held in Africa, each attended by 12-15 Americans and 40-50 key African mathematicians and educators. Texts and materials for grades 1, 2, and 3, and grades 7, 8, and 9 have been written and tested in schools. 

Teachers' guides have been produced for these grades and were used in 12 teacher training institutes held in 10 different African countries. Over 500 teachers have participated in these programs. In addition, 2 institutes for teachers of teachers were held in Nigeria and Tanganyika which over 100 senior instructors and professors of mathematics education attended.

At present over 400 classes in Ethiopia, Ghana, Kenya, Liberia, Nigeria, Sierra Leone, Tanzania, Uganda, and Zambia are using the texts on an experimental basis. It is anticipated that by 1968 a large part of the textbook production will have been tested and completed. teacher training activities will be at an advanced stage, and the local governments will be able to phase their resources into the project as AID support phases out. 

PROJECT TITLE.-SYMPOSIUM ON COMMUNICATION RESEARCH AND THE DEVELOP- MENT PROCESS Contractor.-Michigan State University. 

Project objectives 

The objectives of this symposium are: (1) To bring existing knowledge to bear on the role of communication in economic, social, and political development; (2) To assist AID in developing a sound strategy for programing its communication research effort; (3) To mobilize the best available research talent for this effort; (4) To produce a volume summarizing the symposium's findings in the above areas for wide dissemination to donors and recipients of technical assistance. Justification AID recognizes that the success of many of its development programs (e.g., public health, population growth, community development) depends on improving the form and content of, and institutional arrangements for, communication. 

It is now important to marshal the resources of the research community to increase understanding of the ways in which ideas and information are communicated in less developed countries. This symposium, which will include some 25 leading communications specialists, was organized as the most effective means of initiating this effort. 

Accomplishments The symposium is scheduled for early fall 1965. 

Several preparatory meetings have been held to formulate and help refine key issues.

REDUCTION OF EMPLOYEES AND CONTRACT SERVICES 

The CHAIRMAN. It has since been suggested that one way this is brought about is to take a number of people off your direct payroll and to let contracts to perform the duties, which does not, in effect, reduce the number. It merely changes them from being your employees to those of a contractor who hires them. Is this true?

Mr. BELL. I think that possibly to some small extent this has taken place. There has been a trend-which I have strongly encouraged in recent years-toward using the contract arrangement to a larger ex-, tent. This has two great advantages from the standpoint of the 

AID program. 

First, by contracting with universities, with cooperatives, with labor unions, with profit and nonprofit business, and private institutions, we can draw upon higher talents and greater competence than we could maintain on our permanent payroll. This is particularly valuable in the case of technical assistance projects where you need the highest and the best talent you can get from the American economy and society if you are to achieve the results you are after. 

Second, from an administrative standpoint it is vastly preferable to have a contract to handle and to carry out a technical assistance project because then when the project is finished and the contract is ended, the persons involved are not Government employees with some claim on continued Government employment. 

Part of the difficulty that we have today with personnel in our Agency clearly stems from the fact that 10 years ago people were taken on as direct hire, U.S. Government employees, to do a particular project. When that project was ended, they were shifted to some other work for which, in many cases, they were less well qualified, and they have continued in this sort of status to this day in many instances, not doing a first-class piece of work. In the process they have lost, many of them, the special technical competence that they had originally in a professional field, so that they do not now have the option of returning to their professional field, and they are involved in a program in which they are less than fully satisfactory Government employees. 

Now, this is the kind of situation which faces us today, and we are trying to do something about it, as this committee knows. But, nevertheless, it is a fact and one which we can avoid insofar as we handle our technical assistance projects by contracting with organizations that can get the competence or have it already. And when the project is finished, the people involved have another career and another employer to take care of them. So it is for these two reasons: (1) We believe we can get better competence this way; and (2) it fits far more naturally the nature of the work and the kind of system of doing business that is appropriate for our Agency, that we are relying more on contracting today than we have in the past. 

Now, coming back to your question about the reduction in our overall strength, if I remember the figures correctly, between the end of January 1964 and January 1965, we have cut about 1,400 employees, and the employees of our contractors doing this sort of technical assistance work have gone up by 295 during this same period so that there has been by no means a full offset. 

The CHAIRMAN. That is overall, including foreigners and everybody. 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; that is right.

Mr. BELL. That sounds right.

Mr. BELL. Roughly. I assume those figures came from our Agency.

APPRAISAL OF ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS

There are still certain countries [deleted] in which it would not be proper to say that the Alliance is fully operative, but in Brazil and Chile, in Central America, in Colombia, Peru, Ecuador, Bolivia-all with qualifications obviously-in Venezuela, in

Panama, there are strong and active programs underway. which are having some results.

PHYSICAL RESULTS OF ALLIANCE 

Mr. ROGERS. I think, Senator, if I can build on what Mr. Bell has said, we have seen a number of things in these last 12 months which are sources of quiet hope for us with respect to the Alliance. Solely with respect to the limited question of the U.S. effort, as you know and as is reflected in the presentation book here, the U.S. assistance to Latin 

America remained quite low compared to other regions in the world until the Alliance began. It has only been in the last 2 or 3 years that we have been increasing our level of assistance down there. We are now at the point just with respect to U.S. aid programs where we are beginning to see payout, and as the committee knows, I am sure, the physical results of the aid efforts are now becoming more and more apparent.

For example, during the current fiscal year, there will have been by June 30-solely as a result of U.S. assistance efforts to which the local countries make contributions-124,000 houses and roughly 12,000 classrooms built, more than 5 million school books distributed, several hundred mobile health centers, hospitals and health centers put in operation. We are touching the lives of a vast number of people with our programs.

NEED FOR SELF-HELP RECOGNIZED 

The second point, I think, that deserves emphasis, however, is the second point Mr. Bell made quite clear. These U.S. assistance programs are not conducted in isolation. They are taking hold now at the same time as the Latin Americans themselves are realizing more and more clearly what the Alliance is all about. Fundamentally the 

Alliance is a cooperative effort, in which the major burden of responsibility is on the Latin Americans, and this is now becoming clear to them. We saw this dramatically, I think, at the Lima meeting of the 

Inter-American Economic and Social Council to which the committee had its staff representative, on the verbal level and on the action level. The Latin Americans now realize that U.S. assistance, regardless of how generous, will not do the job of development, and they themselves are coming around and making the hard decisions. We are seeing this I think specifically in country after country. In Brazil we are now dealing with a government which for the first time since. the Alliance began seriously understands the problems of development, the problems of stabilization, the problems of reform, and is doing something about it. It has articulated a comprehensive program which runs across the board from credit restraints, a sensible foreign exchange policy, to effective land reform, increased taxes, and the other kind of things that have to happen in Brazil if we are ever going to have a sensible, decent, viable economy, society, political system in that country.

We are now dealing with, working with, cooperating with, supporting that kind of an effort in Brazil. hat kind

The same sort of thing is happening in Chile. We now have there for the first time a progressive reform-minded Government which is really dedicated to the Alliance. 

In Peru much the same thing is happening. Mexico, by the same token.

The results of this effort, I think, have become fairly important. 

TheAlliance has a very clear blueprint of the type of self-help reform efforts required. We total up the list with respect to tax reform. Nine countries have made major tax reform efforts. In the area of land reform-although the progress here frankly has not been as rapid as it has been in some other field-some dozen countries within the Alliance now have legislation which is the basis from which an effective land reform program can go forward. 

On national development planning, which was a keystone effort under the Charter of Punta del Este, some 10 countries have already completed the articulation of their plans and have submitted them for review.

In the housing field, very substantial progress, a legislative base for effective housing programs in some 15 different countries. With

Development banks, I think it is fair to say the result has been spectacular, both in private and public development banks. respect to the major effort that has to be made for capital marshaling institutions, since the Alliance began, some 13 countries have organized themselves with respect to development banking both in the private and public area.

Other areas of major progress: I think, progress toward regional integration in Central America, is particularly heartening. 

This is not to say, obviously, that the Alliance has finished its work. 

The problems of Latin America are profound as many of us who have worked there fully realize. What I think we are seeing now is pretty good evidence that the Alliance has set up the structural, theoretical, doctrinal framework, that the Latin Americans are coming to accept the things that they agreed upon in the Charter of Punta del Este; that they are realizing in country after country that the major responsibility is theirs and that ours is an effective supporting role, which only makes sense to the extent that the Latin Americans themselves are prepared to take the burden. 

MULTILATERALIZATION OF ALLIANCE 

And finally, the responsibility, the direction, the policy thrust of the Alliance is more and more becoming a multilateral institution, operation and effort. In this respect, of course as you know, the inauguration and first year's operation of CIAP has proved the effectiveness and desirability of that kind of multilateralization of what must in the last analysis be a cooperative effort. 

This, I think, is a sketch of some of the reasons why we feel, as I say, mildly and quietly encouraged that the Alliance is becoming more and more a viable effort in Latin America. 

Senator SPARKMAN. All right. Do you wish to add to that?

Mr. VAUGHN. I have nothing to add to that as regards the increasing optimism that we can share with regard to the physical and the structural institutional accomplishment of the Latin countries. I

think it is worth noting that sometimes we feel that there is backsliding because of political developments where there is a coup and a military dictator or military group takes over. I view this as something that is going to continue to happen occasionally. History shows that it has happened over and over again in the past 100 years, but that this essentially is a result of the problems in Latin America instead of a cause of the problems. 

When there is this overly centralized power and the social, economic, and political injustices, there will continue to be this ferment which will result in one group or another taking over temporarily. 

PARTICIPATION OF OTHERS IN THE ALLIANCE 

Senator SPARKMAN. Let me ask this question of either or both of you. When the program was set up, it was anticipated that we would have public and private participation by this country, that there would be participation by other countries of the free world, and that there would be participation by the Latin American countries themselves. I wonder how well that has been achieved to date. 

Mr. ROGERS. The rough breakdown, Senator, as you recall, that came out of the meeting at Punta del Este was that there would be a requirement over the 10 years of the Alliance for investment of all kinds, on an order of magnitude of roughly $100 billion. The charter made clear that $80 billion of that at least would have to be generated by Latin America itself. The history of the first 3 years of the 

Alliance indicates that the rough ratio between foreign-both public and private investment--and domestic, that is to say Latin America, on the order of four-fifths Latin America and one-fifth outside, that that ratio has been more than preserved. 

The fact of the matter is that the investment generated within Latin America has exceeded the approximately 80-percent figure that was discussed at Punta del Este. 

In addition to that, we have seen, I think, a growing flow of funds into Latin America, particularly in the last year or so, from two sources which I would note. One, the increased private U.S. net investment in Latin America.

You will recall that in 1962 there was a net drain. U.S. investors were taking money out more rapidly than they were putting it in. 

The number was minus $32 million. In 1963 the net U.S. investment was plus $64 million, and the preliminary data from the Department of Commerce indicate that net new U.S. private investment in 1964 was roughly approaching $150 million, which indicates a rising curve of private U.S. investment in the hemisphere. 

FLOW OF EXTERNAL RESOURCES TO LATIN AMERICA 

In addition to that, in terms of flow of external resources into Latin America, the flow from Europe and from Japan has likewise increased in a fairly healthy fashion, in part as a result of some of the efforts that we have been making with respect to the Europeans through the 

DAC and otherwise.

I might also mention that I think there is an encouraging development with respect to that, Senator. As you probably know, in part because we are so desirous of an expanding European participation,

we have made an effort with respect to the Europeans to interest them in participation in the CIAP country review process. Our theory has been that if they had an opportunity to participate in this coordinated multilateral analysis of the country development effort, they themselves would understand the opportunities with respect to further assistance on their part to Latin America and, furthermore, would be able to better coordinate their aid efforts in Latin America. 

This has been fairly successful. Already two of the countries have indicated that they are prepared to participate in these country reviews formally through letters to Dr. Sanz de Santamaria, and the other countries have informally said to us that they are quite interested in participating in the CIAP country reviews which will be formed this year, so we are hoping this will be another step toward more effective participation of Europeans in the Alliance effort. 

Senator SPARKMAN. In other words, your report is to the effect that overall it is following pretty much the pattern that was laid down. 

You say it even exceeds the Latin American participation. 

Mr. ROGERS. Even exceeds. The private U.S. investment in the earlier years has been lower than the figure that was talked about at Punta del Este; it was an arbitrary $300 million figure. 

Senator SPARKMAN. How does the curve look?

Mr. ROGERS. The curve is up, and I think largely as a function of what is happening in Brazil, I anticipate that the curve will go up even further. 

DEVELOPMENTS IN ARGENTINA Senator SPARKMAN. [Deleted.] In Argentina has the curve been due primarily to political instability?

Mr. ROGERS. I think the political point is the one that needs to be touched on first. As you will recall, Senator, since the Alliance was instituted, there was a military coup in the country. President Frondizi was ejected from office. After about a year of interim government, the present civilian government headed by President Illia was elected. 

He has been in office now for 17 months if my recollection serves. 

Two things have been at work. No. 1, the whole country has been looking toward the elections which occurred yesterday, and the anticipation of those elections was colored by several things. One, the threatened return of ex-President Peron, who tried and failed, as you will recall, to get back in. [Deleted.] And second, the extent to which the Peronista party would be allowed to participate. 

You will recall in the presidential election in 1963, the Peronista parties, largely as a result of the limitations laid down on their participation, the extent to which they could campaign for Peron and what-have-you, refused to vote and cast a large number of blank ballots. The question was whether or not Illia could go forward with an election yesterday which would allow the Peronista parties to participate fully without, in effect, endangering the democratic process. 

He did this. 

You know the results of the election which primarily indicate more or less a standoff between the Illia party and the Peronista party. My own instinct-although I am not the world's greatest expert on Argentina-the fact that the election occurred and there was full participation by the Peronistas and peaceful participation and there was in

effect a democratic election is itself a tribute to the possibilities of democracy in Argentina. 

But in effect, as a result of this long history of political instability, there have been some problems. 

In addition to that, the Illia party has been working on the development of a national development plan. They are about finished with that. Their Government is looking toward presentation of the plan to the CIAP, and the analysis of possible lending opportunities by the World Bank. 

Senator SPARKMAN. Let me ask you this question for a quick answer:

I take it that you feel encouraged over the Brazilian situation? 

Mr. ROGERS. Very.

PUBLIC VERSUS PRIVATE INVESTMENT IN LATIN AMERICA Senator HICKENLOOPER. What are we doing in Latin America under this program to encourage not government-supported projects, such as housing and land development, but business development. Are they really selling stock to the public in ventures and enterprises,

bond issues, stock issues, and all that, where the public puts up the money under a private enterprise system, or is it foreign aid money and some alleged Government money that goes into these enterprises? 

The reason I say that is I have learned of two or three places in Latin America where they have finally got around to being able to sell stock issues to the public so there is a wide participation in that business, like the A.T. & T. in this country or something like that. But I have also heard, I should say, about a lot of attempts that have been made down there but the government machinery has so fouled it up that the potential investors can talk about these things but they cannot actually do them. The government steps in and wants to participate in these matters and refuses or circumscribes private investment opportunities which otherwise might further the middle-class development and participating ownership by the public in these things. 

What is the situation there?

Mr. ROGERS. My own rough feeling about it, Senator, is that really effective private stock markets of the kind that we have here and in Europe, sir, may be one of the last things you get in the development process.

In part, this is a result of the fact of long tradition of Latin American restricted ownership of individual firms, and also the fact that in many cases countries don't have the legislation to protect minority stockholders that we have here, and hence it is very easy to lose your shirt if you invest in a minority position in Latin American countries. 

I don't want to put too fine a point on the difficulty of really creating a large private stock market, but it is there in most Latin American countries, and it is bucking a long tradition. We have been working on the problem in a number of ways. 1 

Senator HICKENLOOPER. Of course, we are bucking a tradition in 

Latin America of a thin veneer of the elite at the top who have run the economic and social and political problems for 400 years. 

Mr. BELL. Exactly. 

Senator HICKENLOOPER. I had hoped that under our system we could try to show them the way to break that order down. That is to say not to demand they do exactly as we do, but to try to convince them that the road to prosperity is in the creation of a strong middle class, and about the only way you can do that is to have the middle class participate in the economic development of the country. 

If we just say, "Oh, well, it's their tradition; they have always done it that way and we can't buck it; we will turn the money over to the government and let the government get in here to do this." I would think we would, in a measure, be contributing to the continuation of that tradition of the top echelon running the show all the time and being in control. 

Mr. ROGERS. Let me tell you what we are doing in respect to this, Senator. What we are trying not to do is turn the money over to the government and leave it to them. 

I think one of the most important things we have thought for a long time, one of the things we could get at, was the problem of middle class getting a sense of investment, savings, homeownership, that kind of thing. We have made major effort with respect to savings and loan associations, credit unions, cooperatives, outside the govern-

ment itself, largely in order to stimulate private investment, private savings, and middle-class ownership. 

Certainly, we have done an awful lot with respect to the intermediate credit institutions such as development banks, particularly in Central America where we just about have completed the establishment of private development banks in each country in the Central American area. What we are trying to do through these development banks is expand the sense of stock ownership, expand the little guy's chance to get credit on reasonable terms so that he can set up his own industry and expand the number of owners and entrepreneurs. 

In fact, one of our men in the inspection staff just came back from Central America, took the trouble to go out and talk to some of the little fellows who for the first time had access to these banks as a result of their establishment in Central America. He was told over and over again that the loans they had been able to get from these private banks were the things which had saved their enterprises and that they would not be in business at the present time had it not been for this access of credit to small and growing industries in the Central American region largely inspired by these private development banks. 

GOVERNMENT INTERFERENCE IN PRIVATE INVESTMENT Senator HICKENLOOPER. I have been to South America several times, but on special trips to some particular place for a purpose. I haven't been to South America on a sort of round robin visit for some little time. But I remember beginning 6, 7, or 8 years ago, we thought there were a number of very good ideas on the part of private investors down there. They said there was a vast market for houses; that is, for private investors.

I think Senator Carlson had one man appear before us here who said: "We are willing to put in a lot of money. We want some guarantees. We want some backing." This is private money. This is selling houses to middle-class people. But they say: "We run up against the bar of government. We run up against the law. There is a very limited amount we could do. We can do five times as much." 

One witness had charts and programs. His was a very reputable outfit. I talked to three others down there in various countries. They may have been exaggerating a little-I don't know-but they said: "This is what we could do if they would just let us go." 

Mr. ROGERS. That is right.

Senator HICKENLOOPER. They say, "These people are avid to buy these places and we can't furnish as much as a tenth because we are chopped off by our own government, by credit, and by the local governments. The government officials want to have their finger in the promoting and financing of these things and we are stymied." I wonder if that is breaking down somewhat. 

Mr. ROGERS. I think this, Senator, is one of the things relevant to that list of reforms I was talking about before. Housing legislation has been enacted by a number of countries, in part through technical assistance that we have provided-experts to draft housing legislation-which has opened up the housing picture a little bit. And in addition, of course, you have our all-risk guarantees on housing which

are now all ready by the 31st of December at the $84 million level, and we hope to finish Senator HICKENLOOPER. Do you think we are making progress along that line?

Mr. ROGERS. I don't want to overstate it because the housing gap is enormous. The problem of creating secondary mortgage markets, for example, and getting modern legislation throughout Latin Amer ica to solve the housing problem is enormous. It is going to take time. 

Senator HICKENLOOPER. Yes. 

Mr. ROGERS. But we are seeing something done, I think.

Senator HICKENLOOPER. Mr. Bell, offhand I think I can see some merit in your using contract people to do certain work rather than to use Government employees. I think there is some validity in your argument that if you use a capable contractor to do some of this work, that when the work is finished the employees don't have Government tenure, so they don't have all the protection that goes along with civil service. You don't have them frozen on the Federal payroll, so you have to find something else for them to do.

EXAMINATION OF FOREIGN AID REQUEST 

Mr. Chairman, I have a great many questions to ask the administration, not only in my behalf, but in behalf of a substantial number of Senators who vigorously oppose the Fulbright bill, who vigorously oppose a substantial number of recommendations made in the total foreign aid program by the President. 

We feel that we have an obligation, of course, at least to offer to try to make a record before the committee, whether it is done in a day or a fortnight. But I respectfully point out to my colleagues in this committee that great time will be saved if we go about in good faith meeting the convenience of members of the administration and the committee in making this record. If the record is not made here, it is going to be made upstairs on the floor of the Senate. 

I had hoped that the progress that was made, I thought, prior to adjournment last fall, in trying to work out some informal conferences with AID and the State Department concerning the objections that of us had made in the past 2 years, might have avoided the timeconsuming discussion that is now going to take place around this table or on the floor of the Senate. some The then Assistant Secretary for Latin America, Mr. Mann, said there was a desire down at the AID-State Department level-to discuss with a group of us the minority reports that the senior Senator from Oregon, not in his own behalf alone but in behalf of others,

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, made during the last 2 years to see to what extent we could narrow our areas of disagreement. He can speak for himself. I only want to say I was very pleased with the comments he made about the obvious desire on the part of State Department people and AID people to see if we couldn't reach better understandings. For I interpret his comments to mean, as I have interpreted some of the comments of the chairman of this committee to mean, that there is a recognition that there is a considerable amount of merit to some of our objections to the foreign aid program. I wanted to make a little statement at the beginning of my first round of questions this morning. 

I think the procedure that is being followed in the handling of the foreign aid bill this year cannot be sold to the American people, and I think that that is going to be demonstrated in the months ahead. But be that as it may, of those of us that disagree both with the procedure and the substance, I intend to use every right we have as Senators to make our record.

ADMINISTRATION RECOMMENDATION ON LEGISLATION 

My first question, Mr. Bell, will you tell the committee why you think the Johnson administration has changed the parliamentary strategy this year by sending up the President's message but notfollowing the past practice, I think, going back to the Marshall planaccompanying it with a request for the introduction of a bill which carries out the recommendations of the message. 

Mr. BELL. The President's position, sir, has been that he has placed his substantive recommendations before the Congress. 

Furthermore, as a drafting service the executive branch has made available to the relevant committee staffs and to any individual members who are interested, different forms of legislation in which these substantive recommendations could be embodied. There has been, as you know, sir, a difference of view between some of the key leaders in the Senate and their opposite numbers in the House as to whether it would be preferable to have the recommendations all embodied in one piece of legislation, or in two. The position that the President has taken thus far is that that is a matter for the Senate and the House to consider, and his hope is that the Congress will adopt legislation whether in one bill or two which will carry out the recommendations he has made.

Senator MORSE. It is true, is it not, that that was not the parliamentary policy followed by Presidents Truman, Eisenhower, and Kennedy in regard to submitting foreign aid programs to the Congress? 

Mr. BELL. I am not sure that I can speak with authority on those occasions. I do recall in 1961 President Kennedy considered very seriously the possibility of having military and economic assistance in separate legislation. 

Senator MORSE. That is not what I am talking about, Mr. Bell. I am talking about whether or not Presidents Truman, Eisenhower, and Kennedy sent to the Congress, accompanying their foreign aid messages, a recommended bill carrying out their messages. This I respectfully submit is the responsibility of any President, and Congress has its responsibility to modify that bill in any way it wants to.

My question is this: Can you cite to me a single year in which past 

Presidents have not made recommendations for the passage of an obnibus bill?

Mr. BELL. I think, sir, as I understand what was done in the past, the President, as he did this year, sent recommendations, sent a message which embodied and included recommendations as to the amount of the assistance that he asked to be authorized, amendments to the existing legislation that he would like to have passed, and so on. It was the practice as far as I am aware, to send to the Congress a form of legislation which would carry out the President's recommendations. 

I am not aware of a year in which-although I repeat I haven't checked the records-I am not aware of a year in which, like the present year, two or three alternative forms of such legislation were sent to the Congress. 

Senator MORSE. Now, Mr. Chairman, I make my first request for a staff memorandum. I shall make a good many in the days ahead. 

My first request for a staff memorandum is that Dr. Marcy prepare or have prepared for me, for insertion in the record, a memorandum, in answer to the question I have just asked, setting forth the procedures that have been followed by Presidents Truman, Eisenhower, and Kennedy in the matter of submitting foreign aid messages to the Congress and bills relative thereto. (The information referred to follows:)

Memorandum to: Senator Morse. 

From: Carl Marcy. 

MARCH 17, 1965.

Pursuant to your request at the committee meeting on March 15, there is attached a memorandum setting forth the procedures that have been followed by Presidents Truman, Eisenhower, Kennedy, and Johnson in submitting foreign aid messages to the Congress and bills relative thereto. 

In those cases where the memorandum does not specify whether a draft bill was formally or informally transmitted, it is the staff's recollection that in all instances a draft bill embodying the recommendations of the administration was furnished by the executive branch. The printed records of the committee (calendars, legislative histories, and committee reports), however, do not show this information and a lengthy search of the legislative files, many of which are at the National Archives, would be needed to verify the staff's recollection.

EXTENT OF DOMESTIC PROCUREMENT 

Senator CARLSON. Mr. Chairman, I thought we were going to continue on the Latin American Alliance for Progress. I am not an expert on that nor am I in any field. I do have some questions on the general policy of foreign aid, and I do have some on Latin America, but if the chairman does not object, I would like to dwell on the overall policy.

I have some problems with the statement that has been made for years, that for 80 percent of our contributions to foreign aid, purchases are made in the United States. Therefore it has no effect on the balance of payments. I noticed in the statement submitted to the committee here it says 85 percent.

Mr. BELL. Of new commitments, Senator. 

Senator CARLSON. Of new commitments, and I think February 12 

of this year you issued a release that AID procurement in the United States hit a record of 94 percent. 

Mr. BELL. That was commodities only, Senator.

Senator CARLSON. I have tried to get this clear, because I have always had difficulty with that problem on how we are going to get this money back. Kindly explain it to me. 

 On Friday, I believe it was, I offered and the committee accepted for the record a statement I made before the 

Banking and Currency Committee last Tuesday. I mention this only because that was an attempt to provide a full and careful statement as to the exact situation. 

Senator CARLSON. That will help me. I have had some problems with it for years, not just now. 

Mr. BELL. Let me say it quickly this way. The appropriations. which had been voted under the heading "Economic assistance" are as you well know, spent under loans or grants for goods and services. 

At the present time of the total amount of economic assistance avail-

able under the responsibility of my agency, about a little over 85 percent is being committed for expenditure in the United States, directly for U.S. goods and services. When we make a loan, for example, to 

Brazil for a power station, that really consists of a letter of credit. 

We are saying to the Brazilians, "We will make you this loan for purchases in the United States, the equipment, engineering services and other things that you will need and when you buy them in the United States, we will pay for them with the dollars voted to you by the Congress."

That is the typical pattern of the loans we make today. All of our development loans in that sense are tied to procurement in the United. States.

The expenditures as against the current commitments, the actual expenditures made by AID in calendar year 1964, there was almost exactly $2 billion of expenditures and the offshore part of that expenditure was $403 million. It was almost exactly 80 percent spent in the United States, 20 percent spent abroad. 

Now, the new commitments being somewhat higher than that, the expenditure proportion being spent in the United States will gradually rise further. We think that we are about at the maximum. 

We think 85 to 90 percent is as high as we are going to be able to make the proportion spent in the United States because there are three elements of our program which involve oversea dollar costs. 

OVERSEA DOLLAR COSTS 

First of all, we have people stationed around the world. To some extent they are going to be spending money where they live. We have run surveys on this, and the figures show that they spend abroad about 30 percent of their salaries. The rest they spend in the United 

States or bank it for savings. They spend it for schooling or payments on their houses back here, and so on. But nevertheless there is some offshore expenditure necessarily associated with people being stationed abroad, and this program can't be run without having people stationed abroad. This applies to direct-hire people and it applies to the employees of our contractors. 

Secondly, a part of this bill, as you know, represents contributions. to international organizations, to Paul Hoffman's special fund, and to the Indus Basin Fund, and so on. Such contributions by the unbroken international traditions since the end of World War II are always made in convertible currency and on the Department of Commerce books they show as a direct outflow of dollars. In fact, some of them are spent in the United States. Nevertheless, on the books they show as an outflow. 

Senator CARLSON. Do you count this as part of the 85 percent??

Mr. BELL. They are part of the 15 percent, sir, of the dollars. 

Senator CARLSON. That is on the other side.

 And in addition to this we have thus far, and we expect to continue, to permit some limited portion of our expenditures of expenditures under economic aid, particularly under supporting assistance-to be made not in the advanced countries of Europe and Japan, but in the less developed countries. Therefore, some of the things we are providing today, say in Vietnam, like cement, we are

buying not in the United States but in Taiwan, to save the taxpayer obviously a very large amount of money. It is a small part of this 15 percent net dollar drain. We think that it is, on balance, appropriate and proper to do this. 

Because of these three elements we think, as I say, that the proportion spent in the United States is not going to get much higher than 85 to 90 percent. But that is pretty good. It means that the net dollar drain cost of the foreign assistance program is now below $500 million, and getting smaller, and that doesn't take account of repayments. 

Last year, in the calendar year 1964, there was received some $150 million in repayments. This was dollars or local currency in countries where the local currency is as good as dollars, from previous AID loans and interest on previous AID loans or loans made by our predecessor agencies; so that the net cost wasn't $400 million but $250 million last year.

INDIRECT EFFECTS 

This is, in a nutshell, what I said to the Banking and Currency Committee. These figures that I have been using are essentially accounting figures. They are related to the Department of Commerce's system for calculating the balance of payments. 

Economists feel, and quite correctly, that they are an inadequate set of figures, because they don't reflect indirect effects, and there are indirect effects in both directions. Of the funds that we make available to the United Nations, for example, some are spent back in the United States. They call this the feedback effect. Of the fund that we tie to procurement in the United States, to some extent that offsets purchases which might be made commercially by the country where we make the loan.

The best economic calculations that we have been able to make indicate that these two indirect effects offset each other, and that the accounting estimate of 80 or 85 percent is as accurate as you can get an estimate of the real economic impact of the foreign assistance program on the American balance of payments. Does this respond to your question, sir?

DOLLAR GRANTS 

Senator CARLSON. Do you not make dollar grants to countries? 

Mr. BELL. No, sir, typically we do not make dollar grants. Typically we make grants of goods and services which are valued on our books in dollar terms. 

Senator CARLSON. Has that always been the policy?

Mr. BELL. No, sir, it has not. It has been changed very sharply in recent years. Ten years ago the typical arrangement was that the AID appropriations were spent wherever in the world prices were lowest. 

But beginning in 1959 this policy was very sharply changed and today the situation is as I have described. 

Now, there are one or two remaining cases. I think the testimony, as I indicated, showed as stated that in calendar 1964 we did make dollars available to the extent of $66 million of this $2 billion total; $36 million of that was in Jordan alone, which was paid out month to month to meet Government expenses-not to provide foreign exchange. 

We expect that the actual dollars granted under the AID program in the calendar year 1965 will be down to the order of $40 million, and it will continue to diminish. 

There will still be a few odds-and-ends cases where some AID purpose can only be served by actually making dollars available, but it is a very tiny proportion of the total.

MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO LATIN AMERICA 

Senator PELL. Finally, I have a basic philosophical objection to giving military aid to any of these Latin American countries, and usually tend to vote against it. What is the rationale? In the end it seems to me that one man gets it and then the man next door wants it and in the end the government changes and they are pointed against us. 

One man gets a destroyer and the next man wants a cruiser. Is there

any thought of ending military assistance to these underdeveloped nations?

Mr. BELL. The essential point with respect to Latin America-and my colleagues may wish to supplement what I am going to say nowis that over the last 3 or 4 years we have shifted very sharply from a military assistance program which was intended to build a hemispheric defense that was the theory of it, that was the pattern or plan-to a program which is directed toward helping these countries have sufficient and appropriate military forces to insure internal stabilityinternal security primarily against guerrilla-type activities, led and fomented from Cuba and by the various Communist movements down there and to a lesser extent to contribute through civic action to the economic and social progress of the country, through the work of engineer battalions, and that sort of thing. 

Now, this change in philosophy has been very dramatically reflected in the kind of equipment which is provided. We do not today provide tanks and destroyers and heavy equipment. We do provide jeeps and communications gear and engineering equipment and this sort of thing. 

Now, when you make this kind of a change it must be done gradually, but it is perfectly clear that the change has been made. 

Senator PELL. Is our distributing 10,000 police truncheons or 20,000 

45's and small arms not philosophically offensive?

Mr. BELL. No, sir; I don't see why that should be offensive at all. 

Our police assistance program has been, I think, extremely successful and one of the reasons it has been successful is the attitude of the people who have been running it; the training that we have been giving has been so clearly informed and based on the philosophy of law and order within a democratic framework. 

Senator, I would urge you and I would be delighted to make arrangements, if you are willing to do this, to come out and visit the police academy that we are operating out here in Georgetown, some rooms made over from that old Capital Transit headquarters building. 

We rent space out there. There is ordinarily a group of police officers from Latin America in training there, and we also have a worldwide training course.

Senator PELL. It is one thing to train a man and another to send out equipment. My query is not on the training. It is on sending out the equipment which might be misused. 

Mr. BELL. If you are going to train them, as we have been doing, for example, in Caracas, to operate against urban terrorists, they will need jeeps, they will need radios, and we have helped to provide that sort of thing and have made some equipment grants of that kind. 

Now, you are entirely correct. Both military and police organizations represent an organized force and they are subject to misuse in any society, including our own. 

We attempt to promote the development of democratic societies and through our training, through our continuing advice and efforts of our diplomatic representatives, through the international organizations that we are a part of, to contribute to the use of such elements of social force in the direction of democracy, and of a free society. We certainly would not claim 100-percent success. 

Senator PELL. Thank you, Mr. Bell. Would you like to add anything?

MILITARY TRAINING OF LATIN AMERICAN OFFICERS IN THE UNITED STATES 

Mr. BELL. Before responding to that, Senator, could I add one word about the comments that you quote [deleted] about training in the States. We do, as he said, bring officers to the United States, not only to Leavenworth but to other military schools, and in the last 2 or 3 years there has been a substantial effort while those men are here to expose them to more than simply the military training at that school, and to expose them, to let them see something of our society and how our economy works, to visit people in their homes, to visit businesses, farms, and so on, so that they get a much broader impression of the American society than they would simply from their attendance at the military school.

The results of the training over the years of Latin American military officers and those from other parts of the world seem to be very promising and very encouraging. These men do come to understand something about the potential role of a responsible military force in a democratic society, and there is overwhelming testimony that the younger and rising leaders in Latin America are far less inclined to think of themselves as potential dictators, and are much more inclined to think of themselves as participating in a process of economic, social, and political progress in their own country. 

Furthermore, quite contrary to what your fellow told you, the policy of the U.S. Government is to bring young Ecuadorians to American universities. We are not afraid of that at all. We have got lots of them here, and we hope to have a lot more, and we have several important contracts with American universities to work with Ecuadorian universities which involves bringing Ecuadorians to the home base of that university to prepare them to become instructors and so on.

Senator CLARK. And getting some training in administration, I believe. 

Mr. BELL. That is right.

EFFECT OF TERMINATING MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

Now, to come to your question about what do we think the effect would be. This is really a question that I should perhaps defer to 

Jack Vaughn. My impression, however, if I may state it first, is that with the organized and strongly led subversive type of training and supply of equipment and cadres of leadership stemming from Cuba and from other places, from behind the Iron Curtain and in Communist China that is going on, that it would be very unwise of us to terminate the strong program we now have both in the police field and in the military field to improve the competence of the Latin American forces for dealing with the internal security problem. 

I do not think we are by any means through with the period in which there are serious risks of guerrilla-type activity in a number of the Latin American countries. 

Senator CLARK. [Deleted.] That is all I have, Mr. Chairman. 

The CHAIRMAN. Senator Hickenlooper, do you have a question?

IMPORTANCE OF MILITARY TRAINING Senator HICKENLOOPER. Of course I am not familiar with all of the details, but it is my considered opinion that if it had not been for the training that we gave the military in the Latin American countries, you would see Peron back in Argentina, Brazil down the drain by now, Colombia and Venezuela very far toward Communist influence. 

The military in these countries, and in several others, have been the real safety valve on this thing. I do not know of any of those countries where the military has stepped in and become an oppressive dictatorship, that is, in modern times. 

That was the case a few years ago, but these new officers that are coming along have been trained probably more efficiently in the responsibilities of self-government than they have in the military. I am not so sure very many of them are very expert in the military field, but I think they really got a lot of ideas about responsible self-government. 

So far as I have been able to observe, they are the safety valve in this picture. When they have to step in, they step in to protect their country from going clear over the brink into-I do not know whether it is practical communism-but complete collectivism that would be associated with what we call international communism. They have been caretakers, and when the situation stabilized itself, they have turned the power back in almost every case to civilian government. I think they have not turned it back yet in Bolivia, but I have talked to some Bolivians in the last month or so-one of whom I have known for some little time, and another one I knew about, and who were fundamentally oriented, I think, toward self-government and to the private responsibility system-and they say very frankly that they do not particularly like military government, but that this particular five-

man junta they have now is basically directed toward the stabilization of that situation and is looking toward elections that will support the private responsibility system. 

I think our activities with the military down there in these training programs have been very successful, and they have held the lid on down there. It was the military and the military alone that saved 

Brazil. If it had not been for the stabilizing effect of the military in 

Brazil, they would have been over the brink, and we don't know what would have happened down there.

STATEMENT OF HON. WILLIAM PROXMIRE, A U.S. SENATOR FROM THE STATE OF WISCONSIN 

Senator PROXMIRE. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Chairman, I might say that we did call the committee to find out how much time I might have, and it was indicated there was no limitation. Now, I am going to be as rapid as I can. 

This is a very complicated situation, but I will put as much as possible in the record.
