SUPPORTING OIL PRICE BILL, S. 1069 

Senator PROXMIRE. Mr. Chairman, I am appearing before your committee today in support of my bill to prohibit the payment of "posted" prices for oil by the Agency for International Development as well as the payment of any barter agent's commission by anyone other than the supplier of barter commodities or the country receiving barter aid.

This bill was first introduced in the last session of Congress in the form of an amendment to last year's Foreign Assistance Act. It was incorporated into the act after discussion with Chairman Fulbright 44-834-65-15 217

resulted in its modification on the floor of the Senate. However, the amendment was rejected in a conference between the two Houses on the Foreign Assistance Act. This rejection was due in part to the fact that the House had not had a chance to take up the proposal in committee and in part to an adverse recommendation by the executive branch-that is, the Agency for International Development. 

By reintroducing this legislation as S. 1069 on February 9 of this year, I have given the House Foreign Affairs Committee ample time to carefully consider its implications. It is my purpose in appearing before this committee to point out the many inaccuracies and badly reasoned criticisms contained in the executive branch comments. 

SUBSTANCE OF SECTION (1) OF S. 1069 

First, I would like as briefly as possible to outline the substance of S. 1069 and indicate the problems it was meant to correct. 

The first part of the bill would require petroleum products procured with AID funds to be purchased at a "price generally charged by the supplier in comparable export sales from the source company at the time of purchase" or, and this is a very important "or," to which I will refer later in my testimony, under formal competitive bid procedures. The term "comparable export sales" as used in the bill does not include sales to affiliates. 

Why are sales to affiliates excluded from consideration by S. 1069?

Simply put, it is because transactions between the seven international oil companies and their affiliates are conducted at purchase rates, termed "posted" prices, fully 20 to 40 percent above competitive world prices for petroleum products. There are good reasons for these artificial transactions. Basically they are meant to give the international oil companies certain tax breaks. 

For example, a company has oil production facilities in Saudi Arabia and a processing affiliate in France. Prices posted at the wellhead are 20 to 40 percent in excess of the competitive world price. 

The French affiliate pays the abnormally high price, deducts it as a cost of doing business from its tax return and thus escapes the high French tax rate on the extra money it paid to the Saudi Arabian operation for its oil. Saudi Arabia charges a uniform per barrel tax on oil produced within its boundaries, regardless of the price paid by the French affiliate. Consequently, the extra amount paid by the 

French affiliate for the oil is not taxes in Saudi Arabia. 

This may make good sense in terms of the internal transactions of international oil companies. But it does not make sense for the 

Government to pay these posted prices. Nevertheless, AID currently pays posted prices which, I repeat, are used by seven international oil companies in transactions with affiliates to gain tax advantages. 

This is the situation the first part of my bill was framed to meet. 

SUBSTANCE OF SECTION (2) OF S. 1069 

The second part of my proposal provides that none of the funds made available under the Foreign Assistance Act shall be used to pay any barter agent's commission in any case in which commodities or defense articles furnished to a recipient are procured through the barter of other commodities or articles. It also requires that "any such commission, charge, or fee be paid by the supplier of the commodities or defense articles so furnished or the recipient country."

At the present time a barter transaction is used to facilitate the purchase by a country receiving American aid of products which are not available from the United States, without disrupting further our balance-of-payments situation by using American dollars to buy the needed commodity overseas. It works this way: 

A country receives, let's say, $100 million in foreign aid funds from the United States. The country wishes to use this money to purchase $10 million worth of an item not available in the United States. Under a barter arrangement it authorizes the transfer of $10 million to the Commodity Credit Corporation, which in turn releases $10 million worth of American commodities such as wheat or corn to a barter contractor. These commodities are sold to an eligible country by a barter contractor for American dollars. The contractor then uses these dollars to purchase on the international market the commodity needed by the country receiving foreign aid from the United States. 

Until recently, when AID began to request that the Commodity Credit Corporation pay barter agents with additional commodities, barter agents were paid by the foreign supplier of the product needed by the country receiving aid. This was done through a reduction of the supplier's anticipated profits from the sale of the goods required by the aid recipient.

I want to emphasize that this was a standard procedure which was not in dispute. The Commodity Credit Corporation does not pay an agent's commission unless requested to do so by AID. In fact, the initiation of this practice in the area of oil is setting a dangerous precedent for other Government commodity transactions. My bill is intended to nip this practice in the bud. 

EXECUTIVE BRANCH COMMENTS TO PROPOSALS IN S. 1069 

I would like to turn to the executive branch comments I mentioned earlier in my presentation as one of the reasons my proposal was knocked out of the Foreign Assistance Act by a conference of both Houses. Let me say at the outset that this memorandum is composed of half-truths, unsubstantiated statements, and perfectly acceptable statements of fact, which, however, are irrelevant to the questions raised by S. 1069.

In commenting on the reasons why AID opposes the posted price prohibition contained in my measure, the memorandum makes a number of points. The first, as I understand it, is that the proposal would result in no savings to the Government but would merely mean an increased administrative burden. 

DISCREPANCY BETWEEN WORLD AND POSTED OIL PRICES 

AID is incorrect in stating that there would be no savings to the Government. In order to point up the discrepancy existing between posted prices and world competitive prices I would like to read to the committee a statement made by Mr. Howard W. Page, a director of the 

Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey, at a symposium at Princeton Univer sity in 1963:

Whatever price stability or rigidity may have existed in international oil is a thing of the past as a result of rapidly changing conditions in the last 5 years. Actual sales prices for Persian Gulf crudes have fallen 45 cents a barrel for the heaviest grades to as much as 65 cents for the lightest crudes since their 1957-58 peak. This is a drop of about 25 to 30 percent in actual

prices, compared to a decline of not more than 14 percent (26 to 28 cents per barrel) in posted prices. In considering crude oil prices, it is important to distinguish clearly between posted prices and actual prices. Posted prices are used to determine government revenue in the Middle East. There is sometimes a tendency to equate posted prices with the actual market. Unfortunately, this is no longer the case, and rigidity in posted prices should not be taken to imply rigidity in actual prices for crude oil and in realization from the ultimate sale of products. Prices of fuel products declined nearly $1.20 a barrel or almost one-fourth, between 1958 and 1962, in five European countries with free markets not controlled by the government. 

POSTED PRICES ARE PAID BY AID FOR OIL 

In the body of the executive memorandum, AID admits that posted prices are being paid for approximately 55 percent of AID-financed petroleum sales of approximately $100 million. In other words, $55 million worth of these sales are being financed at posted prices. Assuming the posted price markup was an average 30 percent, the saving to our Government through paying competitive rather than posted prices would be approximately $161/2 million. 

Bulk fuels (gasoline and kerosene) constituted 50 percent of AIDfinanced sales of petroleum products in 1964. Of this 50 percent, half went to Korea and was financed under competitive prices through the use of Defense Department stocks. Forty percent went to Vietnam and Laos at posted prices. AID contends that affiliates own storage and distribution facilities in the recipient countries, Vietnam and Laos, and must buy from the major suppliers at posted prices. 

I know of no law that requires affiliates to buy oil from major suppliers. I hope that this committee will question AID as to the legal basis for such a statement. In my estimation, this sort of a requirement is not only illogical and immoral but is illegal under the accepted standards set up by our Federal antitrust laws. 

If, as AID indicates in the memorandum, there is virtually no discounting from posted prices for movements of bulk fuels into the Far East, AID should encourage competition to develop by requiring advertised bidding. It may be true that the comparable export sales which my bill would ask AID to use as a yardstick do not exist but my proposal does not require the use of such a yardstick if the purchase price of oil is determined under formal competitive bid procedures. 

How can we expect a competitive market to develop if AID does not permit competitive bidding for that market? 

DEFENSE DEPARTMENT BUYS OIL AT WORLD PRICES 

As pointed out in the AID memorandum, the Defense Department does procure under "highly favorable, long-term, large-quantity contracts." In fact, the Defense Department has never to my knowledge buckled under by paying these exorbitant posted prices. If the Defense Department, which buys oil all over the world, under all kinds of circumstances, does not pay posted prices, how can AID justify such a policy?

The AID memorandum calls the Defense Department transactions noncomparable because of the "quantity factor as well as other factors." What are these other factors? Does the quantity factor alone account for the 30 to 40 percent price difference between Defense Department prices and posted prices? These are the sorts of vague, generalized statements that AID should be forced to back up with facts and figures.

AFFILIATES ONLY BUY FROM PARENT OIL COMPANY 

Lubricants constituted 35 percent of AID-financed sales of petroleum products in 1964. Two-thirds of these lubricants were in bulk form and were paid for at bulk prices, once again because they were imported by affiliates of the major oil companies. AID claims "they must be imported by affiliates of major oil companies because they are the firms with the facilities to receive, blend, and/or package bulk shipments."

Why should these affiliates not be required to receive, blend, and package bulk shipments procured under a competitive bidding procedure? If this is not possible the vertical integration of the oil industry calls out for application of our antitrust laws with a vengeance. 

If antitrust laws are not effective in such circumstances, advertised competitive bidding procedures would at least provide the basis for a competitive market and lower prices in the future. 

One-third of these lubricants were purchased in finished form. 

AID admits that there is a price differential of from 5 to 10 percent in contrast with purchases by independent importers under competitive bids. AID justifies this difference because "the major suppliers sell through their affiliates under brand names and conduct continuing programs of research to maintain and improve the quality of the brand name product."

Surely these brand name sales are made to nonaffiliate customers. 

I am sure that no major oil company would want to destroy its outside markets by selling inferior products to nonaffiliates. 

ANSWERS TO EXECUTIVE OPPOSITION TO S. 1069 

Why does AID feel that my bill would result in a greatly increased administrative burden? First, the agency points to the difficulty of finding comparable export sales. The solution to this problem, as I indicated above, is a simple one-formal competitive bid procedures which are provided for by my amendment. AID then talks in ominous terms about litigation, saying that it is unlikely that a price based on comparable export sales would stand up in court. I find it difficult to believe that a U.S. court would rule in favor of an international oil company bringing a suit based on the argument that AID is no longer permitting the company to charge prices 30 to 40 percent in excess of competitive world market prices. If independent oil companies brought suit because AID was refusing to apply the standards of my measure and so get the lowest competitive price, I say more power to them.

The executive branch comments claim that my measure would complicate the administration of foreign exchange laws by setting up à double standard wherein by converting to non-AID dollars a country could get around the competitive bidding and comparable sales requirements.

AID fails to submit any evidence that this is so. My amendment makes no differentiation between AID and non-AID dollars if such dollars result from funds made available under our foreign aid program. I intend to apply it to both. I believe my bill does. If AID can suggest language to satisfy itself that it does so, I will gladly accept it. However, I would hope that AID could eliminate the problem by a wise application of administrative regulations.

In discussing this complication, AID points to the corruption which could take place if a premium were placed on non-AID dollars. However, AID does not mention the corruption that has already taken place because of the noncompetitive situation fostered by AID's posted price policy. This sort of a situation is bound to foster great political pressures and collusion. 

PRESENT AID OIL BUYING POLICY HURT U.S. BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

Before I conclude with a brief discussion of barter agent's fees, I would like to make a few general comments concerning the damage that AID's posted price system is doing to us both at home and abroad. 

First, there is the balance of payments situation. Over 17 percent of the AID-financed program has been handed on a platter to foreign suppliers-virtually all at posted prices. Much of this business is going to French companies at a time when the French Government is doing everything in its power to not only embarrass the United States Government but to force change in world monetary policies that would have serious repercussions on the status and position of America in the free world.

I am not advocating that all AID oil be purchased from American companies, although I believe that this would be the result of a competitive price situation. I am suggesting, however, that it is highly unwise for this country at this time to increase our balance of payments difficulties by paying prices to foreign oil companies that are 20 to 40 percent in excess of competitive prices. 

POSTED-PRICE OIL BUYING DAMAGES U.S. FOREIGN POLICY 

The executive branch memorandum states: 

AID cannot distribute petroleum products itself and cannot encourage foreign governments to do so through the expropriation of storage and distribution facilities or the establishment of competitive facilities. 

In actuality AID, by forcing recipient countries to use foreign aid funds to buy oil at prices 20 to 40 percent in excess of the market price, is encouraging these countries to take action to control oil facilities. 

For example, the Governments of Ceylon and Syria have expropriated all oil facilities. Tunisia and Ghana have built their own refineries. The damage that AID's posted price policy does to our foreign policy deserves this committee's earnest attention. 

PAYMENT OF BARTER AGENTS' COMMISSION 

I would like now to turn to the problem of barter agents' commissions. I am afraid that AID's executive branch memorandum betrays a deep misunderstanding of the purposes of my amendment. AID asserts that the stipulation that barter agents' fees must be paid by the foreign supplier or recipient country does not prohibit the Commodity Credit Corporation from paying such fees. I submit that the bill on its face is incapable of this interpretation. However, I again would be pleased to receive AID's suggestions for a technical change to eliminate this possible misunderstanding. 

AID states that my proposal would make it impossible to use barter arrangements. This statement seems to ignore the fact that suppliers have been paying agents' fees under barter arrangements, as I indicated

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 223 1965 above, since the program has been in operation. In fact, the executive branch memorandum admits at a later point, and I quote: 

Payment is made by a foreign supplier through a reduction of anticipated profits from the sale of goods required by AID. 

My bill most definitely does not preclude the inclusion of the barter contractor's charge in the price of the goods financed by AID, as the executive branch comments claim. Rather it prohibits the payment by an agency of the Federal Government of these fees in the form of additional agricultural surpluses or otherwise. It is entirely possible for a barter agent to receive a double commission, one from the supplier and a second from the Commodity Credit Corporation, at the present time. This additional Government subsidy, which is used almost exclusively in AID oil transactions, would be eliminated by my barter provision.

PROPOSED 1963 AID REGULATIONS ON COMMODITY TRANSACTIONS 

In closing, I would like to draw the committee's attention to proposed AID regulations on commodity transactions financed by AID, published in the Federal Register of December 31, 1963. These regulations, which were never finally approved, stated under section 

201.63 (c):

Comparable export sales within the meaning of this paragraph shall not include sales to affiliates.

That would have knocked out this whole posted price situation that was proposed by AID and then reversed. 

In other words, AID, by this proposed regulation which was never finally approved, would have eliminated the posted price system in the same way that my bill does. This is the language that has been so roundly criticized in AID's executive branch comments. What a difference a year makes.

I urge this committee to disregard AID's second thoughts and to implement legislation which it at one time regarded highly enough to include in its proposed regulations. 

I apologize for reading so rapily but I know the committee is under considerable pressure. 

Senator AIKEN. Thank you, Senator Proxmire.

The term 'comparable export sales' as used in such clause shall not include sales to affiliates." (2) Amend section 604, which relates to procurement, by adding the following new subsection (e): "(e) None of the funds made available under this Act shall be used to pay any barter agent's commission or other servicing charges or disposal fees in any case in which commodities or defense articles furnished to a recipient country are procured through the barter of other commodities or articles, and any such commission, charge, or fee shall be paid by the supplier of the commodities or defense articles so furnished or the recipient country." 

(The AID memorandum referred to follows:) EXECUTIVE BRANCH COMMENTS 

SPECIAL PRICE TEST FOR PETROLEUM PRODUCTS FINANCED UNDER THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE PROGRAM The Difference 

The Senate version would establish a new price test for petroleum products financed under the Foreign Assistance Act. It would preclude the supplier of petroleum products from charging a price in excess of the price he charges in comparable export sales from the source country at the time of sale. The comparable export sales price test would not apply to purchases under formal competitive bids or to commodities traded on exchanges. In determining the supplier's comparable export sales price, sales to affiliates must be excluded. 

The House version contains no comparable provision. 

Executive branch position

The executive branch strongly opposes the Senate amendment. 

The amendment is based on assumptions which are incorrect. Under the 

Senate amendment there would be no effective savings to the foreign aid program. Further, the amendment would have the following adverse effects: (1) The amendment would increase the administrative burden on AID in carrying out its pricing regulations without compensation in savings. For example, it would involve AID in costly, time-consuming arguments and possible litigation. (2) The amendment will make the administration of the foreign exchange laws and regulations of foreign countries more difficult and will invite fraud and corruption in the administration of those laws. (3) The actual result of the amendment would be to deprive AID, in many cases, of any effective control over prices charged in AID financed petroleum sales.

BACKGROUND 

As part of its commodity import programs AID financed sales of petroleum products have averaged about $100 million per year. In the current year the products financed are: crude oil (about 10 percent of the program), bulk fuel (about 50 percent of the program); lubricants about 35 percent and specialty items such as waxes and asphalt about 5 percent. With the exception of a larger than normal crude oil component the foregoing percentages are characteristic of past years and are likely to continue. These products are essentail to private industry in recipient countries and their importation contributes significantly to economic development. 

There are two classes of purchasers of petroleum products: (a) purchasers who use the products themselves and (b) purchasers engaged in the distribution of products in recipient countries. Users normally buy on a competitive basis. 

Distributors, however, generally do not purchase on a competitive basis because they are affiliated with the major suppliers through ownership or by contractual arrangement. About 75 percent of bulk crude and fuels and at least 90 percent of lubricants in world trade move in inter-company transactions. These affiliates operate the complex storage and distribution facilities through which petroleum products reach private consumers in recipient countries. Since most of the distribution facilities in recipient countries are controlled by the affiliates, AID must finance the affiliate's purchases from the major international petroleum

! suppliers if the foreign aid program is to help private industrial and other private consumers in recipient countries meet their petroleum needs. AID cannot distribute petroleum products itself and cannot encourage foreign governments to do so through expropriation of storage and distribution facilities or establishment of competitive facilities. 

PETROLEUM PRICING PRACTICES AS RELATED TO AID'S PETROLEUM PROGRAM 

Underlying the Senate amendment is the assumption that the major international petroleum suppliers sell to their affiliates in recipient countries at socalled "posted prices" which allegedly exceed prices established in competitive sales to other purchasers by 20 to 35 percent. The amendment is apparently intended to preclude AID from financing posted prices. They

The executive branch believes that these assumptions are incorrect. do not accurately reflect either pricing patterns in the petroleum industry or the facts of AID's petroleum program. The facts are as follows: 

(1) Crude Oil.-(Ten percent of current aid program.) Sales of crude oil by international petroleum suppliers to nonaffiliated purchasers are generally made at prices well below posted prices. However, with the exception of small amounts of crude oil for Israel in 1957 and 1958, AID has not financed any crude oil shipments between 1952 and the current year in which a $12 million import program has been undertaken for Tunisia. The Tunisian crude oil program is being handled on a competitive bid basis and AID finances the discounted price rather than the posted price.

If AID finances crude oil in the future-it will -as in the Tunisian programinsist on competitive procurement. Moreover, the Agency will be in a position to assure that its demands are carried out because crude oil imports are for refineries. Refineries own their own storage and handling facilities and are in a position to procure on a competitive basis. Thus, in the case of crude oil, the 

Senate amendment will not result in savings to the program. (2) Bulk Fuels.-(50 percent of the current program.) 90 percent of AID financing of bulk fuels (i.e., gasoline and kerosene) has in the past been for 

Vietnam, Thailand, Cambodia, Korea, and Laos. AID is no longer financing bulk fuels for Thailand and Cambodia. Of the current program, requirements for 

Vietnam, Korea, and Laos will represent nearly 90 percent of AID's financing of bulk fuels.

The program for Korea is 50 percent of the entire AID bulk fuel program. In this case, the fuels are taken from the large U.S. military stocks in Japan, obtained by the DOD under highly favorable long-term, large-quantity contracts. 

By drawing upon these stocks for its Korean program, AID takes advantage of these favorable prices.

For Vietnam and Laos AID cannot draw upon DOD stocks in Japan because (i) unlike Korea, virtually all storage and distribution facilities in Vietnam and Laos are in the hands of the affiliates who must buy from the major suppliers, (ii) because vessels supplying the oil to the DOD in Japan are too large to be diverted to Vietnam and Laos, and (iii) because shipping costs from Japan and Vietnam and Laos would offset any savings. Therefore, for Vietnam and Laos AID currently finances bulk fuel imports at posted prices. 

This does not mean, however, that the Senate amendment would force a change in this practice and result in a savings to the program. Imports of bulk fuels for civilian use into Vietnam and Laos and into the other major importing countries of the Far East are virtually all made at posted prices. In other words, except for purchases by the U.S. Government (DOD) for its Japanese stocks and perhaps isolated purchases by other end users, there is virtually no discounting from posted prices for movements of bulk fuels into the Far East. Thus, for the AID Far East bulk fuel program (90 percent of the total), the Senate amendment would result in no savings to AID. AID could not, even under the Senate amendment, require that imports by affiliates into Vietnam and Laos be at the prices paid by the U.S. Government for its purchases in Japan. The quantity factor as well as other factors make these transactions noncomparable. Even if there are isolated purchases by other end users in the Far East at less than posted prices, it is improbable that these transactions would be comparable to AID financed transactions in terms of the time and period of contracting, quantity, quality, use of U.S. flag vessels, shipping costs, and source country. 

The remainder of the current AID program in bulk fuels is a $600,000 program for Mali; a $500,000 program for Bolivia (handled on a competitive bid basis), and an approximately $3,000,000 program for Tunisia. In 1962 AID financed a one time $10,000,000 bulk fuel program for the Congo.

Because storage and distribution facilities in Mali and the Congo are controlled by affiliates of the major international suppliers, there are no bulk fuel imports into these countries by nonaffiliated purchasers. This pattern holds true for the countries in sub-Sahara Africa. Since sales in this market area are made through affiliates, there is no basis upon which AID could predicate a claim for a discount from posted prices. The Senate amendment would result in no savings to these programs. 

In Tunisia $1.5 million of the $3,000,000 bulk fuel program was handled on a competitive basis. The balance was bought by affiliates at posted prices which for some types of fuels were higher than the prices in the competitive purchases. 

Financing of imports by the affiliates, however, was undertaken by AID to meet an emergency need of private industry until the recently constructed Tunisian refinery became operational. The new refinery will eliminate the need for further AID financing of bulk fuel imports by affiliated companies in Tunisia. (3) Lubricants (35% of current AID program). AID finances lubricants in either of two forms: (i) finished lubricants in containers (i.e., base lubricant stocks mixed with additives and placed in drums or cans), or (ii) bulk shipments of finished lubricants or of base lubricant stocks. The high cost of blending, packaging, and shipping means that finished lubricants in containers cost AID up to 100% more than the bulk shipments, and AID, therefore, finances lubricants in containers only when the purchaser lacks the facilities to receive and/or blend and packaged bulk shipments. Two-thirds of AID financed lubricants are in bulk form. Bulk lubricants, however, must be imported by affiliates of the major oil companies because they are the firms with the facilities to receive, blend, and/or package bulk shipments. With regard to bulk lubricants, therefore (% of AID financed lubricants) no price differential exists and the Senate amendment would result in no savings to this part of the program. 

Finished lubricants in containers are imported by both independent importers and affiliated companies. Here there is evidence, although somewhat speculative, that invoice prices charged AID for packaged lubricants purchased by affiliated companies are 5 to 10 percent more than purchases by independent importers under competitive bids.

There is, however, clear evidence that in AID transactions price differential is normally based on legitimate business considerations. The major international petroleum suppliers generally provide customers of their affiliates with the services of lubricating engineers to develop special lubricants for the customer's plant. The major suppliers sell through their affiliates under brand names and conduct continuing programs of research to maintain and improve the quality of the brand name product. The major suppliers also provide their affiliates with sales promotion services. It is highly unlikely that any of these additional cost elements will be present in sales to nonaffiliated customers. 

ADVERSE EFFECTS OF THE SENATE AMENDMENT 

The Senate amendment would result in the following adverse effects: (a) Increased burden on AID in carrying out its pricing regulations. 

In effect, the Senate amendment would have AID test prices charged in intercompany sales (75 to 90 percent of world trade in petroleum products) by reference to prices charged in sales between nonaffiliate companies (10 to 25 percent of world trade). In the case of petroleum movements to aid recipient market areas, the percentage moving in intercompany transactions is much greater than in the case of the world market as a whole. 

Such an

Under the amendment AID must test the price of any sale by a major supplier to its affiliate by reference to a comparable sale to a nonaffiliate. exercise would impose an enormous administrative burden on AID and would invite costly and time-consuming arguments and possible litigation over whether a sale to an affiliate is in fact comparable to a nonaffiliate transaction in terms of all the factors which enter into price, such as time and period of contracting, quantity, quality, use of U.S.-flag vessels, shipping costs, and source country. 

The full dimension of the administrative problem can be seen by analyzing the situation in the two major product lines which AID finances (bulk fuels and lubricants).

Nearly 90 percent of AID's bulk fuel program is in the Far East. Leaving aside the Korean program, which would be unaffected by the amendment, to test the prices charged in its Vietnam and Laos programs. AID would have to search about to find some purchase of bulk fuels by an end user in the Far East on a competitive basis and then attempt to ascertain whether such purchase was comparable to the AID-financed sale. The DOD purchases for Japanese stocks

are clearly not comparable. The chances of finding other competitive purchases in the Far East area which could be compared to AID-financed purchases is highly unlikely. First, such a transaction would have to be found. It would not, of course, be AID financed. Second, the parties to the sale would be under no obligation to disclose the terms of the sale to AID and would probably be unwilling to do so. Third, even if such a transaction were found and the terms disclosed, AID would have to sustain the burden of showing that the sales are, in fact, comparable or would have to determine the specific price allowance that should be made to render the transactions comparable. Such an exercise would be time consuming, costly, and productive of litigation. 

With respect to sales of finished lubricants in containers, AID would have to undertake elaborate cost and specification analyses to determine the extent that any price differential between a particular sale to an affiliate and a particular sale to a nonaffiliate was attributable to legitimate factors, such as quality differential, services, and research. This difficult task would not justify any minor savings that might result. (b) The Senate amendment would complicate administration of the foreign exchange laws and regulations in foreign countries and would promote fraud and corruption. 

As stated above, it is only with regard to finished lubricants in containers that there is some recurring evidence of higher prices (5 to 10 percent) in sales between affiliated companies than in nonaffiliated companies' transactions. If, therefore, it is the purpose of the amendment to force AID to take advantage of this differential, the Senate amendment would complicate administration of the foreign exchange laws and regulations in foreign countries and would promote fraud and corruption in the administration of those laws. 

When AID agrees to finance commercial imports by a foreign country, the dollars AII) agrees to make available become part of the total dollar resources of that country. The country's total dollar resources (AID) dollars and dollars from other sources) are controlled by the foreign government and are made available to commercial importers through an import licensing system in exchange for local currencies.

Since the Senate amendment applies only to the dollars AID agrees to make available, a petroleum company selling finished lubricants to an affiliate (ie., importer) who has been licensed to use non-AID dollars, could charge the regular industry price, while a petroleum company selling to an affiliate licensed to use AID dollars would, under the Senate amendment, have to charge less. This would place a premium on obtaining non-AID dollars. To insure that each company operating in a particular country received its fair and equitable share of non-AID dollars, recipient governments would have to assume a substantial additional administrative burden. Because the non-AID dollars would be more desirable it would increase the temptation to use political pressure and other devices to obtain these dollars rather than AID dollars. 

Over the last 10 years, the foreign aid program has had some unfortunate experiences with maladministration, including corruption, of the foreign exchange laws of several countries, particularly in Latin America and Korea. 

The 1956 report of the General Accounting Office on abuses in the administration of the foreign exchange control system of Korea, demonstrates the susceptibility of this area to political pressure and collusion. (c) The Senate amendment would eliminate any price standard for foreignaid-financed petroleum sales from parents to affiliated companies. 

The Senate amendment establishes a special price test for petroleum products. A petroleum company would no longer be held to the prevailing market price as would suppliers of other goods. The petroleum company could charge only the price it normally charges in comparable sales. What is a comparable sale? As stated above, the problem of comparing AID-financed bulk fuel and lubricant sales to affiliates with sales of these products to other classes of customers is extraordinarily difficult and even if a comparison is made, it is highly unlikely that the comparison will stand up in court. At the same time, the Senate version expressly states that an AID-financed sale to an affiliate is not to be considered comparable to non-AID-financed affiliate sales. Therefore, were the Senate version accepted, it would as a practical matter be virtually impossible for AID to hold a petroleum supplier to the price he charges nonaffiliated customers and under the Senate amendment the supplier could not be held to the price he charges in non-AID-financed sales to affiliates. Thus, there would be no price standard for petroleum sales to affiliates.

The difference PAYMENT OF BARTER AGENTS' COMMISSIONS 

The Senate version would add a new subsection to section 604 of the Foreign Assistance Act, providing that no funds available under the act shall be used to pay a barter agent's commission or other servicing charge or disposal fee when commodities furnished to an aid recipient country are procured through barter arrangements. Any such commission, charge, or fee is to be paid by the supplier of the commodities so procured or by the recipient country. 

The House version contains no comparable provision. 

Executive branch position The executive branch is strongly opposed to the Senate version. It could make it impossible to use barter arrangements in an effort to assist the U.S. balance of payments and expand exports of U.S. agricultural commodities. At the same time, in carrying out a barter transaction the executive branch requires that the price paid by AID conform to statutory and administrative price standards applicable to nonbarter AID-financed procurement. 

When AID finds it necessary to finance the goods of which the United States is a net importer (e.g., jute), the barter arrangement can serve three purposes beneficial to the United States. First, it permits AID to finance the goods (e.g., the jute) from a major exporting nation (e.g., the Philippines) thereby making it unnecessary to increase U.S. imports. Second, it permits such offshore procurement to take place without an outflow of AID dollars, Third, it can assist in increasing exports of U.S. agricultural surpluses. 

Under barter transactions, a U.S. firm (the barter contractor) contracts with the Commodity Credit Corporation, on a competitive bid basis, to export from the U.S. surplus agricultural commodities to selected countries. The surplus commodities, or the sale proceeds thereof, are then, in effect, used to pay the foreign supplier of the goods which AID requires for its program (e.g., the Philippine supplier of jute) and AID pays the Commodity Credit Corporation the price of the goods it requires. For his service the barter contractor makes a charge which may be figured into the price of the goods AID is financing or may be paid by the Commodity Credit Corporation in the form of additional agricultural surpluses. 

Depending upon which method is used to meet the contractor's charge, the Senate version would have the following consequences: To (1) If the barter contractor's charge is figured into the price of the goods financed by AID (e.g., jute), AID will indirectly be paying that charge. preclude such payment-as the Senate version would do-would defeat the whole barter arrangement. The foreign supplier of AID financed goods (e.g., the jute supplier) is not normally a dealer in agricultural commodities so that the barter contractor is a vital link in the transaction and must be paid. That payment is made by the foreign supplier through a reduction of anticipated profits from the sale of the goods required by AID. The Senate version would preclude such a barter arrangement. It must be emphasized that, under this form of barter arrangement, AID pays to the Commodity Credit Corporation the contract price of the goods required by the AID program. That price is determined by competitive bidding, reviewed by AID before CCC makes any agreement with the barter contractor, and must conform to applicable statutory (§ 604 (a) of the Foreign Assistance Act) and administrative price standards. These are the same standards applicable to AID-financed procurement handled without barter. (2) If the Commodity Credit Corporation pays the barter contractor's charge in the form of additional agricultural surpluses, no AID funds will be used, directly or indirectly, to pay the barter contractor's fee and the Senate version would appear to have no effect whatsoever. The executive branch does not construe the stipulation in the Senate version that any "such commission, charge, or fee" be paid by the foreign supplier or by recipient country as prohibiting the Commodity Credit Corporation from absorbing such fee. The executive branch interprets this stipulation as relating solely to commissions and fees which, but for the prohibition in the Senate version, would be charge able to foreign aid funds (i.e., the arrangement discussed under (1) above).

A STRATEGY OF WORLD ECONOMIC AND SOCIAL DEVELOPMENT" 

On page 5, our Nation has done well on such constructive programs, but larger, more demanding challenges and opportunities lie before us as a nation at the zenith of wealth and power. 

Toward a strategy for world economic development. For some years now, we in the National Council of Churches, in cooperation with. our colleagues around the globe in the World Council of Churches, have been calling for "a strategy of world economic and social development."

In this, our Nation would have to concert our efforts more fully with those of other countries, making maximum use of regional and international organizations, including the United Nations. This means, first, however, that we as a nation, both Government and people, must clarify our own minds as to what mutual aid is all about, articulate our motives and our purposes more rationally in relation to the new realities in our world, and dedicate ourselves more completely to the long-term, tremendous responsibilities which devolve upon us at this stage of history. 

HOPE FOR AN INTERNATIONAL "GREAT SOCIETY" 

Can we hope that our Government and the administration in the concern for the Great Society, will take more cognizance of its meaning not only for our own Nation but also for international relations and the world community? In our concern for poverty, education, health and the economic, social and spiritual well-being of our people in our own land, are we not bound by both moral obligation and the international facts of life in growing interdependence, to be also increasingly concerned about the poverty, education, health, and the economic, social and spiritual well-being of the whole human family? "Greatness" cannot be an island of selfish or uncaring affluence on a small planet where, in the economically underprivileged two-thirds of the world, most human beings are ill fed, ill clothed, ill housed, illiterate or ill. 

Through the achievements of science and technology and other modern developments, it is now realistically possible to think and act in ways which can largely eliminate mankind's heretofore persistent enemies: hunger, poverty, illiteracy and disease-if we will. Such tremendous tasks will demand a larger and more long-term commitment than most of our citizens and even most of our leaders have yet begun to realize.

The National Council of Churches is continuing this year to make one of our three annual emphases in international affairs the concern for world economic development. In this we continue seeking education and action among our constituency in our churches across our land. In this process we are grateful when imaginative and constructive impetus is given by governmental leaders in the Congress and in the administration.

THE CHURCHES' EXPERIENCE AND COMPETENCE THROUGH MISSIONS AND SERVICE

CHURCHES SEE URGENT NEED FOR PUBLIC AS WELL AS PRIVATE PROGRAMS 

Out of long, fruitful, widespread experience, the churches have come to realize that there is urgent, continuing need for voluntary, private, and public programs of mutual aid, expanded to the extent of our national capabilities and the absorptive capacities of the underdeveloped areas. 

RELIGIOUS AND MORAL FOUNDATIONS FOR CONSTRUCTIVE FOREIGN AID 

There is general acceptance of the competence of the churches to speak on religious and moral questions. It is on these grounds that we primarily base our support for constructive foreign aid. Here we are dealing ultimately with questions of life and death, of the nature of man and his destiny. These are moral and religious questions which rest on theology and religious faith. 

While the churches have a basic concern for religious and moral issues, they, recognize as well many of the so-called practical arguments for foreign aid; these also have moral values involved in them. Such arguments are those of security, military necessity, good business and sound economics for our own 

Nation and others.

More basic, however, are certain religious, moral, and humanitarian considerations which we believe compel us as a nation to greater responsibility in constructive foreign aid programs: the interdependence of humanity under God our Creator; our stewardship as a wealthy nation in a world of poverty; what happens to men and nations as they do or do not have a real concern for others in need; the importance of these programs in sustaining human life which we hold sacred.' 

Foreign aid programs go beyond material realities and attain moral and spiritual dimensions in human relations. 

MORAL CONCERNS AND NATIONAL SELF-INTEREST COMPLEMENT EACH OTHER IN CONSTRUCTIVE AID 

In constructive foreign aid, the practical and the moral are not in conflict but in agreement; realism and Christian idealism meet in accord: self-interest and altruism are joined. From the perspective of religion and morality, we believe that our national self-interest at this moment of history is best fulfilled in recognizing that our destiny is inescapably bound with the destiny of the world. 

SOME GUIDING PRINCIPLES FOR OVERSEA AID PROGRAMS 

Based on our experience in oversea service and our moral concerns in international affairs, the churches have evolved through the years several principles which we believe essential for making our Government's foreign aid programs as effective as possible. These principles have clear implications for possible legislation for the foreign assistance program for 1966-and beyond: (1) A long-term basis is necessary in financing, programing, and administering aid programs. (2) Greater emphasis should be placed on the use of international instruments such as regional organizations and the United Nations and its agencies and programs. (3) Although all parts of our foreign policy are interrelated, programs of technical and economic aid should be planned and administered in relation primarily not to political and military considerations but to economic and social needs and opportunities. This means that we support the principle of separating the military and defense support programs and the economic devel opment and technical cooperation programs. (4) As to magnitude, the need is not to cut funds for economic development, but urgently to expand them toward the full extent of our capabilities as a nation and the absorptive capacities of cooperating nations. (5) Programs of technical cooperation should be increased. (6) Larger sums of capital should be made available for economic development. (7) Both public and private programs need to be strengthened and expanded. 

PROGRAMS MUST BE IMPROVED AND PLANNED ON A LONG-TERM BASIS 

We are well aware that some mistakes have been made in programs. But errors in operation do not invalidate the duty to persevere in seeking to fulfill the purpose and attain the goal for which the operation is undertaken. They

only mean that such errors must be corrected and improvements and necessary reforms must be initiated. Trial and error seem to be inescapable accompaniments of human progress; they need not be feared in the realm of aid programs so long as the lessons of the past are wisely used as guides for the future.

THE MORAL AND SPIRITUAL CHALLENGE TO US AS A NATION 

The United States is the wealthiest nation on earth. Yet we are surrounded by a world, as in Asia, Africa, and Latin America, where over a billion people are in desperate need of aid to help them help themselves out of the depths of poverty, hunger, disease, illiteracy, and early death. Our Nation's gross national product continues to rise year by year; it has passed the half-trilliondollar mark, and indeed is now well over $600 billion per year. 

Thus, actually, for many years now, the United States has been putting proportionately less and less of our national capacity into economic aid programs for world development. 

Meanwhile, in many of the economically underdeveloped areas, conditions such as grinding poverty, lack of education, and population explosion mean that there are actually more hungry and suffering people every year than the year before. As a nation, we can afford financially to do vastly more in economic development than we bave so far done even at our best in our mutual aid program. Can we afford, morally, with any sense of stewardship in God's creation, to try to cut what we have been doing? Or are we under moral and spiritual judgment in the necessity to increase our efforts to help feed the hungry and help bring to all men of all nations a more abundant life, such as most of us believe God wills for his whole human family? The nations, too, stand under the sovereignty of God and can in realistic ways, even in keeping with their own self-interest, serve the good of all in a world community of nations. 

OUR NATION MUST INCREASE ITS ROLE OF RESPONSIBLE LEADERSHIP 

Our Nation has done well in such constructive programs, but larger, more demanding challenges and opportunities lie before us as a nation at the zenith of wealth and power. We may even be able, by the grace of God, to help make a new type of history if we are willing to keep moving ahead into even greater constructive world leadership for more justice, freedom, and peace. But we must take the necessary steps year by year toward such a more mature, responsible role in the world of nations, and at times take major moves of a more strategic nature.

TOWARD A STRATEGY FOR WORLD ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT 

For some years now, we in the National Council of Churches, in cooperation with our colleagues around the globe in the World Council of Churches, have been calling for "a strategy of world economic and social development." In this, our Nation would have to concert our efforts more fully with those of other countries, making maximum use of regional and international organizations, including the United Nations. This means, first, however, that we as a Nation, both government and people, must clarify our own minds as to what mutual aid is all about, articulate our motives and our purposes more rationally in relation to the new realities in our world, and dedicate ourselves more completely to the long-term, tremendous responsibilities which devolve upon us at this stage of history.

All this we may not be able to do in this year. But can we not together, as government and people, each with our respective opportunities and responsibilities, at least seek to hold the line this year and, looking forward to next

year and the years to come, commit ourselves to a truly major undertaking of rethinking and renewing our initiative in world leadership, in the fullest possible cooperation with other nations, so that we can all share in a more creative, constructive, and effective strategy for world development? 

"THE GREAT SOCIETY" IN THE WIDER WORLD 

Can we hope that our Government and the administration in the concern for "the Great Society," will take more cognizance of its meaning not only for our own Nation but also for international relations and the world community? In our concern for poverty, education, health, and the economic, social, and spiritual well-being of our people in our own land, are we not bound by both moral obligation and the international facts of life in growing interdependence, to be increasingly concerned about the poverty, education, health, and the economic, social, and spiritual well-being of the whole human family? "Greatness" cannot be an island of selfish or uncaring affluence on a small planet where, in the economically underprivileged two-thirds of the world, most human beings are ill fed, ill clothed, ill housed, illiterate or ill. 

Through the achievements of science and technology and other modern developments, it is now realistically possible to think and act in ways which can largely eliminate mankind's heretofore persistent enemies: hunger, poverty, illiteracy, and disease-if we will. Such tremendous tasks will demand a larger and more long-term commitment than most of our citizens and even most of our leaders have yet begun to realize. 

COMMITMENT FOR THIS YEAR AND THE FUTURE 

The National Council of Churches is continuing this year to make one of our three annual emphases in international affairs, the concern for world economic development. In this we continue seeking education and action among our costituency in our churches across our land. In this process we are grateful when imaginative and constructive impetus is given by governmental leaders in the Congress and in the administration. 

More significant than what may happen this year in a somewhat business-asusual program, which must be maintained at the least, is what can happen by next year with the most inspired leadership that can be given by our President and the administration, by our leaders in the Senate and the House, and by citizens and their responsible organizations, toward a larger, more effective strategy for world economic and social development. 

To this, we pledge a major effort of our National Council of Churches. Our general board has set for this triennium in the national council's major emphasis a "priority on peace." Our international affairs commission has reaffirmed that one of the major dimensions of working for peace is a strategy for world economic and social development. In moving toward that goal we shall be seeking to work in the fullest, most effective cooperation with other major religious bodies. We shall also seek to work in this endeavor in mutual encouragement with other responsible nongovernmental organizations. Meanwhile, we shall be hoping for continued and increasing leadership of an informing and inspiring nature by those of you in strategic positions in our Government. Thus, we hope that we as a nation, under God, may move forward in moral and spiritual world leadership for strategic economic and social development in a greater society for the whole human family.

Mr. VOORHIS. Thank you.

STATEMENT OF JERRY VOORHIS, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR AND PRESI- DENT OF THE COOPERATIVE LEAGUE OF THE U.S.A. 

Mr. VOORHIS. Well, Mr. Chairman, let me apologize first for not being here when my name was called. This is inexcusable, and I can only say that this committee is considerably ahead timewise of any committee that I ever knew of before, and I assumed it started at 

10 o'clock. I am ashamed of it.

Senator AIKEN. We didn't lose any time at all. 

Mr. VOORHIS. Thank you very much. Mr. Chairman, I want to say what I have to say as quickly as I can and, therefore, I am not going to read my statement but I would like to ask that it be printed in the record, if I may.

Senator AIKEN. Very well, we will accept the whole statement for the record.

APPEAL FOR MORE PEOPLE-TO-PEOPLE AID 

Mr. VOORHIS. What I have to say principally is to make an appeal for more people-to-people aid in connection with the whole foreign aid program. 

I feel that when you provide things for other countries, which has got to be done, these may be understood and appreciated and they may reach their goal and they may not. But if you can win the hearts and minds of people you have something of inestimable value and something that isn't likely to be lost, and I would quote James Russell Lowell to the effect that "The gift without the giver is bare," and I would say that our foreign aid program should be conducted as much as possible through the development of people in this country and peoples in other countries of coordinate, cooperative relationships. 

UNITED STATES AID OTHERS TO HELP THEMSELVES 

A second thing I would like to say is that if as a result of our help the people of another country can develop institutions of their own, institutions which they lack and desperately need and which they can down through the years use to raise their living standards, to broaden ownership, and to increase their self-dependence we will have made real progress. 

I will just try to illustrate what I am trying to say here, Mr. 

Chairman. 

If my neighbor has a piece of broken-down machinery and I want to help him out there are three ways I can do it. I can go over and because I have got plenty of money I can say, "Look, I am going to give you a new machine," and then he goes and tells his wife, "Well, the neighbor is going to give us a new machine," and she says, "Aha, you don't amount to much, do you." 

Or, I can go over and say to my neighbor, "I am not going to give you a new machine but I am going to fix yours for you," and even then I haven't increased his stature very much. 

But if I go over there and patiently show him how to fix the machine so that he can do it, and he learns to do it, then, indeed, I have given him something of great value, and this is what we in the cooperative organizations of the United States are trying to do with our fellow human beings in these sorely pressed and needy countries. 

I think that we have made some progress. 

COOPERATIVE OWNERSHIP HELPS DEVELOPING COUNTRIES 

I think we have to remember that these countries are trying to thresh their way out from under the old colonial system under which they lived, economic as well as political. That necessarily they are going to live under turmoil while they do it and that only as each small farmer and as many other people as possible in their new societies

have a personal stake in the ownership of significant things will they have built a firm basis of the kind of stability and conservatism in the sense of conserving values that are worthwhile, that we are trying to build and, therefore, we feel that since the level of capital stimulation is so very, very low in these countries that the cooperative method of private ownership is the most practical one and one that we need to vigorously promote.

We also know that this is an acceptable method of private ownership. 

That it is popular in those countries, as popular as it should be here, and, therefore, that we get a good acceptance. 

Mr. Chairman, I would just like to relate as quickly as I can some things that have happened in Latin America. 

COOPERATIVE ORGANIZATIONS IN LATIN AMERICA 

In 1955 the National Catholic Rural Life Conference called a conference in Panama City of the countries around the Caribbean to consider what their economic and social problems were and to specifically propose what might be constituted cooperatives and credit unions and similar organizations. 

We were invited to participate and I turned out to be a member of the continuation committee despite the fact that with my nice green tie here I don't happen to be a Catholic but still I got on the committee and we formed out of that a Caribbean confederation of which the Cooperative League of the U.S.A. was one member, and the other members were from the other countries, and the cooperative organizations around the Caribbean basin. It carried on a modest program of training of people for a number of years, but with continuing demand on the part of organizations in the rest of Latin America that they be allowed to participate also, and consequently a meeting was called in Bogotá in 1961, and we expected 200 people, instead of that we had 400. They came at their own expense from every country of Latin America except Cuba, Haiti, Paraguay, and the Dominican Republic, all of which were under dictatorships. Every other country had representation, and out of that came a directive that a constitutional assembly be called to form a hemispheric organization.

AID FUNDS FOR LATIN AMERICAN SURVEY 

An organizing committee was appointed and it met in Mexico City, made one request. It didn't ask a lot of money. It asked $30,000. 

It asked us if we could get a $30,000 grant from the AID, from the Alianza Para El Progresso, in order that they might make a survey to find out where they were, what their resources were, how far cooperative organizations had actually developed in Latin America, what was wrong with them, where they needed strengthening, and what indeed their contribution might be to a betterment of social and economic conditions.

Gratefully we received a grant of $30,000 with which amount of money a complete survey of Latin America was made because no member of the commission received 1 cent for the time they spent. None of the hundreds of people in these countries that collected this data

were paid 1 cent. The only people who were paid were four people who actually assembled these data and wrote the reports and who worked full time. 

ORGANIZATION OF COOPERATIVES OF AMERICA 

I thought it was rather good that this was what they wanted. Anyway, this was done and then we had the meeting in Montevideo and we have, to make a long story as short as I can, we now have in being the Organization of Cooperatives of America, and it has members throughout the hemisphere.

When we started these meetings there was particularly on the part of certain Latin American countries repetition very often of anti- U.S. sentiment of one kind or another. There was great resistance to our locating the headquarters of this organization in Puerto Rico, for example, because this was regarded as putting it in Uncle Sam's backyard and they wanted to be more independent. 

As of today, I can assure the members of the committee that there is a warm feeling of friendship and companionship in effort on the part of every single one of the cooperative organizations of these countries of Latin America toward our country, not just toward our organization, but toward our country, and I think this speaks rather well. 

AID GRANT FOR THE OCA JOURNAL 

Since this time, Mr. Chairman, we have asked and have received from AID a grant of money to provide staff workers in four regions of Latin America, we ourselves, our organization, the Cooperative League, is paying the salary of an editor of a magazine which is now circulating in Latin America both in English and Spanish. He is a citizen of our country who went to work in Honduras before he took this job, and this journal has very good acceptance and, needless to say, it tells a story about our country that they don't get other places and gives them a feeling that we are doing the same kind of things they are, and trying to help them to build the institutions that they need.

I submit that money couldn't be better spent than this. 

There is a board of directors of the Organization of Cooperatives of America (OCA). I am one member. There are 11 members, the other 10 members all come from other countries, of course, of Latin America and yet they chose a U.S. citizen as the editor of their paper. 

Some practical work is being done, too, Mr. Chairman, and gentlemen of the committee. This same man who is now editing this journal went to Honduras through the help of some Catholic priests who had been there for some time and he learned about some groups of fishermen on the coasts. These fishermen caught their fish, brought them up on the beach and sold them there to a man waiting to buy them for practically nothing, and Mr. Torres is the man I am referring to, asked them why they didn't form a cooperative so that they could refrigerate their fish and they said, "Oh, we can't do that, we haven't got any money."
