(Mr. Voorhis' statement follows:) STATEMENT OF JERRY VOORHIS, EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR AND PRESIDENT OF THE COOPERATIVE LEAGUE OF THE U.S.A. 

As spokesman for the Cooperative League of the U.S.A.- -an organization which has had much direct experience in the foreign aid program-I thank the committee, Mr. Chairman, for the opportunity of being heard this morning. 

The first thing I want to say, Mr. Chairman, is that where foreign aid is carried forward on a people-to-people basis it can be made a most effective instrument for winning sincere and lasting friends for our country and for strengthening the commitment to freedom and democracy on the part of people in other lands.

In his fine poem, "The Vision of Sir Launfal," James Russell Lowell wrote the immortal line "The gift without the giver is bare." 

This we need to bear in mind when we consider our foreign aid program. 

Money, weapons or things cannot do the job. Only dedicated people can make our foreign aid program what we all want it to be. 

The kind of assistance that is the best kind-and which will be most effective in realizing our nation's purpose is that which helps the people to help themselves. If, as a result of our help, the people of another country can develop institutions of their own, institutions which they lack and desperately need and which they can use down through the years to raise their living standards, to

broaden their ownership, and to increase their self-dependence, then we shall have made real progress. 

When we speak of human resources we must include both the human resources of the recipient countries and our human resources-leaders in all the forms of community action needed by the economies of the new and developing coun tries. These include self-help projects, person-to-person encounters, and all those ingredients of commitment and involvements which are the social mortar to give permanence and durability to our efforts. 

It must be remembered, Mr. Chairman, that many of these nations we try to help are in the stage of threshing out from under a blanket of colonialism just to achieve a political identity of their own. We have only to look at our history to realize why for them this is a period of turmoil and uncertainty. 

For them, as it was for us, it will not begin to calm down and promise continuity until each small freeholder, each family head knows that in the new society he will have a personal stake to call his own. As with our frontier farmers, having something to defend and conserve must come first-only then will he feel a reason to become politically discreet and conservative. 

Fortunately, this best kind of foreign aid is also the least expensive kind. 

But it depends wholly for its success upon the people-to-people relationship. 

Let me illustrate what I mean. In 1955, the National Catholic Rural Life 

Conference called a meeting in Panama City to discuss how cooperative institutions could help the people of the Caribbean area. The Cooperative League participated in that conference. Out of it there developed the Caribbean Cooperative Confederation, an association of people's cooperative organizations in the islands of the Caribbean and the countries bordering it. The CCC, as it was called, carried forward, with considerable support from the Cooperative League of the United States, which was one of its members, a modest program of training people in the organization and successful management of credit unions, farmer cooperatives and similar enterprises. 

As the years passed, the requests from other Latin American countries to be allowed to become a party to this international confederation became more and more insistent. So in the fall of 1961, a conference was called by the Caribbean 

Cooperative Confederation in Bogotá, Colombia, to consider enlarging the CCC into a hemispheric-wide organization. We expected about 200 people to come. 

Instead, almost 400 came from every country of the Western Hemisphere, except Cuba, Paraguay, Haiti, and the Dominican Republic. Hubert H. Humphrey, then a Senator, now Vice President of the United States, made the concluding speech at that conference and took it quite "by storm." 

The Bogotá conference decided to form an organization open to all bona fide cooperative enerprises and associations in the Western Hemisphere and set up a committee to plan a constitutional assembly for this purpose. 

The organizing committee met in Mexico City in May of 1962, at which time the first request for assistance from the U.S. Agency for International Development was made. The request was for $30.000 with which a survey would be made of existing resources and stage of development of cooperatives in Latin America, their usefulness to the people of the various countries, and a general plan for their improvement outlined. For this purpose AID did make a grant to the Cooperative League which our organization in turn used to finance the survey. There was not 1 cent paid to any of the commission members nor to any of the hundreds of Latin Americans who collected the information for that survey. Only the four people who received the data and spent full time writing the report were paid. 

In February 1963, the constitutional assembly met in Montevideo to form the Organization of Cooperatives of America. The meeting lasted day and night for a week. There was at that time, as there had been at Bogotá, a certain amount of anti-U.S. feeling expressed. There was especially obiection to having the headquarters of the OCA in Puerto Rico. But it was finally decided by a considerable margin to do that. And today in all the cooperative organizations in Latin America there is, I can assure the committee, a warm and friendly attitude toward our country. This is undoubtedly a priceless asset for our country. 

And the basic reason for this is that cooperative organizations in the United States have been working with similar organizations in the Latin American countries on a basis of people-to-people relationship. The OCA has a board of directors of 11 members. One of them represents the cooperative organizations of the United States. All the others are from Latin American countries, and yet that board has selected a citizen of the United States as editor of the OCA

magazine-a publication that is beginning to circulate all over the Latin America and which tells about the progress of the people's cooperative businesses in their countries and in ours. 

If I may suggest, this is an opportunity to reach the minds of people that is worth an incalculable amount of money. The salary of this editor is paid with money raised by the Cooperative League itself. The OCA headquarters and its staff in Puerto Rico are supported by the dues from its members, the Cooperative League and other U.S. organizations among them. But from the Alliance for Progress we have requested and obtained a grant to make it possible for OCA to have five field representatives in five regions of Latin America whose principal job is to build membership for the hemispheric organization to give assistance to cooperatives and to work toward development of training programs for improving their operations. Another grant from the Alliance for Progress pays for the first 2 years the publication costs-other than the editor's salaryof the OCA magazine. Funds could hardly be better used. It will leave behind it, we hope and confidently believe, a confederation of cooperative organizations throughout the Western Hemisphere through which the people of all the countries will work together to establish, improve, and make more useful their credit unions, farmer marketing cooperatives, cooperative housing programs, and other institutions for the betterment of their lives through their own efforts and their own institutions. The fact that U.S. cooperative organizations, like Credit 

Union National Association, National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, Cooperative League of the U.S.A., as well as the Alliance for Progress helped to make this possible will not be forgotten in Latin America. We are building genuine, lasting, firm friendships for ourselves and for our country. 

Meanwhile, some immediate, practical work is being done-much of it related to the OCA in one way or another. To begin with, the man, Mr. James Torres, who is now the editor of the magazine of OCA, started his work in Latin America as a representative of the Cooperative League in Honduras. This was our own program financed by our own organization's efforts. 

Let me give the committee just one glimpse of what Mr. Torres accomplished in Honduras. Through acquaintance with two Catholic priests who were working there and helped the development of cooperatives, he was put in touch with a group of fishermen. He found them deeply discouraged. They could catch their fish all right, but they had no means whatsoever of preserving and marketing them. Consequently, the fish were sold to a middleman who drove his truck down onto the beach and paid the fishermen what he pleased for their catch. 

Mr. Torres went many times to meet with them. At the first meetings, they told him there was nothing that they could do about the situation for they had no money. He finally convinced them there was something they could do about it. He asked that we try to get together $2,000 and send it to him, which we did.

With this small amount of money, these fishermen purchased necessary materials and built themselves a refrigerated storage plant. They then requested from CARE a refrigerated truck. The $2,000 I just mentioned was advanced to them as a loan, and every single member of the cooperative which Mr. Torres had formed signed the note to repay the loan either in writing or with their thumb prints if they could not write. Today those fishermen are receiving for their fish in the capital city no less than 10 times what they used to get for them on the beach. Perhaps this is one reason why our Latin American friends were so glad to accept Mr. Torres as the editor of the magazine of the hemispheric organization.

I could tell similar stories about cooperatives formed among cattlemen in Brazil, the Indians of the villages of Peru, and other groups of very poor people in many other parts of the world. 

As time passed, we were asked to sponsor Peace Corps projects, and as of today, we have five such projects where the Peace Corps volunteers are working with the people of the villages of Colombia, Panama, Peru, and Kenya, assisting them in the development of cooperatives to get for farmers decent prices, to build simple homes, and above all, to free themselves from the burdens of unpayable debt.

Our biggest project thus far is one where we have undertaken to develop in four Latin American countries cooperatives among the artisan and handicraft workers of the mountain villages to develop also central marketing cooperative companies in each of these countries for the assembling of the handicraft and for their sale in the United States and elsewhere. Our objective is to get for these handicraft workers a fair and decent price for the beautiful work which

they so often do. If, as we confidently expect, this project can be made a reasonable success, there will be an increased income for the very poorest people in these four countries, and it will have come about because of the relationship between these people in Latin America and the people of what might be called sister cooperative organizations in the United States-in this case, the Cooperative League. This project work is financed with AID funds. Our resources could not touch so big an undertaking. 

Meanwhile, the Credit Union National Association, the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association, the Farmers Union, and some other cooperative organizations in our country, are carrying on similar people-to-people projects. 

We all are using as much of our own resources as we can, but also using funds from AID or the Alliance for Progress. 

I could go on about many other similar stories-about northeast Brazil and cooperative housing in Colombia, and about credit unions in Mexico where a contribution of only $3,500 from the Credit Union National Association has made it possible for them to hire three fieldmen to go out into the villages and organize credit unions.

Perhaps our most important project, however, is one headed by Mr. J. D. 

Lawrence, former president of the Bank for Cooperatives in Columbia, S.C., through which we are hoping to establish institutions patterned on our cooperative farm credit system in the countries of Latin America. The cooperatives in those countries will help to capitalize these institutions. Some loans will be made by the Alliance for Progress, and in a few years, we hope and believe many of the Latin American countries will have their own financing and supervising agencies through which they themselves can carry forward the development of their cooperatives. 

Our man, Richard Owens, is at work in the slums that surround Lima, Peru, where more than a million people have moved in from the impoverished countryside and live in makeshift shacks. Mr. Owens works directly for the Cooperative 

League and is paid out of funds raised by the voluntary contribution of cooperatives and their members in the United States. He was elected by the Peruvians to be the director of their institute where people are trained for work in cooperative housing.

All these things will continue to be possible if the foreign aid program is designed to give cooperatives and other segments of our private enterprise system a fruitful role to play in our foreign assistance efforts. The history of U.S. cooperatives, and indeed the history of our country generally, illustrates that it is the people's private institutions, which they organize themselves, which they operate themselves, and which they control themselves, that are the keystones of the unique economic and political democracy we have forged for ourselves over the years. A century and a quarter ago the French traveler, De Tocqueville, noted and commented on this while traveling here. What the perceptive Frenchman saw and wrote about takes on added significance when we recall thatexcept in the cities-the new countries we are trying to help have about the same amenities, or lack of them, which the frontiersmen of early 19th century America had. If through cooperative organization we can give a coherent social pattern to these emerging people at the community level, a dollar of foreign aid can be made to do the work of 10. This multiple effect is achieved because we will be creating the social mechanisms to channel aid out of the capital cities and into the hands of a locally involved leadership, known and trusted by those people we most want to help. 

The amount of money appropriated for foreign aid is a subject of annual debate. But it is our opinion that the difficulty of getting an adequate level of support will begin to solve itself when we as a people come up with the right "mix" of human and monetary resources and the right "mix" of energies from the public and the private sectors of our economy. The human resources are useless, of course, without financial support, but assurdely the financial outlay is wasted unless enough wisely directed human energy is used to insure that it is spent effectively.

This is where the cooperative presence is of greatest importance. The cooperative technique seeks to keep alive a human involvement with the people being assisted. A particular achievement of American cooperatives for which they are understandably proud-one that has now proved itself beyond debate-is in the State of Wisconsin. I refer to the International Cooperative Training Center on the campus of the University of Wisconsin at Madison. This increasingly well-known

center is the product of the dedication, the devotion, the resources, and the hard work of literally scores of the leadership in cooperatives in our country. 

It has made the Wisconsin campus in one sense the hub of world cooperative development because a steady stream of students from dozens of the new, young countries are coming there to learn how to become leaders or become better leaders of the cooperatives in thir homelands. Here they study intensively in one of the most pleasant academic settings in our country. They not only study but get a chance to see at firsthand how cooperatives work in the United States. 

These young Africans, Latin Americans, and Asians (and some of more mature years) go back to form the nucleus of leadership in their countries. We do not speculate on this point. It is already happening, although the training center is only a few years old. 

In the 1963 testimony of the president of the Cooperative League, Murray D. 

Lincoln, he touched upon a point about all this which is frequently overlooked or insufficiently appreciated. He said that when we use the road of self-help and the building of people's institutions at the local level, we are thus providing the means for our own graceful disengagement when our role is finished. He meant when we have done our part we can get out and leave the job to the people we have been helping. Then it becomes truly their project, their cooperative bank, their credit union. Not only must we go in upon the showing of a need for our help expressed by the people themselves, but we must provide in our planning to withdraw as quickly as possible and leave the responsibility to them as they develop the leadership and know-how to run these things by themslves. 

Mr. Chairman, and gentlemen of the committee, we are doing the best we can, but we cannot even scratch the surface of the need and opportunity with our own funds. If we are really to affect the economies, the opportunity of the people for ownership, or the hopes of the people of Latin America there must be adequate funds in the Alliance for Progress. But because of this method of carrying on the work on a people-to-people basis, we can multiply the effectiveness of every dollar of AID funds in the cause of people and democracy many, many times. 

We hope the bill will pass without reduction by the Congress. 

I could tell similar stories about our work in India where a rural sociologist from the United States heads our mission; where 2 men from the Ohio Farm 

Bureau have been working for 2 years; where even high officials of the Indian 

Government depend very greatly on the advice and counsel of these Americans, and where I myself have seen with my own eyes a meeting of representatives of some 30 cooperatives formed in the villages of 1 section of northern India where life really has been transformed and hope revived for a far better life tomorrow by the work that has been done up to now. Most of it has been financed out of funds that we have raised ourselves, but we are at a point now, if it is really to take hold in the Indian economy, as India so much wishes it to do, that our efforts will have to be supplemented substantially with AID funds. 

I only wish there were time to document our story more completely. If the committee wishes us to submit further information, we will be glad, indeed, to do so.

Senator SYMINGTON (presiding). The next witness is Mrs. Lois Van Valkenburgh of UNICEF.

STATEMENT OF MRS. LOIS VAN VALKENBURGH, DEPUTY EXECU- TIVE SECRETARY, CITIZENS COMMITTEE FOR UNICEF Mrs. VAN VALKENBURGH. Mr. Chairman, and Senator Aiken, I am 

Mrs. Lois Van Valkenburgh, Deputy Executive Secretary of the Citizens Committee for UNICEF. The Citizens Committee for UNICEF is an informal clearinghouse of legislative information serving a number of national organizations which support continued participation by the United States in the work of UNICEF, the United Nations Children's Fund. These organizations have authorized me to present the following joint statement in support of a contribution of $12 million by the United States for fiscal 1966. 

NATIONAL EFFORTS FOR UNICEF SUPPORT 

Over the years when a member of our cooperating groups has appeared before this committee to testify, there has been consistent agreement on the part of all of these organizations that UNICEF commands the support of the American public. Members of these organizations are in favor of a contribution by the U.S. Government to the Children's Fund as a sound, humanitarian program and as an investment in a better future world for our own children and for children everywhere. Members of our organizations have also given much leadership to the private campaigns to raise supplementary funds for the Children's Fund through their own personal efforts in the Halloween Trick or Treat for UNICEF collections; and many have served as volunteer salesmen to promote the sale of the UNICEF cards and calendars. Thus, do they demonstrate their deep devotion to the cause of children. 

The names of the national organizations which have asked me to testify in their behalf are listed at the conclusion of this statement. 

UNICEF'S STEADY AND CONSISTENT PROGRESS 

We do not see UNICEF in the daily headlines of our news stories. 

No dramatic conflicts of opinion cause ill-tempered debates among the 30-nation members of the UNICEF Executive Board. No threats to withhold contributions penalize sick and hungry children because men of small vision or petty tyrants seek to impose their will on the weak and helpless. On the contrary, all of us can take pride in the steady progress that the Children's Fund continues to maintain amid the turmoil of daily international confiicts. The enduring stability of UNICEF's commonsense and fundamental approach to the needs of children provides ample justification for the rightness of its direc tion. It is, also, and equally important, an inspiring affirmation of our faith that mankind can indeed learn to cooperate instead of destroy each other.

FOCUS ON THE NEEDS OF CHILDREN 

UNICEF's outstanding contribution: The development of human resources: Our country's experiences during the history of our aid programs, beginning in the days of the Marshall plan, demonstrate with increasing clarity that economic and technical development, higher standards of living, indeed most progress, depend on the de-

velopment of human beings. If the developing nations of the world are to benefit by their own rising aspirations, their children must be adequately prepared from birth to take their place in society as selfsustaining and contributing individuals. Children's needs, however, cut across many lines of governmental and private activity. The 

United Nations Children's Fund is the only U.S. organization that focuses primarily on these needs of children, just as our own Children's Bureau is charged with the responsibility for promoting the safety and welfare of America's children and youth. 

HALF OF UNICEF FUNDS FOR HEALTH PROGRAMS 

UNICEF, for the present at least, will continue to concentrate well over 50 percent of its assistance on health programs. The mass campaigns against the crippling diseases to which children are most easily prey-trachoma, malaria, leprosy, tuberculosis-will continue to receive support while UNICEF also encourages the establishment of permanent health centers. A second major focus during the past year has been the improvement of child nutrition in 74 countries. 

Here the emphasis has been placed on producing more and better proteins at the local level and on teaching children to eat these foods. 

On the basis of the idea that the best way to a child's stomach is through the mind of his mother, such programs have required the training of mothers in the preparation of healthful, well-balanced diets. UNICEF's direct contribution to this work has been made by providing for the education of local teachers to work with mothers in the maternal and child welfare centers. 

UNICEF A COOPERATIVE PROGRAM 

In 1964, 112 countries or territories in Asia, Africa, and South America received aid in a total of 556 long-term projects benefiting children and mothers. As this committee knows, UNICEF aid is a catalyst offered to induce a country to assist its own children. To qualify for UNICEF assistance a country must request UNICEF aid, must agree to match in goods and services the funds received from UNICEF's central account, and must have a well-planned program that will assure continuing benefits to their children after the international phase of the program is terminated. UNICEF help is self-help; it is not a global giveaway. The cooperative nature of the program is further demonstrated in subsequent paragraphs regarding contributions.

COUNTRY-BY-COUNTRY CONTRIBUTIONS TO UNICEF 

While the U.S. contribution to UNICEF has remained at $12 million for the past 6 years, and is recommended again for the coming year, other governments, impressed by the effective work that is being accomplished, have increased their pledges to UNICEF's central account by about $1 million each year. Examples of impressive increases in new pledges for calendar 1965 include Canada, which is increasing its annual contribution to $1 million. It is interesting to note in this connection that Prime Minister Lester Pearson said, in making his announcement of the increased pledge, that one factor in

arriving at his government's decision to increase its contribution had been the nationwide support for the work of UNICEF, as demonstrated in the Halloween and greeting card campaigns conducted by the Canadian Committee for UNICEF.

Sweden is also increasing its contribution to $1 million for 1965 while Denmark, making an increase of $53,500, will be raising its pledge by 25 percent over previous years. Finland, with an increase of $31,500 will be making a 50-percent increase in contributions. 

Based on provisional figures for total governmental contributions in 1961 the top 20 contributors to UNICEF's central account are ranked below in order of their contribution: 

United States of America Federal Republic of Germany 

France 

United Kingdom and Northern Ireland India Norway Switzerland Iran Brazil 

New Zealand Denmark

Sweden

Another interesting point, in any discussion of contributions to UNICEF's central account, is the fact that the developing countries themselves account for every seventh dollar contributed to the central account (which is over and above the matching funds that they are required by UNICEF regulations to furnish for work within their own borders).

An impressive number of governments-53-contributed to UNICEF proportionately as much or more, in relation to total government contributions to UNICEF in 1964, than they were assessed by the U.N. in its regular 1964 budget. This list, available if the committee wishes to have it, includes nine of the so-called developed countries. Altogether a total of 120 countries contributed to 

UNICEF in 1964.

With approximately $30 million available for program aid by UNICEF in 1964, we understand that almost $9 million more could have been directed into programs benefiting children had the resources been available. The need continues. 

TRIBUTE TO FORMER UNICEF EXECUTIVE DIRECTOR 

On January 19 of this year Maurice Pate, Executive Director of the Children's Fund, died of a heart attack. Mr. Pate, who was once labeled by the late President Hoover as "the most efficient human angel I have ever met," had directed UNICEF's activities since its founding by the United Nations General Assembly in 1946. 

From the outset, Mr. Pate attempted to win government support and financial backing that would enable UNICEF to meet its goals. 

Mr. Pate believed firmly that UNICEF should be absolutely above international politics. He once said, "My personal position is simple. 

I believe in universality based on the factor of needs. I believe in extending relief to children without distinction, either within countries

or between countries." Always foremost in his mind were the questions "What can we do? What action can we take now?" In accord with his pragmatic approach, UNICEF took whatever form was needed to unlock local resources. 

Mr. Pate believed that sick children, hungry children, children deprived of schooling, were not only a burden to humanity's conscience, but a criminal waste of humanity's resources. 

In tribute, U.S. Ambassador Adlai Stevenson termed Mr. Pate: 

A man whose devotion to people knew no geographic or political boundaries. 

But it is not without a sense of pride that I add that Maurice Pate was a citizen of the United States. The measure of our grief and loss is the sincerity with which we pledge ourselves anew to the tasks which claimed his love and devotion. 

Along with the millions of children throughout the world who have been helped by UNICEF, we who have known Mr. Pate will miss him greatly. At this time we can only echo the New York Times editorial: 

No monument could be more imposing than UNICEF, which will carry on because needy children are not going to disappear. As Mr. Thant said, UNICEF is a name known, respected, and loved throughout the world. It will continue to be so, and this is the greatest honor that could be paid to Maurice Pate. 

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

STATEMENT OF J. ORRIN SHIPE, MANAGING DIRECTOR, CUNA INTERNATIONAL, INC., PRESENTED BY A. A. BAILEY 

Mr. BAILEY. Yes, sir.

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, my name is A. A. 

Bailey, and I am here, as you said, for Mr. J. Orrin Shipe, managing director of CUNA, who is having engine trouble in Georgia. 

First of all, I want to thank you for the privilege and time you have afforded us in allowing us to appear before you this morning. 

BACKGROUND AND GOALS OF CUNA 

CUNA was organized in 1934 as a national association of credit unions in the United States. In 1940 Canada was admitted and in 

1946 membership was expanded to include credit unions in the western hemisphere.

Since 1957, all credit unions throughout the free world are eligible for the services which CUNA International provides. 

CUNA's specific goals are to promote the organization of new credit unions; perfect credit union laws in the States, Provinces, and countries in which credit unions operate; improve methods and techniques of credit union operation, and coordinate and direct the efforts of all credit unions in their drive to give the people throughout the world an opportunity to economic, social, and educational advancement through self-help.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 253 1965 1 The world development program of credit unions began in earnest a decade ago when our association established a world extension department. Since then, we estimate that the credit unions of the United 

States and Canada, their leagues, and our association, have expended over $1 million for this program. 

PURPOSES AND SUCCESSES OF CUNA INTERNATIONAL 

The purpose of CUNA International in providing technical assistance to underdeveloped countries was to foster international tranquility and a redistribution of income in places where it was necessary, through increasing thrift and responsibility in the local communities of these countries. This has developed in the people an awareness of the obligation to participate in their countries' development. 

Because of the success that has attended this approach, a greater spirit of self-determination has developed along with a more practical appreciation of the value of democracy. We record among the greatest achievements of our own work this development of local leaderships. These leaders, now imbued with ideas of free enterprise and self-help in local communities, have brought about the achievements we record in our statement. Drawing on our own successful experience over the past decade, we can give unqualified support to the technical assistance aspects of the foreign aid program. Our contributions have been primarily directed toward credit union development in Latin America, the Caribbean, and Africa. By the end of 

1961, the results of our program showed that there were approximately 

400 credit unions in South America and 400 in the Caribbean area.

HUMPHREY AMENDMENT AIDS GROWTH OF COOPERATIVES 

At that time, Congress took note of the accomplishments of cooperatives in providing technical assistance to underdeveloped countries and enacted the Humphrey amendment to the Foreign Assistance 

Act, thereby making it the policy of the U.S. Government to utilize the experience of cooperatives in its foreign aid programs. 

Our own CUNA-AID program is a direct outgrowth of the Humphrey amendment. The technical assistance made possible by the participation of the Agency for International Development has greatly accelerated the growth of credit unions in Latin America. 

The number of credit unions has now doubled, and 600 more are awaiting chargers. There are now 420,000 credit union members in 

Latin America, with savings of about $16.5 million. 

These credit unions now have loans outstanding of $22 million. 

Since 1962, the Latin American credit unions have loaned an estimated $45 million. Another interesting statistic is the fact that the average credit union member in Latin America earns less than $100 per year.

CUNA HELPS TEACH PROCESSES OF GOVERNMENT 

However, we are always wary of stating the success of the CUNA- AID program in terms of statistics. We feel that there are better ways to judge its success. We are finding, for example, that credit unions expand their members' horizons. Credit unions serve as training centers in the process of government.

The cardinal rule of credit union operations is one member, one vote. To us in the United States, who are used to voting for everything from class president in grammar school to President of the United States as adults, the notion of voting and the democratic process seems natural.

But we find that voting for directors and committeemen, and then voting on matters of policy, is a rare experience for many Latin Americans among the people with whom we work. 

They approach the idea cautiously at first. They are suspicious, and distrustful of their fellow members. But then the CUNA-AID technician steps in, and points out that the credit union has worked elsewhere under similar circumstances and that it will work here. 

Encouraged by the technician's enthusiasm, the members take their first halting steps in democracy. 

Gradually they build up a confidence, not only in themselves, but in the other members. Suspicion gives way to hope, and hope to confidence. In very short order, the credit union members are playing a full role in the operation of their credit union. 

CREDIT UNIONS VEHICLE FOR COMMUNITY IMPROVEMENT 

Equally as important from the standpoint of U.S. foreign policy, the credit union is proving to be a vehicle for the implementation of community action programs of various types. The credit union gives the people a new self-reliance, a new initiative. But it also provides capital for any number of purposes they may want to launch. A fine example is the community credit union in Iquitos, Peru. Iquitos is an isolated town in the jungle not far from the headwaters of the Amazon River. Organized in the poorest section, the credit union is now the largest in Peru. It has more than 3,500 members who have saved about $1 million. These figures alone stand out as a remarkable achievement. But the people of Iquitos are using this capital to improve their community. Much of the $1 million is now helping finance a low-cost housing project for its members. 

I might add that the results I am very briefly describing here are not automatic. For example, our training center in Lima, Peru, and other sites in Latin America have been the scene of over 120 seminars for 4,000 Latin Americans.

EXPANSION OF THE CUNA-AID PROGRAM 

I should also point out that CUNA also has contracts with the Peace Corps. Under this program, credit union projects are underway in Ecuador and Chile. But by far the laregst efforts, the acceleration of our efforts have been made possible by the CUNA-AID program. I am filing, of course, the statement which I mentioned earlier which will give you this information in much greater detail. 

Studies currently are going ahead for expansion of the CUNA-AID program into Africa and Pakistan and India. We are very hopeful that activity in Africa will begin this year. This will greatly assist our African program, which, up to now, has been funded by our association and our U.S. leagues alone.

Mr. Chairman, it is our opinion that we in our participation, have lived up to our commitments under our various projects to organize credit unions in Latin America. We know, of course, that authorization for the appropriation of these funds has been approved each year by Congress. It is our firm belief that the money spent in 

Latin America for the CUNA-AID program has been money well spent. For this reason, we support the administration's request for continued funding of the Agency for International Development.

AMOUNT OF COOPERATION BETWEEN AID AND CREDIT CORPORATION 

Senator AIKEN. Mr. Bailey, do you think there has been full cooperation between AID and the credit unions of Latin America to which you refer?

Mr. BAILEY. It varies from country to country, and I think that I could agree with Mr. Voorhis, who is of the opinion that it often depends on the amount of knowledge of cooperative development that exists within the AID missions. This is one factor. 

I know there are other factors. I know the AID missions have many other considerations that we are probably not aware of. But 

I will say this: that where we have within a mission or among the mission staff people who are well informed or well experienced on the value of cooperative development it seems to us that the cooperation we get is probably better.

Now, there could be other reasons for this. 

Senator AIKEN. You get pretty good cooperation, you say? 

Mr. BAILEY. Oh, yes, we do. 

Senator AIKEN. Does AID give you technical assistance in the establishment of credit unions or building and loan associations? 

Mr. BAILEY. Yes. The AID assistance is mainly in providing technicians. In most of the countries in which we have worked AID provides one experienced credit union person and provides him with local assistance, the objective being that within a period of, say, 3 to 5 months or maybe a little longer, these local assistants, the responsibility for them will be taken over by the local credit union movement, and from there on it will be a program financed by the local people.

After that time, the U.S. technician, of course, will be withdrawn. 

BORROWING POLICY OF CREDIT UNIONS 

Senator AIKEN. Do the building and loan associations and credit unions borrow from AID or from the funds which have to be approved by AID?

Mr. BAILEY. In our program we do not provide what is usually described as seed capital. As a matter of fact, we oppose it. But 

I will say when these credit unions have reached a stage of development where they can command credit from ordinary commercial channels than AID funds have been made available, not directly, but through banks set up under the AID program. 

Senator AIKEN. Does AID require them to go through a third party in order to borrow the money and perhaps pay a higher rate of interest?

Mr. BAILEY. We know of no instance in which AID has lent money directly to a credit union, the objective being that in the building up a credit union they must reach the stage where they have a credit rating, if I may use the term, or where their development has made credit available to them from normal commercial channels AID is involved as you know, in lending through commercial channels like the cooperative banks. 

But it is not a special loan, it is a normal bank loan made through a cooperative bank even though the funding of the bank might have come through AID and that might be through the International Bank. 

Senator AIKEN. Do you know of any instance where AID has made direct loans to any corporations seeking to establish branch establishments in Latin America? 

Mr. BAILEY. No, I am not aware of that. 

Senator AIKEN. You don't know about that? 

Mr. BAILEY. None has been made to credit unions, I know. No direct loans have been made to any credit union. 

Senator AIKEN. What I was trying to find out is whether AID is more favorable to strictly private corporate establishments than it is to a cooperative establishment in Latin America although a credit union is a private establishment, too? 

Mr. BAILEY. I am not aware of that. 

Senator AIKEN. You would not want to pass on that? 

Mr. BAILEY. No.

STATEMENT OF MRS. MYRON R. BLEE, NATIONAL CHAIRMAN, COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION, PRESENTED BY MRS. THOMAS KOUZES, MEMBER, COMMITTEE ON LEGISLATION, NATIONAL CONGRESS OF PARENTS AND TEACHERS, WASHINGTON, D.C.

NATIONAL PTA SUPPORT FOR UNICEF 

The National Congress of Parents and Teachers, now comprising approximately 12 million memberships in 50 States, the District of Columbia, and the European Congress of American Parents and

Teachers, has consistently supported UNICEF from the inception of that agency in December 1946 as an emergency program to provide postwar relief for needy children. Our organization, dedicated since 

1897 to the health, education, and welfare of American children, encouraged the development of UNICEF into a permanent organization concerned with the health and welfare of all children in the world. 

Each item in the policy statement of our national legislation program has been recently reviewed and acted upon State by State. Of the 46 PTA State congresses that have now reported their action on this item, 43 approved PTA support of UNICEF legislation-an overwhelming confirmation of the stand our organization has taken throughout the years.

Just as we consider our children our greatest national resources, we must also consider all children of the world the future force on which depends international peace. In light of the classic concept of healthy minds in healthy bodies, it is not enough to indulge in sentimental observations when we know that so often the instigations of international unrest and conflict are historically correlated with hunger, despair, and disease within a country. And these children of the world are the potential leaders of tomorrow who will work with our children as adults in an increasingly interdependent world. The work of UNICEF is vital in this respect, and indeed spectacular within the limitations of its budget. 

INCREASED U.S. PARTICIPATION IN UNICEF REQUESTED 

The UNICEF program, with its own requirements for matching funds from recipient countries, is now, more than ever, achieving notable success among participating countries, in the best tradition of "self-help." In recent years, the average contribution by each country aided was $2.70 for every dollar of UNICEF money spent. Last year, unfortunately, UNICEF projects amounting to $9 million could not be approved because of insufficient funds. 

For the past 6 years, despite the worldwide population explosion, our Government has recommended the same figure for our yearly contribution to UNICEF. In 1964 a total of 118 governments contributed to UNICEF. In view of this increased international participation in the goals and achievements of UNICEF and the fact that this is International Cooperation Year, we would hope that we could increase our U.S. contribution. Can't we further strengthen 

UNICEF as it extends its hands and its heart to contribute in a very real way to the welfare of millions of young people to prepare them for useful lives in a rapidly changing world. 

With an awareness of our country's leadership in building this better world for our heirs, that they may grow and live in peace, we are especially grateful for this committee's consideration of this important item. 

Thank you very much.

STATEMENT OF N. R. DANIELIAN, PRESIDENT, INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC POLICY ASSOCIATION 

Mr. DANIELIAN. Mr. Chairman, I would like to note with pleasure the opportunity this committee has given us again to express ourselves on the foreign aid program. 

In view of the limitation of time imposed, I shall bypass any qualifying statements. I shall state our conclusions and hope that questions will elicit the facts on which they are based. 

Our group has carefully weighed the operations of the foreign aid program particularly in the light of our present balance-of-payments situation when we have come to the following conclusions. 

AID RELATIVE TO BALANCE-OF-PAYMENTS PROBLEM 

1. In spite of tied aid, "program loans" are still adding to our balance-of-payments deficits. They also result in waste of aid funds in current consumption and maintenance of unproductive employment. Therefore they should be curtailed. 

This is a departure from previous positions of our organization. 

Until now we have never taken any position on the amount of money involved in the bills, but this year the group, after careful consideration, has come to the conclusion that in view of the effect of the program loans on our balance of payments they should be curtailed. 

2. As between long-term, no-interest, soft loans to underdeveloped countries, and income-bearing private investments, we feel that the latter should be favored. They will bring income to the United States thus helping in our payments deficits. They will lead toward greater political stability by giving lucrative employment in private business. 

They will mobilize know-how and technology for more efficient development. 

3. The meaning of persistent balance-of-payments deficits since 

1950 (except 1957) is this: The average Government expenditures of $7 to $8 billion a year abroad, sometimes going up to $9 billion or more, cannot be carried by the private economy based upon existing price levels and exchange rates. Private international transactions are in balance. The deficit is in the Government account. The major attention in solving the balance-of-payment deficits should therefore be directed at the Government account. Any attempt to solve this problem by forcing the private economy to meet this challenge will have adverse effects.

!

FEAR FOR PROTECTION OF INDUSTRIAL PROPERTY RIGHTS 

4. There is a worldwide attempt, particularly in underdeveloped countries, to undermine industrial property rights (patents, trademarks, copyrights, et cetera). Since economic aid, as well as private investments in underdeveloped countries, contemplate massive transfer of technological information, protection of these rights becomes a matter of first importance. 

U.S. AID DELAYED COUNTRIES' SELF-HELP EFFORTS 

5. Intergovernmental loans for economic development cannot possibly meet the capital needs of developing countries. To lead them to believe that the United States will solve their problems by continued massive aid programs is misleading, retards local initiative, and will end in frustrated expectations. In most aid receiving countries, the the problems are population control, food production, training of local leadership, education, the inspiration and the drive to work, and the creation of a favorable climate for private industrial enterprise and for private savings and investment. Too much reliance on U.S. aid has delayed the necessary self-help measures to solve these problems. Somewhere we lost sight of President Truman's point 4 program and jumped into massive Marshall plan type of aid that has proved to be inappropriate in many countries. We feel that Government aid should be confined to education, leadership, vocational training, particularly in the areas of food production, health and sanitation, and to necessary public works and public services. Industrial development should be left to local and foreign private capital. 

Based upon these recommendations we recommend and to accomplish these purposes, the following specific steps.

RECOMMENDATIONS FOR THE AID PROGRAM 

1. Phase out intergovernmental program loans, balance-of-payments loans, and budgetary assistance to other countries, beginning with a 20-percent cut in sections 202 and 252 appropriations for fiscal year 1966, I believe will amount to about $450 or $500 million. 

2. To compensate for the reductions in development loans funds, the Congress should enact the 30-percent tax credit for incremental qualified private investments in underdeveloped countries. This will give more economic development at less cost to the Treasury. 

Advocated by President Kennedy in his foreign aid message of 1963 (Apr. 2, 1963), as a necessary measure "for mobilizing and assisting the capital and skills of private business in contributing to economic development", this tax credit has been twice requested by President Johnson, in his foreign aid message of March 19, 1964, and his message of January 14, 1965.

While the administration keeps sending up requests for billions of dollars of direct appropriations for foreign aid, somehow this proposal has remained dormant. It is time to keep faith with the announced policy of encouraging private capital to undertake developmental financing. This committee can render a great service by urging the administration to send up its recommendations while the foreign aid bill is being considered by the Congress, so that a fair judg-

ment can be made between the contributions that private capital can make and the need for direct appropriations for foreign aid. 

3. Substitute in the authorizing provisions of the act (secs. 201 (b) and 251(a)), new language to institute a lend-lease type of assistance in place of monetary loans. 

4. Enforce the provisions of sections 202 and 252, which require that 

40 percent of development funds should be used for economic development through private enterprise. This is not now being done. 

5. Make more effective use of Public Law 480 local currencies in economic development through private business by expanding Cooley amendment funds and their use of working capital, as required by law. 

6. Amend section 620 (e) to include protection of industrial property rights. 

7. Do not discourage direct private investments in developed countries, because this is one of the two principal ways in which the United States can earn income abroad, the other being exports, both of which we need badly authorized to be able to continue the extensive Government operations abroad.

FURTHER DOCUMENTS SUPPLIED FOR THE RECORD 

We had appended to this statement the following documentation: (a) Proposed changes in the authorizing language of sections 201(b) and 251(a) to convert the program to a lend-lease basis. (b) A tabulation on the private and Government sectors of the U.S. balance of payments, which shows that the deficit is in the Government sector. (c) A tabulation indicating that the U.S. share of Latin American imports has been going down in spite of increases in foreign aid. 

This piece of evidence, admittedly not exhaustive, brings into question the claim that 80 percent of our aid is successfully tied. (d) A tabulation of foreign aid requests and appropriations in 

1965, and requests for 1966. (e) Finally, a memorandum prepared by our organization which delineates what economic activities under foreign aid we believe should be in the public and private sectors, respectively. 

Since several bills dealing with foreign aid have recently been introduced, and others are promised, I would like to have the privilege of submitting a written commentary if it appears useful and desirable to do so. 

Mr. Chairman, that concludes my statement. (The appendixes referred to follow :) 

APPENDIX A 

Strike out the language contained in section 201 (b) and replace it with the following language: "The President is authorized to make available by purchase in the United States, and through sale, transfer of title, exchange, lease, lend or otherwise dispose of any commodities, raw materials and capital equipment produced, grown or extracted in the United States for specific projects to promote the economic development of less developed friendly countries and areas with emphasis upon assisting projects contained in a coherent, balanced, long-range program designed to develop economic resources and increase productive capacities. In so doing, the President shall take into account (1) whether financing could be obtained in whole or in part from other free-world sources on reasonable

terms, including private sources within the United States, (2) the economic and technical soundness of the activity to be financed, including the capacity of the recipient country to repay the loan at a reasonable rate of interest, (3) whether the activity gives reasonable promise of contributing to the development of economic resources or to the increase of productive capacities in furtherance of the purposes of this title, (4) the consistency of the activity with, and its relationship to, other development activities being undertaken or planned, and its contribution to realizable long-range objectives, (5) the extent to which the recipient country is showing a responsiveness to the vital economic, political and social concerns of its people, and demonstrating a clear determination to take effective self-help measures, and (6) the possible effects upon the United States economy with special reference to areas of substantial labor surplus, of the loan involved. Loans shall be made under this title only upon a finding of reasonable prospects of repayment."

Section 251 (a) of the Foreign Assistance Act is amended by striking out the last sentence of subsection (a) of Section 251 and substituting the following language: "The President is authorized to make available by purchase in the United States, and through sale, transfer of title, exchange, lease, lend or otherwise. dispose of any commodities, raw materials and capital equipment produced, grown or extracted in the United States or technical assistance from the United States for specific projects to promote the economic and social development of the countries and areas of Latin America with emphasis upon assisting projects which are a part of a coherent, balanced, long-range program designed to develop economic and human resources and increase productive capacities."

APPENDIX E GUIDELINES ON PRIVATE ENTERPRISE ABROAD 

Projects or activities proposed to be financed under any U.S. grant, aid, or loan program, either in dollars or local currencies, will fall into one or the other of the following categories: 

1. Public services: Roads, harbors, airports, sewage treatment and disposal, schools and similar non-revenue-producing, public-type facilities. These must necessarily be public activities. 

2. Utility services: Railroads, airlines, buslines, navigation companies, water supply, dams, electric power, communications and similar services which are income producing. Although these services are private enterprise activities in the United States, in countries where it is traditional practice to conduct such activities on a governmental basis or where the nature of the particular project (such as size of investment) presents some insuperable obstacle to private enterprise undertaking, the project will of necessity fall in the public sector. The 

United States will respect local customs. It is not the purpose of U.S. economic policy, however, to finance the transfer of such activities from the private to the public sector. 

3. Manufacturing, farming, mining, smelting, drilling and similar production of basic materials, and the processing of raw materials and food. In these fields, the following categories or choices are given in the order of preference of the U.S. Government: 

(a) Private financing, ownership, and operation. (b) Combination public and private financing, and private ownership and operation. (c) Public financing, but private operation and control. (d) Public financing, public ownership, but private management, with provision for spinning off stockownership to private investors, management, workers, customers, etc., over a period of time. (e) Public financing, public ownership, and public management: This is the end objective of Communist ideology, inconsistent with personal freedom of individuals in society, and should not be financed by U.S. taxpayer money, except for the most pressing reasons of military security or political alliances. 

Even in these cases, an effort should be made to obtain provisions for later transfer of control, management, and ownership to private hands through distribution of the ownership rights to citizens of the country. 

4. Wholesale and retail distribution: commercial, professional and technical services, including small businesses like the butcher, baker, shoemaker, plumber, electrician, grocer, private housing, etc. These should be financed, owned, and operated primarily in the private sector, and where public funds are used, steps should be taken to insure ultimate private ownership and management. 

5. Private financial institutions, such as investment companies, private banks, building and loan associations, farm credit banks for the purpose of facilitating saving and investment in the private sector of the economy, should be encouraged, with a view also of gradually reducing interest rates to foster private business activity.

Naturally, the most immediate problems in some of the underdeveloped countries have to do with the sustenance of life and the development of basic services without which economic growth is seriously impeded or made impossible. The cultivation of land for the provision of food is moreover of vital importance to buttress any industrial expansion. Consequently, the institution or expansion of agrarian reform measures by the governments of these newly developing countries is to be actively encouraged, with as much emphasis as may be practicable in the circumstances on the private ownership of land and its produce. 

Where conditions permit, the local government should be encouraged to make land available for acquisition and ownership by candidate farmers, such acquisition to be financed by long-term loans or comparable credit arrangements, preferably through private local agencies. But whatever the form or source of the financing, technical assistance to new farmers through local training must, wherever possible, be made available to increase their chances of success and independence.

There is need in such countries for lending or other farm credit agencies not only to finance the acquisition, or interim rental, of farmland but also to provide working capital to the farmer for the procurement of seed, animals, implements, and supplies (in relationship to his need for, and his ability to use, such items). Such

agencies should preferably be private institutions, though perhaps governmentally assisted, to make credit available for new private enterprises. 

There is also need for industrial and commercial lending or credit agencies for longer term developmental financing, privately managed, to encourage new private enterprises to meet the growing needs and markets that will develop as a result of the basic economic program. Interest rates in relending publicly provided capital must be reasonable in order to encourage private enterprise. 

In order to insure efficiency and economy, to expedite the work, and to allow time for the training of native personnel in the conduct of the basic public and utility services being financed, it is recommended that qualified private organizations be utilized to build the project, directly or through subcontracts, and to operate it until local personnel have been trained in the management, operation, and maintenance of the project. Only in that manner, rather than by releasing funds unconditionally to the local government to build the project on its own, will there be assurance that the country will benefit fully from the expenditures made for the new facility. 

In supporting the use of the institution of free private enterprise in the situations above indicated, the Government of the United States does not purport to accept or condone all of the practices of private employers in every part of the world. In fact, it is recognized that in certain instances the practices followed have been such as would offend the conscience of public opinion in the United States. Therefore, it must be stated here that although the U.S. Government does no interfere in the internal affairs of other countries, our concepts of enlightened private enterprise support the gradual improvement of wage standards and health and welfare measures, within the limits of productivity of the country's economy and its industry.

MILITARY EXPENSES AGGRAVATE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

Senator SYMINGTON. When you say military expenses, you mean offshore military expenses?

Mr. DANIELIAN. Offshore military expenses, direct military expenses of U.S. forces abroad. So what the Government is engaged in is an attempt to ship out this amount of wealth to sustain this effort. Now, the commodity surplus of $5 billion, it was $6.5 billion last year, but generally it is between $5 and $6 billion, is not enough to compensate for the Government expenditures of $8 billion or so abroad. This is why there is continually a shortfall in our balance-of-payments accounts. 

When you consider that the private accounts, including short-term movements of capital, are in balance, and the private account is in fact making a contribution toward the Government's expenditures abroad, but it just is not able to reach up to a point where it can meet all of these obligations. Now, in 1947-48 our commodity exports surplus used to be about $8 billion because we were the only source of dependable source of materials at that time. We have not been able to reach that scale since, so there is a shortfall in the private economy's ability to earn money abroad in the amount of about $3 billion a year to meet the Government commitments.

U.S. AID SENT TO LATIN AMERICA NOT TIED TO BUYING U.S. GOODS 

You say our aid to Latin America has increased on a straight bilateral basis from $212 million in 1956 to $630 million in 1963, but at the same time our share of the imports of Latin America has declined consistently by about 1 percent a year over 1956 and 1963. 

You say:

These facts indicated to us that letter of credit sales of U.S. goods and services to Latin American countries are substituting for commercial sales and that the foreign exchange saved in the process is being used to purchase goods from third countries.

That is interesting. Would you explain that in more detail to the committee?

Mr. DANIELIAN. Yes. The foreign exchange resources in a country which is receiving U.S. aid consists of its cash earnings, part of which of course are cash earnings in the United States from exports to the

United States, as for instance in the export of sugar or coffee to the 

United States. 

In addition to that, we make foreign exchange available to them in dollars by letters of credit from the foreign aid program. So that its cash dollar resources will be the sum total of private earnings plus the Government aid we have given. 

We have observed by a study of the behavior of our exports to these countries, that in spite of the fact that foreign exchange resources are increasing by our foreign aid contributions to them, their purchases in the United States do not go up correspondingly in spite of the claimed 80-percent tied loan concept. On the contrary they are buying more and more from other countries. Their total imports are increasing, but their imports from the United States are not increasing commensurately. In fact, they are not increasing by the amount of the foreign aid we are giving them. This means that the increased foreign exchange resources they obtain are being diverted to purchases in other countries. 

Now, the tied aid does not help in this situation because it means that we are still losing dollars to other countries. 

This was admitted by Mr. Bell last week before the Senate Banking 

Committee in connection with the balance-of-payments testimony, although he said that this is compensated by other means. It is called the principle of substitution. The Senator will recall that we brought this matter to the attention of the committee in December 1963 in connection with the operations of the Inter-American Bank and the IDA. This has now been admitted by the administration of the AID 

Agency as it previously had been admitted by the Executive Director of the Inter-American Bank. 

Now, how to correct this situation is quite a serious problem. It is for this reason that we are recommending a change in the nature of foreign aid from a balance-of-payments credit transaction to a lendlease type of operation.

ANALYSIS OF PROBLEMS IN INDIA Senator SYMINGTON. Now, let us talk about India specifically. You have been to India recently, and I am much impressed with some of your observations. You said before the House committee:

One cannot come away from India after even such a short visit as I made- 18 days-without being moved to sympathy for their plight, without admiration for their valiant efforts, without awe at the magnitude of the task. It is not a problem that has arisen overnight nor is it one that will be solved in a short time or even in the foreseeable future. But we as well as the Indian Government must face up to the fact that its problems are not going to be solved by massive foreign aid for an indefinite period of time. Population control, food production, Vocational education, leadership training, and work, work, work, and the habit of work and an appreciation by the Government that freedom of enterprise is as important an economic program of the nation as the ability to put an X on a piece of paper in the ballot box. 

You continue:

That there is growing appreciation of these facts by leaders of the Indian Government, and in all my travels I have never met a more dedicated and able group of public servants as those in our Embassy in Delhi. Ambassador Chester 

Bowles and his aids are doing a superb job. However, the basic decision with regard to the levels of dollars aid and the duration in light of our other problems, the conditions of aid and strategic conditions underlying our commitments must be made here by the President and the Congress.

BALANCE-OF-PAYMENTS PROBLEMS HURT U.S. FOREIGN POLICY 

-pay- I do not believe France would have been in a position to render economic aid to either Red China or North Vietnam if it were not in such a balance-of-payments-surplus position where he, on the one hand, is able to threaten us with embarrassment by pulling down the gold exchange standard through withdrawal of gold because he is holding the chips in his hands and, at the same time, turning around and offering to make loans to other nations that are not friendly to us. 

We would not have gotten into this situation if we had paid more attention to this question of the balance-of-payments and the accumulated short-term liabilities in the hands of other countries, and this is a direct and immediate expression of the things that I have been warning about, and you have been warning in your speeches in Congress; and it seems to me that we have some very hard choices to make as between helping with dollar loans some country that may need it, on the one hand, which may cause a continued balance-of-payments

drain and, therefore, takes away our power to influence other nations' actions and, on the other hand, to maintain our ability to extend our foreign policy objectives and influence our friends. This is a direct result, it seems to me, of the fact that we have allowed this balance-ofpayments situation to get out of hand, and it is not helpful at all. It will not be helpful over the long pull unless we have a complete reexamination of our economic policies. 

I think since 1958 this country has been going through a transitional period, and the signs of this transition have not been read accurately by the policymakers, and those of us who have occasionally tried to raise this issue have been pounced upon and been accused of being reactionary or conservative or isolationists, and anti-this and antithat.

It is not that at all. We are just concerned about the maintenance of the power position of this country in the economic field as well as in the military field.

U.S. AID FOR SOCIALIZED OPERATIONS 

Senator LAUSCHE. Now, what is your opinion of our conduct when we provide money for socialized operations of normal industrial plants?

Mr. DANIELIAN. I have submitted with my statement a memorandum which defines our organization's position with regard to this problem. We have very clear-cut definitions of what areas are fit subjects for government assistance, and what areas are not, and we except public services and public works, non-income-bearing activities as proper areas of government activity. 

But when it comes to industrial enterprises we believe they should not be financed by Government funds. 

Senator LAUSCHE. If it is good for the Communists to insist upon socialized operations of normal profit-producing businesses, would it be fair to infer that what is good for the Communists on this subject would not be good for our country?

Mr. DANIELIAN. There is no question about it, Senator, that a great struggle between communism and ourselves involves the control of property, control of the means of production. This is the major difference. This has been proclaimed ever since 1848 in the Communist 

Manifesto, and everywhere they go, Mr. Mikoyan and everyone else from that side of the Iron Curtain, when they visit different countries they advocate the taking over of property without compensation. 

So this is the first line of the struggle, the control of the means of production, and so I do not, from my point of view, I do not see how we can be opposing it unless we have a sharp division on this issue, and it seems to me that political democracy cannot be conceivable if the government owns all of the means of production, and everybody has got to depend upon one employer, and so if you are for political democracy, for freedom of the individual, you have got to provide him opportunities for working wherever he wants, and being an independent entrepreneur if he wishes to, and this multiplicity of employment units in a community is what make a person free. Otherwise,

if a person goes to a ballot box and makes a sign-we saw a picture of a very prominent citizen recently in Moscow dropping a ballot in the ballot box-it does not give freedom to the individual. 

U.S. AID NOT TIED TO SALES FROM THE UNITED STATES

Will you explain that to the committee?

Mr. DANIELIAN. Yes.

Well, even though the $100 million aid is supposed to be 80 percent tied, let us say, $80 million of it should be an increase in our exports to them, when we study the figures, we will find that the total imports from our country are not $280 million, they still remain about $200 million. 

Senator LAUSCHE. Yes.

Mr. DANIELIAN. And yet their purchases from other countries are increasing, the total imports are increasing.

United States. We release their money to be used in purchasing in other countries; is that correct? 

Mr. DANIELIAN. Yes.

Mr. DANIELIAN. That is true. I think there are- 

Senator LAUSCHE. Do you have a table on that?

Mr. DANIELIAN. Yes. In Latin America we have a table that shows our proportion of exports to Latin America have been going down, although our aid has been going up. But there is a variation between countries. Some countries like Colombia, Peru, Chile, the situation is much clearer.

In other countries such as India, I think India imports from the United States almost equal to our total aid to them.

(The memorandum referred to follows:) MEMORANDUM IN SUPPORT OF THE STATEMENT OF DR. N. R. DANIELIAN, PRESIDENT OF THE INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC POLICY ASSOCIATION, BEFORE THE HOUSE FOREIGN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE THAT "A READING OF THE STUDIES OF THE INTER- AMERICAN COMMITTEE ON THE ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS MAKES IT CLEAR THAT SERVICING OF PAST DEBTS IS ONE OF THE PRIMARY FUNCTIONS OF OUR AID" 

A careful perusal of pages 12-23 of part I of the report (attached hereto) of the Inter-American Committee on the Alliance for Progress (CIAP), presented to the third annual meeting of the Inter-American Economic and Social Council which met in Lima, Peru, November 30 to December 14, 1964, leads to the conclusion that substantial portions of U.S. aid to Latin America make possible the servicing of that area's huge external public and private debt-mostly short term. 

Table A on page 13 gives a projection of the balance of payments of the countries of Latin America for 1965. This table shows that Latin America expects a deficit on current account for 1965 of $1,078 million, has external public and private debts coming due in 1965 of $1,898 million, and projects an increase in Latin American international liquid assets of $262 million. Thus, the projected requirements of Latin America for 1965 are $3,239 million. 

A transitional balance sheet on page 20 projects net inflow of private capital to Latin America of $131 million for 1965 thus reducing Latin America's projected requirements for external financing to a net figure of $3,108 million. 

This same balance sheet demonstrates how it is expected that this deficit will be financed: $1.3 billion will come from disbursements from already contracted loans, including AID loans, Eximbank loans, Public Law 480 shipments, IBRD and IDB loans. It is projected that $400 million of additional financing will come from new development loas from the IBRD, the IDB, Eximbank, AID, Public Law 480, Europe, etc. Still another source from which to finance the external debt is the U.S. Treasury's stabilization fund. 

It should be clear from this analysis that the estimates of aid for Latin America in 1965 are based upon (a) their current account deficits for imports, and (b) their interest and amortization payments coming due in 1965. 

It should be noted parenthetically that in 1963 we had a trade deficit with Latin America and only a slight surplus in 1964, notwithstanding "tied aid." Therefore the huge current account trade deficits of Latin America are with other countries-which do not provide "soft loans." This means that 

U.S. aid is also needed to finance the Latin American trade deficit with other parts of the world.

The following excerpt (from pp. 12-23) of the CIAP report to the Third 

Annual Meeting of the Inter-American Economic and Social Council in Lima, Peru (November 30-December 14, 1964) bears out these conclusions.

V. REQUIREMENTS FOR EXTERNAL FINANCING 

At São Paulo CIAP was instructed to prepare annually a report on Latin American requirements and availabilities of external financing, looking 2 years ahead. As noted above, the secretariat has prepared such a document deriving its calculations directly from the country review procedure. As was already emphasized, the reviews were handicapped by existing gaps in Latin American data and planning. For example, the national plans for certain countries have not yet been completed, including countries with considerable weight in the overall estimates. Moreover, as the final reports on the reviews indicate, the estimates of requirements are subject, in the case of some countries, to wide margins of uncertainty. Nevertheless, the secretariat summary lays before us certain overall magnitudes worth examining and it dramatizes certain critically important problems which require concerted action within the Alliance for Progress. 

To understand the situation and prospects for financing in Latin America, it is essential that we be conscious of the differences among three groups of countries in Latin America.

First, there are two nations whose capacity to earn foreign exchange is such that they require special (soft loan) external assistance either for the first few years or for the whole development decade only in support of certain sectoral projects where the return to the economy and the society is likely to be long delayed.

Second, there is a large group of Latin American countries moving forward in development whose current plans and projects appear to be adequately matched by current and foreseeable external assistance. 

Third, there are several large nations in Latin America-whose situation and prospects are quite correctly given heavy weight in any overall review of the region-where the position is characterized by these three facts: (a) They are in the midst of major structural adjustments in their domestic and foreign economic policies whose character and dimensions pose major challenges to the Alliance for Progress; (b) Their governments are now launching policies and lines of action of great promise; and (c) Their external accounts are characterized by a massive and abnormal volume of short-term credit obligations which require extremely heavy amortization payments.
