Behind the overall figures at the base of the table are a number of assumptions which, of their nature, had to be tentative, but which represented the most balanced approximations which a combination of all available evidence and analysis permitted, in each case, at the time of the review. It was notably the lack of adequate domestic investment data—and of fully developed national plans in most of the cases-which required that this first effort to estimate Latin American requirements and availabilities be based primarily on a balance-ofpayments approach. In some cases the balance-of-payments approach could be related to a domestic investment program which was studied and evaluated; in other cases the shortage of data and time required that provisional estimates be established in the country review, mainly on the basis of data presented by the governments.

A balance-of-payments approach to an estimate of external requirements rooted in the country reviews leads to an estimate that Latin American exports will increase in 1965 by about 3 percent. This deceleration from the 1964 increase of about 7 percent derived from the judgment that the 1964 increase in the volume of some exports (which were based on exceptionally good crops) may not be sustained and that Latin American export prices, as an average, will level off. It also leads to an estimate that a level of imports for 1965, 10 percent higher than 1964, is required to supply the goods from abroad necessary to match at home what might be called Punta del Este self-help performance and investment rates. Although a 10-percent increase in imports in 1965 may appear an ambitious target, it should be remembered that the import figures for 1961-63 were abnormally low due to exchange stringency or to the depressed state of a few major Latin American countries. It is from these and other key assumptions accumulated from the country reviews that the gross deficit figure of $3.1 billion emerges.

The question then arises: Is some such order of magnitude for external financing for 1965 within the range of possibility? 

The answer to this question, in turn, depends on the answer to three subquestions.

First, are development resources likely to be available in adequate amount for requirements other than the amortization deficit in the public and monetary sectors?

Second, does it appear possible that the 1965 amortization payments can be dealt with on a transitional shortrun basis? 

Third, can the longer run problem posed by the existence of these disproportionate short-term debts be dealt with by the Alliance for Progress? 

We shall address ourselves to each of these problems in turn. 

With respect to development financing, as table A notes, the pipeline of obligated funds of about $3 billion will yield in 1965 disbursements of the order of $1.3 billion. After examining the possibilities for additional development lending in 

1965, we consider that, with a maximum development effort in Latin America and a maximum effort by those responsible for development funds outside, additional resources might be generated in 1965 which could supply long-term funds of the order of $400 million in availabilities in that year. Such additional development resources might come via loans from the IBRD and its affiliated institutions, IDB, and AID; from the Export-Import Bank; from Europe; and from other countries interested in Latin American development. 

It is clear from table A, however, that the critical issue is that which centers around the immediate and longer term handling of repayments of the debt (characterized by a very high short-term component) which have been built up in past years and which come due in 1965 at a level of $1.9 billion. 

Of the total for such repayments in 1965, about $1.4 billion is owed by three countries: Argentina, Brazil, and Chile. In the cases of Brazil and Chile, we were informed that concerted efforts are now underway to deal with their 1965 balance-of-payments problems and their debt structures. In the case of 

Argentina, a year of substantial balance-of-payments surplus has been used to reduce considerably its short-term burden. That government, which is now completing its national development program, has not yet indicated the policy it intends to pursue with respect to its debt structure.

Before assessing the possibilities for dealing with the short-term repayment problem, it should be recalled that it is wholly normal that a certain volume of such debts constitute a part of a nation's financial structure; and it is normal practice for certain types of such debts to be renewed almost automaticallyfor example, lines of credit from foreign private banks and regular suppliers of capital equipment. 

It is not possible to state dogmatically what proportion of these scheduled payments should be regarded as normal and what part as abnormal. 

What we can say is that the present level of such debts-and the burden they impose on the balance of payments-is abnormal in a number of Latin American countries. 

We are, in short, facing a situation that requires immediate and longer term action to restructure the balance of capital accounts for a number of Latin American nations. This will require extraordinary action both by them and by the external community. 

The object of our common policy must be to achieve this restructuring of debt while maintaining the volume of imports, the levels of employment, and the rate of growth of those countries. The domestic shifts in policy and reforms required cannot be achieved without social disorder unless the transition is effected in an environment of reasonably full employment. 

The broad lines of policy which ought in such circumstances to be followed by both borrowers and lenders in order to shift to a more rational debt structure, are discussed at length in sections VI and VIII below. Here it is sufficient to note that the problems of putting domestic and foreign financial accounts in order are closely interconnected. Repayment of debt alone, without securing additional capital inflow, would not solve the problem. Serious economic crisis is not an appropriate or even possible environment for financial reform. Debt conversion operations are, therefore, in some cases a necessary step to put the development process on a sound basis. On the other hand, a conviction that the countries concerned are seriously committed to financial reform and that practical measures to this end are actually underway, so that such situation should not recur, is a condition for generating the appropriate levels of external financing.

Assuming acceptance of this approach to the transition, it seems likely that the balance of the amortization burden in 1965 may be covered in the following ways:

First, it is proper to assume some new renewed or extended lines of banking and suppliers credits which would be a part of normal business practice, including the renewal of some swaps. A rough estimate of this possibility comes to the order of some $600 million. 

Second, there is the possibility of increased lending by the IMF which may be accompanied by funds from the Treasury Stabilization Fund of the United States. Here the scale of possible lending depends on the monetary stabilization policies projected and carried out in the Latin American countries concerned. 

Third, there is, as argued in section VI, a legitimate need and possibility of rolling over, rescheduling and refunding of outstanding short-term debts, in the case of some countries. 

Taking these second and third categories together, since they are often related in rollover packages, an order of magnitude of $600 million appears within the range of possibility. 

An additional possible source for meeting Latin American requirements is the possibility of long-term private investment not included in the balance-ofpayments projections of the individual countries. Once the movement toward financial stability becomes established in a context of continued economic momentum, such private long-term capital flows often emerge on a larger scale than had been anticipated. Information has been received that certain longterm capital arrangements beyond those envisaged for 1965 in the country reviews, are well advanced in negotiation. In addition there is the possibility of further long-term investment from private institutions in the United States and elsewhere, including guaranteed investments in housing mortgages. Assum-

ing a continued favorable trend in the Latin American economies and governmental policies and in the international environment, an estimate of an increment of $200 million in availabilities for 1965 does not appear excessive under the heading of additional private foreign capital. There is the further possibility of some capital repatriation, beyond that envisaged in the country reports, which we are not in a position to estimate. 

Excepting possible increments in long-term private investment, these types of assistance are, however, transitional in character. They leave still to be considered, therefore, the question of an appropriate longer run policy toward the debt structure of the Latin American countries now mainly burdened with a short-term debt problem.

VI. THE PROBLEM OF LATIN AMERICAN SHORT-TERM INDEBTEDNESS 

The Alliance for Progress cannot, evidently, be satisfied with a continuation of so large a role for short-term financing of Latin American development. 

We must aim to produce, as the result of a purposeful transitional effort, a debt structure much less reliant on short-term sources of finance. 

To correct the problem, one must begin by identifying its origins. 

In its Mexico City report CIAP noted that there were four major forces which had converged to lead certain Latin American countries to acquire a disproportionate volume of short-term debts: "(1) The past lack of development plans and policies which would justify receipt of long-term financing; (2) the unfavorable terms of trade of the last decade; (3) the fact that certain capital exporting nations almost exclusively have granted medium-term financing, much of it in the form of suppliers credit; (4) the absence of centralized control in the countries over the contracting of foreign debt." 

The problem has also been complicated by the impulse in certain Latin American countries to launch quickly certain projects of believed high political impact-a tendency which can only be countered by the formulation and acceptance by the governments and peoples of longrun national development plans. 

It has been the interplay between these domestic and external forces which yielded the disproportionate volume of Latin American short-term debts; and it will require a concert of policy and action by the Latin American nations and external suppliers of credit to bring this problem under control and, especially, to yield in the future a more rational debt structure for Latin America. 

A sound debt policy requires that Latin American nations- (a) Conduct monetary and development policies which enable them to obtain longer term forms of international financing; (b) Institute firm and effective policies of control over the contracting of external debt; and (c) Those countries which face unmanageable short-term debt problems undertake negotiations with the relevant public and private entities to reduce the burden of repayment of some of those debts. 

With respect to the governments and public and private entities concerned on the lending side, a solution requires that they- (a) Cooperate in the refinancing necessary to reduce the burden of repayment to manageable proportions in terms of the foreign exchange earning power of the Latin American nations; and (b) Move toward forms of financing where the terms of repayment conform to the character of the project being undertaken and to the borrowing country's ability to service the debt. 

A considerable proportion of these short-term debts derive from the excessive proportion of financing in Latin America which has assumed the form of shortterm suppliers credit and swaps. It is to be hoped that in the future those who now grant such credits to Latin America will not merely lengthen the terms of financing to the type of project being financed, including the periods of grace related to gestation of such projects, but also contribute in higher proportion to the long-term development needs of Latin America.

To achieve in 1965 a balance in Latin America's international accounts at this level and by these means would constitute a considerable but not impossible achievement. A 10-percent increase in imports would be provided for as well as some shift in the composition of Latin American debt toward longer term types of financing. Roughly speaking the balance sheet for 

1965, as estimated here, would raise the proportion of current long-term development financing for Latin America from a figure of 50 percent of the total in 1964 to about 60 percent of the total in 1965. It is impossible to estimate with existing data precisely how the fulfillment of this balance sheet would affect the composition and structure of Latin American debt except to note that it would be a significant marginal change in the right direction; that is, toward longrun forms of development financing. 

But, evidently, Latin America's reliance on short-term financing will remain excessive. One goal of the Alliance for Progress should be the reduction of Latin 

American debt service to proportions compatible with the repayment capacity and its development requirements. 

What, then is our answer to the three-questions posed early in this assessment of Latin American requirements and availabilities? 

First, development resources are available or potentially available for requirements other than those posed by the amortization deficit. 

Second, a transitional program for 1965 to cover the amortization deficit in the countries mainly concerned, by a mixture of extended and expanded short-, medium-, and long-term lending, appears within the bounds of possibility with a maximum effort by all parties concerned. 

Third, such a transitional program for 1965 would leave Latin America with a debt structure less dependent than in 1964 but still excessively dependent on short-term financing; and, therefore, we must look within the Alliance for 

Progress for substantial expansion in long-term lending and borrowing. 

What does this mean?

It means the relevant Latin American nations must put themselves in a position to lay claim to long-term financing on a larger scale; and it means the external financing agencies must move to enlarge the availabilities of long-term development resources. 

This is by no means an impossible task. The IDB is in the process of expanding its capital resources; the IBRD commands a considerable reserve lending capacity, as does the Export-Import Bank. The U.S. Government has also indicated that increased resources might well be required in the light of recent developments in Latin America. The level of private foreign investment, which

is grossly beneath the level appropriate to a vital expanding Latin American economy, can be expected to increase.

But in the midst of this critical transition the need for action is urgent. Movements to expand the flow of long-term investments in Latin America during 1965, beyond the level set out in our rough transitional balance sheet, would not merely ease the transition itself, at a critical turning point in Latin American affairs; they would also hasten the day when Latin America's capital accounts could assume a more normal and healthy structure. 

The Alliance for Progress stands at an interval of momentum and of hope, but enormous problems confront the Latin American nations and those committed to assist them; in modernizing rural life; in bringing and keeping inflation under control; in the improvement of planning; in accelerating the development and execution of projects; in finding an enlarged and stable role for domestic and foreign private enterprise; in enlarging the capacity of Latin 

America to pay its way through export earnings; in promoting higher levels of education, health, and housing; and in overcoming the short-term debt problem and preventing its recurrence, in those critically important countries where it now exists.

Let us underline a point made earlier in this report, which has been driven in on us again and again in our work. There is a double interrelation which exists concerning each item in the balance sheet of the Alliance. On the other hand, what the nations of Latin America can do with respect to self-help is dependent in part on the scale and continuity of the external support they will receive; equally, it is true that what can be done for the nations of Latin 

America from outside depends on their domestic performance. 

These interconnections, of course, have important political meaning, but they are fundamentally technical. 

Projects cannot be financed unless feasibility studies are made; but the external financing agencies have the possibility of assisting substantially in identifying investment opportunities in the preparation of feasibility studies. The rate at which funds committed can be disbursed depends upon the speed and efficiency with which projects are executed. 

The scale at which the balance of payments of Latin American countries can be supported by private investment is dependent on the opportunities they may perceive in the expanding economies of Latin America and on the sense of confidence and security which external members and investors may feel in the policies being pursued by the individual countries and its consistency and continuity; and there are policies which can be pursued by the private investors and steps which can be taken by the external agencies and countries committed to the Alliance for Progress, which would make private lending and investment more attractive and feasible. 

On the most immediate problem of all-namely, the high level of short-term debts-once again the possibilities of solving the problem depend on what both the nations of Latin America and the external community are prepared to do. 

On the one hand, the Latin American nations mainly concerned must build their development around a diminished dependence on short-term suppliers' credits and they must present to the external community a vision of monetary and investment policy which makes credible an expansion which will not in the future be as dependent as it has been in the past on suppliers' credits. On the other hand, the external community must be prepared not merely to reduce the backlog of short-term credits but to shift to lending policies which are consistent with the maintenance of a lower proportion of short-term borrowing and a higher proportion of long-term borrowing in their dealings with Latin America. 

And so it is with each of the other major dimensions of Alliance policy including the great issue of trade, where the interconnection between actions taken within Latin America to expand export earnings and purchasing capacity and trade policies pursued outside are dramatically linked. 

It follows from these interdependencies that no one figure in an analysis of Latin American requirements and availabilities is to be regarded as an independent variable. It is the task of the Alliance for Progress and for all its partners-within Latin America and outside-to work together in such a way as to move Latin America toward the Alliance for Progress goals of sustained economic development and social justice and toward a position of self-sustaining growth within the shortest feasible period of time.

Mr. HICKS. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I am 

W. B. Hicks, Jr., executive secretary of Liberty Lobby, representing the more than 100,000 persons who subcribe to our legislative reports. 

Liberty Lobby has always¹ opposed the continuation of foreign aid, for practical and constitutional reasons. On practical ground, we have opposed foreign economic aid because we believe that it is harmful, both to our friends abroad and to the economy of this Nation. 

Foreign economic aid has caused many of the problems faced by the U.S. economy today. It has subsidized oversea industry in competition with our own unsubsidized industry. In this way it has caused unemployment and economic displacement in America, with a resulting loss of tax revenue and higher welfare costs.2 It has led in great part to the ultimate imbalance of world trade and our current gold deficit and prospective inflation. Proponents of foreign economic aid do not contend that it is good for our own economy, and it is not. 3 Foreign economic aid is harmful to other nations in the long run. 

It has served to hold back development of initiative and self-help by recipient nations. It has encouraged the creation of artificial markets that will eventually lead to depressions when the markets collapse. 

It has encouraged the growth of topheavy foreign bureaucracies in small nations that really cannot afford to have bureaucracies. It has aided in the establishment of despotism through its support of these bureaucracies. Thus, in the long run, foreign economic aid is harmful to the recipients. 

1 Liberty Lobby was formed in 1958 and it is with this date in mind that always should be taken. This statement is not meant to condemn the use of foreign military aid when such aid is in the interest of the United States. It should not be taken in reference to the aid rendered during the chaotic years immediately following World War II when prostrate nations without adequate military safeguards were in danger of open Soviet 

Imperialism. 

One good example of this occurred in the displacement of textile industries in New England. Japanese textile mills were allowed to buy U.S. cotton for less than it cost to produce the cotton. The price they paid was thus much lower than U.S. mills paid for the same cotton. With this advantage the Japanese were able to undercut U.S. prices. 

The mills suffered only until they moved to the South where the cost of labor was less, thereby enabling them to continue competing with foreign-made goods. As usual it was the small taxpayer who suffered the most. In this case the millworkers of New England lost jobs, the small businessmen lost business, and the community faced a situation of mounting welfare costs.

The book, "A Nation of Sheep," while espousing as ideology at variance with that of Liberty Lobby, has amassed a great deal of useful background data in support of this contention.

In many cases, the latter are in open violation of the letter of the law, as the Congress has repeatedly said that our aid should not go to aggressors. In giving aid to Communist nations such as Poland and Yugoslavia, and to aggressor nations such as Egypt and Indonesia, the spirit of the foreign aid program is completely violated." 

Liberty Lobby does not believe that the American people have intended that foreign aid should either help our enemies or hurt our friends. Least of all, it was not intended to hurt us. Yet it does all these things. These results have nothing in common with the original purpose of foreign aid as understood by the American people, or as explained to them by this and past administrations. The original purpose of foreign aid, and the purpose that is expressed by the administration, is to aid in the defensive position of the free world. 

As to this bill, Senate bill 1367, and the amendments which the chairman intends to propose, Liberty Lobby finds that it is a radical departure from the justification of foreign aid as understood by the 

American people.

The author has explained in detail the reasons for this radical departure, and there has been no attempt to justify this bill as a defense program. Not only has the President's request for more than $1 billion in military aid been completely eliminated from this bill, but the author has suggested that to some extent, the foreign aid program may become an instrument of reconciliation with the Soviet Union.8 

Certainly, the American voter does not see foreign aid in this light. 

The author of this bill has himself so stated, when he said that- For 20 years we have thought of foreign aid as a weapon in the cold war-a humane and intelligent one, to be sure, but nonetheless a weapon in the global struggle against communism." 

Liberty Lobby agrees with the author of this bill, that the American voter does look on foreign aid as a weapon against communism. We do not believe that the American voter has indicated any change in this basic attitude; which is not to say that the voter will never change his attitude, but simply to point out that it is premature to assume that the voter will understand or support such a radical departure In these latter examples not only the spirit but the letter of the law has been violated. 

Pt. II, sec. 620 (1) of the Foreign Assistance Act forbids the President to extend aid to nations engaged in aggression, or cooperating in the aggression of other recipient nations. 

The stockpiling of Iron Curtain arms in Egypt and the open transport of those arms across the Sudan to Communist rebels in the Congo, is only the most recent example of the blatant violation of this section without administrative counteraction. Indonesia's incursions against Malaysia, India's conquest of the Goa enclave would be other examples.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, from the presently accepted justification of foreign aid at this time.10 

The proposed amendment which would extend the authorization of economic programs for a period of 2 to 4 years is not justified. While we recognize the difficulties caused by annual authorizations, we would point out that these problems are a natural part of the democratic process. In a rapidly changing world, the temptation to seek stability is great, but in a democracy the people must have their say. You, their representatives, must retain the power to review the situation and make changes. When the Nassers and Sukarnos of the world tell us to go to hell with our aid, we should not have to wait 2 to 4 years to get started. 

On this same point, Liberty Lobby opposes multilateral administration of the taxpayers' dollars. If American aid money is unacceptable to others on a bilateral, nation-to-nation basis, the aid should be turned off, not turned over to a middleman agency, neither responsible to nor responsive to the American taxpayer. 12 This bill is offered as a means of achieving truth in packaging.¹ 

Liberty Lobby agrees that there is much room for more truth in the presentation of foreign aid to the American people. For example, the 

President has told the people that his foreign aid program "will impose the smallest assistance burden on the American people since the beginning of the Marshall plan in 1948." 13 This the President told us, even though it is not true. On the contrary, if the administration's request were to be granted, it would be not the smallest assistance program, since the beginning of the Marshall plan, but the largest program in 6 years.14

Liberty Lobby, too, wants more truth in packaging. However, we feel that the total effect of this bill will simply alter the nature of the confusion that surrounds the topic of foreign aid. For example, the proposal that military aid be transferred into the Defense budget not only confuses the concept of what constitutes defense," but also creates the illusion of a net reduction in foreign aid spending.

STATEMENT OF MRS. DONALD BROWN, NATIONAL PUBLIC AFFAIRS COMMITTEE, NATIONAL COUNCIL OF JEWISH WOMEN Mrs. BROWN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

I am Mrs. Donald Brown, a member of the National Public Affairs 

Committee of the National Council of Jewish Women, and one of the major interests of our organization, which was established in 1893, with a current membership of 123,000 in 329 communities, is to promote effective international relations. We believe that U.S. foreign policy must be directed toward insuring conditions of peace in which the dignity of the individual everywhere will flourish in a climate of free institutions, political independence, and social and economic progress. 

ECONOMIC EXPANSION AND DEVELOPMENT 

In 1946, we adopted a resolution, which has been reaffirmed in principle at every biennial convention since then, which urges the United States to support economic development and expansion of economic opportunity throughout the world through assistance programs to both new and developing countries so that they may achieve the economic, social, and educational standards necessary for independence and effective self-government, and by channeling such aid, where possible, through multilateral agreements. 

As an organization, we have believed strongly in the validity and importance of the foreign assistance program since its inception as the Marshall Plan in 1948 and throughout the ensuing years as it has become modified to meet the changing needs of the world. Our various sections, as well as our National Public Affairs Committee, have put much effort this year into reevaluating the program, with particular attention being given to the various criticisms and antiaid arguments currently being put forth by both congressional and public sources. 

AID PROGRAM-A CONTINUING ENTERPRISE 

As we did so, however, it became apparent to us that none of these arguments invalidated the moral, political, and economic reasons which have made in the past our foreign aid program a most important instrument of responsible American foreign policy. Quite the opposite, we feel that aid must be considered as a continuing progress-producing enterprise, not as a postdisaster effort or magic cureall for the ills of the world. 

In 1961, President Kennedy pledged that we would continue our assistance efforts for whatever period is required: "Not because the 

Communists may be doing it, nor because we seek their votes, but because it is right. If a free society cannot help the many who are poor, it cannot save the few who are rich." We believe that America still has this responsibility and that it is imperative that we show ourselves capable of sustained interest in such a massive task.

8 On the political side, statistics tell us that the Communist world has intensified its efforts during 1964 to use aid as a lever in achieving the highest total since their aid program started 10 years ago, over $1.3 billion during the past year. It occurred to us that this dramatic rise in new commitments would not be necessary if the Communists considered our aid program as much of a failure as some of our own critics maintain it is. In view of this, would it not seem unwise for the United States to slacken its own efforts at the present time? 

Although this organization is understandably concerned with some of the disturbing anti-American demonstrations presently taking place, we do not believe that we should allow the intemperate words and actions of irresponsible leaders to irritate us to a degree that we become blind to the successes of the program in other countries and the desirability of continuing it elsewhere. Our broad foreign policy decisions should not be controlled by our enemies or by temporary ire. 

COUNCIL'S ENDORSEMENT OF CURRENT POLICY 

The National Council of Jewish Women fully endorses AID's current policy of careful selectivity and emphasis on self-help, stressing aid to those countries where the U.S. interest is most urgent, which are in a position to make the best use of our help, and where other donors cannot supply all the aid needed. We would also recommend, however, that the President be given sufficient flexibility to make full use of the program as an efficient tool of our foreign policy. The complexities of world affairs and our manifold interests and commitments abroad cannot be adequately protected through a standard set of rules and regulations.

From an economic point of view, we considered the facts that 85 percent of all aid dollars is now committed directly for the purchase of U.S. goods and services resulting in a substantial export business for 

American private enterprise; that American products and industrial know-how are being introduced to new markets; that our exports to 

European markets have more than doubled and those to Japan more than quadrupled since the beginning of the foreign aid program. 

Statistics further show that Israel, Japan, and Taiwan have already become cash customers for U.S. commercial exports. Mr. David Bell states: "A cut of $1 billion in appropriations for foreign assistance would slice something under $100 million from the deficit in the balance of payments, but something over $900 million from U.S. exports of goods and services." Undeniably, the economic development and expanded trade opportunities for free countries is in the long-term interest of our own economy. 

IMPORTANCE OF AMERICAN PUBLIC BEING WELL INFORMED 

The National Council of Jewish Women feels very strongly, and we have testified to this effect in the past, that much of the broad criticisms directed against foreign aid and much of the adverse public opinion reflects a lack of current and correct information about the present direction of aid as well as of the continuous efforts being made to strengthen and improve the program. Well-published failures, frustrations, and international crisis constantly overshadow actual 

600.02 Bebivota 

Delivery 47

aims and accomplishments. We cannot overemphasize the importance for all available media to provide the American public with updated and realistic evaluations of the foreign assistance program. 

In conclusion, the National Council of Jewish Women wishes to reiterate its strong endorsement of the recommendations made for the Foreign Assistance Act of 1965, with its stress on long-term loans, multilateral action, self-help requirements and emphasis on the use of private enterprise and initiative. We urge that this committee give it its favorable consideration.

STATEMENT OF BONNER FELLERS, BRIGADIER GENERAL, U.S. 

ARMY, RETIRED, CHAIRMAN, CITIZENS FOREIGN AID COMMIT- 

TEE General FELLERS. Mr.

Chairman and members of the committee, my name is Bonner Fellers. I am chairman of the Citizens Foreign Aid 

Committee, a committee to aid American taxpayers. I served in the 

U.S. Regular Army for 30 years, 10 of which were spent in the Orient. 

For 2 years, 1940-42, I was the U.S. military observer of combat with the British in the Libyan Desert. In 1943 I joined the staff of General of the Army MacArthur as Chief of Joint Planning. I remained on his staff until my retirement in 1946. 

Beginning in 1959 and each year thereafter our committee representatives have appeared before your committee. We have endeavored to point out fallacies in the U.S. foreign aid program. 

Today I shall endeavor quickly to review the 1959 stand of our committee on military assistance and, in the light of subsequent events, draw some conclusions. 

SHORTCOMINGS IN FOREIGN AID PROGRAMS 

Weaknesses in collective defense: 

From President Eisenhower's statement on mutual security to the 

Congress March 13, 1959, I quote: 

Our friends among free world nations make available to us for the use of our forces: 250 strategic bases; 5 million ground forces; 30,000 aircraft of which 

14,000 are jets; 2,500 combat vessels. 

These glowing figures led the President to conclude:

Dollar for dollar our expenditures for the mutual security program, after we have achieved a reasonable posture for ourselves, will buy more security than far greater additional expenditures for our own forces. 

Today where are these 250 strategic bases? Where are the 5 million ground forces, the 30,000 aircraft, the 2,500 combat vessels, all "available for us for the use of our forces"?

The United States fought a war in Korea. We provided 450,000 troops. All other U.N. countries sent 45,000 and we paid the bills.

Where are the allies which foreign aid has made available "to us for the use of our forces" in South Vietnam? able to us for

There are inherent weaknesses in the collective defense into which our aid program has poured some $34 billion. 

In the British desert campaigns against Rommel, before a British offensive could be launched, permission had to be obtained from each Prime Minister of the Commonwealth countries and of the Free French. This was, the British claimed, an almost insuperable handicap.

ΝΑΤΟ Initially a 100-division NATO strength was discussed. Then step by step division requirements were lowered until today the goal-not yet reached-is 30 divisions. And today no one, except inexperienced dreamers who have never experienced combat, believe that the less than 30 NATO divisions now in West Germany could defend Europe against the Red army. 

Of the NATO defense commitments only the United States has honored its agrement. And the United States has done far more. American taxpayers have contributed $18 billion in military assistance and $27 billion in economic aid to NATO countries. In addition, U.S. strategic striking forces extend a protective umbrella over the NATO countries and the U.S. 6th Fleet patrols the Mediterranean. 

Nevertheless, NATO today is in disarray. Britain is toying with the idea of withdrawing some of her NATO troops. The French have withdrawn their fleet from NATO command. Before he left office, former President Eisenhower had called for a plan to withdraw the bulk of our West German garrison. President Kennedy contemplated similar troop pullback but European protests prevailed. 

U.S OVERSEA FORCES 

Today, something on the order of $3 billion is being spent annually by and for our oversea troops. In view of our chronic unfavorable balance of payments, approximately $1 billion could be prevented from falling in foreign hands if the bulk of our ground forces in West Germany and South Korea were pulled back to the United States. As token forces our West Berlin battle groups, and small units in West Germany and South Korea should remain. 

The West German pullback could be safely accomplished because this garrison is not an effective war deterrent. One must keep in mind that "deter" means "to prevent from action by fear of consequences." 

The Red Army needs no fear of the NATO ground forces in West Germany. Our strategic striking forces, heavy bombers and missiles have the capability of destroying the Soviet war potential. If the Kremlin has aggressive intent, it is clear that aggression is being prevented by fear of consequences.

In South Korea where our two divisions pulled out the remaining 600,000 South Korean troops would have the support of our 7th Fleet air arm and a powerful U.S. Air Force based on Okinawa. 

European NATO population is 400 million. European NATO countries, thanks largely to U.S. aid, are exceedingly prosperous. 

These countries are capable of creating and arming such forces as appear necessary for NATO defenses.

As matter of economic necessity U.S. divisions in West Germany and South Korea should be withdrawn.

Since it is a fact that NATO, more than ever before, is in disarray it, is likely that European NATO leaders will call on the United States for additional economic aid and military assistance. They may do this at a time when France and perhaps the other five members of the European Common Market are buying a huge largesse of what remains of our gold reserve. To meet this possibility the Congress should stand firm. U.S. troops should be pulled back; no more aid should be extended to NATO. 

U.S. MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

As of June 30, 1964, U.S. military assistance to the Near East and south Asia totaled $6 billion. This is more than ample to provide internal security. None of these countries has a modern war capability. 

None of these countries has a modern war capability. Additional military assistance for fiscal 1966 is not indicated. Latin American states have no external military threat. Some $800 million for military assistance has already been granted. These states need no military assistance. In Africa it would be a serious disservice for the United States to extend any military assistance to those emerging countries. Europe has already received far more military assistance than the United States could afford. No additional is indicated. 

War in the Far East requires such military assistance as is necessary for victory. Americans in southeast Asia inherit the antipathy which Asians hold toward English, French, Dutch, and German imperialism. Partially to offset this antipathy, the South Vietnamese and the United States should, with adequate safeguards, invite Japan, the Chinese Republic, and the Philippines to help bring the war to a successful conclusion.

The Honorable Otto E. Passman, chairman, Foreign Operations 

Subcommittee on Appropriations, has determined that military assistance funds, available for expenditure in fiscal 1965, now total $3,110,513,324.

In the light of our planned deficit spending at home, of our chronic unfavorable balance of payments abroad and the resultant flight of gold, the Congress should not appropriate a single penny for military assistance for fiscal 1966. This the Citizens Foreign Aid Committee urgently recommends. Thank you.

Mr. FELLERS. Yes, sir.

STATEMENT OF ELGIN GROSECLOSE, ECONOMIC CONSULTANT, CITIZENS FOREIGN AID COMMITTEE Mr. GROSECLOSE. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, thank you for the privilege of again appearing before you in regard to the foreign aid authorization. To conserve your time I will ask that a statement of my qualifications as a witness be filed and made an addendum to my oral testimony.

Senator LAUSCHE. That will be done.

Mr. GROSECLOSE. I first testified before a committee of the Congress in 1956 as I have done frequently since, and in that 1956 appearancebefore the House Committee on Foreign Affairs-I made this statement:

It is a paradox of the conduct of our foreign policy that we have shown greater concern for the fiscal stability of foreign governments than for that of our own. 

FOREIGN AID AND THE GOLD DRAIN 

We have indeed spent billions to cover the deficits of foreign economies while our own economy has suffered deficits in our international transactions in every year but one in the past 15 years, or since foreign aid began. The result of all this foreign aid expenditure is that the balance-of-payments problem has become one of the gravest the administration is facing, so that the President recently held a conference devoted to that subject.

Meantime, since 1945 we have provided France with nearly $9 billion in foreign aid. In addition, the spending of other billions indirectly through the maintenance of our military forces in France and on the Continent has materially boosted French economy. So prosperous is 

France that President de Gaulle now publicly attacks "American economic imperialism" and adds to our fiscal embarrassments by drawing down large quantities of gold from our reserves. In January of this year we had to deliver to foreigners some $262 million of gold to maintain the stability of the dollar, which steadily grows weaker as the reserves continue to drop-now at lower than prewar and current reports are that France will draw down another $800 million before the end of the year.

It is plain that unless measures are taken to restore the balance in our payments the world distrust of the dollar will spread, and other countries beside France will convert their holdings of dollars into gold. 

Total holdings abroad, convertible directly or indirectly into gold, are on the order of $29 billion. The measures taken so far have been half measures and ineffective, and the balance of payments will be restored only by a cessation of foreign aid spending. 

THE ROSTOW THEORY OF FOREIGN AID 

In my testimony of 9 years ago I questioned the validity of the theories upon which foreign aid is based, particularly the Rostovian thesis, which has now become official since Professor Rostow propounded it in a document for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in 1957 and subsequently became head of the Planning Office of the Department of State. This doctrine teaches that foreign aid "offers the best means of encouraging politically mature, democratic societies, and can within two decades catalyze self-sustaining growth in the underdeveloped countries."

Even before Professor Rostow had provided the framework and language that has beguiled so many into acceptance of this heresy, it had become the philosophical logic for the foreign aid policy first announced by President Truman in his 1949, inaugural address. I challenged this doctrine in my 1956 testimony. I stated, from my per- 44-834-65--20

298. 

sonal observations in the Middle East-supported by the evidence and writing of such authorities as Margaret Mead, the anthropologist, and other observers, such as Clement Johnson, Fereidoun Esfandiary, Prof. 

Helmut Schoeck, and Prof. Peter T. Bauer-that "the aid program has frequently demoralized traditional livelihood systems and created the very unrest which it was designed to allay.' 

TURKEY, AFGHANISTAN, INDIA EXAMPLES OF ECONOMIC INSTABILITY 

I cited specifically the program then underway in Turkey whereby American-made tractors were being provided almost as a gift as elements in a program of forced draft industrialization of that country. I questioned the policy of an effort to "impose a tractor economy upon a people that had since Roman times been getting along with an 'ox and wooden plow' economy." I called attention to reports from our representatives in that country, telling of mounting economic difficulties, restiveness, and public dissatisfaction that were beginning to affect United States and Turkish relations, if not the stability of the Turkish regime.

Four years later the blow fell; public unrest finally exploded over the inflation, the heavy taxes, the increased statism and autocratic control under the guise of economic planning, and Government corruption fostered by so much largess from abroad. A military coup overthrew the Government; the Chief of State was brought to trial and executed. Turkey has not been stable politically since, and as the evidence available to the committee shows, its economic problems are graver than ever.

Senator LAUSCHE. Do you know the name of the person brought to trial and executed? 

Mr. GROSECLOSE. Menderes. 

Senator LAUSCHE. Menderes, I see. Mr. GROSECLOSE. We promoted a TVA-type of program in Afghanistan at the cost of millions of the taxpayers' dollars, and the result was also political disquiet, and Afghanistan is now outside the orbit of U.S. influence. The New York Times, reporting in the March 18, 1956, issue on the Afghanistan fiasco, stated that the aid program "has become a bitter burden that seriously threatens the Afghan economy and presents the United States with a critical problem in a politically strategic area." Nevertheless, the Times, like so many among the electorate and in Congress, remained bedazzled and hypnotized by the glitter of foreign aid and the belief that we could buy the world's peace with U.S. dollars. 

We now have the problem of India, where we have given $3.5 billion, with its monetary reserves exhausted, with famine stalking the country, all traceable to efforts to industrialize under U.S. encouragement at the expense of agriculture. 

In my testimony I did not-nor do I now-argue against modernization of the underdeveloped countries. I pointed out that this was a task for missionary and philanthropic agencies whose personnel dedicate their lives to the people they serve. It is not a job for U.S. 

Government officials who go out for 2-year stints and who inescapably stand in the eyes of those people as representatives of a distant and alien power.

FOREIGN AID ALLEGED TO FOSTER COMMUNISM 

In my 1956 testimony I pointed out thatwhile the domestic policy is to preserve the system of private enterprise among us by getting the Government out of business- I am afraid I was speaking rather naively of domestic policy despite the fact that the administration then in power was of the mainstream 

Republican sort in the conduct of our foreign policy it is putting foreign governments increasingly into business, financing programs that promote statism and socialism and in other ways weakening attachment to the system of private enterprise. 

I stated specifically thatthe United States is, in fact, doing concretely what Soviet Russia has been doing through propaganda: it is pouring out vast sums to promote totalitarian and communistic economic and political systems. If fosters 5-year plans, 7year plans, state planning boards, imitation TVA's; it has put governments into the electric power business, into cement manufacturing, into slaughter and meat processing, textile manufacture, tanning, sugar refining, milk processing, and other commercial undertakings.

Mr. GROSECLOSE. Unfortunately, this evidence was ignored by the great captains of industry who by their testimony before congressional committeess and by their speeches and other declarations have extolled foreign aid because of its supposed benefits in promoting U.S. trade and investment abroad. It is not lost upon this committee, I am sure, that the chief argument today advanced by Secretary Dillon and other official advocates of foreign aid is that supposedly 80 percent of foreign aid appropriations go to buy U.S. goods and services. This, of course, is meaningless, so far as the balance-of-payments deficit is concerned for it means that by financing foreign purchases with aid money, we are relieving foreign governments of that expense and allowing them to spend their cash to buy our gold. This was well documented by the previous witness. 

Senator LAUSCHE. That is by Mr. Danielian?

Mr. GROSECLOSE. Yes. Dr. Danielian gave you concrete data particularly in regard to Latin America that hardly requires documentary evidence, because it is so obvious that if we give foreigners free goods they have the money available to buy other products, our gold or products in Europe or elsewhere. It is particularly true in Brazil where we buy enormous quantities of their coffee with cash, and give them enormous quantities of foreign aid which they are able to use to buy goods elsewhere.

SEIZURE OF U.S. INVESTMENTS ABROAD 

We now see the consequences of what I pointed out in 1956. We have the example of Indonesia which we practically created by our pressure upon the Dutch to leave the country, and which we nurtured with some three-quarter billion dollars of foreign aid. The press of last week announced that Sukarno is now seizing U.S. investments in rubber plantations in Indonesia of a value of $90 million. We have the example of Brazil, which we have aided with $1.5 billion and which has expropriated properties of U.S. citizens. Add Bolivia, Ceylon, and Egypt to the list that have been encouraged along the path of socialism with the consequence of taking over private business enterprises in which U.S. citizens have invested. 

WHO ARE "OUR FRIENDS"?

I referred in my earlier testimony to the State Department speaking reassuringly of "our friends" abroad and added- But who in the Department or outside can say which are our friends and which are not? The unkind words of our French friends uttered a few days agoand this was written in 1956come like an echo of the 1920's. Who can predict what allies we may have in case of war? The armies of Asia and the Middle East that we are equipping, do we know that they will fight, or if so with what zeal, or that they will remain neutral, or possibly turn their American-made weapons against the very people who supplied them?

These questions rise again with the anguish of a tormented conscience that asks how have we betrayed our trust, voting billions to sow dragon's teeth throughout the world? Can we count on the friend-

ship of Pakistan to which we have given nearly $2 billion, and which I is now paying court to Red China? India, to which we have given nearly $3.5 billion, is leader of the neutrals. Even the friendship of the 

Philippine people has become doubtful in recent days, despite a long friendship and $1.5 billion in aid.

I may again quote from my earlier testimony: 

One can but wonder at the lack of official courage in coming to grips with the true causes of unrest in Asia and the spread of communism ***. The dollar approach to the world's ills, the theory that "greater production is the key to prosperity and peace" ignores, or dismisses as inconsequential, the political and social causes of unrest, such as the faulty organization of government, official laxity and corruption, government intervention in the market, statism, inequitable taxation, imperfect judicial systems, and venal courts, police brutality, chaotic civil service, nepotism, uncertain paydays, bureaucracy and overstaffing, loss of morale, official impotence and feeble leadership-these and others that could be named.

FAILURE OF FOREIGN AID IN SOUTHEAST ASIA 

We are now expending the blood of American soldier boys and preparing to expend the treasure of our citizens to justify this monstrous and unfortunate experiment in foreign policy in southeast Asia. As early as 1957, Clement Johnson, a former president of the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, after making an official study of foreign aid in southeast Asia for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee reported as follows: 

It doesn't take a graduate economist to reach the inescapable conclusion that, if the present massive U.S. expenditure is continued for 2 or 3 years and then is either discontinued or is materially reduced, a condition of near chaos would almost certainly ensue. The bisbanded soldiery would probably resort to banditry, the hill folk who once led a marginal but reasonably contented existence, unaware of manufactured goods *** would suddenly be made unhappy by finding all these desirable things beyond their reach. (Senate Foreign Relations committee print. Survey No. 7, March 1957.)

We now see the ghastly effects of the failure to heed this sound counsel.

For 9 years we have been repeating these observations before various committees of the Congress, and elsewhere in the public press and platform, adding new data as they arose, answering new species of specious arguments made by the official proponents of aid. 

OFFICIAL RELUCTANCE TO ADMIT ERROR 

It has not been an easy task; we have met with derision, scorn, indifference; we have seen those who should be heeding and examining the facts we presented rise in self-righteous indignation and leave our hearing. We have had condemnatory and scurrilous letters from the clergy, excoriating us for our hardheartedness and want of Christian charity. Professionally we have seen firms like the one I head garner 

Government contracts in the millions while we have had to seek our livelihood in other fields.

But it is easy to be self-pitying. We rejoice rather that at last men are rising in the Congress to join that clearheaded minority who have long seen the errors of the foreign aid heresy. We rejoice that for one reason or another influential figures in the Congress who have hitherto supported foreign aid are beginning to take a second look and to have doubts and to raise a voice of caution.

TERMINATE ALL FUTURE AID AUTHORIZATIONS 

We conclude, therefore, by urging this committee to cast aside their hitherto held convictions regarding foreign aid, to reject the pressures from the other end of Pennsylvania Avenue, and to examine foreign aid in the light of the facts and objective reason. We are confident that having done so, you will reverse the tide and move toward the abandonment of an experiment in foreign policy that has proven so negative in its promises, so costly to the taxpayer, and so disastrous to U.S. prestige and influence in the world. As a beginning, your committee should forthwith terminate all further aid authorizations, since ample is already available in existing authorizations to phase out this disastrous experiment. Thank you. 

(The addendum to Mr. Groseclose's statement follows:) ELGIN GROSECLOSE 

Elgin Groseclose, Ph. D., financial and investment consultant of Washington, D.C., has been acquainted with the Middle East since 1921 when he taught in a mission school in Persia (now Iran) and did relief work in the Soviet Caucasus. 

Subsequently he became the Department of Commerce specialist in Far Eastern finance, and authored "Money: The Human Conflict" (University of Oklahoma 

Press, 1935), republished in 1962 as "Money and Man." During World War II he served as Treasurer General of Iran, and in the years since he has frequently visited the Middle East on business, on behalf of clients, or as head of Welfare of the Blind, Inc., a Christian agency for the sightless of the Middle East, which he founded in 1956. He is the author of "Introduction to Iran" (Oxford University Press, 1947), a standard reference work on that country, and five other books relating to the Middle East. Since 1944, he has been head of Groseclose, Williams & Associates, financial and investment consultants of Washington, D.C. He is also founder and executive director of the Institute for Monetary Research, Inc. 

Senator LAUSCHE. Senator Pell. 

Senator PELL. Thank you, Senator Lausche.

ECONOMIC PROBLEMS CREATED BY AID PROGRAM 

Dr. Groseclose, I was impressed with your statement that you question the policy of imposing a tractor economy upon a people that in normal times had gotten along with oxen and wooden plows. Is it my understanding of your statement that as to those nations that are used to the oxen and the wooden plows, it is best to let them remain that way and not get into a tractor economy?

Mr. GROSECLOSE. In my statement further on I said I was not opposed to this. I do not argue against modernization, but it has to proceed under the recipients' own impetus and their own steam. The attempt to force growth-I was in Turkey in 1951 and observed it there. Prior to foreign aid Turkey was an exporter of wheat. Turkey has not been an exporter of wheat since foreign aid began. 

Senator PELL. Because the tractor replaced the plow?

Mr. GROSECLOSE. It created economic problems that they have not been able to overcome. It created inflation. It diverted energies from agriculture to industrialization, and we have had to aid them ever since.

The same is true in Pakistan and India. We have diverted their energies, encouraged them to divert their energies from agriculture, and improving their agriculture, to massive industrialization with the result today that India is starving. They have no monetary resources,

which are vanishing, and they have a condition in some areas almost of anarchy.

Senator PELL. I was also impressed by this theory, but I am not necessarily in agreement. 

General Fellers, I was in some agreement with you. Perhaps from different premises we arrive at the same conclusion which is that military aid extended to Africa and Latin America and the underdeveloped nations is better ended because in the end you know which way those guns are pointed, and if you give to one you have to give to another to balance it out. 

But as a professional military officer, I had always thought that military aid given to allies like the British would be, perhaps, of considerable advantage to us. Would you disagree with that?

General FELLERS. No, sir. I do not disagree with that. My point is they are dragging their feet in NATO, and we are carrying the burden, and we are in no position to go on with it, and I think we have had enough, that is all. They have had $17 billion in foreign aid, I believe it is, I mean in military assistance. 

Senator PELL. I think your point is well taken. In Vietnam we have, according to the latest report I have received, under 400 allies working with us there, and I have often though we would do very well if we could get some Asiatic allies to help us. That is all. 

Senator LAUSCHE. All right. Thanks very much for your presentation.

General FELLERS. Thank you. 

Senator LAUSCHE. Mr. John O. Teeter, vice president of Pfizer International.

STATEMENT OF JOHN O. TEETER, REPRESENTING THE CHAMBER OF COMMERCE OF THE UNITED STATES 

Mr. TEETER. All right. I may summarize a point or two then, and 

I would like to have it inserted. 

My name is John O. Teeter, vice president of Pfizer International,

New York City. I am here to present the views of the Chamber of 

Commerce of the United States on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1965.

I serve on the chamber's joint subcommittee on foreign aid, composed of representatives from seven chamber policy committees. This morning I am accompanied by Jay H. Cert, on my left, manager of the chamber's foreign commerce-foreign policy department, and John 

Donaldson and Jack Gilbert of the staff.

My company is engaged in manufacturing pharmaceuticals and chemicals. We do a substantial oversea business and are therefore close to international developments, particularly in the less-developed areas of the world.

CHAMBER SUPPORTS ADMINISTRATION OF AID PROGRAM 

In presenting the national chamber's position on foreign aid, I want to emphasize that the chamber: 

Supports effectively administered aid programs designed to achieve U.S. foreign policy objectives. 

Encourages greater reliance on, and participation by, private enterprise in projects which can be carried out more effectively by the private sector. 

Recommends a gradual reduction of foreign aid fund levels over a period of years to the point in each country at which self-sustaining economic growth, political stability, and military security permit a phasing out of the program. 

Both Democratic and Republican administrations have endorsed foreign aid programs as vital to the conduct of our foreign policy. 

These programs can help provide the economic base necessary for vital private investment and enterprise which can gradually eliminate the need for government-to-government assistance as in the case of Taiwan.

We are not engaged in a popularity contest with foreign aid as the lure. Foreign aid successes, measured by self-help programs that encourage development of free societies, underscore the worth of aid programs. Since 1945, 17 nations have become self-sustaining economies. Fourteen additional countries are approaching this stage of development.

PRESIDENT GIVEN FLEXIBILITY IN ADMINISTERING PROGRAM 

We realize that the magnitude of the aid program subjects it to inevitable weaknesses. The American public is understandably concerned about recent anti-American demonstrations in Indonesia and Egypt. The U.S. Chamber heartily deplores these and other actions which are stirred primarily by the leaders of these countries. Recognizing the value of maintaining an American presence in these countries, the chamber believes the President should be given flexibility in administering aid programs. 

FUNDS FOR DEVELOPMENT 

Support for the principle of foreign aid does not necessarily imply approval of all the various programs known as foreign aid nor of every budget authorization request. The comparative budget analysis included at the end of this statement shows chamber support for roughly a 2-to-1 ratio of economic assistance to military aid-or a $3 billion ceiling for fiscal year 1966. 

MODERATE REDUCTION IN FOREIGN AID FUND LEVELS 

In line with the reduced foreign aid budget request, we support a gradual reduction of foreign aid fund levels over a period of years to the phaseout point. We believe the Congress will authorize the necessary dollar amounts for each program account.

1 Major budgetary emphasis should be placed on specific long-range economic development programs that make self-help efforts a basic criterion for negotiating loans. 

Every effort should be made to phase out grant programs and to put foreign assistance on a businesslike basis. Wherever possible, foans should be encouraged. Voluntary, private groups should receive prime consideration. We are encouraged that AID is placing increased reliance on nongovernmental technical assistance programs, and urge that it push its contracting policies to the fullest. 

IMPACT OF FOREIGN ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS ON THE U.S. BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

In his February 10 balance-of-payments message, President Johnson urged the business community to be prudent about its oversea investments. One week later, the President called business and banking leaders to the White House, urging them to devise voluntary controls on the outflow of American capital. Recognizing that the 

President's remarks were directed primarily at Western Europe, the National Chamber believes that direct investment in the developing countries, stimulated by the private enterprise provisions of foreign assistance programs, can promote foreign markets which will continue to import U.S. goods and services even after Government assistance is phased out.

If I may, Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a little statement in addition to this, since the testimony here concerns foreign aid primarily, and we are stressing the phase of the developing countries. 

However the balance-of-payments problem is something that encompasses both the developed and developing countries. My own company has a major interest abroad, and we are operating in both developing and developed countries. Virtually 50 percent of our business is done outside of the United States as a result of foreign investment and sales that we make. Therefore, it is of vital concern to all of us here, and I think I would like to quote from a statement I made with regard to our position with reference to the balance of payments and the President's request. 

PFIZER'S CONTRIBUTION IN REGARD TO BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

We have already put into effect many steps now recommended by the Government since 1951, and since 1951 Pfizer's operations abroad have made a net contribution to the plus side of the U.S. balance of payments of approximately $370 million. The major portion of this inflow, some $270 million, has come from our exports of U.S.made goods, and equipment to our oversea installations, most of which would not have been possible without prior direct investment in these installations.

The remainder, some $100 million, has come from such items as dividends, interest, royalties, and service fees also largely resulting from these investments.

As to investment policy, for many years all Pfizer investments abroad have been made from foreign borrowings and foreign handling, which continue to finance the future investment needs for such

purposes. I am quite sure many other firms are in the same position, and feel very much the same as we do. 

In the overall, I think direct investments we would find have resulted in the net surplus of $3.2 billion in the year 1963. Of this portion, Europe is $1.2 billion. Figures from other U.S. Department of Commerce Survey of Current Business were used as a source for this information, and since I was called rather hastily to testify, I prepared this yesterday, and with the permission of the Chair I should like to extend my remarks by submitting these to you, in the form of some explanatory remarks, because I think they will carry out the point very well. 

Senator LAUSCHE. That may be done. (The information referred to follows:)

SUPPLEMENTARY REMARKS MADE BY MR. JOHN O. TEETER 

At this point, Mr. Chairman, I should like to depart from my printed testimony which you have before you to develop a point more fully. 

Foreign aid is essentially directed toward the developing nations. However, the balance-of-payments problem encompasses both developed and developing nations. My company has installations abroad in both categories, and since almost half the total sales volume of our entire operations is sold outside the United States, we are vitally concerned with this subject. 

With your permission, Mr. Chairman, I should like to quote a statement of our balance-of-payments position, a statement which I feel is fairly typical of the record and attitude of many firms whose operations are similar to our own. 

QUOTE TEXT OF PFIZER'S POSITION 

A careful analysis of properly adjusted statistics based on the U.S. Department of Commerce balance-of-payments data published in the Survey of Current Business indicated that the total surplus from all direct investments reached $3.2 billion in 1963. On the other hand, trade accounts (import-export) similarly adjusted, produced a surplus of about $900 million. If we take manufacturing direct investments in Europe alone, analysis shows a surplus of $1.2 billion.

With the Chair's approval, I should like to request permission to extend my remarks for the record. As you know, I was called to testify on very short notice and consequently two charts which have been prepared, as well as a supplementary statement in connection with the figures that I have just recited, could not be included in the printed testimony. 

The attached charts, schedules 1 and 2, have been prepared to illustrate that direct investments abroad contribute favorably and substantially to the balance of payments. A popular but erroneous misconception is that our payments deficit is a direct result of such investments. The basic reasons for this misconception are: (1) Inflating trade accounts by including in exports goods financed by AID which do not earn dollars, (2) including in exports goods shipped to U.S. affiliates, that is to say direct investments abroad, and (3) understating the contribution of direct investments by not adding to the net of the capital inflows and outflows, also exports to affiliates abroad and royalties and service fees, in addition to returned profits. 

To clearly illustrate these points, statistics obtained primarily from the U.S. 

Department of Commerce Survey of Current Business have been regrouped. 

We have added to the direct investments capital account (capital inflow and outflow on direct investments) the royalty and service fee income together with repatriated earnings, and we have further added the current account effect of direct investments; that is to say, the excess of exports over imports to and from direct investments abroad.

As indicated on schedule 1 the only estimate we have made covers the importation from nonmanufacturing direct investments abroad, such as oil imports, foodstuffs, minerals, etc. It has been necessary to make an estimate here, since no figures have been published. aloidy odb

TP. If you will refer to schedule 1, you will note that the total surplus from all direct investments is approximately $3 billion in 1962 and $3.2 billion in 1963. 

We do not have final figures for 1964, and it is possible that the surplus picture is not quite as good, although it would be hard to believe that they were not of the same order of magnitude. 

An examination of schedule 2 reveals the figures for the trade accounts, after making the deductions previously mentioned from the export side. To balance this, we must deduct from the import side those shipments which arise from direct investments. Here you will note that in 1962 and 1963 the figures come to $1 billion and $900 million respectively. 

It appears obvious, therefore, that direct investments rather than visible trade currently provide the bulk of the private surplus for the balance of payments, with which necessary governmental activities, such as military disbursements and foreign aid, are financed. Surplus created by direct investments is about three times as large as the surplus created by visible trade.
