PFIZER'S POSITION REGARDING PRESIDENT JOHNSON'S BALANCE-OF-PAYMENTS STATEMENT (DIRECT INVESTMENT ABROAD) 

We will cooperate with the President's program and are now examining ways and means of doing so. We have, however, already had in effect many of the steps now recommended by the Government and since 1951 Pfizer operations abroad have made a net contribution to the plus side of the U.S. balance of payments of approximately $370 million. The major portion of this inflow ($270 million) has come from our exports of U.S.-made goods and equipment to our oversea installations, most of which would not have been possible without our prior direct investment in these installations. The remainder ($100 million) has come from such items as dividends, interest, royalties, and service fees also resulting largely from the investments. As to investment policy, for many years all Pfizer investments abroad have been made from foreign borrowings and foreign earnings, and we intend to continue to finance future investment. needs abroad by these means. 

As we understand the President's program concerning direct investment abroad and the further explanation of it by Secretary Connor, the Government now recognizes the very substantial favorable effect of direct investment abroad by American business on the U.S. international balance of payments. 

Having come to this full recognition of the situation, the Government is not asking us to curtail the growth of our businesses abroad but rather, in continuing their normal growth, to take every means possible to enhance the favorable impact of direct investment upon the balance of payments. We think this is a fair and reasonable approach to a difficult subject. Secretary Connor has suggested several specific and constructive methods of accomplishing the Government's objectives such as expanding exports, increasing use of American-flag carriers, avoiding or postponing marginal projects, making greater use of funds raised abroad to finance direct investments in other countries, trying to repartriate a larger share of income earned abroad, minimizing the outflow of shortterm financial funds invested abroad solely because of more favorable interest rates, etc. The international business community should give careful consideration to all of Secretary Connor's suggestions and undoubtedly can comply with many of them, the exact compliance in each case depending on individual circumstances. The net effect should enhance the present substantial return on direct investment.

PRIVATE INVESTMENT INCREASES INTERNATIONAL TRADE GROWTH 

Mr. TEETER. In addition to stimulating the U.S. economy-U.S. private investment abroad increases the international trade growth rate of developing countries, thus expanding world trade and providing vital foreign exchange needed by these countries to stimulate economic development through their own efforts. We have charts listed on this page which indicate the situation from 1960 to 1963. 

U.S. private investment in the developing countries, as compared to U.S. Government economic assistance, has a direct relationship to the growth of international trade illustrated above. The following graph brings home the fact that aggregate U.S. private enterprise direct investment in the developing countries has grown at a greater rate than Government assistance since 1960 as AID placed increased emphasis on private sector development. 

IMPLEMENTING FOREIGN AID 

National chamber foreign aid recommendations continue to urge increased reliance on private enterprise and initiative in foreign assistance programs. Significantly, increased emphasis has been placed on the need to direct U.S. private capital and knowledge toward the encouragement of private enterprise in the developing countries. 

In this connection, the national chamber is maintaining contact with

the advisory committee on private enterprise in foreign aid, chaired by chamber member Arthur K. Watson of IBM. 

Bilateral and multilateral aid practices must be reassessed by developed nations in light of increasing demands from developing countries for economic assistance. It is clear that the industrialized nations need to coordinate their aid efforts if the developing countries are to be put into a position from which their free, economic growth can be generated by self-help programs. As pointed out in the national chamber's attached "Statement in Furtherance of Policies on Mutual Security," terms of development loans should take into consideration the overall debt management position of recipient countries.

Some efforts at improving the business climate are being made through such aid programs as investment surveys and investment guarantees. I submit that the trend toward placing increased emphasis on private enterprise suggests the desirability of AID becoming more of a lending agency while allowing the technical, operational aspects of aid programs to be administered by the private sector.

FOCUS ATTENTION ON POPULATION EXPLOSION IN RELATION TO ECONOMIC GROWTH OF DEVELOPING COUNTRIES 

In providing foreign assistance, intensive study should be given to the problems of countries whose economies are substantially dependent on their terms of trade or whose economic well-being is threatened by population increase. Although attention has been given from time to time to the impact of the population explosion on economic growth, increased emphasis should be placed on demographic studies in the developing countries. Excess U.S.-owned local currencies are an available source for promoting these studies. 

ENCOURAGING AN IMPROVED INVESTMENT CLIMATE 

Up to this point I have emphasized primarily the stake of private enterprise in foreign assistance because we believe that the less-developed countries need vastly more capital and know-how than the governments of developed nations will or can supply. We also believe that the road to economic development is through the private sector, complemented by appropriate governmental infrastructure programs. An improved investment climate can be fostered by encouraging new investment through- Development banks, regional banks, and other credit facilities. 

Corporate educational training and housing facilities in host countries.

An international convention for protection of property rights. 

People-to-people programs such as the Michigan County-Cali, Colombia project and Partners of the Alliance. 

Development of an international legal system referred to in item II-B of the attached furtherance of policy statement. 

I would like to turn now to specific foreign assistance programs.

DEVELOPMENT LOANS 

Priority should be placed on development loans to those countries whose programs provide significant roles for domestic and U.S. private enterprise. Before committing these funds, the President should receive from recipient countries progress reports with respect to selfhelp and reform measures, both planned and achieved. The President should also ascertain what external aid from other sources is being considered and take steps to make international lending terms more equitable.

THE ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS 

The Alliance must be coordinated through other institutions and programs in order that hemisphere needs can be dealt with on a hemispheric basis. Guidelines recommended by the Alliance's new 

Inter-American Committee (CIAP) hold great promise for new Latin American efforts to encourage economic and social development and to improve the investment climate. Recent fiscal reforms designed to curb inflation in Brazil are a key case in point. We are hopeful that the new Businessmen's Council for Latin America, on which we are represented, can help the Alliance find new roles for the private sector. 

INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS 

Multilateral foreign aid, to which other industrial nations contribute through such international lending institutions as the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, should be emphasized as a practical alternative to U.S. financing alone. Although the national chamber recognizes a need for a U.S. bilateral program, multilateral assistance often can be more effectively conditioned on recipient country performance than bilaterial assistance. 

MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

The national chamber recommends that an adequate budget be provided to support present commitments in countries on the Sino-Soviet periphery. However, other industrial nations should bear more of the cost for new military assistance programs. 

SEPARATION OF ECONOMIC AND MILITARY AID 

The chamber reiterates its position that the cost to the United States for military assistance should be accountable to the Department of Defense. We are aware that a shift of appropriation responsibility would involve committee jurisdiction. However, the U.S. national interest would be served by properly identifying foreign economic assistance with the stated purposes of long-range economic development. We urge a separation of economic and military aid accountability that provides appropriate review authority for pertinent congressional committees. 

U.S. CHAMBER RECOMMENDATIONS 

In summary, to provide necessary assistance to the developing countries and to further U.S. interests, the national chamber recommends continued refinement of a foreign aid program that will-

Increase reliance on private sector assistance, and reduce Government programs accordingly. 

Base loan commitments on demonstrated self-help and reform measures.

Take steps to coordinate aid programs and terms with other developed nations. 

In conclusion Mr. Chairman, I request that the attachments to this statement be made a part of the official record of your hearings. 

I will be happy to answer your questions. 

Thank you very much, sir. (The complete statement of Mr. Teeter, with the attachments referred to, follow :)

STATEMENT IN FURTHERANCE OF POLICIES ON MUTUAL SECURITY I. BASIC CHAMBER POSITION ON FOREIGN ASSISTANCE 

A. Foreign aid continues to be a proper element of U.S. foreign policy. Its objectives and principles have long been endorsed by the chamber. 

B. The need to improve the program continues. Progress should follow the effective guidelines established by the AID Administrator. The program objectives should be continually clarified as they relate to U.S. foreign policy. The U.S. public demands clear justification of its foreign aid investment. 

C. The objectives of the Act for International Development of 1961 must be fully met. Particularly, it must provide an effective base for the exercise of private enterprise and initiative in foreign economic and social development. 

II. CHAMBER PROGRAM PROPOSALS 

A. Long-range economic planning and development must be emphasized. Although long-term aid investment seldom has dramatic impact, in general it can yield far higher returns than short-term "gimmicks." Economic planning need 3 beds

not mean a government "planned economy" in underdeveloped countries. On the contrary, recent experiments with long-range planning have given considerable emphasis to both the private sectors of the local economies and the need for private foreign investment, particularly from the United States. This recognition of private enterprise must be encouraged and expanded. Private enterprise and government should cooperate in their efforts to locate opportunities and improve means for greater reliance on private enterprise in the development of free and viable economies. B.

The Government's efforts along these lines have been laudable. But a still more 

Government incentives to U.S. private foreign investment must be improved. positive approach is imperative, centering around the need to build an economic and political framework in which the profit motive can operate at full potential. 

Certain provisions in the Revenue Act of 1962 on taxation of foreign income are punitive and self-defeating. 

The United States should suspend foreign assistance to any nation which takes discriminatory or confiscatory action against U.S. private investment in such nation without taking appropriate steps to discharge its obligations under international law including prompt and full compensation or relief. Courts in the 

United States should determine and apply principles of international law in appropriate cases to encourage the development of an international legal system that will contribute to the improvement of the investment climate, and the protection of private property abroad. 

C. Development loans should receive priority. The trend toward Government lending to, and for the express development of, private institutions and organizations should be accelerated. Terms of development loans should take into consideration the overall debt management position of recipient countries. 

D. Military aid should be limited. A limited program of military assistance to selected allies is essential to total short-range, free-world security. Military assistance should be held to a minimum, particularly in Western Europe and Latin America. The cost to the United States of such assistance should be accountable to the Department of Defense. 

E. Multilateral development financing and technical assistance should be emphasized as an essential instrument of U.S. foreign policy. In some instances this approach is more practical and effective than the bilateral approach. Private international consortia should be utilized to the fullest extent possible. Congress and the administration should propose new means to achieve U.S. foreign economic development objectives through international institutions in collaboration with other industrialized free world nations provided the United States has voting rights commensurate to its contributions. major role to the private sectors of both donor and recipient nations, and the administrative cost of such programs must be equitably shared by the respective Such programs must assign a national governments. The chamber recognizes a continuing need for a sub- stantial U.S. bilateral program. 

F. Aid should be selective. The administration should apply great selectivity in choosing which nations and projects are to be aided from among ever-increasing requests for assistance. Self-help criteria should be rigorously applied, to the point where local reforms are a prime factor in qualifying for U.S. aid. Assistance should be based on results. 

3. aid. Ass

The chamber believes that the food-for-peace program, under Public Law 480, title II, serves in general the best interests of U.S. foreign policy. It realizes that particular programs may raise serious special questions and believes the final determination has to be made by the President of the United States in terms of the national interest.

G. Intensive study should be given to the problems of countries whose economies are substantially dependent on their "terms of trade" or whose economic well-being is threatened by population increase. 

H. The Alliance for Progress must be moved forward along the sound lines recommended by its Inter-American Committee (CIAP). The original concept of the Alliance cannot be carried out if it is administered or just another aid program.

At least three criteria must be met if the Alliance is to progress: 

1. The Alliance must be coordinated through other institutions and programs in order that hemisphere needs can be dealt with on a hemispheric basis. 

2. The objectives of the Alliance must be realistically determined, with particular regard to the efforts which can reasonably be expected of the

Ond den forg the se ee D

me! 71 cooperating Latin American countries and to the availability of external resources. 

3. Alliance programs must generate a massive infusion of free enterprise by creating the necessary atmosphere of stable development planning in which private investment and initiative, local and foreign, can operate beneficially. 

I. The aid task must be more justly shared. The United States should constantly and increasingly enlist greater cooperation from other industrialized nations in assisting less developed countries. The Development Assistance Committee of the OECD has an important duty as an instrument to serve this purpose. 

It is hoped that its future role will be indicative of its increasing activity in enlising free world economic cooperation toward this end. 

J. Agency for International Development administration. In order to assure effective execution of the foreign assistance program, steps should be taken to improve the quality and reduce the number of its personnel, both domestic and Overseas. The administrators of the program must have the legislative authority to carry out this objective.

STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH CAMPBELL, COMPTROLLER GENERAL OF THE UNITED STATES; ACCOMPANIED BY ROBERT KELLER, GENERAL COUNSEL; OYE STOVALL, DIRECTOR, INTERNATIONAL OPERATIONS DIVISION; VICTOR LOWE, ASSISTANT DIRECTOR, ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS GROUP, INTERNATIONAL OPERATIONS DIVISION; JAMES DUFF, ASSISTANT DIRECTOR, MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS GROUP, INTERNATIONAL OPERATIONS DIVISION; AND GILBERT STROMVALL, SUPER- VISORY ACCOUNTANT, INTERNATIONAL OPERATIONS DIVISION Mr. CAMPBELL. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, we are appearing before the committee in response to your invitation to discuss some of the findings from our test reviews over the past year relating to the economic assistance program, and to present our views concerning particular elements which we believe may be of interest to the committee as subjects for remedial legislation or otherwise for committee consideration.

During the past year we have submitted to the Congress 26 reports on foreign aid matters. Of these, 13 have related to economic assistance.

In this presentation we have endeavored to identify significant areas or elements of the operations of the economic assistance program in which our findings lead us to believe that improvements are needed. 

Some of these could be accomplished by action within the executive branch, but in each situation we believe there is an opportunity as well as significant need for strengthening of the management processes through either clarification of reiteration of legislative intent and purpose.

PURPOSE OF GAO REPORTS ON AID 

Before discussing specific areas of our findings, Mr. Chairman, I believe it might be well to identify the purpose of our reviews of economic assistance activities and our objectives in making such reviews as well as the general guidelines under which our staffs operate. We try generally to direct our available manpower resources to the areas which in our opinion will be most productive of significant findings and recommendations for improving the operations and achieving greater efficiency and economy.,

Accordingly, our work and our statements here today are in no way intended as views on basic foreign aid policy questions or, to any degree an overall evaluation of the economic assistance program. Rather, our efforts are directed to identifying from our findings specific areas in which we believe that improvements are most needed in the financial management and operational control of the programs, within the basic purposes established by the Congress. 

Our efforts and suggestions go particularly to seeking out areas in which we believe that the purposes of the particular program or projects can be accomplished at less cost, or those areas in which our findings indicate that the objectives of particular projects or functions are not being accomplished. The matters presented are primarily from reports which we have issued to the Congress, but also include some of

T SE I E our current findings contained in report drafts which are still in the final stages of review and completion for issuance within the near future.. 

USE OF FOREIGN CURRENCIES 

We would like to present for your consideration today five problem areas, with some suggestions which we believe may be of assistance to the committee in seeking ways for improving financial management of the programs. They concern- (1) More effective use of U.S.-owned foreign currencies; (2) Improved fiscal management of our foreign currencies to obtain interest on the large accmulations; (3) Clarification of purpose in relation to country capability to utilize economic assistance furnished; (4) Greater use of excess property in lieu of dollar expenditures; and (5) Emphasis on individual responsibility and accountability in the management and administration of the program. 

From our reviews we have found that maximum use has not been made of U.S.-owned foreign currencies in lieu of dollar expenditures. 

It is generally recognized that it is in the U.S. interest to use these currencies wherever possible in place of dollars, particularly in view of the current balance-of-payments situation. 

We are aware that the executive agencies are placing considerable emphasis on making the best possible use of these foreign currency funds. However, we believe that there is a continuing major opportunity for management improvement throughout the Government, as well as in the foreign aid program, in the utilization of foreign currencies already owned by the United States. 

We reported in October 1962 that dollar expenditures could be reduced if better use were made of U.S.-owned foreign currencies. 

Expenditures were being made in dollars even though excess foreign currencies were available. In other cases foreign currency balances were being held for specific purposes, even though there were other current needs for which dollars were being spent. Dollar expenditures could have been reduced and the outflow of dollars postponed if owned currencies reserved for specific purposes but not currently needed were made available on a replacement-when-required basis. Subsequently, legislation was passed to permit such use. 

The Treasury Department and the Bureau of the Budget have estimated that this legislation made available at least $75 million of administratively reserved foreign currencies. Purchases of foreign currencies for other purposes will thus be substantially reduced and the outflow of dollars curtailed. 

A recent review disclosed that AID unnecessarily spent $3.8 million to finance goods produced in one aid-receiving country for shipment to other aid-receiving countries. 

The United States had sufficient foreign currency in the producing country to have purchased the goods and an agreement with the country permitted such usage; instead, dollar purchases were made. Our review showed a need for procedures in the Agency under which full

consideration would have to be given by appropriate levels of Agency management to the use of U.S.-owned foreign currencies for financing procurement by aid-receiving countries. We also believe that there is a need for more direct assignment of responsibility within the Agency for assuring that all possible utilization of foreign currencies is realized. 

USE OF DOLLARS RATHER THAN FOREIGN CURRENCIES IN TRAVEL BY SOME GOVERNMENT AGENCIES 

We have noted that various Government agencies have expended dollars rather than foreign currency for air travel by Agency personnel even though the United States owned considerably more foreign currency than its operating requirements in the countries concerned, and U.S. agreements with these countries permitted payment of this expense with foreign currencies. The agencies involved have generally agreed that tighter controls are needed over their oversea travel and have informed us that necessary changes are being made in their regulations and review procedures.

This is primarily a matter for administrative action by the executive agencies. However, maximum use of U.S.-owned foreign currencies means using not only currencies where U.S. balances are considered by the Treasury Department to be excess, but also other currencies whose supply while not sufficient to be declared "excess" is also above immediate U.S. needs. This is particularly important where inflationary pressures in a foreign country might cause U.S.-owned currency balances to deteriorate in value if they are not used. 

Generally speaking, we believe that economies can usually be realized by using available foreign currencies regardless of the amount of Treasury holdings when such use results in the deferral or elimination of an equivalent amount of dollar expenditures. Executive branch policies recognize that it is advantageous to the United States to use foreign currencies in many cases even though they may not have been declared to be "excess."

Section 612(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 now provides that "The President shall take all appropriate steps to assure that, to the maximum extent possible, United States-owned excess foreign currencies are utilized in lieu of dollars" and defines "excess foreign currencies" as *6* * * foreign currencies or credits owned by or owed to the United States which are, under applicable agreements with the foreign country concerned, available for the use of the United States Government and are determined by the President to be excess to the normal requirements of departments and agencies of the United States for such currencies or credits and are not prohibited from use under this subsection by an agreement entered into with the foreign country concerned."

We suggest for your consideration that to establish a basis for more effective usage of U.S.-owned foreign currencies the committee might wish to consider revision of present legislation, particularly of section 612 to broaden the policy so that it will not be restricted to "excess" currencies.

INTEREST OF U.S.-OWNED FOREIGN CURRENCIES 

We have on several occasions reported on losses of interest income which might have been earned if U.S.-owned foreign currencies had been deposited in interest-bearing accounts. 

In our most recent report on this subject, we pointed out that a potential $7 million in interest was lost in the Republic of China in a 2-year period because U.S. agencies had not sought the agreement of the Chinese Government to pay interest on the large holdings of U.S.owned foreign currency in that country. We found that the decision against attempting to obtain interest appeared to have been made by State Department personnel; however, the management of foreign currencies has been so diffuse in the Departments of State and the Treasury and the Agency for International Development that we have been unable to determine specifically why such losses were allowed to occur or the individuals responsible for this situation. The diffusion of management responsibilities is, in our opinion, a basic reason for the limited action taken on the findings and recommendations made in our previous reports on the same subject. 

In our report on interest losses in the Republic of China, we made a number of recommendations designed to affix management responsibilities and to make decisions reached a matter of record, subject to periodic review at appropriate management levels. We also expressed the belief that the Congress might wish to consider the enactment of legislation requiring that agreement be reached with countries receiving economic assistance on the payment of interest on U.S.owned foreign currencies.

We recently have been advised by the Agency for International Development that a plan has been developed to extend the interestearning principle on a worldwide basis in a manner which is in substantial accord with the recommendations in our report. 

Despite the Agency's assurances that appropriate corrective action will be taken administratively, this committee may wish to consider the adoption of an appropriate legislative requirement to obtain interest income on U.S.-owned foreign currencies. We are making this proposal because of the historical failure of responsible agencies to act meaningfully on similar reports we have issued in the past and because there is no real assurance that a continuity of effective action will be taken in the future. Also, it would appear that the current initiative may be emanating from the Agency for International Development in this matter, whereas we believe that any permanent improvement should be rooted in a more comprehensive exercise of top fiscal responsibility by the Treasury Department. 

A legislative requirement could also serve to strengthen the position of the State Department in its negotiations with certain foreign countries, since they might otherwise resist efforts to negotiate for the payment of interest on U.S.-owned foreign currencies in deposit accounts. 

COUNTRY CAPABILITY TO UTILIZE ASSISTANCE 

A number of our reviews have shown that the amount of economic assistance furnished has, in significant instances, been excessive in relation to the capability or willingness of the recipient countries for effective utilization. In many cases, the United States has agreed

to provide dollar assistance in the form of equipment, facilities or material; whereas, the recipient country has agreed to provide foreign currency funds for operating and maintenance expenses. These agreements have not been adhered to completely in a number of cases because of the inability or unwillingness of the recipient country to provide the necessary foreign currency. In other instances, we have found that the recipient country lacked the trained manpower, facilities, or other basic capabilities to assure effective utilization of the assistance.

The above situations have led to an inability to meet important program objectives and an underutilization of U.S.-furnished material. For example, reviews we have performed in Turkey and the 

Republic of the Philippines have disclosed widespread conditions of ineffective use of assistance furnished for purpose of developing the economies of these countries. 

For example, in our examination of assistance furnished Turkey, we reported that the Turkish bituminous coal industry continued to suffer from inefficient operations despite U.S. dollar and foreign currency aid of at least $68 million; and that about $18 million had been provided to three enterprises for the procurement and erection of facilities which were barely used although they had been completed for 2 or more years. The assistance furnished had contributed little toward improving operations of the enterprises. 

Similarly, in a recent review of economic assistance furnished to the Republic of the Philippines, we observed that about $54 million in grant aid assistance for development projects had been furnished which substantially exceeded Philippine capabilities to effectively absorb, maintain, and utilize with the limited country funds allocated for this purpose. We found, as a result, that the projects had not achieved the economic development benefits that could have been reasonably expected had adequate levels of support been made available by the Philippine Government. 

We believe that it is incumbent on U.S. officials administering economic assistance programs to carefully consider the availability of country resources needed to support proposed program activities before committing or disbursing U.S. funds to these programs. While we recognize that this is primarily an administrative task for the Agency for International Development, this committee may wish to consider the enactment of legislation which would require appropriate officials in the Department of State and the Agency for International Development to certify that the recipient country has sufficient available resources to devote toward proposed programs to assure that they are carried out effectively. 

We believe that a legislative requirement would tend to assure more careful scrutiny of proposed projects and would also require continuing analysis of the principal U.S. objectives in furnishing assistance. 

We have observed that a number of economic assistance projects have been justified both on economic and foreign policy grounds. Under these circumstances, it becomes difficult from a management viewpoint to ascertain what the predominant U.S. objectives are, so that a meaningful standard of achievement can be established. 

For example, a project justified primarily on economic grounds would require a different type and degree of management control and

零食 ​its success or failure would be appraised in entirely different terms from a project justified primarily on foreign policy grounds, where the principal objective may be to retain a favorable climate for the continued access to oversea bases, to demonstrate support of a recipient government, or to offer an economic alternative to Sino-Soviet assistance.

We believe that a legislative certification requirement could serve to specifically identify the primary U.S. interests involved, serve as a standard for appraising project performance, and be of assistance both to the administration and the Congress in their continuous review of economic assistance matters. 

A legislative certification requirement for economic assistance would be in line with existing legislation pertaining to the military assistance program. 

EFFECT OF LEGISLATION SUGGESTED BY GAO 

For example, our reports on the military assistance program over the past 7 years had shown one basic deficiency in the administration of the program to be the failure of the Department of Defense to limit materiel deliveries in line with the capability of the recipient countries to maintain and utilize effectively, even though this was required by the agency's own regulations. We, therefore, suggested that the Congress might wish to consider the enactment of legislation requiring additional safeguards before delivery of military as sistance program materiel. Public Law 88-633 approved October 7, 

1964, added section 513 to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, to require a certification of recipients' capability.

Mr. CAMPBELL. Mr. Duff, you have been on that. 

Mr. DUFF. Yes, sir.

On our current reviews we are looking into this thing, and the certifications started coming in about the 4th month after the bill was passed. Our current reviews will evaluate this and we will report on how it is working out. 

Mr. CAMPBELL. And we have just been at it about 3 or 4 months.

USE OF EXCESS PROPERTY Mr. CAMPBELL. From a recent test review in five aid-receiving coun tries, we found that excess Government-owned property is being used as supplemental assistance over and above regular approved projects, but is not being applied to any appreciable extent as a substitute for new purchases. Our report to the Congress is now being prepared. 

Our review in the five countries disclosed that U.S.-financed property purchases and planned purchases estimated at approximately $3 million could have been avoided if excess property already owned by AID or available from other Federal agencies had been used. On the basis that comparable conditions prevail in other countries, very substantial amounts can be saved annually if AID's oversea missions give full consideration to the use of excess property in lieu of new procurement.

Section 102 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 provides that- *** it is the sense of the Congress that assistance under this part should be complemented by the furnishing under any other Act of surplus agricultural commodities and by disposal of excess property under this and other Acts. 

AID's stated policy regarding excess property isto promote the optimum utilization of excess property in the implementation of aid projects and programs. 

This policy is in accordance with the Federal Property Management Regulations which provide that each executive agency shall, to the fullest extent practicable, utilize excess property as the first source of supply, AID's policy also stated thatin addition, utilization of excess property to "complement" AID economic assistance programs is in accordance with and serves to implement congressional policy.

Although considerable excess property has been transferred to AID recipients, we concluded from our review that very few U.S. dollars were saved directly as a result of such transfers in the five countries because the excess property was generally not substituted for proposed new procurements, but was provided as additions or supplements to regular approved agency projects and programs. 

The CHAIRMAN. Was this primarily agricultural commodity you had in mind?

Mr. Lowe. No, sir; this was excess equipment- 

The CHAIRMAN. I wasn't sure. 

Mr. Lowe (continuing). Such as tractors and trucks and that sort of thing.

Mr. CAMPBELL. While we do not question the furnishing of excess property as supplemental assistance, we are concerned with AID's failure to place primary emphasis on those uses of excess property which would result in direct dollar savings to the United States. We believe that the management processes should provide that consideration first be given to the use of excess property in AID-financed projects and programs, and only after it is assured that such property is not needed for these activities should AID allow it to be transferred as supplementary assistance.

Our concern is with the way in which the broad legislation is being interpreted in actual practice with insufficient emphasis on the use of excess in substitution for new purchases. 

We believe that before economic assistance funds are allowed to be used for procurement of new property for public projects, responsible agency personnel might be required to certify that (1) no suitable excess property was located after due and diligent search, or (2) that suitable excess property found to be available was not used in lieu of the procurement of the new property for clearly stated reasons. We believe that such certifications would assign a personal responsibility for conservation of U.S. Government funds and would also document the reasons for nonuse of available excess property for Agency management and planning purposes.

Although improved administration in this area is not necessarily dependent on legislative action, you may wish to consider guidelines to the administering Agency, particularly with respect to the relative emphasis that should be accorded excess property as substitutes, rather than supplements, for new procurement.

אוד

I V In that connection the committee may wish to clarify the intent of the broad legislation that is now being interpreted in actual practice in a fashion that minimizes the use of excess property as a substitute for new purchases. 

INDIVIDUAL RESPONSIBILITY AND ACCOUNTABILITY 

We continue to find situations in which the original purposes and intent of a particular AID project or program seem to be modified or diluted along the way without apparent good reason, or where the original terms of an agreement are modified and relaxed during the administration of a project or loan without evident justification. 

Some of these have the effect of providing supplemental assistance through the relaxation of terms of the agreement as, for example, in not requiring adherence by a country to the terms of its agreement in relation to maintenance of value, or in accepting conversion rates which have the effect of providing additional dollar exchange to the country concerned. 

Frequently, the records supporting these changes or modifications are inadequate to show the reason or the advantage to the U.S. Government resulting from such change and, in some situations, we find it impossible to pinpoint with any degree of certainty just where and by whom a particular decision was made. This is true to a greater extent in the food-for-peace program, but it does apply to economic assistance and it is not limited to any particular area. 

We recognize the difficulties under which these programs are administered and the considerations of international relations which enter into the decisions made in negotiating and administering foreign. assistance. This is accentuated by the degree to which the management decisions require recognition of the broad interest of the United States, political and military or other, in addition to the purely economic features.

In this connection, we have been increasingly concerned from our findings over the past 2 or 3 years in relation to governmental management systems generally with the need for a greater sense of individual responsibility for economy in Government operations and with the additional costs that have been and are being incurred because of an inadequate sense of fiscal responsibility with respect to U.S. 

Gnment interests on an individual basis. dent

A most important underlying reason in our opinion for the management deficiencies which we continue to find is the tremendously complex operation-and-management structure in the Government, and the resulting decentralization or fragmentation of management responsibility. This has led to the development of and reliance upon operation of management systems which are based on the "managementby-exception" principle; that is, a system is presumed to be operating correctly except where the contrary is shown. Costly and wasteful deficiencies usually result from the failure of one or a number of individuals to properly carry out their duties. When this occurs, the error made by one person is compounded or leads to others, because each individual is concerned only with his own specific activity.

Management systems, as now administered, frequently lack in sufficient degree the essential ingredient of responsibility for individual performance. In the area of foreign aid the problem is compounded by the necessity for recognizing the interests of more than one agency and the consequent clouding of individual responsibility that goes with a multiagency performance. 

We do not intend an indictment of management systems as such or of the many hard-working devoted persons participating in these programs; nor do we propose any simple solution to the problem. 

It seems only reasonable, however, that the greater the size and complexity of the activity and the resultant reliance to be placed on the operation of the management system, the greater the need for emphasis to assure (1) that the relative responsibilities of the different agencies are clearly understood; (2) that each individual involved fully understands the nature of this function, the part it plays in the system, and his responsibility for his acts in terms of the results; (3) that means be provided, through supervisory surveillance and independent internal review, to evaluate the performance of both workers and supervisors against this yardstick; and (4) that individual accountability for mismanagement thus determined at any level be dealt with by appropriate administrative action. 

As I mentioned earlier, these problems are present to the fullest degree in the foreign assistance programs; not only because of the sensitivity and complicated nature in many cases, but also because of the participation of more than one department or agency in the management decisions. 

We have found it most difficult in many situations to identify the official in the decisionmaking process who was actually responsible for the particular decision and its consequent administration. In some cases it is difficult to identify the agency which played the dominant role. While the Agency for International Development generally has primary responsibility, such responsibility is often diluted by the interests of other agencies, particularly the political elements of concern to the Department of State which may be overriding but not acknowledged in the record as the basis for the decision or action.

We believe that the prospects for improved financial management would be materially enhanced by a clearer requirement for pinpointing responsibilities within the Agency for International Development and for requiring clearer identification of the decisions made by personnel of other agencies in the conduct of the economic assistance programs.

In summary, we believe that these five topics we have discussed represent areas in which there remains room for substantial improvement in the operation and management of the economic assistance program, and while most of these could be accomplished within the executive branch, we believe that they are matters which the committee might wish to consider for clarification or reiteration of congressional intent and purpose through a committee position or other legislative consideration that would tend to strengthen the efforts toward greater effectiveness and economy in management of these programs.

This concludes my statement, Mr. Chairman.

EXAMPLES OF POSSIBLE SAVINGS TO AID BY SUBSTITUTING EXCESS PROPERTY 

The CHAIRMAN. I want to go a little further on page 15. You say "very substantial amounts can be saved annually if AID's oversea missions give full consideration" to these problems. You mention this is not just commodities. Can you develop that a little further. 

Mr. Lowe. Yes, sir; if I may. 

The CHAIRMAN. You you have some examples? 

Mr. Lowe. I do; yes.

Our report on this matter should be out soon, Mr. Chairman. For example, we found these four or five items which we are going to recite in our report, but there are many, many others along this nature.

Back in 1961, when the Foreign Assistance Act as it is presently constituted was passed, AID asked for and was given authority to set up a revolving fund to acquire excess property from other government agencies in advance of any known specific need on the basis that they knew the types of property and equipment that would be needed generally throughout the AID program. 

And in addition they have access directly to all of the property declared excess by the government agencies throughout the world, particularly overseas. But some of the items we picked up, for example two new dump trucks costing $15,000, were financed for Thailand when AID had similar trucks which were suitable for these required trucks in its own inventory of excess goods acquired in advance. 

They already had it in their own inventory. 

Senator SYMINGTON. Whereabouts? 

Mr. Lowe. This would have been in Japan, I believe. They have a big depot in Japan.

Another example, we found they had financed two new crawler tractors for China, this is Taiwan, of course, at a cost in excess of $49,000, and we located a number of similar tractors that were available in 

AID's own inventory. They financed two new 72-ton dump trucks for Turkey at a cost in excess of $40,000. We went to the Turkish officials who operate the Ministry that acquired these two trucks, through the AID program, and we presented the trucks that we had located in excess property and they advised us that they would have been suitable for the two trucks that they acquired at a cost of about $40,000.

Now, these are very clear-cut examples, I think. But in every case in this particular report that we are referring to, we either had confirmation from the AID technician or from somebody inthe host country that this appeared to be substitutable material for the material that was actually being purchased or had been purchased. 

The only time we did not get this confirmation was when the item to be acquired was so specifically stated that it was readily identifiable with another item in the excess property.

DIFFICULTY IN WRITING ADEQUATE LEGISLATION 

In connection with those things we attempted to get guidelines written into the bill from time to time but we don't seem to get administrative compliance with vigor, at least, let's say. We get some compliance. I think Mr. Bell, who is head of the Agency, is really trying to do a heroic job to get some more order into this thing, but we have had reports of our own from time to time that we have had too many "square pegs in round holes" in these places around the world. While 

I think some attempt to get more adaptable and more qualified people into these spots has been made, I do feel there is a certain amount of, let's say, lack of vigor in carrying out what otherwise would be a program that this committee has already reauthorized. 

The difficulty that I find in legislating is that it is practically impossible for a legislative body to write the details of administrative activity. About all you can do is write the guidelines and the policy and hope that you can get administrators that will really devote themselves to implementing that policy-I won't say in good faith because I don't want to question the good faith of people. We must hope, however, to get administrators in various places who will really get down and try to administer these policies with the same vigor as if it was their own business and thereby save the Government money. 

You pointed up this problem clearly in your statement here. 

I don't know what the answer is beyond what we have done. We can again reiterate our policy in this bill that people should be efficient, that they should do many of these things, and yet we come up year after year and find out that they just don't do it. 

I see no real reason why in the administration of this program certain regulations can't be laid down and if people violate them, they will have to go look for a job someplace else. 

We have problems in the military, which is not necessarily in our bailiwick, where fairly high military officers violate the law in the expenditure of the money that is available to them. 

I haven't heard of one of them being disciplined for clear violation of the law or the regulations, in the expenditure of money. I don't know what you do with officials in administrative government, who don't obey either the letter or the spirit of the law. 

I know the chairman has, in years past, and some of the rest of us who have been on this committee a long time have, had reviews of these things. Some of us have been abroad repeatedly. Those things have been reported back here, and the deficiencies have been called to our attention, and I think they have resulted in a number of cases of so-called alterations of the law or the rewriting of the guidelines. 

I still think that a legislative body can't write the details of administration; all we can do is write the principles and then the administration has to take over and follow these principles. 

SUGGESTION TO COLLECT INTEREST ON FUNDS 

I am intrigued by the suggestion that we begin to collect interest on these funds that are reserved for us; that is, these local currencies that are reserved for our particular use in these countries. I don't know that we have devoted any particular time to considering that

particular issue in the past, but I think it is one that we should look into.

I see no reason whatsoever why administration from the top of this Agency down, couldn't lay down very rigid specifications which require the holding to account of individual and local administrators of this program to see that they make sure-for instance in this surplus property that is available that could be used rather than buying new property-that there is no surplus property in these depots or anything else that could be substituted already owned by the Government. 

I have maintained for a long time that if people on the ground in a lot of these foreign countries have a Federal checkbook with any kind of leeway, or, if they can get away with it, it is a lot easier to write a Federal check than it is to go out and do a little work and turn up substitutes or see that these countries do what they are supposed to do in return for the receipt of American aid and American property. 

It makes it very difficult for a great many of us, I am sure, who don't want to see the AID program completely eliminated, who believe that it has a place and who believe there is a responsibility. But one has to be increasingly apologetic for this AID program because of these deficiencies that show up year after year and don't seem to be corrected. That is one of the reasons why on the floor of the Senate and over on the floor of the House the resistance to these aid programs is increasing. It is going to keep increasing if the administration of this program doesn't show more evidence of efficiency of results or a greater percentage of results for the money we put in. And it is going to have increasing difficulty.

Now, after all of that, may I get around to a question?

However, we have gone about attempting to find out how a decision was arrived at, there have been occasions when we actually haven't been able to. The records just don't tell the story and it is difficult to find individuals who were on the ground when the decision was made.

Do you wish to add something, Mr. Stovall?

Mr. STOVALL. I might add our concern is not as much with the policy as with the actual doing, the carrying out or failure to carry out.

CLASSIFICATION OF GAO REPORTS 

Senator WILLIAMS. Mr. Campbell, I want to join the rest of the committee in congratulating you on the job you have done. Over the years I have followed your reports with great interest, and I am wondering if a part of the problem we have in this connection is an undue use of the word "secret" or "confidential." I have read many of these reports you have sent down here that have been classified. I try to read all of them if I can and, in some of them, I can see some reason for marking them secret. However, from a security standpoint, it didn't make sense to me to classify all of them unless it was not to embarrass the Agency. Do you think all of this confidential classification is necessary?

Mr. CAMPBELL. We have had occasions both in Defense and also in 

State where we have wondered why they have classified certain information.

We had an experience not many years ago when a report of ours was classified, and I mean classified, practically every page. It was

a very substantial report and, yet, when the chips were down, and the matter became a really hot issue where the particular agency in Defense needed declassification to defend itself, that report was declassified and it was due to pressure by one of the committees on the other side.

This happens rather frequently. 

Senator HICKENLOOPER. I have seen that happen right in testimony before a committee, where a man has taken it and declassified it right then when it was convenient for him to declassify it. 

Mr. CAMPBELL. Mr. Stovall would like to say something.

Mr. STOVALL. I would like to elaborate just a little more on our working procedure with the Defense Department and the State Department and AID on our reports. We try in every way possible to keep our reports unclassified and we sit down in each case with the Agency at the time that they have an opportunity to look at our report draft and ask them to tell us page by page the specific classification which they put on the report, and we frequently have found that by going back and asking them about a particular paragraph we find if we rephrase it slightly or delete a sentence or something of this order that we can get it declassified. We have been actively working with the agencies on this and in quite a few instances have been able to make our point and make the facts available in an unclassified report. 

Senator WILLIAMS. I have often wondered why the committee didn't review these reports as a committee and declassify some of them. If they let the Agency know they are going to be publicized, that, in itself, would be a deterrent to some of this waste that they are trying to cover up. I have read many of these reports. For example, I am not excusing the release of it, but I don't see how you are going to embarrass us from a military standpoint to point out that we are buying new equipment when we have plenty of old equipment over there in the area.

Mr. STOVALL. We do in the final analysis, of course, respect the classifications.

Senator WILLIAMS. I understand that. 

Mr. CAMPBELL. We have no alternative. 

Senator WILLIAMS. I appreciate that, but I just wonder if the

Agency itself was not trying to use this to cover up embarrassing situations, rather than to protect the security of the country? 

Mr. CAMPBELL. Of course, Senator, one of the important aspects of this is that there are a good many men in the Congress who do not have facilities to handle classified reports. I know many men who would like to have these reports and would read them but they fear responsibility for a "leak" and, therefore, they ask us not to deliver or send classified reports to them.

Senator WILLIAMS. That is the reason why they really don't get the circulation they should have in the Congress itself. 

Mr. CAMPBELL. That is correct.

UNITED STATES SENATE, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN RELATIONS,

Present: Senators Fulbright, Morse, Pell, Hickenlooper, Aiken, Carlson, and Williams.

I believe you have a short statement this morning, do you not, Mr. 

Bell? I think you might as well proceed. We might as well get used to the fact that we proceed with less than a quorum or we do not proceed at all.

STATEMENT OF DAVID E. BELL, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT; ACCOMPANIED BY JOHN H. 

FUNARI, COORDINATOR, LEGISLATIVE PRESENTATION, AID COORDINATION OF MILITARY AND ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE 

Mr. BELL. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I welcome the opportunity to discuss with the committee the coordination of military and economic assistance programs. 

The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, in section 622 (c), directs thatunder the direction of the President, the Secretary of State shall be responsible for the continuous supervision and general direction of the assistance programs authorized by this Act including, but not limited to, determining whether there shall be a military assistance program for a country and the value thereof, to the end that such programs are effectively integrated both at home and abroad and the foreign policy of the United States is best served thereby. 

The Secretary has delegated this responsibility to me as the Administrator of the Agency for International Development.

There is full agreement, in the executive branch as well as in the Congress, on the need for central coordination of our military and economic assistance programs to make sure they are effectively integrated and best serve the foreign policy of the United States. Specifically, it is necessary to make sure that military assistance programs, like economic assistance programs, have been examined from the standpoint of the U.S. interests they are expected to serve. Furthermore, it is necessary to consider the continuing defense costs which are being undertaken by a country receiving military aid, in relation to the economic prospects and requirements of the country and any economic aid we are considering there. Finally, there are often detailed relationships between military and economic assistance in a country con- 359

cerning such matters as internal security, civic action, the programing of local currency proceeds of Public Law 480 sales agreements. 

All these aspects of the coordination responsibility are, we believe, provided for under present arrangements. With the committee's permission, I will outline briefly the organizational arrangements and the procedural system under which this coordination responsibility is carried out. 

As the committee knows, the Department of Defense has operational responsibility for the administration of military assistance. This comes to a focus in Washington under the Assistant Secretary of Defense for International Security Affairs and the Director of Military Assistance who will be testifying before this committee later this week. 

And of course, as the committee knows, the Secretary of Defense is personally involved and feels, as he should, personally responsible for the operational aspects of the military assistance program. 

COORDINATION IN THE FIELD AND AT HOME 

The field organization of this program is directly parallel to that of the Department of Defense for other purposes, running through the regional unified commands; such as, CINCPAC in Hawaii and 

CINCSOUTH in Panama. These commands have responsibility both for U.S. forces and defense operations in their theater, and for the conduct of military assistance activities in that theater. 

Military assistance in the recipient country is administered by a Military Assistance Advisory Group which, like the economic assistance mission, is responsible to the Ambassador. 

The Department of State and the Agency for International Development maintain continuing communication with this Defense organization in Washington through small staff groups in the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs, where Ambassador Thompson is now acting, and in AID's Office of Program Coordination. Moreover, specifically designated liaison officers in the 

AID and State regional bureaus are in continual contact with the regional military assistance officers in the Office of International Security Affairs as military assistance problems evolve, and our country desk people are in frequent contact with their opposite members in the 

Pentagon on common problems.

In each aid-receiving country, the Ambassador, frequently with the help of a full-time special assistant, is deeply involved in the overall policy direction of military assistance and with maintaining balance between this and other programs in the country for the most effective and economical pursuit of U.S. interests there. In addition, there is a substantial working relationship between the AID mission and the military assistance advisory group in each aid-receiving country on problems of financial support, civic action, internal security, et cetera. 

CYCLE OF BUDGET PREPARATION AND PROGRAMING 

Within this structure, the coordination effort centers on the annual cycle of budget preparation and program decision. The starting point is the military assistance guidance document which goes to the field each spring, stating general policies for the program and specific objectives and target-planning levels for each country. This is

prepared in the Department of Defense in close coordination with Department of State and AID staff, and is issued with my concurrence.

On the basis of this guidance, each country's Military Assistance Advisory Group prepares a proposed assistance program indicating the priority needs for training and equipment. 

The Ambassador reviews this recommended program with his staff and reports his endorsement or any differences of view he may have, based on political considerations or a different judgment of priorities, to the Departments of State and Defense in Washington and to the unified commander.

The unified commander reviews the program presented by the country mission in terms of military priorities within the theater, relationship to U.S. defense requirements, and a techniqual critique of the military judgments on which the recommended proposals are based. 

The revised plans of the unified command are reviewed in Washington within the Department of Defense and in a series of interagency review sessions participated in by my staff as well as other officers from the Departments of State, Treasury, and the Budget Bureau. This process culminates in reviews conducted by the Secretary of Defense and by me, on which we base our recommendations for the President's program and budget proposals for the coming year. 

Following action by the Congress on these proposals, the Department of Defense prepares specific program implementation proposals on the basis of which, following thorough staff coordination, and whatever discussion may be necessary with the Secretary of State, I authorize the level and general content of military assistance for each country. 

SUMMARY 

For the most part, this coordination effort is smooth and reasonably quick. It involves more than just the formal approval of documents; it involves a great deal of informal consultation among the regional bureaus and country desks of AID, the Department of State, and the Department of Defense as problems evolve. This is particularly true as conditions change from those anticipated during the annual programing process; new threats arise or governments shift requiring changes in program plans. Such shifts that is, such changes in program plans are generally initiated either by the Ambassador or by the unified commander, and frequently involve intense personal review by the regional assistant secretaries of state and assistant administrators of AID as well as by the military assistance officials in the Defense Department and my own coordination staff, before I authorize a change in the approved program. On major and important problems; such as, the shifts which have been required this year because of the large increases in requirements in southeast Asia, the Secretary of State and the President are consulted before final decisions are made. 

In this brief account, Mr. Chairman, of the organizational and procedural arrangements through which we carry out the coordination responsibility, I have made no attempt to discuss the substantive questions which are our daily concern. I thought, however, it would be useful to the committee to have a clear statement of the arrangements under which we work. I shall be very pleased to respond to 44-834-65-24

any questions concerning these arrangements, or any other aspect of the problem of coordination. 

The CHAIRMAN. Mr. Bell, have you been informed about our session with the Comptroller General by Mr. Funari? 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; I have.

FURNISHING MATERIAL TOO SOPHISTICATED FOR COUNTRIES' USE 

The CHAIRMAN. What is the explanation of the examples which he gave of supplying sophisticated material, particularly electronic and modern materiel, to countries which have no capability of utilizing it? He had 13 reports last year of military assistance that had gone wrong in one way or another. What is the matter with this procedure which you described here, which is rather complicated, that it allows this to happen so often? 

Mr. BELL. I am not sure, Mr. Chairman, that the Defense Department would agree with the Comptroller General in every case that the equipment that was furnished was badly designed for the purpose. 

The CHAIRMAN. No; I did not make myself clear. I did not say that. I think what he said is that the people in these countries are unwilling or unable and often, I got the impression, incapable of utilizing the kind of equipment they have been given. 

Mr. BELL. Let me respond positively. The military assistance program, in a sense, consists of providing equipment which is more technical and more sophisticated than that which the Armed Forces of the recipient country had before. The plans for military assistance are a continuing process of improving the capability of the defense forces in the recipient country to handle more sophisticated equipment. The training programs and the equipment provision programs are designed and planned to go hand in hand and side by side. 

Now, there are certainly instances in which it has turned out to be infeasible to upgrade the technical capability of the receiving military forces as rapidly as the Military Assistance Advisory Group anticipated when the plan was laid out. In a case like that, there may well be, and I am sure there have been cases in which it turned out that the equipment was overly sophisticated for the time being, and these would be cases which are quite legitimately pointed out by the Comptroller General. They would represent mistakes in judgment which should be corrected insofar as they can be. 

But it is important to emphasize, it seems to me, Mr. Chairman, that the entire process is one in which we are deliberately anticipating the improvement of the capability of the military forces in the recipient country to handle more modern equipment. The training plans which are a part of the military assistance program are designed precisely and exactly to enable the military forces in these countries to use this more sophisticated equipment. 

Now, coming back to what I was saying, this is why I believe that there are likely to be instances in which there would be a difference of judgment between the Comptroller General's auditors and the military people.

08 

EQUIPMENT ARRIVING BEFORE TRAINING IN ITS USE IS FINISHED 

The CHAIRMAN. Do you think there could be any difference of judgment as to whether the machinery has actually been used? Would they differ as to whether this electronic equipment or these planes were actually used or not used? 

Mr. BELL. Not whether actually in use, but whether it is arriving and is there at a time when the training is close enough to completion so that it was legitimate and proper for it to arrive, or maybe the slippage was very brief. 

I repeat, I am sure there have been cases, Mr. Chairman, in which the plans turned out to be in error and in which the training job could not be carried forward as rapidly as the original plans indicated. This is a matter which we are very sensitive to ourselves. I have seen many instances on the economic side of the program in which I consider that mistakes of this character were made, and the training program and the plans for helping to establish an organization to operate and maintain equipment, for highways or something like that, in fact could not be developed as rapidly as the people who made the plans thought it could. Therefore, we have delivered equipment which at [ that time turned out not to be useful or not to be fully usable. These are mistakes. We have to keep pressing our field managers extremely hard on this sort of thing so that they are continually under the gun to feel the pressure of our insistence that they recognize the difficulty of developing the operation and maintenance capability of the people who are expected to be able to operate this more sophisticated equipment.

There was some reference, I believe John Funari told me, on the military assistance side of the case in Thailand, where I know there was at least one of the issues between the Comptroller General and the Defense Department. I think the Comptroller General is probably wrong. He said, and correctly, that equipment was delivered for 100 percent of troop strength for units which were only 80 percent filled. 

That was the plan, and that is what we have in this country. 

We have mobilization reserves--I do not know that the proportion is always 100 to 80, but it is a perfectly legitimate and appropriate objective to have equipment on hand ready for additional mobilization to full troop strength as and when that decision is taken. 

But that is just one element, I am sure, in the Comptroller General's judgments about Thailand. I repeat, in many instances I am sure he is entirely right, and we have found him to be so in the reports that he has made on our activities. 

DUPLICATION OF SUPPLIES 

The CHAIRMAN. He also gave examples of purchases of new material when you had it on inventory; particularly in Japan I think he gave two or three examples where he thought there was very poor coordination. 

Do you have any comment on that?

Mr. BELL. Only that I agree and have agreed. I have been pressing this point within our organization for a long time. It was first called to my attention, I believe, not by the Comptroller General but by Mr.

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, Mansfield, the Inspector General in the State Department, something over a year ago. We looked into it, and he was quite right. 

I put out a very stiff instruction to our own staff. We have been following it up since, and I am sure there has been a substantial improvement. I certainly would not wish to claim that we are doing the job today 100 percent. 

What happens as you know, Mr. Chairman, when you get engineers, technical experts in a country who are trying to help establish, for example, a road maintenance organization-they are going to provide some equipment for such an organization. It is easy for them, mistakenly, to say, "Well, I do not trust that reconditioned equipment that is shown as being up in Japan. I know the Army has been using it for 5 years. My guess is it is probably pretty well beat up, and I would rather have a nice new road grader or crawler tractor or what not." 

Now, our instructions are perfectly clear. Our people in the field are expected to and required to determine specifically that the items available through excess property-we have catalogs printed and continuously brought up to date, and in the hands of all of our missionsthey are specifically required to look through those catalogs and to use every piece of equipment they can get in that way that will do the job, before they buy anything that is new. 

RESPONSIBILITIES FOR MISTAKES 

The CHAIRMAN. He commented in that connection it is almost impossible to identify who is responsible for the mistake. 

Do you have any comment on that?

Mr. BELL. Well, I do not believe that is the case. I have insistedthis is a point I stressed when I was Budget Director, and I try to follow my own prescription in this job-we have a very clear, clean, and simple chain of command in the AID organization that runs from me to the assistant administrator for the region to the country director. 

This is a very short, clear line of responsibility, and I would burn the tail off any country director in which this sort of thing happened when it has, and when we find out about it. 

He understands that this is one of the elements of his responsibility, and he in turn puts the responsibility on an officer. He is instructed to put the responsibility on an officer in his field mission.

COMMENTS ON A PARTICULAR PROGRAM IN TURKEY 

The CHAIRMAN. May I ask one more question? The Turkish situation I just remembered was quite a specific one that the Comptroller mentioned. I think it was a large amount $54 or $60 millionwhich had been utilized very, very little I think. 

Are you familiar with that case?

Mr. BELL. Roughly. I am not familiar in detail. 

The CHAIRMAN. This was not military. 

Mr. BELL. No; this was economic. 

The CHAIRMAN. It was a case where they were quite strong in their view.

Mr. BELL. Yes; but this is also a case in which there was quite a sharp difference of opinion. 

The CHAIRMAN. As to its utilization? 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; and the basic purpose of the enterprise and how to evaluate the results.

For example, one of the conclusions that the Comptroller General reached was that this coal operation in Turkey is running at a very severe loss, and that this was related to the inadequate use of the equipment that we provided and engineering services and so on. 

This is disputed by our people. I think there are some grounds for the argument. They say that the Government of Turkey has held the price of bituminous coal deliberately below the world price level. 

Now, the wisdom of that policy can be challenged if you like, but in assessing the economic significance of the coal business in Turkey, the alternative cost of coal should be considered. If it were, it would be found and if you did, you would find that these coal mines in Turkey are running not at a loss in the broad economic sense but at a substantial gain in contrast to buying coal externally, and that economically speaking, therefore, the coal mines are showing a return. 

I think the figure is 15 to 20 percent on this basis of valuing the coal at the world price level.

Now, that is an entirely legitimate economic point, and indicates quite a different conclusion than the one that the Comptroller General reached.

The CHAIRMAN. I understood him to say it just was not producing coal. It was not being utilized. I do not recall that he emphasized the fact that it was produced at a loss. 

Mr. BELL. No; it is being produced and utilized. 

The CHAIRMAN. In any new capacity? 

Mr. BELL. I believe so, yes.

The CHAIRMAN. I must have misunderstood him. 

Mr. BELL. Another point in the case is that the purpose of the additional equipment that the United States furnished was to enable the coal production to be maintained and slightly increased because the problems of mining the coal were becoming more difficult. They were running deeper mines and more distant faces under the ground, so that the purpose of the additional equipment that we made available was not to expand coal production greatly, but instead to enable them to maintain and slightly increase the volume that they had been producing, and that this made economic sense.

Now, I repeat I have not been all the way through this particular issue myself, and, again, I am not trying to say that we are right and the Comptroller General is wrong in the majority of cases. Quite the contrary, most of the reports that I have seen from the Comptroller General have been very helpful. They have pointed out things that we do need to improve, and we have tried to follow up on them and improve them.

But there are cases-and this may well be one-in which some of his conclusions may have been overstated.

The CHAIRMAN. Senator Morse. 

Mr. BELL. Excuse me; may I just add one more sentence?
