PRESERVING AUTHORITY OF STATE DEPARTMENT 

Senator MORSE. As I think you know, I am very much concerned about the authority of the State Department to run our foreign affairs, subject to the approval of the President. I am concerned about a tendency in this system of government of ours to delegate in depth authorities that are invested in the first instance in the heads of departments in this instance the Secretary of State-to organizations and officers below him. Even when filled by the best men with which they can fill them, nevertheless, such delegation in my judgment tends to dilute our system of checks. 

It has been my observation from both ends of the Government, legislative and executive, that the tendency to delegate in depth waters down our control system. The delegator, busy with other things, tends to rubber stamp the decisions of the individuals in the offices to whom the delegation has been made. 

So in this instant case, I am very much interested in trying to find out from you to what extent the Secretary of State in fact exercises control-not retains it nominally, but exercises it. To what extent in this very important field in fact have you become the Secretary of State?

RELATIONSHIP OF AID DIRECTOR TO SECRETARY OF STATE 

I would like to have you discuss in a little greater detail for the record the relationship between you and the Secretary of State in determination of final affirmation of policy in respect to military assistance. I would like to have you direct your attention to that fear.

My present surmise is that the Secretary of State and I think rightly so far as your ability is concerned-may be inclined to say "Let Mr. Bell do it." What are your relationships with the Secretary of State in seeing to it that the Secretary of State in fact assumes the responsibility, which I think this law, that I shall return to momentarily, places in him to render the judgments on military assistance? 

Mr. BELL. I can say the following things about that, Mr. Morse, and of course you may wish to get the Secretary's own views also. In the first place, I feel that my relationship to the Secretary is intimate, close, and continuous. I attend his staff meeting every morning in the week. This is a brief, small staff of four or five people who meet every day. At that meeting I am expected to raise with him the current questions that are on the agenda. It is not a time at which we discuss at any length particular policy issues. But it is a time at which I am expected to keep him continually advised as to points of difficulty or issues that are before us which he should know about and on which I will be informing him or will be seeking his advice. 

Secondly, I feel that it is quite clear, and I think he does too, that he expects me to bring him personally into the discussion or make sure he is brought personally into the discussion and consideration of

any issue which is of sufficient significance and there are many of them.

The [deleted] case I cited a few minutes ago would be an illustration. The Secretary was personally involved in that at the appropriate stage to make sure that he agreed with us that we should oppose this request [deleted]. 

There have been important issues of policy respecting military assistance in recent months affecting Indonesia [deleted] and affecting Jordan, affecting Israel, affecting India. And also affecting Vietnam obviously, and Laos in which the Secretary is intimately and continually involved.

In all of these cases, just to cite illustrations that I recall easily and without looking up any records, the position which was taken by the Secretary was established personally, after considering the pros and cons, and hearing the issues, the arguments on both sides of the issues.

Now furthermore in a broader sense, at the time that we prepare by the means that is described in my brief statement-the budget recommendations, the program recommendations and the resulting budget recommendations to the President in the fall of each year, that of course is gone over with the Secretary, and he is personally satisfied before it goes forward. 

When the Congress has approved the appropriation at the end of the annual legislative process and we have the documentation, the basic approval letters that I sign-again the issues and the important elements of those letters are gone over with the Secretary, and I sign in a proper sense on his behalf, not without his paying any attention to it or just on my own initiative, but acting from him as the delegation implies. 

Now, I do not want to exaggerate the point, Senator. The Secretary has an enormous volume of material on his desk every day. 

There are many decisions in this program which I make without discussing with him. He expects me and I understand it to be part of my job-to decide which issues are appropriate for me to sign off on, without requiring him to examine the papers and the issues personally. 

I do feel that on all major issues, the Secretary is personally involved, as he should be. It may be something we can handle very quickly-I can handle with a 3-minute phone call. It may be something on which I will ask to see him for 5 minutes, or it may be something on which we will get a group of people around, and the Secretary will sit through an hour or two argument as to what ought to be done in given circumstances. Or it may be something which comes back to him several times before it is finally decided. 

But I believe I can honestly assure you that, recognizing there may be difference of judgment as to what elements of the program are appropriate for me to sign off on as against his being in it personally, I think, and I believe he thinks, that he is personally involved in all of the major issues in which he should be involved. 

AID CONFERRING WITH DEFENSE DEPARTMENT DIRECTLY 

Senator MORSE. In keeping with the liaison coordinating procedure with the military that you have outlined in your statement this morning, do you sometimes-and to what extent-find it necessary to con-

fer directly with the Secretary of Defense when you feel there ought to be some modification in the recommendation of the Pentagon Building? 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir, I do; and if you will pardon me, may I go back and add one other point to what I was saying about the Secretary of 

State? Because I think it is highly relevant.

One of the problems in any delegation is the question of how much reliance you place on the delegee to bring forward issues that are of sufficient significance to be brought up. 

In the case of the military assistance program, there is in a sense an independent check, because the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs is continually informed on the military assistance program and all issues under it, and the Deputy Under Secretary of State, Mr. Thompson, who is also in the small staff meeting every morning, also has direct access to the Secretary and to the Under Secretary. In any case in which he might feel that the matter should go to the Secretary's attention and I might be prepared to sign off but he might feel that it ought to go to the Secretary's attention, he could mention that to the Secretary or to me so that in that sense I do not recall any cases of this kind-in that sense there is a protection, so to speak, for the Secretary against my assuming a greater responsibility than I ought to in settling an issue without consulting him personally.

Coming back to the point you were just making, yes, sir, there are cases in which I have talked to the Secretary of Defense and should talk to him, need to talk to him, and there are lots of cases in which the Assistant Secretary for International Security Affairs, John Mc Naughton now, is involved where I talk with him or Mr. Gaud or one of our other people.

AID RELATIONSHIP TO AMBASSADORS OVERSEAS 

Senator MORSE. About the relationship that exists between the AID organization in Washington and in the field, and the Defense organization in Washington and in the field, vis a vis the work of the ambassadors in the given country where the problem arises, would you explain for the record what the procedure is in carrying out the duties of your office in relationship to an ambassador in any one of these trouble spots?

I ought to supplement my question with the explanation of my interest. There have been some indications that the ambassadors have been placed in a secondary position in their representation of our Government through the Department of State by the operation of AID and military officials in a country. Within the embassy they have the military attachés, they have the AID representatives, and they attend the ambassador meetings. But there is a feeling-that is perhaps the best word to use in some instances that the ambassadors have been shuttled to the background, and that in some countries AID and the Pentagon Building have really taken over some of the functions of the embassy that they should not. 

Mr. BELL. I would say, Senator, that quite the contrary has been the thrust we have intended. Throughout the last 4 or 5 years that I have known anything about this matter, both in the Budget Bureau and

in my present job, our continuing thrust has been to enhance the position of the ambassador. We have done this in several ways. 

POSITION OF AMERICAN AMBASSADOR 

As you will recall I am sure, in the early days of the Kennedy administration, President Kennedy wrote a special letter to the ambassadors around the world which was intended not as a personal letter to each of the men in those jobs, but as a formal statement of doctrine. It was not dissimilar in purpose to something that President Eisenhower had also done a year or two earlier. In some ways it was a somewhat stronger statement, although the legal position was not markedly different. The intent of that letter was to assert that the President of the United States expected the ambassador in each country, to be the principal officer of our Government there and to have under his control and direction the elements of our Government agencies-military, economic, information, whatever else and to act as the controller and supervisor of all such units. 

We have tried, as I say, to follow this line continually. With specific reference to the military assistance coordination, the instructions and the procedure are entirely explicit and very clear. The ambassador is required to put his comments on top of the recommendations of the Military Assistance Advisory Group in that country. 

This is also true, incidentally, on the economic side. When recommendations come from our AID missions in the country, the ambassador is required to put his comments on top. He can approve them, and normally if he is a strong minded ambassador and has worked effectively with these units in the country team, there will have been a program worked out which has his approval. 

However, there are obviously instances--and should be instancesin which there will be a disagreement, in which event we would expect the MAAG chief or the AID mission chief to put forward his views and the ambassador to say, "I agree with all except the following points, with which I disagree, and here are my reasons." 

But to repeat, the ambassador is required to state his views, and there cannot be any bypassing of the ambassadors with respect to the programing decisions. 

Now furthermore, I have personally talked to many ambassadors. 

I have tried to follow this relationship as closely as I can, especially when I have a chance to visit the field. My impression is, although obviously one's impression can be erroneous-and there certainly may well be differences of views among different ambassadors but my impression is that ambassadors with any experience say today that their control over the U.S. country units, the country team in the broad sense, is better today than it has ever been. 

When a man's abilities are correctly assessed to appoint him an ambassador-there are obviously some men who have not turned out to have the ability to be ambassadors but obviously the man with ability to be ambassador can in fact exercise appropriate command over the elements of the American official family in his country. 

I think you would find, whether you look at Win Brown in Korea or 

Graham Martin in Thailand or Lincoln Gordon in Brazil, in cases where the previous are very complicated and wide ranging, or Chet Bowles in India, wide ranging U.S. presence in missions of a variety

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 371 1965 I of kinds, that these men are on top of them. They do not feel that they are unable to exercise adequate command and control. 

Now I repeat, I do not want to exaggerate the fact. It has been an extraordinarily diverse and difficult job for an ambassador to run a big U.S. program, as in the countries I have cited. I think it is extremely important, and I believe that this has been an increasingly important criterion for the selection of ambassadors, that they be chosen because they are considered to be capable of managing very large enterprises.

We have hundreds or thousands of Americans doing dozens of different things in these countries, and they are major enterprises and require major management skills.

IMPROVEMENT OF MANAGEMENT 

Mr. BELL. Well, my particular response is, as I started to say, that 

I have tried to stress improvement in the management of this organization and its program. The day I arrived in it, I had the feeling as 

Budget Director that the Agency was an agency which, for various reasons, had come to have somewhat too loose management standards, that the level of the personnel in the Agency was not all that it should be, that the system of management was rather slow and cumbersome, and I have taken a series of steps which I hope have made some impact on that problem.

I certainly would not claim by any means that we have done everything that we should do, or that the Agency is running as smoothly and efficiently as you would like or I would like. I would, however, if I may, indicate some of the things we have been able to do. 

I think anyone who looked at the situation would agree with me that the caliber of our mission directors around the world is today

substantially better than it has been any time since the Marshall plan, when really a very remarkable group of men was involved. It is far from perfection, but the quality is rising rather than staying level or declining. This is extremely important because, as I indicated earlier, I think the chain of command between myself, the Assistant Administrator and the mission director is the heart of the management process in the AID program. 

The mission director has to be an extremely competent man with a very strong ability in the management field and a very strong interest in management matters if we are to have the degree of efficiency that we want.

Now, I have not made as much headway as I would like to have made on upgrading the rest of the personnel of the Agency. This committee recalls that we asked for special authority last year, which the Congress did not give us, which would have helped, in my opinion, to have upgraded the quality of the civil service employees. 

On those whom we have appointed under the Foreign Service Act, the Foreign Service Reserve officers, which is most of the people we have overseas, we have put into effect the selection out authority which the Congress gave us, had given us in the act of 1961. We have been using that authority. We are on our third round of selections out now, and this has exerted, in my opinion, a very healthy effect throughout the organization in toning up- Senator CARLSON. Mr. Bell, that deals with the personnel of the 

Agency, which I fully agree is important.

Mr. BELL. This is a matter that we have been pressing and improving steadily. If I remember correctly, in Mr. Funari's report, the 

Comptroller General emphasized or mentioned that we had not used local currency in all cases that we should have to pay for transportation of our people to and from the countries where excessive currencies exist.

He was correct. We have improved that. We had instructions which were clear, but we had to pursue them harder, and we have been doing that, and our record today is a lot better than when he looked at this-than when his people looked at the record. 

Senator CARLSON. Some are advocating that we use these local currencies for tourist travel. Has that been given any study or thought? 

Mr. BELL. It has. We have studied that frequently. 

You have to recognize, Senator Carlson, that when we originally make a decision to accept local currency in return for Public Law 480 commodities, we make that decision because we judge that the country cannot afford to pay dollars or undertake a dollar obligation in re-

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 377 1965 R payment for these commodities. That judgment is made because of the weakness of the country's balance of payments. 

If the country's balance of payments were strong enough, we would not accept the local currency in the first place. 

Now then, having accepted it and made that decision and having accepted the local currency, then the question is should we undertake action which in effect would require that country to convert some of the local currency into dollars or its equivalent? We may do that to some small extent, and we are trying-we are working on the question for tourists and the use of foundations, for example, and others in various countries. 

But it has to be recognized that that is a reversal of the decision that we made when we decided it was proper and appropriate to take the local currency in the first place. 

INTEREST ON FOREIGN CURRENCY ACCUMULATIONS 

Senator CARLSON. Then he makes a further suggestion for improved fiscal management of our foreign currencies to obtain interest on these large accumulations. 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir, on that he was quite right that this has not been given adequate attention. Since his report we have worked with the 

Treasury and the State Department. We now have a very firm understanding, a very clear procedure. 

The Treasury Department has accepted responsibility and understands that it has responsibility. It is in charge of all U.S.-owned currencies, of course, anywhere in the world. But they understand that their responsibility is to get those amounts into interest-bearing accounts except in any case where the State Department advises the Treasury in writing that there are some foreign policy reasons which prevent it. 

Furthermore, each of these cases will be reviewed by State, AID, and Treasury jointly at least once a year, in each case where the moneys are not in interest-bearing accounts. 

A point came up-if I may make clear for the record-when that was under discussion, as I understand it, with the Comptroller General, which may have been misleading to the committee. 

In the case where the currencies are on deposit in non-interest-bearing accounts, they are not in commercial banks. They are in the central banks of the country in question. Therefore, there is no question of a windfall accruing to some commercial operation in the country in question.

I do not mean that we should leave them in non-interest-bearing accounts if we can possibly avoid it, and therefore my response to this i one, Senator, is that we accept the Comptroller General's view. We agree with his judgment. We should put all these moneys in interestbearing accounts unless in some unusual case there is an overriding foreign policy objection, and under the system we have now set up, as Ï said, the Department of State would have to so indicate to the Department of the Treasury in writing, and that decision would have to be reviewed at least annually.

How CENTRAL BANKS IN UNDERDEVELOPED COUNTRIES UTILIZE PUBLIC LAW 480 GENERATED LOCAL CURRENCIES 

It is difficult to generalize on how central banks in various less-developed countries make use of Public Law 480 title I generated currencies because of the differences in laws and regulations governing their activities. Whether the central bank is directly owned by the government or set up as an autonomous body apart from the government, it performs a variety of fiscal functions for the government, including acting as a depository, loaning funds at no interest to the government, and generally acting as the government's agent in its broad fiscal activities.

Most central banks are not commercially oriented although in many cases they maintain commercial departments alongside the department devoted to the central banking function. These commercial departments make loans to corporations and individual entrepreneurs and receive commercial rates of interest for their loans. Unsegregated deposits or deposits available to the commercial department of the bank would influence total loan capacity. In this respect U.S.-deposited local currency, if sizable in amount, would presumably have some effect on the bank's lending capacity and its periodic profitand-loss position. 

However, many central banks are precluded from carrying on commercial business. Under the overall central banking function the position of the bank is not influenced greatly by the size of its deposits because the bank can create credit without deposits. Whether the bank has deposits or not it can make advances to the government and can make loans with no deposits. Of course, long-term deposits are to the advantage of the central bank and to the government which it serves. 

In view of what is said above, it is apparent that in those cases where the central bank is carrying on commercial lending, the existence of U.S. long-term deposits would enhance its revenue earning ability. In cases where it has no commercial business, the U.S. deposit might assist the government in its general fiscal operations. In the case of India where the United States carries relatively large deposits, the central bank does pay interest to the United States. 

Senator MORSE. Pardon me; another question. 

Senator CARLSON. Go ahead.

Senator MORSE. To what extent do they use their international funds to finance projects within their country that do have commercial connections, such as the structure of public works that are built through their own contractors and the private segment of their own country?

Mr. BELL. I assume that in most cases at least, and again I will supplement this if I may for the record, that if the government wishes to obtain funds from a central bank, they normally would borrow. 

Now, the rules under which they borrow are different in different countries. I suppose there are some countries in which they borrow

T I 3 at no interest, others in which they borrow at an exceptionally low interest like India, others in which they borrow on commercial terms. (The following material was subsequently furnished for the. record :)

USE BY CENTRAL BANK OR BY ASSISTED COUNTRY OF PUBLIC LAW 480 CURRENCIES FOR DEVEOPMENTAL, INCLUDING COMMERCIAL, PROJECTS 

It is the intention of the United States in its Public Law 480 agreements to provide funds in local currency to assist the country with development projects, including those of a commercial type which contribute to economic development. 

Public Law 480 104(g) loans are provided for such purpose as are the 104(e) Cooley loans. Generated currencies from title I sales for these purposes may be deposited for limited periods of time in central banks or in commercial banks as the U.S. Treasury determines. However, it is executive branch policy that loan agreements directing these funds to specific development or commercial purposes shall be developed and signed as quickly as practicable in order that the funds may be disbursed for such agreed purposes. All such funds remain in Treasury accounts in local banks until loan agreements are signed and the funds are disbursed to the borrowers. 

In order to speed up the use of such local currency funds all Public Law 480 title I agreements in recent years have set a 3-year limit on the availability of these funds both for 104(g) or Cooley loan purposes. If, at the expiration of that time, these funds are not used, they revert to the U.S. Treasury for other use. During the time between generation and deposit in the local bank and the signature of the 104 (g) or Cooley agreements, it is true that the funds remain on deposit and may or may not earn interest. In view of the fact that the funds must be ready for disbursement as soon as the agreements are signed, it is doubtful that the local bank or central bank could make extensive use of these funds for non-U.S. agreed purposes. In exceptional cases, where agreements are long delayed, it is possible that this acretion to the assets of commercial banks would enhance their lending capacity for other than U.S.-agreed purposes, because assets are generally fungible. However, the bank, whether central or commercial, must be ready to disburse on short notice all funds deposited to the U.S. Disbursing Officer account. In view of the fungibility of the bank's general assets it would be difficult to prove that the specific deposits of the United States were in any given case used for a non-U.S.-agreed purpose.

PHILIPPINE PROBLEMS 

Now, the Comptroller General is entirely correct. We have had a lot of difficulty in the Philippines. It stems from a situation which I think had some understandable aspects. It extends from the period when Magsaysay was trying to beat the Huks in the early fifties, and Magsaysay's program, which as you know turned out to be very successful, involved building many roads, digging many wells, doing many other things in the countryside which would represent quick progress for the rural people. 

Under that well-drilling program, for example, several thousand wells were dug in very short order. Approximately 17,000 wells were dug during the life of the project. Now, the Comptroller General points out, and quite correctly, that over the ensuing years some wells, less than 10 percent of the total, were not maintained and went out of order. That is not good. But it was recognized, and it was quite an appropriate decision, that we were starting something on a very rapid scale designed deliberately to exceed the current operation and maintenance capability of the Philippine Government. 

The agreements with the Philippines were clear. They were going to hire people, budget for the operation and maintenance and so on. 

They did not succeed in doing so. It has been a continuing and difficult point between them and us. We have continually hammered on this year after year. We have been pressing them to do what they agreed to do, and what they were supposed to do. 

In a number of those cases the situation is still not satisfactory. 

Now, because this had been true, in 1962 we undertook in the Philippines as a special measure, because we had not been satisfied by the Philippine Government, we undertook an arrangement-for any new project we insisted that not only the Filipinos agree to provide the operation and maintenance financing and the people and the organization, but that in fact they put the money in escrow in effect; that they not only put it in the budget but that they appropriate it and they put it in the bank in an account, a fund really which is available for

this purpose, and since 1962 they have done that and we do not have this problem with new projects begun since then.

Senator CARLSON. Barges and dredges.

Mr. BELL. Yes; this was river and harbor dredging, if I am not mistaken.

Mr. BELL. No, the pier is a case in which they were slow, but it has now moved. Since the date of his report, half of the pier has been finished, and the rest of it is in the process of being contracted. 

Incidentally, while I do not want to make very much out of it, there are some differences of judgment on the actual situation. For example, the U.S. Bureau of Public Roads, who have been associated with this road-building endeavor from the beginning, tell us today that the Comptroller General is just plain wrong, that large parts of those roads are in very good shape, and others, while not in as good shape as they should be, are quite passable. That, however, I only repeat. I do not emphasize it very much because the basic thrust of the Comptroller General's report, in my opinion, was quite correct. 

We did move fast on some works which we wanted to move fast on and did have a big impact, but the Filipinos were not always successful in providing the followthrough, the operation and maintenance costs and organization.

There are aspects of that problem which we are still working on today.

FUNDING OF TRAVEL BY PRIVATE GROUPS PARTICIPATING IN THE PARTNERS OF THE ALLIANCE PROGRAM 

The partners of the Alliance is a private sector program which establishes direct working relationships involving business, professional, civic, educational, labor, and other groups in the United States with counterpart groups in areas of 

Latin America. 

The U.S. private groups organize area or statewide partners committees which then send program development teams to their Latin American partner area. 

These teams work with their counterpart partners committees in developing programs and projects which can be implemented through private sector funding. 

The cost to the U.S. Government consists of funding a major portion of the costs of the program development teams. 

The AID partners coordinating office in Washington or the AID mission in the partner country may suggest that the program development team include certain technical representatives-such as in the fields of marketing, education, public health, or labor. The selection of the committee's team representatives, however, is, as it should be, made by the State partners committee. 

In response to the specific question concerning the team participation of members of the press, the list of team delegations reflects that only one press representative has served in a program development capacity. A second representative of the press has been selected to serve on a program development team by a recently organized partners committee. 

Following is a list of the people who have traveled to Latin America in the development of the partners of the Alliance program; they reflect a broad range of private participation on program development teams.

RISING PUBLIC DEBTS IN LATIN AMERICA 

Senator WILLIAMS. The President, in his message, is discussing the 

Alliance for Progress and he said: 

We are particularly concerned about the terms of aid. The burden of debt borne by the developing countries is rising. Their accumulated public foreign debt now runs to about $30 billion. The volume of repayments comes to nearly $5 billion per year, and it is rising by 15 percent each year. 

I am quoting from page 7 of the President's message.

3 Senator WILLIAMS. As I understand it, the loans which we are making in this area are long-term loans with a nominal rate of interest in the beginning or maybe the interest deferred; is that correct? 

Mr. BELL. As a result of the action of the last two congressional sessions, Senator, our rates of interest today are no longer as low as they were a couple of years ago. The rate today is a minimum rate, 1 percent up to a 10-year-grace period, and 21/2 percent thereafter, and our loans can be up to a maximum of 40 years. 

Senator WILLIAMS. That is right, but that is still a low rate of interest. 

Mr. BELL. Oh, yes.

ARE U.S. LOANS USED TO PAY OFF OTHER LOANS? 

Senator WILLIAMS. The question I am asking, is: they are having to pay $5 billion a year on $30 billion loans. That means they are paying either a sizable rate of interest, and or a substantial amount on the principal. I am wondering whether they are using our loanslong-term and easy loans to make the repayments on the loans that are being granted by these other countries? Are we paying off their debts?

Mr. BELL. Let me answer that if I may by making two points, Senator.

In the first place, we provide, under a loan, a letter of credit which they can use to buy American equipment, facilities, engineering services, et cetera. So that the specific objectives of our loans are to make available to them goods and services from the United States. 

Senator WILLIAMS. I appreciate that, but we both know that when we put up $1 million and we earmark that it must be used for a certain project, the fact that we pay for that project means that the dollars which they have accumulated otherwise can be used in some other direction.

I am not trying to follow the identity of the dollar. What I am wondering, are we, in effect, paying off these loans of the other countries because they are collecting at the rate of about $3 to $4 billion per year on their principal?

Mr. BELL. This is the second point I want to make. 

Senator WILLIAMS. While we are not collecting anything, as you know, to speak of.

Mr. BELL. It depends on where you are looking. In Latin America, for example, the Export-Import Bank is receiving high flows and rates of interest.

Senator WILLIAMS. We are not speaking of the export-import countries.

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; that is included in those debt figures. But nevertheless, the point I want to make here is that we are deeply concerned about the heavy debt burdens of these countries, and we have participated in rescheduling of debt for Brazil and for Chile in recent months. The Europeans have extended the terms of debts owed to them in most cases, and to some extent also the Export-Import Bank. 

We had very little owed to us and obviously, therefore, did not participate extensively in the rescheduling. 

But in addition, in the Chilean debt renegotiation, the principle the standard was accepted that what would be rescheduled was the prin-

cipal of the obligation, and not the interest, so that those countries which had made loans of a relatively shorter term provided the bulk of the rescheduling. Since our terms had typically been longer, we provided for a lesser share. 

Senator WILLIAMS. You recognize the danger of your point.

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; we have, and we have been working against it. 

We have also, as you know, Senator, been working hard to try to get the other countries to reduce their terms. There has been some progress along that line, not all we would like, but some. 

LIBERALIZATION OF OTHER COUNTRIES' LOANS 

Senator WILLIAMS. I notice Canada has undertaken a program of lending under terms which are even more liberal than ours. 

Senator WILLIAMS. I assume that European countries are the ones you are referring to that have these hard terms. 

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; the Canadians have established a loan fund on the same terms as the IDA, which is up to 50 years, 10 years' grace, and three-quarters percent interest.

Senator WILLIAMS. What rate of interest do the European countries have?

Mr. BELL. The Europeans have been increasing, improving the terms of their obligations. The Germans are now making a substantial part of their loans available on 25 years' maturity, 7 years' grace, and 3 percent interest. 

Senator WILLIAMS. What were their rates of interest prior to that?

Mr. BELL. Five years ago they did not make any loans more than 

10 years and less than 51/2 or 6 percent rate of interest. 

Senator WILLIAMS. By these liberal loans that we have been making-almost waiving the interest-we have been practically paying or providing the source of funds whereby the interest could be paid at this higher rate before. 

Mr. BELL. Well, it has not been an equitable situation, and we have been hammering hard on it. I repeat there has been some progress, though not as much as we would like. 

The British last year began a system under which they make loans, a large part of their development loans at 30 years maturity, 7-year grace period on the payment of principal, and no interest rate at all, a zero rate of interest during the grace period, and then a 5or 6percent interest rate to completion of the loan. 

If you average that out, it is about the same as 30 years, with a 

312-percent rate overall.

Now the British, when I was in London about 3 weeks ago, the new head of the British Ministry of Overseas Development-they have just set up an aid ministry for the first time-the Cabinet Minister in charge is Mrs. Castle, and she told me that the British are considering a further softening of rates on their loans. [Deleted.] 

So I repeat, we have not regarded the situation on long terms as equitable. We have been pressing very hard on the matter, on all the other countries. There has been some real headway, but we still believe that there is a distance for the other countries to go. 

Now, as you know, Senator, this is a very complicated matter. For example, the French, while the terms on their loans are fairly hard,

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 391 1965 W ¡ make a higher percentage of grants than any of the rest of them. 

The 80 percent plus of the French aid program is a grant program, not loans at all.

Senator HICKENLOOPER. Where do those grants go? To former 

French colonies, do they not?

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir; but nevertheless it is perfectly legitimate aid, and it is doing the same work that the development loans do. 

At the present time in our opinion the Japanese and the Italians are the two countries that need to make the sharpest adjustments and do the most in the direction of liberalizing, and we have been running into very heavy weather in getting those two countries to reduce their interest rates and lengthen their maturities. They are running a little softer but not nearly enough.

Mr. BELL. Yes, sir. I am sure it is very small, but I will check the point, insofar as we know.

The Norway one, as I remember it, primarily related to ships and aircraft; the Danish one, likewise. The Italian one I have forgotten. 

In any event, no new commitments of this kind are being entered into. These run to 1966 and in some cases 1967, and one of them runs up, I think, 1970.

Now, I am not trying to defend the wisdom of each of these commitments at this time. I have really forgotten the considerations. 

Several of them had to do with cases in which there were sort of tie-in sales.

MILITARY ASSISTANCE IN COMPETITION WITH MILITARY BUDGET 

Senator MORSE. My next question, Mr. Bell, goes to section 504 (b) 

of chapter 2, "Military Assistance," which reads as follows: 

In order to make sure that a dollar spent on military assistance to foreign countries is as necessary as a dollar spent for the United States Military Establishment, the President shall establish procedures for programing and budgeting so that the programs of military assistance come into direct competition for financial support for other activities and programs of the Department of Defense. 

My question is this: With the military assistance program in process, what factors are considered? What are the priorities of allocation of resources? In other words, is military assistance considered to be in competition with roughly $50 billion Defense budget funds or with roughly $3 billion-plus of foreign aid funds? 

Mr. BELL. With both, sir, but specifically on the military side, the 

Secretary of Defense personally-and I can verify this because I have been involved in discussions of this both as Budget Director and in my present job, the Secretary of Defense personally reviews the military assistance budget, each element in it, just as he personally reviews

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 395 1965 18 each element of the main Defense Department budget, and sees himself that that requirement of law is being met and, indeed, has stated I believe consistently before the Congress that the dollars-that if reductions were to be made in the Defense Department budget or the military assistance budget combined, they should first come out of the Defense Department budget because the marginal value of the dollars in the military assistance budget in his opinion, in terms of American interest, is greater than the value of the marginal dollar in the 

Department of Defense budget. 

In other words, it is his judgment that there is a very high value to the U.S. interests in these military assistance dollars. 

Now, so far as the comparison, the competition between the military assistance and economic assistance funds, this is something that my office is responsible for in the first instance. We take that responsibility seriously, and the Budget Bureau and the President's staff also review, of course, the same question. We have felt that the balance, the mix that was presented to the Congress, has been an appropriate one in terms of the national interest. 

Senator MORSE. I know that as you have related it is the position that the Secretary of Defense has taken. I have never found it at all convincing, but I am going to help him along this year. If we are not able to cut this military aid-and I am very hopeful that we will be able to—I shall give the Congress an opportunity to cut it out of the defense budget.

CRITERIA FOR SETTING UP PRIORITIES 

To get back to my question, you render the judgment as you say you do. What factors do you consider and what priorities and allocations of resources do you apply in determining military assistance abroad in competition with our own national defense budget? 

Mr. BELL. We regard the economic assistance funds and the military assistance funds as having to stand against the criterion of what the United States needs to accomplish in a given country and in a given region.

We apply this comparative or competitive standard case by case, country by country. We expect the ambassador and his staff to answer that question when they send us their recommendations. We review their recommendations from this point of view. 

Now, this is not something obviously that one can do by applying a slide rule or a mechanical calculation. We certainly ask how important is it to the United States that this country, the country in question, have a Military Establishment of a specified size and force from the point of view of defense against external aggression or from the standpoint of internal security. We ask what is the relationship between the costs of the Defense Establishment in that country that we would be contributing to through military aid, to the budgetary strength of that country, its projected revenues. Is it going to be able to afford this Military Establishment over a period of time? 

We are interested in getting each country, as you know, into a situation as rapidly as possible when it can provide for its own further development and its own defense with its own resources and without any

aid from us. That is our purpose and our objective everywhere we work.

Therefore, we are exceptionally, we are extremely conscious of the need to avoid saddling a country with unnecessary defense costs which will limit the extent to which it can put its own resources into development and investment, and thereby speed the day when it can operate without any more aid from us. 

That is a general indication, sir, of the kind of questions that we try to ask and try to get answered before we decide on the recommendations to the President and the Congress for both military and economic assistance.

JUSTIFICATION OF MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO PAKISTAN 

Senator MORSE. On the basis of the policy criteria that you have just outlined, could you-not at great length but to whatever extent you think necessary-give this committee your explanation of the justification for the military aid that we have given now for some years to Pakistan which is renewed each year? There is criticism on the Hill—and it is going to be very intensive this year, let me forewarn you-of the aid that we have been giving to Pakistan and the relationship of that aid to India. I believe we cannot separate it from India. 

The official position announced by the Foreign Minister of Pakistan some months ago was that they had no intention of rendering assistance to us in South Vietnam. How can you justify the aid that you have approved for Pakistan from the standpoint of their own economy and from the standpoint of their own military need, when that same amount of money or a large portion of that same amount of money invested in economic projects in Pakistan would do something about developing their ability to finance themselves in 25 to 50 years? 

Mr. BELL. With respect to the last point first, the combined program of military and economic assistance which we have been making available to Pakistan for some years now, and, of course, the additional assistance that they have been getting from other countries, from the World Bank, and so on, has not hampered or has not prevented a very encouraging rate of progress in the Pakistan economy. 

The rate of growth in agriculture, in industry, education, other fields in Pakistan the last several years has been very encouraging indeed, and rather surprising to me, since I worked there about 10 years ago and would not have expected such rapid progress to have been possible.

Now, therefore, it is, I think, not the case that the military assistance we provided, or speaking more broadly, the military establishment. that Pakistan has maintained, has in fact prevented very sizable and rapid economic progress. However, that is not adequate, is not a sufficient answer to your question, because your question is why should we have helped the military establishment in Pakistan at all. 

The answer to that is that it has been judged by the responsible officers in the U.S. Government, in this instance repeatedly including successive Presidents, that it was valuable to American interests to have some improvement in the Pakistan military forces. As you know, it is not a huge military force, but it is a sizable one, several divisions, some air strength, some navy.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 397 1965 ere of veli Wet end ம் exte ST Pakistan has continued to reflect a policy in agreement with ours as against the potential spread of Communist control in that part of the world, as represented by the Soviet Union. In the last 2 or 3 years excuse me, this policy has always been one which was complicated by the fact that the Indians were regarded by the Pakistanis as their main enemies. In the view of the Pakistan Government there was a potential threat all right from the north, from the Soviet Union, but their much more immediate concern and threat they felt was and is from the Indians. 

When the Chinese attacked India a couple of years ago in October 1962, and we decided to respond to the Indian request for some assistance of a military nature, this was very upsetting to the Pakistan Government, and at that time they began-and they have continued to this day-to engage in discussions with the Chinese Communists. 

This has needless to say been a matter of very great concern to us which has been repeatedly expressed to the Pakistan Government. 

Only recently President Ayub was in Peiping, and his statements at that time were in our judgment surprisingly and very unfortunately favorable to the Chinese Communist point of view on this matter. 

Now, the judgment that has been made continuously, and is still our judgment, is that despite the flirtation between the Pakistanis and the Communist Chinese, it remains true that the Pakistan Government is a strong Government and a strongly anti-Communist government, and that it is valuable to the United States to have some minimum or some significant military force in Pakistan with which we are in continuous association, which could be used under certain circumstances. 

As you say, it is not being used today in southeast Asia, but on the other hand, there have been circumstances envisioned under which it might very well be that Pakistan forces could be used and would be very helpful. 

We are very distressed by the continuing controversy, the continuing latent hostility between Pakistan and India. This is not our opinion of a healthy basis for the defense and the progress of either country. We have been unsuccessful in all of our efforts to persuade them to come to an agreement over Kashmir, which we think would probably take a lot of the heat out of this relationship. 

It is a very complex situation, one on which there can obviously be a difference of judgment, but the judgment of the executive branch is as I have indicated, sir. 

EFFECT OF TERMINATING MILITARY AID TO PAKISTAN AND INDIA

Senator MORSE. "But we are perfectly willing to negotiate with you a transfer of what we now provide you as grant military aid to a program of project by project economic assistance." 

Do you think that that would in any way jeopardize the security of India and Pakistan?

Mr. BELL. I think they would continue to obtain about as much and perhaps more military equipment by purchase as they now do by grant. 

Senator MORSE. Who would they buy it from?

Mr. BELL. Well, they might try to buy it from us. They would also they could buy it from Britain, from France, from Germany. 

ROLE OF INDIA AND PAKISTAN IN U.S. SECURITY

Indian Army would be of no help to us whatsoever. 

Mr. BELL. It depends on what kind of a war. 

Senator MORSE. They could very well be a hindrance if we got into a war with Russia.

Mr. BELL. It depends on what kind of a war it was. 

Senator MORSE. A nuclear war is the only kind of war we will ever have with Russia.

Mr. BELL. If we got into a nuclear war 

Senator MORSE. You do not think the Russians are going to engage us in a conventional war?

Mr. BELL. The Russians could very easily do the kind of things that [deleted] the kinds of subversive activity and the kinds of local uprisings and the kinds of small brush fire stimulated wars and outbreaks in which it would be very valuable to have Pakistan and Indian forces.

Senator MORSE. I have a series of questions on the kind of military aid that I have always supported to help a country keep down Communist coups. But the kind of activity that you are referring tothe stirring up uprisings within a country in order to endanger that country by creation of revolutions within it through the staging of a Communist coup-is not the type of military aid I am talking about nor is it the type of military aid you are making available to India and Pakistan. The aid which you are giving India and Pakistan is for the building up of military power to conduct external war against another nation. I find it very difficult to reconcile that with the language of the statute which says that this aid shall be given from the standpoint of the competition for the defense dollar between our own Defense Department needs and the protection of our Nation's interest and between the aid you give in my hypothetical to Pakistan and 

India.

TO 

T the security of my country. To the contrary, I think this endangers the security of my country because it increases the possibility of a war between India and Pakistan which my country has to get into. We cannot stand by.

The very aid that we are giving in some instances is bound to involve us in case these countries exercise their sovereign right to make war. You say they can get the equipment elsewhere. Let them get it elsewhere, but let us not be a party to building up their war machines. Let us help them with the type of military assistance that they need for truly internal security, which is all the difference between high noon and black midnight. 

I raise only this one hypothetical. I shall in the course of debate this year raise a good many other instances where we are doing the same thing in other parts of the world. I think we are doing it in the Middle East. I think we are doing it in Greece and Turkey. I just do not see what criteria you have set forth in your explanation this morning that meets the language of this law. 

LESSON FROM SINO-INDIAN INCIDENT IN 1962 

Mr. BELL. Senator, the fact is that in October 1962 the Chinese did attack the Indians. It was an actual outright aggression. The 

Indians were very poorly equipped and prepared to respond to it. 

The kind of equipment and training that we are giving them is directed related to mountain warfare and to light, quickly moving forces, and so on. 

Furthermore, there is, as you know, very great uncertainty as to what the Chinese may be doing in the years ahead in a broader sphere than simply the Indian border, and it is not at all out of the question that the Indian forces and the Pakistani forces could be useful in southeast Asia. They are not now under present circumstances being used, nor could they be used. 

Senator MORSE. It is made clear they do not intend to use them. 

Mr. BELL. At the present time and under the present circumstances, but it seems to me, sir, that if these programs have any-well, in thinking about these programs, one must look fairly far ahead. The development of the Chinese military force is plain and clear and growing.

Senator MORSE. You see where you and I have this fundamental difference. You build up these other war machines. You place in the hands of the controllers of these machines a course of action that could very well get us into a war. Coming back to your Indian- 

Chinese 1962 incident, I would much rather have the United States, Great Britain, and other free nations move right in there and say, "We are going to give you an opportunity to settle it by peaceful procedures or we are going to stop the war." 

I think you would lessen in the long run to a much greater extent the danger of an international conflagration. We keep hearing all this talk about the Indian incident of 1962. Yet if you get up to the 

United Nations as I have and talk to representatives of the various delegations up there, it is clear that the story has never been told. 

The confusion exists with regard to boundary rights even in that incident.

The assumption our administration has constantly made is that 100 percent of the wrong was all on the Chinese side. I would like to believe that it is, but you have a good many representatives of free nations in the world-not Communist nations-that point out that it was not that clear.

But let us assume that it was, and that India was 100 percent right and China was 100 percent wrong in regard to that boundary dispute. 

I do not want to be pouring military aid into India or into Pakistan to put them in a position where they can call the tune as to whether or not we go to a military war as a result of their actions. 

If China or Russia or any other Communist nation proceeds to violate the sovereignty of free nations, let them understand that we are not going to stand by and permit that kind of an invasion. 

I am very much of the opinion that much of this military aid is not in our national interests at all, but endangers it. And I do not think you could pick a better spot in the world than Pakistan and India to prove it.

Mr. BELL. I think probably, sir, the crux of our agreement would revolve around my feelings that if we are going to give what amounts to a security guarantee to these people and I do not differ that we, in effect, do and should-that it makes sense to have them to some extent in a position where they can help in their own defense, rather than looking forward to a time when if anything happened, we had to do it all ourselves.

I do not mean to say this as if it were an open and shut question. 

It is obviously one on which there can be different judgments. But I think that would be probably the crux of the reply that I would make to your last comment.

Senator MORSE. Of course, it goes to the matter of degree. I am for them developing their own military establishment but not with our aid. I am for trying to help them so that we are going to have a viable country from the economic aspects and to help them, as you have heard me say so many times, develop their economic freedom. If we do that I think it will take care of their political freedom. 

I think we have to reappraise this year as we never have, to a greater degree than we ever have before, this whole military aid program of the United States. I do not think it is strengthening our security, but weakening us.

STATEMENT OF POLICY 

The administration is requesting the addition of the following sentence to the statement of policy contained in section 102 of the act: 

Congress further urges that the United States and other free world nations place an increasing portion of their assistance programs on a multilateral basis and that the United States continue its efforts to improve coordination among programs of assistance carried out on a bilateral basis by free world nations. 

The President, Secretary Rusk, and Mr. Bell have already stressed the importance we place on both multilateral aid giving and effective coordination of bilateral aid. We stand ready to increase our contributions to multilateral agencies as rapidly as other nations are prepared to do likewise. Also, we are continuing our efforts to increase and strengthen bilateral and multilateral coordination of aidthrough the Development Assistance Committee, through consortia headed by the World Bank and the OECD, through the consultative groups in being or soon to be established under the leadership of the World Bank, through the new Inter-American Committee for the Alliance for Progress (CIAP), or through direct contacts on a bilateral basis with aid donors in particular recipient countries. 

We believe these efforts reflect the will of Congress as well as the administration. Addition of the sentence quoted above to the basic statement of policy of the act will give added recognition to the importance the United States puts on improved multilateral coordination of assistance.

AMERICAN SCHOOLS AND HOSPITALS ABROAD 

Sections 214 (a) and 214(b) of the act authorize the furnishing of support to certain schools and hospitals outside the United States founded or sponsored by U.S. citizens. The administration is requesting the repeal of section 214 (b) as of June 30, 1966.

Section 214(b) was enacted in 1959. Although its authority is expressed in general terms, its original purpose was to enable the United States to contribute U.S. owned Polish currency to building the Polish 

Children's Hospital in Krakow, Poland. In 1961, it was broadened to include dollar assistance when it became evident that the hospital could not be built without contributions of foreign exchange as well as local currency. Funding necessary for construction was completed in fiscal year 1964.

We believe that the special authority of section 214 should be limited to the support of institutions whose primary function is education and research, whether in medicine or in other fields. Such assistance can be furnished under section 214(a). We do not consider it wise to go beyond this and support, through a special authorization such as section 214, institutions whose primary or sole purpose is to provide medical treatment. There are said to be more than 300 such 

American-supported hospitals in existence today. Their needs and requirements should be assessed in comparison with the other developmental needs of the countries in which they are located so that a realistic order of priorities may be established. Such would be the case were section 214(b) repealed.

Some Members of the Congress have expressed concern about repeal of section 214 (b) for fear that some of the institutions which have

been receiving support under that section might need further support after fiscal year 1966. They are four in number: The Polish Children's Hospital, Project Hope (which would in any case be eligible for assistance under sec. 214(a)), the Admiral Bristol Hospital in

Turkey, and the Seagraves Hospital in Burma. We would have no objection if the repeal of section 214(b) were accompanied by a "grandfather" clause which would permit continued support to those specific institutions which have received assistance under that section. 

Senator MORSE. Do you mind if I interrupt at that point? 

Mr. GAUD. Not a bit. 

Senator MORSE. It will probably save time, if the Chairman does not object.

On page 5, the second paragraph, "There are said to be more than 300 such American-supported hospitals in existence today." Then you comment on only 4 of the 300. Are any of the other hospitals of similar importance to these four?

Mr. GAUD. Well, I suppose in the eyes of their sponsors they are, Senator. Our basic proposition here is that we do not believe when the Congress put section 214 (b) in here, it meant to start a new aid program. It was put in here really for one institution. We are already helping four. We are getting requests for help from a good many others, and we just think it is time to shut the door. 

Senator MORSE. On what basis are we supporting the others of the 

300 On Section 214(b)?

We do not think we ought to carve out this exception here for hospitals which are doing nothing more than giving medical treatment. If a hospital has a medical school attached to it, if a hospital has a nursing school attached to it so that it is training people in the country, then we can support it under section 214 (a) as it now stands. That kind of an institution we have no problem with. 

But we do not want to lay ourselves wide open here to an exception which will enable every American-sponsored hospital abroad to come in here and ask for aid, because sometimes it is darn hard to turn them down.

INVESTMENT GUARANTEES 

Mr. GAUD. The executive branch has proposed a number of amendments designed to extend and facilitate the use of our investment guaranty programs. 

This committee has been furnished with figures showing the rapid growth of the specific risk investment guaranty program-the program which affords protection against inconvertibility, expropriation, and war risks. In calendar 1963 the Agency issued 186 contracts

Ir.

TO 

22 with a coverage totaling $426 million. In 1964 we issued 486 contracts with a total coverage of $708 million. To meet the rising demand, we are requesting that the total face amount of specific risk guaranty contracts that may be outstanding at any one time be increased from $2.5 to $5 billion (sec. 221 (b) (1)).

Other proposed amendments relating to the investment guaranty program are as follows: 

1. Section 221 (b) (2) of the act now limits the size of extended risk guarantees of loan investments to $25 million and of equity investments to $10 million. Institutional investors, whose funds this authority is designed to attract, are often interested in large projects. 

We are requesting removal of these limitations. 

2. Our authority to issue extended risk guarantees now expires on 

June 30, 1966 (sec. 221(b) (2)). We are requesting extension of this authority to June 30, 1967. 20 3. Section 221 (c) provides that no guaranty shall extend more than years from the date of its issuance. Long-term institutional lenders such as insurance companies and pension funds often extend credit for more than 20 years. We propose, therefore, to eliminate the 20year restriction on guarantees of loan investments-but not on guarantees of equity investments. 

4. Section 222 (b) of the act now permits the use of fee income to meet managerial and custodian costs incurred with respect to assets acquired by the Government when it pays a claim and takes over the investment of a guaranteed investor. But it does not permit the Government to use fee income to pay the costs of investigating and adjusting claims prior to payment. We are requesting this added authority. 

5. The act now permits guarantees to be issued to foreign corporations owned by one U.S. corporation, but not to foreign corporations owned by more than one U.S. corporation, or by individual U.S. citizens or by U.S. partnerships or other noncorporate U.S. organizations. 

This anomaly is removed by the addition of a new section 223 (c) which includes such foreign corporations in the definition of eligible U.S. investors.

HOUSING PROJECTS IN LATIN AMERICAN COUNTRIES 

Section 224 of the act now authorizes the issuance of $250 million face amount of extended risk guarantees on investments "in pilot or demonstration private housing projects in Latin America of types similar to those insured by the Federal Housing Administration and suitable for conditions in Latin America." We are requesting continuation of this authority and an increase from $250 to $350 million in the total face amount of guarantees that may be outstanding at any one time. However, the $100 million increase in issuing authority may be used only to guarantee investment loans of eligible U.S. investors in 

First. Credit institutions in Latin America engaged directly or indirectly in the financing of home mortgages; such as savings and loan institutions. 

Second. Housing projects in Latin America for lower income families and persons, which projects shall be constructed in accordance with maximum unit costs established by the President for families and persons whose incomes meet the limitations prescribed by the President.

Third. Housing projects in Latin America which will promote the development of institutions important to the success of the Alliance for Progress; such as free labor unions and cooperatives. 

Fourth. Housing projects in Latin America, 25 percent or more of the aggregate of the mortgage financing for which is made available from sources within Latin America and was not derived from sources outside Latin America, which projects shall, to the maximum extent practicable, have a unit cost of not more than $6,500. 

This change is based on our belief that the time has come to move on from encouraging the construction of pilot or demonstration housing projects. Its purpose is twofold: first, to assure that the focus of the housing guarantee program will be to stimulate the development in Latin America of institutions similar to those which in the United States have so successfully mobilized private capital for the financing of new homes, and to stimulate the growth of other institutions important to the Alliance; such as labor unions and cooperatives; second, to assure that the guarantee program will stimulate the development of low-income housing. 

One other change is requested in section 224 of the act. It would apply to guarantees under the Latin American housing program the same definition of "eligible U.S. investors" as applies to all other guarantees issued under the act.

The executive branch believes that other technical assistance programs carried out by the ISVS serve the best interests of the United States. We are requesting removal of the existing prohibition to enable the United States to contribute to these technical assistance activities.

STANDBY AUTHORIZATION FOR VIETNAM 

Section 106 of the executive branch requests for fiscal year 1966 an authorization of $50 million for the contingency fund together with a special standby authorization which can be used only for economic and military assistance to Vietnam. 

Senator AIKEN. That is a contingency fund to be used for either economic or military assistance? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes.

The CHAIRMAN. It can be used anywhere? 

Mr. GAUD. That is right: $50 million is obviously a minimum request. We hope it will prove to be adequate. However, future requirements for Vietnam are so uncertain that we feel obliged to make the standby request. It authorizes such additional appropriations in fiscal year 1966 as may be necessary for use in Vietnam only. 

It is impossible to predict now whether it will be necessary to use this standby authority. Its purpose is to save a legislative step, thus adding to the speed and flexibility with which we can deal with the situation in Vietnam. It is to be noted, however, that the proposed amendment expressly requires the President to present to this committee and the House Foreign Affairs Committee the programs to be carried out with appropriations requested under the standby authority. 

Senator MORSE. Let me interrupt there. I do not want to take very much time, Mr. Chairman, and I certainly do not want to argue the point, but just state my caveat.

I am a little bit at a loss to understand why the President would want this when it is so easy for him to come up here on an emergency basis with any supplemental request he needs for this kind of a national emergency. The very process of getting it is so informative to the 

American people and is so consistent with our system of representa-

at. tive government, where the legislature and the executive can work together immediately on a given problem. 

My objection to this kind of an approach is that it involves, for want of a better descriptive term, what I call a blanket grant of authority to be exercised at the discretion of the President. I do not care how you term it. It is at least once removed from the application of a congressional judgment or check on an existing need, where the facts of that need are presented. I am only talking of a hypothetical and it is too bad we use South Vietnam as a hpyothetical. But it may very well be that 6 months from now or 9 months from now the American people, or the Congress representing the American people, might think a check ought to be exercised on a President. I do not care who he is. 

Yet we will have given to him in advance of the opposing facts existing at a given time the authority to use his unchecked discretion. 

The time factor I think is a weak argument. With what he has in general contingency fund, he can meet an overnight emergency. Then he can get himself up here and say, "These are the facts that warrant more funds for this specific purpose.' 

Many do not share my fear, but I think it is a mistake for the executive branch of Government to make this kind of a request for what I call blanket authority in futuro. That is a question I ask. I think it is bad policy.

Mr. GAUD. Well, I would only like to comment briefly, if I may, sir. Last year we asked for authority to do this. We were given the authority to do this with respect to only 20 people. We have 20 people going through such training now. We could easily hire more. FAMINE AND DISASTER RELIEF 

Mr. GAUD. Under existing law the President can, notwithstanding other statutory prohibitions on assistance to a country or its government, furnish famine and disaster relief to the people of a country, either directly or through voluntary organizations such as the Red 

Cross. 

We are requesting an amendment which would broaden existing authority in two respects in order to improve our ability to demonstrate the humanitarian concern of the United States for the plight of people who suffer disaster.

First, it would permit us to do whatever is necessary to meet the needs of famine or disaster victims during the initial emergency period, including dealing directly with the government or furnishing items of more lasting benefit to the country than food, clothing, and temporary shelter. The executive branch would consider the initial emergency period as being no longer than 60 days from the date the disaster strikes.

Second, the amendment would permit us to meet shortrun rehabilitation requirements which cannot be handled during the immediate emergency period. The executive branch would limit this rehabilitation assitance to programs that can be completed within 90 days after plans have been drawn up and funds made available. 

I would now like to mention actually two additional matters although only one is referred to here in the statement. 

Senator AIKEN. There is no limitation with respect to the time it takes to draw up the plans, however. 

Mr. GAUD. No, sir.

Senator AIKEN. It might be 2, 3 years?

Mr. GAUD. That is a good point. The assumption is that it would be an immediate proposition. 

Senator AIKEN. The assumption is there, but the wording is not. 

Mr. GAUD. You are quite right.

FOREIGN DISASTER EMERGENCY RELIEF, JANUARY-DECEMBER 1964 

For the 10 years prior to 1964 foreign disaster relief by the U.S. Government was handled through ad hoc groups. Foreign emergency assistance was conducted on a worldwide basis but treated as a one-shot temporary expediency. 

The change that took place at the end of 1963 was a determination by State, AID, and DOD to coordinate U.S. Government foreign disaster operations. A classified State circular issued in 1958 contained some guidelines and there was a draft DOD directive but not one single manual order existed. A first requirement of coordination was the adoption of instructions of equal authority in State, AID and DOD. By October 1964 they were issued and all of them appear in the AID Manual Orders Series, 1562.1 to 1965.1, inclusive. 

During the time the manual orders and directives were being shaped, formed and approved a number of foreign disasters occurred, providing pertinent and immediate experience in foreign disaster relief operations. 

Therefore, this first year of operation has been one of formulating instructions, gaining experience and trying to reach the high goal of effective, rapid, and meaningful coordination.

In calendar year 1964, the U.S. Government and the U.S. voluntary agencies (registered with the U.S. Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid, including the 

American National Red Cross) provided assistance in 62 foreign disasters. 

This report brings together, for the first time, an accumulation of data on foreign disaster relief. It is not possible to know or record everything. For example, no mention is made of what each country did for itself. The aid reported begins from where the local resources were exhausted and outside help was needed. It is usually provided for a period of 60 days, with the exception of food. When disaster strikes in a foreign country, the U.S. ambassador immediately extends the sympathy of the President and the people of the United States to the disaster victims and to the country for the damage suffered. 

When outside help is needed, the ambassador offers assistance, consistent with U.S. foreign policy goals. Ambassadors may, under the Foreign Assistance Act, use the authority delegated to them to make grants ranging in amounts up to $25,000. Larger amounts had to be approved by State/AID headquarters. 

Major disasters require massive action, quick response, and timely delivery of disaster relief personnel, drugs, food, blankets, beds, clothing, shelter, field hospitals, and other disaster supplies. All U.S. resources must be coordinated to provide this added measure of help to the foreign disaster victims. 

To put this into practice, disaster relief coordinators have been set up in State, Defense, HEW, and AID-supported by the newly issued policy, procedure, and operations manual orders.

Working relationships within the U.S. Government and voluntary agencies were coordinated to expedite exchange of facts on disasters; determine needs and how best to meet them; speed up supply and transportation; avoid overlap and waste; maintain the humanitarian spirit and motivation; give accurate public information; and demonstrate U.S. concern and effectiveness in assisting disaster victims of the world.

The U.S. voluntary agencies took a vital and meaningful role in foreign disaster relief. Their historical, detailed knowledge of areas and people, their experience in distribution of emergency food and supplies, and their dedication were indispensable.

U.S. Government personnel overseas, representing the U.S. Embassy, AID, USIS, Peace Corps, military assistance groups, as well as the American women's clubs and private U.S. citizens, contributed not only their personal funds but also their services to aid foreign disaster victims.
