INDUCEMENTS TO SERVE IN VIETNAM 

First, we face a situation in Vietnam which may necessitate a request for certain additional authorities with respect to our civilian employees who serve in that country. During the period February 

11-14, the dependents of all U.S. employees in Vietnam were evacuated. Our recruitment problems in Vietnam were already difficult, and thereupon became more difficult still. It has also become harder for us to induce those of our employees who are already in Vietnam to remain for an additional tour of duty. 

Further inducements may be necessary to persuade our personnel in Vietnam to sign on for another tour of duty. Further inducements may also be necessary to enable us to recruit more personnel to fill existing and future vacancies. Before the committee concludes its consideration of the bill, we may have some specific requests to make in this area.

Then finally, Mr. Chairman, if I may- 

PEACE CORPS ACTIVITIES IN VIETNAM AND INDONESIA 

Senator CARLSON. Do we have a Peace Corps operation in Vietnam?

Mr. GAUD. No, sir; we do not. Mr. Shriver or the administrationconsiders that Vietnam is not an appropriate place for the Peace Corps. We do, however, have a contract with the International Volunteer Services under which we have up to 80 IVS volunteers in Vietnam working in the fields of education, health, and agriculture, and they perform essentially the same functions as the Peace Corps would.

Senator AIKEN. We have a Peace Corps in Indonesia, however. 

Mr. GAUD. Yes; we do.

Senator AIKEN. The last I heard they were encountering no difficulties.

Mr. GAUD. That is true. They have not had any difficulties to speak of. At the same time you cannot help but worry about the Peace 

Corps in Indonesia, because most of them are serving out in the boondocks, and they can get into trouble an awful lot faster and be a great deal harder to protect than some of our other people there. 

DEADLINE FOR ENTERING INTO INVESTMENT GUARANTEE AGREEMENTS 

Mr. Chairman, one final word if I may. The committee is familiar with section 620 (L) of the act which provides that we cannot give any assistance to any country after December 31, 1965, unless that country has entered into an investment guarantee agreement with us covering the risks of inconvertibility and expropriation. December 31, 1965, is now right around the corner, you might say. 

In the last couple of years, we have managed to get a good many more countries to sign these agreements. At the end of 1962 we had agreements with only 47 such countries. Today we have agreements

i 3 with 63. But there is still a number of countries which have not entered into agreements with us, and some of these are of considerable importance. Brazil, for example. We have entered into an agreement with Brazil on the administrative level, but it has not been approved by their Congress. Mexico will not enter into an agreement as a matter of principle. Peru has not entered into an agreement for coverage other than that for inconvertibility. 

There are a number of small countries in which the likelihood of American investment is almost nil. The Yemen, a number of the sub- 

Sahara countries, others. [Deleted.] 

But the Brazilian agreement will be submitted to their Congress we hope this week. [Deleted.]

But nevertheless it is only fair to say to the committee that before you finish your consideration of the bill, we will request that the terminal date of December 31, 1965, be extended for 1 year. 

The CHAIRMAN. It will give more time to enact the bill; that is all. 

Mr. GAUD. In the case of some of these countries it is a matter of giving them more time to enact the bill. In the case of a good many of the countries, most of them that have not entered into them, the agreement really is of no significance. 

Senator AIKEN. A change of government would nullify it anyway, would it not?

Mr. GAUD. It might, if the new government were prepared to disavow an outstanding contract. They would have to go pretty far. 

Senator AIKEN. If their political philosophy changed with the government, the agreement would automatically be rescinded. 

Mr. GAUD. That is right. If we had had, for example, an agreement with Cuba prior to the takeover by Castro, I have no doubt that Castro would have disavowed it and we would have been in for a good many claims.

EFFECT OF NOT EXTENDING THE DEADLINE 

Senator MORSE. Let us look at this for a moment. What about the countries that have signed agreements. Are they not going to have a sort of feeling that we are going to let them down? They cooperated with us; they signed the agreements. We speak about these other countries. I know there are other countries in which we do not have investments. We ought to reduce the number of countries we are aiding anyway. We ought to work with the countries that keep faith with us on a matter which is very important, taking the picture as a whole.

Mr. GAUD. A country which has entered into an agreement has been benefited because it is getting much more American investment. A country which has not entered into an agreement with us has considerably less opportunity of inducing American investments. There is the real benefit of entering into the agreement, it seems to me. 

Take the countries which have not entered into it up to today. It seems to me that we ought to look at this in a perfectly coldblooded way- 

Senator MORSE. Absolutely. 

Mr. GAUD (continuing). From our standpoint. Is it worth more [deleted] to us to cut off aid to [deleted] a country because she has

not entered into this agreement, or is it worth more to us from our standpoint, not from [deleted] the country's viewpoint to continue an aid program in [deleted] the country? That is the issue. 

Senator AIKEN. Mr. Chairman, I would like to ask how come that, without any agreement, Mexico is getting more American investments than any other of the states in Latin America? 

Mr. GAUD. I am sure you will agree, sir, the climate for investment in Mexico is a good deal better than it is in almost any other Latin 

American country.

Senator AIKEN. We are there without any agreement. 

Mr. GAUD. With or without, because manifestly the existence of the agreement is only one of a number of factors that investors look at. 

The climate in Mexico is much healthier for foreign investment than it is almost anywhere else in the Southern Hemisphere. 

Senator AIKEN. My experience with Mexico indicates that they are very sensitive about any help that looks like a handout or relief.

PAYMENTS MADE UNDER INVESTMENT GUARANTEES

The CHAIRMAN. Four claims.

One is an expropriation claim arising out of an investment in Iran, and the amount of that claim is between $10,000 and $12,000. There is another one, an expropriation claim arising in Haiti, where the Valentine Petroleum Co. says that their concession was canceled by the Government of Haiti, and that they are asking for $1 million. 

We are not very far along in our investigation of that claim.

Claims.

CONGRESSIONAL LIAISON OFFICE OF AID 

How many congressional liaison people do you have in the AID organization?

Mr. GAUD. I would have to supply the exact figure, but it is not over 10. 

Senator MORSE. You are sure it is not 20?

Mr. GAUD. Positive; there are seven professional positions in the congressional liaison staff of AID. 

Senator MORSE. Maybe it is a matter of definition.

Mr. GAUD. We are talking AID, Senator, not State Department?

Senator MORSE. AID. 

Senator MORSE. Mr. Funari is certainly not a congressional liaison man. 

Mr. GAUD. No, sir; not in my judgment. 

Senator MORSE. No; nor in mine either.

Mr. GAUD. No; our congressional liaison people are all in one outfit headed by Mr. Gibbons, formerly by Craig Raupe who left the Government a few months ago, and the staff is quite small. 

Senator MORSE. What are their duties? 

Mr. GAUD. Their duties. They handle the correspondence between the Congress and AID. They try to keep in touch with Members of the Congress, keep them posted on what is going on in the AID program, answer their requests for information, all that sort of business and keep us posted on the attitudes in the Congress. 

Senator MORSE. I can understand that. Would you say that these

AID liaison people really are members of your organization who are as familiar as Mr. Funari with the substance of the AID program? 

Are these liaison people by background and training qualified to really sit down with us as you and Mr. Funari and others are, to discuss policies of AID and the facts about the administration of AID? 

Are they more than sort of congressional public relations people for you, to do a type of lobbying for the executive branch of Government on the Congress?

Mr. GAUD. I do not think any of them are as familiar as Mr. Funari is with the program. One of Mr. Funari's jobs is to prepare this book which sets forth our entire program, and he gets probably a closer look at the entire program than almost anyone else in the Agency. 

But I feel very strongly that our legislative liaison people are not worth their salt unless they are familiar with the substance of the program. They obviously cannot do their job unless they know as much as possible about what we are doing. This is one of the reasons we have them handle the correspondence, by answering or helping to answer scores and at times hundreds of letters, they see a good deal of the operation.

The Legislative Liaison Office, like most of our offices in the Agency, is set up on a geographical basis. I used to be, for example, sir, the 

Assistant Administrator for the Near East and south Asia region. One member of the liaison staff was assigned to my region. He came to all of my staff meetings. I made a point of seeing to it that various members of my staff lunched with him regularly, that he was kept up to date as completely as I could keep him up to date with what was going on in my region.

Now obviously these fellows have to spend a good deal of time out of the office, so that they do not have as much time to get into the program as people would who are in the office all day long. But we make a conscious and deliberate effort to acquaint them as much as we can with the substance of the program, and I think we have to. 

Senator MORSE. You say they handle congressional correspondence.

You mean in some instances some Senators and some Congressmen follow a procedure that we call bucking over correspondence. They have letters from their districts or States, and they send those letters

DISTINCTION BETWEEN CONGRESSIONAL PRESENTATION AND CONGRESSIONAL LIAISON 

Senator MORSE. You have told about Mr. Funari's preparation of these workbooks. I suppose there is no one in your organization with whom members of this committee work more closely with than Mr. 

Funari. I want to find the line of distinction between Mr. Funari's work and a congressional liaison official of AID. 

Mr. Funari really is on the policymaking level-as far as the preparation of the substance of the program of AID is concerned-at a much lower echelon than you and the Director, I understand. But you do consider him one of your policymakers, while these congressional liaison men are not at the policymaking level? 

Mr. GAUD. I would not describe it exactly that way. The distinction that I draw in my own mind is this. Mr. Funari is in the Program 

Office of the Agency. Now the Program Office deals with the why's and wherefore's of the AID program, how much money we have, how we can divide it up, what we ought to be doing in this or that country, SO it is on all questions of policy, as you say. So that he is on the program side.

The legislative liaison people are assigned to a specific operational function. They could not possibly prepare the congressional presentation themselves. They are not deep enough in it. 

At the same time, Mr. Funari, working on the program side, has to work with the legislative liaison people. In other words, here is a function, the presentation to the Congress, which really crosses a number of lines in the Agency. We have to bring our comptroller into it; we have to bring our congressional liaison people into it; we have to bring our program staff into it. We obviously have to bring in Mr. 

Bell-or bring me in on his behalf. So that we work really as a group.

But you are quite right, sir. Essentially Mr. Funari is on the substantive side. The other fellows are on the operating side.

INVESTMENT GUARANTEES AND THE BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

Senator GORE. With our stringent balance-of-payments problem, I have wondered if we should continue with the same volume and vigor the program of guarantee of foreign investment. Would you relate that program to the balance-of-payments problem? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir. The position of the administration on that is clear. The President has drawn a distinction between continued private investment in the developed countries and continued private investment in the underdeveloped countries, and it still remains the policy of the administration to encourage private investment in the underdeveloped countries. To date the amount of investment in those countries has not been sufficiently large, and in our view, in the President's view the benefits from it, including the transfer of technical and managerial skills, have been sufficiently great so as to continue that type of investment. 

Senator GORE. What exactly is an underdeveloped country?

Mr. GAUD. Well, an underdeveloped country is defined in the Executive order issued by the President under the interest equalization tax legislation. I have not got that in front of me, Senator. It would not include any of the countries in Europe. It would not include 

Japan. It would not include Canada. It would include most of the rest of the free world to which we are giving assistance.

INVESTMENT GUARANTEE PROGRAM IN TAIWAN 

Senator GORE. Why should we undertake to guarantee further investment in Taiwan? Have we not done enough for that particular part of the world?

Mr. GAUD. No, I do not think so. After the end of this fiscal year, all things being equal, conditions not changing, AID will make no more loans to Taiwan. But Taiwan still, you might say, has gone only a very short way down the road to economic independence. The per capita income of her people is $150 a year. She has a good base, a much better base for development than she had a few years ago, but it is still a very fragile situation and it seems to me that it is to our advantage to continue to encourage American investment in Taiwan. 

Senator GORE. Why? 

Mr. GAUD. Well, because Taiwan is not nearly as strong, Senator, nearly strong enough so that you can look at Taiwan and say it is done, we can be sure it is done. Much of the recent growth of its economy took place in the private side. American know-how has a particularly significant role to play at this stage of Taiwan development. Taiwan has not anywhere near the strength, for example, that 

Japan has, or that most of the European nations have or that we have. 

Senator GORE. Do you think we should undertake the burden of making Taiwan as strong as Japan?

Mr. GAUD. No, but the question of whether and to what extent 

Taiwan is going to continue to develop is certainly still open, and investment guaranties are about as cheap a way of continuing to strengthen strong private sector development as I can imagine.

NEED FOR GUARANTEEING INVESTMENTS IN TAIWAN 

The CHAIRMAN. It would help matters if you cut off those on which we agree. Mr. Bell has been very proud of the fact, he has told us, that you have cut off economic aid to Taiwan. I think it is rather logical that if you get a country to that point, you might as well cut off the extension of guarantees. There is no urgency in inducing the 

American business to go into Taiwan. There are lots of other places which need it worse, Latin America, for example. 

Mr. GAUD. That may be true. The way we would look at it, sir, a country like Taiwan passes through various stages in its transition from a country that is wholly dependent on aid to one that gets along without any aid. In the case of Taiwan it has reached the point where we do not feel that it needs any more grant economic assistance. 

It has reached the point also where it does not need any more loans on concessional terms. It still needs military assistance and loans from the Eximbank on investment terms. It still needs, in our judgment, the kind of technical and managerial assistance, which can best be supplied by American private enterprise and our investment guaranties are designed to facilitate the process. 

The day will come certainly when American money or other money from the rest of the free world will move into Taiwan without that encouragement, and then we can cut it off. It is a question of judgment. In our judgment that point has not yet been reached with Taiwan.

Senator GORE. I am afraid in my judgment it has. You say she is still unable to completely care for herself. Do you ever envision the time when Taiwan in and of herself could have an adequate defense? 

Mr. GAUD. There would have to be quite a change in the world situation before that would happen.

REVIEW OF COORDINATING PROCEDURES 

Yesterday we were asking Mr. Bell about the extent to which he vetoed recommendations of the Military Establishment in respect to military aid. We discussed the law which specifically gives the Secretary of State veto power over the Pentagon Building, subject, of course, to the action of the President. We brought out that the Secretary of State has delegated this function in the first instance to Mr. 

Bell, and he, working through the AID organization, reviews the military aid program of the Department of Defense.

DISTINCTION BETWEEN PROGRAM AND PROJECT LOANS 

Senator MORSE. Can you give me a clear distinction between the program loans and project loans. 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir, clear to me. I hope it will be clear to you.

A project loan is a loan that we make to cover the foreign exchange costs and sometimes local costs under the letter of credit procedure of a specific project such as an irrigation project, a powerplant, or other physical installation. 

A program loan, on the other hand, is not tied to a specific project. 

It covers the cost of importing from the United States raw materials, spare parts, machinery, commodities-sometimes expressly defined and limited, sometimes not. 

These program loans we make to only six, seven, or eight countries. Those are countries in which we are carrying on a fairly large developmental effort, and where we feel we have a clear notion of the foreign exchange requirements of the country, and where we also have confidence that they are making sensible use of their resources, and of the resources that we are putting into the country. 

The primary purpose of the program loan-in addition to enabling the country to buy things overseas when it lacks the foreign exchange to do so is to provide the raw materials, the spare parts, the machinery, and equipment needed for what you might call the existing plant of the country. 

Most of these items which are imported under these loans go to the private sector, and they keep the existing businesses in the country going.

Senator MORSE. Mr. Reporter, there is one clarification I want to ask Mr. Gaud on another subject matter. 

Mr. Gaud, did I understand you to say to Senator Aiken some time ago in the hearing this moring that foreign aid could have been used in Vietnam to pay for fire bombs and the material used in these gas attacks?

Mr. GAUD. It could have been. I do not know the facts, but the equipment which was used in these attacks I assume could have come

from either of two sources, either U.S. stocks or materials supplied to the Vietnamese under military aid. 

Senator MORSE. That was my understanding of what you said, and

I wanted to be sure. 

Mr. GAUD. And I want to emphasize I do not know the facts. 

Senator MORSE. I understand that. I think you made that clear before.

Now, we come back to projects and loans. Does the World Bank give program loans?

Mr. GAUD. The World Bank has made, so far as I know, one program loan and that is to India. They are considering making others. 

We are urging them to make others. 

NEED FOR PROGRAM LOANS 

Senator MORSE. What would you think of a requirement that all 

U.S. loans be for project purposes?

Mr. GAUD. I think that would hurt, would cripple, the aid program about as successfully as any single thing I can think of other than taking all our money away. 

Senator MORSE. Tell us why.

Mr. GAUD. Well, may I talk about the case of India. 

Senator MORSE. Take any case.

PROGRAM LOANS TO INDIA 

Mr. GAUD. India has a development plan. She operates on a series of 5-year plans, as you know. We furnish our aid to India through the Indian consortium which is headed up by the World Bank. The 

World Bank-in addition to the input that the World Bank and we ourselves put into the drawing up of India's 5-year plans each year the World Bank sends a team out to India which reviews the position of India, the Indian economy, how they are doing, what their requirements are, and so forth and so on, and comes up with a statement of what is necessary to keep the Indian economy going in the next year.

Now, this is in two parts: one, local currency-which comes from inside India-the other, foreign exchange. These foreign exchange requirements are then presented to the consortium, after deducting the amount of India's own foreign exchange and after deducting the amount of foreign exchange that it is estimated she will get from the bloc countries that are giving her aid. 

You come up with a net requirement of foreign exchange, and let us say for a given year-recently it has been anywhere between $900 million and $1 billion annually. And each year for the last few years we, the World Bank, and the other members of the consortium have come up with that amount of aid. 

If we could give India nothing but project loans, all we could do would be to continue to build more powerplants, more irrigation projects, more factories in India. India would not have the foreign exchange to buy the raw materials, the spare parts, the machinery, and the like that she needs to keep her existing plant going. 

All we would end up by doing would be giving her large loans of $1 million on up for specific projects. We would not be able to take

care of the small Indian manufacturer, the small Indian industrialist whose requirements are a few thousand dollars to $100,000 or a few hundred thousand dollars a year, who has to import stuff in order to keep his plant going. 

When the World Bank comes up with its statements of requirements for India, it says how much of this is needed in the way of nonproject loans-how much they need to keep their present industrial plant going and the Bank also makes recommendations as to how much more should come up by way of project loans to increase the existing plant.

If we could not make program loans to India, or if the Germans did not or if the British did not or if nobody did, the Indian economy would collapse tomorrow. Because India has not got the foreign exchange to buy the raw materials and the spare parts and the machinery that she needs to keep her plant going. That is point No. 1. 

PROGRAM LOANS TO LATIN AMERICA 

Let me switch now to the situation in Latin America, to give you another example of how we make use of the program loan, in addition to its being, as I see it, essential for the economy. 

The World Bank-and this is true of other international lendersdoes a superb job, in my judgment, of passing on the validity of specific projects and deciding whether or not a given powerplant is needed in a given country at a given time. They have addressed themselves much less to the question of how a particular country is using its own resources, whether it is fighting inflation, whether it is collecting enough taxes, whether it is incurring too much short-term debt, that sort of business.

In our relations with the Latin American countries to which we are giving a lot of aid, and the same thing is true of India, Turkey, and Pakistan, we have been trying to devise ways and means of dealing with the state of the economy as a whole rather than dealing with the efficiency of a particular project, and as Mr. Bell may have already told you, we have made in the last year or two sizable program loans to Brazil and Chile. [Deleted.] 

The point is that by agreeing at the beginning of the year that over the next 12 months we will make available a million dollars in four installments, provided they carry out their stated stabilization program we affect the whole economy and make our aid dependent on performance.

We have followed this procedure in Brazil and in Chile. If conditions should change in [deleted] we will try to do the same thing there. 

We were doing this in [deleted] and until the Government takes the steps [deleted] necessary to deal with their monetary and fiscal situation we will not give them any program assistance this year. 

We have done more or less the same thing in India where we have conditioned a program loan specifically on their taking certain steps to increase fertilizer imports. We have done the same thing in Pakistan, where in this last fiscal year we made a program loan available on their relaxing certain restrictions on their import licenses, freeing up their economy, as a result there are a lot of factories in Pakistan today that are working 24 hours a day instead of 8 hours a day because Pakistan did take these steps to eliminate these restrictions.

3 3 So, to sum up, sir-this has been a very long speech-program loans are essential, as we see it, first in order to keep an economy going, to supply something more than new plants. 

Second, they are extremely useful devices in getting performance from these countries. 

Senator MORSE. I want to say, Mr. Gaud, that this is the clearest and best statement that I have heard from AID yet in regard to your policy with respect to program loans. 

This explanation leads me to conclude to a remarkable degree your program loans have many restrictions attached to them. This results in their being somewhat a hybrid between outright program loans from the U.S. Government to government X, Y, or Z to do what they want to do at their own discretion, and a program of loaning which says to them in effect, "We are going to give you so many millions of dollars on a quarterly installment basis, provided you spend that money under a program of reform." 

Mr. GAUD. Exactly. 

Senator MORSE. You can put restriction taxwise, I suppose, interestwise, administrativewise and whatever else you want to that will assure us, or leave us with the feeling of assurance, that the money is being wisely spent. 

Mr. GAUD. That is right.

NEGOTIATING A PROGRAM LOAN 

Senator MORSE. Under this type of program loaning, am I to understand that when we turn it over I am not talking about the World Bank or any other international body; I am talking about simply a direct bilateral arrangement-that although you have a program loan, with these other restrictions that I have just referred to, in additiontake India as an example-the officials of the Indian Government sit down with you in negotiations, and they in effect do say "We want this money for these purposes." To all intents and purposes they do talk to you about the project or the purposes, so to speak, for which they are asking for the money, but they are left a considerable amount of leeway in carrying out their administration of it? 

Mr. GAUD. That is right. In the Indian case you are working in a framework of a development plan, and of course you are working there in a highly controlled economy.

The Indians control their foreign exchange within an inch of its life, and it isn't like some other countries in some other parts of the world [deleted] where Tom, Dick, or Harry can go out and incur shortterm indebtedness on whatever incredible terms he likes. 

You can't do that in India, so that you are working within a framework of a development plan which you are reviewing constantly, and you have a particularly big review every year before the meeting of the consortium when the World Bank goes out there. 

Now, meanwhile, throughout the entire year John Lewis, our Mission Director in India, and his staff are working with the Government from day to day. But essentially what we are doing when we make a program loan to India is to make a million dollars available to India to be used within the framework of an agreed-upon plan to meet foreign exchange requirements which have been reviewed, screened,

and approved by the World Bank, by ourselves, and by the other members of the consortium. 

Senator MORSE. I will stay with India a moment longer. Could

IS THE UNITED STATES TOO CLOSELY IDENTIFIED WITH BORROWING COUNTRY UNDER PROGRAM LOANS?

As I said earlier, we make them on a very selective basis, six or seven countries only, and we don't make a program loan unless we think the government then in power is making sensible use of its own resources and of the money we are going to give it, and unless it will take necessary reforms in the fiscal field, the financial field, or what have you.

In other words, we will only make a program loan to a government that we are prepared to support. Now, we did not do it, as you recall, with the former government in Brazil. We had a program loan agreement with them. [Deleted.]

In [deleted] we made a program loan in 1964. [Deleted.] 

Whether we make one in 1965 will depend upon satisfactory performance in fiscal and monetary fields. In other words, we do this on a very selective basis. 

We are prepared to support the governments to which we make these program loans. We think they are good governments, that they are trying to deal with the country's problems. Otherwise we won't make the loan.

APPENDIX A TECHNICAL AND OPERATIONAL AMENDMENTS TO THE FAA OF 1961 REQUESTED BY THE EXECUTIVE BRANCH SECTION 252-AUTHORIZATION FOR ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS 

It is proposed to amend section 252 which relates to the authorization for the Alliance for Progress, in two respects: 

1. To include in the Alliance for Progress authorization language similar to that contained in the Development Loan title (sec. 202(a)) which would authorize an additional appropriation in fiscal year 1966 of an amount equal to the difference between the amounts authorized to be appropriated for fiscal years 1963-65 and the amounts actually appropriated in each of those years. 

2. To authorize up to $85 million of the funds appropriated in fiscal year 1966 to be used for technical cooperation grants. 

SECTION 451 (b) -REPORTING USE OF FUNDS APPROPRIATED UNDER SPECIAL STANDBY AUTHORIZATION FOR VIETNAM 

Amendment is requested to section 451(b) to exclude funds appropriated under the special standby authorization for Vietnam, if any, from the quarterly reports on the programing and obligation of the contingency fund. Funds under the special standby authorization are different from contingency funds in that the executive branch, if it seeks an appropriation under this special authorization, will make a full presentation to both the authorizing and appropriating committees of the Congress on the proposed use of those funds. Their actual use will then be reported in the annual reports under section 634. 

SECTION 605-REUSE OF REFUNDS 

Amendment of section 605 which relates to retention and use of items is requested in the following respects: 

First to change the section heading to read "Retention and use of certain items and funds."

Second, to add a new subsection (c) to section 605, under which refunds received by AID as a result of failure of a transaction financed by AID to conform to the statutory or regulatory requirements of the United States or to the terms of any agreement or contract, may be credited to the appropriaion, fund, or account used to finance the transaction or to the appropriation, fund, or account currently available for the same general purpose. This will permit these refunds to be reused for economic assistance purposes. Under current law, and 

AID agreements with the General Accounting Office, refunds can be reused only for the foreign country making the refund, even when it is the country's failure to comply with AID regulations or agreements that gives rise to the refund. AID believes that refunds received from aid-recipient countries should in most instances be reprogramed through AID's normal budgetary process rather than to the country making the refund. This amendment would permit adoption of this policy. In a limited number of cases, primarily where a supplier or contractor has committed the default (rather than the recipient country), AID proposes to reprogram refunds back to the original aid-recipient country. 

SECTION 612-USE OF FOREIGN CURRENCIES 

Amendment is requested to section 612 which relates to the use of foreign currencies, by redesignating subsection (c) as subsection (b). Section 2 of 

Public Law 88-638 (October 8, 1964) redesignated subsection (b) of section 612 

as section 104 (t) of the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954 (Public Law 480). 

SECTION 624 (B)- -SUCCESSION AMONG STATUTORY OFFICERS 

Amendment is requested to section 624 (b) which presently authorizes the President to fix the order of succession among the Assistant Administrators of AID, to authorize the fixing of such order among the statutory officers of that Agency. This change is a technical change necessitated by the amendments to section 624 (a) made by section 305 (42) of the Federal Executive Salary Act of 1964 (title III of the Government Employees' Salary Reform Act of 1964) 

(Public Law 88-426).

SECTION 624 (D)-STATUTORY OFFICER 

Amendment is requested to subsection (d) of section 624 by striking out all references to Public Law 86-735 and substituting the short title of that law, "the Latin American Development Act, as amended." 

SECTION 630-REIMBURSEMENT FOR PERSONNEL DETAILED TO FOREIGN GOVERNMENTS AND INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATIONS 

Amendment is requested to section 630 relating to the terms of detail or assignment, to provide that when detailing any officer or employee of the United States to a foreign government or international organization on a reimbursable or advance credit basis, the President may require the foreign government or international organization to pay an amonut equal to the cost to the United States of any "benefits" payable to the employee in respect of the period of his assignment or detail. At present, paragraphs (2) and (4) of section 630 provide for reimbursement or advance credits measured solely by the "compensation, travel expenses, and allowances" payable to the officer or employee assigned or detailed.

This amendment will permit AID to reuse any amounts received from the foreign government or international organization in respect of "benefits" in the same way it can now reuse payments for the other listed items. 

SECTION 635-SALE OF BUILDINGS AND GROUNDS 

It is proposed to amend section 635 by adding a new subsection (1) to permit the President to sell buildings and grounds in foreign countries acquired in carrying out economic assistance activities, and to use the proceeds of such sales toward the purchase, construction, improvement, and preservation of other properties or hold them for later use. A proviso to the new subsection requires the President to report all such transactions annually to the Congress along with the budget estimates for AID. This language would extend to AID authority similar to that now vested in the Department of State under section 9 of the Foreign Service Buildings Act of 1926 and is important to promoting efficiency in the handling of these properties. 

SECTION 636 (F)-PROVISIONS ON USES OF FUNDS 

Amendment is requested to section 636 (f) by striking out "Act to provide for assistance in the development of Latin America and in the reconstruction of Chile, and for other purposes" and substituting the short title of that act, to wit: "the Latin American Development Act".

SECTION 638-PEACE CORPS ASSISTANCE 

Amendment is requested to section 638 by striking out the reference in that section to famine or disaster relief under title II of the Agricultural Trade Development and Assistance Act of 1954. This is a conforming amendment made necessary by the executive branch request relating to famine and disaster relief (new sec. 639).

SECTION 642 (A) (2)—STATUTES REPEALED 

Amendment to section 642 (a) (2) which relates to statutes repealed, is requested in the following ways:

First, to repeal section 143 of the Mutual Security Act of 1954, which relates to aid to Yugoslavia but is now obsolete, having been superseded by the far broader provisions of section 620 (f). 

Second, to repeal the proviso authorizing the continuation under the FAA of certain programs authorized by sections 405 (a) (c) (d) and 451 (c) of the Mutual Security Act of 1954 until enactment of separate legislation relating to such programs. Enactment of separate legislation-the Migration and Refugee Assistance Act of 1962-renders this savings clause obsolete. 

SECTION 645-UNEXPENDED BALANCES 

Amendment is requested to section 645 by striking out "Public Law 86-735" and substituting the short title of that act, to wit: "the Latin American Development Act." (Whereupon, at 12:35 p.m., the committee adjourned to reconvene at 10 a.m., Wednesday, March 24, 1965.)
