The committee met, pursuant to recess, at 10:05 a.m. in room S-116, the Capitol, Senator J. W. Fulbright (chairman) presiding. 

Present: Senators Fulbright, Mansfield, Lausche, Pell, Clark, Hickenlooper, Aiken, Carlson, and Case.

 Some of the members may come in later, but this is a very difficult committee to get together. We want to make a record anyway. 

I notice both of you have prepared statements. I think you might as well begin. 

STATEMENT OF HON. ROBERT S. MCNAMARA, SECRETARY OF DE- FENSE, AND GEN. EARLE G. WHEELER, U.S. ARMY, CHAIRMAN OF THE JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Mr. Chairman, I do not know whether you would wish me to review the statement, reading portions of it, or simply to speak from it. I think perhaps the latter may suit your purpose.

The CHAIRMAN. I think it would be better if we put the entire statement in the record, and you draw attention to the most significant parts of it. (Secretary McNamara's and General Wheeler's statements in full follow :)

STATEMENT OF ROBERT S. MCNAMARA, SECRETARY OF DEFENSE 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, almost 4 years have passed since I first testified before this committee in support of the military assistance program, yet I can repeat without reservation a statement I first made in June 1961: "Overall, the military assistance program is a vital element of our national defense and an essential tool of our foreign policy." 

It is still my conviction that military assistance to friendly nations should be viewed as an extension of the United States own defense structure, and that adequate support of the program is essential to our own national security. There is, in short, an indissoluble relationship between our national security and the collective security pacts which we are associated. 

Cooperative effort and joint commitment by allied and friendly nations have created a free world military posture which represents a total strength far greater than the strength of any single nation. Singleness of purpose and cooperative effort are what have enabled us to maintain a military strength and strategic flexibility commensurate with the threat posed by the Communist bloc nations. The need for this strength and flexibility has not diminished, nor is it likely to do so within the foreseeable future. 447

Indeed, as U.S. retaliatory capabilities have made the certain destruction involved in a full-scale nuclear exchange increasingly obvious to any potential aggressor, aggression has sought new and more subtle outlets. But if free and independent nations are to survive in the world, limited, nonnuclear aggression must be deterred no less effectively than we have deterred the use of nuclear weapons and all-out, general war. 

As I told our NATO partners last December, deterrence is no more than the shadow cast by the actions we are prepared to take and would have to takeshould deterrence fail.

The "we" in that statement is collective: It means the United States and all other free and independent nations which share our determination to resist Communist expansion. Determination, however, must be given substance and credibility by the maintenance of armed forces trained, equipped, and deployed in positions from which they can respond promptly and effectively to acts of aggression. Such forces are the tangible evidence to any potential aggressor of the actions we are prepared to take. The shadow they cast is deterrence. 

Although U.S. military strength represents the major element of that deterrence, contributions from other nations are essential to it. These nations can and should provide the military strength essential to their own internal security, and they must be able to resist or repel at least the initial thrust of attempted aggression. Their ability to do so is not only vital to themselves, it is also in the interest of the United States. 

An attempt on our part to provide, unilaterally, the armed force essential to insure both national and collective security would be both self-defeating and dangerous. Self-defeating because it would not develop in other free world nations the will and the military self-sufficiency required for their security; dangerous because it would greatly increase the chance of U.S. involvement in every local or limited war. 

Any such effort would also be prohibitively expensive. It would require us to maintain a military force structure of such magnitude as to be enormously costly in terms of both American manpower and American tax dollars. can

Our solemn commitment to the common defense of the free world is embodied, as you know, in multilateral and bilateral agreements with many allied and friendly nations, as well as in other assurances and declarations by the President and by the Congress. The question which confronts us here is not the validity of that commitment, but how we now plan to act upon it. We c either help our partners help themselves in the development of an agreed military posture which will minimize their need for outside assistance, or we must be prepared, in case of emergency, to assume the whole burden ourselves, deploying U.S. forces and accepting the consequences which may result from our direct intervention.

The options available to us are three in number: 

1. We can drastically revise our foreign policy to the lasting advantage of communism. 

2. We can raise our own force structure to a higher-and vastly more costlyplateau of strength. 

3. Or, we can assist friendly nations with the equipment and training required to enable them to carry their share of the collective defense burden. 

If we continue to exercise the third option, then we must maintain a carefully planned and adequately funded military assistance program. 

FISCAL YEAR 1966 REQUEST 

The authorization and appropriations we are requesting represent, in my judgment, the minimum necessary to promote the security of the United States and to provide a solid foundation for our foreign policy. In support of those objectives, we are asking $1.170 billion in new obligational authority, $1 billion of which represents what, for want of a better description, we have designated the "base line" program. This $1 billion reflects the success of our continuing effort to allocate military assistance on a selective and austere basis. 

The remaining $170 million provides for the special combat needs in Vietnam and Laos, in addition to the portion of the $1 billion which funds goods and services for these countries under the "normal" program. Both countries are, abviously, being subjected to Communist pressure in a more dynamic and dangerous form than that confronting other recipients of military assistance; their needs are accordingly substantially greater and more urgent.

ར་ Regarding Vietnam, there are two paramount reasons why we must succeed in helping that country resist the aggression mounted against it by North Vietnam. First, a Communist victory in South Vietnam would immediately open the way for further adventures by the Hanoi regime, and by China, in other neighboring countries. Laotian neutrality and independence would be gravely threatened, and the other nations of southeast Asia would be vulnerable. Second, it is vital that the United States prove to the world that the form of aggression being tested in South Vietnam is not the "wave of the future.” 

As I have previously stated, we may be certain that if the Communists established their control over South Vietnam, they would press their subversive operations in Laos and then in Thailand and we would have to face the same problem all over again in another place or permit them to have all of southeast Asia by default. Thus, the choice is not simply whether to continue our efforts to keep South Vietnam free and independent but, rather, whether to continue our struggle to halt Communist expansion in Asia. If the choice is the latter, as I believe it should be, we will be far better off facing the issue in South Vietnam.

In Laos, we continue to support the 1962 Geneva settlement which was aimed at preserving the independence and neutrality of that country. In the face of continued Communist attacks against the Lao Government, we are responding to that Government's request by providing military assistance necessary to enable its forces to meet these attacks. 

The “base line” military assistance program for Vietnam and Laos is included as part of the basic $1 billion and is enumerated on the regular country pages for Vietnam and Laos in the presentation document before you. The extraordinary costs incident to providing additional support to these two especially beleaguered nations are itemized on supplementary country pages and amount to $170 million. I must warn you, however, that the total of $170 million may represent a conservative estimate, since it is based upon our current analysis of possible developments over which we do not have full control. 

Indeed, the sharply rising costs of our effort there have so reduced current resources for military assistance that the President is making a $50 million transfer of economic aid funds to military assistance under section 610 of the act. 

This transfer will facilitate accommodation within the fiscal year 1965 program of some high-priority requirements which we might otherwise have been forced to defer at the expense of our national interest. 

PROPOSED PROGRAM FOR FISCAL YEAR 1966 

The program we are proposing for fiscal year 1966 is based on total obligational authority in the amount of $1.258 billion-$1.170 in new obligational authority plus $88 million in reappropriations and estimated recoupments. The total obligational authority of $1.258 billion is distributed as follows: almost 

86 percent of the total, $1.077 billion, will be used for assistance to individual recipient nations, with 84 percent of that total, $905 million, allocated to 11 key countries on the periphery of the Sino-Soviet bloc. The balance over and above the country programs will provide for nonregional and other costs, including administrative expenses, which are not appropriately chargeable to individual country programs. 

These figures clearly indicate the emphasis we place on the need for indigenous forces to help hold the line against further Communist aggression at the edges of the Iron and Bamboo Curtains. They also reveal the comparatively modest amount of assistance we are planning to provide to all the other countries included in the fiscal year 1966 program. 

Again this year, we have sought to facilitate your consideration of our proposals by presenting them to you in terms of objectives to be accomplished, rather than on an arbitrary regional basis. The six categories into which the program is thus divided are the same as those used in last year's presentation. Each category is composed of individual programs which have as their common denominator a particular objective of U.S. military strategy or foreign policy. The first five include individual country programs only, and are designated: "Forward defense," "Alliance for Progress," "Military bases," "Grant aid phaseout," and "Free world orientation." The sixth is named for its major components: "U.S. forces support, and military assistance program administration." It also includes various miscellaneous items not chargeable to individual country programs, which I shall describe.

FORWARD DEFENSE PROGRAMS 

The importance of the first category-"Forward defense programs"-is readily apparent from a glance at the map. The 11 key countries in this category- 

Greece, Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, India, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, the Philippines, and the Republics of China and Korea-form a wide protective arc which stretches, along the boundaries of the Communist world, from the southern flank of NATO to the Western Pacific. Our past actions, as well as mutual defense agreements with certain of these allied nations, demonstrate that we will come to their assistance in case of Communist attack or infiltration beyond their capability to resist or repel. These nations are situated, both geographically and psychologically, on the front lines of the free world's common defense. 

Their total military strength of 32 million men is, therefore, a large and vital asset in an area which contains almost half of our planet's land mass and more than three-fourths of its population. 

This vast area, with its enormous human and natural resources, is a prime target for Communist aggression. It is fortunate, therefore, that the 11 key countries, whose continuing independence and territorial integrity are at stake, are in a position to supply the bulk of the manpower required to hold the line against intrusions. As I have said, indigenous forces can and should be able to assume major responsibility for providing the necessary on-the-spot deterrent and prompt and effective military response to attempted aggression. 

They cannot do so, however, without substantial U.S. military assistance. 

None of the forward defense countries is economically capable of supporting, with its own resources, a modern military establishment. The average per capita gross national product of these 11 countries is $168.55, compared with $3,239 for the United States. And while their per capita gross national product is only one-twentieth of ours, the percentage of GNP which they spend for defense is more than 50 percent of ours. Considering the relative burden, it can hardly be said that recipients of our aid make no effort to help themselves. Many of these countries are simultaneously supporting forces important to the common defense, and undertaking major efforts to achieve the social and economic development vital to their long-range survival. It is in our own self-interest for us to fill the gap between what our partners can do on their own behalf and what must be done to maintain an adequate common defense capability. 

The $905 million investment in the forward defense program generates maximum free world military strength at minimum expense to the United States. 

The average annual cost of pay and allowances, subsistence, and clothing for a forward defense country soldier is $497. The comparable cost for a U.S. soldier is almost 10 times that amount-$4,347. In other words, U.S. military assistance makes it possible for those 11 countries to deploy sizable forces all along the frontiers of freedom, from Greece to the Republic of China, at approximately one-tenth of the cost per man if we were deploying U.S. forces. 

The reason we must earmark such a high percentage of total obligational authority for forward defense country programs is that we are still trying to make up for the sharply reduced appropriations for fiscal year 1964. That reduction compelled us to defer urgently needed replacement of obsolete and wornout equipment, prevented important force improvements originally planned, and thus affected the parity between allied forces and the constantly modernized Communist forces they oppose. The capabilities of these allied forces cannot safely be allowed to deteriorate further for lack of adequate materiel. 

Accordingly, we have sought, within the limits of the proposed fiscal year 1966 military assistance program, to reevaluate both the force structures and the competing requirements of the forward defense countries and thereby to determine the optimum distribution of available funds. In so doing, we have had little leeway because almost 70 percent of the total amount allocated to this category, $623 million, must be applied to essential operating and maintenance costs. The comparatively small balance is all that remains available for no longer postponable force improvements.

I have personally reviewed these programs and have satisfied myself that they represent the best use of the funds we are requesting. They support a program which substantially enhances our national security, at rockbottom cost to the American taxpayer and with minimum risk of U.S. involvement in local wars along the farflung frontiers of freedom.

ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS SECURITY 

Closer to home, we also count upon military assistance as an effective instrument of U.S. policy with respect to Latin America. In the second category, entitled "Alliance for Progress Security Programs," we therefore propose to provide some form of military assistance to 18 Latin American nations, all of which are Rio Pact adherents and partners with us in the Organization of American States. The amount allocated to this category is $77.3 million, or about 6 percent of the total obligational authority upon which we have based the fiscal year 1966 military assistance program. Within this amount, the defense items programed will not, of course, exceed the $55 million ceiling imposed by the Congress on the provision of materiel to Latin America. 

All 18 programs proposed for Latin America, 2 of which provide training only, are generally oriented toward the maintenance of internal security and the encouragement of civic action projects through which indigenous forces can contribute to nation building; and all are, as you know, subject to the required presidential determinations. The general orientation of our military assistance effort in Latin America is clearly revealed by the functional distribution table which appears on page 55 of the classified presentation document. It shows, in summary, the funds allocated to Latin America will be used as follows: 

To strengthen the internal security capabilities of indigenous forces, 56.6 percent, $44 million;

For support of civic action projects, 15.8 percent, $12 million; 

To enhance the defense of maritime areas, 15.8 percent, $12 million; 

For general training, 4.9 percent, $4 million; and 

For supply operations, 6.9 percent, $5 million. 

Because of the importance we attach to both the direct and indirect benefits accruing from the training of Latin American military personnel, I want to emphasize the fact that the total amount which will be used for this purpose, including both that distributed by function and that of a general nature, is $13 million, or 17 percent of the $77.3 million for grant aid allocated to the entire region.

Each of these functions is designed to support and promote the basic objectives of the Alliance for Progress by helping to create an environment free from fear of lawlessness, banditry, and insurgency. Such freedom is a prerequisite to economic and social progress. It is also our purpose to provide only that amount and kind of military assistance which will exert a desirable influence on the Latin-American military and contribute to the stability of constitutional governments.

I While we must accept many of the risks inherent in any military assistance program for Latin America, the one risk we cannot accept is that of failing to deal with the threat to subvert these countries posed by Communist Cuba. need not remind you that the reality of that threat has been fully validated by the finding of the Organization of American States that Communist Cuba was indeed guilty of aggression against Venezuela. I do, however, want to recall the fact that internal security training provided as military assistance and equipment provided through sales to that same country helped the government of former President Betancourt to hold elections a year ago last December, despite all the efforts of Castro-supported subversive elements to prevent them. 

On balance, therefore, I am fully satisfied that the proposed fiscal year 1966 military assistance program for Latin America clearly accords with our national and hemispheric defense interests, and that it will serve its primary purpose of countering the threat to the entire area by providing equipment and training which will bolster the internal security capabilities of the recipient countries. 

MILITARY BASE RIGHTS 

The third category, "Military base rights," comprises countries in which the United States has access to oversea bases or facilities essential to maximum effective deployment of U.S. military strength, and to the accomplishment of our forward strategy.

The role of military assistance with respect to such base rights should be clearly understood. Military assistance to countries in which we have base rights makes the U.S. presence more readily acceptable and strengthens the capabilities of indigenous forces responsible for maintaining the climate of security essential to our full and free use of the bases themselves.

The arrangements of September 26, 1963, for extending the Spanish base agreements assure us of Spanish cooperation in the use of the bases until September 1968. That agreement provides not only for our continuing access to facilities which are of strategic importance to our global military posture, but also for the assumption of a greater role in Western defense by Spanish forces. Those forces will be strengthened through a combination of grant aid and Spanish purchases from the United States. We anticipate, furthermore, that such purchases will partially offset U.S. expenditures in Spain, thus mitigating their adverse impact on the balance of payments. Together with grant aid, they will also generate additional purchases of spares, replacements, and follow-on equipment from the United States. 

The amount allocated to this category in support of our base rights interests is $38.9 million, or 3.1 percent of the total obligational authority upon which the proposed fiscal year 1966 military assistance program is based. 

GRANT AID PHASEOUT 

The designation of the fourth category, "Grant aid phaseout," reflects a continuation of the trend which has already resulted in the termination of all grant aid materiel programs for the United Kingdom, the Federal Republic of Germany, the Netherlands, Belgium, Luxembourg, France, and Italy. No new commitments are being made to the three economically recovered nations-Norway, Denmark, and Japan-remaining in this cateogry. Accordingly, grant aid military assistance to these three countries will be limited to the fulfillment of prior commitments and to a small amount of training. Most of the prior-year commitments take the form of U.S. participation in previously agreed cost-sharing undertakings which generate indigenous effort and contribute to the strengthening of the common defense posture.

This rapidly shrinking category offers tangible evidence of the success of our persistent effort to eliminate grant-aid programs for countries which are capable of providing for their own defense requirements, and it accounts for only $39 million; 3.1 percent of the total fiscal year 1966 program. 

FREE WORLD ORIENTATION 

The next category, "Free world orientation," accounts for even less of the total obligational authority, $16.9 million, or 1.3 percent. The primary objective of these programs is to preclude or minimize Communist bloc influence. At the present time, there are 18 countries in this category; but our continuing efforts to encourage their free world orientation will, of course, vary in response to the changing tides of international relations. A very recent case in point is the suspension of Indonesia from the roster of free world orientation countries. 

Of the remaining 18 countries for which programs are currently planned, 8 are in Africa and the other 10 are scattered throughout the Near and Middle East and south and southeast Asia. Most of the countries included are small ones; and only three of the individual country programs are in excess of $1 million each. 

The relatively modest amounts of equipment and training we plan to provide are designed to serve one or more of several purposes, depending upon the needs of the situation in each individual country. Thus, although the specific objectives may vary, the basic justification common to all programs in the free world orientation category is the need to manifest U.S. interest and prevent a weighting of the scale which would upset the delicate balance of certain nonalined nations and cause them to fall quickly and finally to the Communist side. The desirability of precluding such an outcome is obvious. 

The proposed programs presently included in this category are as essential to the attainment of our national security objectives as those in any of the other categories.

U.S. FORCES SUPPORT AND MAP ADMINISTRATION 

I shall touch very briefly on the sixth and final category, "U.S. forces support and military assistance program administration." Of the $181 million allocated to this category, some 28 percent will be used to provide credit assistance essential to maximize purchases of military equipment by foreign governments which do not have the means to buy for cash. It is obviously in our national interest to facilitate such purchases, both as a highly desirable alternative to grant aid and as a means of improving our balance of payments. Funds used for this purpose will be repaid, reused to finance additional sales, and eventually

returned to the U.S. Treasury. In the interim, they will have served a very useful function by encouraging military purchases from the United States. 

Another 49 percent is required to meet the costs associated with U.S. participation in NATO infrastructure and international military headquarters and agencies, which could very properly be considered costs of U.S. forces support even though they have traditionally been funded as military assistance. If there had not been such a program, they would have had to be borne in the regular Defense budget.

The United States and other NATO nations are currently negotiating a new cost-sharing agreement in which we seek a reduction in our share of the next annual program. Incomplete or unstarted projects which are part of previously approved programs will continue to be funded at the percentage rate in force at the time of their approval. 

With respect to the remaining items in the sixth category, I want to assure you that each represents the minimum amount necessary for efficient administration and optimum use of the military assistance and sales program in the attainment of its authorized objectives.

TRAINING AND CIVIC ACTION 

There are two forms of military assistance which merit special mention because they make a rather unique and increasingly significant contribution toward the attainment of our objectives. These are the training of foreign military personnel, and the encouragement and support of civic action. I have said before, and I think it bears repeating, that in all probability the greatest return on any portion of our military assistance investment-dollar for dollar-comes from the training of selected officers and key specialists in U.S. schools and installations. 

These students are handpicked and screened by U.S. military personnel; they are the coming leaders of their nations. It is of inestimable value to the United 

States to have the friendship of such men. Accordingly, appropriate training is strongly stressed throughout the proposed fiscal year 1966 military assistance program. We are continuing our concerted effort to maximize the benefits of this program, not only to the trainees and their countries, but to the strength and solidarity of the free world common defense posture. 

We are also placing increased emphasis on the support of civic action projects, through which indigenous military forces participate in the economic and social development of their country. Civic action projects afford the civilian populace visible evidence that their government and their military are endeavoring to improve the lot of the average citizen. The resulting increased confidence in constituted authority, in or out of uniform, substantially lessens the vulnerability of a people to the subversive efforts of Communist agents, who prey upon the discontent of the underprivileged. 

SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE 

Although supporting assistance is not a part of the military assistance program, and is included in the economic aid request, I consider it a vital adjunct to military assistance. A supporting assistance program of $389 million, is proposed for fiscal year 1966. Over 80 percent of the total will be concentrated in four Far Eastern countries-Vietnam, Korea, Laos, and Thailand—all of which, as you will note, are included in our military assistance key forward defense category. More than half of the $389 million will go to Vietnam alone. These funds are absolutely essential to our effort in that country. 

LEGISLATION 

I would like briefly to mention certain changes which we propose in the legislation this year.

Most of the proposed changes concern the sales program. In line with our general approach of handling sales transactions on a businesslike basis, we are requesting as the major change in this program that we be allowed to make firm price commitments to foreign countries during negotiations. Firm prices will facilitate our negotiations by making it possible for foreign ministries of defense to ascertain what their obligations will be should they elect to order defense articles and services from the United States. They also will afford the purchasing country a means for determining whether a proposed purchase is within its budgetary capabilities, and facilitate arrangements for any credit terms required to conclude the sale.

The major change in the provisions relating to military assistance concerns the "drawdown" authority of section 510 of the Foreign Assistance Act. As the law now reads, the military assistance program is authorized to make use of Department of Defense stocks and resources for military assistance, subject to subsequent reimbursement therefor, when the President determines such action to be vital to U.S. security. Reimbursement is made through subsequent appropriations to the President for the military assistance program which in turn reimburses the appropriate DOD account or fund. The statutory limit on that authority is now fixed each year for the current fiscal year at $300 million. 

We propose two changes to section 510. The first would authorize reimbursement to be made, at the discretion of the Appropriations Committees, either to the President for the military assistance program or directly to the Department of Defense. Since such anticipated reimbursements would be an element of the overall DOD financial plan, it appears appropriate that there be an option to have them considered by the executive branch and by the congressional committees concerned during the annual examination of the Defense Department budget itself. In that context, it would be possible to make an informed judgment as to whether the items drawn down should be replaced in kind, whether the anticipated reimbursement should be applied to the procurement of other defense items, or the extent to which other funds available to the military departments should be reprogramed because of the transfer to the military assistance program of these items. The second change would make the statutory limit of $300 million a continuing limit for each fiscal year. 

I wish to emphasize, however, that the proposed option in the appropriation structure would not change the existing requirement that this authority be used only when the President determines it vital to the security of the United States. 

As you know, to date, we have not found it necessary to utilize this authority which was first granted to us in 1961. It is our firm intent not to use it except as a last resort.

I also want to call the committee's attention to the new sentence which the executive branch proposes that you add to section 451 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1931, as amended. This new sentence provides that there be authorized to be appropriated to the President for use in Vietnam such sums as may be necessary in the fiscal year 1966 for economic and military assistance if he determines such use to be important to the national interest. The purpose of this amendment is to give the President additional flexibility in dealing with presently unpredictable changes in the Vietnamese situation. 

CONCLUSION 

I have not undertaken to set before you on this occasion more than a few of the salient facts and figures which support our conviction that the authorization and appropriations we are requesting for fiscal year 1966 represent the bare minimum consistent with our national security and the common defense of the free world. 

I believe that the fiscal year 1966 military assistance program which we present to you today merits the full support of this committee and of the Congress. 

No other defense expenditure by the United States produces greater value. 

I have stated to the committee on a previous occasion, it would make little sense to spend almost $50 billion a year on our own military forces and refuse to spend 2 percent of that amount to support the forces of our allies who stand beside us in the collective defense of the free world. As

STATEMENT BY GEN. EARLE G. WHEELER, U.S. ARMY, CHAIRMAN OF THE JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I welcome this opportunity to appear before you in support of the military assistance program for the fiscal year 1966. I consider this program an integral part of our national military strategy and feel a personal responsibility to support this program as an essential complement to our own national military programs. 

I see no evidence that would justify any relaxation of our own national security efforts or those of our allies. The forces of communism and nationalism-in some areas so intermixed by Communist exploitation as to be indistinguishable pose an increasing threat to our worldwide interests and to the interests of our free world allies. There is no evidence of a decrease in Soviet military capabilities or of any change in the long-range political objectives of

their Communist Party leadership. Chinese Communist military capabilities, to which has now been added the threat of a nuclear capability—seem to be on the increase. And certainly, Peiping's politico-military adventures in southeast 

Asia, Africa, and Latin America are trending upward. Moreover, conflict in the areas of insurgency, penetration, and guerrilla warfare takes such forms that properly trained and equipped indigenous security and defense forces are the most effective counterforce against Communist domination. As you know, one of the first goals of the typical subversion plan of the Communists is to infiltrate, if possible, the armed forces of the chosen victim government; failing that, to attempt then to drive wedges of distrust between the armed forces, the populace, and the government. If there are some who place little value on the armed forces of our less affluent allies, you may be assured the Communist planners are not among them-they are well aware of the true value of these forces. 

The Joint Chiefs of Staff fully appreciate the significance of these allied military forces. As members of this committee may know, the Joint Chiefs of Staff use the same strategic planning document to establish the requirements both for our U.S. forces worldwide and for the military establishments in friendly countries which we need in support of our national strategy and collective security. 

In other words, we examine concurrently, on a worldwide bases, our own forces and those which we would like to see maintained by our friends. In the end, the military assistance we recommend is pared down to those countries that are of particular importance to our security and to those military forces within those countries that bear a particular complementary relation to our own. Thus, we in the Joint Chiefs of Staff are constantly reminded of the interlocking relationships existing between our national military programs and those of military assistance. I trust the committee will also keep in mind this important relationship.

The Joint Chiefs have viewed the level of the military assistance programs of the last 2 years with deep concern. Annual appropriations at the current level will barely provide the required day-to-day operating costs of ships, aircraft, and equipment necessary to prevent backsliding in current capabilities. Many well-planned force improvements in the original fiscal year 1964 program submission, which was severely reduced by the Congress, have had to be deferred indefinitely. This deferment is all the more significant since the quality of the equipment of the armed forces of the Soviet Union, Communist China, and the other Communist-controlled nations is improving steadily. While we are not unmindful of the fact that there are considerations other than military, such as our ultimate political and economic objectives for the several areas, which must be evaluated in determining the level of the annual military assistance program, we are of the opinion that further reductions below the current level are not justified by the military situation confronting the United States and its free world allies today and in the near term. 

Nearly three-fourths of this year's program will go to support force levels in the 11 countries on the periphery of the great Communist landmass. These funds will enable them to maintain over 3.5 million men under arms in collective defense of mutual security interests; i.e., those which we share with them. It would be far more expensive if we had to replace any part of this 3.5 million men with men from our own Armed Forces. None of these peripheral countries have the capacity to assume full support of these forces which are essential to our mutual security interests. It is appropriate for them to accept these burdens in the interests of our common defense, and it is appropriate for us to assist them. To reduce our assistance is to weaken forward defense forces and is an invitation to Communist effort to occupy the power vacuums that could result. In my opinion, reduction of the funds allocated to the forward defense country programs would be the poorest kind of economy for the United States, and one for which we might ultimately have to pay many times over. 

Of the small remainder of the annual program, the assistance to our Latin American neighbors is extremely important. Our country programs under the 

Alliance for Progress are oriented primarily toward internal security. Not to recognize the era of social, economic, and political change our Latin American neighbors are facing would be to ignore a key trend of our time. Change is a traditional feature of Latin American politics, and in recent years it has been the military establishment which in many instances has provided the greatest stabilizing factor for orderly change and continuity of constitutional government. 

There are others, of course, who would gladly offer military assistance to our Latin American friends in order to gain opportunities for political infiltration.

In short, this is no time for the United States to reduce this part of the military assistance program below a level that will further these ends. 

Those remaining funds programed for military base arrangements, grant aid phaseout, and free world orientation, while relatively small in dollars, are significant since they are tied to our own special interests and specific obligations. The military assistance program as a whole is a very tightly constructed package this year. I can assure you that it has the full support of the Joint 

Chiefs of Staff. 

As you know, this year's program includes $170 million over and above the basic $1 billion new obligation authority to meet the special combat requirements in Vietnam and Laos. I think it particularly important to recognize this special requirement as such. To lump the special funding requirements of combat situations with those of the remainder of the long-range force development plans would impair the orderly programing and execution of the balance of our military assistance programs. 

With regard to the situation in South Vietnam, let me state first that if we were to fail to continue to assist our Vietnamese friends, who have turned to us for help in their bitter struggle to maintain freedom, we could only expect a decline in the trust in which we are held by our other allies who are exposed to the threat of Communist subversion or aggression. Secondly, I would remind all: (1) That for a period of over 10 years, the Republic of Vietnam has sustained the most vicious Communist subversive campaign faced by any nation in our time and is still free; (2) that despite the obvious setbacks and distractions on the political scene, the Vietnamese regular armed forces have remained intact, vital, and disciplined; (3) that the armed forces have remained the single governmental organization to continue functioning and constitute the most effective government organism in Vietnam today; and (4) that the Vietnamese armed forces continue to show improvement in their military operations despite the stepped-up efforts of the Vietcong to force the issue. These are positive accomplishments which should not be ignored at a moment of great difficulty in Vietnam. It is my belief that the elements essential to the success of the counterinsurgency program in Vietnam still exist, and I strongly support the additional military assistance for Vietnam in this program. 

In conclusion, I suggest that President Johnson placed our military assistance program in its proper perspective when he stated "Military assistance makes it possible for nations to survive. It provides the shield behind which economic and social development can take place." While the details of the economic aid program are beyond my purview, I support the economic aid program in principle, since it is the program that can best promote the ultimate self-sufficiency of the recipient nations. The military assistance program is providing a necessary shield and the fiscal year 1966 program is essential to its sustenance. Again, I assure you the program submission before you has the full support of the Joint 

Chiefs of Staff. 

Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

APPLICATION OF HICKENLOOPER AMENDMENT TO MILITARY SALES 

Section 620 (e) (1) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, the Hickenlooper amendment, requires the suspension of assistance under the act to countries which confiscate property owned by American citizens. As the law now stands, therefore, applicability of the Hickenlooper amendment to a particular military sales transaction depends upon whether the circumstances and terms and conditions of the sales transaction are such that the transaction constitutes assistance within the meaning of the act. If the sales transaction does involve assistance, it is subject to the Hickenlooper amendment; if the sales transaction does not involve assistance-for example, does not utilize any funds made available under the act, does not involve any concessional elements, does not result in any unreimbursed cost to the U.S. Government, the transaction is not subject to the Hickenlooper amendment. 

Several drafts of legislation for fiscal year 1966 are now before the House 

Foreign Affairs Committee and the Senate Foreign Relations Committee. The draft which the House Foreign Affairs Committee is actively considering does not change in any way the scope of the applicability of the Hickenlooper amendment. The only bill dealing with military assistance and sales which has been introduced in the Senate, and hence the only bill formally before the Foreign Relations Committee, is S. 1524, the bill introduced by Senator Morse on March 

15, 1965. That bill restructures part II of the Foreign Assistance Act by placing in separate chapters of part II military sales and grant aid. As part of this restructuring, the bill makes it clear that military assistance includes only grant aid and that the Hickenlooper amendment applies only to the grant aid program. 

In this context, the executive branch prefers the Senate bill. As an overall matter, it believes that, in view of the fact that the sales program is of approximately the same dollar magnitude as the grant aid program, separate congressional examination of and legislation for, sales is warranted. In particular, the executive branch believes that considerations which may justify the imposition of a particular restriction on grant aid transactions may not equally be applicable to sales transactions, and hence that existing restrictions, and such restric tions as may be proposed in the future, should not be applied to sales unless the factors which justify the restrictions on grant aid are equally applicable to sales. 

Senator HICKENLOOPER. We will also see. The interpretation or the assumption may be wrong. There are elements I think in the executive end of Government that try to get rid of that amendment. There are other elements that would like to keep it because they think it would be very helpful. But be that as it may, we will see what we can do.

USE OF GAS IN VIETNAM 

Senator LAUSCHE. Just one question further. This is away from what we are discussing today-the use of this riot gas in Vietnam. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes? 

Senator LAUSCHE. May I ask a question on that? I would like to have the Secretary comment.

The CHAIRMAN. I was going to. I thought somebody would have before this; there is so much in the press. I think this is a good opportunity to explain that and napalm both. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. First, let me describe the three gases that are involved here, and then relate the circumstances under which they have been used.

The three are known as DM, CN, and CS. DM is a pepperlike irritant which causes irritation of the eyes and the mucous membranes, viscous discharge from the nose which is similar to that caused by a cold. It causes sneezing, coughing, headache, tightness in the chest, nausea, and vomiting. It incapacitates on the average for periods of from one-half hour to 2 hours.

CN is a lachrymatory agent-tear-producing agent which is also an irritant to the upper respiratory passages, and it may also cause irritation to the skin. It incapacitates on the average of approximately 3 minutes.

CS is a more recently developed lachrymatory agent-tear-producing agent-which causes more severe irritation to the eyes than does

CN and more severe irritation to the nose and respiratory tract. It is usually accompanied by pains in the chest, by choking, and by violent coughing. Concentrations of CS can lead to nausea and to vomiting. On the average CS incapacitates for from 5 to 15 minutes. 

All three of these agents are commonly known as riot control agents. 

Senator AIKEN. What is the life of the gas itself? 

General WHEELER. It disappears almost immediately. It is lighter than air.

Senator AIKEN. You mean one attack, unless the gas is renewed, will General WHEELER. Dissipate almost immediately, Senator. the 

Senator AIKEN. Three minutes?

General WHEELER. A couple of minutes I would say, at the most in open air.

Secretary MCNAMARA. Three minutes incapacitation allows the police to move in.

Senator AIKEN. I am sorry I interrupted. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. In any event, all three of these agents are distributed worldwide for riot control purposes. For example, here is a catalog, a 1964 catalog of one of the distribution sources. This is from the Federal Laboratories, Inc., which is a private firm in 

Saltsburg, Pa., which, as you see from the cover, provides a worldwide distribution service for these. 

Senator AIKEN. Who controls the company?

Secretary MCNAMARA. It is privately owned. I do not know the owners or 

Senator AIKEN. It is independent?

Secretary MCNAMARA. It is independent, that is correct. There are several of these corporations. For example, one is Fisher Laboratories in New Jersey, and another is the Lakery Corp., in Cleveland, Ohio. The only one for which I have a catalog is the Federal Laboratories. They show, for example, on page 4 of their catalog, the ads for CN and for DM, and on page 6 of their catalog, they show the ads for CS.

Now, I show this to you only to indicate that these are common riot control agents used by police departments and other law enforcement agencies worldwide.

They were provided by the United States-

INSTANCES OF TEAR GAS USE 

Secretary MCNAMARA. No, sir; that is a judgment I will leave to you. But in any event, these agents are provided to law and order forces worldwide, and they were provided to the South Vietnamese forces, both the military and police, for the purpose under the military assistance program over the past years. They have been used, to the best of my knowledge, only three times. They were first used on the 23d of December last year in an operation that had as its objective the extrication of American prisoners who were believed retained in the area. Their second use was on the 25th of December. 

Again the operational objective was the extraction of American prisoners believed retained in the area.

Their third use was on the 28th of January of this year when Vietcong Communists mingled with villagers in Phu Yen Province, and in an attempt to separate the Vietcong from the villagers and to avoid firing upon the village, these riot control agents were used. 

They are the same kinds of agents that have been used elsewhere in the world on many, many occasions. One of them, for example, the more severe lachrymatory agent known as CS, has been supplied by the British to Venezuela, Cyprus, Trinidad, Belgium, British 

Guiana, Gambia, Ghana, Northern Rhodesia, Switzerland, South

Africa, Sweden. 

So far as we were able to determine from the Federal Labs, which is this corporation, it has been sold to Bolivia, Dominican Republic, France, Peru, and South Vietnam. The agents have been used in

USE OF NAPALM 

The CHAIRMAN. While we are on this subject, do you wish to comment on the use of napalm?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes, Mr. Chairman. This is an entirely different weapon. I want to emphasize that CS, CN, and DM are riot

control agents, are nonlethal, and are used customarily by law enforcement agencies as substitutes for lethal weapons. 

In contrast, napalm is a munition of war used as an optimum agent under certain circumstances to achieve destruction of military targets. 

In the case of our operations against North Vietnam and the operations of the South Vietnamese against North Vietnam, it has been used a few times. [Deleted.] Those sorties that have carried it have done so because they were directed against military targets separated from civilian areas which military targets could be destroyed most effectively by napalm.

It is both the most effective weapon against some targets and it is also the weapon which minimizes potential fatalities to U.S. troops. 

I say that for the reason that the launch of a high explosive bomb requires that the aircraft launching the bomb rise above its initial altitude if it has been coming in at low altitude, in order to avoid the surface-to-air defense. 

If you visualize an airplane coming in at say 200-500 feet, you can recognize that if it were to drop a bomb from that altitude, the explosion very likely would damage the aircraft. For that reason, the pilot must rise to a higher altitude, something on the order of 3,500 4,000 feet, before he makes his dive from which he will launch the bomb, and when at the higher altitude, he is exposed to the antiaircraft fire to a greater degree than were he to be able to maintain the low altitude. 

Napalm can be launched from a lower altitude, and therefore when it is optimum in its effect on the target, it is highly desirable that the aircraft carry that weapon in order to minimize the danger to our own forces, and for both reasons, therefore, we authorize its use under certain specified and restricted conditions.

SEPARATION OF MILITARY AND ECONOMIC AID 

The CHAIRMAN. I know the administration thinks this is a matter for Congress to determine. If you do not care to comment on it, it is quite all right. Secretary MCNAMARA. Mr. Chairman, I will be happy to comment on the question. I did so a little earlier today, but I will repeat it here because it is important. 

I believe it is a mistake to lump together the economic aid and military aid in a single bill, and I say this without any reference to the committees of Congress that would be involved in considering separate bills. I think that is an issue for Congress to decide and not for me to even make a recommendation on. 

But I do believe that it confuses the public and I think also the Members of Congress to lump together such disparate subjects as military aid, which is primarily developed on the basis of military requirements, with economic aid, which is designed to serve a quite different purpose, when these two subjects are covered by a single bill, it confuses the review of each.

I am certain it confuses the public, and I think it confuses the Members of Congress.

There is no question in my mind but what military aid is far more comparable to the other items of the defense budget than it is to the economic aid, and it ought to be considered in relation to the defense budget.

I am not suggesting now how it should be handled in the Congress, what committees should consider it. I am simply pointing out that it ought to be considered in relation to the defense program, and if the Congress feels that either military aid should be increased or decreased in contrast to the recommendations of the administration, it

should do so only after it has considered how that change, increased or decreased, would affect the other portions of the defense budget. 

This it can do best if it considers the military aid separate and apart from the economic aid.

USE OF GAS BY EGYPTIANS IN YEMEN Senator HICKENLOOPER. Secretary MCNAMARA. I do not believe that concentrations of any one of these three gases, CN, CS, or DM will cause death, and I think that is why they are classified in our manuals as nonlethal agents, and I believe that is why they can be sold by a private corporation without any restriction.

Senator HICKENLOOPER. Do you have any knowledge, General 

Wheeler, of the chemical type of that gas?

General WHEELER. No; I do not, Senator. I received essentially the same reports that you heard.

I would say this. That these particular gases we are discussing now, these riot control agents, we use routinely in the American Army for training. I have had doses of all three of them at various times in gas training, gas mask drills, and so on, going back to 40 years ago when I first joined the service. Just like any other gaseous substance which is not air, if you were confined in more or less an airtight room and you pump the room full of such a substance in the long term I do not know whether it would kill you or not, but it certainly would not do you any good. But normally in tactical use where people can move about they can get out of it very rapidly, because it does not persist.

Senator HICKENLOOPER. So I understand. 

General WHEELER. In fact the object of the use of these riot control munitions is to make the crowd disperse, to make them move and get out of the area.

Senator HICKENLOOPER. I understand, General Wheeler, that we have discussed the gas we have used there. 

General WHEELER. I have no personal knowledge of the characteristics of this other gas.

SEPARATION OF AID WILL NOT AFFECT CONSULTATION

Secretary MCNAMARA. That is correct.

Secretary MCNAMARA. That is correct.

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes; I think it would depend upon whether you authorized such transfers in a separate economic aid bill, if it were separated. 

The CHAIRMAN. Yes; but it has been suggested, you know, that the military aid should be proposed by you, perhaps subject to the approval of the Department of State or of Mr. Rusk. This is not necessary; is it?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I am always amused by the fact that the foreign aid bill requires that the Secretary of State exercise a certain authority over the military assistance program, as if to imply that the Secretary of State has no interest in or authority to comment upon the defense program, the defense budget, which is the foundation of our foreign policy, and which if it were different from what it is, would require a change in our foreign policy, and which therefore absolutely requires that the Secretary of State certify that the defense program is balanced with the foreign policy objectives. 

I am amused because by legislation we are required to consult on a very small part of a very large problem, whereas there is no legislative requirement to consult on the heart of the problem. 

The CHAIRMAN. But the necessity of which is obvious, and you do. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Which is obvious and fundamental. 

The CHAIRMAN. Yes.

Secretary MCNAMARA. And which the President recognizes, which 

I recognize and which the Secretary of State would insist upon if I did not recognize. 

FORMER ATTITUDE OF DEFENSE DEPARTMENT TOWARD SEPARATION 

The CHAIRMAN. I want to put in the record part of an exchange that took place in 1954 and 1955 on this same subject to illustrate that this is not a new problem. 

In 1954 in the hearings on page 263 this exchange took place. I said-I was not chairman then "Mr. Chairman, may I ask why this $1.1 billion is not in the military budget?"

General Stewart, who was then representing the Defense Department said:

Senator, my answer was that it was my understanding there were two bills, the foreign aid bill and our own Defense Department bill, because it was the will of the Congress to control and designate the funds which would be specifically used in support of the foreign policy as opposed to those funds which would be used for the maintenance of our own forces. 

Senator FULBRIGHT. What do you mean the will of Congress? Who told you that?

It has been going on now for about 4 or 5 years. Senator. 

This is General Stewart. 

The question has been raised among those of us who tried to administer this bill a number of times on how much easier it would be for us as the working people if this was all part of one budget, and that is the answer that I have been told. I do not remember who told me, but it has been discussed many times.

Senator FULBRIGHT. I do not see any reason why this money should be in this bill at all. It is somewhat deceptive in a way because it is essentially military as you say.

General STEWART. That is right. 

That was the attitude of the Defense Department 10 years ago. 

And in 1955 a very similar exchange took place. I will not read it all. This is with Admiral Radford. I asked very much the same questions. I said then :

It seems it would be wise to include at least this 50 percent which is for direct military support in your defense budget and thereby cut down the amount for foreign aid. You would have a much easier time getting it through. If I could accept literally what you say about the significance of this appropriation being so directly military in nature that it might as well be included in your budget, do you see any objection to that procedure? 

Admiral RADFORD. No, sir; I do not.

So it is not anything new. This has been an attitude I think of the 

Defense Department at least for 10 years.

Secretary MCNAMARA. My attitude is a little different than that, Mr. Chairman. I not only see no objection to it, I think it would lead to a more logical rationale and comprehensive review of the defense program. 

The CHAIRMAN. I do, too. 

I said then, "Can you give any reason, perhaps Mr. Hensel can"who was then the Counsel for the Department-"why these items are included in foreign aid rather than the Defense Department?" 

Mr. Hensel said, "I think, Senator Fulbright, it is a matter of history." He could not give any better answer, so it is not something new cooked up to try to deceive anybody.

Senator CLARK. May I ask one question on that?

The CHAIRMAN. Yes. 

PENTAGON INFLUENCE OVER STATE DEPARTMENT 

Senator CLARK. Mr. Secretary, there is a wide school of thought, to which I do not necessarily belong, that the Pentagon rather constantly pushes the State Department around and is in effect conducting the foreign policy of the United States with the aid of what General Eisenhower used to call the military-industrial complex. 

I take it you do not share that view. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. The fact of the matter-the reason that school of thought exists-is that you never see in the press a divergence of opinion between Secretary Rusk and myself. The reason you do not is because we consult fully on these matters, and because I believe very strongly in the subordination of defense policy to foreign policy. 

Senator CLARK. And you do not attempt to run foreign policy.

You have enough to do in the Department of Defense. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. I do not, and I do not think anyone can point to a single instance in which we have endeavored to impose our will on the State Department. 

Senator CLARK. Sometimes possibly at lower level?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I doubt even that, because I think that the 

Joint Chiefs feel just as I do, and I think the other civilian and military personnel of the Department do, and in the last 4 years during the time I have been associated with the Department, we have sought to insure that every individual in it understand this single point, that defense is a tool of foreign policy, and it must be subordinated to foreign policy, and there must be a balance between our foreign policy objectives and our military forces and defense program. 

USE OF GAS IN VIETNAM 

Senator CLARK. Without regard to the wisdom or lack of wisdom of the use of gas in Vietnam, that was not cleared in advance with the 

State Department, was it?

Secretary MCNAMARA. I would like to go off the record here. 

Senator CLARK. Why the great excitement yesterday?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Because the initial press reports confuse the use of riot control agents on the one hand with the use of "gas" in gas warfare on the other hand, and one is deplorable and considered uncivilized. The other is accepted by every major nation in the world as necessary and required. The press did not distinguish between the two.

Senator CLARK. I was asked four times on television in Philadelphia yesterday whether I approved of the use of poison gas in Vietnam. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. The answer is obviously no, nor have we used it. 

General WHEELER. May I add a footnote here, Senator? 

Senator CLARK. Yes, indeed.

General WHEELER. [Deleted.]

8 Senator LAUSCHE. Might I say that the putting of the question to 

Senator Clark four times left with the public an implication that we did use poisonous gases.

Senator CLARK. It is perhaps an evil arising from the fact that we live in a democracy, and Senators have to answer those questions, sometimes with inadequate information. 

The CHAIRMAN. Senator Aiken. 

WHO AUTHORIZED USE OF GAS? 

Senator AIKEN. Commenting on the effect of the reports whether correct or erroneous, last night the news quoted President Johnson as saying he was shocked that gas would be used without his knowledge. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. He did not say that.

Senator AIKEN. Nevertheless, it went out. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. That is a complete misquote, because he has never said that, I am certain. 

Senator AIKEN. Does the Secretary of Defense have knowledge that gas would be used? How far down the line does autonomy in the choice of weapons extend? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. There is no autonomy in the choice of weapons. Each weapon is certified at the time, and at the time of certification all elements of the Government that could properly be involved in the decision are brought into the decision. Now, the fact is that these particular so-called weapons-and I think we misuse the term "weapon" when we apply it to this these so-called riot control agents were certified for use years and years ago, and at that time I am certain that the State Department and other appropriate authorities, including the upper echelon authorities, were brought in. 

There is no weapon used by the defense forces of this country that represents a new use that is not approved by the Joint Chiefs and by me, for example, and I never approve one without review by the Secre tary of State. [Deleted.] 

Senator AIKEN. About the use of the gas, has that been certified? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. It was certified at the time the riot control agent was introduced into our inventory, but that was years and years ago.

Senator AIKEN. Was the use of gas certified for military purposes or for control of riots?

Secretary MCNAMARA. It was certified for use in situations where you were endeavoring to separate friend from foe rather than kill them, and that is exactly what we are trying to do. 

Senator AIKEN. That would be for military purposes? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. I would say either military or civilian.

When you are trying to recover American prisoners, I do not know whether it is a military purpose or not, but what we were trying to do was avoid firing on groups, and this weapon, if you want to call it a weapon, is certified for use under those circumstances. 

The point I am trying to make, Senator Aiken, is there is no failure to consult at upper echelons at State or Defense on significant changes of weapons, changes in policies, or changes in operations. We have consultation at the highest level on changes in weapon policy or operation. Every single message referring to every one of these three areas

of activity is personally reviewed by me and personally reviewed by the Secretary of State or his designee, sometimes George Ball, for example.

Senator AIKEN. Not necessarily by the President. 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Not necessarily the President.

Senator PELL. My second point is in connection with one which has been covered here: gas. As I understand it, while we have not ratified the Geneva Convention, we did say we would go along with it.

Secretary MCNAMARA. That is right, absolutely not.

Senator PELL. Is my conception of the present policy correct in that apparently in order to get the North Vietnamese to say "Uncle," we are willing to move quite far, but we will not use any nuclear weapons, and we will not use poison gas?

First, we have no intention of using poison gas. We have no authorization for the use of poison gas. There has been no consideration given to the use of poison gas. 

Senator PELL. Would it have to be authorized? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Absolutely. Quite frankly it would have to be authorized by more than me. There is absolutely no authorization or consideration of it. I have never even given it a thought. I think it is rather unfortunate that it has become common practice to apply the same term "gas" to a lethal agent, poison gas, and a riot control agent, CS, CN, and DM, which is used in control of civil disturbances. It is only the latter that we have supplied.

Secretary MCNAMARA. But these three agents do not fall under that protocol. 

Senator PELL. It is not under gas.

Secretary MCNAMARA. Not under the terms of that protocol. 

Senator PELL. Has that point been established?

Secretary MCNAMARA. It has been established. 

Senator PELL. I haven't seen the reference.

Secretary MCNAMARA. There is legislative history under which this is recognized. That is why the British have supplied it to that list of nations that I read, and that is why they used it in Cyprus, and that is why it is used in West Berlin today and why it is used by other nations. 

Senator PELL. Who buys this? Ladies not wanting to be attacked in the subway?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Police departments primarily, but not only police departments, governmental agencies buy it. I think, for example, there is a certificate in there they can sign for tax exemption. 

Others who buy it are not tax exempt.

INVESTMENT GUARANTEE PROGRAM 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, in accordance with your request, I propose to discuss further today AID's specific risk investment guarantee program and its extended risk guarantee program.

There is a great need for investment capital in the underdeveloped countries.

Senator GORE. Would you digress to explain the difference in the two terms you have just used?

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir. The difference between the two is this, and I will come to it later in the statement. The specific risk investment guarantee program guarantees the investor against political risks; it may be inconvertibility, it may be expropriation, it may be war risk. 

The extended risk guarantee program, on the other hand, is the program authorized by the act under which we can insure an investor against business risks up to 75 percent of the investment. 493

Senator GORE. Thank you. Mr. GAUD. There is an equally great need for strengthening and expanding private enterprise in those countries. The participation of 

American companies in business in underdeveloped countries helps meet these needs. It also brings with it technology and know-how that no governmental program can duplicate. 

The investment guarantee program is the core of AID's many efforts to induce American business to invest in underdeveloped countries. 

The evidence-in terms of increased guarantees and applicationsindicates the importance that businessmen attribute to it. 

Investment in any foreign country carries with it difficulties in dealing with unfamiliar languages, currencies, business practices, and customs. In the less-developed countries, these difficulties are compounded by fears of political instability. 

Many American businessmen tell us that the availability of investment guarantees is a significant factor in their evaluation of the climate for investment and their decision to invest in a particular underdeveloped country. Others have indicated they could not obtain necessary funds for foreign investment unless their investment were insured against political risks. Such insurance is not generally available commercially.

The investment guarantee program can be particularly useful in countries making substantial progress toward development. AID ends its dollar assistance programs, not when a nation becomes fully developed, but when progress toward development can be sustained without dollar inflows on concessional terms. At such a stage-and we believe that Taiwan is there today-a nation faces a critical need for continued foreign investment. The investment guarantee program provides an effective means to induce such investment from private sources.

I would like now to say a few words about each of the two programs.. 

SPECIFIC RISK GUARANTEE 

Specific, or political risk, guarantees have been available since 1948. 

They provide coverage against loss from the political risks of (a) inconvertibility, (b) expropriation, and (c) war, revolution, or insurrection. More than $2.2 billion of such guarantees were issued through 

December 31, 1964, and almost $1.7 billion were still outstanding as of that date. 

Senator LAUSCHE. May I ask a question at this point? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir.

Senator LAUSCHE. Do these guarantees cover investments in undeveloped countries alone or both developed and undeveloped? 

Mr. GAUD. Only undeveloped. 

Senator LAUSCHE. Undeveloped? All right. 

Mr. GAUD. Since the adoption of Senator Aiken's amendment in 

1958, there have been no investment guarantees issued for investment in developed countries, Senator Lausche. 

Senator LAUSCHE. All right. 

Mr. GAUD. Guarantees are limited to the value of the investment made plus retained earnings thereon. In the case of a loan, the amount of such earnings that may be covered is limited to accrued interest. In

the case of an equity investment, the amount of such earnings is generally limited to an amount equal to the original investment. The liability of the United States is automatically reduced as the investor recovers the principal of his investment. 

The investor does not have to take out all three risk coverages. He may elect the coverage he desires within the limits described above. 

For each type of coverage, the investor pays one-half percent on the amount of insurance in force, and one-fourth percent on amounts reserved for future coverage. 

Senator CASE. Would you explain what that means?

Mr. GAUD. Yes, that is a standby fee. For example, an investor who is making a loan may take out inconvertibility insurance on the total amount of interest payments that are coming to him over the period. of the loan. But until the interest is earned, it is only a standby arrangement, and he pays one-fourth of 1 percent during that period. 

Senator CASE. And he pays the balance as time goes on. 

Mr. GAUD. As it comes into effect the fee goes up to one-half of 1 percent.

Senator CLARK. Are these annual charges or just one-time charges? 

Mr. GAUD. They are annual, Senator Clark. 

Senator CASE. Are you quite sure about that? Suppose it is a 30year loan. Do you pay one-half of 1 percent each year?

Mr. GAUD. Yes. If the loan is going to be made by the bank or the institution to the borrower at 5 percent, let us say, this increases the rate of interest which he charges by one-half of 1 percent for each of these coverages per year. 

Senator WILLIAMS. What has been your loss ratio on this?

Mr. GAUD. I am coming to specific figures on that if I may, sir, very soon.

We are requesting that the Congress increase the amount of specific risk guarantees that may be outstanding at any one time from $2.5 billion to $5 billion. I discussed with you Tuesday a number of other changes in the legislation which we are requesting to make the program more effective. 

EXTENDED RISK GUARANTEE PROGRAM 

Under the extended risk guarantee program AID can guarantee investors against loss up to 75 percent of an investment against all risks other than fraud or misconduct on the part of the investor. This program also permits guarantees of up to 100 percent for housing loans similar to the Latin American housing guarantee program. 

Past interest in the extended risk guarantee program has been a disappointment. We have to date issued only three guarantees totaling approximately $8.3 million. But we think we have now developed a set of policies that will generate more activity while preserving the share-the-risk concept inherent in the 75-percent guarantee authority. 

The major emphasis of the program will be to encourage financial institutions such as insurance companies, pension funds, and banks to extend long-term industrial loans in the developing countries. 

Under the new policies, AID is prepared to provide extended risk coverage to the late installments of a long-term credit. There would be only a specific risk guarantee to the institutional lender on the first

25 percent of the payments; the extended risk guarantee would fully cover the last 75 percent.

Mr. GAUD. Of the first 25 percent. Let us say if it is a 12-year loan, the lender will carry the commercial risk, 100 percent, for the first 3 years' installments.

AID EXTENDED RISK GUARANTEE POLICY 

In July 1964, AID issued a draft policy paper on extended risk guarantees for loans. At that time, AID envisaged guaranteeing 75 percent of the amount of a loan outstanding at any time. In subsequent discussions with institutional investors it became evident that they were unwilling to carry 25 percent of the business risks over the life of a long-term loan. After these discussions, and a review of other U.S. Government programs for guaranteeing private lending, such as FHA, Maritime Administration ship financing guarantees, and Eximbank suppliers' credit guarantees, AID decided to offer the extended risk guarantee on the late maturities of a loan.

Under this new policy issued in December 1964, AID is prepared to consider proposals for applying the extended risk guarantee against the later maturities of a loan, while allowing the percentage of the loan not covered by such a guarantee to constitute the early maturities. If the Agency guaranteed none of the commercial risk for installments equal to the first 25 percent of the principal due, the remainder of the installments could be 100 percent guaranteed. 

An extended risk guarantee includes specific risk coverage. A lender may increase his coverage against the specific risks of inconvertibility, expropriation, and war by taking supplementary coverage (e.g., for the remaining 25 percent or more of his investment) under the specific risk program. 

Should a default in a credit occur at any time due to one of the specific political risks, the investor could collect up to 100 percent of the outstanding investment and accrued but unpaid interest. 

Should a default occur as a result of commercial risks during the early period when the maturities not covered by an extended risk guarantee are outstanding, the lender would lose the amount of the early, unguaranteed maturities. If the loss occurred at any time after repayment of the early maturities on which there was not extended risk guarantee coverage, the lender could collect up to 100 percent of the outstanding investment and accrued but unpaid interest. In no case would payment under an extended risk guarantee be more than 75 percent of the total amount of the original credit. 

AID would perform a technical and financial analysis of a project for which extended risk guaranteed financing is requested to assure that the amount of the financing corresponds to the cost of the project. In the guarantee contract AID would prohibit prepayment of the early loan installments not covered by extended risk guarantees.

Mr. GAUD. This policy only applies in the case of loans, Senator Aiken.

Mr. GAUD. This is on a guarantee of an equity investment? In this case, we guarantee the U.S. investment in a single project. When the investor withdraws his money, this reduces pro tanto the extent of our guarantee.
