Senator LAUSCHIE. Mr. Chairman, may I ask a question?

The CHAIRMAN. Yes. 

Senator LAUSCHE. I want to get this clarified in my own mind. 

Under the present practice and law, you guarantee up to 75 percent on what you call extended or business risk. 

Mr. GAUD. That is right, sir.

Senator LAUSCHIE. The banks understand that that 75 percent is available, but they want it under a formula which will relieve you from coverage of the first 25 percent on extended risk loss. 

Mr. GAUD. That is right.

Senator LAUSCIIE. They cause you to adopt 100 percent on the last 

75 percent of loss.

Mr. GAUD. That is correct. That is it exactly. 

Senator LAUSCHIE. Does that mean that in the end you still are only covering 75 percent? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir.

Senator LAUSCHE. And why do they want it set up that way? I have my own idea.

Mr. GAUD. The banks are perfectly willing to take the early maturities of the loan, and then they lay off or they discount the late maturities to the insurance companies. The insurance companies will not take those late maturities without this guarantee. 

Senator LAUSCHE. What about the political risk coverage?

Mr. GAUD. The political risk coverage, if they want to pay for it, goes up to 100 percent. 

Senator LAUSCHE. 100 percent. 

Mr. GAUD. Yes.

Senator LAUSCHE. So you must consider this in two packages-one political risk and the other extended risk. Is that right?

Mr. GAUD. That is right. The normal investment guarantee that we make is purely of the political risks.

FEES PAID FOR GUARANTEES 

Senator LAUSCHE. Yes. This further question. You identify the premiums that are paid? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir.

Senator LAUSCHE. You say, "For each type of coverage, the investor pays one-half percent on the amount of insurance in force." 

Senator LAUSCHE. You may have how many types of coverage?

Mr. GAUD. Three. 

Senator LAUSCHE. That is the political risks? 

Mr. GAUD. Three political risks. 

Senator LAUSCHE. What about the extended? Is that separate?

Mr. GAUD. I have not come to that yet. 

Senator LAUSCHE. So that would be a maximum of 11/2 percent premium.

Mr. GAUD. Yes; and the fees under the extended risk program are 

134 percent. That, of course, includes the others.

Senator LAUSCHE. Does it include this one-fourth of 1 percent on amounts reserved for future coverage? 

Mr. GAUD. No; if you take out the extended risk guaranty, this guarantees you against everything except fraud or misconduct on the part of the investor. In other words, it includes the political risks, and the charge for that is 134 percent. 

Senator LAUSCHE. That is the whole charge. 

Mr. GAUD. It is the aggregate charge. 

Senator LAUSCHE. And you get full coverage-political and extended. 

Mr. GAUD. You get full coverage up to 75 percent on the one and the 100 percent on the other. 

The CHAIRMAN. Is that one-half of 1 percent for each category, inconvertibility one-half of 1 percent expropriation one-half of 1 percent, and war one-half of 1 percent? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir.

The CHAIRMAN. He can take all three of those. 

Mr. GAUD. That is correct.

The CHAIRMAN. He can buy risk against inconvertibility for onehalf of 1 percent.

Mr. GAUD. That is correct. Now, normally in the average case all of your money is not risked at the same time as far as the inconvertibility thing is concerned, particularly in the case of a loan. The average effective rate at any given moment for a man who takes out all three types of insurance is about 114 percent. 

Senator WILLIAMS. They would normally add that onto the 5 percent. 

Mr. GAUD. That is right.

Senator WILLIAMS. And the net effect of it is they have a guaranteed 

Government mortgage of 5 percent. 

Mr. GAUD. Guaranteed against certain risks.

Senator CASE. Political risks. 

Mr. GAUD. Yes; political risks, such as expropriation. 

Senator WILLIAMS. Business failure risk.

Mr. GAUD. If you had the business failure risk guarantee it would cost you 134 percent, and it is only good up to 75 percent of your investment, so you are at risk for 25 percent. 

Senator WILLIAMS. You are at risk, but as Senator Case points out; if you jockey around, you can safeguard your first 25 percent. 

The CHAIRMAN. This is a proposal. He is talking about the way it is. The proposal would be that way. 

Senator WILLIAMS. The way it is now, I understand. 

Mr. GAUD. Yes. 

DEFINITION OF MISCONDUCT 

Senator LAUSCHE. May I put one more question? You have been saying that "misconduct" not being covered. Is that in the present law? 

Mr. GAUD. That is in the law.

The CHAIRMAN. You put it in there, Senator. 

Senator LAUSCHE. I did not know whether it went out. 

Senator GORE. Nobody knows what it means. nobody knows what that Mr. GAUD. Courts decide that from time to time. 

The CHAIRMAN. Just like negligence means until it is decided in a specific case. 

Go ahead. Maybe we will clarify it.

Mr. GAUD. There are a few more facts which will appear here as I go along.

The CHAIRMAN. All right. Go ahead. 

Mr. GAUD. We are also prepared to consider extended risk guarantees for equity investments in exceptional cases. 

Fees under the program-this is the extended risk program, as I said-will be 134 percent of the amount of the extended risk guarantee in force on the estimated amount of disbursed and outstanding credit.

The CHAIRMAN. Let me make clear, extended risk here includes not only the business but also these other three, does it not? 

Mr. GAUD. That is correct.

The CHAIRMAN. That is right. 

Mr. GAUD. Before closing, let me comment on two points about which some concern has been expressed: The extent of our exposure under the political risk program and the balance of payments. 

EXPOSURE TO LOSSES 

The amount of all three types of political risk guarantees outstanding totals almost $1.7 billion, but our actual exposure to loss is far less than this amount. Many investments are protected by all three types of coverage. It is unrealistic to expect that loss would occur on more than one coverage for any single investment. 

Senator AIKEN. They pay a separate fee for each type of coverage? 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir. Guarantee agreements are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. Government. Furthermore, we had available, as of December 31, 1964, reserves totaling $278 million to meet losses under the program, including almost $22 million in fees collected. We see no need to fund these reserves further at the present time.

The CHAIRMAN. What made up those reserves besides the $22 million?

Mr. GAUD. It is primarily notes, that is to say authorization to spend from the public debt which were authorized in the very early days of this program, in the late forties and early fifties, Mr. Chairman. 

Senator WILLIAMS. That is the $278 million?

Mr. GAUD. Yes; I will tell you how it breaks down. There is roughly $22 million of fees. There is $80,000 proceeds from the sale of assets in a case where we had to take over a claim. Transfer from Development Loan Fund appropriated funds, $27 million. In fiscal year 

1963 the Congress appropriated $30 million for this purpose, and then in earlier years the authorization that I spoke of, $199 million. This all totals about $278 million. 

Senator WILLIAMS. Were the losses you sustained taken from that, or is this after those losses have been written off? 

Mr. GAUD. That is after the losses. We have had only one loss, and 

I am coming to that right now. 

LOSSES TO DATE 

Losses to date, on political risk guarantees, have been small. We have paid one claim, which resulted in no loss. 

Senator LAUSCHE. Where was that loss?

Mr. GAUD. Why do I not distribute these papers right now. I was going to do it in a minute, but you will have the facts in front of you. 

I have here, Mr. Chairman, which I would like to submit for the record if you would like, but certainly for the information of the committee at the moment, a statement showing all the claims that have been filed under the specific risk guaratee program, under AID, under the extended risk guarantee program (of which there are none); and also under the DLF program under the Mutual Security Act of 1954 which was repealed in 1961. 

I would like to distribute those around.

Senator WILLIAMS. This $278 million of funds, is it invested? 

Mr. GAUD. They are in the Treasury, and I just do not know the answer to that question.

Treasury also?

Mr. GAUD. That is right. The $57 million in appropriations has never actually left the Treausry. As I say, we paid one claim which resulted in no loss. Three others are pending, with a total exposure of less than $1 million.

There have been no losses under the extended-risk program. 

Indeed, we have only guaranteed three investments under that program. Under the old Development Loan Fund all-risk program, which went out of business in 1961, we have made one payout of $650,000.

EFFECT ON BALANCE OF PAYMENTS 

Finally, let me comment on the relationship of the guarantee programs and the balance of payments. Since 1959, investment guarantees have not been issued to cover investment in developed countries. 

They are available only for investments in underdeveloped countries. 

The President made clear in his balance-of-payments message that the United States still seeks to encourage private investment in the less developed countries. 

We believe that the $708 million in political-risk guarantees written in calendar 1964 will cover actual investment of about $250 million. 

We estimate about 80 percent of the total invested will be spent in the 

United States.

It should be borne in mind that this investment generates substantial remittance of earnings to the United States. Investment in the less developed countries also helps build future markets for U.S. goods. 

I have attached an appendix which contains summaries of five actual investments which are covered by the political-risk guarantee program. I think these specific examples of investments covered under the program will be of interest to you. 

(The appendix referred to follows:) APPENDIX-REPRESENTATIVE EXAMPLES OF POLITICAL RISK GUARANTEES 1. PHELPS DODGE COPPER PRODUCTS CORP., EL SALVADOR 

Investment: $600,000 equity, $300,000 technical assistance fees. 

Guarantees: Convertibility, $1,500,000; expropriation $1,300,000.

Phelps Dodge Copper Products Corp. has established a corporation under the laws of El Salvador for the first electrical wire and cable fabricating plant in the Central American common market area. The investor received 50 percent of the equity interest in the corporation for its $600,000 investment. The other 50 percent of the foreign concern's initial capital stock will be owned by the Institute Salvadoeno de Fomento Industial (Insafi). One-half of the concern's profits will be retained in El Salvador for use by Insafi in developing other industries. 

The investor will also furnish technical assistance, know-how, and personnel training in return for fees based on the net sales of the foreign enterprise. The benefits to El Salvador and the Central American area will result from the employment of approximately 100 local personnel in the first year of operation and more in later years, the use of local raw materials, the provision of electrical products to the Central American countries. 

2. CONTINENTAL GRAIN CO., MOROCCO 

Investment: $200,000. 

Guarantees: Convertibility, $200,000; expropriation, $200,000; WRI, $200,000.

Continental Grain Co., of New York City, has invested $200,000 for new shares of capital stock in Cellulose du Marc, S.A., in Rabat, Morocco. The funds will be used to acquire equipment to increase the production of wood pulp for papermaking from 25,000 to 36,000 metric tons per year. Most of the wood pulp will be

exported to France, England, and Holland to be used for the manufacture of high-grade paper. This has and will result in increased foreign exchange to the country.

The foreign concern owns large eucalyptus forests and the planting, care, cutting, and transportation of the trees requires the employment of approximately 1,000 workers. The increase in capacity will increase employment in the forest and in the plant. 

Investment: $127,597. 3. S. B. PENICK & CO., ECUADOR 

Guarantees: Expropriation, $175,000.

S. B. Penick & Co. started the cultivation of pyrethrum in Ecuador over 12 years ago. During these years it has increased the production and processing of pyrethrum flowers to the point where it now employs several thousand people and utilizes several thousand hectares of land which previously had been idle. 

The recent investment guarantee covers additional equity to expand the company's operation.

The dried flowers are used both for export and delivery to two local factories which process the flowers to make pyrethrum extract for insecticides. The dried flowers have been exported to, among other places, Argentina for the preservation of stored grains, and to England for experimental use. As Ecuador further develops agriculturally, it is estimated that the demand for insecticides and fungicides will reach 3,500 tons annually by 1970. 

Investment: $3,250,000. 

4. THE BORDEN CO., ARGENTINA 

Guarantees: Convertibility, $6,500,000.

The Borden Co. is investing $3,250,000 in shares of the common stock in Cia 

Casco, S.A.I.C. in Argentina. The foreign enterprise will construct new facilities to manufacture methanol and phenol molding compounds, basic materials for Argentina's rapidly expanding plastics industry and for other industrial activities. The present investment is the first stage in a plan to increase production of methanol. The current investment will allow the Argentine company to produce about 12,000 tons per year. Subsequent expansions look toward annual production of 33,000 tons by 1967. 

5. OLIN MATHIESON CHEMICAL CORP., INDIA 

Investment: $756,000. 

Guarantees: Convertibility, $1,512,000; expropriation, $1,512,000.

Olin Mathieson has subscribed an investment of $756,000 to obtain capital stock of Synbiotics Ltd., a pharmaceutical company located at Ahmedabad, India. 

Fifty-two percent of the foreign concern is owned by an Indian firm, which has manufactured and distributed fine chemicals for 50 years. The enterprise is licensed to manufacture, subdivide, use, and sell certain squibb pharmaceuticals and inorganic chemical preparations including tetracycline and streptomycin.

Synbiotics has purchased a small Indian firm which had a license for the manufacture of penicillin that was not being utilized. This production facility has been rehabilitated and expanded to enable India to meet its needs for penicillin.

An additional investment is contemplated to enable Synbiotics to purchase the essential equipment in the United States to provide for an increased production of tetracycline and amphotericin in India. 

These investments will assure an adequate supply of essential pharmaceutical and fine chemicals of local manufacture, thus, saving foreign exchange for India.

COVERAGE GREATER THAN INVESTMENT 

Senator WILLIAMS. May I ask a question in connection with these examples? I notice that your guarantees cover approximately double the amount of the investment. What does that mean? 

Mr. GAUD. On the political risk guarantee

The CHAIRMAN. Are you looking at the Phelps Dodge investment? 

Let us follow one and see if we can understand it. 

Senator WILLIAMS. Phelps Dodge; yes.

Mr. GAUD. The explanation of that is that we will issue a politicalrisk guarantee for the amount of the original investment plus earnings up to the equivalent of the face amount of the investment. The investment here in equity is $600,000, so we will cover that $600,000 plus potential earnings in an equivalent amount which brings you to $1.2 million. 

Senator GORE. You mean potential or actual? Do you guarantee that it will earn or do you guarantee the nonexpropriation of retained earnings?

Mr. GAUD. We guarantee that if they actually earn earnings up to the face amount of the original investment, we will guarantee that those earnings are not expropriated, that they may be paid in convertible currency; but they have to earn the money. 

Senator GORE. You used the word "potential" though, and I did not think it meant that. 

Mr. GAUD. Well, at the time you issue your guarantee, they are all potential. They are in futuro. 

Senator GORE. You do not guarantee a potential. You guarantee actual earnings realized and retained. 

Mr. GAUD. That is correct; if earned. 

Senator GORE. Then you did not mean "potential."

Mr. GAUD. I stand corrected. 

Senator LAUSCHE. Go back to Senator Williams' question, if you will, please. 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir.

We have here an investment of $600,000 in equity. We will guarantee for political risks that $600,000 plus $600,000 of earnings if earned. 

That makes $1.2 million. In addition, Phelps Dodge under this arrangement had a contract for technical assistance fees of $300,000. 

We guarantee that against expropriation or against not being collected. 

The CHAIRMAN. You mean that the country, El Salvador, is going to pay that?

Mr. GAUD. That is right, for management services and the like, so that the total that we guarantee in this case is $1.5 million, the maximum we could guarantee is $1.5 million. 

Now, this particular company chose to take out full coverage for convertibility. It did not choose to take out full coverage for expropriation. This is their option. 

Senator CASE. How long a term in time?

Mr. GAUD. Twenty years. The statute now limits the quarantees to 

20 years. We are asking this year that that restriction be lifted as to loans, not as to equity investments.

Senator CASE. So in the case of Phelps Dodge an equity investment- 

Mr. GAUD. Would be good for 20 years.

HOW DOES A GUARANTEE OPERATE? 

Senator CASE. I am not sure just what it means. Take convertibility. 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir?

Senator CASE. What does it relate to? Suppose they want to leave their money. 

Mr. GAUD. No problem. Suppose they want to withdraw some in the shape of dividends, or if this were a loan, it would be principal payments or interest payments. Convertibility would be important. 

Senator CASE. They would have the right, in other words, to bring back $1.5 million within 20 years, any time they want to, out of their investment. In effect, that is what it is. 

Mr. GAUD. If they get it out of their investment. 

Senator CASE. Yes, that is right. Of course, we know they made the investment of $600,000. We know that they rendered services to the extent of $300,000. You are only talking about $600,000 in any event. 

Mr. GAUD. That is right.

Senator CASE. If they want to sell this corporation next week, they can do so and you will be guaranteeing it. 

Mr. GAUD. That is right.

Senator WILLIAMS. Suppose they have earned this $600,000. I understand that they would have to earn $1.2 million because they only have 50 percent interest. This is only their percentage. 

Mr. GAUD. The total equity interest in this corporation is $1.2 million, and they own 50 percent of that. 

Senator WILLIAMS. In this company whether they own 50 percent or more, you are only insuring that portion of the earnings which is represented by their percentage of ownership. 

Mr. GAUD. That is right.

NO GUARANTEE AGAINST DEVALUATION 

Senator WILLIAMS. Suppose that they have this moving along, and they have earned the $600,000. They decide to leave it there for the time being. Naturally it would be deposited in the currency of the country where they are. Then they get a complete devaluation of that currency. Do you pay it off in the old valuation or are you guaranteeing it against the valuation at the time that they are operating? 

Mr. GAUD. There is no devaluation coverage. 

Senator WILLIAMS. In other words, they have $600,000 earnings insured which they have already actually earned as their portion of the investment. That is carried on deposit and they get a devaluation in which the value of the unit of currency in El Salvador is cut by half, you only owe them $300,000. 

Mr. GAUD. That is right. We do not guarantee that the currency will not be devalued. There is no maintenance of value provision. 

Senator WILLIAMS. They take that loss. 

Mr. GAUD. They take that risk.

The CHAIRMAN. Wait a minute, that has to be, though, in the form of currency. They would be very improvident to leave that kind of money in local currency. Of course their property stands there, and it is not devalued.

Mr. GAUD. They would be more likely to invest it. 

The CHAIRMAN. They would be very foolish to have this in a drawing account in a bank, would they not? They might have some. 

Senator WILLIAMS. They might have some. I just assume this, suppose that they had not drawn this money back? A lot of the companies do want to leave it down there because the moment they bring it back, it is subject to tax. 

The CHAIRMAN. But they do not like to leave it, I would think, in a savings account. They would have it in something, I would think, if they are good businessmen. 

Senator WILLIAMS. They could not very well deposit it in dollars down there. 

Mr. GAUD. No. 

Senator WILLIAMS. It would have to be in currency. 

Mr. GAUD. If they are prudent, they either bring their money back here, or they invest it down there. They certainly do not leave it in local currency.

The CHAIRMAN. They would have it in property which would not be affected.

Senator HICKENLOOPER. Suppose they invest it down there, and it is a bad investment, and they lose it. 

The CHAIRMAN. This guarantee does not cover it specifically. 

Mr. GAUD. That is their tough luck. 

That would be another investment.

EXTENDED RISK GUARANTEES TO DATE 

Mr. Chairman, I have here another statement. I said earlier that we have made three extended risk guarantees to date. 

The CHAIRMAN. Where are they? Are they in the appendix?

Mr. GAUD. No. I have copies of a paper listing these. There is one in Argentina, there is one in Colombia, and there is one in Somali. 

AID EXTENDED RISK GUARANTEES ISSUED UNDER THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT OF 1965 ARGENTINA-PASA PETROCHEMICALS. 

Date issued: October 11, 1963. 

Duration of guarantee: 10 years.

Total investment in project: $98,000,000. 

Amount of guaranteed investment: $15,500,000. 

Percentage of guaranteed investment covered: 50 percent. 

Maximum U.S. liability: $7,749,500. 

Guaranteed investors: U.S. institutional investors.

Project: The project consists of seven integrated petrochemical units near 

Rosario, Argentina, 230 miles northwest of Buenos Aires which will produce synthetic rubbers and associated chemicals using local raw materials. The foreign exchange savings to Argentina could be as high as $29 million annually, when the full project is in production. 

The owners are Continental Oil, Cities Service, U.S. Rubber, Fish International and Witco Chemical Co. Additional financing comes from the investors equity and other long-term debentures held by equipment suppliers. The 50 percent of the debenture not covered by extended risk is covered by specific risk guarantees.

COLOMBIA, CABOT CARBON BLACK Date issued: February 10, 1965. 

Duration of guarantee: 10 years.

Total investment in project: $3,800,000, being a Cabot equity of $1,600,000 and 

Colombian loans of $1,400,000 in addition to the guaranteed loan. 

Amount of guaranteed investment in project: $825,000 in loan. 

Percentage of guaranteed investment: 75 percent. 

Maximum U.S. liability: $618,750.

Guaranteed investor: Cabot Corp. 

Project: This project is the establishment of a Cabot subsidiary near Cartagena in Colombia to produce 15 million pounds per year of carbon black for existing tire factories. The foreign exchange savings to Colombia are estimated at $1.5 million annually, when the plant reaches full production. 

The extended risk guarantee of the loan is conditioned on the future offer of 10 percent of the share capital of the company to Colombian citizens. The 25 percent of the credit not covered by extended risk is covered by specific risk guarantees.

SOMALI REPUBLIC, SOMALI AMERICAN FISHING CO. 

Date issued: March 12, 1965. 

Duration of guarantee: 20 years. 

Total investment in project: $1,500,000. 

Amount of guaranteed investment: $222,320. 

Percentage of guaranteed investment covered: 50 percent.

Maximum U.S. liability: $111,160. 

Guaranteed investor: Quincy Market Cold Storage & Warehouse Co. 

Project: The project involves a tuna catching operation and a freezing plant at Ras Faluch on the north coast of Somalia. It is planned to process 5,000 tons of tuna per year for sale in Italy, which should earn $500,000 annually in additional foreign exchange for the Somali economy. Fifty percent of the equity is owned by Somalis.

The most pertinent consideration, as I see it, is how much of an effect, how much of an impact, on the balance of payments is it going to have if we continue with these present policies. 

Now, as far as the investment guarantee program is concerned, our best estimate is that in 1964, taking into account all the investment guarantees that we issued, taking into account the extent to which we were guaranteeing investments representing goods shipped from the United States rather than bought abroad, our best estimate is that the impact on the balance of payments was $50 million for the entire calendar year, for these programs which I have been testifying about this morning.

So the only question at issue, it seems to me, is whether it is worth $50 million a year balance of payments wise to continue these programs. Now the answer to that seems to me pretty easy, that it is.

You add on top of that a fee of 12 percent and before you know it you are at 6 percent or above. 

India cannot afford very many of those loans, and therefore we make direct loans to India under the AID program primarily. 

Now, Taiwan, nearer the other end of the scale, has sufficient foreign exchange reserves, and has a sufficiently good balance-of-payments position, so that she can borrow a lot more money on the kind of terms that you get if the capital is going in there under an investment guarantee program. Mr. GAUD. Let me say a word about why we are asking for this increase, and the sort of thing we are going to do with it. I will give you one or two examples.

EXAMPLE OF INDIAN INVESTMENT 

In India probably the most serious problem today is food. The 

Indians have come, as we see it, rather slowly to realize this and to do something about it-more particularly to do something about their fertilizer business, the production of fertilizer. Originally they had the notion that they would not allow any fertilizer plants in India unless they were in the public sector, and they would not let any private investment into the fertilizer business. 

Well, we broke that barrier a couple of years ago, and the California 

Chemical Co. and the International Minerals & Chemicals Co., both

U.S. firms, worked out an arrangement with the Indian Government to set up a fertilizer factory run by the Coramandel Co. They own 47 percent of it, and an Indian firm and the Indian public-no Indian Government money-own the balance of it. That was done in large part because we made two loans to this company. 

A year later or less, Allied Chemical went into another arrangement with an Indian firm and worked out arrangements for another fertilizer factory. Allied Chemical owns 32 percent, the Indians-no 

Indian Government money again-own 68 percent. This was made possible very largely by a Cooley loan. 

Now today, the Indians realize the importance of this fertilizer business, and a consortium of American companies-the two spokesmen are Mr. Bechtel from California and General Clay-are trying to work out arrangements with the Indians to set up four fertilizer factories and a refinery. 

Now, here is the $64 question. Are those loans to the extent that they are to cover the import of machinery and equipment into India which can only be bought with foreign exchange-are those loans to be made by AID in which case the U.S. Government would put up all the money in the first instance, or can we do a good part of this job with investment guarantees of private loans?

It seems clear to me, Senator, that we can do a lot of this job with investment guarantees. Indeed, it may not be necessary for these people to come to us for any loans whatsoever if we can give them investment guarantees.

Now, there is a specific example, as I see it, of where this program is going to make a tremendous contribution as far as India is concerned. 

The CHAIRMAN. Extended risk guarantee or specific guarantee? 

Mr. GAUD. Probably some of both. It will save the U.S. Government-it will be much cheaper for the U.S. Government to go into this project on a guarantee basis than on a loan basis. 

Senator GORE. I concur in your assessment here of all of the needs in India. I have had an opportunity to observe them in a limited way. 

The production of food for an adequate diet is the greatest. 

Mr. GAUD. Yes, sir. 

Senator GORE. And nothing can be more basic.

Mr. GAUD. No. 

Senator GORE. And much of their soil is so depleted of the necessary elements that its fertility, its production is low. Fertilizer is definitely and obviously an answer. I think this would be in one category.

AID COMMENTS ON TESTIMONY OF THE COMPTROLLER GENERAL 

The Agency for International Development agrees with the Comptroller General in the objective of improving, where needed, the financial management and operational control of the foreign assistance program and the need of reviews to assure that the program is being conducted within the basic purposes established by the Congress. In recognizing this need for reviews and evaluations the AID has for several years conducted internal audits and made evaluation studies of

the various programs of assistance being furnished under the Foreign Assistance Act. These audit reports and evaluation studies have materially assisted the responsible officials in effecting improvements in the management and operation of the programs. Similarly the reports submitted by the Comptroller General have been helpful in reviewing the programs of assistance and in evaluating the courses to be taken in the future to best achieve the objectives of the foreign assistance program. 

As the Comptroller General has indicated, the reports issued by his office, as well as the internal audit reports issued by the AID, do not, to any degree, constitute an overall evaluation of the total economic assistance program but are directed only to specific areas, usually where there is some previous indication of a need for improving operations and achieving greater efficiency. The effectively operated programs and successful achievements obtained by the foreign assistance program are not audited or reported with the result that only areas where recommendations for improvement are indicated become highlighted and publicized. 

It is necessary to recognize, as the Comptroller General has stated, the difficulties under which these programs are being administered. These programs are being conducted in developing countries where people unfortunately do not always have the degree of sophistication in management and operational techniques that is to be desired. AID programs will continue to stress the importance of effective management and assist in achieving better operational control. There will, however, be instances where reviews will indicate that additional improvements are needed. In this context the reports and recommendations of the 

Comptroller General's staff help to strengthen the effort the AID is making to improve the management of the economic assistance program. 

The following comments relate to the individual reviews referred to in the 

Comptroller General's testimony. 

UNNECESSARY DOLLAR COSTS INCURRED IN FINANCING PURCHASES OF COMMODITIES PRODUCED IN BRAZIL 

The objectives expressed in the report of utilizing, to the maximum possible extent, the excess local currencies owned by the United States are very worthwhile, and are being aggressively pursued. However, in the situation to which the report addresses itself, the action proposed would have run counter to an AID program of balance-of-payments support for Brazil. 

In each of the 3 fiscal years covered by the draft report it was in the interest of the United States to help meet Brazil's balance-of-payments deficits in the aggregate amount of $150 million. Because Brazil has been a friendly country receiving such assistance, it qualified under AID policies as a source country for the procurement of certain types of AID-financed commodities. With respect to the instances cited in the draft report, it would not have been consistent with the U.S. objectives to worsen Brazil's already precarious foreign exchange gap by denying export earnings at the same time we were helping Brazil with balance-of-payments support. The principal commodity involved, sugar, could have been freely sold by Brazil for dollars on the world market during the period covered by the GAO draft report. 

FAILURE EFFECTIVELY TO UTILIZE EXCESS U.S.-OWNED FOREIGN CURRENCIES TO PAY INTERNATIONAL AIR TRAVEL TICKET COSTS BEING PAID IN DOLLARS 

AID has taken steps to correct the situation disclosed in the report by issuing a circular airgram to all of AID oversea missions and on AID notice to the Washington area which includes participating agencies and training officers connected with the International Training Division. These notices reemphasize the necessity to utilize foreign currencies in payment for air travel costs to the maximum extent possible.

A recently issued uniform State-AID-USIA procedures and guides for foreign service travel also contains a complete section on the use of excess foreign currencies for travel and transportation.

In addition to issuing the directives referred to above, AID intends to give this operation continuing close supervision so as to achieve maximum compliance with the Agency directives.

LOSS OF INTEREST ON U.S.-OWNED FOREIGN CURRENCIES IN THE REPUBLIC OF CHINA (TAIWAN) 

Agreement has been reached with the Chinese Government for the transfer of U.S.-owned local currencies from non-interest-bearing accounts in the Bank of Taiwan to interest-bearing accounts in the branches of two American banks that have recently been established in Taiwan. 

AID has also developed procedures to extend this interest earning principle on a worldwide basis. The procedures are as follows: The Treasury Depart ment will provide the Department of State a statement of U.S.-owned foreign currencies, showing for each country the amounts held in interest-bearing and non-interest-bearing accounts, and recommend that the Department of State take action to conclude intergovernmental agreements with particular countries which will permit the United States to obtain interest on balances currently maintained on a non-interest-bearing basis; the Department of State will respond in writing to the Treasury Department that it either will undertake to accomplish the action recommended or that for foreign policy reasons it would not be in the best interest of the United States to pursue the matter further; AID and the Departments of State and Treasury will review this matter annually to assure that all U.S.-owned local currencies allocated to the Agency are in interestbearing accounts, or that the reasons for not depositing them in interest-bearing accounts are fully documented in writing. 

EXAMINATION OF ECONOMIC AND TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS FOR TURKEY, FISCAL YEARS 1958-62 

The report recommended that AID initiate, or encourage the Turkish Government to initiate a study to correct inefficiencies in the operations of the Zonguldak coal mines. AID in its relations with the Government of Turkey has for a long time accorded a high priority to reform of state economic enterprises, of which the Zonguldak coal mines are a part. Efforts toward this goal received impetus in the immediate post-revolutionary period when the new government set about investigating the operations of the state economic enterprises and exploring the prospects for reform. Experts were furnished to advise on overall reform and to study 12 of the enterprises, including TKI, which operates the Zonguldak mines. The principal recommendations of these advisers were later incorporated in the Turkish 5-year plan and satisfactory progress in implementing them has been made. In the operation of the Zonguldak mines, the labor force has been reduced by 3.500 over the last 2 years. production has increased and, in 1963. Zonguldak showed a profit of over $1 million. Turkish efforts are being closely followed by AID and by the OECD Consortium for assistance to Turkey.

INEFFECTIVE AND UNECONOMICAL ASPECTS OF ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE PROVIDED TO THE PHILIPPINE ISLANDS FOR DEVELOPMENT PURPOSES 

The concern that the Philippine Government has not contributed sufficiently to the support of certain projects is shared by AID. Contrary to the implications in the report, however. AID has taken action to persuade the Philippine 

Government to devote enough resources to permit effective maintenance and utilization of U.S. assistance after its delivery. Numerous official undertakings by the Philippine Government to this end are embodied in project agreements. 

The basic problem in the Philippines is not United States failure to plan for and obtain a commitment for local currency financing in advance. Rather, under the Philippine system executive agencies signed agreements in good faith and adequate funds are usually "appropriated." but inadequate revenues are collected to fund these appropriations and inadequate procedures and practices create problems in making use of available funds. The AID program has been directed at these fundamental problems for several years, particularly in tax and customs administration, civil rights, budgeting, management of financial and material resources, and maintenance of equipment and facilities. In 1962, in a further effort to solve this problem, AID gained Philippine adoption of a procedure under which the local currency component to finance new projects must be included in the Philippine national budget and deposited to a special fund prior to initiation of the project. 

The AID mission is aware of the peso support problem and has taken action to prevent similar problems from arising in future projects.

AID has stated that it is prepared to consider future loans only if the projects are supported adequately with local currency. 

INEFFECTIVE UTILIZATION OF EXCESS PERSONAL PROPERTY IN THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE PROGRAM 

The report concludes that AID personnel are not sufficiently aware of, nor sufficiently impressed with the importance of, the economic advantages of utilization of excess property. 

On April 13, 1964, the Administrator of AID directed a memorandum to various assistant administrators, titled, "Utilization of Excess Property in AID Program." That memorandum set forth positive policy guidance from the Administrator to strengthen areas cited as deficient in the January 7, 1964, report rendered by the Department of State's Inspector General of Foreign Assistance. 

It is significant that the Administrator's April 13 memorandum recognized the need for the same corrective action as now recommended in the GAO draft report. It is the Agency view that appropriate implementation by AID generally of the letter and the spirit of the Administrator's memorandum will satisfy the three major recommendations of the draft report. 

Specific examples of implementation of that policy guidance are found in the records of the Far East and Near East South Asia Bureaus of AID. On 

May 19, 1964, the Far East Bureau issued a circular message to Far East missions, requiring them to submit lists of all major equipment items needed for implementation of their fiscal year 1965 projects. Of 836 major items listed, excess procurement has been substituted for new in 54 instances. Continuing screening, both within AID/W and in the field, can result in additional substitutions being made. The Near East South Asia Bureau established a procedure to insure that proposed AID loans, which would later involve commodity procurement be reviewed from the outset of their consideration to determine whether or not the commodity procurement element was generally susceptible, in some degree, to satisfaction through the use of excess property. If deemed to be so, a clause is inserted in the loan agreement when prepared, authorizing and encouraging maximum consideration for the use of excess property as substitutes for new procurement. This reviewing practice has subsequently extended to include all AID loans. 

QUESTIONABLE JUSTIFICATION FOR BUDGETARY SUPPORT LOANS MADE TO THE GOVERNMENT OF ECUADOR 

The GAO suggests that the two budget support loans could have been reduced if, as a precondition to loan disbursement, the Government of Ecuador had been required to make full use of its internal borrowing authority from the Central Bank. At the time these loans were negotiated, the Government of 

Ecuador's requirements were estimated. It was concluded that the Government of Ecuador would have to borrow from the Central Bank up to the maximum limit approved by the IMF as being noninflationary and that the amounts of the loans were additional requirements above the IMF ceiling. For this reason the suggested precondition to loan disbursement was not included in the loan agreements. This suggestion is a useful one and will be followed in future transactions.

The GAO questions whether the loans could not have been substantially reduced and correctly points out that as of December 31, 1961, and September 30, 1962, the Government of Ecuador and the public sector agencies owed the Central Bank $4.3 million and $1.6 million less than the credit ceilings approved by the IMF. The Agency believes there are two relevant considerations that were not brought to the GAO's attention. First, since the Ecuadoran fiscal year at that time effectively ended on March 31 rather than December 31, certain disbursements under the Government of Ecuador budget year were made during the first 3 months of the following calendar year. Second, there had been in the years prior to these loans (and still is) a heavy drain on all sources of internal borrowing during the first half of each year. The reason for this heavy drain is that revenue yields traditionally are lower than they are in the latter half of the year. Because of these considerations the magnitude of the unused IMF credit ceiling should have been determined as of the end of the periods of low revenue yield. If that had been done, April 

30, 1962, and May 31, 1963, would have been used, and on these dates the

9. The unused credit ceiling limits stood at $0.7 and $0.8 million, respectively. 

Agency agrees the loans could have been reduced by these amounts.

DISTINCTION BETWEEN PROGRAM AND PROJECT LOANS 

Would you distinguish, Mr. Bell, your understanding as to the differences between project and program loans under the Alliance for 

Progress title of the act? 

 The distinction is not an absolutely sharp line, but, in general, a project loan is one which is made for the facilities, that is, for the equipment, the commodities, the engineering services related to the construction or performance of a specific limited project such as construction of a single plant or a power station or highway or port, or the provision of funds for a credit institution such as a home loan bank or an agricultural credit institution. 

A program loan normally provides for a broader financing of equipment and supplies-materials not related to a particular project or ordinarily to a particular set of projects--but instead for a broader import or group of imports or a broader economic purpose. 44-834-65- ——36

554 

44 Senator, as you know, we make project loans quite widely. We make program loans in a very limited number of cases, only to six or eight countries.

The reason is that it is obviously a kind of loan which, if it were not related to a very tight set of economic policies, could result in our simply financing part of a country's import burden without making sure that that was contributing to a solid, rapid economic progress toward self-support. 

Therefore, we make program loans only in those cases where they fit into a complete set of economic policies affecting the use of the country's own resources and all the external resources that it can get. 

Therefore the complete flow of resources is before us when we make a decision of this kind, and we are confident that this particular group of economic inputs are part of a program which is going to move that country as rapidly as possible toward economic progress and self-support. Under these circumstances we have found that this kind of loan is extremely valuable because it provides a flow of materials and equipment, construction items, investment goods, which are extremely helpful in stimulating the private sector. This was the case in Pakistan, India, Brazil, and other places. For this reason, we regard it as an especially valuable technique for making sure that we are not putting our money simply into large public sector projects, but instead are contributing to a much more broadly based and more widely dynamic private economy.

DISTINCTION BETWEEN PROGRAM LOANS AND SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE COMMODITY PROGRAMS 

Senator MORSE. How do these loans differ from commodity loan programs financed under supporting assistance?

Mr. BELL. The supporting assistance commodity programs traditionally were related to a different objective. They were related to the objective of maintaining a military or defense capability in a country. A calculation that used to underlie the supporting assistance requirement was how much military force of that country was it in the interests of the United States to maintain, what economic requirements did that imply, and what, therefore, did we need to provide to fill an import gap or a budget gap, as the case might be. 

Now, over the last several years, as this committee knows, we have been shifting away from that concept of assistance. We have eliminated supporting assistance in country after country, because it was essentially when one looked at it that way, it was a "maintenance" process, and we don't want to be in a "maintenance" process, we want to be in a development process to get a country on its feet, and then to get out.

We have dropped 14 countries to which we were providing supporting assistance 5 years ago. There is a very limited group of countries receiving supporting assistance now. For fiscal year 1966, some 88 percent of the supporting assistance request will go to only four countries, Vietnam, Laos, Korea, and Jordan, and there are perhaps as many as half a dozen more in which we expect to use supporting assistance to a small extent.

1 1 Now as we have made this shift from a supporting assistance concept to a development concept in country after country, we have found that we can use supporting assistance in some cases in a similar manner to what I have described, but this is a rare case. This is the case right now in Korea. Over the last 2 or 3 years we have been working with the Koreans to try to persuade them to improve their policies so that they are engaged in a full-scale development effort. 

They have worked out with an IMF stabilization program under which IMF just last week, as I remember it, maybe the week before, gave them a standby, as they do when they are satisfied that a country's financial and monetary policies make sense. [Deleted.] 

This is not, however the standard or normal pattern for using supporting assistance in commodity support. More typical under supporting assistance is the Vietnamese or Lao situation in which supporting assistance is very important and very valuable but in which none of us would claim that it is contributing to a very rapid progress toward economic independence [deleted]. 

PROJECT LOANS VERSUS PROGRAM LOANS 

Senator MORSE. It is said by some critics of the program loan in contrast to the project loans that the program loan tends to underwrite an existing regime in a country which even at the time may be an undesirable regime or which may turn into an undesirable regime, while a project loan is related not to a government but to a dam or a refinery or a specific capital investment. Therefore, it is better to relate your loans to projects in the first place and, in the second place, it gives you more a direct check on the expenditure of the funds than if you turned the money over to a government through a program loan. 

Mr. BELL. Two points on that, Senator. First, whatever type of loan we provide, whether it is a project loan or even a technical assistance project or a program loan, we are faced with the question: Are we, by taking this action, contributing to the strengthening of policies or of a government which we don't want to strengthen or support? 

This is a general problem and it is a very vexing one and one of the most significant that the United States faces in handling an aid program in any country. 

Our general experience has been that in some instances, particularly in the past, we have gotten ourselves publicly committed to a government or a set of policies we didn't like. 

I think we have learned better in recent years. For example, the experience under the Alliance for Progress shows that it has been possible for us to commit ourselves to progress in Latin America without committing ourselves to any particular government. 

Even in Brazil and Chile today, while we are supporting strongly the existing governments, I believe the situation is clear that we are supporting them because they are progressive and working toward objectives that we think are appropriate and necessary, and not because of the particular individuals who are involved. We could be just as strongly in support of an alternative government so long as it

- 

pro- was headed in the same direction and was committed to the same p gram of reform, stabilization, and progress. 

Now, I don't think, sir, there is very much difference between project and program lending in this context. 

Suppose there were a major project in a country, and the government of that country wanted us to support it because it was symbolic or would be symbolic of our support for that government, we would have to face this issue and we might very well decide not to do it. 

The fact that it was a project loan would not protect us from the question of whether we were, by making the loan, tying ourselves or relating ourselves to policies or individuals that we did not want to be related to.

EFFECTIVE USE OF PROGRAM LOANS 

Conversely, we have used program loans very effectively, I think, in three cases in Latin America-Colombia, Brazil, and Chile-and I do not think that we have, by so doing, found ourselves trapped in supporting a government we didn't want to support. Quite the contrary, in the Brazilian case, you will recall in 1963, we made the kind of agreement with Santiago Dantas, then Finance Minister, which represented a strong and complete economic program on their part, and we were prepared to make program loans in support of it. 

When he was not backed by his own Government and that policy was not followed through, we withheld the program loan, and did not proceed to make the funds available to the Goulart government. 

Indeed, in that case, the program loan proved to be a more flexible instrument. If we had committed ourselves to projects for the same amount of money we might well have felt ourselves so bound to the particular construction effort that it would have been hard for us to back out. But the program loan is a more flexible instrument which we typically release quarterly in these Latin American situations. As soon as it became evident that the Goulart government was not following through, we stopped immediately further action on that loan. 

This was a means of making it plain that we did not agree with and support that particular government of Brazil and its current policies. 

We would have been prepared to support them had they followed a more sensible policy. So that I think that this is the way that we see it; namely, that the program loan is not a difficult instrument to handle from the point of view of this very serious question, which is a real question we always do have to look at. 

Senator MORSE. Let me dwell on this just a moment longer. In connection with program loans, am I to understand that when we enter into a program loan agreement with government X you do it on an installment basis-I think that you used the word "quarterly"in the sense that the loan is to be made available on a time installment? If you find that the government is following a course of action that you think is inimical not only to the loan objectives but inimical to the United States itself outside of the loan, could you hold it up? 

Mr. BELL. I would add two qualifications, Senator.

Firstly, in all cases we relate these program loans to programs of and commitments of self-help and reform which the countries themselves undertake. We do not necessarily relate them to-you used the phrase "broader U.S. interests." I want to qualify and make plain

that we normally do not relate them to political relationships, that is, a broader framework. The question of political relationships is a broader framework, within which all of our aid, of course, has to fit. 

But the program loan is normally related to a set of fiscal policies, balance-of-payments policies, priority plans for investments, a development program in the full-scale economic sense and, as I indicated, this can be done in only six or eight cases at the present time.

The second qualification is that in the Latin American instances, Brazil, Chile, and Colombia, in each case we have used this system of quarterly reviews and disbursements. We have not done that in the Indian, Pakistan, Turkey, Tunisia cases which I think are the only other cases there are. 

I am not sure we shouldn't. But we have not done so thus far. 

We have felt that India and Pakistan particularly and Turkey in the last 2 or 3 years, and Tunisia [deleted] have not had the very severe and instant problem of inflation. They have not had to make as much of a reform in their own policies and, therefore, we have felt up to now that we have been able to make a basic agreement that could run for a year.

Now, I repeat we have been quite impressed with the effectiveness of the Latin American technique. [Deleted.] 

Whether we should use the quarterly system in other parts of the world we haven't yet decided.

HYPOTHETICAL CASE 

Senator MORSE. To be sure I understand your policy, discuss with me this hypothetical case. You make a program loan to country Y and you pay it in the first quarter. If you notice in beginning of the second quarter that the government is moving further and further to the left and you became satisfied that the government is going to go communistic, do you then reserve your right under your program loan policy to give them no more money after the second quarter? 

Mr. BELL. It is a question we haven't faced in exactly that form and I will have to give you a hypothetical answer. 

Senator MORSE. I know.

Mr. BELL. All of our loans, and particularly our program_loans, carry some sort of general phrase, the exact legal language I have forgotten, that we can suspend this at any time in the interests of the United States-in just about as broad language as that—and therefore, my answer to you is that we would not only have the ability under the terms of the loan to hold it up, but the policy question would depend on the exact circumstances of the case. [Deleted.] 

Senator MORSE. I do not imply that I think you should follow this course of action, but to lay out in this record an evaluation of criticisms from the two types of critics of your program holding completely opposite views, I raise this. One group of critics says that foreign aid is used by the United States in many instances to influence the development of a type of government that the United States thinks ought to be developed, pro-Western, pro-United States, and the United States puts aid money in to develop that type of government.

Critics on the other side say that the United States should not use aid to influence the internal politics of a country, and they claim that the United States does it time and time again and, therefore, they oppose aid.

CRITERIA FOR GIVING ASSISTANCE 

My question is in the administration of our foreign aid program, has the State Department and the AID administration taken into account, as one of the criteria that we apply in granting aid, the internal politics of a country and guaranteed aid or made loans in order to influence the governmental policy? 

Mr. BELL. It is a very important question, it is not a simple one to respond to. Let me say two or three things about it. 

Senator MORSE. I understand. 

Mr. BELL. First of all, we are quite clearly and definitely seeking to encourage policies which will lead toward economic and social progress in societies that are essentially built around the concept of free institutions, open societies, pluralistic societies. 

We are necessarily starting from where each country is. They all have different backgrounds and all have different historical roots. 

We are normally working with groups, individuals, within a government. Normally there is an internal battle going on in a country where we are working, and normally we would prefer to see one set of policies adopted rather than another. We will be interested in policies leading toward stability in an inflation sense, toward economic development, toward a broader based democracy, and so on. 

Now, the instruments we are using through the AID program are not directly related to the political process in the country in question. 

We can and do bring quite a few people to this country who see, incidental to their training in a technical field, something of what our society is like, and typically when they go home they are interested in trying to move their society in a similar direction. 

We can and do contribute to the development of broader based institutions in the country. 

For example, we are contributing very strongly right now as much as we can to the development of savings and loan associations, co-ops of various kinds in Latin America because we believe these will have very valuable political effects as well as good economic effects. 

People who run co-ops, who learn to sit of boards of directors, to choose managers, to dispose of group funds and so on are learning something that is important politically. 

Now, there are plainly important ways in which we can communicate what we mean, what we are interested in supporting, what we mean by economic and social progress and the kind of projects we are interested in supporting, and the kind of program we might be willing to support with a program loan. 

In this sense our attitude is known, and the political forces within a country are working with the knowledge of our attitude. Quite plainly, for example, the Government of Indonesia knew for the last 2 or 3 years we were not prepared to provide economic assistance unless they were prepared to undertake a serious attack on their own inflation and on their other economic difficulties. [Deleted.]

Now, there are also cases where we get to the point of making a decision or a judgment as to whether a particular decision on a loan usually, normally a project loan, or a technical assistance project even will strengthen the chances for a particular man or party to be elected or a particular policy to be adopted, and sometimes that fact is weighed, and it does weigh, heavily in the decision, which is the precise point that you were asking about. 

I think myself this is a very risky kind of thing to do. It is, by no means, the standard of the decisions that are taken in the AID program. 

I do not think it is necessarily wrong. I do not think it is necessarily wrong to allow such an immediate decision to weigh in the balance, but I think it is more important for the United States to be clear that it desires to support economic and social progress in that country, and the movement toward free institutions rather than that it be known as supporting a particular party or a particular individual, and we try to act that way. 

Senator MORSE. This has been helpful. 

AID TO "QUESTIONABLE" REGIMES 

I want to move from a hypothetical to a few specific cases. It is said by some critics that the United States has used its AID program to shore up and support some very questionable regimes [deleted]. 

Some also point out that under the Geneva accords we had no right at all to involve ourselves in the establishment of a government in Vietnam, which Dulles obviously did when we set up the Diem government.

The Geneva accords on the truce line provided for an election in 1956, which we did our best to prevent. Therefore, we used aid in 

Vietnam to influence the type of government that was set up. 

Irrespective of the rightness or wrongness of it, my question is, what is your defense of the AID program to these governments which, in the instances I mentioned, are anything but democratic governments? [Deleted.] 

Mr. BELL. Evidence of what I was saying earlier about working with economic instruments which have only a limited and indirect effect, but within those limits we certainly try to help the groups and forces which are, from our point of view, progressive, democratic, and reform minded. [Deleted.] 

The way it looks to me sitting at my desk is that most of the things we are doing, most of the time, certainly most of the money, is involved in situations where this is not in issue. 

In India, for example, we are not involved; the Indian political evolution has been moving along. We generally approve of it, but we have not had anything to do with it, and our aid is not directly connected with it. 

The same is true in Pakistan, the same is true in Turkey, in Nigeria, in Brazil. We did not have anything to do with the Castelo Branco regime coming in.

So the bulk of the situations that cross my desk, and the bulk of our funds are used in ways that are not directly related to political issues, but there are cases in which these political matters are very much involved. [Deleted.] Wive

END-USE CONTROLS 

Senator MORSE. Mr. Bell, what are the checks that AID imposes. to prevent AID money from being siphoned off for corrupt purposes, such as making wealthy men out of generals in South Korea, where we have heard many criticisms of misuse of AID funds, as well as in Vietnam and other trouble spots of the world? What do you do to assure that, for want of a better term, the money is not stolen? 

Mr. BELL. The first and most important point, Senator, is that except, with very rare and unusual exceptions, we do not provide money to anybody. We provide goods. The money is spent, as you know, under today's system, 85 percent or better in the United States for specific commodities, products, and services. 

Senator MORSE. I will save time if I interrupt at this point. They do not take the money, but they take the goods and sell them in the black market and make money that way. 

Mr. BELL. Therefore, our checks are primarily concerned with making sure that the products and goods and services go where they are supposed to go, and are used for the purposes they are supposed to be used for. We have, internally, a very careful, quite elaborate, program of auditing and end-use checks on exactly that question. 

We have in each of our major missions auditors in the mission whose job is, in part, the one you just cited. Furthermore, we have a set of inspectors who travel and whose job it is to follow up any hint or suggestion of graft or corruption we get from anywhere, a local country, via an American citizen who saw something suspicious, or whatever.

Then outside of AID, there is Mr. Mansfield, the inspector general, who reports to the Secretary of State, not to me, and he has people continually traveling.

There is the GAO system, and they have teams at work all the time around the world, and there are, of course, congressional committee staffs who travel and who are alert to this sort of thing. 

I think the most difficult problem, in my observation, is the case in which we are financing, as we try to do through private trade; that is to say, we are making financing available for something that is supposed to be handled through a private importer in the country in question, and a private exporter in the United States, and to follow those transactions we require thorough documentation, exactly what the product and goods were that were bought, the price that they were bought at, the shipping costs, the commissions, if any, that were paid, the price level.

We require competitive bidding, demonstration that the price was competitive, and these are all followed up. We have various instances in which we have spotted something irregular and have brought it to the attention of the Justice Department, and the people in question have been prosecuted. 

We also have a continuing flow of cases in which items were improperly charged to AID financing in which we placed a claim against the government of the country in question, and are constantly and continually recovering funds that were improperly applied.

Now, none of this is 1,000 percent sure. But my observation is that the system has been getting steadily better. I have considerable confidence in it now. 

We have not had, in the last couple of years, any evidence whatever of anything that reflected a major leak or a major drain. 

Now, we could be wrong, but our system strikes me as quite good, and neither Mr. Mansfield nor the GAO has identified any major difficulty with it. They are continually identifying, and we are continually following up, on important points where something has gone awry or where we need to tighten our system, and we are. I, personally, have insisted that these matters be handled in a way that I am involved, so that people in the agency know that I am concerned when Ken Mansfield or the Comptroller General finds something that we should have found and should have corrected before it ever came to their attention. That is a general answer, sir. [Deleted.]

TRANSFERS BETWEEN ECONOMIC AND MILITARY AID 

Senator CARLSON. One other point. It concerned me when you stated-and I believe you did this past year you have been able to transfer funds of military aid from one country to another when you needed them in Vietnam.

If you can do that, can you do it also for economic aid? 

Mr. BELL. Well, the system in both cases, Senator, has been, since the beginning as far as I am aware, to present to the Congress a request for authorization and appropriation of a certain amount of money justified by showing a plan to justify what purposes, what country, and so forth. It has also been the practice from the beginning within appropriations, to recognize that there would be changes in the situation during the year to come, the future year, and to permit the President authority to reprogram. So where he planned to use a certain amount of money for X country, if he found the money was more needed in Vietnam he had authority to put it into Vietnam. 

Now, so far as transfer between appropriations is concerned there always has been some limit on that but nevertheless there is an authority within limits and on certain finding to do that, too. That is what I had in mind. We anticipate quite honestly and properly what we planned to use the money for, and then under the way the law is written, we are required to and do report during the year the changes, if any, that are made to respond to changes in the world situation.

ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS LOAN FUNDS TO ENCOURAGE ECONOMIC DEVELOP- MENT THROUGH PRIVATE ENTERPRISE 

Mr. Bell, the last sentence of section 251 requires at least 50 percent of Alliance for Progress loan funds to be used to encourage economic development through private enterprise. 

Can you tell the committee what percentage has, in fact, been used?

Mr. BELL. A much larger percentage than that, Senator. There have been some problems of definition about that. We have understood that to mean funds which have gone to support the development of the private sector in the Latin American countries. That is to say, loans directly to private businesses, loans to financial institutions established to make loans and to otherwise support the development of the private sector businesses or individual farmers or homeowners or savings and loan associations or co-ops; also loans-our program loans, as I indicated, are primarily to finance equipment, materials, supplies going to private hands and intended for private use in the Latin American countries.

Now, these, I think, are all quite clear elements of the definition, and they add up to much more than 50 percent. However, it is also true that loans to help expand power production, to help expand transportation, to help build ports, all of these are obviously necessary

elements to the development, and expansion of private business activity. If you include those, the loans we make for those purposes, we actually come up to a percentage, I think it is well over 90 percent, as I recall it. 

Now, I repeat, you can draw your definitions in various ways, but that is about the story, sir. 

Senator MORSE. I am glad to have that.

WHO DECIDES ON WHAT PROGRAMS FOR A COUNTRY? 

One of my contentions, Mr. Bell, is that Congress has lost control of the foreign aid program. In fact, we have given to the AID administration, to the Department of State, Department of Agriculture, Department of Defense, blanket control to run programs as they see fit. I am bothered about who is in charge in the executive branch of the Government. Where does the power lie to determine whether country X has (1) a development loan program; (2) a military assistance program; (3) a food-for-peace program; (4) a Peace Corps; (5) a World Bank or IDA or United Nations technical assistance program, insofar as the United States can influence that? 

Mr. BELL. The first several, that is to say the development loan program, the military assistance program, food-for-peace program, and Peace Corps program, the answer is essentially the Secretary of State, operating, however, in slightly different ways for each of those. 

For the first two my office is the control point. For the third—well, I beg your pardon, my office is the control point for food for peace as well as military assistance and development assistance. 

Regarding the Peace Corps, Mr. Shriver, of course; reports directly to Secretary Rusk. I am not involved in the decision as to whether there shall be a Peace Corps program in any particular country. 

So far as I am aware of how that process works, Mr. Shriver makes his recommendation to Secretary Rusk who reviews them and makes a decision one way or the other. 

The international agencies you speak of, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the World Bank, and its subsidiary, the IDA, there is an American, a U.S. executive director who, in recent years has been the Assistant Secretary of the Treasury for 

International Affairs.

The Secretary of the Treasury takes the formal position for the United States. Before doing so, however, my office is consulted and does express itself. We express ourselves and indicate, sometimes quite strongly through the U.S. executive director, that we oppose or would like to prevent, would like to avoid a loan to a particular country under particular circumstances. 

These matters are matters of some delicacy, obviously. These are international bodies, but the United States has a very strong weight in the World Bank and, of course, we have a majority or veto power in effect, in the Inter-American Development Bank. We have used our authority in both banks when the situation seemed to warrant it, and the State Department and AID have been involved in all instances. 44-834-65-37

IMPORTANCE OF CONGRESSIONAL CHECKS 

Senator MORSE. As I have indicated so many times in the last 2 years, I am greatly concerned about the delegating of authority by the Congress to the executive branch of Government in this and many other fields, but I will devote my attention to this. 

I think of the blanket authority that the Congress has given the executive branch of Government in the field of aid and the retention of the checks-and I highly approve of the retention of those-in domestic aid, and then I think of the troubles that delegations from Northwest States have had in recent months in getting both the execuive branch of the Government and Congress to act on this shocking disaster situation in the Northwest which the congressional committees, I say most respectfully, and the Bureau of the Budget haven't faced up to. Our delegations are told, "You have to go through these various steps and checks." I would only that the Senators and the 

Representatives, on those committees and the executive branch of Government answer my mail for me. You cannot justify those checks domestically and have people in my State pointing out how unchecked our policies are in regard to foreign aid as far as Congress is concerned.

ADMINISTRATION OF PUBLIC LAW 480 

With respect to Public Law 480 the situation is not so clear. I quite agree it would be better were the Public Law authority placed in the Secretary of State rather Agriculture. But every time this matter has been raised with the relevant congressional leaders, it has been made plain there would be tremendous opposition in the Congress to any such change. This, I recall very distinctly, was considered in the early days of the Kennedy administration when the extent of centralization was stepped up when AID was established-in consideration of exactly the points the Senator is making-when the Development Loan Fund and then ICA were consolidated so you have technical and capital assistance in the same agency, when the guarantee investment and Cooley loans were taken out of Export-Import Bank and placed in AID again to centralize responsibilities and have an agency which would be more responsible for a larger area of the 

American aid effort. 

At that time it was the question was raised whether it would also be feasible and desirable to place the authority, basic authority, for Public Law 480 in the Secretary of State. It was felt that this would not be acceptable to the Congress. 

I don't know whether that decision was right, but that is a consideration of very great magnitude that is involved. 

Assuming that that is the case or that it might be the case, then the question was, How can we be sure that the resources made available under Public Law 480 do contribute to a consolidated and sensible and appropriately sized American assistance program in an aidreceiving country?

We certainly don't want the Secretary of Agriculture putting in a volume of resources unrelated to the rest of American aid effort, and that point, I do believe, is quite satisfactorily handled by the interagency machinery which does exist. There is no case in which a Public Law 480 program is approved unless I am satisfied with it, again speaking for the Secretary of State, and there are many cases in which there are discussions between Secretary Freeman and myself in which we are discussing what is the right solution to a series of possibly conflicting interests, the American agricultural interests, the AID interests, the political interests, and other interests that may be involved.

So that, while the authority is in the Secretary of Agriculture, he exercises it in consultation with me, and we have not had difficulty in agreeing on the logical outcome and I feel satisfied that we are using our Public Law 480 resources in a combined American aid program that does make sense. 

It is not only at our end of the avenue, of course, but up here as well, that it is difficult to make sure of that and to bring it together because, of course, it is handled by a different committee than this one. 

ADMINISTRATION OF PEACE CORPS 

Now, with respect to the Peace Corps, at the time the Peace Corps was originally established there were a number of people in the executive branch-I was Budget Director at the time and I rather leaned this way, I must say who thought that it would be best to have the

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, Peace Corps as sort of an independent unit within the Agency for International Development. This was not done. It was not done, in part, to make sure that the Peace Corps had the drive and the esprit and the elan that would come from its being a quasi-independent organization.

Certainly, I believe that the results do make a strong case for the wisdom of having the Peace Corps as independent as it has been. 

There has been an enormous spirit in that organization which I think would have been largely diluted had they been part of the AID. 

We have lost something in the process. We have had some difficulty, which I think is now largely overcome but not completely, of making sure that the Peace Corps volunteers in various countries around the world were contributing to the maximum extent to projects and purposes which the United States had in that country, and where they could effectively be related to AID program. So today we have a lot of programs now around the world in which Peace Corps volunteers are working and there are also AID resources, frequently of a material nature.

For example, in Ethiopia, the Peace Corps volunteers are teaching in the high schools and AID is deeply involved in providing textbooks for those same high schools and we are working together intimately to achieve the best combined result. 

I think there is still some improvement in coordination needed in that field.
