1. AID TO INDONESIA, UAR, AND VIETNAM AID TO INDONESIA 

From its inception in 1945, aid to Indonesia has been primarily designed to help a new and important nation achieve economic viability and prevent or inhibit a Communist takeover. During the period 1945-50, the U.S. Government, through the Marshall plan and other means lent the Government of the Netherlands $70 million and gave some $60 million in grants for use in Indonesia. 

Indonesian independence was recognized in 1949, and in 1950 an economic cooperation agreement was signed between the U.S. Government and Indonesia. 

Under this agreement, the United States began providing technical assistance, concentrated in agriculture, industry, health, education, and internal security. 

During the period 1950-61, technical assistance and other ICA programs amounted to about $150 million; Public Law 480 title I sales totaled nearly $170 million in the same period, and approximately $7 million surplus commodities were distributed through voluntary relief agencies. Export-Import Bank loans during the 1950-61 period totaled over $160 million for capital projects, such as cement and fertilizer plants, and transportation equipment, airplanes, locomotives, and trucks. Three DLF loans also were made in this period totaling

$11.6 million to improve transportation facilities. Military assistance amounting to $60 million during that period provided equipment for the Indonesian Army and Navy and training in the United States. 

In 1961, the United States took an important step toward establishing better relations with Indonesia. President Kennedy met with President Sukarno in 

April 1961, and sent an economic survey team to Indonesia. Meantime, Indonesia's balance-of-payments position took a sharp turn for the worse, and the pace of economic deterioration accelerated. Indonesian preparations for military campaign to annex West New Guinea by force were a major factor in this deterioration. During the same period, the U.S.S.R. and its satellites sharply increased their programs of economic and military assistance. 

The peaceful solution of the West New Guinea crisis in August 1962 and a subsequent revival of Indonesian interest in economic stabilization and development provided the basis for harmonious relations and expanded economic cooperation between the United States and Indonesia. The flow of U.S. assistance both economic as well as military was stepped up and reached a peak of $136 million in fiscal year 1963, compared with $40 million in 1961. The technical assistance activities accounted for $18.4 million and the balance consisted of a $16.9 million loan for raw materials and industrial spare parts, $86.4 million for surplus agricultural commodities to alleviate shortages of food and fiber, and $13.9 million for military assistance.

In the spring and summer of 1963, a serious effort was made to launch a large scale stabilization program in Indonesia through a consortium of western nations working with the International Monetary Fund. 

In September 1963, Indonesia proclaimed a policy of hostile "confrontation" against Malaysia, invalidating the trade and fiscal assumptions on which the stabilization program was based. This policy necessitated substantial readjustments in our aid programs in Indonesia, which we began to put into effect within a few days of its proclamation. At the same time, it offered the Communists a further opportunity to extend their subversion. It was determined, accordingly, that those forms of aid which might tend to encourage or support confrontation would be terminated, while those related to the training of Indonesia's future leadership, eradication of malaria, and relief programs would be continued under close surveillance. 

Since September 1963, our aid activities in Indonesia have been restricted to preexisting programs in the field of technical assistance. No new commitments of financial support and no Public Law 480 agreements have been made since that time.

During the current fiscal year, we have been continuing only existing programs in technical training, university affiliations, and malaria eradication. There have been no Public Law 480 title I deliveries. Public Law 480 food donations to U.S. and international charitable organizations working in Indonesia were continued. AID technical cooperation programs have been successively restricted, as a consequence of the deteriorating prospects for meaningful cooperation. Obligation of fiscal year 1965 technical cooperation funds has been limited to a minimum of costs in ongoing programs primarily for U.S. technicians and participant training. A total of $1.9 million had been obligated as of 

March 31, 1965. Most activities other than university affiliations and training of participants have been terminated and the U.S. staff is being withdrawn.

UNITED STATES AID TO THE UNITED ARAB REPUBLIC (EGYPT) 

During the years 1952 to 1956 the point IV program consisted of such elements as agricultural development, transportation and communications, industrial development, health, education, public administration, community development, and housing. One of the more outstanding projects of this period was EARIS (Egyptian American Rural Improvement Service), which was begun in 1953 to help the United Arab Republic with a pilot project to reclaim land in northern Egypt for settlement of landless families. 

Relations between the United States and the United Arab Republic, which were cordial from 1952 to 1954, sharply deteriorated in 1955. Following the outbreak of hostilities in 1956, the U.S. aid mission was withdrawn and the program suspended. 

Assistance was resumed late in 1958, in an atmosphere of improving relations, with a sale of wheat for Egyptian pounds (title I, Public Law 480). The U.S. aid mission was reconstituted in March 1959. Since that time the following development loans have been authorized:

AID TO VIETNAM 

Our aid program in Vietnam has changed throughout the years to respond to the changing political and economic scene. The partition of the country in 

1954 left the new Republic of Vietnam facing a major task of reconstructing an economy devastated by World War II and the Indo-Chinese war. This task was further complicated by the influx of upward of 900,000 refugees from the north. A major feature of our program at that time was a large commercial import program designed to keep the economy operating and to combat inflationary pressures that threatened and help rehabilitate the country. By the end of 1957 the inflationary and refugee crisis had ended; the United States reduced the volume of aid for commercial imports and in 1959-60 the program was put on a balance-of-payments criteria rather than budgetary support. The aid level continued to fall for the next few years. 

Other major features of the program were institutional development, technical assistance, and expansion of private industry. Educational and health systems were reinforced. The National Institute for Administration was developed to train better Government administrators. A series of vocational schools were established. Teacher training was expanded and upgraded. The number of children enrolled in elementary school has tripled since 1954. Hospitals, clinics, and health stations have been greatly expanded in number and upgraded. Cooperatives and agricultural credit have also received a great deal of attention and support. AID has assisted the establishment of over 700 medium and small industries in Vietnam.

In 1962 with the renewed and intensified Vietcong insurgency activity, our aid rose to support the Government of Vietnam's resolve to counter the military and civil insurgency.

Today the program represents an integrated counterinsurgency effort designed to assist the nationwide pacification plan. 

Particular emphasis during fiscal year 1966 will be given to rural development within the counterinsurgency program, encouraging domestic private industry, needs of the urban population, and further development of crucially needed national and local public administrators. All programs are geared to specific needs of the war effort. 

The fiscal year 1966 program contains three major elements: (1) Balance-of-payments support in supporting assistance funds to finance essential imports such as fertilizers, pharmaceuticals, chemicals, iron and steel products, and industrial machinery needed to maintain the economy of Vietnam and prevent serious inflation. Most of the commodities will be purchased in the United States and less-developed countries. This assistance will be supplemented by sales of agricultural commodities of wheat, flour, evaporated and dried milk, tobacco, and raw cotton under title I of Public Law 480. (2) Commodities and technical assistance for the overall counterinsurgency effort directed in large part in fiscal year 1966, at rural development, communications, public works programs, and the national police.

These programs assist war refugees, relocation of disaster victims, and defectors through the provision of food, clothing, and simple construction materials. 

Other activities meet the people's felt needs quickly by helping to construct marketplaces, schools, health, and irrigation facilities. A contract with International Voluntary Services provides volunteers to work in the provinces in agriculture, health, and education.

Further, AID assistance will provide improved seed, fertilizer, and pesticides to farmers; wells and surface water facilities; repair and maintenance of war damaged highways and railroads, dredging of waterways, assistance in rural health services by improving provincial hospital facilities, and increasing the number of rural health workers. The police program will aim in fiscal year 

1966 at augmenting the force and its effectiveness while in the communications field new programs are being designed to extend the Saigon telephone network and increase the effectiveness of communications media in combating Vietcong propaganda.

AID assistance is supplemented by the distribution of U.S. agricultural surpluses of corn, bulgar wheat, vegetable oil, and nonfat milk under title II of Public Law 480. In addition, foodstuffs will be provided under title III for distribution by voluntary agencies. (3) A technical cooperation program to provide technical skills, advice, and training to assist the Vietnamese in developing their ability to govern effectively throughout the country. In fiscal year 1966 it is planned to double the number of graduates from the National Institute of Administration; extend the system of inservice training; and make efforts to improve the tax assessment and collection system. Through continuing contracts with Southern Illinois and Ohio 

Universities, technical advice in all phases of curriculum planning, vocational education, and teacher training are intended. In the field of public health the malaria spraying program will continue; and the provision of a teaching hospital is planned. The labor program will concentrate on participant training and providing demonstration and training equipment. In industry, AID will provide experts to help develop local industries.

2. CRITERIA FOR INITIATING NEW AID PROGRAMS 

Since the circumstances under which new nations become independent vary widely, there is no standard procedure for determining whether a new nation is to receive U.S. assistance. In all cases assistance is given only in response to a request from the new nation, although if a request is anticipated the executive branch may begin to consider whether aid should be given before receiving a formal request. In all cases consideration is initiated by the Department of 

State. The executive branch does "not proceed on the assumption that it is incumbent upon the United States to have a program of aid in every country or that it is U.S. policy to undertake aid programs on a universal basis." (Circular 

CG-1066, June 1961). The following three basic criteria are used to determine whether a new nation should be aided, and if so, what the nature and extent of our assistance should be. 

1. The nature and extent of U.S. foreign policy interests in the country.-Such interests reflect a number of factors, including the country's size, location, population, and resources; its political stability or vulnerability to subversion; the extent and nature of its influence in regional and international councils; special 

U.S. historic or other ties with the country (such as those with the Philippines). 

Since most countries which have recently became independent or may become so in the future have a colonial history, the U.S. Government carefully considers whether diplomatic, aid and cultural relations between the new nation and its former metropole will adequately maintain a Western orientation within the country, or whether the United States wishes to establish more extensive ties with the new nation than diplomatic relations alone permit, in order to bolster the country's Western orientation and/or to promote more specific U.S. interests. 

Changes in a country's situation may lead the executive branch to reverse an earlier decision not to extend aid, in order to meet an increased threat (military assitance to Malaya) or to demonstrate support for much improved policies or a new and constructive regime. 

In several of the east and southeast African countries which have become independent since 1960, U.S. economic aid programs were initiated before independence in an effort to establish working relations and begin building influence with the emerging leaders and groups. In these countries, the U.S. choice at the time of independence was not whether to begin, but whether to continue or terminate existing programs. 

2. The effectiveness with which aid can be used in the country to promote economic development and/or other U.S. objectives.-The U.S. Government may judge that accelerated economic and social development will strengthen an already Western-oriented and responsible government, or is a necessary (though not sufficient) condition for increased political stability or more constructive role in international affairs. The levels and types of U.S. assistance which the country can effectively use to speed its growth will be largely determined by the level of development it has already reached and by the vigor of its self-help efforts. 

3. The availability of external resources on adequate terms from other sources. In general, the U.S. Government follows the principle that ex-colonial powers should assume primary responsibility for assisting newly independent countries. The former metropole has personnel with experience in the country. 

The institutions and procedures of the new nation are usually modeled after those of the former colonial power. People in the newly independent country are familiar with the language, educational institutions, and products of the former metropole and therefore find it easier to take training or study courses, order equipment, and otherwise deal with the ex-metropole. 

However, total reliance on the former colonial power is often politically unacceptable in the newly independent state. Moreover, the U.S. position on, for example, issues before the U.N. may differ from that of the former metropole. 

In such cases a modest U.S. assistance program may "sweeten" and thereby make possible continued primary reliance on the formed metropole, and/or may demonstrate U.S. concern and interest and thereby increase receptivity to U.S. views on international issues. 

There have also been some cases where a newly independent country is capable of holding and attracting substantial new private foreign investment, thus reducing need for concessional aid from any source. Southern Rhodesia and 

Malaya are examples. Under these circumstances U.S. economic assistance may serve no significant U.S. interest. In a few cases such as that of Malta, income

from United Kingdom facilities plus tourism largely meet external requirements, so that there is no significant requirement for U.S. assistance. 

These criteria reflect the fundamental purposes of U.S. foreign assistance, as set forth in section 102 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended. 

More specific legislative guidelines applying to initiation of new programs, such as the requirements of section 620 (a)(3), (b), (c), (f), (i), and (1) are also observed. 

3 AND 4. PLANNING COUNTRY PROGRAMS AND REGIONAL APPORTIONMENT 

Decisions on the nature of the aid programs planned for each country for the following fiscal year, and decisions regarding allocations of funds among geographic regions, are both the outcome of a program planning and budget cycle spanning about 15 months. The process differs slightly for economic and military assistance. Therefore, the economic assistance planning and allocation process is described in some detail below, using Turkey as an example. This description is followed by a briefer account of the military assistance planning process and the points at which the two programs are coordinated. 

1. Planning guidance I. ECONOMIC ASSISTANCE A. FORMULATING PROGRAM PROPOSALS 

The initial proposals for economic aid programs in the coming year are drawn up by the field mission. In formulating program proposals, the mission is guided by standing policy guidance set forth in the AID program guidance manual, and by guidance messages from the Administrator and from the regional bureau in Washington flagging subjects to which special attention should be given in preparing proposals for the coming fiscal year. The mission also has as a starting point the current year's country assistance strategy statement reflecting the conclusions reached during the year regarding U.S. goals in Turkey and the strategy and program content designed to move toward those goals. 

2. What the mission considers in formulating program proposals 

During the time since the mission submitted to Washington the previous year's program proposals, the mission has been keeping close track of Turkish economic trends and of Turkish Government policies and programs. Mission staff have consulted with Turkish officials as closely as possible to ascertain their views of Turkey's problems and their plans for meeting these problems. The mission then examines the following topics in order to arrive at a recommended U.S. economic assistance strategy and program for Turkey: (a) The recent record.-Trends in the Turkish economy during the past year. and the reasons for good or poor performance, including Turkish self-help efforts, important changes in the political or security situation, and the implications of these changes for the Turkish economy. (b) Prospects for the next few years.-Prospects for economic growth and political stability during the next few years. These estimates are based on stated assumptions about Turkish policies and programs to be pursued, aid expected from other donors, the probable volume of private foreign investment, and other key variables. The analysis spells out the most important self-help measures Turkey must take to accelerate progress. The discussion may compare the results, in terms of economic growth, of several different sets of assumptions to test how big a difference specific reforms or alternative levels of aid might make. 

In Turkey and in other countries supporting large defense establishments, the projections are also based on stated assumptions about military expenditures, and they may be used to examine the probable results of alternative levels of military expenditure. (c) Appraisal of the past effectiveness of aid.-An examination of the extent to which U.S. economic aid has met our goals, including increased production in particular sectors, improved institutional capacity, changes in Turkish policies, and increased aid on better terms from other donors. (d) Proposed U.S. assistance program and strategy.-On the basis of the above, the mission recommends a program for the coming fiscal year, and indicates the general magnitude of aid and the broad strategy it feels should be pursued for the next several years. "Strategy" includes fields of concentration 44-834-65-38

for capital and technical assistance, the balance between project and nonproject aid, ways of encouraging and supporting more vigorous Turkish measures to improve key policies, ways of encouraging fuller coordination with, and increased aid from other donors. Mission proposals take into account expected military assistance, Export-Import Bank loans, and Peace Corps activities, and make recommendations concerning Public Law 480 programs and use of U.S.owned or U.S.-controlled local currencies as well as direct AID dollar assistance. 

The proposals for the level and composition of the fiscal year 1967 program are backed up by detailed project sheets describing the purpose, proposed plan of action, and expected costs of both continuing and proposed new activities. 

B. WASHINGTON REVIEW OF PROGRAM PROPOSALS 

1. The review process

The mission analysis and conclusion are presented in a country assistance program book (CAP). The CAP is reviewed by the Ambassador and submitted to 

AID in Washington with his approval. The CAP is carefully examined by the responsible officers in the regional bureau in Washington, who consult with their counterparts in the Departments of State and Defense and the Peace Corps, and with the Export-Import Bank, Department of Agriculture (concerning Public Law 480) and other agencies as appropriate. If any points are not clear, or if additional material is needed to evaluate a proposal, the mission is asked to provide additional information. The regional review culminates in a meeting chaired by the Regional Assistant Administrator and attended by representatives from the Departments of State and Defense and, usually, the Bureau of the Budget. Major programs, plus smaller programs which present special problems or are being substantially modified from the previous year, are then reviewed by the Administrator or the Deputy Administrator, with appropriate interagency representation. In autumn 1964, Mr. Bell and Mr. Gaud reviewed strategy and program proposals for fiscal year 1966 for 19 countries. 

2. Factors considered in reviewing program proposals 

The Washington review goes over the field mission's analysis of the country's economic situation and prospects. It reappraises the country team judgment regarding the urgency of U.S. foreign policy interests in the country, and compares these interests with those in other countries. In assessing the firmness of proposed aid levels for a country, Washington carefully examines the likelihood that all of the loan projects the mission has included in the proposed loan total will actually be ready for financing by the close of the coming fiscal year. 

The rationale for proposed technical assistance activities and their consistency with overall country assistance strategy is considered. Since the Washington staff knows what other missions are requesting, and has received from the Bureau of the Budget a planning figure for the total AID budget, it is better able than the field to judge whether financing and personnel can be provided to carry out the programs proposed for a particular country. 

The Washington review not only permits comparison of priorities among countries, but also brings to bear considerations the field staff may not take into account. For example, Washington staff are both more likely and in a better position to take into account the demonstration effect in third countries of U.S. actions in any one country. Since the Washington staff may have fuller communication with their counterparts in other donor capials, they may reach different conclusions than field staff regarding what can be expected from other donors and how they can be encouraged to increase aid, improve terms, and cooperate with us in pressing for better recipient performance. 

Since the review culminates about 3 months after the CAP is sent to Washington, the final decisions will also take into account any important changes in the country situation during that period. 

3. The country assistance strategy statement 

The decisions reached in the review process are reflected in a revised and approved version of the country assistance strategy statement (CASS). The 

CASS is a brief-5 to 10 pages-document stating U.S. economic assistance objectives, summarizing the key aspects of the country situation, and setting out the aid strategy and the magnitude and content of the aid program through which the goals will be pursued. After interagency clearance and approval by

the Regional Assistant Administrator or the Administrator (depending on the importance of the program), the CASS is sent to the Embassy and mission. It provides guidance for decisions during the year and a starting point for the program planning process the following year. 

4. Reviewing specific loan and technical cooperation project proposals 

In addition to the broad program reviews described above, each loan and technical assistance project proposal is carefully reviewed for technical and economic soundness, priority in the country's development program, and consistency with the country assistance strategy before approval and allotment of funds. This review of both new and continuing activities continues for some months after the overall program review has been completed. Only very large projects or those presenting special problems are brought to the attention of the Administrator.

C. FORMULATING THE BUDGET AND ALLOCATING AID AMONG GEOGRAPHIC REGIONS 

The field missions formulate their program proposals during the early summer, and submit the CAP's to Washington in July or August. (Full detail on project proposals may be sent somewhat later.) The review process described above takes place in September and October. By October the Agency has sufficiently close estimates of the proposed levels of country programs for the coming fiscal year to put together a budget request, which is submitted in November to the Bureau of the Budget. Before October the Agency will have received planning levels from the Bureau of the Budget regarding the total AID budget. The regional bureau reviews of proposed country programs permit an estimate of the total level of programs deemed feasible and desirable in that region. If this total seems too high when combined with desirable amounts for other regions, the regional bureau will consider which parts of which country programs can be reduced with least harm to U.S. objectives, while the central program coordination staff will discuss with other regional bureaus the effects on their programs of transferring some funds to the hardest pressed region. The resulting budget represents the Agency's best judgment as to the distribution of aid within a target total which will most effectively promote economic growth and protect priority political and security interests. Cuts required by the Bureau of the Budget before the presentation to the Congress, or resulting from the action of the authorizing and appropriating committees of the Congress, are allocated among regions by a similar process of consulting with the regional bureaus and comparing the importance to U.S. foreign policy of the activities and programs which would be reduced in each region if that region absorbed a large share of the cut. 

II. MILITARY ASSISTANCE A. PROGRAM FORMULATION 

Like economic aid proposals, the proposals for military assistance for the coming fiscal year are initially formulated by the Military Assistance Advisory Group (MAAG) or its equivalent in the field. MAAG's are guided in their planning by a guidance manual including both worldwide policy guidance and individual country guidance statements summarizing the broad purposes of U.S. military assistance in the country, the nature of the threat, and the general content and approach the programs should pursue. The military assistance guidelines reflect both national security policy as expressed in congressional legislation, Presidential policy statements, instructions from the National Security Council and interagency national policy papers, and more specific national military plans and policy. The relevant regional unified commander-for Turkey, the U.S. Commander in Chief for Europe (U.S. Cinceur)-supplements this guidance with detailed instructions and suggestions based on changes in the U.S. military situation or in the regional situation, experience during the past year, GAO reports and other considerations. 

Unlike the AID field missions, each MAAG receives a specific dollar ceiling for the proposed military assistance program in its country. These country planning figures are formulated in Washington in the context of a 5-year plan for the worldwide military assistance program and are approved by the Secretary of 

Defense.

The MAAG prepares specific program proposals within the dollar ceiling and consistent with the guidance provided by Washington and by U.S. Cinceur, or, where necessary, requests a higher level of assistance and justifies the request. 

MAAG consults with both the AID mission and the Embassy on the economic capability of Turkey to support given force levels and military expenditures, and the relationship of the military program as a whole to political, information, training, and other aid programs. 

B. PROGRAM REVIEW 

MAAG then forwards its proposals to U.S. Cinceur, which modifies the proposals as seems necessary, taking into account U.S. military posture in the region, proposals from other MAAG's for assistance to other countries in the region, and the possible alternative combinations of U.S. and other friendly forces in order to be prepared for various kinds of possible threats. Copies of the military assistance planning book prepared in U.S. Cinceur, plus extensive machine-run data on the precise equipment and material to be supplied, are sent back to the MAAG and Embassy in Ankara for their comment, and are also forwarded to the 

Office of Internal Security Affairs (ISA) within the Department of Defense in 

Washington. Mr. Bell as the Coordinator for Foreign Assistance makes sure that the views of each ambassador are sought and considered in Washington at this and earlier stages of program formulation. 

ISA further reviews the program proposals for Turkey and all other countries, consulting with the Joint Chiefs, AID, and the Department of State. In the interagency review process, the relationship of military to economic assistance is carefully analyzed, particularly in respect to local currency generation for Armed Forces use under AID and Public Law 480 programs, civic action projects involving both agencies, joint projects in the field of communications and transportation, economic impact of military credit sales activities, and other points of potential conflict, omission or duplication. At this stage the urgency of needs in different countries in different regions must be compared. In general the forward defense programs have priority over other programs, but since many of the "Western orientation" and other programs are very small the large programs would gain very little and other U.S. foreign policy interests may be substantially injured by transferring all resources to the forward defense programs. The process of comparing marginal claims in different countries in order to arrive at regional totals as essentially the same for military as for economic assistance.

It is the AID Administrator's responsibility in his capacity as Coordinator for Foreign Assistance to resolve interagency differences of opinion regarding competing claims for funds, or to refer issues to the Cabinet level (i.e., the Secretaries of State, Defense or the NSC, as appropriate) or President for decision. The final budget proposals for the military assistance program must be approved by the Coordinator as well as by the Secretary of Defense. 

AID TRAINING PROGRAMS FOR OVERSEA ASSIGNMENT 

Attachment A is a chart showing statistics for fiscal year 1964 covering training activity designed to prepare U.S. personnel for oversea assignment. The following explanatory remarks are provided to clarify terms used in attachment A:

Junior officer training.-Special training for selected personnel entering the Foreign Service at the FSR-8 through FSR-6 levels. Training normally consists of 6 months in rotational assignments in Washington; language training, where necessary; and an additional 6 months in on-the-job training assignments at post. Promotion normally follows satisfactory completion of the total (1 year) training plan. 

Orientation.-A 6-week course of training in Washington for all employees prior to departure for oversea duty. The program, conducted in-house and at the Foreign Service Institute, presents an introduction to and appreciation of policies, procedures, programs, area studies, Americana, the Federal Government, American foreign policy, and advisory techniques. Special long-term orientation training, including extensive language instruction is offered for certain personnel assigned to Vietnam, Laos, and Thailand. (A copy of the orientation program is attached.)

Language training.—All positions in the Foreign Service have a designated language requirement. Those employees who lack the required degree of language proficiency for their positions are eligible for training at FSI, commercial facilities, or in FSI language programs in the field. French and Spanish instruction accounted for approximately 90 percent of the language training given in Washington in fiscal year 1964. Special intensive training in Vietnamese, Laos, and Thai was introduced in fiscal year 1965; this new program could result in as much as a 30 percent increase over fiscal year 1964 totals. 

In-service training.-Specialized training for in-service (as opposed to new-hire) employees to keep them abreast of new developments in their fields, foster their career development, impart new skills, and generally to increase their effectiveness as Foreign Service employees. The facilities used include AID in-house facilities; FSI; private institutions, associations, societies, etc.; colleges and universities; and other Federal agencies. 

In addition to the training described above, the Agency conducts programs of a more specific nature which are not represented in attachment A. The more significant of these include: 

Training of Foreign Service personnel initially assigned to Washington under section 625 (d) (2) of the Foreign Assistance Act 

Present authority permits up to 20 such appointees at any one time for duty in Washington not to exceed 2 years. A training plan is prepared for each of these appointees, individually tailored to their individual needs as preparation for eventual oversea assignment. The plan sets forth such elements as job assignments in AID/W, kinds and amounts of formal study, travel to oversea posts for temporary periods, research, etc. The training plans so prepared are reviewed and endorsed by the Assistant Administrator prior to implementation. Progress reports are prepared on completion of each unit of training. 

Extended preservice training for certain employees appointed for duty in Laos and Thailand

A 10-month training program was recently instituted for this group. Training includes 3 months at the University of California in special study relating to their ultimate assignments abroad; 24 weeks of language training in Washington; area studies; counterinsurgency training; and a stopover in Pakistan en route to post for 2 weeks of field training. Twenty-two new appointees entered the first class at the University of California (Berkeley) in February 1965.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 

UNITS FOUR AND FIVE 

Monday, April 5, through Friday, April 16, 1965 

Area studies

This section of the orientation program is presented at the Foreign Service Institute and is designed to provide knowledge and understanding of the diverse political, economic, and cultural aspects of the various countries and areas of the world.

Area studies concurrently include Eastern Europe; Latin America; Near 

East and North Africa; Africa, South of the Sahara; South Asia; Southeast 

Asia; and East Asia.

The flow of study includes two parts: the first or "situation" week emphasizes the peoples, geography, history, religion, and society of the various regions; the succeeding 2-week portion emphasizes the transitional and sometimes revolutionary aspects of those societies, religions, economies, and political patterns.

A detailed schedule for each course will be furnished you on arrival at the Foreign Service Institute. 

NOTE.-Shuttlebus service will depart from the 22d Street entrance of New 

State Building to the Foreign Service Institute at 8:30 each morning and will return at 3 minutes past the hour.

CONCEPT OF THE UNIT TWO PROGRAM 

The unit two lecture series is designed to provide you with general insight regarding the AID program, with an understanding about the efforts of other members of your team, and to provide you with a substantive perspective for your individual skills in order to enhance your effectiveness in the program. 

Included will be sessions on the nature of underdevelopment, the problems faced by the developing nations and the various methods that AID and other organizations are using to help these countries help themselves. 

One of AID's most valuable resources is the extensive range of professional and technical skills among its employees. Such skills, to be most effective, must not only be properly focused upon the immediate task, they must be correlated by the broader long-range objectives of AID; and they must be congruent with the other program endeavors. 

The lectures this week will not attempt to tell you how to do your job, whether your job is in Washington or in an AID mission. Such knowledge is largely yours already by virtue of your academic training and experience. 

Your technical backstop office will augment such knowledge by explaining the nature of your specific job and discussing the special problems or techniques associated with it. 

To deepen your understanding of the program and where you fit into it, each session will be divided into two parts. The first half generally will be given over to a lecture on the assigned subject by a staff member who specializes in the field; the second half will be an informal seminar in which the participants exchange ideas and clarify concepts. The lecturer will serve as discussion leader. Your active participation will help make this part of the program successful.

Self-study source materials pertinent to the week's program will be distributed in advance in order to gain more benefit from other presentations. 

You are urged to prepare yourself for the sessions by a careful reading of this material. 9:00-9:15 9:15-11:00

How many State congressional liaison people are there, how many Defense, Agriculture, White House, Disarmament Agency? I have, in talking to other

Senators, found that there is, at least, say, a misunderstanding about the liaison program. I think we ought to get, for your interests, if for no other, an answer to these questions and those I may add. 

ARE AID FUNDS USED TO PAY AMERICAN CREDITORS? 

Next, Mr. Bell-and I shall soon be through-to what extent and in what amounts are AID funds in effect and in fact used to pay the American creditors of some country, whether it is Brazil or X, Y, or Z. 

Mr. BELL. Well, there is no-I know of no case, in which there is a direct relationship in the sense that we make money available to a country and they, in turn, pay the money to an American firm. 

Indirectly, I would suppose the proper response is the following: 

There are American obligations or obligations to American firms. 

Most of those are normal commercial obligations. If a country is in short-run balance-of-payments difficulty, it is not our business, not AID's business, where we can possibly avoid it and we normally can, to bail them out. It is the obligation of the country, in consultation with the IMF to organize a program to meet their short-run balanceof-payments difficulty.

In recent years, in a couple of cases, Brazil is one and Chile is another, this has involved in part a rescheduling of debts. The American 

Government has urged that in such cases debts to private people, Americans and other private people, should be included in the rescheduling, and this was done, for instance, in the recent Brazil case. 

It was not only the governments to which Brazil owed money that agreed to stretch out the payments over several years, but also the Brazilian Government undertook [deleted] to work out arrangements with private creditors in the United States and in Europe, and have done so under which the private suppliers' creditors agreed to a rescheduling of the debt.

Now, when those reschedulings have been made the result, is of course, of part of the future balance-of-payments picture of that country, and it is against that future balance-of-payments picture, among other things, that we will be considering with the country how much assistance might be needed and of what kind, and in that sense certainly there is a relationship between the obligations not only to American private creditors but also the Export-Import Bank, for example, as to what the AID program in a country will be. 

You may also have in mind the recent settlement of the American foreign power case in Brazil in which the settlement involved primarily the retention in Brazil in alternative investments of payments made to the American foreign power company by the Brazilian Government to buy out that electric utility. But there were also some amounts to be repaid to the company in the United States. It is not very much but it is something. 

It obviously is part of the future balance-of-payments situation to which their economic program must be related and to which, in turn, our AID program is related. But certainly we are not in the business of making aid available to bail out American creditors of a given country.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 599 1965 1 Senator MORSE. It has been alleged in the past that some years ago there was an arrangement entered into with Argentina that resulted in a loan with the understanding that part of it would be used to pay off American creditors. I wish you would go into that question and give us a memorandum on it. 

Mr. BELL. I will, sir. It is not a case I am familiar with and I will check it. How long ago, Senator, roughly, 2, 3, 4 years?

Senator MORSE. Maybe 5 or 6. 

Mr. BELL. I will be glad to look into it and provide it for the record.

(The information referred to follows:) EXPORT-IMPORT BANK LOAN TO ARGENTINA 

In March 1963, when political uncertainty was causing a balance-of-payments crisis in Argentina, Export-Import Bank authorized a $20.0 million loan to provide balance-of-payments assistance. This loan was authorized with the understanding that it would be used to: (a) Refinance maturities due under the Bank's various exporter programs, as well as, (b) Refinance principal repayments due U.S. suppliers and private financial institutions.

Because of the subsequent improvement in its balance of payments, Argentina was able to meet its maturities in the United States without this Export- Import Bank assistance and the credit was never utilized for the above purposes. Instead, agreement was reached to apply this $20.0 million commitment to finance U.S. exports destined for specific projects. AID loans were not involved in this transaction. 

MILITARY ASSISTANCE LIMITED TO CIVIC ACTION PROGRAMS 

Senator MORSE. On the question of military aid, do you think it would be feasible to limit our military aid in most countries to programs whereby the military would do the type of thing that the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers does, and require the country concerned to raise its own money for maintaining its defense establishment as such?

Mr. BELL. In some countries, of course, that is our policy, mostly in the case of some of the smaller African countries, where we get involved at all, this is basically our policy. 

The question, however, would apply primarily to Latin America and to the countries of Asia where the bulk of our military assistance is going at the present time.

I would think, Senator, that in the cases, the large cases, Greece, Turkey, Iran, Pakistan, India, and so on around to Taiwan and Korea, that this would not be feasible, at least not until after a long period of transition.

We have a relationship which has been built on an entirely different basis. It is a relationship which is very important to our security as well as theirs, to our interest as well as theirs, and if one tried to do this in the short run, the immediate response would be presumably that the country only has resources of its own for a certain total of development and defense expenditures. We agree that the defense expenditures are sensible, then if we are not prepared to help meet them through military assistance we would presumably ask-be asked to help them through economic assistance indirectly.

Now, over time we have made, as I have indicated, we have made a considerable movement in this direction in Latin America, a gradual change, but as I have indicated to Senator Clark, in many cases there is still an appropriate degree of regular military strengths, you might say, in addition to civic action capability. 

I think, if I might sum it up, I believe we have headed in this direction and are moving well toward it in Latin America. I would not think that we should move more than we have. In Africa in a number of cases we are following such a policy and will continue to do so. Not in all, not in all, in Africa. 

In Asia I doubt whether this would be an appropriate way to pursue what I understand to be the American interests in those countries. 

Senator MORSE. You see the problem I am troubled with is that this leaves so much to the discretion of the executive branch and so little to the imposition of policy on the part of the Congress. Under this revised program that I am going to introduce in the Senate this year, I am not stripping the executive branch of all discretion but I am at least going to try to build a framework of congressional control within which the executive branch has to operate. Military aid greatly concerns me. I would double the amount of economic aid for every dollar of military aid that we subtract. I think if we did that you would strengthen not only the security of the United States around the world but you would greatly strengthen freedom around the world. 

Senator CLARK. Would the Senator yield?

Senator MORSE. I yield.

BALANCE BETWEEN ECONOMIC AND MILITARY

I think that has been a movement in the right direction, and the directionthe percentages are continuing to change that way.

GAO REPORT ON SHIPMENT OF CARS 

Here is a point that, perhaps, does not involve you at all. My attention was intrigued by a case in Friday's New York Times, I think. 

It says that the Comptroller General charges the military wastes more than $1 million by following servicemen's desires rather than regulations by bringing privately owned cars back from overseas. 

The congressional watchdog over executive spending said some 3,400 vehicles were involved in excess costs incurred in the 4 years through 1964. Campbell noted regulations generally provide Government payments for private cars shipped to American ports nearest to a serviceman's next domestic duty post. 

Nevertheless, he found that in many cases cars landed from Europe at Atlantic or gulf ports had then been shipped to western ports hundreds of miles distance from new duty stations.

A case in point was an Air Force officer's Rolls Royce. It was shipped from 

Britain to New Orleans, and then to Oakland, Calif., at a cost of $925, although the officer's next post was in Ohio, 2,396 miles from Oakland. 

It would appear from this that, at least, Air Force officers and possibly other officers will buy a Rolls Royce in England, ship it to

Chairman. 

Our problems with cars have usually been in the other direction, namely, people who take American cars with them, as they are authorized to do, and then sell them on a very highly inflated local market. 

This is a problem, for example, in Brazil and other Latin American countries and some of the countries in Asia.

The CHAIRMAN. Do you pay the transport of an American car to Brazil?

Mr. BELL. Yes; we do, assuming the man and his family are going to a 2-year duty tour. We do not pay for shorter tours. 

Now, we have, I have, personally strongly objected to our people earning or receiving these large gains from the sale of their automobiles. We did not send them abroad to be used car dealers. We sent them abroad to serve in a job for the U.S. Government, and the State 

Department and ourselves and USIA and the Defense Department are now all signed to a new policy which was put out about 6 weeks ago, namely, that individuals who sell cars abroad are not entitled to take out anything more than the cost to them of that car, and if they receive more money than that they are required to put it into some kind of a charitable foundation or an embassy foundation or whatever the local arrangements may be in a local situation. 

Now, we have received a lot of protests about this. Americans like to sell their cars abroad and make several thousand dollars on them. 

But we do not regard that as appropriate and proper, and we are quite prepared to take disciplinary action to forbid it. 

Now, you are citing the opposite case. It would not apply to us because the countries where our people work you cannot buy a Volkswagen or a Rolls Royce, for that matter, at a low cost, and bring it back to the United States where it would have a higher value. Quite the other way around.

We do not have people stationed in England or in Germany or in France or whatnot. But I repeat, I will check the point. (The following information was subsequently furnished:) 

AID REGULATION RELATING TO SHIPMENT OF VEHICLES OWNED BY AGENCY PERSONNEL 

AID regulations (manual order 560.2) permit shipment of a personally owned vehicle to the United States at Government expense only in the case of employees who are assigned to duty in the United States or who resign or are separated from service. The automobile must have been in the possession and use of the employee during his last oversea assignment and not acquired while enroute back to the United States. The Government will pay expenses only for shipment to the employee's new assigned post in the United States or his residence. 

Subject to the foregoing general limitation, a foreign car may be shipped to the United States at Government expense only in the following limited situations: 

1. The employee owned the car prior to March 1, 1961 (when AID's present policy on shipment of foreign vehicles went into effect). 

2. The employee owned such vehicle at the time of his appointment. 

3. The employee acquired such vehicle at a post where foreign-made vehicles were authorized because reasonably adequate commercial vehicles did not exist for the maintenance and repair of motor vehicles manufactured and assembled in the United States. 

4. The oversea employee purchased the foreign-made vehicle from another employee who had purchased it prior to March 1, 1961. 

5. The employee acquired the vehicle at a post where the use of a right-hand drive motor vehicle was mandatory.

U.S. AID PROGRAMS IN SMALL COUNTRIES 

Before Senator Case leaves, may I come back for just one moment to this matter of small countries? I repeat the real question as to whether our interests can be served through multilateral agencies rather than bilateral, that is a real question. But I think there is a difference between the chairman and myself as to the general net effect of the aid relationship on the relations between the United States and these countries. 

By and large, in most cases we are able to conduct our aid program with good effect, not bad effect, on the general relationship between ourselves and this other country. This is true in the bulk of these small 

African countries. The net effect is a good effect, not a bad one. 

In cases where there are bad relations, I should say, between the United States and the country in question, like Indonesia and like the United Arab Republic, the bad relationship does not stem from our aid program, but stems from basic political differences which would be there whether we had any aid program there or not. 

So I feel very strongly, I have looked at this question very carefully, and I am not arguing that I am right, but what I am saying is that my quite firm judgment is that we do know how to conduct an aid relationship in a way that will contribute to good overall relations to the friendship and cooperation between ourselves and the country in question, and we will not end up with resentment, exacerbation, unhappiness, unpleasantness. That is stated a little more strongly than I would with all the careful qualifications stated, but I really feel this way, and I wanted to make this point before you went out. 

Senator CASE. I appreciate your making it. I appreciate the chairman letting me say this: How much experience is this judgment based on-and I have great respect for yours?

Mr. BELL. In my own case I have been in this particular job for a little over 2 years, 2 years and 4 months now, but I have watched it since 1954 when I first went to Pakistan on a project for the Ford Foundation.

I watched it through the late fifties when I was at Harvard teaching economic development, and I have been concerned with this matter for better than 10 years now, not as a Government official, and it strikes me as extremely pertinent. There are obviously ups and downs in our relationships.

WEDNESDAY, APRIL 7, 1965 UNITED STATES SENATE, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN RELATIONS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met, pursuant to recess, at 10:10 a.m., in room S-116, the Capitol, Senator J. W. Fulbright (chairman) presiding. 

Present: Senators Fulbright, Mansfield, Morse, Pell, Gore, Lausche,

Church, Smathers, Clark, Hickenlooper, Aiken, Carlson, Williams, and Case. 

We are very pleased to have the Secretary of Defense and the Acting Secretary of State with us this morning. 

By way of background, I might say that the committee in a preliminary way acted last week to reduce the President's request for military assistance authorization from the figure of $1,170 million to $1,055 million, which is the figure for this year's program and is a reduction of $115 million from the request. 

We also decided against an open-end authorization of additional military and economic assistance to Vietnam, but in partial compensation therefor increased the sum requested for contingency purposes from the $50 million to a hundred million dollars. 

I think I express the sense of the committee in stating that the reduction in sum authorized for the military was motivated not by a desire to reduce such funds for Vietnam but rather by a desire to reduce military assistance to certain other nations [deleted]. At least they were the ones that were discussed in connection with that matter.

As a result of conversations subsequent to that it has developed that these military programs really involve very strongly the political policy in these particular areas and, therefore, when it was suggested we might reconsider that action, the committee decided that, before taking any action on the motion to reconsider, we invite both the Acting Secretary and the Secretary to come and give us their views on these matters. 

Since this involves a military request, I assume it is appropriate to ask the Secretary of Defense to lead off and then be followed by the 

Acting Secretary of State; I don't care. If you wish the Secretary of State to start it first it doesn't matter to me. 621

Senator CLARK. Would you give us in just a few sentences, Mr. 

Secretary, the justification for maintaining the Spanish bases? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Yes, sir; we have two primary justifications. 

One is that we use the southern coast of Spain for naval purposes. 

We have Polaris submarines based there and by so doing we reduce the number of Polaris submarines required. 

Alternative bases would be in Scotland, and we reduce the number of submarines required by the difference in transit time from Scotland to the southern coast of Spain, and this is of great value to us. This is by far the cheapest way to achieve deployment of a number of [deleted] submarines under the water in the Mediterranean. 

Assuming for the minute that we could agree on the number of submarines to be deployed under the water in the Mediterranean it would cost us far more to keep that number there if we were forced to use Scottish bases than if we used Spanish bases. 

Senator CLARK. How about the airbases? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. Well, the most important base by far is the 

Rota Naval Base for the submarines. 

Senator CLARK. Excuse me, how much of the rent goes for the naval base?

Secretary MCNAMARA. We don't divide it that way. When I call this rent, actually it is military assistance, not rent, and because it is military assistance we don't try to divide it between rent for Rota and rent for the airbases. In the past the airbases have fulfilled two functions: one, our advanced bases for the B-47's and strategic bombers. 

These, I don't believe we need any longer, and we have, therefore, forced the redeployment of B-47's out of Spain back to this country. 

And when we did that, we asked that Spain take over the responsibility for its own air defense. [Deleted.] 

They have chosen themselves to operate these and we have turned them over to them. This has substantially reduced our domestic budget costs because those were not military assistance funded but funded through the basic defense budget. 

In any event, the airbases serve first the function of advance bomber bases and second, the function of in-transit bases. We are continuing to maintain them for that purpose, although we have reduced the number of bases required for that purpose, and reduced the number of personnel at those bases. 

Senator CLARK. Aren't they becoming obsolete? 

Secretary MCNAMARA. No, sir, not for in-transit bases. [Deleted.] 

FUTURE NEED FOR OVERSEA BASES 

Senator CHURCH. Is it your present plan, Mr. Secretary, given the changing function of these bases and projecting into the future beyond the term of the present agreement, to retain some kind of permanent airbase in Spain or have you decided on that?

Secretary MCNAMARA. Let's assume the present agreement runs through 1969, I believe I am correct in saying that it does, it is either 1969 or 1970, by that date we will have longer legged aircraft in both our tactical fighter units and our airlift units and it is conceivable at that time these transit bases will not be as important to us as they are today.

The F-111 has a much greater range than any of the current fighters. 

The C-141 which will be coming in as a basic airlift aircraft has a longer range than our other airlift aircraft, and we could, perhaps, reduce the reliance on transit bases. 

I frankly just haven't studied the situation in sufficient detail to answer the question. [Deleted.]

And I neglected to mention that as a subsidiary agreement to the basic rental agreement with Spain, they have agreed to purchase, I believe it is [deleted] million dollars worth of military equipment in this country, and pay for it standard prices.

EFFECT OF TURNING FACILITIES OVER TO SPAIN

INVESTMENT IN SPANISH BASES 

The bases and facilities which have been used by the United States jointly with the Spanish under the provisions of the 1953 Defense Agreement include: (a) Three major bases, Zaragoza, Torrejon, and Moron. (b) A support base at San Pablo. 

(c) An emergency fighter base at Reus. 

(d) A 485-mile POL pipeline with associated underground storage. (e) A major Navy base and air station at Rota. (f) Seven aircraft control and warning stations. (g) Navy fuel and ammunition storage facilities at El Ferrol and Cartagena. 

(h) Communications stations. 

The total cost of U.S. construction in Spain is approximately $359 million, of which $132 million was provided by the Spanish Government from 60 percent of the counterpart funds accruing from the proceeds of U.S. economic assistance.

SIMULTANEOUS ASSISTANCE TO INDIA AND PAKISTAN 

Senator LAUSCHE. I would like to ask, what explanation do we give with respect to this apparent conflict of helping both India and Pakistan?

Secretary BALL. Well, the explanation is that our assistance to 

Pakistan is based upon developing Pakistan as an effective bastion against the historic movement of the Soviet Union down into the subcontinent through Afghanistan and the Khyber Pass and also on strengthening the defense of the whole SEATO and CENTO area. 

Now, the problem of India again is simply to respond to a demonstrated vulnerability of India across the high mountains to the north which was shown in 1962 when the Chinese launched their aggression. 

India then went through a sudden wakening. [Deleted] India decided that it had to begin to protect itself and called on us, and the British to help them. Working together we were able to assist them to build a defense which can be a very real deterrent against Chinese aggression and which can move, and already has moved, the Indian people toward a much more realistic appreciation of the facts of life.

So, India [deleted] is actually being very helpful to us during this period.

In addition there is another factor which I think we have to take into account and which affects not only India and Pakistan but Taiwan and Korea as well and that is the repercussion of the development of a nuclear capability on the part of the Chinese which is something which gives especial sensitivity at the present time so far as their feeling of security is concerned.

REAPPRAISAL OF FOREIGN POLICY 

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make the observation that the discussion we have had today over what is a relatively small amount of money seems to me to have implications far, far deeper than the question as to how much money we give Greece and Korea. I am at complete sympathy with the publicly expressed views of the chairman that our foreign policy today is being conducted on the basis of a good many myths and not enough reality. 

I think there ought to be a massive reappraisal, not in the Defense Department at all, but in the State Department, of the overall implications of our foreign policy. I think the Russian threat should be reappraised. I think we ought to think a good deal more in the line of Walter Lippmann and George Kennan instead of Foster Dulles and Hanson Baldwin.

[From the New York Times] TOKYO INVESTIGATOR SCORES UNITED STATES AFTER VIETNAM STUDY (By Robert Trumbull) 

TOKYO, April 6.—U.S. policy in South Vietnam came under fire today in a report by a senior diplomat sent to survey the situation in Vietnam by Premier Eisaku Sato. The diplomat, Shunichi Matsumoto, expressed doubts as to Washington's view that the Vietcong insurgency was predominantly a Communist movement. 

He implied that the American side was rigid in the belief that the conflict could be won by military means. The Japanese special envoy considered this view highly questionable. 

Concluding that the U.S. course in Vietnam would prolong the fighting, he said that "Japan has a duty to grasp a good opportunity to talk to the United States and to appeal to world opinion" in an effort to find a peaceful solution. 

OPINION MOSTLY OPPOSED 

Mr. Matsumoto, a former Ambassador to Britain, is an adviser to the Foreign 

Ministry. His views are highly significant here because of the influence they are likely to have on Japanese attitudes toward the American role in Vietnam, especially since his report seems to confirm the skepticism already felt here. 

Judging by the leading Japanese newspapers and magazines, it would seem that only the various spokesmen for Mr. Sato's stanchly pro-Western government approve the U.S. position in Vietnam. Other expressions have been overwhelmingly negative. reply to a

Government's pro-American stand was underscored again today in its note from the Soviet Union demanding that Tokyo prevent the United States from using Japanese bases to support the operations in Vietnam. 

The Japanese Government said that Communist aggression and infiltration was the main problem in South Vietnam. The question of bases was turned aside. 

Mr. Matsumoto's views were given in an article he wrote for the influential newspaper Asahi, which circulates widely throughout Japan. The article was printed today in both English and Japanese editions of the newspaper. "It seems that the basic thinking of the United States is that Communist China or the Soviet Union is connected with North Vietnam and the Vietcong in a sort of parent-child-grandchild relationship," Mr. Matsumoto said. "However, there is no one who can define clearly the true character of the Vietcong "Even the people of Saigon," he continued, estimate the Communists in the 

Vietcong to be "at the most, 30 percent."

RESISTANCE LIKENED TO WAR'S 

Containing "nationalist” elements and "some who are simply dissatisfied with the present government," the Vietcong "could possibly be called a movement somewhat similar to the resistance of the French underground during World 

War II," Mr, Matsumoto declared. "It can be said that the Vietcong is not directly connected to Communist China or the Soviet Union. "Consequently, it is not certain that the Vietcong will give up fighting because of the bombing of North Vietnam ***. In Vietnam I often heard it said that the Vietcong is a nationalist movement. This means the Vietcong will not give up resistance until they have achieved their objectives." "If North Vietnam shows no inclination for peace even if the bombing of North Vietnam is continued and if the Vietcong does not suspend its guerrilla activities, the United States probably will be forced to restudy its policy," the 

Japanese diplomat stated.

Mr. Matsumoto talked with Ambassador Maxwell D. Taylor, among others in 

Saigon. He also visited Cambodia and Laos.

"I heard not a word about peace from the U.S. side in Vietnam," he said. "At any rate," he added, "I learned in Vietnam that both the U.S. State Department and the Defense Department have strong opinions. There is no possibility of the United States first bringing about talk of peace." 

Mr. Matsumoto suggested that Japan should contribute strongly to the economic improvement of South Vietnam. 

[From the Washington Post, Mar. 7, 1965] TWIN ATTACK PRESSED BY RED CHINA (By Charles Taylor) (Toronto Globe and Mail) 

PEIPING, April 6.-While the crisis in Vietnam remains explosive, China is preparing major diplomatic moves against both the United States and the Soviet Union.

This drive will come to a climax at the Afro-Asian Conference in Algiers in June. It is a long-range campaign which reaches far beyond Vietnam, although the fighting there provides the Chinese with useful arguments. Its goal is an 

Afro-Asian world which looks to Peiping for revolutionary leadership and which rejects all American and Soviet aid and influence. 

Most observers say Peiping expects to avoid a direct military clash with the

United States over Vietnam, in spite of its offer to send men. 

PEARSON IGNORED 

The Chinese are also set against a cease-fire and immediate negotiations. It is probably significant that the Chinese press has not reported Canadian Prime Minister Lester Pearson's call for a temporary end to U.S. airstrikes, even though this would support the favorite Peiping thesis of a disintegrating Western alliance.

Rather than seeking a quick settlement, the Chinese seem to hope that North Vietnam can endure U.S bombings until the anti-Communist drive in the south collapses through military, political, and diplomatic pressures and the Americans are forced to withdraw.

This would discredit Soviet theories of peaceful coexistence with the West and strengthen Peiping's revolutionary line. It would also leave two exhausted 

Vietnams much more susceptible to Chinese influence. 

ESCALATION RISK 

This is a perilous course. It runs the risk that U.S. intervention will increase to the point where China must retaliate. But if there are any alternatives up the Chinese sleeve, they have yet to be disclosed. 

Yet the Chinese leaders are far from waiting on events in Vietnam. They are pressing the pace of diplomatic activity in order to outflank both Washington and Moscow, not only in Vietnam, but throughout the developing world. 

This is seen as the major reason for Premier Chou Enlai's short visit to Algeria, Egypt, Pakistan, and Burma, and Foreign Minister Chen Yi's trip to Afghanistan, Pakistan, and Nepal. It is also connected with the current African tour of a Chinese parliamentary delegation headed by Liu Ning-yi, Secretary General of the standing Committee of the National People's Congress. 

It is part of a process which began this year with visits to Peiping by key 

Afro-Asian leaders-Foreign Minister Subandrio of Indonesia, President Julius Nyerere of Tanzania, and President Ayub Khan of Pakistan. 

TRIP TO INDONESIA SET 

It will continue when Chou and Chen travel to Indonesia later this month for the 10th anniversary of the Afro-Asian Conference at Bandung. At some point, the Chinese leaders will make their east African tour of Tanzania, Kenya, and Uganda, postponed from last year because of the military uprisings.

In each case, there were specific bilateral issues to be discussed by each visit has given the Chinese a chance to press their case for a militant stand by the whole Afro-Asian world against the two superpowers. 

In return, the Chinese are giving welcome support to their friends-praising Indonesia for its U.N. withdrawal; reaffirming their backing for Pakistan over 

Kashmir; and strongly supporting Arab opposition to Israel and West Germany. 

These are more than merely polite noises. They indicate a growing determination that Peiping's voice should be heard, and heeded, on all major world issues.

To some extent, the Chinese campaign looks like fencemending. China's first atomic explosion and its attack on the U.N. evoked Afro-Asian responses that were more worried than warm. 

The Chinese are also working hard to have the Soviets excluded from the Algiers meeting. Diplomatic sources in Peiping say the issue is still in doubt, and must have been a major talking point during the recent tours of Chou and Chen.

The news that Japan will send a high-powered delegation to Algiers can hardly have pleased the Chinese. To turn the Conference into a sounding board for their militant doctrines, they must outmaneuver such moderate powers as Japan and India.

The CHAIRMAN. He goes on about what our policies will result in according to his views, which are all directly contrary to our assumptions, aren't they?

Secretary BALL. Well, I think that it is certainly no secret that there is opinion in many places in the world, that it is fundamentally an indigenous revolt. That this is what the Communists represent it to be.

Additional statements and letters submitted for the record by non- Government representatives. 

Hon. J. W. FULBRIGHT, SILVER SPRING, MD., April 1, 1965. 

Chairman, Committee on Foreign Relations, U.S. Senate. 

DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: Concerning foreign aid appropriations to encourage 

American citizens to invest in Latin America, I would like to bring to the attention of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations an instance where American citizens endeavored to carry out the aims of such a program in the Republic of Panama. However, instead of encouragement on the part of the local government, they have been faced with a long period of harassment, the imposition of discriminatory taxes, and virtual expropriation of their property. 

I would appreciate your views as to whether this should be brought to the Subcommittee on American Republics Affairs, or the Committee of the Whole. Sincerely,

CHARLES H. WHITAKER. 

SILVER SPRING, Md., April 2, 1965. 

STATEMENT TO THE COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN RELATIONS OF THE U.S. 

SENATE CONCERNING FOREIGN AID APPROPRIATIONS 

I have lived in Latin America for 13 years and am interested in the economic development of Latin America as expressed in the Alliance for Progress program. I have been a foreign service officer of the Department of State for 

21 years, and during this time made many speeches about how the foreign aid program would prime the pump in underdeveloped countries, and then private investment would come in and carry on where the Government aid programs leave off.

The reason that I am particularly interested in the foreign aid appropriations is that two able young American investors came to Panama in good faith, did just what our Government said they should do to further economic development through private industry on a well-conceived project, and met with only continuing harassment.

Mr. Kingdon Gould and Mr. D. F. Antonelli, Jr., experienced American businessmen with substantial property and business interests in Washington and other places, came to Panama in 1956 and actively engaged in a private industry project that fulfilled in every aspect steps that President Eisenhower and Assistant Secretary of State Henry Holland in published policy statements said that socially conscious American businessmen should take to help bring more prosperity to countries of the Western Hemisphere. 

They brought in modern equipment, experienced management, and adequate private financing. Through no fault of their own, but through the indifference of the local government, and its failure to carry through on commitments made before they agreed to undertake the project, they lost $500,000. This stopped further development work on the Boston Panama Company and the Boston Panama Coconut Company projects which were, in my opinion, both wellconceived and, under their management, well-executed. 

The above projects are exactly the type of desirable economic development projects that our Government is currently spending substantial sums of public funds to try to encourage with its technical assistance programs. They would have supplied a large part of the needs of Panama for edible oil which it now 653

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, imports in quantities of millions of dollars of copra per year from the Philippines and other distant places. From the standpoint of many new jobs, new capital investments in Panama, the fuller utilization of available local natural resources, and every other economic aspect, these are the types of projects that would be good for the economy of Panama which we are trying to encourage with U.S. public funds. 

Since financial circles are extremely sensitive and very well informed, experiences like this are bad for the implementation of the aims of the Alliance for Progress program, and impede the flow of U.S. private capital and know-how to the friendly nations of the Western Hemipshere. This situation should be remedied, and provision should be made so that it will not happen again. 

For 9 years, in spite of costly time-consuming discussions, and continuing efforts, it was not possible to make any progress towards reaching an equitable solution with the local government concerning certain tax and boundary matters which would make it financially possible for the two companies to operate in the manner as originally planned when the present owners were invited to come to Panama until the adoption of the Long or Hickenlooper amendment in the foreign-aid legislation of 1962. Only at that time did there appear to be any desire on the part of the Panamanian Government to reach any settlement. 

While the Hickenlooper amendment, section 620(e) of Public Law 87-565, the Foreign Assistance Act of 1962 provides that the President shall suspend assistance to the government of any country to which assistance is provided under this act when the government of such country*** (1) has seized 

or enforced discriminatory taxes," repeated official representations of the Boston Panama Co. have so far elicited very little concern or interest on the part of either the United States or the Panamanian Government. 

I still believe American private investment confidence to be essential to Latin American economic development, and hemispheric solidarity generally. 

But any businessman who wonders whether confidence in such investments is justified must "ask the man whose made one." The Gould/Antonelli investment in Panama is now nearly 10 years old, and continues to constitute a severe loss. Their experience is hardly encouraging. It is in fact a storm signal for any would-be investors at least in that country. 

American businessmen must assume risks in any ventures, at home as well as abroad. But the risk of expropriation, de facto or de jure, is too high a burden of risk for private business to assume. If the U.S. Government wishes to see investments go forward in the developing countries of this or any other hemisphere, it has to be prepared to provide either for an indemnity program of its own against expropriation, or, which is more reasonable and appropriate, provision in its aid program, bilateral and multilateral, which serve notice that aid moneys will be withheld from any government which indulges in this practice. Such protections should be demanded and accorded the governments and private interests of all participant countries in a multilateral aid venture so its benefits are not restricted to the United States. 

What is fair for one is fair for all but it is manifestly unfair and unwise as a matter of foreign or domestic policy to put our public shoulder to the wheels of economic progress oblivious or indifferent to the efforts of private businesses which, in the long run, are the kingpins that keep those wheels rolling.
