U.S. Government Support." APPENDIX No. 1 BACKGROUND CONCERNING THE Boston PANAMA Co. 

1976 toda

Buvies In 1955, Mr. D. F. Antonelli, Jr., and Mr. Kingdon Gould, who have substantial business interests in Washington and other parts of the United States, purchased

1 a U.S. company which since 1905 had expended over $1,250,000 in developing a coconut plantation in Panama. They began an active program to rehabilitate the plantation and develop the natural and human resources of the area for which purpose they brought in $250,000 additional capital. 

They demonstrated that their business experience gained in the United States would also work under favorable conditions in Panama by organizing in addition with Panamanian associates, a successful vegetable oil plant in Panama City. 

However, they have found that their efforts to establish a Panamanian source of raw material for their vegetable oil plant which now purchases substantial quantities of peanuts and copra from Africa and the Far East, and to bring doctors, schools, access roads, markets, and better living conditions to the people in the plantation area who now have an extremely low standard of living with little hope for improvement, instead of finding encouragement from the local Government, have met with obstacles at every turn. 

A "denuncio" for uncultivated land tax, which the company does not feel is due because of the exemption allowed for 5 hectares of uncultivated land for each hectare of cultivated land that is suitable for cultivation, has resulted in a tax lien against the property of over $1,800,000. Strenuous efforts since 

1955 to settle this matter have met with indecision and apparent indifference on the part of the local Government. Squatters and lack of police protection have further complicated the problem. According to law the company must now make a cash deposit of $1,804,254.40 before it can contest this case in 

Panamanian courts. This is discriminatory because the uncultivated land tax is not being paid by other landowners. For example, no uncultivated land tax was collected during the year in which this tax in the amount of $1,804,254.40 was levied against the company. Nor was it collected in the 2 previous years, nor the 8 years following except for a payment 1 year of only $139, nor is it currently being collected.

This project is clearly within the scope of the aims of the Alliance for Progress program, and if encouraged, could result in a higher standard of living for a large number of people, and increased utilization of the natural and human resources of the Republic of Panama. It would also make possible the production of raw materials in Panama for which the local economy is well adapted and which now have to be imported, in substantial quantities from outside the Americas. This project already has the human interest of Americans who are experienced, and well established in U.S. business, real estate, and financial markets and could bring into play substantial additional financial and human resources.

As financial circles are extremely sensitive, and very well informed, experiences like the above in which projects fail to develop because of artificially imposed cricumstances, harassment, or an unfriendly climate, rather than as the result of conditions related to faulty conception or the intrinsic worth of the project, discourage U.S. investment in private enterprise in Panama and other Latin American countries as conceived in the overall plan of the Alliance for Progress which relies heavily on the private investment sector for economic development in Latin America.

APPENDIX No. 2 PANAMANIAN UNCULTIVATED LAND TAX COLLECTIONS 

Usual land taxes have been paid regularly by the company, and are not under discussion, only the uncultivated land tax. The company's position in regard to the latter is clear. According to the uncultivated land tax law (law No. 8 of January 27, 1956) for every hectare of cultivated land, 5 hectares are exempt from the tax. Swamps, deserts, and lands unsuitable for cultivation are also exempt. More than one-fifth of the cultivable land is now being cultivated whether by the company or the squatters, and therefore the entire area should be exempt from the tax. Furthermore, much of the land being taxed is extremely mountainous, and therefore unsuitable for cultivation. 

This tax is also discriminatory because it is not being collected from other large landowners. The company was assessed an uncultivated land tax of almost $3 million in 1949 which was later reduced to $1,804,254.40. The total

uncultivated land tax collections from all others for the past few years have been as follows:" 1947. 1948.

STATEMENT OF NATIONAL FARMERS UNION 

I am Reuben Johnson, director, Division of Legislative Services, National 

Farmers Union.

Mr. Chairman, we appreciate this opportunity to appear before your committee this morning. It is always a pleasure to visit with you and the distinguished members of the committee to present the views and recommendations of the National Farmers Union. 

I have with me this morning, Dr. John Eklund, who is director of the National 

Farmers Union International Projects Division. As you know, Farmers Union is one of the organizations which cooperates with the State Department to provide technical assistance to many of the developing nations who receive help through our foreign assistance program. Dr. Eklund directs this operation for 

Farmers Union and therefore is an expert and actual eye witness to what our foreign assistance program is and is not accomplishing. 

But before Dr. Eklund presents his views, I would like to make clear that we vigorously support the continuation of this program with a few modifications which we will spell out a little later in our testimony. We believe foreign aid continues to be an independent arm of our foreign policy in building a society of free nations in a stable world. The fundamental reason why we support this program of economic assistance is because, first of all we feel it is the humanitarian thing to do, but even more important is the fact that it supports our own Nation's interest in the broadest sense around the world. Our own Nation's security is bound up with the evolution of a world of independent, peace-seeking nations. It is in our most elementary national self-interest to do what we can to help in strengthening the prospects for peaceful progress in Asia, Africa, and 

Latin America. 

Our support of this program was reaffirmed only last week at our national convention held in Chicago, Ill., where the delegation adopted the following resolution: "Foreign policy of the United States should be shaped to help assure dignity and justice for human beings everywhere. Our power and our strength should be tempered with understanding of others. Our national self-interest should be tempered by recognition of the interests of other peoples, and our firmness of purpose must never exclude humanitarianism and charity. "Food and fiber should be utilized as an essential part of the foreign policy of the United States. We should make full use, in conjunction with other nations which have food and fiber abundance, of a unique opportunity to promote widespread and more rapid economic development in less developed nations through the use of food and fiber. Such a multilateral program should make use of the world food program operated by the Food and Agriculture Organization of the 

United Nations. "We urge greater use of long-term, low-interest rate food and fiber loans, authorized under Public Law 480. Donation programs both direct and through private, nonprofit United States organizations should be used when and where needed to assist needy people. Long-term legislation should be enacted, directing the use of the economic strength of the United States in cooperation with other free nations toward promoting economic development of the less fortunate nations of the world."

Mr. Chairman, I think you and the committee will agree that the membership of National Farmers Union have made their desires and wishes clear, and it is in response to their wishes that we appear before you and your committee today in support of this program. 

Mr. Chairman, with your permission, I would now like to have Dr. Eklund present to you a more comprehensive statement of his views and his own observations of our foreign assistance program as he has personally viewed it during his extensive travels around the world. 

Statement by Dr. John Eklund, director, International Projects Division, National Farmers Union: 

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, this is indeed a rare opportunity for me and a most pleasurable one I can assure you. Having just returned to the States 4 weeks ago from an extensive inspection tour of U.S. AID missions in Thailand, South Vietnam, Korea, and the Philippines, I would like to relate to you some of the things I saw and have seen in the past since being associated with our foreign assistance program. 

First, may I say that National Farmers Union's contribution to the foreign assistance program is one example of the contribution independent organizations are making in partnership with our Government. Our particular effort has been directed to providing technical know-how for the establishment of farmer cooperatives and to encourage and assist farm organizations and rural institutions in these developing nations. 

National Farmers Union has been in partnership with the Government of the United States since late 1961 to carry out this mission. Programs of assistance operate in behalf of the campesinos of five Latin American countries under the Alliance for Progress; Chile, Peru, Venezuela, Bolivia, and Colombia. In 1963 and 1964, 141 leaders from these countries lived in our farm communities, studied our institutions and since their return home have, almost without exception, stimulated and led their own people to improved conditions and independent action.

In community after community, cooperatives have been organized; to market, to process, and to supply farm needs, resettlement programs have been begun and the rural education process has been stimulated. 

In five countries of Africa, Farmers Union is now consulting in inviting the rapid development of national cooperative efforts in marketing, supply, and credit.

Uganda, the first project country, illustrates this assistance. In this country, which achieved independence in 1962, the cooperative movement has grown from less than 100,000 patrons to more than 400,000. The number of successful cooperatives has grown from 70 to more than 700 and a strong effective national cooperative union and educational arm has been given day-by-day consultation. 

Other countries in which Farmers Union is working include Tunisia, Dahomey, Kenya, and Ethiopia. Consultations with four additional countries are underway.

Within recent weeks a program of assistance has been negotiated with the Philippines and the Farmers Union has supplied a consultant to the Afro-Asian rural construction organization. 

In the developing countries of the world, the development of cooperatives is -central to their economic planning, for the farmers of the world make up from 50 to 85 percent of their countries. The hope for a better life depends on their ability to sever themselves from the middlemen and moneylenders and establish their own marketing and supply institutions. 

The democracy practiced in their own cooperatives is today laying the groundwork for their democratic societies, and the preservation of economic and politi- 'cal freedoms.

Needless to say, I am extremely proud of the part I personally play in administering National Farmers Union's commitment to the people of America to assist peoples of these developing nations. 

Continuation of statement by Reuben L. Johnson, director, legislative division:

Mr. Chairman, I want to further add that Farmers Union wholeheartedly supports the President's request for $365 million in new authorizations for U.S. bilateral technical assistance and contributions to United Nations relief and development activities, including the U.N, expanded program of technical assistance and the special fund for U.N. Relief and Works Agency, the U.N. Children's

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, We believe these programs constitute some of the most creative and humani. tarian activities engaged in by the United States because they help people help themselves. The technical assistance projects which Dr. Eklund has been tell. ing you about help raise the educational, technical, and institutional level of the new nations. The United Nations programs are particularly constructive in that they mobilize the human and financial resources of many lands for human betterment.

There are however several modifications of the program which we hope you, Mr. Chairman, and the committee will give serious consideration to. 

First of all, we feel that the economic aid program should be completely separated from the military assistance. We question the assumption that economic aid programs must be included with military aid programs to win support at this time. The food-for-peace, Peace Corps and various international lending programs have won House approval without a military component. Since true economic and social development programs constitute only half the overall aid program, separate legislation would give the American people a better understanding of the size and direction of the U.S. development efforts. 

We do not believe that the U.S. program can function at maximum efficiency unless it is geared to a long-term effort. In this light, we support long-term loans in the form of food so that the peoples of these developing nations might have an adequate diet which is a most important factor in the efficiency level and degree of initiative of the individual. 

In addition, we would like to see the food-for-peace program greatly expanded and the use of food in the administration of our foreign policy given the proper emphasis it deserves. 

I would like to further point out, Mr. Chairman, that at present the annual per capita gross national product of the United States exceeds $3,000 while that of the developing world averages $145. Even in view of this, unfortunately, U.S. aid budgets are going down while the gap between the living standards of the United States and the developing world is increasing. We therefore urge your committee to recommend an increase in technical assistance and development aid.

As you know, Mr. Chairman, National Farmers Union has been very close to this program and a vigorous supporter of the concept of foreign assistance dating back to the early efforts which led to the establishment of the Marshall plan and we are proud of this continued support as we look at the successes in Western Europe, Japan, Spain, Greece, and all the other nations whose destiny hung in the balance after World War II, but who were able to hang on to freedom as a result of our help. 

Thank you very much.

STATEMENT IN SUPPORT OF THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT OF 1965 BY DR. ALONA E. EVANS, AREA REPRESENTATIVE, WORLD PROBLEMS, AND MRS. GEORGE C. HAHN, CHAIRMAN, LEGISLATIVE PROGRAM COMMITTEE OF THE AMERICAN ASSOCIATION OF UNIVERSITY WOMEN 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, we wish to thank you for the privilege of again presenting a statement to this committee. We regret that the short notice we were given prevented presentation of a witness. 

In our many appearances before you since the days when the Marshall plan was being discussed, we have assured you that an overwhelming majority of our membership believes our foreign assistance programs to be a constructive tool of U.S. foreign policy which: (1) Not merely combats communism, but works toward the creation of a world situation in which ideals of freedom and democracy can exist; (2) Promotes the economic growth and social development of the emerging nations which we wish to remain as a part of the free world-thus securing markets for our own production as well as the sources of raw materials we will need in the future; (3) Promotes the concept of creative international relationships advanced in recent years by every administration-a concept stated forcefully by President Eisenhower when he said, "We accept our own deep involvement in the destiny of men everywhere." 

We find in our own membership an unwillingness to give up our foreign assistance programs-for we in AAUW recognize that the long-range security of the free world is at stake in the underdeveloped countries. Nonetheless, in our

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 661 1965 membership, as in the press and in Congress, we have noted a growing disenchantment and a growing lack of understanding of the problems we face. We believe this growing anxiety over expenditures for AID would be largely dissipated if the average American realized that the attacks upon foreign aid programs are upon some foreign and military policies and not intended to undermine the social and economic development programs. Approximately half of the $3.38 billion asked for fiscal 1966 is for military assistance and defense support. We in 

AAUW are not prepared to argue for or against these military assistance programs. But we do believe economic and technical aid is and can be a most effective instrument of foreign policy which must be used at the pace for which it is geared.

In spite of the fact that irritation against our foreign assistance efforts has been building up in this country over current statements of leaders in the Middle and Far East, it is our firm belief that almost everyone recognizes that there are far deeper and longer range implications involved for the future of the United States than this spilling over of frustrations would indicate. These implications, as we have pointed out earlier, make retreat from development programs under the Foreign Assistance Act impossible. 

Because of these much-talked of failures, or so-called failures, in several areas where we have had substantial programs, we believe more light should be shed on the successes of our foreign aid. 

Several years ago it was decided to direct the major part of our aid to those countries most likely to benefit through their own efforts and to work for greater use of multilateral agencies in supporting and distributing economic assistance. 

AAUW recognizes the importance of continuing our bilateral programs but it also recognizes that certain programs, for example programs of social and fiscal reform, are better undertaken multilaterally. 

Our successes in stimulating progress in self-help is evident in the increase in production, in industrial output, and in exports of the less-developed countries of 

Latin America, Africa, and Asia.

We are told that every dollar of U.S. aid granted on a bilateral basis has stimulated expenditure of six local development dollars in those countries where our programs are concentrated. This is indeed success. 

Equal success has attended our efforts to enlist the sharing of responsibility for aiding the developing countries. Today several recipients of our economic aid are themselves conducting substantial assistance programs bilaterally as members of the Development Assistance Committee (DAC) of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). Like the programs supported by the United States, much of this assistance has been in loans rather than grants. It is heartening to note that the interest rates charged on these loans have been dropping. In the face of this trend toward more realistic interest rates on long-term loans made by other countries in the free world, we urge that this committee reject any possible amendments to this legislation, similar to those proposed last year, which would have substantially hardened AID development loan terms. In our view, such action would seriously inhibit the success of our foreign assistance programs. 

Ten years ago, the World Bank was the only mutilateral source of development capital; today the World Bank, the International Development Association, the 

European Development Fund, and the Inter-American Development Bank are also sources of capital and technical assistance funds. In the eyes of the AAUW, this, too, is substantial progress. 

Up to this point we have made no reference to the agencies of the United Nations to which the United States contributes under the Foreign Assistance Act. 

Our members have repeatedly demonstrated, in our opinion polls and by convention vote, their interest in and support for the work of the U.N. family around the world.

In this connection, we would like to draw the attention of this committee to the interest of widespread support for International Cooperation Year, not only in our own organization, but throughout the country. Again it is our contention that cultural exchange, weather, transport, and health programs, to list a few which are conducted on an international scale, are evidence of progress far outweighing the limited numbers of failures which can be listed. 

One of the greatest contributions to a free world, we in AAUW firmly believe, is the promotion of education, particularly in the developing nations. As in the past, we urge upon this committee insistence on more emphasis in future pro-

graming not only on combating illiteracy but on advancing social, political, and technical skills at the highest levels which will inevitably contribute to advances in the health and social climate of the recipient nations, as well as to their economic and political stability. It is also a measure of success that in recent years the investment in education in these countries has increased annually by 15 per cent. Education is a slow business. Changes in social mores and creation of new institutions in government take time which cannot be shortened without raising the levels of education in the less-developed nations. 

From our own experience as an organization making grants to foreign students, we in the association can testify to the appalling need in some parts of Africa, Latin America, and Asia. In the past 7 years, the association has granted over three-fourths of a million dollars, contributed in dimes and dollars by its members, to 297 foreign students from Europe, the Middle East, and Asia, from Africa and Latin America. In this period, we received 915 applications for fellowships. Our fellowships committee was forced to turn down two-thirds of these applications, no matter how deserving the applicant, or how great the need for the skills which might be developed. Because we in AAUW were becoming increasingly aware of the critical shortage not only of teachers but of teachers to teach teachers in African countries, a program of summer studies was initiated 2 years ago and is being continued this coming summer. 

This program, carried out in conjunction with the State Department, brings teachers who cannot be spared in their countries for a full academic year to the United States for a summer of special training. We pay room, board, tuition, and incidental expenses. The State Department provides travel expenses. 

The following excerpt from a letter from one of these African grantees is an illustration of the worth of this effort. "The courses have helped to solve some of my present problems. I teach home economics at the college and now I feel more well informed using the knowledge I acquired. Of course, there are certain problems like lack of adequate equipment, but all the same there is always a way of getting around it. 

I am at the moment getting in touch with various supervisors of home economics to try and include certain items in their study syllabuses which were omitted and I feel are very important, e.g., foods and nutrition, to both boys and girls*** Since we had time in the evenings and over the weekends, we were able to make friends and as such discussed all sorts of general cultural and social interests. We were invited to various social gatherings outside the university." 

We in AAUW are now engaged in trying to work out a similar program with AID for teachers from Latin America for whom we in AAUW will assume responsibility.

Again we urge authorization of at least the full amount requested by the administration for technical assistance and development programs. 

STATEMENT OF U.S. SECTION, THE WOMEN'S INTERNATIONAL LEAGUE FOR PEACE & FREEDOM, WASHINGTON, D.C. 

The Women's International League for Peace and Freedom has long been concerned about the U.S. foreign aid program. Our statements opposing the military aid program and supporting economic aid have been submitted year after year. Some members of the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations and the 

House Committee on Foreign Affairs feel that military aid is an essential part of the foreign aid bill without which economic aid would not be approved. 

Nevertheless, the league believes that military aid should be reduced until it is eliminated and that economic aid should be increased and should be granted more and more through multilateral channels. 

The league believes that military aid does not achieve real security either for the United States or for the recipient country and, in fact, very often it is used to subvert democratic processes. As Senator Morse has pointed out in a speech (August 1964), the U.S. aid program has been resumed in four "junta-ruled countries" the Dominican Republic, Guatemala, Ecuador, and Honduras-where more often than not there are ruling tyrants which with U.S. aid oppress the people rather than try to raise their standards of living. 

The President said in his message relative to foreign aid in January that we would persist in our efforts to put more aid on a multilateral basis. He pointed out that a growing proportion of economic assistance is directly administered by

international financial institutions such as the World Bank, the International Development Association and the Inter-American Bank. This is a good trend on which we should capitalize. It is important that these institutions maintain their international character, but it is even more important that the wealthiest Nation in the world contribute more to the newly developing nations. Therefore the United States should increase its economic aid, whether or not other nations increase their contributions. 

President Johnson asked Congress for only $3,38 billion for his foreign aid program, including military aid. This is the lowest request since U.S. foreign aid formally began in 1948. Yet the needs are greater than ever. As the Washington Post said, editorially, on January 15, 1965, “In the underdeveloped countries of three continents, the rate of economic growth still lags behind the population growth and threatens two-thirds of the people of the world with social disorganization, economic decline, and political disintegration." It cites 

South America especially as a continent where 2 percent of the people own more than half the wealth, 80 percent of the people dwell in miserable shacks, illiteracy grips more than half the population, more than 50 percent of the people suffer from hunger and disease, and the population growth rate exceeds the growth in the production of goods and services. 

These glaring realities mean that the United States must increase its economic aid and, we believe, channel it through the United Nations and other multilateral agencies so that it will be administered with no national strings attached. If, as was proposed at the World Trade Conference held last year, all countries would give 1 percent of their gross national product for foreign aid, the U.S. figure would be $6.4 billion instead of the proposed $3.4 billion. The 

United States, of all the countries at the conference, is most able to contribute such a percentage. The league urges Congress to show more foresight and make sure that the United States measures up to the proportionate amount given by countries with far less national income. Surely 1 percent of the gross national product is not too much to expect from an "affluent society." 

STATEMENT OF J. ORRIN SHIPE, MANAGING DIRECTOR, CUNA INTERNATIONAL, INC. 

(FORMERLY CREDIT UNION NATIONAL ASSOCIATION) 

The Humphrey amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 made it the policy of the U.S. Government to use cooperatives, credit unions, and savings and loan associations to help implement the self-help objectives of our foreign aid program. Their use, it was felt, would add a new people-to-people dimension to 

U.S. Government efforts to assist developing countries. 

To implement this new program, the International Cooperative Development Service was set up in the Office of Material Resources in AID/Washington, and authorized to enter into a series of global open end contracts with U.S. cooperative organizations qualified to help establish cooperatives abroad. To date seven contracts are in force, one with the Credit Union National Association (CUNA), of Madison, Wis., and six other national cooperative organizations. 

CREDIT UNIONS AND COMMUNITY DEVELOPMENT 

A credit union is a cooperative association organized to promote thrift among its members and to accumulate a fund from these savings to make needed loans to members for useful purposes at reasonable interest rates. 

It also has been described as a uniting of the efforts and knowledge of a group of people who have a common bond and share a common need for accumulating savings, providing a source of credit, and developing or fostering among themselves cooperative action. Credit unions are a means by which people get together and work together toward the solution of one of the chief problems affecting developing communities, the satisfaction of basic human needs through self-help.

In uniting efforts toward the solution of their problems through credit unions, each individual in the group participates in the activity which causes the group to improve or develop. 

A credit union can be started in any group: people working for the same employer; people who live in the same small community; people who are members of the same church, labor union, or fraternal order. Membership is open to

everyone in the group. Basically, every credit union is a group of friends and acquaintances who want to help each other. The only purpose of a credit union is service not charity or profit. 

CREDIT UNIONS-A MEANS OF SAVINGS 

Communities in Latin America are assuming responsibility for the management of local affairs. They have to manage their limited capital assets to increase production and to develop and improve their standard of living and way of life.

The pattern of development in Latin American and other less developed countries has had the effect of providing the larger share of proceeds from industry or agriculture, whether in profits or emoluments to the main towns. The re- maining proceeds have been spread among the indigenous population at a low per capital income rate. Millions of people are continually in servitude during most of their lives and in many cases pay interest several times the amount of the principal. Reputable organizations providing natives with credit for personal or productive use are practically nonexistent; in most instances, they are limited to the user. 

The internal mobilization of capital has to be accomplished, first, by using these small sums on a broad base, and the best, indeed, the only way in which this is economically feasible is through a credit union, where the self-help aspect eliminates the administrative cost of the operation. 

Credit unions throughout the world have always maintained truly self-help programs. This feature of credit union development is most important, especially in developing countries where people in these countries often look outside of themselves and their communities for the solution of their problems. 

Even in the cooperative movement itself, at times, due to a lack of this selfhelp feature, development has taken place without this effective financial contribution or active participation in management from the people within the local community. 

CREDIT UNIONS-BASIC FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS 

Credit unions are set up and operated for and by groups of interested people who have some established interests with each other or some existing common bond. They are legally chartered by Government, and are usually supervised by the chartering agency, but are otherwise fully owned and controlled by their members under the one-member-one-vote process. Day-to-day operations are carried on by a board of directors, and a credit and supervisory committee operating under delegated authority from members and according to accepted bylaws and operating policies. 

Credit unions offer numerous benefits and services to members varying from group to group. Basic standard benefits include 

1. Encouraging, motivating, and providing a ready facility to help members practice thrift by systematically saving-even very small amounts of their incomes; 

2. Providing low-cost loans; 

3. Providing finance and budget counseling; 

4. Planning expenditures, keeping out of heavy debt involvement to highrate lenders; 

5. Frequently providing services such as insurance coverages for loans and insurance to match member savings, and insurance protection against losses which may arise in its financial operations; and 

6. Education of members and training of officers in finance management through the democratic process. 

The key to credit union success with low-income people is perhaps the feeling of group solidarity growing out of group action, and the confidence developing in these finance institutions that are member owned and controlled. Credit unions exist-to some degree in some 75 countries of the world and are increasing steadily.

CUNA INTERNATIONAL, INC. 

CUNA was organized in 1934 as an association of credit unions in the United States. In 1940, Canada was admitted and in 1946 membership was expanded to include credit unions in the Western Hemisphere. Since 1957, all credit unions through the free world are eligible for the services which CUNA International provides.

CUNA International, the credit unions' own international confederation, n, serves ets and coordinates this worldwide program. AID is using credit union technicians provided by CUNA to help implement the Humphrey amendment in its cooperative development programs; and helping credit union people extend this worldwide thrift service to the people of developing countries to which CUNA is fully committed.

CUNA's specific goals are to promote the organization of new credit unions; perfect credit union laws in the States, provinces, and countries in which credit unions operate; improve methods and techniques of credit union operation, and coordinate and direct the efforts of all credit unions in their drive to give the people throughout the world an opportunity to economic, social, and educational advancement through self-help. 

CUNA, through its world extension department, has been engaged for more than a decade in channeling assistance for the development of credit unions in many developing countries. This assistance by the people in credit unions did not begin with the creation of the world extension department of CUNA in 1954. 

It was the outgrowth of a desire to insure that assistance as was customarily given by credit union members to less developed countries for this purpose be better deployed and also extended. Prior to this time, many United States and 

Canadian provincial leagues had been assisting credit union development in the 

Caribbean and in South America.

Within the limits of its resources, CUNA has tried to answer the great number of requests for assistance it is receiving at its Madison headquarters. It is with such assistance to local leaders by guidance and training that a sound and stable credit union development is taking place in the Caribbean Islands of Jamaica, Trinidad, the West Indies, and the Netherlands Antilles; in the Latin American countries of Mexico, Venezuela, Ecuador, Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Peru, Panama, Guatemala, El Salvador, Honduras, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, and in the Pacific in the Fiji Islands, Samoa and Korea; and in Tanzania, Kenya, Ghana, and Nigeria in Africa. 

In 1961, following on the Humphrey amendment, the Alliance for Progress decided to include assistance to the South American countries participating in the program for the development of credit unions, cooperatives, and savings and loan associations. Following this, a contract was signed with the Credit Union 

National Association to develop credit unions. 

Under the leadership of CUNA technicians, credit unions have increased in Latin America from 432 in September 1962, to over 1,200 by December 1964, with over 600 additional groups awaiting charters; members increased from 124,000 to 420,000; savings of members from $4.2 to $16.5 million, and loans outstanding to members from $4 to $18 million. Loans are made for some 25 different purposes covering personal or consumer loans, farm production loans, self-help housing loans, and loans to start small business enterprises. 

Growth approximated or exceeded 100 percent in each of these 2 years. Considering that most members earn $100 per annum or less, this overall growth is phenomenal. The new program is saving low-income credit union members of 

Latin America an estimated $3 million or more annually by way of interest charges, and is raising $40 or more in new capital for each $1 of technical assistance cost. In addition, it is establishing a new and completely self-sustaining and self-perpetuating program for the low-income people of Latin America. 

Some of the reasons for credit union success are: 

1. It is a simple type cooperative. 

2. It deals with only one commodity-money. 

3. It creates no new problems; it is set up only to solve problems already existent. 

4. It is less vulnerable to competition because it is self-contained and operates in the closed circuit of its own members. 

5. Other enterprises need capital with which to start operations, but the credit union, in the process of developing capital, is carrying on one of the two main functions of the society-savings. 

6. The credit union can be scaled down to meet the needs of the lowliest people, as well as meet the needs of the most demanding, and it can be brought within the grasp of all people. 

The extent of this unsatisfied need among less developed peoples of the world has been clearly shown by the part that CUNA, with its limited resources, has 44-834-65- -43

The strength of the credit union movement is not its monetary assets, important as they are. Its greatest value is its contribution to the growth and development of its members, its practical demonstration of democracy at work, its development of leaders from among its membership, its demonstration of private enterprise as a means for attaining social, economic and political freedom. 

CUNA has played a dynamic role in these developments. 

Cooperation between AID and CUNA has resulted in the extension and acceleration of credit unions in the developing countries. Since the first agreement in 

1962, the agreement to develop credit union systems in Latin America, AID has broadened the scope of the partnership, in January 1963, to include all other regional areas.

1 As I mentioned in my covering statement to this appendix, the development work carried on by CUNA International takes three forms: the CUNA/AID program, the CUNA/Peace Corps program, and the work of CUNA alone. The figures in the tables above give a good indication of the progress of each of these programs.

For example, the CUNA/AID contracts have been limited up to now to work in a dozen countries of Latin America: Venezuela, Brazil, Peru, Colombia, Bolivia, Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Costa Rica, Panama, Nicaragua, and

El Salvador. Additional credit union programs can be started in a country under the CUNA/AID program on the basis of a task order worked out by the local 

AID mission. 

Feasibility surveys have been mounted in Ethiopia, Sudan, Nigeria, Tunisia, and Sierra Leone. The average cost per country of a credit union organizing program is $50,000. On the basis of present performance, each technical assistance dollar expended in Latin America has generated over $40 in new capital through credit union savings. 

Activities with the Peace Corps have been confined to Ecuador, where an intensive organizing program has gotten underway. 

The remaining credit union development listed in the above tables is due to the CUNA world extension program operating alone and independent of any Government support. 

Strong areas of credit union development outside of Latin America include 

Australia, Jamaica, Netherlands Antilles, Trinidad-Tobago, Fiji, and the Philippines. We are proud of the support of credit union leagues in the United States and Canada which has made this development possible. Out of this development have come many heartening examples of what credit unions are accomplishing. 

A peasant woman in Arequipa, Peru, near the Chilean border, exercised her credit union membership rights by borrowing the equivalent of $22, not a significant sum, but nevertheless, an amount of money sufficient to enable her to buy three used beds for her nine children, the first time any member of the family had slept off the ground. 

In Peru, the poor people in the isolated jungle town of Iquitos, not far from the headwaters of the Amazon River, have shown how a credit union can influence an entire community's growth. Organized in the poorest section of the town, the credit union is now the largest in Peru. It has more than 3,500 members, deposits approximate $1 million, and has started financing low-cost housing projects among its members. 

From September 1962, to December 1964, savings held by Latin American credit unions have increased at a phenomenal rate: from $4.2 to $16.5 million, in excess of a threefold increase.

There are other examples of opportunities opened by credit unions: a loan permitting a young lawyer to pay for his license to practice; a newly licensed dentist to buy his equipment; a mechanic to open his own tire recapping shop. 

Credit unions also expand people's knowledge. They act as training centers, teaching people with limited training a basic understanding of the truth about their country's development, and having them participate in this development in a democratic manner. For the first time, in most cases, they practice the basic principles of democracy. 

Credit unions are also bringing people and their communities out of isolation. 

Through uniting their savings into significant sums, they are being brought into the mainstream of their country's economic life, and are becoming an integral part of their country's development. 

This remarkable progress is directly attributable to the education and training programs; programs designed not only to instill technical competence, but also to develop local leadership.

CUNA has provided this type of training to more than 4,000 volunteers in over 

120 seminars throughout Latin America.

Among local communities, it is in the awakening of the recognition of this need, capacity, and ability to help themselves that the credit union has made its best contribution to development. Only those who have seen the self-reliance, self-respect, and initiative which a credit union engenders can fully appreciate the extent to which this is true. Credit unions, simple as they may seem, have tapped the greatest national resource of many countries through their success in bringing about this awareness by their self-help cooperative program. Where this recognition is awakened, there will be a great willingness to participate fully and freely in development ventures. Without this recognition, all other efforts are likely to fail in the long run.

STATEMENT BY THE AFL-CIO EXECUTIVE COUNCIL ON FOREIGN AID 

The AFL-CIO reaffirms its support for a practical and humanitarian foreign economic policy. America is rich enough in spirit and material wealth to support the expansion of freedom in the world. The national interest is not served by cutrate approaches to foreign aid. 

In about two decades of existence, the foreign aid program has met both success and failure. Success can be the benchmark for future gains; failure must be the reason for improvements. But the Nation cannot afford to undermine its security by denying world realities and continuing past mistakes. 

Neither propaganda nor promises can substitute for specific efforts to help less developed countries establish viable economies and strong, free institutions. Such assistance to friendly developing nations, which need our help and will cooperate with us, is essential in the fight against the world Communist menace.

U.S. production has risen more than one-fifth since the decade of development began in 1960. The U.S. can afford to spend 1 percent of its total national output for aid to the less developed countries-the goal of the decade of development. Present aid proposals amount to less than one-half of 1 percent of our gross national product. Yet pennypinchers in the Congress are already attacking even such a limited objective as too expensive. Others would divide foreign aid into segments, as if security were a piecemeal proposition. 

Moreover, with the bulk of foreign aid procurement placed in the United States, the charge of "giveaway" is a distortion. AID-generated exports provide business for American companies at home and add to American employment. 

The United States must continue, extend, and improve its efforts to assist developing nations to establish economically viable, free societies. The need for roads, schools, and the other underpinnings of modern economies should be assisted by U.S. grants and long-term loans to the governments of friendly developing nations. However, Government programs cannot do the whole job. Private capital and the efforts of private groups must be a supplement to, but not a substitute for, essential governmental help. 

U.S. business should receive and has received assistance for investing in less developed countries, in the forms of guarantees and tax incentives. But the proposal that American taxpayers pay 30 percent of a company's investment in a developing country, through a 30-percent tax credit for investments in developing nations, would provide a windfall to business operating overseas and add to balance-of-payments difficulties. 

The United States should continue its support for international financial institutions and for the multinational aid. The Alliance for Progress deserves continued and expanded support. The principles underlying the Alliance should guide U.S. economic and technical assistance projects to the developing countries. 

The AFL-CIO supports a foreign aid program designed to show that the United States is able and ready to foster the expansion of freedom by assisting the developing nations to establish, in their own ways, the foundations of strong, free societies.

STATEMENT BY THE AFL-CIO EXECUTIVE COUNCIL ON PUBLIC LAW 480-FOOD-FOR- PEACE PROGRAM 

Recent congressional discussions of U.S. foreign policy have brought into bold relief the urgency of avoiding certain obstacles to its effective execution. On the one hand, some have proposed restrictions on the President's mobility in ex-

ecuting the Nation's foreign policy. On the other hand, proposals have been offered which tend to undermine responsible congressional bipartisan participation in our country's fulfillment of its international responsibilities. The vital necessity of avoiding these dangerous obstacles to the effective execution of sound U.S. foreign policy has been most clearly underlined in our country's experience, to date, with the application of the food-for-peace program (Public Law 480). 

The executive council maintains that the aforementioned obstacles can be largely avoided by providing additional safeguards for the national interests of our country. Toward this end, we propose that any agreement with a foreign government which seeks the benefits of the food-for-peace program shall be operative only as long as its purpose of promoting peace through aiding people in need is not converted or distorted into a food-for-work program. The use by any foreign government of American surplus food as full payment for work done on various projects would put our country in the indefensible position of enabling the said regime to wield awesome dictatorial powers over the lives of its working people. Such abuse of the purpose of Public Law 480 would, in effect, constitute a form of forced labor and a flagrant violation of the ILO Convention on Forced Labor-for the adoption of which American labor took world initiative. 

The executive council further proposes that benefits accruing to a foreign government from a Public Law 480 food-for-peace agreement into which it has entered with the United States shall cease the moment the said government fails to protect or covertly or overtly instigates, incites, or promotes mob violence against citizens, representatives, establishments, or property of the United 

States. 

In addition, the executive council recommends that such benefits shall likewise cease to accrue to any foreign government the moment it disrupts peace by engaging in direct or indirect (subversion) aggression against any country with which the United States has diplomatic relations. 

We propose the aforementioned clarifications solely in the spirit and aim of the policy enunciated by President Lyndon B. Johnson, when he declared in his state of the Union message that: "We are prepared to live as good neighbors with all, but we cannot be indifferent to acts designed to injure our interests, or our citizens, or our establishments abroad. The community of nations requires mutual respect. We shall extend it-and we shall expect it."

STATEMENT OF THE LEAGUE OF WOMEN VOTERS OF THE UNITED STATES IN SUPPORT OF FOREIGN ECONOMIC AID TO THE SENATE FOREIGN RELATIONS COMMITTEE BY THE LEAGUE OF WOMEN VOTERS OF THE UNITED STATES 

The League of Women Voters of the United States wants to reaffirm to this committee our members' support of economic aid and technical assistance to the developing countries. Delegates representing the 1,150 local leagues in all 50 

States and the District of Columbia expressed this support at our biennial convention in Pittsburgh last spring. League support for economic aid is nothing 

It goes back to the days of the Marshall plan and has continued as the aid programs have changed direction to meet changing world conditions. new.

We have given this support to aiding developing countries knowing full well that it is no easy matter to bring millions of people living in century-old condi-

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, tions into the complex 20th century. We believe that it is high time that Congress gives recognition to the long-range reality of economic development aid by taking a hard look at the procedures it has set up for annual authorization of these programs, a time-consuming and divisive technique. We believe that Congress has a responsibility for keeping a watchful eye on the operation of the programs, but it seems to us that this could be accomplished through a system of reports by the executive agencies to the congressional committees most involved. Authorization of programs for more than 1 year at a time would give these agencies and the countries they are aiding a chance for better planning and better evaluation of programs in being. If the authorization were passed early in the first session of each Congress and interim reports submitted to that Congress we do not believe that congressional oversight would be weakened or destroyed.

We are glad that more aid is being channeled through multilateral agencies and we encourage increased use of such channels insofar as additional contributions-both financial and technical-from the United States can be effectively utilized. We have supported the increase in capital resources of the International Development Association and believe that merging the Alliance for 

Progress Social Progress Trust Fund with the Fund for Special Operations of the Inter-American Development Bank was another step in the right direction. 

We support voluntary U.S. contributions to the United Nations specialized agencies for we recognize that aid given through these agencies is often more acceptable than aid through bilateral programs. 

However, we also believe that the bilateral technical and capital assistance program still has an important part to play in the overall plan for bringing the overall plan for bringing the developing countries into the present-day world. 

We do not think that the magnitude of assistance needed to move these countries toward self-sustaining growth could begin to be reached if we completely cut out bilateral programs. But we would urge that our bilateral assistance increasingly became genuine "development assistance," geared to each recipient country's own desires and needs and tied into effective self-help efforts by these countries. 

We applaud increased use of various new devices, such as the consortium technique, which can effectively coordinate the various bilateral and multilateral assistance to a particular country in a way mutually beneficial to all parties concerned.

In closing we thought you would be interested in the account of a "go see" trip made by one of our former board members who recently returned from a trip to Africa with her husband, a member of the International Housing Committee of the National Association of Home Builders. She was so impressed by what she saw of the U.S. technical assistance program in action that she wrote a letter to the editor of the league's National Voter. She wrote: "***Almost the first thing we learned-a point that was evident as we went from country to country-is that while these newly emerging nations face almost insurmountable problems of their way toward development, the basic problem is development of the people themselves. The real need is to furnish them not only with the basic elements of food, clothing, and shelter, but to help them educate and train themselves in order to be participating members of their developing society. But this is a painfully slow process. Cultural patterns are not altered overnight, nor are people of many separate tribes molded into a cohesive nation in a wink. Thus economic development will be a slow, very slow process, and there will be need for aid and technical assistance from the developed countries for a long, long, long time to come * * *. "Overall, the changing face of Africa shows not only a redrawn map, but a changing pattern of living as well. Sleepy little towns of 20 years ago have almost overnight become roaring cities, overcrowded and underplanned as the rural population treks to the city in search of jobs. Teeming, filthy, tumbledown shantytowns almost floating in seas of mud are mute evidence of this rapid urbanization. Strikingly obvious is the need for planning for roads, schools, hospitals, water supplies, sanitation. But no need is greater than housing.ws "Nigeria is making the biggest strides toward meeting housing needs in cities. 

Perhaps this is because it seems to be further advanced than many other African countries. It is blessed with great diversity of natural resources, and has broad diversification of industry. It has enjoyed relative stability in its economy and 

"Over and over again, country by country, we were told of the high priority that education was being given in development plans. In most places the literacy rate runs about 20 percent. Each country claims compulsory education,

but it is more of a hope than a reality because there are just not enough trained teachers, nor school buildings, nor even books. In Kenya, for instance, 70 percent of children up to 10 years old attend school, 20 percent up to age 14, and only 2 percent go on to secondary schools. Thus very few are prepared to receive the specialized training necessary to enable them to fill positions of leadership. AID is supplying both personnel and construction funds to help break this bottleneck. No investment will yield greater returns than that applied to training teachers who in turn will educate the children. "We came away somewhat dejected and discouraged by the enormity of the problems these countries face, but with a deep respect for their optimism and eagerness. We are more than ever convinced that thoughtfully planned and carefully administered technical assistance is of inestimable value. Development is a long, slow process, and whatever assistance we can give will help these people help themselves to a higher standard of living. I have firsthand proof and renewed conviction about the merits of foreign aid." 

We hope that this committee will recommend authorization of the full amounts requested by the President for economic aid in fiscal 1966. 

NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF HOME BUILDERS,

DEAR SENATOR FULBRIGHT: I would appreciate having the attached statement included in the record of hearings on S. 1367, the proposed Foreign Assistance 

Act of 1965, which is now before your committee. Sincerely, Enclosure.

BURL A. JOHNSON, Chairman, NAHB International Housing Committee. 

STATEMENT OF BURL JOHNSON, CHAIRMAN, INTERNATIONAL HOUSING COMMITTEE, NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF HOME BUILDERS OF THE UNITED STATES 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I submit this statement to you on behalf of the National Association of Home Builders of the United States which, as you may know, is the trade association of the American homebuilding industry. 

For many years, the association, with some 43,000 members in 387 affiliated local and State associations in every State of the Nation, including Alaska and Hawaii, and in Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands, has worked toward the improvement of housing conditions in other countries. As far back as 1950, it established relationships with similar associations representing homebuilding industries in other countries. It maintains a close and cordial relationship with 

11 assocations in 8 countries.

The comments of the association on the proposed bill coincide with my own personal views, based on my experience during the last 5 years as a builder of housing abroad for my own account and as a consultant to others in that field. In one of those capacities or as a member of study committees of the 

National Association of Home Builders, during 1964 I have traveled some 180,- 000 miles and visited 40 foreign countries on every continent. 

Both NAHB-and I personally-strongly agree with the purpose of section 224 of the Foreign Assistance Act to stimulate private homeownership and assist in the development of stable economies in Latin America. 

I will go further. It is no overstatement to say that it will be impossible for most Latin American countries to maintain a democratic form of government unless we can effectively assist them in fostering private homeownership as we know it in this country. 

It has been strikingly evident that the one thing which most impresses nations of other countries visiting the United States is the widespread ownership of homes by persons of modest means. To them, it is literally an economic miracle that salesmen, clerks, white- and blue-collar workers alike own their homes in this country. In Puerto Rico (if further illustration be needed) we have strikingly demonstrated the stimulating economic and social effects of a private enterprise homebuilding industry and of increased homeownership.

This and the vigorous Puerto Rican stateside American homebuilding industries which built these homes and which are mainstays of the economy of their countries-was made possible by the encouragement provided by the Federal Housing Administration system of mortgage insurance, by veterans' loan guarantees, and by savings and loan associations organized into the Fed eral Home Loan Bank System. 

A small, but highly creditable and successful beginning in bringing homeownership to foreign lands has been made during the past few years, under section 224 of the Foreign Assistance Act-particularly since the Agency for International Development has called on the Federal Housing Administration for technical assistance in processing applications. Projects have been built under this section and are, in my observation, outstanding successes both in providing good housing and in fulfilling the threefold objective of the act to stimulate a local homebuilding industry, to develop a stable economy, and to provide the highly desirable social pattern of private homeownership in the nations sought to be assisted. 

It is important to remember that this has been accomplished without any expenditure of appropriated Federal funds but by guarantees which should result in very little call, if any upon the Federal Treasury and possibly actually produce a profit if our own FHA pattern is any indicator. 

The program has evoked tremendous interest on the part of American builders and lenders. Applications for many thousands of units have been filed with AID. 

In practically every case, projects which have gone forward have been built by American builders in cooperation with local builders. As pilot projects, they have provided the faint beginnings of a homebuilding industry in these countries. 

The National Association of Home Builders, which strongly urged this program be established, believes it is working and could be even more effective. 

Therefore, limitations in the proposed amendment to section 224, contained in the bill before you come as something of a shock. Instead of continuing and expanding this vital effort to stimulate private howeownership, section 103(e) of the bill would amend the existing act so that, in effect, hereafter it could not be used by the American private homebuilding industry. 

This results from- (1) The proposed wording in subsection (a) of section 224 which enjoins AID to place "particular emphasis" on projects of cooperatives and of free labor unions, and (2) The limitation in subsection (c) which, in increasing the total amount of guarantees proposed from $250 to $350 million, would confine projects not in those categories or not intended for "low-income families" to the previously existing authorization. In short, no part of the increased authorization would be available to U.S. builders to help in development of a private homebuilding industry as known in this country. 

This, we submit, is in conflict with the stated objectives of section 224. The objectives of private homeownership and a stable economy go hand in hand with a vigorous homebuilding industry. Without such an industry, they are not possible of attainment.

Projects of the types sought to be favored by the bill should, of course be encouraged. Cooperatives and labor union projects have their place. The need for housing in these countries is so great as to warrant use of all tools to develop a supply of homes. But this should not be done to the virtual exclusion of the type of project which has heretofore gone forward and which, we submit, is essential in developing a free, stable economy. 

In addition to the Latin American guarantee authority contained in section 224, housing guarantees for countries outside of Latin America are also authorized under section 221 (b) (2) of the act. Last year, AID internally set aside for housing $50 million of the $300 million available under this section. Today, this program is just getting underway, although I would estimate that the formal applications already being processed and indications of interest from builders far exceed the $50 million available by AID. 

We recommend- (1) That portion of the amendment to subsection (a) of section 224 which would require "particular emphasis" on cooperatives. free labor unions, and savings and loan assoications, be stricken from the bill to end (a) after the word "programs." (2) The restrictions contained in the first proviso of the proposed amendment to section 224 (b) be stricken from the bill. (3) The amount of authorization be increased to $500 million.

(4) Section 221(b) (2) should be amended to expressly provide that $150 million of the guarantee authority thereunder be utilized for middle-income housing projects in other than Latin American countries. 

Some critics of the housing guarantee program point to it as a source of aggravation to the already serious balance-of-payments problem which this country is presently experiencing. We would like to make it clear at this time that the program, in fact, has very little, if any, adverse effect on our balance of payments. 

As you know, many of the less developed countries themselves have serious shortages of foreign exchange. AID attempts to mitigate this shortage by making dollar grants or so-called program loans to these countries to enable them to finance their hard currency imports. We submit that through the use of the housing guarantee program in such countries, AID can and should be able to multiply the otherwise minimal advantages which it gains through its grant aid program. In short, guaranteed loans for housing result in the construction of crtically needed housing in these countries and at the same time serves to replace grant aid as a result of the net dollar inflow to be derived from the housing loan.

On the other hand, many of the less developed countries, while badly in need of adequate housing, are not experiencing a shortage of foreign exchange. In these instances, we feel strongly that AID, FHA, and the U.S. builders involved should constantly seek ways to maximize procurement of construction materials from U.S. sources. The experiences of many U.S. builders who have heretofore participated in the program indicate that with little difficulty at least 35 percent of the principal amount of the guaranteed loan can be constructively used for procurement of materials from U.S. sources. Such dollar procurement in the 

United States, coupled with the profits remitted to the U.S. builders, underwriting and commitment fees, shipping charges, insurance and engineering, architectural and design fees, results in reducing the net dollar outflow in the case of a guaranteed loan for housing to a negligible amount. 

STATEMENT OF HERMAN WILL, JR., ASSOCIATE GENERAL SECRETARY, BOARD OF CHRISTIAN SOCIAL CONCERNS OF THE METHODIST CHURCH 

I am Herman Will, Jr., associate general secretary of the Board of Christian 

Social Concerns in charge of the Division of Peace and World Order with offices in Washington, D.C. The board is an official agency of the Methodist Church. 

I appreciate this opportunity to place in the record the official position of the Methodist Church on world economic development as adopted by the general conference of the Methodist Church, the highest authoritative body of our denomination. The general conference, numbering approximately 900 persons, half laymen and half clergy, meeting in Pittsburgh, Pa., on May 8, 1964, adopted the following statement: 

"WORLD ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT 

"The desperate unmet needs of people in this world are of grave concern to Christians. The economic gap between the rich nations and the poor nations is widening as time elapses. The population explosion further jeopardizes the stability and progress of many lands. "We believe that economic assistance, which seeks to make the benefits of scientific advance and industrial progress available for the improvement of underdeveloped areas, is an example of both Christian love and practical international brotherhood. "All programs of technical assistance and economic aid should be designed primarily to benefit the people of underdeveloped countries and their economies rather than to serve political or military purposes. For maximum effectiveness, it is important that these programs be on a long-range basis. "The provision of development assistance should be conditioned on the undertaking of land reform, equitable taxation, sound fiscal policies, and careful economic planning by the recipient countries. Strong encouragement should be given to the formation and growth of self-help institutions. "We endorse the principle of multilateral assistance, especially through the U.N., and urge upon the nations wholehearted and generous participation in 

U.N. development programs. The Bible and the history of mankind contain ample warning to affluent peoples who will not share their abundance." * 

*

I turn now from the official statement in order to add some words of interpretation and comment.

It is clear that the official leadership of the Methodist Church views the widening economic gap between the prosperous, developed nations and the less developed, poverty-stricken lands with grave concern for at least two reasons. 

First, as religious persons, the members of the Methodist General Conference are keenly aware of the abject poverty, the continual hunger, the blinding ignorance, and the chronic illness that afflict hundreds of millions of their fellow men. Churchmen have sought to meet these conditions and alleviate this suffering through missionary service and oversea relief for a century and more.

Today, Methodist leaders believe that the needs are of such great proportions that economic assistance on a scale available only to the governments of the developed nations is essential if any significant impression is to be made on the problem. They also believe that the expression of compassion for human suffering ought not be limited to church channels but can properly be expressed through government as well. Virtually everyone supports the extension of emergency aid by governments to the victims of disasters. Surely, human suffering is no less real nor should it be less compelling because it is chronic rather than temporary. 

Methodist leaders also are convinced that the growing gap between "the rich nations and the poor nations" is fraught with danger. The continuance and the widening of this gap not only threaten the political stability and economic progress of the world but also constitute a serious obstacle to the creation of the conditions needed for the maintenance of peace. This is why the general conference looks at economic assistance as a matter of "practical international brotherhood."

The official leaders of the Methodist Church have expressed their conviction that "technical assistance and economic aid should be designed primarily to benefit the people of underdeveloped countries and their economies rather than to serve political or military purposes. Obviously, no complete separation of purposes is possible. Nevertheless, one step in this direction that can and should be taken is to separate the authorization and appropriation bills for economic aid from those for military assistance. 

The Methodist General Conference also stressed the importance of aid programs being put on a long-range basis for maximum effectiveness. While some nations may not need assistance for more than a few years, there are several, including a few very large ones, which will require efforts lasting many years if any appreciable improvement is to result. Surely, this is a case where the United 

States should not weary of well-doing, and because the job is worth doing, it should be done well. 

Finally, I wish to point out the endorsement by the Methodist General Conference of the principle of multilateral assistance. It is not suggested that this should be to the exclusion of bilateral aid. However, there are many advantages to United Nations and other multilateral programs, including the increasing involvement of other developed lands, the disentanglement of assistance from bilateral political issues, and the strengthening of international organization. 

May I express again our appreciation for this opportunity to present the official statement of the Methodist Church and to add these words of comment. 

STATEMENT OF THE NATIONAL RURAL ELECTRIC COOPERATIVE ASSOCIATION 

Mr. Chairman and gentlemen of the committee, my name is Robert D. Partridge.

I am the legislative representative for the National Rural Electric Cooperative Association. NRECA is the national service organization of 977 rural electric systems operating in 46 States. These rural electric systems operate on a nonprofit basis, providing electric service to farm and other rural consumers in 2,700 of the Nation's 3,200 counties. NRECA is a nonprofit cooperative, providing its members with legislative, management, information, and insurance services. 

Membership in NRECA is entitrely voluntary.

In our statement to your committee last year, we described the development since 1961 of NRECA participation in the program of the Agency for International Development. Our members have been active participants in the effective development in this country of cooperatives as the principal means of accomplishing area coverage rural electrification. We have long held the view that the cooperative REA pattern is adaptable to the needs of other countries, and that for most of the developing countries, cooperatives afford the best

. form of business organization for accomplishing many of the economic and social goals of our AID program. 

The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 includes a declaration of policy placed in the act by an amendment proposed by the then senior Senator from Minnesota, Hubert Humphrey, which reads as follows: "It is declared to be the policy of the United States to encourage the development and use of cooperatives, credit unions, and savings and loan associations." NRECA supported this policy statement, and we are proud to have taken part over the past 4 years in its implementation.

Until late 1962, NRECA assisted in the AID program on an informal basis. 

On November 1, 1962, an NRECA-AID contract was signed in President Kennedy's 

Office. Substantial progress has been made in developing feasible plans for rural electrification cooperatives in several Latin American countries, and we are beginning work in other areas of the world. We have undertaken this work on a nonprofit basis; AID pays only reasonable and necessary expenses incurred. 

More than 40 people from NRECA and its member systems have completed assignments of various terms abroad in this joint program with AID. A summary of our efforts to date is as follows:
