NOTE. In addition to the principal specialists listed by country, the following have assisted in one or more countries: Clyde T. Ellis, general manager NRECA; 

Robert I. Kabat, director NRECA, management services department; James E. 

Ross, former coordinator, Latin American program; Thomas M. Venables, coordinator, AID-NRECA, global contract program; Leon E. Evans, administrator, AID-RECA, Latin American program. 

The progress being made in exporting the REA pattern abroad is evident when one examines the status of efforts underway in the 17 countries listed above. 

1 Now being worked.

In a few countries, the work has progressed to the point that substantial numbers of rural people will soon receive electric service. Rural electric cooperative systems are under construction with AID loan funds in Nicaragua and in Ecuador. 

Another rural electric sysetm is in actual operation in Columbia, although AID loan funds for additional construction and extension of service has not yet been released. An AID loan has been approved in Chile, where 14 small rural electric cooperatives were already in existence. A loan application has also been made to AID for three rural electric cooperatives in Costa Rica, and AID expects to take action on these during fiscal year 1965. 

The use of cooperating country funds to develop electric cooperatives, following technical assistance provided by NRECA under the AID contract, is a relatively new and encouraging development. The experience in Venezuela is illustrative. 

The AID mission in Venezuela provided a technical assistance grant in 1964 for an NRECA specialist to make a survey of Venezuela to determine the possibilities for developing rural electric cooperatives. Mr. Paul Richter, manager, Todd-Wadena Electric Cooperative, Wadena, Minn., was selected for the task. 

Mr. Richter recommended two areas in Venezuela as being most feasible for rural electric cooperatives, one near Lake Maracaibo and one near the Carribean coasts. After careful consideration by the Venezuelan Government, that Government has decided to make funds available for the development of these two electric cooperatives. USAID/Venezuela is providing a four-man team under the 

NRECA contract to organize the two cooperatives, make engineering studies to determine feasibility, and to develop the loan application for consideration by the appropriate agencies of the Venezuelan Government. 

The Venezuelan solution to rural electrification needs is one which AID and we hope will occur in every area of Latin America; that is, the indigenous governments funding such development programs as rural electrification and executing them with the necessary technical assistance provided through AID. 

The rural electric cooperative organized at Santo Domingo, Ecuador in 1963 is one from which worthwhile operating experience has already been derived. 

The cooperative began operation of a small existing electric plant in March 1964 and has now completed 1 year of operation. The benefits to the small rural community served by this cooperative are amazing. Electric service is now available around the clock, instead of a few hours a day, as had previously been the The revenues of the cooperative have increased substantially without a corresponding increase in operating expenses. With 24-hour electric service available, new industries have begun to develop. A half-dozen small industries are taking electric service from the cooperative. case.

The Santo Domingo cooperative has increased its consumers from 350 to 650 without the use of AID loan funds. This has been made possible through assistance provided by rural electric cooperatives in Kentucky, who donated more than 40,000 pounds of line materials and equipment to the Ecuadorian cooperative. This material was in good, usable condition but was obsolete so far as the 

Kentucky co-ops were concerned, because their loads had grown beyond the capacities of the transformers and other items. The way was cleared for the transportation of this material from Louisville, Ky., to Santo Domingo, Ecuador without charge, as truck drivers and a banana company volunteered their services along the way. 

This assistance has enabled the cooperative to near the break-even point on its operations, in contrast to the earlier expectation that the cooperative would have a substantial deficit during its first 12 months of operaion. The development of this cooperative to its present operational status has established a sound base for the further expansion of the cooperative to reach additional rural people presently without electric service. 

Our specialists who have visited the Santo Domingo cooperative report the enthusiasm of the people for the cooperative which is providing good electric service at reasonable rates. The same contagious enthusiasm for rural electrification is reported by many who have been in other AID mission countries. People are anxious to do something for themselves, particularly as regards rural electrification and the adaptation of the REA program as we know it in the United States to their needs. 

Training is an important part of the work we are doing in Latin America. 

Training begins with the work which our specialists do when they are assigned to various phases of these rural electrification projects abroad. We have also participated in training which is conducted in this country. In July 1963, 12 1

prominent Latin American leaders, active in cooperatives in their own countries, completed the first AID-supported training program. A similar training program was conducted in 1964, and included participants from India and Ethiopia in addition to the Latin Americans. This training program is sponsored jointly by AID, NRECA, REA, and the International Cooperative Training Center at the University of Wisconsin. The course provides foreign specialists an opportunity to study American cooperatives and the REA pattern firsthand. In addition to classroom study, the participants receive training at rural electric cooperatives in the United States. The NRECA Management Services 

Department has designed institutes to meet the needs of these specialists as regards management principles, tools, and techniques. 

The heartening experience in developing rural electricfication in Latin America has stirred considerable interest in other areas of the world. NRECA has received numerous inquiries from African and Asian countries, as have the AID missions in those countries. Several of the African and Asian countries show promise for adaptation of the Latin American experience in developing rural electrification; these include South Korea, Taiwan, the Philippines, Thailand, India, Nigeria, Liberia, Sierra Leone, Tunisia, and other established and stable countries on the two continents, CONCLUSION 

Our rural electric cooperative leaders who have been in Latin America have been particularly impressed with the determination of rural people in those countries to develop cooperatives as a means of providing themselves with electric service. Electricity has a very high priority in the scale of goods and services desired by most Latin Americans, and understandably so, because of the great improvements in living conditions which electricity makes possible. The work under the AID-NRECA agreement has received enthusiastic acceptance in all areas of Latin America in which the program operates. 

We believe that the successful experience in Latin America justifies the optimism we expressed to the committee last year, that the program has applicability in other areas of the world where we have a foreign aid program. 

Our objective continues to be to develop pilot rural electrification projects in these countries, as a demonstration to the people and to their governments that cooperative rural electrification can be accomplished; that it will increase the productivity of labor; that it will raise the level of living in the home and in the community; that it will foster democratic action by promoting individual participation in self-help activities; and that it will materially assist in carrying on effective programs in education, health, and other public services which these countries badly need. We are seeking to develop credit and service institutions similar to the REA, to extend the development of cooperative rural elec trification beyond the pilot project stage. 

The people from this country who have served abroad under the AID-NRECA agreement have witnessed firsthand the effectiveness and the importance of our AID efforts abroad. They are doing an effective job of telling the story of this worthwhile effort to people in their home communities upon their return. 

Twenty-four of those who have returned from foreign assignments and who are employed by rural electric systems have spoken to more than 47,000 people, have been or more than 160 radio programs, and have had more than 400 newspaper articles written about their assignments and experiences. 

The initial projects in Latin America are showing the way for others to follow. 

We believe that other countries will follow the example of Venezuela in providing assistance to accomplish rural electrification, and that the primary need for assistance in these countries will continue to be the technical assistance and know-how which we are providing under our AID contract. At the same time, we recognize that there will be cases in which the indigenous government cannot provide the loan funds required for rural electrification projects, and that there will be a need in those instances for financial assistance from AID. 

We believe that very few development programs match rural electrification in respect of the widespread and immediate benefits to people. Cooperative rural electrification is making a unique and successful contribution in our foreign aid efforts, and we respectfully urge the members of this committee to give continued consideration to the cooperative approach in making all aspects of the foreign aid program more effective.

STATEMENT BY COMMITTEE FOR INTERNATIONAL HOUSING THROUGH PRIVATE INVESTMENT 

Mr. Chairman, I am Abner Sibal, an attorney with offices in Norwalk, Conn., and Washington, D.C. I am most appreciative of the opportunity which this committee has given to me to appear this morning as counsel for the Committee for International Housing Through Private Investment.

This committee, very recently organized, is only now in the process of formation. As its name implies, the committee is concerned with the encouragement of privately supported housing projects, particularly in less developed nations. 

Our committee at the moment is enlisting private home builders, investment bankers, mortgage bankers, and representatives of long-term lending institutions. We are hopeful that as the work of the committee increases, we will encourage membership from people in the academic community, interested sociologists and economists, private citizens who are interested in the private development of additional housing in less developed nations, and others who may be engaged in the business of building and financing homes overseas. 

I have some idea, Mr. Chairman, of the difficulties in Congress of bringing out of committee this early in the session a major piece of legislation. I want to congratulate your committee on having moved this year so rapidly in bringing the Foreign Assistance Act of 1965 to this point with only 2 months of the session having passed. 

Our interest in the bill which your committee is considering relates specifically to the continuation of authorization for investment guarantees for self-liquidat-

ing housing projects in Latin America nations, so-called section 224 guarantees, and the use of authorization under section 221(b) for housing guaranties in other areas. The specific sections of the bill to which my comments this morning are addressed are contained in title 3, section 103 (e) beginning on line 17 of page 4 of the committee print and section 221(b) (2) referred to in section 103 (a) begining on line 1 page 3 of the bill. 

Our committee's interest in these sections of the bill is twofold. First, since most of the individuals and businesses who are participating in the formation of this committee are in the business of building or financing homes, we are understandably concerned with continuing and expanding commercial opportunities for American businessmen abroad. Secondly, we are deeply impressed with the magnificent way in which section 224 has in the brief period since the program was begun in 1961 helped demonstrate in less-developed countries in Latin America some of the great strengths of the private enterprise system as applied to one of the most basic needs of all nations-housing. 

I know that it is unnecessary to remind this committee that the section 224 Latin American housing guarantees provision was initiated by the Congress having been added to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 by amendment. The amendment was aimed at introducing into Latin American nations financing arrangements heretofore unknown in Latin America whereby private longterm home financing would be available to middle class families of a type similar to that insured by the Federal Housing Administration in this country. 

The program differed significantly from almost all other Alliance for Progress programs in the housing field, most of which were aimed at slum clearance and low-cost housing projects financed with appropriated funds. It was intended to provide moderately priced houses for those individuals with some savings and steady employment who could afford fixed monthly payments to purchase their own home. While public housing projects can be built on a government-to-government aid basis, it was conceived that through this FHAtype housing financing, the private sector could assume its proper responsibility in attempting to meet the housing deficit in Latin America-currently estimated at 4 million dwelling units. In the original Senate floor debate on this provision, Senator Smathers explained the objectives of this legislation: "One other factor which I feel is of extreme importance, and which the pending amendment is designed to accomplish, is a stimulation of private homeownership and the encouragement of free enterprise in the American Republics. In this way our foreign aid will operate on a people-to-people basis. "This, in my opinion, is a most effective way to combat the Communist economic offensive which poses such a threat to not only Latin America but to the security and economic well-being of all the Americas." 

The success of the program to date, Mr. Chairman, has more than vindicated the vision and wisdom of its original congressional authors. In testimony before the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate just last year, William D. 

Rogers, Deputy U.S. Coordinator of the Alliance for Progress stated: "Although the program excited little attention in the early months following its enactment in 1961, through 1962 and particularly 1963, there was increasing interest among builders in the United States. By the summer of 1963, applications on hand had risen to more than $200 million, even before AID's authority was raised to the $150 million level." 

Mr. Rogers went on to explain that in order to handle the rapidly increasing volume of applications, a permanent staff had been established in AID and detailed arrangements had been concluded with the Federal Housing Administration in order that FHA could provide technical services in determining the feasibility and eligibility of projects. Mr. Rogers indicated in his testimony that AID had received complete cooperation from FHA and that the new arrangements for processing were working "extremely well." He noted that the first homes had been delivered to homeowners in Lima, Peru, and that over 5,000 units were under construction in Peru, Colombia, and Mexico only 2% years after the program was initiated. The Senate committee report on the Foreign 

Assistance Act of 1964 which granted $100 million in additional authority noted with approval the progress made to date on section 224 housing and at the conclusion of its report on this section of the bill stated that "the committee hopes that this program will be pushed more vigorously." 

As of last December, 10 projects with over 12,000 dwelling units were under construction, approximately 25 percent of which had been completed and sold.

All that has been accomplished by this program to date, it should be noted, has been accomplished without the investment of a single U.S. tax dollar. We are talking solely about the investment of private funds from U.S. private financing sources in the construction of private projects. There is every reason to believe, in fact, that the program, rather than costing the U.S. Treasury, will actually return a profit through the payment of the 2 percent guarantee fee. 

It is our belief, Mr. Chairman, that no program more effectively demonstrates the advantages of the U.S. private enterprise system than the section 224 housing guarantee program. It is our feeling also that there is no more basic and fundamental need than to supply decent housing at a reasonable cost for persons in less well developed nations. We could not even hope to scratch the surface of the housing needs of these countries if we were to double or even triple the amounts of U.S. Government funds that we invest in public housing projects nor would we meet the pressing demands of the middle class. By the introduction of techniques and methods for private home construction through long-term financing, however, we may in the long run assist these nations to help themselves in overcoming their tremendous housing shortages. If we are successful in encouraging the establishment of long-term financing facilities, then the return on the investment which we make through section 224 housing may be multiplied many times over in these countries. 

It is important to remember also that the concept that we are introducing has very real political implications in encouraging free democratic institutions in the countries affected, particularly for the middle class which has such a profound influence on a nation's economic and political destiny. When a man buys a home, as distinguished from renting in a public housing project, he is making an investment in his country as well. He becomes concerned with the preservation of private property values. He becomes concerned with the stability of his country's government and of his country's economy. He becomes in a very real sense a private capitalist. This point was very well made in a report entitled "A Study of International Housing" by Rodman C. Rockefeller, a part of the 

1963 Senate Banking and Currency Committee Symposium on Housing. 

"In many cases, these damaging impacts of the cruel housing shortage are most keenly felt by the very groups that the U.S. effort is most anxious to reach, the struggling middle class whose whole future may be blighted by lack of a decent home. The middle class is universally the leadership class, if not of the present, then certainly of the future. It shares certain expectations and certain aspirations, which if frustrated can turn it antidemocratic, radical, and revolutionary. This is the group of which private action is best designed." 

In a report entitled "Types of Assistance Programs" by Don L. Dise, part of the same symposium, it was noted that: "The middle-income group, which in most less-developed countries is rapidly expanding in number, is capable, anxious and willing to purchase a home if a good home were available at a reasonable price and on reasonable terms. For many reasons this middle-income group should be among the first to be considered for housing. The upper income group already is being taken care of by existing means. "By providing housing for the middle-income group, employment would be provided for large portions of the lower income groups, enabling them to eventually purchase homes of their own. "The middle-income group, which is intelligent, educated, and employed, is also among the most effective agitators of leftwing movements against existing free governments, brought about in most cases by dissatisfaction with the deplorable living conditions in which this group is forced to exist.” 

In a third report in the symposium, Norman P. Mason, formerly Administrator of the Federal Housing Administration, pointed out: "These countries (South American) need, most of all, political and economic stability. In the light of present social trends, this sort of stability will come only if there is created an ability on the part of the common person, the great middle class, economically, the ability to be owners of real property. Only through such a group can we have pressures executed on political leaders to preserve values. *** The major part of our effort should be to assist in the building of housing for the rapidly developing middle-income group.' 

In the ultimate transition of the Alliance for Progress from a purely government-to-government aid arrangement to one which encourages private economic activity, section 224 housing can perform an invaluable service. 

I ask your permission, Mr. Chairman, to insert at this point in my remarks an editorial 99 44-834-65- -44

which appeared in the New York Times of December 10, 1964, which noted with approval the fact that the Alliance was beginning to invite an increasing contribution of private investment, both domestic and foreign. 

I would also like to ask your permission, Mr. Chairman, to insert in my remarks an article which appeared in the Wall Street Journal of February 16 of this year which very well describes the increasing interest on the part of the U.S. home construction industry in building private homes abroad and in meeting the tremendous housing shortage of Latin America. 

The account is especially significant in that it points out areas in which U.S. industry can participate in the growing foreign home market. 

You have before you in the committee print of the bill which will become the Foreign Assistance Act of 1965, authorization for the continuation of this program but in a very significantly modified form. These modifications which are contained in the bill before you would for all practical purposes eliminate the section 224 program as it exists today as an FHA-type insured housing program. All that has been accomplished to date will be for naught if your committee continues the guarantee program only in the modified form proposed in the bill. The bill at present calls for an additional $100 million of guarantee authority but specifically to be used for local mortgage financing institutions, low-cost housing projects sponsored by cooperatives or labor unions, and projects involving substantial local financial participation with a unit price ceiling of $6,500. The bill in fact specifically eliminates further authorization under subsection (b) (1), the kind of projects I have been describing this morning, even though the entire $250 million which has been authorized to date for these types of projects has been substantially exhausted. We are not questioning the merits of the new types of guarantee authority. In fact, I want to compliment the American Institute for Free Labor Development for the tremendous job which it has done in this program to date. To continue or expand labor union activity in this field is undoubtedly of great merit. Whatever the merits may be of the new types of guarantee authority contemplated in the committee print, it seems to us disastrously shortsighted to eliminate entirely the privately sponsored, privately built, middle-income housing projects of the kind that have been so successfully undertaken to date under the authority of section 224. We urge, therefore, that the committee grant an additional $100 million of guarantee authority for projects described in the bill in section 224 as "similar to those insured by the Federal Housing Administration." We ask, in effect, that the committee continue authority for middle-income housing projects on the same basis that the amendment was originally sponsored in the Congress in 1961 and on the same basis it has been renewed and increased by the Congress each year since. There is nothing in the present program that argues other than for its continuation on an ever-increasing basis. 

We recommend also that the committee urge the AID to allocate an additional $50 million of the $300 million of loan guarantee authority presently contained in section 221 (b) (2) of the Foreign Assistance Act for housing projects in areas other than Latin America. At present, $50 million of the $300 million authorized under this section has been reserved for housing. 

It may be argued that the bill in its present form would still permit private U.S. homebuilders and private financing institutions to participate in the program through the authority which provides for construction in accordance with a maximum unit cost, proposed by AID at $6,500 per unit. In many instances, middle-class housing may be constructed within this limitation or, in fact, at even lower costs. In many other instances, however, this limitation would prove wholly unrealistic and unworkable. Such an inflexible limitation overlooks the fact that this is a privately sponsored housing program, designed for middleincome families, who are capable of purchasing their own homes. This is not a question of public charity or of government-to-government grants. In evaluating the feasibility, and most important the salability, of the housing to be constructed, the laws of the market as in any other private undertaking must govern. As Mr. 

Rockefeller pointed out in the study of international housing: "We are speaking of the need for freedom, not assistance. Neither U.S. private enterprise, nor local private enterprise can be considered assistance." 

We are not in the slightest unmindful of the serious problem of our balanceof-payments deficit. I know that it is a matter of great concern to your committee as you shape the authorization of our foreign assistance programs in the coming year. In his balance-of-payments message on February 10, 1965, the 

President made it clear, however, that it is our national policy to encourage an increasing flow of private investment to the developing nations of the world.

The President noted that there was little adverse impact on the balance-ofpayments problem as a result of such investments. Net capital outflow to the developing nations is less than one-quarter of our total capital outflow. It should be noted also as you consider the continuation of section 224 guarantees that while this program does involve an outflow of capital, it is in the form of loans rather than grants. Every dollar which flows out of the country as a result of this program will ultimately return with interest. Moreover, it is a flow of private capital rather than Govenment funds. Much of it can and does return to the United States in terms of purchases from U.S. manufacturers. 

Most importantly, this program has no more adverse effect, perhaps even less, than any other form of foreign assistance. There is no more logic to curtailing this program than there would be to curtailing any other aspect of our foreign aid program. The significant difference here is that we are concerned with private investment and private dollars, not government-to-government aid or U.S. 

Treasury funds.

This statute, Mr. Chairman, is an attempt to encourage private homeownership through long-term financing in countries which do not have the local institutions or resources to accomplish it themselves. It is an attempt to encourage the lowest income group which is capable of purchasing its own home to do so. It is an attempt to encourage a sense of values and a sense of responsibility among middle-income families. It is an attempt to export American know-how both in methods of mass home production and in financing and to encourage other nations to develop this know-how themselves. Viewed in the light of its short life to date, it has been an enormous success. American builders and American financing institutions have responded nobly to help meet the middleclass private home needs of Latin America. 

We submit, Mr. Chairman, that it would be a terrible defeat to the cause of encouraging and expanding private enterprise in the less developed nations of Latin America to permit this program now to fail. We urge you to continue the housing guarantee program in its present form, whether additional modified proposals are undertaken or not, at least at its present level of authority. We submit that American private industry has proven that it is ready and willing to step up to the challenge and to meet its responsibility toward private economic development in Latin America. 

Hon. J. W. FULBRIGHT, AMERICAN FARM BUREAU FEDERATION, 

Washington, D.C., April 2, 1965.

STATEMENT OF THE AMERICAN FARM BUREAU FEDERATION WITH REGARD TO THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT OF 1965 

(Presented by John C. Lynn, legislative director, and Gustave Burmeister, assistant legislative director) We appreciate the opportunity to present the views of the American Farm Bureau Federation with respect to authorizations for the fiscal 1966 foreign aid program. The new spending authority requested (NOA) in the budget message totals $3.4 billion ($2.2 billion for economic aid and $1.2 billion for military assistance). This amount compares with $3.5 billion authorized and $3.2 billion appropriated by the Congress for fiscal 1965. 

Farm Bureau is the largest farm organization with a voluntary paid membership of over 1,647,000 families in over 2,750 county farm bureaus in 49 States

and Puerto Rico. These families are much concerned, as are many other groups of citizens, with respect to Federal budget deficits, the national debt, our balance of payments, and foreign policy decisions because all of these problems have a direct bearing on their well-being and prosperity. Through a program of policy development at county, State, and National levels, they have given thoughtful consideration to these problems and the official voting delegates of the member 

State farm bureaus concluded in part as follows: 

The United States is an example of the progress possible in a free society. 

Our assistance to underdeveloped nations should be based on long-range plans carefully prepared and agreed to by the underdeveloped nations with proper consideration of their ability to utilize this aid. 

Requests for foreign aid funds should be justified, nation by nation, and presented to Congress for approval. Congress should authorize appropriations on an annual basis only after careful review and reevaluation of the progress of the plans. Such a program of assistance should be designed to aid those whose allegiance is to the free world and whose governments oppose international communism.

We believe future commitments should be predicated upon : (1) A well defined program to provide technical assistance at a level consistent with each nation's current stage of development; (2) Granting loans on the basis of sound commercial standards when there is reasonable expectation of repayment; (3) Continued military assistance where this is determined to be essential to nations demonstrating a strong will to resist Communist aggression; and (4) An overall plan designed to make clear the source of the aid and the economic system that made it possible. 

The Peace Corps should be an integral part of our foreign technical assistance effort, with emphasis on selection of volunteers who have practical experience and training. Careful training of volunteers is essential and should include special emphasis on courses which will enable and inspire them to explain and defend the American private competitive enterprise system. 

The above policy resolution reflects a strong belief that major changes should be made in the magnitude and direction of our foreign aid effort. Our specific recommendations are designed to make a start in this direction. 

We believe that the Congress should continue both its review and its direction of the operation of this program. 

It is evident that aid continues to have difficulty in developing sound programs based upon the needs and desires of the recipient countries and the foreign policy objectives of the United States. It appears that there still are excess funds in the pipeline and that a further tightening of requirements and expenditures: can be made.

Experience clearly demonstrates that we cannot buy friends and cooperation with money and that we cannot remake people or governments in our own image. 

We should continue to try to help those who need and want our help, providing only such amounts as they can use efficiently and effectively. 

We should give assistance only on the basis of soundly conceived plans that show good possibilities of achievement.

We should insist that private enterprise, both domestic and foreign, be encouraged in countries that are seeking aid for economic development. 

We should continue to insist that our economically strong allies assume the aid responsibility for the areas where they have a major trading and political interest.

We believe that the money should be fitting to the plans, rather than the plans. to the money.

MILITARY ASSISTANCE 

Last year we raised the question with respect to whether military assistanceshould be included as a part of the foreign aid program or as a part of the appropriation for national defense. We note that the responsibility, operations, and funds have been transferred to the Department of Defense. We recommend again that all foreign military assistance be made part of our overall defense program. 

Most of the military assistance is to countries on the periphery of the Communist bloc. Greater care must be taken to limit this aid to countries which are willing and able to fight for freedom and against Communist aggression. For

example, Indonesia, Egypt, and Syria have taken our assistance and then moved definitely toward close cooperation with the Communists. 

In view of this situation, we recommend that the military assistance program be carefully reappraised and that for fiscal 1966 the authorization be reduced to $900 million. It is our belief that this amount, together with the unexpended balance, will be ample to cover all requirements. We note that the President, in his message to Congress, said that if more funds should be needed he would not hesitate to request a supplemental authorization. 

DEVELOPMENT LOANS 

The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, included an authorization for development loans, totaling $1.5 billion for each of the fiscal years 1965 and 

1966. However, for fiscal 1966, the administration estimates that only $780 million will be needed-about the same as was appropriated for fiscal 1965-but about one-half the amount authorized in advance. Despite the sharp cuts in appropriations in recent years the unobligated balance at the beginning of fiscal 1966 is estimated at $468 million. Thus, it is evident that the loan program is not nearly as large as indicated by the budget request. 

Under this program, repayments of loans and interest earned remain in the fund for future loans. Repayments plus annual increments from new appropriations have created a capital loan fund of more than $4 billion. 

It is interesting to note that the United States has six major direct foreign aid loan programs in operation with loans outstanding totaling about $10 billion as of the end of fiscal 1964. By the end of fiscal 1966, this total is scheduled to exceed $13 billion. The programs are as follows:

In addition, there are available funds of the Eximbank, totaling $9 billion, and the dollar pledges of the United States as capital to the International Monetary Fund, the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development, the International Development Association, the International Finance Corporation, and the Inter-American Development Bank, which add to a total of $16.3 billion. Therefore, in all of these institutions there is slightly more than $25 billion of U.S. public funds available for foreign assistance loans. The interest earned and repayments from loans by all of these institutions are available for reloaning. Also there is about $500 million of Public Law 480 foreign currencies becoming available annually for loans to recipient countries, and $400 million for grants. 

On the basis of the administration's request and the unobligated balance, new development loan obligations for fiscal 1966 totaling $867 million are planned. 

This compares with $848 million scheduled for fiscal 1965 and $845 million actually obligated in fiscal 1964. We believe that the development loan program can be held to a much lower level and that the estimated unobligated balances totaling $468 million, can be reduced. If these suggestions are followed, a new authorization of $500 million should be ample for fiscal 1966. 

ALLIANCE FOR PROGRESS 

The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, included an authorization for the Alliance for Progress totaling $600 million per year through fiscal 1966 with the proviso that not to exceed $100 million shall be available for grant

aid. It is now proposed that the latter figure be changed to $85 million for fiscal 1965 and 1966. The spending authority requested totals $580 million for fiscal 1966 compared with $510 million appropriated for fiscal 1965. Since $85 million is set aside as grant funds, the amount requested for development loans totals $495 million for fiscal 1966 compared with $425 million appropriated for fiscal 1965 and $375 million for fiscal 1964. 

In addition to the authorizations and appropriations for grants and loans given above, a total of $2.2 billion has been provided for loans through the 

Inter-American Development Bank since the beginning of the Alliance for Progress to date. This amount includes the recently enacted $750 million increase in the Bank's fund for special operations. 

In fiscal 1964 about $310 million was obligated for new loans, and it is planned that the level will be increased to about $434 million in fiscal 1965 and to $546 million in fiscal 1966. We believe that conditions do not warrant such a rapid increase, and we recommend that the level be no higher than $400 million. 

On this basis, the loan program can be financed with new obligational authority of about $300 million plus a reduction of about $100 million in the unobligated balance which is estimated at $265 million. For grant aid we recommend $50 million.

We also believe that American private enterprise could supply nearly all of the development capital required if the Latin American governments provided a favorable climate. This would be particularly true if private enterprise was encouraged to use the increased loan resources of the Inter-American Development Bank.

ECONOMIC GRANTS 

The economic grant program includes funds for technical cooperation and economic development, American schools and hospitals abroad, supporting assistance, contingency fund, the Alliance for Progress (grant programs), international organizations, and administrative expenses. 

The spending authority requested for these categories totals $935 million, or $61 million less than was appropriated for fiscal 1965, but about the same as appropriated for fiscal 1964. 

It is noted that $210 million is included for development grants for other than the Alliance for Progress, $369 million for supporting assistance, $50 million for the contingency fund, and $7 million for American schools and hospitals abroad, or a total of $636 million for these four categories. Since these funds actually are used for practically the same purposes, we recommended last year that they be merged into one fund and labeled as "development grants." We so recommend again, and suggest that the authorization for fiscal 1966 be reduced to $400 million. It should be noted that this amount, together with a large carryover, will be more than adequate to cover the anticipated expenditures in fiscal 1966, totaling about $677 million. It is necessary to reduce new spending authority now in order to bring the program level down in the future. 

Development grants are intended primarily for technical assistance, demonstration, and training to provide the developing countries the knowledge with which to increase their standard of living. This program has been in progress in many countries for more than a decade, but it is difficult to measure how much has been achieved. 

The Peace Corps apparently is popular in the developing countries. We believe that it is serving much the same purposes as the old technical assistance program and that in some cases it is more effective and efficient. 

Last year we suggested that these programs be combined so that similar functions in the same country can be coordinated. We again so recommend. 

Supporting assistance is another form of development grant made to bolster the economy and political stability of countries receiving military assistance. 

It is indicated that most of these funds are spent in three countries-South Korea, Vietnam, and Jordan. This means that these countries received large amounts from this source in fiscal 1965 which, together with a large input of military aid, make them heavily dependent on the United States. Now it appears that, with the exception of Vietnam, conditions have improved sufficiently that our contributions can be sharply reduced in this area in fiscal 1966. 

We strongly recommend that the programing of grant aid be made on the basis of a sound plan for each country where there is a real need and that funds

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 687 1965 be provided only to fit the plan. If this were done, there would be little need for a large contingency fund. The President said in his message that if a critical need arose, especially in Vietnam, he would not hesitate to come back to Congress with a supplemental request. Thus the contingency fund can be reduced to a minimum. 

The request includes $156 million to be contributed by the United States to international organizations for various and sundry purposes. For fiscal 1966 it is proposed that the U.S. contribution to the United Nations expanded program of technical assistance and the Special Fund, and to the Indus Basin Development Fund be increased. Other programs included here are the United Nations 

Relief and Works Agency, United Nations Children's Fund, and the World food program. It should be noted that many of these programs duplicate our own bilateral aid programs. Also it should be noted that planned expenditures in fiscal 1966 total only $105 million. We believe that the carryover and $80 million of new spending authority will be ample for fiscal 1966. We should effectively resist the attempts of a large number of small countries, which contribute a small proportion of the funds, to extend and enlarge these programs over the objections of those contributing the major share. 

TRANSFER OF THE FOOD-FOR-PEACE PROGRAM 

Last year we recommended that the authorization and appropriation for title II (Public Law 480) donations be transferred from the Department of Agriculture to AID. The voting delegates of the American Farm Bureau Federation at the annual meeting in Philadelphia in December 1964 adopted the following policy on the subject: 

If food and fiber aid is to be continued as an insturment of foreign policy— (1) Programing should be based on the needs of recipient countries; and (2) Aid should be extended in the form of authorizations to purchase commodities on the open market. Under this approach the Government's requirements for aid would become a part of the market demand, and needed supplies would be produced in response to market prices. The cost of such programing should be subject to foreign aid appropriations and not charged to agriculture.

In December 1963 President Lyndon B. Johnson said— 

"Now, on a world scale, the time has come, as it came to America 30 years ago, for a new era of hope-hope and progress for that one-third of mankind still beset by hunger, poverty, and disease. Any man and any nation that seeks peace and hates war-and is willing to fight the good fight against hunger and disease and ignorance and misery-will find the United States of America by their side, willing to walk with them every step of the way." 99 1 

The Honorable Richard W. Reuter, Special Assistant to the President, director, food-for-peace, included the following statement in a memorandum for the President dated September 11, 1964 : "***We have learned during this first decade that- "Our food is a potent force in relieving chronic hunger and malnutrition and in meeting emergencies and postdisaster situations. "Our food, through prudent planning, can provide price stability in basic commodities and help prevent inflation in developing countries. "Foreign currencies generated by the sale of our food can be an integral part of economic development. They also can be used to pay 

U.S. bills overseas which strengthens our balance-of-payments position. "Our food can be bartered for materials, services, and supplies needed by our Government. "Our food can strengthen and enlarge the humanitarian programs of 

U.S. voluntary agencies overseas. 

"Our food can be used as an incentive to motivate people to help themselves in building their own free societies. "And, in the process of all this, our foods can build future markets for the produce of the American farmer * * *"2 

1 20th Semiannual Report on Public Law 480-H. Doc. 365-88/2, p. 9. 

2 20th Semiannual Report on Public Law 480-H. Doc. 365-88/2, p. 3.

From these statements it is clear that the food-for-peace program is for all practical purposes a foreign aid program. It has become an important tool of foreign policy, and has become less and less a surplus disposal or foreign agricultural market development operation. Agricultural commodity aid provided through Public Law 480 represented 47 percent of total net U.S. economic aid supplied to underdeveloped countries in fiscal 1963. 

The shift of appropriations and program responsibility to AID is especially important at this time because of probable changes in Government farm programs. For example, if new legislation transferred a large portion of CCC stocks to a security reserve, and the price support program was changed so that the "trade" carried more of the current stocks, USDA should have only a small part to play in Public Law 480 operations. The agricultural commodities exported under Public Law 480 programs, except title III donations, will be purchased in the market rather than obtained from Government stocks. 

We believe that under these circumstances funds for these purposes should be appropriated directly to AID and that AID should have the responsibility for developing and carrying out the food-for-peace program. 

The spending authority requested for the four titles of Public Law 480 for fiscal 1966 totals $1,710 million compared with the adjusted total for fiscal 1965 of $2,410 million. Details by titles follow:

CONCLUSION 

With the transfer of the appropriation for Public Law 480, totaling $1,710 million, and our proposed authorizations for economic assistance for AID, totaling $1,380 million, there would be available to AID for foreign economic assistance a total of $3,090 million for fiscal 1966. If the foreign military assistance is added, the grand total would be $3,990 million. 

We strongly believe that a country-by-country analysis of the economic assistance programs will show that the United States can curtail its financial contributions abroad. Our recommendations are for reduced spending authority, because we believe that the United States should retrench its programs in many countries where our aid is either not wanted or is no longer needed. 

Because of the huge carryover of funds, it will take several more years to bring annual expenditures into line with the program level which we have proposed. 

We firmly believe that the Congress should carefully consider the problem and move decisively in this direction.

The second part of the table deals with U.S. contributions to the Inter-American Development Bank, the International Development Association, international institutions, the International Monetary Fund, and the food-for-peace program. 

The following comments are pertinent to each item: 

1. Inter-American Development Bank 

The table shows a total of $705,880,000. This is not correct. The total U.S. contribution to the Inter-American Development Bank for fiscal year 1966 is $250,000. The remainder shown in the table is for (a) $205,880,000 as a reserve or guarantee to the Bank to enable it to float bond issues. It is highly unlikely that this reserve would ever be used and it remains in the U.S. Treasury; and (b) $250,000,000 is a supplemental request for fiscal year 1965. This table purports to be a fiscal year 1966 table and thus this amount is erroneously included. 

2. International Development Association 

The table correctly shows that the proposed contribution of the United States to the International Development Association for fiscal year 1966 is $104,000,000. 

3. The International Monetary Fund 

The figure, of $1,031,250,000 should not be included in the table because (a). The 

IMF assists all countries with short-term, balance-of-payments assistance. It 691

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, does not extend development assistance; it is not an "aid" institution. For example, the United States draws funds from the IMF on occasion-in calendar year 1946, U.S. net drawings were $262 million; and (b) In any case, the item shown for the IMF is for fiscal year 1965, not fiscal year 1966. 

4. Food-for-peace program 

The figure shown for this program is correct. 

Public Law 480, which began as a program for the disposal of surplus food and fiber, makes a significant contribution to economic development. However, of the $1,658 million listed for food for peace, $357 million is for title IV sales repayable in dollars over a shorter period of time than development loans; and $200 million is local currencies for U.S. Government uses.

INTERNATIONAL INSTITUTIONS IN THE FIELD OF DEVELOPMENT FINANCE 

Whether or not, and when, our contributions to international development financing institutions have an effect on our balance of payments depends on a number of factors, including particularly the type and form in which our contribution is made. Where the capital structure of an institution involves socalled callable capital subscriptions, such subscriptions are neither paid in or expected to be paid in. They are callable, not to provide funds which may be lent, but only in the event the institution is unable to meet payments on its own obligations. They permit an institution to borrow in world financial markets, but because they involve no payment of funds, they have no direct effect on the U.S. balance of payments. Such callable capital arrangements exist in the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank. 

Where the capital structure of an institution involves paid-in subscriptions, some or all of the contribution may be made in the form of non-interest-bearing notes or letters of credit. Under such arrangements, the funds contributed have no immediate balance-of-payments effect. Because of the lag between the time an international institution commits funds for a project it is financing and the time it requires cash to meet disbursement on the project, actual cash drawings on the notes or letters of credit may not take place for some time and thus only enter the balance-of-payments statistics as a debit to international institutions well after the U.S. contribution has been formally made. It should also be noted that such future calls for cash would be made, not on the United States alone, but proportionately on the other contributors as well. Non-interest-bearing note and letter of credit arrangements exist in the International Development Association and the Inter-American Development Bank. 

Apart from the U.S. contributions to international institutions, the operating transactions of the institutions themselves affect the U.S. balance of payments in a variety of ways. Procurement of goods and services in the United States for projects financed by an international institution is reflected as an increase in U.S. exports and therefore benefits our balance of payments. U.S. companies may win procurement contracts on the basis of international competitive bidding or, as in the case of the Fund for Special Operations of the IDB, procurement with U.S. funds may be explicitly tied to U.S. goods and services. 

In addition to project procurement which may occur in the United States, the international institutions make administrative expenditures in the United States which benefit our balance of payments. If U.S. residents hold bonds issued by an international institution, interest payments on these bonds are a balance-of-payments inflow, against which must be balanced any interest payments to the institution on holdings of U.S. Government obligations and other 

U.S. investments. Although the international financial institutions that borrow on world financial markets use markets other than the United States to the maximum extent feasible, the effects on the U.S. balance of payments of such sales of obligations as do take place here are offset by investment of the pro-

ceeds in the United States pending disbursement. Finally, it should also be noted that transactions in dollars between international institutions and foreign governments do not affect our balance of payments, since they are simply transfers of dollar holdings from one category of foreign holder to another. 

Moreover, since the international financial institutions concerned with lending. for economic development.do not engage in gold transactions, shifts of foreignowned dollars to them tend to lessen potential calls on our gold. 

In terms of actual experience, the World Bank group of institutions, consisting of the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD), the International Finance Corporation (IFC) and the International Develop ment Association (IDA), has carried out its function of providing development financing without imposing any overall burden on the U.S. balance of payments. 

The transactions of the IBRD and IDA together have over the entire period of the existence of the two institutions, had a favorable total effect on the U.S. balance-of-payments position, particularly in the more recent period during which our balance-of-payments problem became serious. In fiscal year 1964, for example, the favorable combined effect of IBRD/IDA transactions totaled $209 million. This figure takes into account the various factors outlined above. 

Transactions of the International Finance Corporation are on a small scale and are considered to have had negligible balance-of-payments impact. 

Based on preliminary information for 1964, including only 6 months' data on procurement, the estimated effect on the U.S. balance of payments of the ordinary capital operations of the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) is an outflow of only about $15 million. This level of outflow is entirely compatible with overall balance-of-payments policy, particularly in view of the major role played by the Bank in the implementation of the Alliance for Progress program.

A similar preliminary estimate of the balance-of-payments effect of the Fund for Special Operations (FSO) of the IDB indicates that there was an outflow of less than $15 million in 1964. A new policy has been adopted covering the $750 million which the Congress recently authorized as the U.S. contribution over a 3-year period to an expansion of the FSO. Under the new policy, the 

U.S. funds would be tied to purchases of U.S. goods and services, so that 90 percent or more of the total will be spent in the United States. There is, therefore, assurance that the balance-of-payments effect of the operations of the expanded FSO will be minimal. 

THE AID RESEARCH AND ANALYSIS PROGRAM 

The charter of the research and analysis program, section 241 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, states: "The President is authorized to use funds made available for this part to carry out programs of research into, and evaluation of, the process of economic development in less developed friendly countries and areas, into the factors affecting the relative success and costs of development activities, and into the means, techniques, and such other aspects of development assistance as he may determine, in order to render such assistance of increasing value and benefit." 

In order to carry out the legislative mandate "to render such assistance of increasing value and benefit," particular emphasis has been placed on restricting the selection of research proposals to projects which not only are scientifically sound, but appear most promising in terms of potentially high payoffs for AID operations. A significant indication of the selectivity of the program is the mortality rate of incoming proposals-out of a total of 260 formal and informal research proposals received between July 1, 1963, and January 8, 1965, only 18 new projects were selected for AID support. 

The attached annex A lists all contracts and interagency agreements for which research funds were obligated through June 30, 1964. Annex B lists the contracts executed thus far in fiscal year 1965. Beyond these, another $5.5 million is now firmly programed, and in part obligated, for (1) projects being implemented under interagency agreements signed in prior years; (2) contract renewals and new contracts in or nearing the negotation stage; and (3) other essential program costs such as consultant and staff services. Additionally, a substantial number of proposals now under review will be funded before the end of fiscal year 1965. The funding ceiling for this year is $12 million. 

Special review procedures have been developed to insure thorough screening of research proposals. The criteria applied are the same for all: relevance to 

AID needs, scientific merit, and feasibility. Other important factors considered

are competence of the principal investigators and their commitment in terms of time to be devoted to the proposed study. 

These procedures call for a number of consecutive steps. The first screening is conducted by the staff of the Office of Research and Analysis. The proposal is then reviewed by all pertinent AID offices and formally constituted internal advisory committees, as well as by the AID missions in the countries where the research is to be conducted. 

To avoid inadvertent duplication or overlap with other research efforts, proposals are submitted to the External Research Staff of the State Department for a careful check against other Government and privately financed research projects. To complement this internal review, proposals are submitted to carefully selected external consultants drawn from the specific disciplines involved. 

If both internal and external reviews are favorable, the proposal is forwarded for review to the Research Advisory Committee (RAC), a group of 16 eminent scientists appointed by the Administrator. 

Finally, if the RAC recommends approval, the proposal and supporting justification for AID support are sent to the Administrator for concurrence before the contract is negotiated. Prior to this final stage, the General Counsel's Office and the Contract Office will have been consulted on the adequacy of the supporting documentation, potential legal problems, reasonableness of cost, and consistency of the proposed contractual arrangements with sound business practice.

This intensive screening process, though time consuming, has paid substantial dividends in terms of quality, soundness, content, and justifiability of the AID research program. As the projects mature, major benefits should accrue in the form of increased effectiveness and improved administration of assistance provided to developing nations.

Research and development in beginning science curriculum for English-speaking Educational Services, Inc. tropical Africa: To produce, for English-speaking countries in tropical Africa, a new and tested elementary school science curriculum stressing scientific thinking, as opposed to rote learning, and keyed to critical problems of daily living such as sanitation, nutrition, and health. 

3. Research and training in land tenure and reform in Latin America: (a) To conduct a program of research studies on the economic, social, political, legal, and administrative aspects of land tenure patterns and agrarian structure in Latin America; and to relate these factors to agricultural productivity and rural development; (b) to make the research findings available, in appropriate form, for use in ongoing AID programs dealing with agricultural productivity and rural development; (c) to increase the number of qualified Latin American and U.S. researchers in these fields by direct participation in the study program. 

4. Diffusion of innovations in rural societies: (a) To evaluate methods of acclerating the spread and use of agricultural innovations aimed at increasing agricultural productivity in developing countries; (b) to develop improved methods for studying the diffusion process under different social and economic conditions. 

5. Research on the process of institution building: Four case studies of educational and training institutions. (a) To examine the process by which new institutions are introduced and fitted into developing societies, acquire the capacity to sustain themselves, and influence the larger environment in which they function; (b) to establish a set of criteria for identifying and evaluating this process, regardless of cultural environment. 

6. The interaction of social values and political responsibility. To illuminate critical problems in starting community activities at the village level, initially in India: (a) by examining how traditional values held by local leaders affect their decisions on community development programs; and (b) by identifying conditions (such as patterns of authority, communication channels, etc.) which can alter the impact of those values on their commitment to such programs. 

7. Symposium on communication research and the development process: (a) To bring existing knowledge to bear on the role of communication in economic, social, and political development; (b) to assist AID in developing a sound strategy for programing its communication research effort; (c) to involve the best available scientific talent in such research programs; (d) to produce a volume summarizing the symposium's findings in the above areas, for wide dissemination to donors and recipients of technical assistance.

ANNEX B 

Research and analysis program-Contracts executed in fiscal year 1965 1-Continued Project title and objective 

Contractor 

Duration Amount obligated, fiscal year 1965 8. Symposium on research on the development of administrative capacity in emerging countries: (a) To identify key research issues involved in improving public administration in emerging countries, and thus to provide guidelines for an effective research program in that area; (b) to produce a volume integrating specially prepared papers, participant discussions, and the conclusions reached at the symposium, which will be widely distributed for use by AID and local public administrators and social scientists engaged in research. 

9. Symposium on research on comparative social change in developing countries: To obtain scientific information on which a sound research strategy can be developed by AID for its programs of research on comparative social change relevant to the development process. Corollary objectives are: (a) to involve the best available scientific talent in such research programs; and (b) to produce a volume summarizing the symposium's findings, for wide distribution to AID and host government personnel responsible for programs of planned social change. 

10. Impact of electric power on rural development.-Pilot project in Colombia: To appraise the economic and social effects of introducing small electric power units in selected Colombian villages, where community self-help programs are underway. 

11. Import substitution and economic policy in economic development: To assess, in terms of economic growth, the relative effectiveness of policies adopted to implement industrialization by import substitution, and to explore practical policy alternatives which may produce more rapid growth. 

12. Capacity expansion planning factors: To provide quantitative guidelines on the amounts of capital and other inputs required to achieve increases in production, adapting data on the United States for use in less developed countries.

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, 707 1965 

AID-SPONSORED TRAVEL 

There are no private sector programs, in which AID participates and for which the U.S. Government provides travel funds, operating in other free world areas similar to the partners of the alliance program in Latin America. 

DEPARTMENT OF STATE-BUREAU OF INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATION AFFAIRS INTERNATIONAL CONFERENCES AND CONTINGENCIES 

This appropriation funds the cost of official U.S. participation in multilateral international conferences, and other international activities not otherwise provided for, that are necessary in the conduct of foreign affairs. This includes (a) participation in conferences of the United Nations, its subsidiary bodies, and specialized agencies; (b) meetings of regional and other international organizations, including inter-American bodies, commodity groups, and other conferences of an economic, political, cultural, or scientific nature; (c) participation in international conferences not directly associated with international organizations; (d) defraying the expenses of participating members of international secretariats to meetings, conferences, and related activities held under U.S. auspices; and (e) contributions to new or provisional organizations. 

Funds in the amount of $3,117,000 were made available in fiscal year 1963 to the Department of State under the appropriation "International conferences and contingencies." Of this amount, $1,322,920 was obligated to defray the cost of transportation and per diem for official U.S. delegation members to international conferences.

Funds in the amount of $1,943,000 were made available in fiscal year 1964 to the Department of State under the appropriation "International conferences and contingencies." Of this amount, $986,966 was obligated to defray the cost of transportation and per diem for official U.S. delegation members to international conferences.

Records are not maintained in a manner from which there can be derived a distribution of the costs of travel by each individual conference or category, i.e., congressional, Department of State, other U.S. Government agencies, and public members. However, there is shown below the total delegation members by cate gory and a listing of the international conferences, fiscal years 1963 and 1964.

DEPARTMENT OF STATE BUREAU OF INTERNATIONAL ORGANIZATION AFFAIRS INTERNATIONAL TARIFF NEGOTIATIONS 

This appropriation provides for continuation of U.S. participation in the multilateral Trade Negotiating Conference-the sixth or "Kennedy" Roundwhich was formally opened May 4, 1964, under the sponsorship of the contracting parties of the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (GATT). The negotiations are expected to continue throughout 1966. 

Funds in the amount of $365,000 were made available in fiscal year 1964 to the Department of State under the appropriation "International tariff negotiations." Of this amount, $33,765 was obligated to defray the cost of transportation and per diem for official U.S. delegation members to meeting preparatory to the sixth round of tariff negotiations. 

Records are not maintained in a manner from which there can be derived a distribution of the costs of travel by each individual conference or category, i.e., congressional, Department of State, other U.S. Government agencies and public members. However, there is shown below the total delegation members by category and a listing of the meetings held during fiscal year 1964.

AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT COMMENTS ON CHAIRMAN PASSMAN'S LETTER 

Chairman Passman's letter makes a number of charges against foreign aid. 

These charges must be looked at more closely. 

1. The letter states that the foreign aid may exceed $7 billion for fiscal year 

1966. The President has requested this year $3,380 million for economic and military assistance authorized under the Foreign Assistance Act, the lowest of any year since 1948. 

There are other programs such as Public Law 480, contributions to international or multilateral institutions, refugee relief, administration of oversea territory, etc. These programs serve other central purposes, e.g., Public Law 480 serves as an outlet for domestic agricultural surpluses, the Cuban refugee program provides for care and settlement of refugees from the Castro regime. 

Normally, these are not considered as "foreign aid” and are not contained in the Foreign Assistance Authorization Act. All are contained, however, in the President's budget and all are reviewed by the Congress in detail. 

The programs of economic and military assistance authorized by the Foreign Assistance Act promote directly the national security and foreign policy of the United States. Adding together all U.S. Government programs which have an international or foreign dimension does not accurately describe "foreign aid," not does such lumping together necessarily increase understanding of the foreign assistance program or these other programs however closely or remotely related. 

2. The letter criticizes AID for deobligating and reobligating funds. In fact, deobligation and reobligation is a sensible management tool by which AID can insure that it gets the most for the assistance dollar. Projects and activities are examined to determine if the funds committed to those projects and activities will be needed. If the job can be done for less money, or if it is necessary to do less of the job in order to achieve our goals, funds may deobligated and made available for use elsewhere in the program. 

The use of deobligated funds has been precisely laid out by the Congress in the appropriations legislation. They must be used within the same appropriations category for which originally committed. In the case of fiscal year money, deobligations must be used only for projects or programs previously justified to the Congress. AID must notify the Appropriations Committees prior to the reuse of any such prior year deobligated funds. 

Estimates of deobligated funds for the budget year are taken into account in preparing the budget request and the total request for new appropriations is reduced accordingly. 

3. The letter implies that AID will have available $11,027 million in fiscal year 

1965. This is simply not true. The Congress appropriated new funds totaling $3,250 million for programs under the Foreign Assistance Act for fiscal year 1965. The Congress also made available an additional $28.9 million in unobligated funds from previous year appropriations; $2,223 million of this amount is available for AID programs. The remainder, $1,056 million, is for the military assistance program. These funds are available for commitment and obligation to carry on the foreign assistance program.

On June 30, 1964, unliquidated commitments to the foreign assistance program (the pipeline) totaled $3,825 million for AID programs and $2,050 million for military assistance programs. This foreign aid "pipeline" consists of funds already committed to finance specific activities but not yet actually spent. These funds are not available to finance other activities. The pipeline exists because foreign aid projects-as construction projects in this country-often cannot be completed within a single fiscal year. 

For example, AID may make a loan to finance the purchase of hydroelectric equipment for a power dam project in a foreign country. The funds become part of the pipeline and remain in the pipeline until construction has proceeded to the point when the equipment is delivered and paid for. Pipelines exist in other government programs and in many business enterprises. For example, the Defense 

Department has an estimated fiscal year 1965 pipeline of $30,700 million. 

It should also be noted that Mr. Passman includes new availabilities and unexpended balances for programs under title II of the Foreign Aid and Related Agencies Appropriations Act. These programs include the Peace Corps, the Department of the Army's administration of the Ryukyu Islands, the Cuban refugee program, the IDB, and the IDA. Not all of these programs are normally considered to be foreign aid; none are administered by AID or the military assistance program. 

4. The letter states that foreign aid will be dispensed in 99 nations and 9 territories during fiscal year 1965. This is a total of all countries which receive any military assistance, economic assistance, or Public Law 480, including the use of surplus American agricultural commodities by private American voluntary relief agencies.

In fiscal year 1966 AID plans to make new aid commitments in 72 countries. 

Our assistance is highly concentrated; 95 percent of AID assistance in fiscal year 

1966 will go to 31 countries in the free world. Military assistance grant programs will be conducted in fewer than 60 countries. 

Foreign aid does end. AID economic assistance has been successful and terminated in 26 countries since the start of the Marshall plan. Some of these are the countries of Western Europe which increasingly are participating in the foreign aid effort as donors. 

5. Mr. Passman states that there are 71,416 people on the foreign aid payroll, including participants. But participants are not on the foreign aid payroll. Participants are foreign nationals who are studying or receiving training under the foreign aid program. More than 33,000 of the 71,416 total cited by Mr. Passman are participants. About 21,000 of them are being trained as part of the military assistance program. 

Participant trainees are not paid wages or salaries by the U.S. Government. 

Their situation is analogous to American students who receive scholarships for college study. They are in no sense employees of the U.S. Government. What they do receive is tuition, living expenses, etc., while being trained. 

AID reduced its direct-hire employment by 1,140 during fiscal year 1964 to a level of 15,642, including 8,954 foreign national employees paid in local currencies at pay rates current in the country where they work. 

6. Mr. Passman's letter says that 57 countries which received about $12.5 billion in foreign aid of all kinds between January 1958 and December 1963 purchased $7 billion of gold from the United States during that period. He implies that resources released by foreign aid enabled those countries to buy $7 billion of gold from the U.S. Treasury. That conclusion does not withstand close analysis. 

Twelve of those countries bought most of the gold ($6.4 billion or 92 percent). 

The same 12 countries actually returned to the United States $916 million more repayments of past aid than the assistance they received during this 5-year period. These countries received nearly $4 billion of assistance, two-thirds of it military aid, but repaid in principal and interest nearly $4.9 billion to the 

United States during this period. 

The 12 major purchasers of gold were Austria, Belgium-Luxembourg, Denmark, France, West Germany, Italy, Japan, Lebanon, Netherlands, Saudi Arabia, Spain, and the United Kingdom. They bought $6.4 billion during the 5-year period. It should be noted that none of these 12 countries have received AID assistance for 2 years or more, and that military assistance has virtually ended to most of them.

It is AID policy to relate proposed assistance to the foreign exchange needs of recipient countries. AID does not provide assistance merely to add to a country's dollar reserves or to be used to purchase gold. 

More than 85 percent of today's AID funds will be expended in the United States. The AID program finances the export of U.S. goods and services for the less-developed countries, and not U.S. dollars.
