Confiscation of Property of Sudeten Germans Case (1948) Ann. Dig. 24, 25 (No. 12) (Amtsgericht of Dingolfing). The court held that plaintiff should recover property seized by the Czechoslovakian authorities pursuant to a decree to that effect because the decree authorizing seizure of enemy property was contrary to international law in that it was discriminatory in nature and provided for no compensation. The court held: "The expropriation without compensation of the property of nationals of a foreign state on the mere ground that they are nationals of that state or of that nation is, accordingly, contrary to international law." 4 376 U.S. 440 (1964).

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, Confiscation of German Property in Czechoslovakia Case (1953) Int'l L. Rep. 

31. The Federal Supreme Court approved the decision of the Munich Court of Appeals which refused to recognize Czechoslovakian confiscation of property of a German national, but remanded the case for reconsideration of an unrelated issue.

The Czechoslovakian expropriations of Sudeten-Germans cases uniformly held that discriminatory expropriation without compensation violated international law and was contrary to the public order of the forum. For comprehensive text authority concerning these expropriations and the disposition of cases by the German courts with respect to property taken, see Graue, Germany: Recog nition of Foreign Expropriations, 3 Am. J. Comp. L. 93 (1954). 

The cases after World War I holding that Russian nationals had validly transferred title were based on a recognition of the Russian expropriations by Germany in international agreements. See Amtsgericht Berlin-Schoeneberg (1928), 

(1928) I.P. Rspr. No. 16; Caucasian Licorice Company v. Katz, Landgericht Hamburg (1924), (1924) Hanseatische Rechts-Zeitschrift 750. 

FRANCE 

French courts consistently review foreign expropriations within the context of the public policy of the forum (ordre public). 

Ropit case, Cour de Cassation (Supreme Court) (1928), (1929) Recueil general des lois et des arrets (Sirey) Part I, 217,55 Journal du droit international (Clunet) 674 (1928), (1927-1928) Ann. Dig. No. 43. The Supreme Court refused to apply Soviet law in a case involving a claim of the Soviet Russian Government to part of a nationalized merchant fleet which had escaped from Russia after the nationalization because confiscation without compensation was contarry to "one of the fundamental principles of our social institutions." 

Volatron v. Moulin, Cour d'appel (Court of Appeals) of Aix (1939), (1939) 

Recueil Dalloz, Recueil hebdomadaire de jurisprudence etc. 329, (1938-40) Ann.

Dig. No. 10. The court held that plaintiff's claim to the proceeds of the sale of a consignment of potash (which consignment was part of the property of the plaintiff confiscated by the Government of Catalonia and sent to France) should be recognized because the expropriatory decree, in the absence of compensation was contrary to French public policy and therefore could not be recognized by a French court.

Societe Potassas Ibericas v. Nathan Bloch, Supreme Court (1939), (1939) Recueil Dalloz 257, 66 Clunet 615 (1939), (1983-1940) Ann. Dig. No. 54. The court in a case with substantially the same facts as in Volatron v. Moulin arrived at the same result: "French courts may not recognize any divestment of a right of ownership, except with consent of the owner, without just and previous indemnity." 

GREECE 

Greek law applies foreign law under the reserve of "public order." 

District Court of Piraeus (1937), (1937) Efimeris Ellinon Nomicon D, 560, reported by Massouridis, "The Effects of Confiscation, Expropriation, and Requisition by a Foreign Authority," 3 Revue Hellenique de droit international 62, 68 (1950). The court refused to recognize the expropriation of a ship seized by the Spanish Government on the ground that the confiscation was incompatible with the "public order."

ITALY Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. v. S.U.P.O.R. Co., Civil Tribunal of Venice (1953), 

(1955) Int'l L. Rep. 19, 47 Am. J. Int'l L. 509 (1953), 76 Il Foro Italiano Part 

I, 719 (1953). The court reviewed the Iranian nationalization of property of a 

British oil company but held it did not violate Italian public order because of provision for compensation.

Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. v. S.U.P.O.R. Co., Civil Tribunal of Rome (1954), 

(1955) Int'l L. Rep. 23, 49 Am. J. Int'l L. 259 (1955), 78 Il Foro Italiano Part 

I, 255 (1955). The court in reviewing the Iranian nationalization of property of a British oil company stated:

"As has been stated above, however, this court holds that the Italian courts have the right and the duty to examine a foreign law, from the point of view of its legality, so as to establish whether it is contrary to * * * international public policy or to any generally accepted principles of international law *** In consequence, the Italian courts must refuse to apply in Italy any foreign law which decrees an expropriation, not for reasons of public interest but for purely political, persecutory, discriminatory, racial, and confiscatory motives. Furthermore, the Italian courts must refuse to apply in Italy such foreign laws as may, even for non-political and non-persecutory motives, decree expropriation of the property of any foreign national without compensation." 

The court found that the Iranian law did not violate these principles. 

JAPAN 

Anglo-Iranian Oil Co. v.

Idemitsu Kosan Kabushiki Kaisha, (1953), (1953) 

Int'l L. Rep. 305, 312. The High Court of Tokyo reviewed the Iranian Oil nationalization under international law and public policy but found no violation of public policy. 

THE NETHERLANDS P. T. Escomptobank v. N. V. Assurantie Maatschappij de Nederlanden (June 6, 

1963). The Court of Appeal at The Hague held that the Indonesian nationalization of Dutch corporations, being confiscatory and discriminatory, would not be recognized by Dutch courts. "[W]hile respecting the rule that in general a Netherlands court may not pass judgment on the lawfulness of acts performed jure imperii by a foreign power, in a law suit between private companies that same court is bound to take no account of such acts of State and to regard them as non-existent if they are at variance with (unwritten) rules of international law for the protection of private interests; 

***** [C]onfiscation of the Indonesian subsidiaries of the respondents with out any compensation * * * constitutes a serious breach of the said rules of international law and as such accordingly cannot be recognized by the Netherlands courts and measures taken in that behalf must therefore be regarded as non-existent."

Bank Indonesia v. Senembah Maatschappij N. V. and De Twentsche Bank N. V., 

(1959) Nederlandse Jurisprudentie 855, portions of decision quoted in 7 Nether lands International Law Review 400 (1960). The Court of Appeals at The 

Hague reviewed the Indonesian nationalization measures and finding them to be discriminatory and without compensation, held that the Indonesian action was in violation of international law and therefore without legal consequence. 

SWITZERLAND 

Rosenberg v. Fischer, (1948) Ann. Dig. 467. The Federal tribunal recognized a claim for the restitution of property seized by the German authorities of occupation in France pursuant to a German decree because the seizure of the property was contrary to international law. "In fact, an object seized from its owner in a manner contrary to international law has, without doubt, the character of stolen or lost property in the meaning of Article 934, par. 1, of the Civil Code * * *." UNITED KINGDOM 

Wolff v. Oxholm (1817) 6 M&S 92. The court refused to recognize a Danish decree confiscating the debt of a Danish subject to a British national because the decree did not conform to the usage of nations. 

In re Helbert Wagg & Co. Ltd., (1956) I Ch. 232, 347-9 (1956). The court reviewed the German legislation which was under challenge, but found it did not involve a violation of international law. On the question of whether an 

English court is entitled to examine a foreign law, sought to be given effect, the court specifically held that: "*** this court is entitled to be satisfied that the foreign law *** is not a law passed ostensibly with that object [protecting the economy], but in reality with some object not in accordance with the usage of nations."

STATEMENT SUBMITTED BY THE NATIONAL ASSOCIATION OF MANUFACTURERS, 

MARCH 30, 1965

NAM ACTION 

To supplement and fortify NAM action taken in August 1964, Robert Murphy, chairman, international economic affairs committee, wrote Congressman Morgan, chairman of the House Affairs Committee on March 9, as follows: 

"You may recall that last year, in my capacity as chairman of the International Economic Affairs Committee of the National Association of Manufacturers, I sent you a telegram which read as follows: ""NAM commends the action of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee relative to amendment to section 620 (e) adding to the Foreign Assistance Act a new subsection providing that no court in the United States shall decline on the ground of the act of state doctrine to make a determination on the merits or to apply principles of international law in a case in which an act of a foreign state is alleged to be contrary to international law. "'NAM expresses the hope that this amendment will be concurred in by the Senate and the House. This amendment is entirely in accord with NAM policy in support of the principles and purposes of the aid act of 1961 as an instrument to strengthen friendly foreign countries by encouraging the development of their free economic institutions and productive capabilities, and by minimizing or eliminating barriers to the flow of private investment captal.' 999 Last year the conference committee adopted the principle of the rule of law or Sabbatino amendment but did so on a temporary basis with the understanding that it would be further considered in 1965 with a view to determining whether the amendment should be made permanent legislation. I am writing to urge that your committee in its consideration of the foreign aid bill of 1965 take the next logical step and make this amendment a permanent one. 

In my opinion, it is extremely important that the United States take a strong position against uncompensated expropriations and indeed against any expropriations which are in violation of international law. One of the ways in which this can be done is to modify in part the principle laid down by the Supreme Court in the Sabbatino case by a reversal of presumptions. This is the gist of the amendment which is now before you which was in turn derived from the recommendation in 1959 of the Association of the Bar of the City of New York after detailed consideration of this problem by a distinguished committee of lawyers, many of them known to you and other members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee. If the amendment adopted last year is made permanent, the effect will be that the competency of American courts to adjudicate questions of international law in an important area will be reestablished and the courts will proceed to settle the rights of private litigants in accordance with international law except in those cases in which the President, or his designee, determines that such adjudication would be contrary to the foreign policy interests of the United States. This is a more limited position than that adopted by the lower court in the original Sabbatino case and it seems to me to be a reasonable accommodation of the interests of the private litigant in securing a court determination and of the Government in avoiding embarrassment in the conduct of foreign policy. "Perhaps in view of my former association with the State Department, I may add a few words regarding the contention that the amendment, as now proposed, will create embarrassment for the State Department. I understand in a theoretical way the point of this contention but I may add that I have not in practice seen any instance in which the application of the rule of the amendment would have been an embarrassment in the conduct of foreign policy. If embarrassment is anticipated under the rule of the amendment, the President has only to speak and the courts will suspend their normal processes and the private litigants will be obliged to desist in pursuing judicial recourse. 99 On March 25, Mr. Murphy wrote Senator Fulbright, chairman, Senate Foreign 

Relations Committee, substantially the same letter as he addressed to Congressman Morgan, and in his communication said he was "writing also to Senators Hickenlooper and Sparkman in view of their sponsorship of the amendment."

YALE UNIVERSITY LAW SCHOOL, 

March 29, 1965.

Hon. J. W. FULBRIGHT, Chairman, Committee on Foreign Relations, U.S. Senate, Washington, D.C. 

DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: Last year I wrote you in suport of the proposed 

Sabbatino amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act. Such an amendment was 

The effect adopted and is now coming to be called the rule of law amendment. of the amendment was to establish the position recommended in 1959 by the Committee on International Law of the Association of the Bar of the City of New York and in thorough accord with worldwide expectations about the requirements of international law. It modified some of the unfortunate consequences of the Supreme Court decision in the Sabbatino case, through the ill effects of the majority opinion in this case will be with us for a long time. 

As one who has long studied and taught in this area of the law, I am writing to urge that last year's amendment, which was adopted on a temporary basis, or some equivalent be made permanent legislation, thus reestablishing the application of appropriate international law as the long-term policy for all 

American courts.

Others will no doubt be expressing their views to your committee about the need for taking steps both to maintain an international economy and to protect American oversea investment from the threat of uncompensated and discriminatory expropriations. This need is very urgent and certainly in my opinion fully justifies, even requires, congressional action. However, I would like more to empahsize an aspect of the Sabbatino decision which is of particular concern to me as a teacher of international law. In my judgment, the most unfortunate part of the Supreme Court decision is that it lays down a rule of legal policy which automatically excludes all courts in the United States from further participation in the development of customary international law in so broad and important an area as that of the protection of international economic activities. 

Historically under our constiutional system, the courts of the United States have played a leading role in the development and application of international law. Chief Justice Marshall was, for example, particularly creative and influential in this regard. His Court handed down some of the landmark decisions which have shaped the broad outlines of contemporary international law. These decisions, and others by his successors, have been followed by the courts of other countries all over the world. 

My greatest concern in this matter is, thus, that the United States should set a good example for other countries in the development and application of an international law designed to protect a free world society. In an interdependent world, with widely dispersed resources and skills, this must of necessity include the protection both of an international economy and of some private participation in wealth activities. Similarly, in a world without centralized legislative, executive, and judicial institutions most of the decisions about the development and application of international law must continue to be made, as during the past several hundred years, by the officials of particular nation-states. Any suggestion that our courts are not competent to continue to participate in the development and application of an international law, whether related to economic affairs or to other affairs, is fundamentally inimical to our own long-term national interests and the comparable interests which we share with other states. 

I have seen the various objections urged against the amendment before you, and I find them both inaccurate and wholly unpersuasive. The amendment does not in any way interfere with the President's authority to conduct foreign affairs, since he has unfettered discretion to waive the application of the amendment. 

All the amendment does is reconfirm the historic policy of this country, and of other countries-in entire accord with the requirements of international lawthat courts should apply international law in cases properly before them. Its particular specification of confiscation cases is made necessary only by the unfortunate decision in the Sabbatino case. The courts of other countries do not accept the doctrine of automatic and compulsory abstention from examining the acts of other governments. It is difficult enough in some of them to secure the honoring of acts of state which are in accord with international law. The amendment, if made permanent, will greatly increase the protection for American investors abroad by making clear that our own immensely important internal markets cannot be made an outlet for confiscated properties. The fact that some of the Communist countries may disagree, and demand a lew embodying the design of a different kind of world, is no reason why we should not attempt to maintain an appropriate international law for a genuine international economy with such countries as are willing to cooperate, and many of them are so willing. 

I very much hope that the committee will vote to make the rule of law amendment permanent legislation. 

Because of their cosponsorship of the amendment, I trust that it is not amiss for me to send copies of this letter to Senators Hickenlooper and Sparkman. 

Very sincerely,

MYRES S. MCDOUGAL, 

Sterling Professor of Law.

STATEMENT OF PROF. MYRES S. MCDOUGAL TO THE HOUSE FOREIGN AFFAIRS COMMITTEE IN SUPPORT OF "SABBATINO" AMENDMENT TO SECTION 620 (e) OF THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, you have my warm thanks for this opportunity to appear before you about a matter which I regard as of the utmost importance. I am sterling professor of law at the Yale Law School and for some years have specialized in teaching and writing in the field of international law.

The issues at stake in the Sabbatino amendment cut deep into the potential future effectiveness of all international law and most vitally affect that particular part of international law which is designed to promote and secure an international economy.

Your committee must have the thanks of all of us who are deeply concerned with these issues for affording opportunity for their full and candid examination.

As you may know, I wrote last year to both your chairman and to the chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in support of the enactment of the Sabbatino amendment. My purpose in appearing before you today is very strongly to urge you to make this amendment permanent legislation. 

In giving my reasons for this urgent recommendation, there are a number of fundamental considerations which I should like to discuss with you, and it may be convenient to outline and develop these considerations in the following order:

First, the kind of international law for the protection of an international economy and private rights which we had prior to the Sabbatino decision. 

Second, the way in which, historically, all international law has been made and applied.

Third, the damage which the decision and majority opinion in the Sabbatino case did both to inherited substantive international law and to the processes by which such law is made and applied. 

Fourth, the remedy for this damage embodied in the Sabbatino amendment and the relation of this remedy to the foreign affairs power of the Congress.

Fifth, and finally, the kind of international and national law we continue to require for the maintenance of an international economy and the protection of private rights. 

In the course of our discussion, I will hope both to answer the more important criticisms of the Sabbatino amendment and to suggest the broad outlines of the positive case for making it permanent. 

Let me begin with our inherited international law for protecting an international economy and private rights. The principal function of this law has been to facilitate international cooperation in the production and distribution of goods and services by establishing a stability in people's expectations that they will be protected against arbitrary coercion and can safely commit their energies and resources to creative enterprise. Like any good modern national constitution, this international law has contained two very different components: First, specific grants of competence to make and apply law and, second, principles designed to restrain and limit the arbitrary exercise of the competence so granted. 

The substantive grants of competence-contained within the familiar jurisdictional principles of "territoriality," "nationality," "protection of nationals,' "protection of national interests," and "universality"-authorize states, having many differing degrees of control over persons and goods, to make and apply law for governing the events by which they are substantially affected. 

In an interdependent world, in which everything affects everything else and markets and resources are widely distributed, it should not be surprising that these grants of competence often confer jurisdiction upon more than one state over the same events. In particular, it may be emphasized that the "territoriality" principle does not exclude the application of many other principles. 

The more important restraints upon these grants of competence to statesthe "bill of rights" of international law are the limitations contained in the traditional, customary formulations about "the rights of aliens," and "the responsibility of states." Sometimes of course comparable limitations are explicitly embodied in treaties of "friendship, commerce, and navigation." The range of protection afforded by customary principles is, however, as recently demonstrated by the Harvard Research in International Law [55 Am. J.I.L. 545 (1961)], most extensive, and related to such diverse matters as arrest and detention, denial of access to tribunals, denial of fair hearing, and destruction of and damage to property. The long-established customary rule, about which more will be said below, prohibiting the confiscation by one state of the property of the nationals of another state, is but a dramatic instance of a much more comprehensive policy prohibiting many different kinds of arbitrary deprivations. 

With this perspective, it is now possible to note the function of the genuine, international-law doctrine of "acts of state." Like a "full faith and credit" clause in a national constitution, this doctrine seeks to secure that the basic

substantive policies of international law-including both the jurisdictional policies allocating competence among states and the basic limitations designed to restrain the arbitrary exercise of this competence are made effective across nation-state lines, despite the continuous movement of persons and goods. In the contemporary world in which people and goods can move so rapidly, and do in fact move so frequently, it would obviously be impossible for states to maintain any kind of order if they did not accord a reasonable deference to each other's decisions taken in conformity with international law. It should be observed, however, both that this doctrine does not require the honoring of acts contrary to international law and that it has nothing whatsoever to do with the internal, constitutional allocation of competence among the different branches of a government within a particular state, such as the United States. 

Next, let us turn to how, historically, international law has been made and applied. In the absence of compulsory, centralized structures of authority, most international law has of course been made and applied by nation-state officials. 

Sometimes international law has been explicitly made by great multilateral agreements, such as the Hague Conventions or the United Nations Charter. The great bulk of international law has, however, been made, like our Anglo-American common law, by customary behavior which creates expectations about uniformity and rightness in decision. The officials of one state make a claim with a promise of reciprocity and the officials of other states accept it, as an expression of common interest, or reject it, as an assertion of special interest. Thus, the claims of coastal States to the exclusive enjoyment of subterranean riches of the Continental Shelf were established as lawful in community expectation by a process of unilateral claim and reciprocal tolerance in less than 10 years. Historically legislative bodies have participated in this process: in the famous case of 

The Scotia (14 Wallace 170 (1871)) the U.S. Supreme Court held that a relatively uniform series of national enactments about the rules of the road at sea had created customary international law. The fact that the individual decisionmakers participating in this process have been representatives of nation-states has not commonly been regarded as incapacitating them for clarifying a common interest with the peoples of other states. On the contrary, the fact that the same state officials have had to be, alternatively, both claimants before authority and established decisionmakers for the general community has been regarded as the best incentive, and the most secure sanction, for a genuine clarification of common interest.

The important role which, until recently, our own Supreme Court has played in the making and application of international law has been too many times recounted to require further detailed recital. The numerous cases before the Court have related to almost every facet of transnational activity, and in many instances the decision and opinion of the Court have served as a model for worldwide emulation in the clarification and implementation of common interest. 

The only point I would here emphasize is that in this participation in the customary processes for making and applying international law our Court, like the courts of other nation-states, has been continuously passing upon the lawfulness of "the acts" of other states. In one famous case, Hilton v. Guyot (159 U.S. 113, 163 (1895)), in refusing to give automatic deference to a judgment of a French court, the Court takes explicit note of this fact in words which deserve quotation: "International law, in its widest and most comprehensive sense- -including not only questions of right between nations, governed by what has been appropriately called the 'law of nations', but also questions arising under what is usually called 'private international law' or the 'conflict of laws' and concerning the rights of persons within the territory and dominion of one system, by reason of acts, private or public, done within the dominions of another nation-is part of our law, and must be ascertained and administered by the courts of justice, as often as such questions are presented in litigation between man and man, duly submitted to their determination. "The most certain guide, no doubt for the decision of such questions is a treaty or a statute of this country. But when, as is the case here, there is no written law upon the subject, the duty still rests upon the judicial tribunals of ascertaining and declaring what the law is. whenever it becomes necessary to do so, in order to determine the rights of parties to suits regularly brought before them. In doing this, the courts must obtain such aid as they can from judicial decisions. from the works of jurists and commentators, and from the acts and usages of civilized nations."

Such is the background against which we must appraise the Sabbatino decision. Both the holding and the reasons for the holding in this case are obscure and subject to much dispute among the commentators. It would appear, however, that the Court sought to impose upon itself a blanket prohibition against the examination of a broad class of acts of foreign governments for their conformity or lack of conformity with international law. It is not clear, further whether the Court regards itself as competent to lift this prohibition in a particular case even upon explicit request by the Executive. In its most precise formulation, in Mr. Justice Harlan's opinion for the majority, the Court states: 

66* * * [W]e decide only that the Judicial Branch will not examine the validity of a taking of property within its own territory by a foreign sovereign government, extant and recognized by this country at the time of suit, in the absence of a treaty or other unambiguous agreement regarding controlling legal principles, even if the complaint alleges that the taking violates customary international law." (Banco Nacional de Cuba v. Sabbatino, 376 U.S. 398, 428 (1964)) The Court explicitly recognized that this conclusion was not required by either international or our constitutional law. The reasons given by the Court were cast in terms of deference to "acts of state," but the Court itself noted that in none of its previous decisions were the facts such as to raise the issue about acts in violation of international law, and critics of the Court have correctly emphasized that many of the cases invoked by the Court had no relevance to the policies-designed to protect stability in interactions across nation-state linesunderlying the genuine act of state doctrine. The policies applied by the Court, relating to the appropriate allocation of competences among the different branches of our Government, are in fact those which underlie the "political questions" doctrine, but the Court did not apply the tests for "political questions" which it had so recently announced in Baker v. Carr (369 U.S. 186 (1962)), and it did not find the issue nonjusticiable, as application of the "political questions" doctrine would have required. The doctrine of automatic, blanket abstention announced by the Court is clearly a new, and bizarre, creation. The principal justification which the Court offers for this creation is, further that there is not sufficient consensus (since some of the Communist and other new countries appear not to agree) about the international law it was being asked to apply to the Cuban confiscations. Without "critical examination" and much too broadly, as 

Justice White points out in dissent, the Court adds to the statement quoted above: "There are few if any issues in international law today on which opinion seems to be so divided as the limitations on a state's power to expropriate the property of aliens." 

In a magnificent dissenting opinion, Justice White answers the Court point by point, noting that its decision does in fact "validate" a "lawless act" and make it effective within our country. He summarizes: "No other civilized country has found such a rigid rule necessary for the survival of the executive branch of its government; the executive of no other government seems to require such insulation from international law adjudications in its courts; and no other judiciary is apparently so incompetent to ascertain and apply international law" (376 U.S. 440 (1964)).

The remedy sought by the Congress in the Sabbatino amendment is, despite all the fuss made about it, quite simple. This amendment, as an expression of the Congress competence to participate in the more comprehensive formulation of our foreign policy, sets aside the "Federal act of state doctrine" in certain specified cases and provides that in those cases courts in the United States shall "make a determination on the merits giving effect to the principles of international law ***" To forestall any doubts about its purpose, perhaps having in mind the difficulties which the Supreme Court had exhibited in clarifying the relevant international law, the Congress added its own interpretation of what international law requires as compensation for expropriation by a cross-reference to section 620(e)(1) of the Foreign Assistance Act, which provides for "speedy compensation for such property in convertible foreign exchange, equivalent to the full value thereof." It is worth noting that Attorney General Katzenbach in his testimony before you, though opposing abolition of the doctrine of automatic abstention, apparently agreed with this formulation of the requirements for compensation.

In order to avoid any possible interference with the President's day-to-day conduct of foreign relations, the amendment specifically provides that it is not to apply when "the President determines that application of the act of state

1965 

FOREIGN ASSISTANCE, doctrine is required in that particular case by the foreign policy interests of the United States and a suggestion to this effect is filed on his behalf in that case with the Court." The procedure thus established would appear comparable to that presently employed by the Executive with respect to pleas of state, or "sovereign," immunity and to be entirely adequate to permit the Executive to cope with any unique contingencies which might require judicial restraint. 

It can scarcely be doubted that the enactment of this Sabbatino amendment is well within the Congress competence over foreign affairs. The most direct and explicit testimony comes from Prof. Louis Henkin, of the Columbia Law 

School: "There can be little doubt that the Court would have to follow modifications in act of state by act of Congress or by treaty, even by executive agreement." (The Foreign Affairs Power of the Federal Courts: Sabbatino, 64 Col. 

L. Rev. 805, 823 (1964)). Elsewhere Professor Henkin has more comprehensively summarized the bases for his views of the competence of the Congress. 

He writes: "Under the power 'to regulate commerce with foreign nations, and among the the several states,' Congress has no less authority over foreign commerce than it has over interstate commerce. And since the revolution initiated by Jones & 

Laughlin, it no longer needs citation of authority or argument to show that under the commerce power Congress can reach all interstate or foreign 'intercourse'; it can reach matters precedent to or subsequent to interstate or foreign commerce; it can reach what relates to or affects as well as what is commerce; it can reach strictly local commerce and activities when necessary to make effective a regulation of interstate or foreign commerce. The power of Congress over foreign commerce would then, of itself, support legislation equivalent to a large part of the law 'enacted' by treaty." (The Treaty Makers and the Law-Makers: 

The Law of the Land and Foreign Relations, 107 U. Pa. L. Rev. 903, 914, 915 

(1959).)

Similarly, he continues: "So, in addition to several other broad powers in Congress, we have the 'foreign affairs power.' We may say with confidence that this power supports any reasonable regulation of the rights of aliens; even as to citizens it supports such limitations on freedom of action as may be deemed by Congress reasonably necessary in the interests of U.S. foreign relations. Without inducing or extrapolating too boldly from what the Supreme Court has held and said, it can be asserted that the foreign affairs power of Congress, of itself or, surely, with other powers we have mentioned, can support enactment of virtually any provision contained in any treaty in the history of the United States: in agreements conferring diplomatic and other rights on foreign governments and foreign officials; in disarmament agreements; in treaties of friendship, commerce and navigation; in extradition treaties, even as applied to American citizens; in reciprocal taxation and trade treaties; in status-of-forces and other military agreements which became law in the United States. Congress could without a treaty make such legislation applicable to nationals of other nations or to Americans on a reciprocal or parallel basis. Congress could also, it would seem, enact them without reciprocity in the hope that other nations would do likewise, or because of other impact which such provisions would have or might have on the attitudes of other nations toward the United States and U.S. citizens" (id. 920922). 

Finally, we come to more explicit consideration of the kind of international and national law we continue to require for the maintenance of an international economy and the protection of private rights. 

The first point I would emphasize is that, if we are to take seriously our proclaimed goals both of promoting and securing a more abundant international economy and of protecting private rights, it is incumbent upon every branch of our Government to continue to assert the common interests of all peoples in the maintenance of an international law which prohibits states from expropriating the property of the nationals of other states without making just and reasonable compensation. Despite the doubts expressed in the majority opinion in the Sabbatino case, it would further appear that an appropriate "critical examination" of the available evidence from international and national decisions, arbitral awards, treaties, diplomatic settlements, state practice, official utterances, the writings of publicists, and so on-would still confirm a high degree of consensus among the different peoples of the world that this prohibition is an established principle, as useful today as in the past, of living customary

international law. (For a recent, well-documented, and persuasive survey of authoritative expectations see the amicus brief in the Sabbatino case of the American Bar Association.) A most precise and eloquent statement of the basis for this established principle was made by an American scholar some 40 years ago: "It must be noted that this accepted principle, which safeguards foreign-owned property from confiscation in time of peace, has become part of the law of nations not merely because it represents a universally recognized standard of justice, but also because it is absolutely essential for the welfare of every nation, for without its protection no commercial or financial international intercourse could safely be carried on. "Accordingly, the real basis for the adoption and enforcement of this protective principle in international relations is its appeal to enlightened public opinion, not alone on the ground of inherent justice, but also on account of reciprocal benefits. It derives its real authority and permanence from the universal need by all nations of foreign trade for their prosperity, and in the mutual benefits which nations receive through the investment of foreign capital for the development of national resources. "The investment of surplus capital in foreign countries goes hand in hand with this principle of international law prohibiting the confiscation of foreign-owned property, and all of the indispensable business of international trade and foreign investment will automatically cease whenever the protection of the correlative law of nations against the confiscation of foreign-owned property is repudiated.' (Anderson, Basis of the Law Against Confiscating Foreign-Owned Property, 21 

Am. J. Int'l L. 525, 526 (1927).)

It would not appear fruitful to dispute precisely in what most general terms the measure of compensation required for making an expropriation lawful should be stated-whether in Secretary of State Hull's classic formula of "prompt, adequate and effective," or in the less colorful "just and reasonable" suggested above, or in some other equivalent. Every good lawyer knows that in any particular instance of controversy all high-level principles, in whatever terms formulated, must be given a specific meaning by a very delicate evaluation of many variables, ranging through the whole past history of the relations between the parties and varying potential impacts of alternative decisions upon the parties and others. The formulation of a principle is but a beginning in the specification of its meaning. 

The statement of the requirement for compensation in terms of "prompt, adequate, and effective," so cogently urged by Secretary of State Hull, has, however, much more support than the Sabbatino majority opinion and its supporters would suggest. This was conceded by Attorney General Katzenbach in his testimony before you and is documented in the article on the "Sabbatino Controversy" by Prof. Robert Y. Jennings, already introduced into these hearings. High executive officials of our Government have also found a confirmation of this standard in the United Nations General Assembly's declaration on "Permanent Sovereignty Over National Resources," which provides, inter alia, that: "Nationalization, expropriation, or requisitioning shall be based on grounds or reasons of public utility, security, or the national interest which are recognized as overriding purely individual or private interests, both domestic and foreign. In such cases the owner shall be paid appropriate compensation, in accordance with the rules in force in the state taking such measures in the exercise of its sovereignty and in accordance with international law." [Emphasis added.] (Schwebel, the Story of the U.N.'s Declaration on Permanent Sov ereignty Over Natural Resources, 49 A.B.A.J. 463, 466 (1963).) 

It may be added that at a conference convened by the International Chamber of Commerce in Karachi in December 1960, the representatives from 28 countries, including some generally classed as "developing" (such as "Burma, Ceylon, India, Iran, Korea, Pakistan, Philippines, Thailand, Tunisia, Turkey, United

Arab Republic, Vietnam, and Yugoslavia") unanimously adopted a statement of conclusions which read: "Nationalization—if applied at all-should be nondiscriminatory and accompanied by prompt, effective, and adequate compensa tion." (Snyder, Protection of Private Foreign Investments: Examination and 

Appraisal, 10 Int. and Comp. L.Q 469, 481 (1961).)

The second point I would emphasize is that, if our country is to make its proper contribution to the clarification and implementation of an international law appropriate to our times, our courts must continue to set a model, as they have

historically, in the making and applying of such an international law. Any suggestion-even from the Supreme Court itself-that our courts are not competent to continue to participate in the development and application of international law, whether related to economic affairs or to other affairs, is fundamentally inimical both to our own long-term national interests and the comparable interests which we share with other states. 

The fact is of course that the Supreme Court did apply international law in the Sabbatino case. The international law which it did apply-in honoring the 

Cuban confiscations-were the principles of jurisdiction which confer upon states the competence to act. The international law which it refused to apply were the principles imposing responsibility for acts even within jurisdictional competence the "bill of rights" which would have protected private rights. 

The consequence of this ambivalent deference, to principles which should have been regarded as complementary and equally deserving of deference, was that one set of principles was applied in a way to stultify the major goals of both sets of principles: the minimization of arbitrary coercion and the securing of a stability in people's expectations in cooperative activity across state lines. 

The reason why our courts should apply all international law has been best stated by Justice White: 

"Principles of international law have been applied in our courts to resolve controversies not merely because they provide a convenient rule for decision but because they represent a consensus among civilized nations on the proper ordering of relations between nations and the citizens thereof. Fundamental fairness to litigants as well as the interest in stability of relationships and preservation of reasonable expectations call for their application whenever international law is controlling in a case or controversy" (376 U.S. 453). 

The final point I would emphasize is that it is scarcely credible that the continued performance by our courts of their functions in developing and applying international law could interfere, seriously or otherwise, with the Executive's conduct of foreign relations. The critics who cry havoc discreetly forbear to give any factual illustration of such possible intereference, and even if their fears are not fantasy, the proviso in the Sabbatino amendment authorizing the President to request a suspension of judicial proceedings would appear adequate, as already noted, to nullify any difficulty or embarrassment. 

The argument that the Executive should have complete control over expropriation because the Executive may have more general objectives than those related to expropriation-"other fish to fry" such as combating communism in a particular country-proves too much; it would apply equally to any other judicial proceedings which might have foreign impacts and substantially eliminate the courts from concern with activities transcending state lines. Justice 

White is again most apt: "The assumption, if sound, would apply to any other problem arising from transactions that cross state lines and is tantamount to a declaration excusing this Court from any future consequential role in the clarification and application of international law" (376 U.S. 458). 

The costs, in terms of damage to private rights and other values, of denying our courts a "consequential role in the clarification and application of international law" can only be high; the burden of proof upon those who insist that embarrassment to the Executive requires this denial should be made equally high. 

It is difficult to escape the suspicion that many who foresee "embarrassment" have somehow confused the President's responsibility for the "conduct of foreign affairs" with the more comprehensive responsibility, shared by all branches of the Government, for clarification and prescription of basic community policies which must guide and control the Executive's day-to-day conduct of negotiations. They might do well to remember, inter alia, Professor (now Judge) Jessup's admonition that the Department of State "is not organized in such a way as to facilitate rendering what are essentially judicial decisions" (Has the Supreme Court 

Abandoned One of Its Functions, 40 A.S.I.L. 168, 169 (1946)). Curiously, in cases related to denationalization, and expatriation, as contrasted with expropriation-issues surely highly controversial in their impact on other countriesneither the Supreme Court nor others seem to be concerned about decisions which may "embarrass" the Executive, or even the Congress. (See e.g. Schneider v. 

Rusk, 32 U.S.L.W. 4399.)

The argument that the Executive may be able to secure a greater recovery for expropriated investors through diplomatic negotiations than they can secure for themselves by judicial proceedings is, again, beside the point. The efforts of the

Executive should be made cumulative, rather than substitutive. It is difficult to see how judicial decisions, or legislative enactments, closing the internal markets of our country to confiscated goods could do other than support the hand of the Executive in negotiations designed to secure settlement. Similarly, to argue, as some have, that judicial decisions cannot be made effective protection for investors, since expropriated goods may only occasionally be brought into a country whose courts make such decisions, is to miss the point of the Sabbatino amendment: its purpose is not merely to facilitate the occasional recovery of specific goods or their money equivalent, but rather to restore and confirm a model in principle and procedure which, if generally maintained, could close many important markets to confiscated properties and, hence, provide an effective sanction to the requirements about compensation and perhaps deter confiscation. 

In conclusion, permit me to say again that the principal purpose of the Sabbatino amendment is merely to reconfirm the historic policy of this country, and of other countries-in entire accord with the requirements of international lawthat courts should apply international law in cases properly before them. The amendment, if made permanent, will greatly increase the protection for American investors abroad by making clear that our own immensely important internal markets cannot be made an outlet for confiscated properties. The fact that some of the Communist countries may disagree, and demand a law embodying the social design of a different kind of world, is no reason why we should not attempt to maintain an appropriate international law for a genuine international eocnomy with such countries as are willing to coperate, and many of them are so willing.

I very much hope that the committee will vote to make this amendment permanent legislation. Thank you for your courtesy.

DECLARATION OF NATIONAL FOREIGN TRADE CONVENTION 

New York, N.Y., November 16, 17, and 18, 1964, National Foreign Trade Council, Inc., New York, N.Y.

IX 

Protection of American property rights abroad: The convention notes with growing concern not only the takings of American-owned private property by foreign governments and the increased threats of such action which have occurred during recent years, but also that many owners still have failed to receive adequate and effective compensation for such property. In many cases no provision at all has been made or proposed for such compensation and its prompt payment. The convention is further concerned by the development of new forms of taking, both direct and indirect, such as discriminatory taxation and the application of special tax rates on dividends of corporations of which less than a substantial percentage of shares are owned by local residents. 

American-owned private property abroad comprises not only industrial property, composed of plant, equipment, liquid capital, patents, trademarks, and other assets; it also includes real property used for agricultural purposes and interests in other natural wealth and resources. 

Various programs for "social reform," which have aims that frequently appear meritorious, have been advanced as a justification for the taking of property, e.g., so-called agrarian reform programs. Such programs cannot justify takings of foreign-owned property without proper provision for prompt, adequate, and effective compensation.

Moreover, private property is entitled to be protected against takings that are not pursuant to a genuine public purpose. It is clear that this requirement constitutes a significant limitation on excuses for seizing private property. The determination of what constitutes a public purpose may normally be made by the government exercising the power to seize. However, where a controversy arises over the genuine public nature of a purpose in relation to the taking of foreign-owned property, the issue should be left for determination by an impartial tribunal.

Inherent in those systems which recognize the rights of private property is a basic requirement that contracts between governments and private parties are binding in each case on the government, as well as on the private party. When the latter is a citizen of another country, his rights are protected by international

law, and thus protection extends to reliance, induced by the government, upon official undertakings and assurances. 

The convention also reiterates the position of previous conventions on the matter of compensation. To the extent that compensation for the taking of private property does not represent the full value of the property, or where there is an unreasonable delay in payment, or payment is made in a form that cannot effectively be realized by the party concerned, the taking amounts to a confiscation. Where governments do seize private property, owned by foreigners, elementary morality as well as international law requires that the owner promptly receive full reimbursement for what he has lost and that this be in an effectively realizable form. 

Elementary morality, as well as international law, also requires reimbursement of damages sustained by a failure to fulfill a contract with a foreigner or other undertaking given to a foreigner. Unless reparation for willful injury is required, repudiation of the most solemn promises and assurances would be encouraged. 

To tolerate repudiation leads to a breakdown of private international trade and investment, a slowdown of economic development and a deterioration of international relations. Protection of existing investment is a keystone to obtaining new investments.

The convention again draws attention to the inclusion in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended (the basic act), of a specific directive to the executive branch to discourage nationalization, expropriation, confiscation, seizure of ownership or control of private investment, and discriminatory or other actions having the effect thereof undertaken by countries assisted under the act. It notes with approval that at the time this amendment was adopted the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives stated that: "Countries receiving our assistance should be made fully aware of the U.S. Government's position toward the creation and maintenance of a favorable private investment climate, and the intent of this Government to extend every available protection to the U.S. investor." In this connection, the act, as amended, contains provisions which provide that assistance shall be suspended to governments which confiscate American property or repudiate contracts or agreements made with U.S. citizens or corporations. 

The convention welcomes the inclusion in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1964 of the amendment which provides generally that no U.S. court shall refuse, on the ground of the act of state doctrine, to examine the validity of acts of foreign states occurring after January 1, 1959, which are alleged to be contrary to international law. However, the amendment contains several exceptions, including a provision that it shall not be applicable "in any case in which the proceedings are commenced after January 1, 1966." It is urged that this limitation be removed during the calendar year 1965. 

The convention recommends that treaties protecting private investment be negotiated with additional foreign governments. Further, it is believed that the substance of the draft convention on the protection of foreign property which has been prepared by a committee of the Organization for Economic Cooperation and Development, strengthened in line with provisions traditionally advocated by the United States in the conduct of its foreign relations, should in principle be supported in the OECD by the United States. In this connection, it is also suggested that at an appropriate time the Department of State should seek the views of business with respect to specific provisions of the draft convention.
